names.lutein-zeaxanthin: Lutein and Zeaxanthin (leafy green and macular carotenoids)
names.fisetin: Fisetin (strawberry flavonoid, studied as a senolytic)
names.urolithin-a: Ellagitannins and Urolithin A (pomegranate and walnut compounds)
names.vicine-convicine: Vicine and Convicine (fava bean toxins, favism)
names.furocoumarins: Furocoumarins / Psoralens (lime, celery and parsnip phototoxins)
names.nicotinamide-riboside: Nicotinamide Riboside (NAD+ precursor, vitamin B3 form)

qs.q: A 58-year-old man has crushing chest pain for 20 minutes. He has no allergies and no history of GI bleeding. Which medication should the EMT give first?
qs.a: Chewable aspirin 162-324 mg
qs.x: Aspirin reduces mortality in ACS by blocking platelet aggregation and should be given early when there are no contraindications.
w: Sublingual nitroglycerin 0.8 mg
Oral glucose 15 g
Albuterol 2.5 mg

qs.q: The primary reason aspirin is given to a patient with suspected ACS is to:
qs.a: Prevent platelets from clumping and enlarging the clot
qs.x: Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent; it keeps the clot from growing but does not dissolve it.
w: Dissolve the clot that is blocking the coronary artery
Dilate the coronary arteries to improve blood flow
Relieve the chest pain by blocking pain signals to the brain

qs.q: Which form of aspirin is preferred for suspected ACS?
qs.a: Chewable, non-enteric-coated
qs.x: Chewing non-enteric-coated aspirin gives the fastest antiplatelet effect.
w: Enteric-coated, swallowed whole
Dissolved in water, then swallowed
Rectal suppository only

qs.q: Which finding is a contraindication to giving aspirin?
qs.a: A known allergy to aspirin
qs.x: Known aspirin allergy is a contraindication. Taking daily low-dose aspirin is not a reason to withhold a chewed dose for ACS.
w: The patient takes a daily baby aspirin
Blood pressure of 150/90
Pain radiating to the jaw

qs.q: A 15-year-old with a flu-like illness asks for aspirin for a fever. Aspirin should be avoided because of the risk of:
qs.a: Reye syndrome
qs.x: Aspirin in children and teens with viral illnesses is associated with Reye syndrome (liver and brain injury).
w: Serotonin syndrome
Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Malignant hyperthermia

qs.q: A patient with chest pain reports vomiting dark coffee-ground material this morning. With regard to aspirin, you should:
qs.a: Withhold it because of possible active GI bleeding
qs.x: Active GI bleeding is a contraindication to aspirin.
w: Give it with water to protect the stomach lining
Give double the normal dose
Give it rectally to bypass the stomach instead

qs.q: How long does a single dose of aspirin affect platelets?
qs.a: For the life of the platelet (about 7-10 days)
qs.x: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-1, so the effect lasts the platelet's lifespan.
w: About 4 hours, until the drug is fully metabolized
About 30 minutes
Only while the patient is in the ambulance

qs.q: Aspirin belongs to which drug class when given for ACS?
qs.a: Antiplatelet
qs.x: In ACS, aspirin works as an antiplatelet agent.
w: Anticoagulant
Thrombolytic
Vasodilator

qs.q: Which classic symptom suggests aspirin (salicylate) overdose?
qs.a: Ringing in the ears (tinnitus)
qs.x: Tinnitus, vomiting, and rapid breathing are classic early signs of salicylate toxicity.
w: Pinpoint pupils (miosis)
Slow heart rate (bradycardia)
Low body temperature (hypothermia)

qs.q: Before assisting a patient with nitroglycerin, the EMT must confirm:
qs.a: The BP is above the protocol minimum and no erectile dysfunction drug was recently taken
qs.x: Nitroglycerin drops blood pressure; it is withheld with hypotension and after PDE-5 inhibitor use.
w: The heart rate is below 60 and the patient has already taken a full aspirin dose today
The patient has clear lung sounds bilaterally and a blood glucose above 120 mg/dL
The patient has not eaten anything in the last 4 hours and is lying completely flat

qs.q: A patient with chest pain took sildenafil (Viagra) 6 hours ago. You should:
qs.a: Not give nitroglycerin
qs.x: Nitrates with PDE-5 inhibitors can cause profound, life-threatening hypotension.
w: Give half the normal dose
Give nitroglycerin and lay the patient flat
Give nitroglycerin only if the pain is severe

qs.q: Nitroglycerin relieves anginal chest pain mainly by:
qs.a: Dilating blood vessels and decreasing the heart's workload
qs.x: Venodilation reduces preload and myocardial oxygen demand; coronary arteries also dilate.
w: Increasing the heart rate to pump more blood to the heart muscle
Thinning the blood
Constricting blood vessels to raise blood pressure

qs.q: The usual dose of sublingual nitroglycerin is:
qs.a: 0.4 mg
qs.x: One tablet or spray delivers 0.4 mg, repeated every 3-5 minutes per protocol.
w: 4 mg
40 mg

qs.q: After a nitroglycerin tablet, the patient complains of a pounding headache. This is:
qs.a: A common, expected side effect
qs.x: Headache from vasodilation is the most common nitroglycerin side effect.
w: A sign of an allergic reaction
A sign of stroke that requires stopping all care
Evidence that the tablet was expired

qs.q: Nitroglycerin tablets that do not cause a slight tingling or burning under the tongue may be:
qs.a: Expired or no longer potent
qs.x: Nitroglycerin loses potency with exposure to light, heat, and air.
w: Too concentrated for safe use
Stored correctly and fully active
Allergenic

qs.q: How often can nitroglycerin generally be repeated if chest pain persists and BP remains adequate?
qs.a: Every 3-5 minutes up to the protocol maximum
qs.x: The standard repeat interval is 3-5 minutes, typically up to 3 doses.
w: Every 30 seconds until the chest pain is completely gone
Once per hour as long as the BP stays above 90
Only once, then switch to aspirin for further pain relief

qs.q: The most important vital sign to reassess after giving nitroglycerin is:
qs.a: Blood pressure
qs.x: Hypotension is the major risk after nitroglycerin.
w: Temperature
Pupil size and reactivity
Blood glucose

qs.q: Which route is used for EMT-assisted nitroglycerin?
qs.a: Sublingual
qs.x: Tablets or spray are placed under the tongue.
w: Intramuscular
Subcutaneous
Intravenous

qs.q: A patient took his own nitroglycerin and now feels faint with a BP of 78/50. Your first action is to:
qs.a: Lay the patient supine and raise the legs if no contraindication
qs.x: Nitroglycerin-induced hypotension is managed by positioning and supportive care.
w: Give another nitroglycerin to relieve the remaining chest pain
Sit the patient upright to improve breathing and perfusion
Give aspirin and then have the patient walk to the stretcher

qs.q: A diabetic patient is confused but awake and can follow commands and swallow. Blood glucose is 42 mg/dL. You should give:
qs.a: Oral glucose
qs.x: Oral glucose is indicated for a conscious hypoglycemic patient who can swallow and protect the airway.
w: Nothing by mouth and transport
Insulin
Activated charcoal

qs.q: Oral glucose is contraindicated in a patient who:
qs.a: Cannot swallow or protect the airway
qs.x: Giving anything by mouth to a patient who cannot protect the airway risks aspiration.
w: Has a blood glucose of 50 mg/dL
Is a known diabetic who carries glucose tablets
Took insulin this morning

qs.q: A typical adult dose of oral glucose is:
qs.a: 15-24 grams
qs.x: One tube is usually 15 g; protocols commonly allow 15-24 g.
w: 1-2 grams
150 grams
0.5 grams

qs.q: The best way to administer oral glucose gel is:
qs.a: Between the cheek and gum or swallowed in small amounts
qs.x: The gel is placed between the cheek and gum or taken by mouth in small amounts.
w: Injected into the thigh muscle with an auto-injector
Sprayed into each nostril with an atomizer device
Mixed with water and given only after the patient eats

qs.q: Glucose is essential primarily because the brain:
qs.a: Depends on glucose as its main fuel
qs.x: The brain relies on a constant glucose supply; hypoglycemia rapidly causes altered mental status.
w: Stores large amounts of sugar for later use
Uses fat for most of its energy
Makes its own insulin

qs.q: A patient with altered mental status has a blood glucose of 110 mg/dL. Oral glucose is:
qs.a: Not indicated
qs.x: The glucose level is normal; look for another cause of the altered mental status.
w: Indicated at double dose
Indicated if the patient is diabetic
Indicated to prevent future lows

qs.q: After giving oral glucose to a hypoglycemic patient, you should:
qs.a: Reassess mental status and recheck blood glucose
qs.x: Reassessment confirms that the treatment worked and the patient is improving.
w: Immediately give a second tube
Lay the patient flat and avoid further assessment
Give insulin to stabilize the glucose

qs.q: A patient stung by a bee has hives, wheezing, and a BP of 84/50. Which medication is most important?
qs.a: Epinephrine auto-injector
qs.x: Anaphylaxis with respiratory compromise or hypotension requires epinephrine first.
w: Oral diphenhydramine tablets
Oral glucose
Aspirin

qs.q: The adult epinephrine auto-injector dose is:
qs.a: 0.3 mg
qs.x: Adult auto-injectors deliver 0.3 mg; pediatric auto-injectors (for 15-30 kg) deliver 0.15 mg.
w: 3 mg
1 mg

qs.q: The preferred site for an epinephrine auto-injector is:
qs.a: The lateral thigh
qs.x: The anterolateral thigh gives the most reliable absorption.
w: The deltoid muscle of the upper arm
The upper outer buttock
The abdomen around the navel

qs.q: Epinephrine helps anaphylaxis because it:
qs.a: Constricts blood vessels and dilates bronchioles
qs.x: Alpha effects raise blood pressure; beta-2 effects open the airways.
w: Dilates blood vessels and constricts the airways
Lowers the heart rate and reduces cardiac output
Blocks only histamine receptors in the skin

qs.q: Which side effect would you expect after epinephrine?
qs.a: Increased heart rate and anxiety
qs.x: Epinephrine stimulates the sympathetic system, causing tachycardia, tremor, and anxiety.
w: Bradycardia and drowsiness
Pinpoint pupils and slowed breathing
Hypothermia

qs.q: A child weighing 20 kg has anaphylaxis. Which auto-injector is appropriate?
qs.a: 0.15 mg pediatric auto-injector
qs.x: The 0.15 mg auto-injector is designed for children about 15-30 kg.
w: 0.3 mg adult auto-injector
Two adult auto-injectors
None; children should not receive epinephrine

qs.q: When an auto-injector is activated, it should be held in place for:
qs.a: Several seconds per the manufacturer (often 3-10 seconds)
qs.x: Holding the device in place ensures the full dose is delivered.
w: One full minute to ensure complete absorption into the muscle
Less than half a second, then remove it quickly from the thigh
No time at all; remove the device immediately

qs.q: A patient who received epinephrine for anaphylaxis feels better and wants to refuse transport. You should explain that:
qs.a: Symptoms can return hours later, so evaluation is needed
qs.x: Biphasic reactions can occur, and epinephrine wears off in 15-20 minutes.
w: They are cured and need no further medical follow-up
They should use another auto-injector in 1 hour
They should drink milk to prevent a recurrence of symptoms

qs.q: Anaphylaxis is best described as:
qs.a: A severe, life-threatening, multisystem allergic reaction
qs.x: Anaphylaxis can involve the airway, breathing, circulation, and skin.
w: A localized rash with itching that stays at the sting site
A bacterial infection that spreads through the blood
A heart attack that is triggered by an allergy medicine

qs.q: A patient found down has pinpoint pupils and respirations of 4 per minute. Your first priority is to:
qs.a: Ventilate with a bag-valve mask
qs.x: Airway and ventilation come first; naloxone follows.
w: Give naloxone before any airway care
Check blood glucose
Obtain a medication list

qs.q: Naloxone reverses the effects of:
qs.a: Opioids
qs.x: Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist.
w: Benzodiazepines
Alcohol
Stimulants

qs.q: A common intranasal naloxone dose for adults is:
qs.a: 2-4 mg
qs.x: Prefilled nasal sprays deliver 4 mg; 2 mg given by atomizer is also common.
w: 40 mg
0.2 mg

qs.q: After naloxone, a patient wakes up agitated, vomiting, and sweating. This is most likely:
qs.a: Opioid withdrawal
qs.x: Rapid reversal in opioid-dependent patients precipitates withdrawal.
w: An allergic reaction
Hypoglycemia
A stroke

qs.q: The goal of naloxone administration is to:
qs.a: Restore adequate breathing
qs.x: Naloxone is titrated to adequate respirations, not to full wakefulness.
w: Make the patient fully alert and talkative
Lower blood pressure
Stop seizures

qs.q: Why must a patient revived with naloxone be monitored closely?
qs.a: Naloxone may wear off before the opioid, so breathing can slow again
qs.x: Naloxone lasts 30-90 minutes, which is shorter than many opioids.
w: Naloxone causes delayed seizures in most patients after 1 hour of recovery
Naloxone lowers blood sugar and can cause hypoglycemia later
Naloxone often causes a delayed allergic reaction several hours later

qs.q: Naloxone will NOT reverse respiratory depression from:
qs.a: Alcohol and benzodiazepines
qs.x: Naloxone only antagonizes opioid receptors.
w: Fentanyl and other synthetic opioids
Heroin and prescription pain pills
Morphine and hydromorphone

qs.q: Albuterol relieves wheezing by:
qs.a: Relaxing the smooth muscle of the bronchioles
qs.x: Albuterol is a beta-2 agonist bronchodilator.
w: Reducing airway inflammation over days
Thinning the blood to improve lung perfusion
Slowing the heart rate to reduce oxygen demand

qs.q: A common side effect of albuterol is:
qs.a: Tachycardia and tremor
qs.x: Beta stimulation causes rapid heart rate, shakiness, and nervousness.
w: Bradycardia
Drowsiness
Low blood pressure only

qs.q: An asthmatic patient says she used her inhaler 10 times in the last hour without relief. This suggests:
qs.a: A severe exacerbation needing aggressive treatment and transport
qs.x: Repeated rescue inhaler use without relief signals severe, worsening asthma.
w: An allergy to the inhaler that is causing the wheezing
Her asthma is improving and she needs no further care
She is just anxious and needs only coaching and reassurance on scene

qs.q: A nebulized albuterol dose for an adult is typically:
qs.a: 2.5 mg
qs.x: The standard unit dose is 2.5 mg in 3 mL.
w: 25 mg
250 mg

qs.q: Before assisting with a patient's metered-dose inhaler, the EMT should verify:
qs.a: It is prescribed to the patient and not expired
qs.x: Follow the medication rights (right patient, drug, dose, route, and time) and check the expiration date.
w: The patient's blood glucose is above 70 mg/dL
The patient has taken a dose of aspirin today
The patient is no longer wheezing before you start

qs.q: A spacer is used with a metered-dose inhaler to:
qs.a: Improve delivery of medication to the lungs
qs.x: Spacers reduce the need for perfect coordination and improve lung delivery.
w: Increase the dose of medication delivered with each puff
Slow the onset so the medication lasts longer
Keep the inhaler mouthpiece clean and sterile

qs.q: An asthmatic who was wheezing loudly is now quiet, drowsy, and has minimal chest movement. This indicates:
qs.a: Impending respiratory failure
qs.x: A silent chest with fatigue indicates severe air trapping and respiratory failure.
w: A complete response to albuterol
A patient who is resting comfortably
A mild asthma attack

qs.q: Activated charcoal works by:
qs.a: Binding (adsorbing) certain poisons in the gut
qs.x: Charcoal adsorbs many substances, preventing their absorption.
w: Neutralizing stomach acid so pills cannot dissolve
Causing vomiting to empty the stomach contents
Speeding up the heart rate to clear the poison faster

qs.q: Activated charcoal is contraindicated in a patient who:
qs.a: Has an altered mental status and cannot protect the airway
qs.x: Aspiration of charcoal can cause severe lung injury.
w: Swallowed pills 30 minutes ago and is alert
Is an adult with a normal level of consciousness
Is cooperative and able to swallow without difficulty

qs.q: Activated charcoal is ineffective for which ingestion?
qs.a: Iron or lithium
qs.x: Charcoal does not bind metals such as iron and lithium, alcohols, acids, or alkalis.
w: Acetaminophen
Aspirin
Many sedative medications

qs.q: The usual protocol dose of activated charcoal is:
qs.a: 1 g/kg
qs.x: Toxicology/protocol dosing is 1 g/kg (about 50-100 g in adults); the OTC label lists 20-30 g.
w: 10 g/kg
0.1 g/kg
500 g regardless of weight

qs.q: Before giving activated charcoal for an ingestion, many protocols require you to:
qs.a: Contact poison control or medical direction
qs.x: Charcoal use has narrowed, and consultation is commonly required.
w: Induce vomiting first to empty the stomach
Give a glass of milk to coat the stomach lining
Give oral glucose to prevent hypoglycemia

qs.q: Acetaminophen is used to treat:
qs.a: Mild to moderate pain and fever
qs.x: Acetaminophen is an analgesic and antipyretic.
w: Anaphylaxis and severe allergies
Opioid overdose and sedation
Wheezing and bronchospasm

qs.q: The organ most at risk from acetaminophen overdose is the:
qs.a: Liver
qs.x: Overdose depletes glutathione and can cause liver failure.
w: Lungs
Heart
Bladder

qs.q: Why is it dangerous to leave a patient with an acetaminophen overdose at home, even if the patient looks well?
qs.a: Liver damage may not cause symptoms for 24-72 hours
qs.x: Early acetaminophen toxicity is often silent.
w: Seizures always develop later, usually without warning
Severe hypertension will develop
Internal bleeding will start within minutes of ingestion

qs.q: Before giving acetaminophen, an important question is:
qs.a: Have you taken any other acetaminophen products today?
qs.x: Many combination products contain acetaminophen, risking unintentional overdose.
w: Do you have asthma, COPD, or any other lung disease?
Are you allergic to bees or other insect stings?
Do you take insulin or other diabetes medications?

qs.q: Ibuprofen belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: NSAID
qs.x: Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug.
w: Opioid
Antihistamine
Beta blocker

qs.q: Ibuprofen should generally be avoided in a patient who:
qs.a: Has a history of stomach ulcers or GI bleeding
qs.x: NSAIDs increase GI bleeding risk.
w: Has a sprained ankle with swelling and pain
Has a low-grade fever from a cold
Has a mild tension headache after a long workday

qs.q: Unlike acetaminophen, ibuprofen:
qs.a: Reduces inflammation and affects platelets
qs.x: NSAIDs are anti-inflammatory and have GI, renal, and bleeding risks.
w: Is safe in kidney failure
Has no effect on the stomach lining or kidneys
Reverses the effects of opioids

qs.q: Which of the following is one of the medication "rights"?
qs.a: Right route
qs.x: The rights include the right patient, drug, dose, route, time, and documentation.
w: Right hospital
Right crew
Right weather

qs.q: A medication that is placed under the tongue is given by which route?
qs.a: Sublingual
qs.x: Sublingual means under the tongue.
w: Buccal
Intranasal
Transdermal

qs.q: An indication for a medication is:
qs.a: The reason or condition for which the drug is given
qs.x: An indication is why a medication is used.
w: A situation in which the drug should not be given
An unwanted effect that occurs alongside the desired one
The drug's trade name printed on the package

qs.q: A contraindication is:
qs.a: A situation in which giving the drug may cause the patient harm
qs.x: Contraindications are reasons to withhold a medication.
w: An expected therapeutic effect that the drug is given to produce
The approved maximum dose that is listed on the package insert
An unintended effect that commonly occurs at normal doses

qs.q: A side effect is best described as:
qs.a: Any effect of a drug other than the desired effect
qs.x: Side effects are effects other than the intended therapeutic action.
w: The reason the drug is given to the patient in the field
The drug's generic or official name
The correct dose of the drug for an adult

qs.q: The generic name of a drug is:
qs.a: The official, non-brand name
qs.x: Generic names (e.g., acetaminophen) differ from trade names (e.g., Tylenol).
w: The name given by the manufacturer for marketing
Always capitalized
Used only in hospitals

qs.q: Among these routes used by EMTs, which has the fastest absorption?
qs.a: Inhaled
qs.x: Inhaled medications are absorbed quickly across the large surface area of the lungs.
w: Oral
Rectal
Transdermal

qs.q: Before administering any medication, the EMT must obtain:
qs.a: Online or standing-order approval from medical direction
qs.x: EMTs give medications under medical direction.
w: Verbal permission from the patient's family members only
Approval from a police officer
A normal blood test result from the patient's own physician

qs.q: After giving a medication, the EMT must:
qs.a: Reassess the patient and document time, dose, route, and response
qs.x: Reassessment and documentation are required for every medication.
w: Leave the patient alone for 10 minutes to let it work
Give a second dose automatically to be sure that the first one works
Contact the patient's pharmacy to report the dose given

qs.q: A patient's medication list includes metformin and insulin. This suggests the patient has:
qs.a: Diabetes
qs.x: Both are diabetes medications.
w: Asthma
Seizures
Heart failure

qs.q: A patient's medication list includes an albuterol inhaler and fluticasone. This suggests the patient has:
qs.a: Asthma or COPD
qs.x: Both are respiratory medications.
w: Diabetes mellitus
Hypertension
Epilepsy (seizures)

qs.q: A patient takes warfarin (Coumadin). This is important after a fall because:
qs.a: The patient has an increased risk of serious bleeding
qs.x: Anticoagulants raise the risk of intracranial and internal bleeding.
w: The patient will have dangerously low blood sugar
The patient cannot feel pain
The patient is likely having a stroke from the medication

qs.q: Which medication is supplied as a gel?
qs.a: Oral glucose
qs.x: Oral glucose is commonly supplied as a gel.
w: Epinephrine auto-injector
Nitroglycerin spray
Albuterol nebulizer solution

qs.q: A metered-dose inhaler delivers medication as a:
qs.a: Fine spray or mist inhaled into the lungs
qs.x: MDIs deliver an aerosolized, measured dose.
w: Tablet placed under the tongue to dissolve
Injection into a muscle
Liquid that is swallowed and absorbed in the gut

qs.q: The "right time" in medication administration includes:
qs.a: Checking when the patient last took the drug and when it may be repeated
qs.x: Timing matters for repeat doses and maximum doses.
w: Giving every medication only at night before bed, regardless of symptoms
Waiting a full hour before giving any medication dose
Giving all of the patient's medications at the same time

qs.q: What is the expected effect of medications that dilate the bronchioles?
qs.a: Improved airflow and reduced wheezing
qs.x: Bronchodilators open the airways.
w: Lower blood glucose and improved energy
Pupil constriction and slower heart rate
Reduced bleeding and better clotting

qs.q: Epinephrine is classified as a:
qs.a: Sympathomimetic (adrenergic agonist)
qs.x: Epinephrine stimulates alpha and beta adrenergic receptors.
w: Antihistamine (H1 blocker)
Opioid (mu-opioid receptor agonist)
Anticoagulant (clotting factor inhibitor)

qs.q: A patient in anaphylaxis also takes a beta blocker. You might expect the epinephrine to:
qs.a: Be less effective
qs.x: Beta blockers can blunt the response to epinephrine.
w: Work faster than usual
Cause bradycardia
Have no side effects

qs.q: A patient with chest pain has a blood pressure of 96/60 and your protocol requires a systolic BP of at least 100 for nitroglycerin. You should:
qs.a: Withhold nitroglycerin and contact medical direction
qs.x: Nitroglycerin is withheld when the BP is below the protocol threshold.
w: Give nitroglycerin anyway since pain is the priority
Give two tablets
Give aspirin and nitroglycerin together at once

qs.q: Which patient is most at risk for severe hypotension from nitroglycerin?
qs.a: A patient with an inferior/right ventricular MI
qs.x: Right ventricular infarction makes the heart preload-dependent.
w: A patient with a blood pressure of 180/100
A patient with stable angina that occurs with exercise
A patient with a mild headache and normal BP

qs.q: A patient with chest pain says he already took 324 mg of aspirin 30 minutes ago. You should:
qs.a: Withhold more aspirin and document the dose
qs.x: The full dose has already been taken; repeating it adds bleeding risk.
w: Give another 324 mg
Give an extra 81 mg
Give nitroglycerin instead of aspirin

qs.q: A COPD patient with wheezing receives albuterol. The most important reassessment is:
qs.a: Lung sounds, breathing effort, and pulse oximetry
qs.x: Reassess respiratory status after giving a bronchodilator.
w: Pupil size and reactivity to light in both eyes
Skin temperature and capillary refill only
Blood glucose, temperature, and skin color

qs.q: Hypoglycemia is commonly defined as a blood glucose below about:
qs.a: 60-70 mg/dL
qs.x: Most protocols treat symptomatic patients below 60-70 mg/dL.
w: 120 mg/dL
200 mg/dL
300 mg/dL

qs.q: Which patient is at highest risk for hypoglycemia?
qs.a: A diabetic who took insulin and skipped a meal
qs.x: Insulin without food intake commonly causes hypoglycemia.
w: A diabetic who just ate a large meal
A nondiabetic who just had a snack and some juice
A patient with a sprained ankle

qs.q: Which finding best suggests an opioid overdose?
qs.a: Pinpoint pupils, slow breathing, and decreased responsiveness
qs.x: The classic opioid toxidrome is miosis, respiratory depression, and CNS depression.
w: Dilated pupils, hot flushed skin, and a very high body temperature
Hives, wheezing, and swelling of the lips, face, and tongue
High blood sugar, deep rapid breathing, and fruity-smelling breath

qs.q: Naloxone can be given by EMTs through which routes in most systems?
qs.a: Intranasal or intramuscular
qs.x: EMTs commonly give IN or IM naloxone.
w: Intravenous only
Sublingual tablet only
Rectal suppository or oral tablet

qs.q: Which patient needs epinephrine rather than just antihistamines?
qs.a: Throat tightness, trouble breathing, and low BP after eating peanuts
qs.x: Systemic involvement with airway or circulation compromise is anaphylaxis.
w: Mild itching and redness only around a single mosquito bite on the arm
Sneezing, runny nose, and watery eyes during the spring pollen season
A single small hive on the forearm with normal vital signs and breathing

qs.q: A side effect of activated charcoal is:
qs.a: Black stools
qs.x: Charcoal passes through and turns stool black.
w: Pinpoint pupils
Bradycardia
Hypoglycemia

qs.q: Ibuprofen should be avoided in late pregnancy because it can:
qs.a: Close the fetal ductus arteriosus prematurely
qs.x: NSAIDs taken in the third trimester can affect fetal circulation.
w: Cause high blood sugar in the mother and fetus
Cause an allergic reaction in all patients
Speed up labor

qs.q: Acetaminophen does NOT have significant:
qs.a: Anti-inflammatory or antiplatelet effects
qs.x: Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever but not inflammation, and it does not affect platelets.
w: Fever-reducing (antipyretic) effects
Pain-relieving (analgesic) effects at normal doses
Metabolism by enzymes in the liver

qs.q: An expired medication should be:
qs.a: Removed from use and replaced
qs.x: Expired medications may be less effective or unsafe.
w: Used if it still looks normal
Used at double the dose
Used only for pediatric patients

qs.q: Which is the best example of a trade (brand) name?
qs.a: Tylenol
qs.x: Tylenol is the brand name for acetaminophen.
w: Acetaminophen
N-acetyl-p-aminophenol
Analgesic

qs.q: Medications that are absorbed through the skin over time are delivered by which route?
qs.a: Transdermal
qs.x: Patches such as nitroglycerin and fentanyl are transdermal.
w: Sublingual
Intraosseous
Inhalation

qs.q: Before removing a medication patch, you should:
qs.a: Put on gloves to avoid absorbing the drug yourself
qs.x: Gloves prevent provider exposure.
w: Use bare hands so you can get a better grip on the edge
Leave the patch in place no matter what happens
Cut the patch in half to reduce the dose given

qs.q: A patient uses a fentanyl patch and is now very sleepy with slow breathing. An important action is to:
qs.a: Remove the patch and support ventilation
qs.x: Removing the patch stops further absorption; heat increases absorption.
w: Apply a heat pack over the patch site
Give oral glucose to raise alertness
Give nitroglycerin for the slow breathing

qs.q: A patient with pulmonary hypertension and RV failure on Primacor 0.375 mcg/kg/min becomes hypotensive at 74/40. Which addition makes the most sense?
qs.a: Vasopressin, which raises SVR with little effect on PVR
qs.x: Vasopressin restores SVR and RV coronary perfusion without raising pulmonary vascular resistance much. Large fluid loads over-distend the failing RV and worsen septal shift, and phenylephrine raises PVR.
w: Phenylephrine, which lowers PVR more than it raises the SVR
A 2-liter crystalloid bolus to load the dilated RV
A higher milrinone dose to unload the right ventricle

qs.q: A patient on metoprolol has anaphylaxis with persistent hypotension after three IM epinephrine doses and an epinephrine infusion. Which drug should be added?
qs.a: Glucagon IV
qs.x: Glucagon raises cAMP independently of beta receptors and is the guideline adjunct for beta-blocked patients with refractory anaphylaxis. Steroids do not act fast enough to work as pressors.
w: Atropine 1 mg IV
Calcium chloride 1 g IV
Methylprednisolone as the pressor

qs.q: A crewmember makes push-dose epinephrine by drawing 1 mL from a 1 mg/mL vial into 9 mL saline, believing it is 10 mcg/mL, then gives 1 mL. How much was given?
qs.a: 100 mcg, a tenfold overdose
qs.x: 1 mg in 10 mL is 100 mcg/mL. The usual protocol mix uses 1 mL of the 0.1 mg/mL cardiac syringe in 9 mL saline to make 10 mcg/mL. Concentration mix-ups are a classic push-dose error.
w: 10 mcg, the intended protocol dose
1 mcg, a tenfold underdose
1000 mcg, a hundredfold overdose

qs.q: A patient with an aortic dissection is started on Nipride without a beta-blocker, and HR rises to 128. Why is this a problem?

qs.x: Vasodilators trigger reflex tachycardia and a higher dP/dt, which propagates the tear. Beta-blockade, e.g., esmolol to HR under 60, comes first per guideline, then a vasodilator if BP remains high.
w: Nitroprusside directly stimulates beta-1 receptors
Early cyanide toxicity is causing a compensatory sinus tachycardia
The tachycardia is harmful only if MAP drops below 65

qs.q: A 26-year-old has an irregular wide-complex tachycardia at 240 with varying QRS morphology. BP is 118/70. Which drug is best?

qs.x: Irregular, very fast, changing wide complexes suggest pre-excited AF (WPW). AV nodal blockers can speed conduction down the accessory pathway and cause VF. Procainamide or cardioversion is preferred.

Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV
Metoprolol 5 mg IV

qs.q: A heart transplant recipient has a narrow-complex SVT at 190. How should the adenosine dose be adjusted per guideline?
qs.a: Lower the first dose (e.g., 3 mg), since the denervated heart is hypersensitive
qs.x: Denervated transplanted hearts have exaggerated, prolonged responses to adenosine, so guidelines reduce the dose. Doubling it risks prolonged asystole.

Avoid adenosine entirely and give verapamil as the first-line agent
Use standard 6 mg and 12 mg dosing, since transplant does not matter

qs.q: A patient with SVT takes several home medications. Which one would most blunt the effect of Adenocard?
qs.a: Theophylline
qs.x: Methylxanthines such as theophylline and caffeine competitively block adenosine receptors, so larger doses may be needed. Dipyridamole blocks adenosine uptake and greatly potentiates it.

Carbamazepine
Lisinopril

qs.q: A 70-kg patient has stable monomorphic VT at 170 with BP 110/70. What is the labeled Cordarone IV regimen?
qs.a: 150 mg over 10 min, then 1 mg/min for 6 hr, then 0.5 mg/min
qs.x: The label gives 150 mg over 10 minutes, then 1 mg/min for 6 hours, then 0.5 mg/min. The 300 mg push is the ACLS dose for pulseless VF or VT and can cause hypotension in a perfusing patient.
w: 300 mg rapid IV push, then 150 mg rapid IV push 3-5 min later
5 mg/kg IV over 2 minutes, repeated twice as needed
1 g IV over 1 hour, then 0.5 mg/min for 24 hours

qs.q: A patient with a long baseline QTc has recurrent, self-terminating polymorphic VT with twisting QRS axis. BP is adequate between runs. What is the best first treatment?
qs.a: Magnesium 2 g IV, then overdrive pacing or isoproterenol if needed
qs.x: Per ACLS, torsades responds to magnesium, and raising the heart rate shortens the QT. Amiodarone, procainamide and sotalol all prolong the QT and can worsen torsades.
w: Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes to suppress the runs
Procainamide 20 mg/min until the QRS widens by 50 percent
Sotalol 1.5 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes for rhythm control

qs.q: Corvert is given to convert recent-onset atrial flutter. Which monitoring does its label require?
qs.a: Continuous ECG for at least 4 hours
qs.x: Ibutilide causes polymorphic VT in a small percentage of patients, usually within hours of the infusion. Correct potassium and magnesium first and have a defibrillator ready.
w: Digoxin levels before and after infusion
Hourly glucose for hypoglycemia
Liver enzymes within the first hour

qs.q: A patient with known EF 20% has AF at 160, BP 98/62 and crackles. Which rate-control drug is most likely to cause decompensation?
qs.a: Cardizem
qs.x: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are negatively inotropic and are avoided in decompensated HFrEF. Amiodarone and digoxin are the usual options, with cardioversion for instability.
w: Amiodarone
Digoxin
Synchronized cardioversion if unstable

qs.q: A patient with a regular wide-complex tachycardia, presumed to be SVT with aberrancy, collapses after verapamil. What is the most likely mechanism?
qs.a: Verapamil caused vasodilation and negative inotropy during VT
qs.x: Most regular wide-complex tachycardias are VT. Calcium channel blockers given in VT cause profound hypotension and collapse. Treat wide-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise.
w: Verapamil turned SVT with aberrancy directly into VF
Verapamil prolonged the QT interval and caused torsades
Verapamil blocked sodium channels and widened the QRS complex further

qs.q: A patient in AF at 180 has BP 70/40 and is confused. Per ACLS, what is the appropriate biphasic electrical therapy?
qs.a: Synchronized 120-200 J
qs.x: Unstable AF needs synchronized cardioversion, starting around 120-200 J biphasic per ACLS and the device maker. An unsynchronized shock can land on the T wave and cause VF.
w: Unsynchronized 120-200 J
Unsynchronized 360 J
Synchronized 2 J/kg

qs.q: A patient has third-degree AV block with a wide-complex escape at 30 and BP 70/40. Why is atropine likely to fail?
qs.a: The block is infranodal, below vagal influence
qs.x: A wide escape rhythm suggests block at or below the His-Purkinje system, which vagal blockade cannot help. Move quickly to pacing or an epinephrine or dopamine infusion.
w: Atropine is contraindicated in acute coronary syndrome
The dose must exceed 3 mg before any effect is seen
Atropine works only in pediatric bradycardia

qs.q: A patient remains in VF after multiple shocks, epinephrine, and amiodarone 300 mg then 150 mg. Which electrical change has RCT support for refractory VF?
qs.a: Vector change or double sequential defibrillation
qs.x: The DOSE-VF trial found that anterior-posterior vector change and double sequential external defibrillation improved survival. Long pauses in CPR before shocks reduce the chance of success.
w: Escalating single shocks to 400 J with one defibrillator
Switching to unsynchronized monophasic 200 J shocks
Pausing CPR for 30 seconds before each shock

qs.q: A patient with ICD shocks has received 6 shocks for recurrent VT in one hour despite amiodarone. He is awake and terrified between episodes. Which adjunct best targets the cause?
qs.a: Deep sedation plus beta-blockade to blunt sympathetic drive
qs.x: Electrical storm feeds on catecholamines: each shock and the patient's fear trigger more VT. Sedation and beta-blockade, e.g., esmolol or propranolol, break the cycle. Epinephrine and isoproterenol fuel it.
w: Epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 minutes between episodes
Isoproterenol infusion to suppress the ventricular ectopy and pauses
Calcium chloride 1 g IV to stabilize the cardiac membrane

qs.q: An 80-kg patient on warfarin has an intracranial hemorrhage with INR 5.2. Per the Kcentra label, what is the best reversal?
qs.a: 35 units/kg 4F-PCC (2800 units) plus vitamin K 10 mg slow IV
qs.x: The labeled dosing is 25 units/kg for INR 2 to under 4, 35 units/kg for INR 4-6 and 50 units/kg for INR over 6, with a max per tier. Vitamin K is given with it. Many protocols use a fixed dose instead.
w: 25 units/kg 4F-PCC (2000 units) with no vitamin K given at all
50 units/kg 4F-PCC (4000 units) with FFP 15 mL/kg added
10 units/kg 4F-PCC (800 units) plus protamine 50 mg IV

qs.q: Why is IV vitamin K given together with 4F-PCC for warfarin reversal?
qs.a: PCC wears off in hours; vitamin K restores factor synthesis over 12-24 hr
qs.x: The factors in PCC, especially factor VII, have short half-lives, and the INR rebounds unless the liver resumes making functional factors. PCC factors are already carboxylated and do not need vitamin K to work.
w: Vitamin K binds warfarin in the plasma and speeds its renal clearance from blood
Vitamin K is needed to activate the clotting factors in the PCC vial
Vitamin K prevents the thrombotic complications caused by PCC

qs.q: A 72-year-old on dabigatran has a traumatic subdural hematoma. What is the labeled Praxbind dose?
qs.a: 5 g IV as two 2.5 g vials
qs.x: The label dose is 5 g, given as two consecutive 2.5 g infusions or bolus injections. Idarucizumab binds dabigatran with very high affinity and reverses it within minutes.
w: 2.5 g IV, repeated in 12 hours
50 units/kg IV based on weight
1 mg per 100 mg of dabigatran

qs.q: A patient on Eliquis has a life-threatening GI bleed, and andexanet is not available. Which option is reasonable per guideline?

Protamine 1 mg per 100 units
Vitamin K 10 mg slow IV with fresh plasma

qs.q: A heparin infusion at 1200 units/hr was stopped just before an emergency. Using a common guideline that counts heparin given in the last 2.5 hours, what is the protamine dose?

50 mg
120 mg

qs.q: Which patient is at highest risk of a severe reaction to protamine?
qs.a: A diabetic who has used NPH insulin for years
qs.x: Prior exposure to protamine-containing insulin (NPH), fish allergy, vasectomy and prior protamine exposure increase the risk of anaphylaxis and pulmonary hypertensive reactions. Give it slowly and be ready to treat reactions.

A patient on long-term warfarin for AF
A patient with prior heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

qs.q: A patient who got Lovenox 1 mg/kg 4 hours ago is now bleeding significantly. What is true about reversal?
qs.a: Protamine 1 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin gives only partial reversal
qs.x: Per the enoxaparin label, protamine 1 mg per 1 mg given within 8 hours neutralizes anti-IIa activity but only about 60% of anti-Xa activity. Idarucizumab is specific to dabigatran.
w: Protamine completely reverses enoxaparin, just as it does heparin
Idarucizumab 5 g IV completely reverses enoxaparin
Vitamin K 10 mg IV reverses enoxaparin within hours

qs.q: After 8 units of blood products over 40 minutes, a trauma patient's QT lengthens and BP falls despite more products. iCa is 0.82 mmol/L. What is the cause and fix?
qs.a: Citrate chelating calcium; give calcium chloride 1 g IV
qs.x: Citrate preservative binds ionized calcium, causing hypotension, poor contractility, coagulopathy and a long QT. Calcium replacement is part of massive transfusion protocols.
w: Hyperkalemia from stored blood; give insulin and dextrose
Hypothermia from cold products; warm them and give TXA
An acute transfusion reaction; stop products and give epinephrine

qs.q: Compared with 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate, how much elemental calcium does 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride provide?
qs.a: About 3 times more (13.6 vs 4.65 mEq)
qs.x: 1 g of calcium chloride has about 13.6 mEq of calcium, versus about 4.65 mEq in 1 g of calcium gluconate. Chloride is also more irritating to veins, so a central or large, secure line is preferred.
w: About the same, since both are 10% solutions
About one-third as much as the gluconate
About 10 times more than the gluconate

qs.q: A blunt trauma patient in hemorrhagic shock was injured 3.5 hours ago. TXA has not been given. Per CRASH-2 protocol, what is best?
qs.a: Do not start TXA; late dosing raised bleeding deaths

w: Give 1 g over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 hr as usual for trauma
Give a 2 g bolus to make up for the delay
Give TXA only if fibrinogen is under 100 mg/dL

qs.q: Cyklokapron 1 g is pushed IV over 1 minute instead of over 10 minutes. Which effect does the label warn of with rapid injection?
qs.a: Hypotension
qs.x: Rapid IV injection of tranexamic acid can cause hypotension. Infuse it no faster than about 100 mg/min.
w: Hyperkalemia
Bronchospasm
Hypoglycemia

qs.q: A patient with a penetrating torso injury and no head injury has BP 82/50 after 2 units of blood. Surgery is 40 minutes away. What is the best resuscitation target?
qs.a: Permissive hypotension, SBP about 80-90
qs.x: Until bleeding is controlled, damage control resuscitation accepts a lower BP with blood products to avoid dislodging clot and diluting clotting factors. This does not apply to TBI, where hypotension worsens outcomes.
w: Norepinephrine to a MAP of 65 first
2 liters of crystalloid to restore a normal BP
Push-dose phenylephrine to SBP 120

qs.q: A patient with active heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is on warfarin and needs emergency reversal. Which product does its own label contraindicate?
qs.a: Kcentra
qs.x: Kcentra contains a small amount of heparin and is contraindicated in known HIT. FFP or other strategies are used instead, together with vitamin K.
w: Vitamin K
Idarucizumab
Fresh frozen plasma

qs.q: A patient on Pradaxa with acute kidney injury has a major bleed, and idarucizumab is unavailable. Which therapy can remove the drug?
qs.a: Hemodialysis
qs.x: Dabigatran has low protein binding and is renally cleared, so hemodialysis removes much of it. Apixaban and rivaroxaban are highly protein-bound and are not dialyzable.
w: Plasmapheresis
Protamine 50 mg IV
Charcoal hemoperfusion only

qs.q: A patient with an amitriptyline overdose has QRS 148 ms, BP 80/50 and is seizing. What is the best immediate treatment?
qs.a: Benzodiazepine plus sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV
qs.x: Hypertonic sodium and alkalemia overcome TCA sodium channel blockade. Benzodiazepines treat the seizures. Phenytoin is a sodium channel blocker, and physostigmine can cause asystole in TCA toxicity.

Physostigmine 1-2 mg for the anticholinergic toxidrome signs
Flumazenil to reverse a possible benzodiazepine

qs.q: A TCA overdose patient is intubated after bicarbonate boluses. Which ventilator strategy is best?
qs.a: Avoid hypoventilation; keep the pH mildly alkalemic
qs.x: Acidemia increases TCA binding to sodium channels and widens the QRS. A drop in minute ventilation after intubation can rapidly worsen the cardiotoxicity. Target a pH of about 7.45-7.55 per toxicology guidance.
w: Permissive hypercapnia for lung-protective ventilation
Hypoventilate to retain CO2 and offset the bicarbonate
Any rate is fine; ventilation does not affect TCA toxicity

qs.q: A TCA overdose patient still has QRS 160 ms and runs of VT after the pH reaches 7.55. Which antiarrhythmic is preferred?
qs.a: Lidocaine
qs.x: Lidocaine is a fast on-off sodium channel blocker that can displace the TCA and is the preferred second-line agent. Class IA and IC drugs add to the sodium channel blockade, and sotalol prolongs the QT.
w: Procainamide
Flecainide
Sotalol

qs.q: After an amlodipine overdose, BP is 70/40, HR 58 and glucose 310 despite fluids and calcium. Which therapy is the best next step?
qs.a: High-dose insulin with dextrose per protocol
qs.x: CCB toxicity blocks insulin release and leaves the heart starved of glucose. High-dose insulin euglycemic therapy (toxicology protocol, off-label, e.g., 1 unit/kg bolus then an infusion) improves contractility. The hyperglycemia is a marker of severity, not a reason to withhold insulin.
w: Hold insulin because the patient is already hyperglycemic
Atropine 1 mg every 3-5 minutes as the main therapy
Glucagon 10 mg IV as the definitive therapy

qs.q: After glucagon 5 mg IV for propranolol toxicity, which adverse effect should the crew prepare for first?
qs.a: Vomiting with aspiration risk
qs.x: Large glucagon doses (an off-label toxicology use) commonly cause vomiting, which is dangerous in an obtunded patient. Pretreat with an antiemetic and protect the airway. Glucagon raises glucose.
w: Severe rebound hypoglycemia
Hyperkalemia with peaked T waves
Bronchospasm and wheezing

qs.q: Which beta-blocker in overdose is most likely to cause seizures and QRS widening?
qs.a: Propranolol
qs.x: Propranolol is lipophilic and blocks sodium channels, causing seizures and a wide QRS that may respond to bicarbonate. Sotalol's distinct danger is QT prolongation and torsades.
w: Atenolol
Metoprolol succinate ER
Sotalol

qs.q: A 70-kg patient has an acute digoxin ingestion with a serum level of 12 ng/mL. How many DigiFab vials does the label formula give?
qs.a: 9 vials
qs.x: Vials = (level in ng/mL x weight in kg)/100 = 840/100 = 8.4, rounded up to 9. Each vial binds about 0.5 mg of digoxin.
w: 3 vials
20 vials
1 vial

qs.q: A patient on chronic digoxin has nausea, yellow-tinged vision, a junctional rhythm at 38 and K 5.9. What is the best definitive treatment?
qs.a: Digoxin immune Fab, which also corrects the potassium
qs.x: The hyperkalemia comes from Na-K ATPase poisoning, and Fab reverses both the dysrhythmia and the potassium shift. Digoxin's large volume of distribution makes dialysis ineffective, and pacing can trigger arrhythmias in the irritable myocardium.
w: Calcium chloride 1 g IV, then insulin and dextrose infusions
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate plus hemodialysis
Transcutaneous pacing as the definitive treatment

qs.q: After DigiFab, a lab reports a total serum digoxin level of 25 ng/mL. What does this mean?
qs.a: Expected: the assay counts Fab-bound digoxin
qs.x: Most immunoassays measure total digoxin, including inactive drug bound to Fab, so levels rise after treatment and are unreliable for days. Follow the clinical response instead.
w: Fab failed, so give a double dose at once
The patient has taken more digoxin
A lab error, so repeat it in 1 hour to redose

qs.q: An enclosed-space fire victim has GCS 8, BP 82/50, lactate 11 and SpCO 18%. What is the best antidote plan?
qs.a: Cyanokit 5 g IV over 15 min with 100% oxygen
qs.x: A lactate above about 8 in smoke inhalation strongly suggests cyanide. Hydroxocobalamin (5 g per label) does not impair oxygen delivery. Nitrites create methemoglobin, which further reduces oxygen carrying in a patient who already has carboxyhemoglobin.
w: Sodium nitrite then thiosulfate with 100% oxygen
Methylene blue 1 mg/kg IV with 100% oxygen
Sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg for the acidosis

qs.q: Which finding is expected after hydroxocobalamin and could mislead the receiving team?
qs.a: Red skin and urine with falsely abnormal labs and co-oximetry
qs.x: Hydroxocobalamin's red color interferes with colorimetric labs and co-oximetry and can trigger blood-leak alarms on dialysis machines. It tends to raise BP, not lower it. Draw labs before giving it if possible.
w: Blue-gray skin with a falsely low SpO2 reading on pulse oximetry
Profound bradycardia that needs atropine
Hypotension that needs vasopressor support

qs.q: A patient on propofol and dopamine infusions needs Cyanokit. How should it be given?
qs.a: Through a separate IV line
qs.x: The label lists physical incompatibility with many drugs, including propofol, dopamine, dobutamine, diazepam, sodium thiosulfate and blood products. Use a dedicated line.
w: Piggybacked into the propofol line
In the same bag as sodium thiosulfate
Pushed through the dopamine line

qs.q: A carbon monoxide-poisoned patient has SpO2 99% on a standard pulse oximeter. Why can this be misleading?
qs.a: Two-wavelength oximeters read COHb as oxyhemoglobin
qs.x: Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light much like oxyhemoglobin, so standard oximetry overestimates oxygenation. CO also shifts the curve LEFT, which impairs oxygen unloading to tissues. Use co-oximetry or a CO-capable monitor.
w: CO shifts the curve right, so SpO2 is accurate here
CO creates methemoglobin, which reads as 99 percent
SpO2 is accurate here; it is the PaO2 that is falsely low

qs.q: An organophosphate-poisoned farmer has wheezing and copious bronchorrhea. HR is 128 after 4 mg of atropine. What is the next step?
qs.a: Keep doubling atropine until secretions dry
qs.x: The atropinization endpoint is drying of bronchial secretions and better oxygenation. Tachycardia can come from hypoxia or nicotinic effects. Glycopyrrolate does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
w: Stop, since the tachycardia means full atropinization
Switch to glycopyrrolate for its CNS effects
Give a beta-blocker to control the tachycardia

qs.q: A methamphetamine user has temp 41.2 C (106.2 F), HR 170, BP 210/120 and severe agitation. What is the best first treatment?
qs.a: Large-dose benzodiazepine sedation plus active cooling
qs.x: Benzodiazepines reduce the CNS drive behind the tachycardia, hypertension and heat production. Struggling against restraints worsens hyperthermia and acidosis, and antipyretics do not help agitation-driven heat.
w: Haloperidol 10 mg IM and physical restraint alone
Labetalol 20 mg IV as the first drug for the hypertension
Acetaminophen 1 g PO plus axillary ice packs

qs.q: After cocaine use, a patient develops QRS 150 ms and a wide-complex tachycardia with a pulse. Which drug is most appropriate first?
qs.a: Sodium bicarbonate
qs.x: Cocaine blocks sodium channels like a class IC drug, so hypertonic sodium bicarbonate is first-line. Procainamide adds to the sodium blockade, and beta-blockers given alone are controversial in acute cocaine toxicity.
w: Metoprolol 5 mg IV push
Procainamide
Amiodarone

qs.q: A patient on sertraline received linezolid and fentanyl. Temp is 39.8 C (103.6 F), with ankle clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation and dilated pupils. What is the best treatment?
qs.a: Benzodiazepines, cooling and Periactin via OG tube
qs.x: Clonus and hyperreflexia point to serotonin syndrome. Cyproheptadine, an oral-only 5-HT2A antagonist, is a guideline adjunct. Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist used for NMS and can worsen serotonin toxicity.

Bromocriptine 2.5 mg via OG tube every 8 hours
Haloperidol for agitation plus acetaminophen

qs.q: A patient started on Haldol 4 days ago has rising temperature, lead-pipe rigidity, decreased reflexes, mutism and CK 18,000. What is the diagnosis?
qs.a: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
qs.x: NMS develops over days after dopamine antagonist exposure, with bradyreflexic rigidity. Serotonin syndrome develops within hours with clonus and hyperreflexia. MH follows exposure to volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine.
w: Serotonin syndrome
Malignant hyperthermia, delayed onset
Anticholinergic toxicity

qs.q: A patient with severe serotonin syndrome has temp 41.5 C (106.7 F) and truncal rigidity despite benzodiazepines. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Intubate, paralyze with a nondepolarizer and cool
qs.x: The fever comes from muscle activity, not the hypothalamus, so antipyretics fail. Nondepolarizing paralysis stops heat production. Succinylcholine risks hyperkalemia in a rhabdomyolytic patient.
w: Acetaminophen and ibuprofen around the clock
Succinylcholine boluses to relieve the rigidity
Physical restraints to prevent self-injury

qs.q: Shortly after succinylcholine, an intubated patient has masseter rigidity and EtCO2 rising from 38 to 70 despite increased ventilation. What is often the EARLIEST sign of malignant hyperthermia?
qs.a: Unexplained rising EtCO2
qs.x: Hypermetabolism raises CO2 production before temperature rises, so rising EtCO2 is often the first sign. Hyperthermia is frequently a late finding, and hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia, occurs.
w: Temperature above 41 C (105.8 F)
Hypokalemia with U waves
Bradycardia with hypotension

qs.q: Why is Ryanodex easier to give in a transport malignant hyperthermia crisis than the older 20 mg dantrolene vials?
qs.a: Each 250 mg vial mixes in 5 mL of sterile water
qs.x: Older 20 mg vials each need 60 mL of sterile water, so a 2.5 mg/kg dose for an 80-kg adult takes 10 vials and 600 mL. Both products act on the ryanodine receptor and are reconstituted with sterile water.
w: It works through a different receptor mechanism
It can be given IM when no IV access is available
It is reconstituted with normal saline, not water

qs.q: A diphenhydramine overdose patient is delirious, hot and dry with dilated pupils, but QRS is 132 ms. Is physostigmine appropriate?
qs.a: No; a wide QRS suggests sodium blockade and asystole risk
qs.x: Diphenhydramine in overdose blocks sodium channels like a TCA. Conduction delay is a relative contraindication to physostigmine. Treat the QRS with sodium bicarbonate and the agitation with benzodiazepines.

Yes, because a wide QRS signals cholinergic deficiency
Yes, as long as atropine is given first as pretreatment

qs.q: A fentanyl overdose patient is apneic but easy to bag, with SpO2 94% on BVM. Which Narcan strategy is best?
qs.a: Small titrated doses (e.g., 0.04-0.1 mg IV) to restore breathing
qs.x: Titrating small doses (per protocol) restores ventilation and avoids abrupt withdrawal, vomiting, catecholamine surge and pulmonary edema. The labeled initial dose is 0.4-2 mg. The goal is adequate breathing, not full arousal.
w: 2 mg IV push to fully reverse the opioid in one dose
No naloxone; intubate immediately for airway protection
0.4 mg IM, then midazolam if withdrawal agitation occurs

qs.q: After a topical benzocaine spray, a patient has SpO2 85% that does not improve with oxygen and MetHb 32%. The patient is known to be G6PD deficient. What is best?
qs.a: Avoid methylene blue; consider exchange transfusion or HBO
qs.x: Methylene blue needs NADPH from G6PD to work and can cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, a label contraindication. Exchange transfusion and hyperbaric oxygen are alternatives. Nitrites create more methemoglobin.
w: Give methylene blue 2 mg/kg IV as the usual first-line dose
Give hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV as an alternative reducing agent
Give sodium nitrite to convert the methemoglobin back

qs.q: After an interscalene block with bupivacaine, a patient seizes, then develops a wide-complex bradycardia with hypotension. What does ASRA guidance call for?
qs.a: 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg plus epinephrine under 1 mcg/kg
qs.x: LAST is treated with lipid emulsion and reduced epinephrine doses. Vasopressin, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers and more local anesthetic are avoided. Propofol's lipid content is far too low and it depresses the heart.

Propofol 2 mg/kg for the seizure as the lipid source
Lidocaine 1.5 mg/kg IV for the ventricular dysrhythmia

qs.q: Before transport, an intoxicated patient has a high osmolar gap, early normal anion gap and suspected ethylene glycol ingestion. What does fomepizole do?

qs.x: Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase so toxic glycolate and oxalate are not formed. It does nothing about metabolites already formed, so dialysis is still needed for acidosis or organ damage.

Reverses existing acidosis and kidney injury
Neutralizes the oxalate crystals in tubules

qs.q: A patient with salicylate poisoning tires out and must be intubated. The pre-intubation ABG was pH 7.38, PaCO2 18. Which vent setting choice matters most?
qs.a: Match the high minute ventilation she had before

qs.q: What is the WHO-recommended TXA approach for postpartum hemorrhage?

qs.q: Terbutaline is ordered as a tocolytic. What does its FDA boxed warning address?

qs.q: A preterm labor patient on magnesium is also given nifedipine. Which interaction is the concern?

qs.q: A patient at 30 weeks is in preterm labor and delivery seems imminent. What is the main reason to start magnesium?

qs.q: A 2-day-old with suspected ductal-dependent heart disease is started on Prostin VR 0.05 mcg/kg/min for transport. What should the team prepare for most?

qs.q: A 3-kg newborn has HR 40 despite 60 seconds of compressions with effective ventilation. A UVC is in place. Per NRP, what is the IV epinephrine dose?

qs.q: A preterm infant has an order for caffeine 20 mg/kg load during transport. Why is clarification needed?

Caffeine citrate is twice as potent as the base

qs.q: A neonate in transport has glucose 28 mg/dL and is jittery. What is the best treatment per guideline?

qs.q: A 6-kg infant has SVT at 280 with adequate perfusion after vagal maneuvers fail. What is the PALS adenosine dose?

qs.q: A 15-kg child has HR 48 with poor perfusion despite effective oxygenation and ventilation. No vagal cause or AV block is suspected. What is the first drug per PALS?

Adenosine 0.1 mg/kg IV

qs.q: Two hours into DKA treatment, a 9-year-old develops headache, HR 58, BP 140/90 and a falling GCS. What is the best immediate treatment?

qs.q: An 80-kg patient has seized for 10 minutes, and no IV can be placed. What is the best first anticonvulsant?

qs.x: In RAMPART, IM midazolam 10 mg (for patients over 40 kg) worked at least as well as IV lorazepam. IM lorazepam and IM diazepam are absorbed slowly and unpredictably.

Diazepam 10 mg IM
Fosphenytoin IM load

qs.q: A 70-kg patient remains in status after two lorazepam doses. Per its label, how should Cerebyx be given?
qs.a: 1400 mg PE at up to 150 mg PE/min with ECG and BP monitoring
qs.x: The status epilepticus dose is 20 mg PE/kg at up to 150 mg PE/min. Faster rates risk hypotension and arrhythmias, so cardiac monitoring is required. The 50 mg/min limit applies to phenytoin, not fosphenytoin.

700 mg PE as an IV push over 1 minute
2000 mg PE over 2 minutes, then repeat in 10 minutes

qs.q: A patient with cirrhosis on warfarin remains in status epilepticus after benzodiazepines. Which second-line agent fits best?

qs.x: In ESETT, levetiracetam, valproate and fosphenytoin were equally effective. Valproate is hepatotoxic, and phenytoin has many interactions including with warfarin. Levetiracetam is renally cleared with few interactions.

Phenytoin 20 mg/kg as the preferred second-line agent

qs.q: A patient in refractory status is intubated and given rocuronium for the flight. Movement stops. What is the key problem?

w: Rocuronium itself ends the seizure activity
Paralysis prevents the seizure brain injury
No movement means the status has resolved

qs.q: A TBI patient has a blown pupil, HR 52 and BP 104/60 after other trauma. Which osmotic agent is preferred?

qs.x: Both lower ICP, but mannitol causes an osmotic diuresis that can worsen hypotension in a bleeding patient. Steroids worsen TBI outcomes, and only brief hyperventilation, targeting about 30-35, is a bridge for herniation.

Neither; hyperventilate to EtCO2 20 for the whole flight
Dexamethasone 10 mg IV to reduce the cerebral edema

qs.q: A patient with spontaneous ICH has BP 210/110, and the target SBP is about 140. What is the correct Cardene titration per its label?

qs.q: A dialysis patient has K 7.8 and a sine-wave rhythm with a pulse. Only a peripheral IV is available. What is the best first drug?

Lorazepam alone; correct the sodium slowly over days

Labetalol for the tachycardia

qs.q: A patient with liver failure and anuric kidney failure needs a paralytic infusion for ARDS. Which agent is best?

Recent major burns
Mild hyperthermia

qs.q: At a cabin altitude of 8000 feet, what happens to an air-filled ETT cuff inflated at sea level?

It does not change in a pressurized cabin

Concentration over 3 mg/mL in standard PVC

qs.q: Sodium bicarbonate is pushed through the IV line already running norepinephrine. What are the two main problems?

qs.q: Anectine is stored in an unrefrigerated flight bag. What does the label say about storage?

qs.q: A smoke inhalation patient will get both hydroxocobalamin and blood products. How should they be given?

qs.q: An awake ventilated patient has HR 118 and BP 160/90 and is fighting the vent. The crew wants to paralyze without changing sedation. What should happen first?

qs.q: After chewing aspirin, a 60-year-old chest pain patient has an SpO2 of 98% on room air, is speaking in full sentences, and has clear lung sounds. Which oxygen decision is most appropriate?

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman with chest pressure and nausea reports black, tarry stools for the past two days. BP 118/74, HR 104. She has no drug allergies. Regarding aspirin, the EMT should:

qs.q: A 9-year-old was found with an open bottle of his grandmother's aspirin 2 hours ago. He now has ringing in his ears, vomiting, and rapid deep breathing. What is the best interpretation and action?

w: Give a second aspirin dose to finish the protocol
Give nitroglycerin to treat the ongoing chest pain
Note it as a heartburn reaction and recheck later

qs.q: A 72-year-old man with chest pain becomes confused and can no longer follow commands or swallow reliably before you give aspirin. What should you do about the aspirin?
qs.a: Withhold oral aspirin and manage his airway first
qs.x: Aspirin for ACS is chewed and swallowed, so it requires an alert patient who can protect the airway. A declining mental status makes airway management the priority and oral medication an aspiration risk.
w: Place the tablets in his cheek and let them dissolve
Have a family member help him chew the tablets slowly
Crush the tablets in water and pour them into his mouth

qs.q: A 61-year-old woman with chest pain says she took her usual 81 mg daily aspirin this morning. She has no allergies or bleeding. Following typical ACS protocols, you should:
qs.a: Give the ACS aspirin dose per protocol or medical direction
qs.x: A low daily maintenance dose does not replace the 162-324 mg chewed ACS dose, and most protocols still give it, with medical direction as needed. Withholding it removes a proven early treatment.
w: Withhold aspirin because she already took a dose today
Give one additional 81 mg tablet only, to avoid overdose
Delay aspirin until the hospital can check her platelet count and clotting

qs.q: A 70-year-old man has sudden right arm weakness, facial droop, and slurred speech that began 40 minutes ago. He has no chest pain. His wife asks you to give him aspirin. You should:
qs.a: Withhold aspirin and transport rapidly to a stroke center
qs.x: Prehospital aspirin is indicated for suspected ACS, not stroke; a stroke may be hemorrhagic, and slurred speech raises swallowing concerns. Rapid transport for imaging is the priority.
w: Give chewed aspirin because it helps prevent stroke
Give chewed aspirin only if his blood pressure stays above 160 systolic
Give aspirin with water since he cannot chew well

qs.q: You are assessing a 67-year-old with chest pain before giving aspirin. Which history finding is the most important reason to withhold it?
qs.a: Lip swelling the last time she took ibuprofen
qs.x: Hypersensitivity to aspirin or other NSAIDs is a contraindication, and a prior reaction to ibuprofen suggests NSAID sensitivity. A statin, a prior stent, or a recent meal are not contraindications.
w: She takes a daily statin for high cholesterol
She had a cardiac stent placed five years ago
She ate a full meal about one hour ago

qs.q: You gave aspirin to a 63-year-old with chest pain. During transport he becomes unresponsive, pulseless, and apneic. What is your next action?
qs.a: Begin CPR and apply the AED
qs.x: Cardiac arrest takes priority over every medication decision; immediate high-quality CPR and early defibrillation are what change survival. No oral or sublingual medication is given to a pulseless patient.
w: Give a second dose of aspirin rectally
Assist with his nitroglycerin spray
Give oral glucose in his cheek

qs.q: A 52-year-old man has chest pain that began while shoveling snow. He took acetaminophen at home for the pain. He has no allergies or bleeding history. Regarding aspirin, the best action is:
qs.a: Give chewed aspirin; acetaminophen is not an antiplatelet
qs.x: Acetaminophen has no antiplatelet effect, so it does not replace aspirin for suspected ACS. Waiting or reducing the dose delays a proven early treatment.
w: Withhold aspirin because he already took a pain reliever at home today
Give only half the aspirin dose to avoid an overdose
Wait to see whether the acetaminophen relieves the pain

qs.q: A 45-year-old with chest pain has a history of asthma but has taken aspirin many times without wheezing or rash. She is not wheezing now. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give aspirin per protocol and monitor for bronchospasm
qs.x: Asthma alone is not a contraindication; aspirin-induced asthma or NSAID hypersensitivity is. Because she has tolerated aspirin before, give it and watch for bronchospasm, a known serious side effect.
w: Withhold aspirin because all asthmatics react to it
Assist with her albuterol inhaler first, then give the aspirin afterward
Give the aspirin rectally to avoid any bronchospasm

qs.q: At a family gathering, a 62-year-old has crushing chest pain and a 14-year-old has fever, sore throat, and body aches. Both ask for aspirin. Which plan is correct?
qs.a: Aspirin for the adult per protocol, but not the teenager
qs.x: Aspirin is indicated for suspected ACS in the adult, but it is avoided in children and teens with viral illness because of Reye syndrome. Withholding it from the adult delays a key ACS treatment.
w: Aspirin for both patients, since each of them is unwell and in pain
Aspirin for the teenager only, who is at lower risk
Withhold aspirin from both until hospital arrival

qs.q: A 76-year-old man taking glipizide was found confused with a glucose of 44 mg/dL. After oral glucose he is alert with a glucose of 98 mg/dL and wants to stay home alone. What concern should guide your advice?
qs.a: His low glucose may return for hours, so transport is advised
qs.x: Sulfonylureas such as glipizide can cause prolonged, recurrent hypoglycemia, especially in older adults living alone. Oral glucose works quickly but briefly, so transport and observation are strongly advised.
w: Oral glucose lasts all day, so recurrence is very unlikely
Glipizide raises glucose, so the low reading was an error
His normal reading means he no longer needs any food

qs.q: You are about to give oral glucose to a confused diabetic woman (glucose 39 mg/dL) when she becomes unresponsive with gurgling respirations. What is your next action?
qs.a: Suction and manage the airway; do not give oral glucose
qs.x: Oral glucose requires a patient who can swallow and protect the airway. Once she is unresponsive with gurgling, airway management and ALS for IV dextrose take priority; oral gel risks aspiration.
w: Squeeze the full tube onto her tongue while she is still
Give the gel and tilt her head back to help it go down
Rub the gel on her gums and wait for her to swallow

qs.q: A 7-year-old with type 1 diabetes is pale, sweaty, and irritable after soccer practice but answers questions and swallows normally. Glucose is 52 mg/dL. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give oral glucose per protocol and recheck glucose
qs.x: A child who is awake and able to swallow can receive oral glucose for symptomatic hypoglycemia. Insulin would worsen the low glucose, and rest alone does not correct it.
w: Withhold sugar because children cannot take oral glucose
Give his scheduled insulin dose since he missed lunch
Have him lie down and rest until his color improves

qs.q: A 45-year-old found confused in a parked car smells of alcohol and has slurred speech. His friend says he is diabetic. What is the most important step before deciding on treatment?
qs.a: Check a blood glucose level
qs.x: Hypoglycemia can mimic intoxication, and the two often coexist. A glucose reading decides whether oral glucose is indicated; assuming intoxication can miss a treatable emergency.
w: Assume intoxication and transport quietly
Give oral glucose immediately without any test
Ask him to perform a field sobriety test

qs.q: A 28-year-old diabetic has vomiting, deep rapid breathing, fruity breath odor, and mild confusion. Glucose reads 480 mg/dL. What is the best action?
qs.a: Withhold oral glucose, give supportive care, and transport
qs.x: Hyperglycemia is a contraindication to glucose, and these findings suggest DKA, which needs hospital care. Oral glucose would raise an already high glucose, and vomiting increases aspiration risk.
w: Give oral glucose because the confusion suggests his sugar is actually low
Give oral glucose since it cannot harm any diabetic
Have him take his own insulin and then release him

qs.q: Fifteen minutes after oral glucose, a 60-year-old diabetic remains confused and her repeat glucose is still 46 mg/dL. She can still swallow. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Repeat oral glucose per protocol and request ALS
qs.x: Persistent hypoglycemia calls for a repeat dose per protocol while she can still swallow, plus ALS for IV dextrose. Insulin would worsen the hypoglycemia, and waiting prolongs brain glucose deprivation.
w: Stop treatment because oral glucose has failed
Give her own insulin to help glucose enter cells
Wait another 30 minutes before rechecking glucose

qs.q: A 68-year-old with diabetes has new left-sided weakness and slurred speech. Glucose is 41 mg/dL. He can swallow small sips. Which action comes first?
qs.a: Treat the low glucose per protocol, then reassess deficits
qs.x: Hypoglycemia can cause focal deficits that mimic stroke. Correct the low glucose, then reassess; if deficits persist, continue stroke-focused transport.
w: Skip glucose and go straight to a stroke center
Give aspirin for a possible stroke, then recheck glucose during transport
Withhold glucose since it may worsen a stroke

qs.q: An 81-year-old nursing home resident with dementia is more confused than usual, according to staff. Glucose is 54 mg/dL. She has a weak cough and chokes when drinking water. Which is the best decision?
qs.a: Avoid oral glucose and request ALS for IV dextrose
qs.x: Oral glucose requires the ability to swallow and protect the airway; a weak cough and choking on liquids indicate aspiration risk. ALS can give IV dextrose instead.
w: Give the full tube quickly before she tires out
Mix the gel into a large cup of juice for her
Wait until she becomes unresponsive, then give the oral glucose gel

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman who is 28 weeks pregnant and takes insulin for gestational diabetes is shaky, sweaty, and anxious but alert. Glucose is 50 mg/dL. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give oral glucose per protocol and recheck glucose
qs.x: Symptomatic hypoglycemia in an alert pregnant patient is treated with oral glucose, which also protects the fetus. Supine positioning late in pregnancy can cause hypotension, so the left side is preferred.
w: Withhold glucose because it can harm the fetus
Have her take her scheduled insulin dose to stop the shaking and sweating
Place her supine and give nothing by mouth

qs.q: Which patient is the best candidate for EMT-administered oral glucose?
qs.a: An alert, sweaty diabetic with a glucose of 50 mg/dL
qs.x: Oral glucose is for symptomatic hypoglycemia in a patient who can swallow and protect the airway. Unresponsiveness, hyperglycemia, and a normal glucose are all reasons not to give it.
w: An unresponsive diabetic with a glucose of 35 mg/dL
A confused diabetic with a glucose of 420 mg/dL
An alert nondiabetic with a glucose of 105 mg/dL

qs.q: A known diabetic is sweaty and confused but able to swallow, and your glucometer has failed. He took insulin and skipped lunch. Following typical protocols, the best action is:
qs.a: Give oral glucose per protocol, then reassess mental status
qs.x: Many protocols allow oral glucose for a diabetic with signs of hypoglycemia when glucose cannot be measured; it is low risk in a patient who can swallow, while delay risks brain injury. Insulin would worsen hypoglycemia.
w: Withhold glucose until a reading is available at the hospital
Give his insulin because the reading cannot be confirmed
Encourage him to sleep it off while you monitor him

qs.q: A 50-year-old with chronic alcohol use is confused and sweaty after days of not eating. Glucose is 46 mg/dL. He can follow commands and swallow. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give oral glucose per protocol and recheck
qs.x: Hypoglycemia is treated regardless of diabetic history; poor intake and alcohol use deplete glucose stores. Naloxone is not indicated without signs of opioid toxicity.
w: Withhold glucose because he is not diabetic
Treat as intoxication and let him sleep it off
Give naloxone first to wake him up fully

qs.q: A 60-year-old diabetic with a glucose of 38 mg/dL receives oral glucose. Ten minutes later she is alert with a glucose of 112 mg/dL, but she still has slurred speech and a new right facial droop. What does this suggest?
qs.a: A possible stroke needing rapid stroke-center transport
qs.x: Focal deficits that persist after glucose is corrected suggest a stroke, not hypoglycemia. More glucose is not indicated with a normal reading, and time to stroke care matters.
w: Expected recovery that will improve with more glucose
An allergic reaction to the oral glucose gel
Normal post-hypoglycemia confusion needing no action

qs.q: A 19-year-old type 1 diabetic collapsed during a marathon. She is awake, confused, and sweaty, and she can swallow. Glucose is 55 mg/dL; HR 118. What is the best initial treatment?
qs.a: Give oral glucose per protocol, then recheck glucose
qs.x: Exercise can drop glucose in insulin-dependent diabetics; she is symptomatic and able to swallow, so oral glucose is indicated. Insulin would worsen the hypoglycemia.
w: Give insulin to help her muscles use glucose
Give nothing by mouth at all until she reaches the emergency department
Give a caffeinated drink to raise her alertness

qs.q: An insulin-dependent diabetic who is awake but very confused will not open her mouth for oral glucose and keeps turning her head away. What is the best action?
qs.a: Do not force it; protect the airway and request ALS
qs.x: Oral glucose requires a cooperative patient who can swallow; forcing it risks aspiration and injury. ALS can give IV dextrose while you protect the airway.
w: Squeeze the gel through her clenched teeth
Hold her head still and pry her mouth open
Wait until she falls asleep, then give the gel

qs.q: A 35-year-old diabetic who took insulin is anxious, pale, and sweaty with a pulse of 112. She is alert, and her glucose is 61 mg/dL. Her friend says it is a panic attack. What is the best action?
qs.a: Treat the low glucose with oral glucose per protocol
qs.x: Sweating, pallor, anxiety, and tachycardia with a low glucose after insulin indicate symptomatic hypoglycemia. Treat it now rather than waiting for neurologic decline.
w: Coach slow breathing for a panic attack
Give her own insulin to lower her heart rate
Withhold any treatment until she becomes confused or drowsy

qs.q: A 19-year-old with a known peanut allergy ate a cookie 15 minutes ago. He has diffuse hives, abdominal cramping, and has vomited twice. Breathing is unlabored; BP 118/76. He has a prescribed auto-injector. What is the best action?
qs.a: Assist with his auto-injector because two systems are involved
qs.x: Skin plus GI involvement after a known allergen exposure meets anaphylaxis criteria even without airway or BP changes. Early epinephrine is safer than waiting for airway compromise or shock.
w: Withhold epinephrine because his airway, breathing, and BP are all normal
Give oral glucose to settle his stomach and observe
Wait to see whether his breathing worsens before acting

qs.q: A 10-year-old (35 kg) has anaphylaxis from a bee sting. His parent holds his own prescribed 0.3 mg auto-injector and a younger sibling's 0.15 mg device. Which is appropriate?
qs.a: The child's own 0.3 mg auto-injector
qs.x: The 0.3 mg auto-injector is for patients 30 kg or more, and it is prescribed to this child. The 0.15 mg device is for 15-30 kg and belongs to someone else.
w: The sibling's 0.15 mg auto-injector
Both devices given at the same time
Neither until a dose is calculated

qs.q: Three minutes after an auto-injector, a 45-year-old with anaphylaxis says her heart is pounding and her hands are shaking. HR 118, BP 128/80, and her wheezing has decreased. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Expected epinephrine effects with a good response
qs.x: Tachycardia, palpitations, and tremor are common epinephrine side effects, and improving wheezing with a normal BP shows it is working. Repeat dosing is based on persistent anaphylaxis, not on side effects.
w: An overdose requiring immediate medical direction
Worsening anaphylaxis needing a second injection
A sign she is allergic to epinephrine itself

qs.q: Twenty minutes after an auto-injector, a patient's hives and wheezing had resolved. During transport her voice becomes hoarse, wheezing returns, and BP falls to 88/56. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give a second auto-injector per protocol and request ALS
qs.x: Epinephrine wears off and anaphylaxis can recur; returning airway signs and hypotension call for a repeat dose per protocol and ALS. Albuterol alone does not treat airway swelling or shock.
w: Assume it is anxiety and coach her to breathe slowly into a paper bag
Give her albuterol inhaler only and keep monitoring
Hold further treatment since the first dose worked

qs.q: A patient in anaphylaxis is wearing heavy jeans and has stridor. Which approach to her auto-injector is best?
qs.a: Inject the anterolateral thigh, through clothing if needed
qs.x: Auto-injectors are designed for the anterolateral thigh and can be given through clothing to avoid delay. Removing clothing wastes time, and other sites are not the recommended location.
w: Remove the jeans fully, then inject the deltoid
Inject into the buttock to reach a larger muscle
Inject into the abdomen to avoid the clothing

qs.q: A 30-year-old asthmatic is wheezing after eating at a restaurant. Which additional finding most strongly suggests anaphylaxis rather than an asthma flare?
qs.a: New hives and lip swelling
qs.x: Hives and lip swelling with wheezing after a possible allergen exposure indicate anaphylaxis, which needs epinephrine. An inhaler history, a mild tachypnea, or a night cough do not distinguish the two.
w: A history of using an inhaler
A respiratory rate of 22
A dry cough at night

qs.q: A teenager in anaphylaxis with stridor and BP 80/50 has only an auto-injector that expired two months ago. ALS is 15 minutes away. What is the best action?
qs.a: Contact medical direction about using the expired device
qs.x: A recently expired auto-injector usually retains much of its potency, and in a life-threatening reaction with no alternative, medical direction may approve its use rather than a 15-minute delay. Antihistamines do not reverse airway swelling or shock.
w: Discard it and wait for ALS to arrive with a fresh dose of epinephrine
Give oral diphenhydramine and monitor her airway
Inject it into the deltoid to improve absorption

qs.q: A woman who is 32 weeks pregnant develops hives, wheezing, and BP 84/50 after a dose of an antibiotic. She has a prescribed auto-injector. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give epinephrine and position her on her left side
