qs.a: Give dextrose now; give thiamine as well without delaying glucose
qs.x: Hypoglycemia can cause brain injury within minutes and must be corrected right away. Thiamine is given too, but delaying dextrose for it is not justified.
w: Give thiamine and wait 30 minutes before giving any dextrose
Withhold dextrose because it will cause Wernicke encephalopathy
Give oral glucose only, since IV dextrose is unsafe in alcoholics

qs.q: A 49-year-old man with chronic alcohol use is ataxic and confused, with nystagmus. After dextrose his BG is 112, but the confusion, nystagmus and ataxia persist. What should you consider next?
qs.a: Thiamine 100 mg IV for possible Wernicke encephalopathy
qs.x: Confusion, ataxia and eye movement abnormalities in a malnourished drinker suggest Wernicke encephalopathy, which is treated with thiamine 100 mg IV. More dextrose is not needed with a normal glucose.
w: Another D50 dose since the confusion persists
Naloxone 2 mg IV for possible opioid co-ingestion
Haloperidol IM to manage the confusion

qs.q: A 1-year-old weighing 10 kg has had vomiting and diarrhea. She is lethargic and not feeding, with BG 34. You have IV access. What is the best treatment?
qs.a: D10 IV dosed at 5-10 mL/kg
qs.x: Infants and young children get dilute dextrose (D10) by weight to avoid vein injury and large osmotic loads. Oral glucose is unsafe in a lethargic child who cannot protect the airway.
w: D50 25 g IV push as for an adult
Oral glucose gel between her cheek and gum
Withhold dextrose and give a fluid bolus

qs.q: A 66-year-old man who takes glipizide was found confused with BG 36. After D50 he is alert with BG 104. He wants to stay home. What is the key concern?
qs.a: Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia often returns after dextrose
qs.x: Sulfonylureas act for many hours and can cause hypoglycemia to come back after a single dextrose dose. These patients need observation, so the crew should strongly encourage transport.
w: D50 will cause dangerous hyperglycemia within the hour
Glipizide will interact with the D50 to cause dangerously low potassium
His glucose will stay normal for the rest of the day

qs.q: A 71-year-old woman has new right-sided weakness and slurred speech that started 40 minutes ago. BP 168/94. Her glucometer reads 38 mg/dL. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Treat the hypoglycemia with dextrose and reassess her deficits
qs.x: Hypoglycemia can mimic a stroke, so it must be found and treated first; the deficits often resolve once glucose is restored. Aspirin and BP lowering are not field stroke treatments here.
w: Transport to a stroke center without treating the glucose
Lower her blood pressure first, then recheck the glucose in 15 minutes
Give aspirin for the stroke while the glucose is rechecked

qs.q: A 28-year-old man is naked, sweating, screaming and fighting police. Temp is 40.5 C (104.9 F), and he cannot be safely approached for IV access. What is the best medication strategy?
qs.a: Ketamine IM per protocol for rapid, safe sedation
qs.x: Hyperactive delirium with hyperthermia needs fast chemical sedation, and IM ketamine works quickly without IV access. Prone restraint without sedation risks sudden death, and IV or oral routes are not practical.
w: Haloperidol IV once an IV is started in the field
Keep him prone in restraints until he tires out
Midazolam PO mixed in a drink to calm him down

qs.q: Minutes after IM ketamine for agitation, a patient develops high-pitched stridor, chest retractions, and SpO2 dropping to 84%. What should you do?
qs.a: Jaw thrust and BVM with positive pressure for laryngospasm
qs.x: Laryngospasm is a serious ketamine complication, and positive pressure ventilation with a jaw thrust usually breaks it. Naloxone does not reverse ketamine, and the prone position makes airway management harder.
w: Give a second ketamine dose to deepen the sedation
Give naloxone to reverse the ketamine effects
Place him prone and apply a nonrebreather mask

qs.q: A 74-year-old man with Parkinson's disease is confused and agitated after a fall. He is pulling at his IV. Medical control asks what agent you plan to use. What is the key consideration?
qs.a: Avoid haloperidol; it can severely worsen his parkinsonism
qs.x: Parkinson's disease is a contraindication to haloperidol because blocking dopamine can sharply worsen rigidity and mobility. Look for causes of delirium and use other approaches or agents per protocol.
w: Give haloperidol IV because it acts faster in the elderly
Give double the usual haloperidol dose because of his tremor
Haloperidol is preferred since he has a movement disorder

qs.q: Twenty minutes after IM haloperidol for agitation, the monitor shows a QTc of 520 ms and short runs of polymorphic VT. The patient has a pulse. What is the best action?
qs.a: Withhold more haloperidol and give magnesium per protocol
qs.x: QT prolongation is a serious haloperidol effect and a reason to stop; polymorphic VT with a long QT (torsades) is treated with magnesium. Amiodarone further prolongs the QT.
w: Give a second haloperidol dose to prevent more agitation
Give amiodarone to suppress the polymorphic VT runs
Ignore the runs since they are self-terminating

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman is severely agitated after an argument. Her 12-lead shows a QTc of 480 ms. Droperidol is in your agitation protocol. What is best?
qs.a: Withhold droperidol and use a benzodiazepine per protocol
qs.x: A QTc over 450 ms in a female is a contraindication to droperidol, which carries a QT prolongation risk. A lower dose or another route does not remove that risk.
w: Give droperidol IM, since the IM route avoids QT effects
Give droperidol at half the usual dose with monitoring
Give droperidol and repeat the 12-lead at the hospital

qs.q: Twenty minutes after droperidol for vomiting, a 22-year-old woman is very restless, keeps standing up and says she feels like she has to keep moving. Vitals are stable. What is happening?
qs.a: Akathisia from the droperidol; stop it and treat per protocol
qs.x: Akathisia is a common droperidol side effect and a reason to stop further doses; it is often treated with diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine per protocol. Giving more droperidol would make it worse.
w: Worsening anxiety that needs a second, larger droperidol dose to control it
A normal sign that the nausea is resolving
An allergic reaction that needs IM epinephrine

qs.q: A 27-year-old woman who delivered 4 days ago has a severe headache and had a generalized seizure at home. BP is 164/108. She is now postictal. What is the best medication?
qs.a: Magnesium sulfate 4-6 g IV over 15-20 minutes
qs.x: Eclampsia can occur up to several weeks after delivery, and magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice to treat and prevent seizures. Blood pressure control alone does not prevent recurrent eclamptic seizures.
w: Labetalol alone, since the pregnancy is over
Dextrose, because seizures after delivery are hypoglycemic
Diphenhydramine for a postpartum migraine

qs.q: During a magnesium loading dose for eclampsia, a patient feels warm and flushed and is sweating. RR is 18, patellar reflexes are present and BP is 148/96. What is best?
qs.a: Continue the infusion and keep monitoring reflexes and breathing
qs.x: Flushing, warmth and sweating are common, expected effects of magnesium. Toxicity shows as loss of reflexes, RR under 12, hypotension or bradycardia, and none are present.
w: Stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate IV immediately as an antidote
Stop the infusion because she is having an allergic reaction
Speed up the infusion so the side effects pass sooner

qs.q: A woman has just delivered a full-term infant. The uterus remains large, with the fundus above the umbilicus, and you feel what may be another fetus. Bleeding is moderate. Your partner draws up oxytocin. What is best?
qs.a: Withhold oxytocin until a second twin is ruled out
qs.x: A possible second twin is a contraindication: oxytocin could clamp the uterus down on an undelivered infant. Give it only after all infants are delivered.
w: Give oxytocin 10 units IM to control the bleeding now
Give oxytocin IV fast to speed delivery of the placenta
Give oxytocin, then perform fundal massage firmly

qs.q: After oxytocin 10 units IM and fundal massage for postpartum bleeding, the uterus is firm at the umbilicus, but a steady stream of bright red blood continues. HR 112. What should you do next?
qs.a: Look for a perineal laceration and apply direct pressure
qs.x: Once the uterus is firm, ongoing bleeding suggests another source such as a laceration, which needs direct pressure. More oxytocin targets uterine tone, which is already good.
w: Give more oxytocin, since a firm uterus means it is not working
Vigorously massage the fundus for another 15 minutes
Have her sit upright to slow down the flow of blood

qs.q: A woman delivered 40 minutes ago. Despite oxytocin and fundal massage she is still bleeding heavily. HR 124, BP 86/50. Your protocol includes TXA. What is the correct administration?
qs.a: 1 g IV infused over 10 minutes
qs.x: For postpartum hemorrhage, TXA is given as 1 g IV over 10 minutes, and the dose can be repeated if bleeding continues after 30 minutes. A rapid push can cause hypotension.
w: 1 g IV as a rapid push over 30 seconds
2 g IM divided into both thighs
100 mg IV infused over 8 hours

qs.q: A trauma patient with controlled external bleeding is receiving TXA 1 g IV. Your partner pushed the first part of the dose over about 30 seconds, and BP falls from 104/68 to 82/50. While you reassess for ongoing hemorrhage, what should you do about the TXA?
qs.a: Slow the rest of the dose to run over about 10 minutes
qs.x: Hypotension is a known effect of giving TXA too rapidly, which is why it is infused over about 10 minutes, so the rate is slowed and the BP treated. A drop in BP is not a sign of allergy, and hemorrhage must still be ruled out in a trauma patient.
w: Push the rest quickly so the drug works sooner
Stop TXA and give IM epinephrine for an allergy
Stop TXA for good, since hypotension rules it out

qs.q: A 30-week pregnant woman in preterm labor received terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ by medical control order. Now her HR is 128, and she reports chest tightness. What is the best action?
qs.a: Withhold further terbutaline and obtain a 12-lead
qs.x: A maternal HR over 120 or chest pain is a reason to stop terbutaline. Repeating the dose increases the risk of dysrhythmia and cardiac ischemia.
w: Give the second dose since contractions persist
Give a fluid bolus and then repeat the dose
Give metoprolol to slow her heart rate

qs.q: A woman at 31 weeks has regular contractions. Medical control is discussing terbutaline when you see the infant's head crowning with each contraction. What should you do?
qs.a: Prepare for delivery; do not attempt tocolysis
qs.x: Delivery is imminent, so trying to stop labor is no longer appropriate and could delay care. The crew should prepare for a preterm delivery and neonatal resuscitation.
w: Give terbutaline SQ quickly to stop the delivery
Have her cross her legs while terbutaline is drawn up
Give terbutaline and transport in the left lateral position

qs.q: A 6-year-old weighing 22 kg ate a peanut cookie. He has hives, wheezing and vomiting, BP 70/40. Using 1 mg/mL epinephrine, what is the correct initial dose?
qs.a: 0.22 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh
qs.x: Children under 30 kg receive 0.01 mg/kg IM, so 22 kg gives 0.22 mg. The 1 mg/mL concentration is never given IV push, and antihistamines do not replace epinephrine in anaphylaxis.
w: 0.22 mg IV push of the 1 mg/mL solution
0.5 mg IM in the deltoid muscle
Diphenhydramine first, then epinephrine

qs.q: A 9-year-old in anaphylaxis received IM epinephrine 6 minutes ago. She is still wheezing with hives, and BP is 76/44. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Repeat IM epinephrine and give fluids per protocol
qs.x: IM epinephrine can be repeated every 5-10 minutes when anaphylaxis persists, along with fluids for hypotension. Antihistamines and steroids are slow adjuncts that do not reverse shock.
w: Wait 20 minutes for the first dose to fully work
Give diphenhydramine instead of more epinephrine
Give methylprednisolone and wait for it to work

qs.q: A 2-year-old has a barking cough, stridor at rest, suprasternal retractions and SpO2 93%. Symptoms began suddenly overnight after a mild cold. What is the best treatment?
qs.a: Nebulized racemic epinephrine and calm transport
qs.x: Croup with stridor at rest is treated with nebulized racemic epinephrine to reduce swelling in the upper airway. Albuterol treats lower airway bronchospasm, and agitating the child can worsen the obstruction.
w: Nebulized albuterol for the noisy breathing
Inspect the throat with a tongue blade first
Nebulized saline only, since croup resolves

qs.q: A 4-year-old is sitting upright and leaning forward, drooling, with high fever, a muffled voice and soft stridor. He looks toxic. Your partner wants to start a nebulizer and an IV. What is best?
qs.a: Keep him calm with the parent and transport quickly
qs.x: Drooling, toxic appearance and tripod positioning suggest epiglottitis, where agitation can cause complete obstruction. Avoid upsetting procedures, keep him in a position of comfort, and prepare for a difficult airway.
w: Start the IV first, then give racemic epinephrine
Lay him flat and give racemic epinephrine by mask
Look in his throat to confirm the diagnosis first

qs.q: A 3-year-old has a barking cough at night but no stridor at rest, normal work of breathing and SpO2 98%. What is the most appropriate medication?
qs.a: Dexamethasone PO per weight-based dosing
qs.x: Mild croup without stridor at rest benefits from a single dose of dexamethasone, which reduces airway swelling over hours. Racemic epinephrine is reserved for stridor at rest or respiratory distress.
w: Nebulized racemic epinephrine right away
Nebulized albuterol every 20 minutes
IM epinephrine in the lateral thigh

qs.q: A 46-year-old woman with vomiting and diarrhea remains hypotensive after 2 L of fluid. Her medication list shows long-term daily prednisone for lupus, and she missed doses while sick. What does this finding change?
qs.a: Consider adrenal crisis and give dexamethasone per protocol
qs.x: Long-term steroid use suppresses the adrenal glands, so illness with missed doses can cause adrenal crisis that does not respond to fluids. A corticosteroid such as dexamethasone (4 mg IV per protocol) is indicated.
w: It changes nothing, since steroids do not affect shock
Stop all fluids, since prednisone causes fluid retention
Give extra potassium for steroid-induced hypokalemia

qs.q: A 68-year-old man with Parkinson's disease is vomiting. His medications include carbidopa/levodopa and apomorphine injections. Which is the best decision about ondansetron?
qs.a: Withhold ondansetron because of the apomorphine
qs.x: Ondansetron with apomorphine can cause profound hypotension and loss of consciousness, so it is contraindicated. Changing the route does not remove the interaction.
w: Give ondansetron 4 mg IV as for any adult
Give ondansetron ODT, since the oral form is safe
Give ondansetron and a fluid bolus together

qs.q: A 5-year-old weighing 18 kg has had vomiting and diarrhea for a day. She is alert, mildly dehydrated, and has no IV. Your protocol allows ODT ondansetron. What is the correct dose?
qs.a: 4 mg ODT
qs.x: For children 15-30 kg, the ODT dose is 4 mg. The 2 mg dose is for 8-15 kg, and 8 mg is above the range for her weight.
w: 2 mg ODT
8 mg ODT
0.4 mg ODT

qs.q: An 18-month-old has been vomiting for 6 hours and is mildly dehydrated. A parent asks if you can give promethazine like the older sibling got. What is the best response?
qs.a: Promethazine is contraindicated under age 2 because it can stop breathing
qs.x: Promethazine is contraindicated in children under 2 years because of fatal respiratory depression. An age-appropriate antiemetic such as ondansetron per protocol is the alternative.
w: Promethazine is safe at half the adult dose in any toddler
Promethazine is fine in toddlers as long as it is given deep IM rather than IV
Promethazine can be given if the child weighs over 10 kg

qs.q: A 72-year-old woman with prior abdominal surgery has a distended abdomen, no bowel movement for 3 days, and is vomiting foul brown fluid. What is the best decision about metoclopramide?
qs.a: Withhold it because of suspected bowel obstruction
qs.x: GI obstruction is a contraindication to metoclopramide because it increases gut movement. The surgical history and feculent vomiting strongly suggest obstruction.
w: Give 10 mg IV to speed up stomach emptying
Give it IM so that it bypasses the gut
Give it only after a fluid bolus is complete

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman took a handful of her amitriptyline 45 minutes ago. On arrival she is drowsy, slurring words and her GCS is 11. She is not intubated. What is the best decision about activated charcoal?
qs.a: Withhold charcoal because she cannot protect her airway
qs.x: Altered mental status without a protected airway is a contraindication because of aspiration risk, which is especially high with a tricyclic that can cause sudden seizures and coma. A smaller dose does not solve the airway problem.
w: Give charcoal right away while she can still swallow
Give charcoal mixed with soda to improve its taste
Give half the charcoal dose to lower aspiration risk

qs.q: A 3-year-old drank from a bottle of lamp oil 20 minutes ago. He is coughing and mildly tachypneic but alert. The parent asks about the charcoal they read about online. What is best?
qs.a: Do not give charcoal; it does not help and raises aspiration risk
qs.x: Hydrocarbons are a contraindication to charcoal: it does not bind them well and vomiting increases aspiration risk. The cough already suggests aspiration, so watch his breathing closely.
w: Give charcoal 1 g/kg PO right away to bind the lamp oil before it is absorbed
Give charcoal after making the child vomit at home
Give charcoal through an NG tube to protect the lungs

qs.q: A 33-week pregnant woman has a severe headache and BP 172/114. She uses an albuterol inhaler for asthma and wheezed last week. Medical control asks about labetalol. What is your best response?
qs.a: Asthma is a contraindication; request an alternative agent
qs.x: Labetalol blocks beta-2 receptors and is contraindicated in asthma or reactive airway disease because it can cause bronchospasm. Another antihypertensive should be chosen per medical control.
w: Labetalol is safe in asthma when it is given slowly IV
Give labetalol with albuterol to prevent bronchospasm
Give labetalol IM instead of IV to avoid bronchospasm

qs.q: A preeclamptic patient received labetalol 20 mg IV for BP 170/112. Ten minutes later, BP is 146/94 and HR has fallen to 52. Your protocol calls for 40 mg next if BP is still above goal. What is best?
qs.a: Hold further labetalol because of the bradycardia
qs.x: An HR under 60 is a stop criterion for labetalol, and 146/94 is already out of the severe range that requires urgent treatment. Further beta blockade could cause symptomatic bradycardia or heart block.
w: Give the 40 mg dose since BP is still above 140
Give atropine and then the 40 mg dose of labetalol
Give 80 mg now to reach the BP goal faster

qs.q: A 7-year-old weighing 20 kg ate shrimp and has itchy hives on the trunk. Lungs are clear, no swelling of the lips or tongue, no vomiting, BP 104/66, HR 108. What is the best treatment?
qs.a: Diphenhydramine and close monitoring for any progression
qs.x: Isolated hives without airway, breathing, GI or circulation involvement is a mild allergic reaction that is treated with an antihistamine, with monitoring for progression to anaphylaxis. IV epinephrine is reserved for refractory shock.
w: Epinephrine IV push of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration to stop the reaction
Nebulized albuterol to prevent future wheezing
No treatment and release to the parent at home

qs.q: An 18-month-old weighing 11 kg had a 2-minute generalized seizure with fever. On arrival she is crying and moving all limbs, with normal breathing, SpO2 98% and temp 39.4 C (102.9 F). What is the best approach?
qs.a: Withhold benzodiazepines; treat fever for comfort and transport
qs.x: A short febrile seizure that has stopped does not need a benzodiazepine; acetaminophen is given for comfort but does not prevent recurrence. Aspirin is avoided in children because of Reye syndrome.
w: Give IN midazolam now to prevent another seizure
Give acetaminophen now, since it reliably prevents the seizure from recurring
Give aspirin for the fever and then release her at home

qs.q: A 58-year-old with urosepsis has MAP 56, HR 118 and lactate 4.8 after an initial crystalloid bolus. Her lungs now have faint crackles. Only an 18 g antecubital IV is available, and a central line will take 45 minutes. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Start peripheral norepinephrine and titrate to MAP 65 or greater
qs.x: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock and can be started through a secure proximal peripheral IV with close site checks. Waiting 45 minutes for a central line prolongs hypoperfusion, and more fluid is risky once crackles appear.
w: Hold all vasopressors until the central line has been placed
Start a phenylephrine infusion as the first-line agent
Keep giving crystalloid boluses until the MAP is above 65

qs.q: You pick up a 31-year-old with an open-book pelvic fracture. BP is 74/40 and HR 138. The referring facility started norepinephrine but has not given any blood. What should change first?
qs.a: Give blood and bind the pelvis before relying on the pressor
qs.x: Hypovolemic hypotension is a contraindication to norepinephrine unless used briefly while volume is restored. This patient needs hemorrhage control and blood; raising the pressor dose squeezes an empty tank.
w: Double the norepinephrine rate to reach a MAP of 65 or greater
Add vasopressin so norepinephrine can be weaned
Give push-dose phenylephrine and keep the current plan

qs.q: Twenty minutes into transport, the MAP of a patient on norepinephrine falls from 70 to 46 over 2 minutes. The patient just had a line change at the referring bedside. HR and rhythm are unchanged. What is the best first action?
qs.a: Trace the line and pump to confirm the drip is infusing
qs.x: A sudden MAP drop right after a line change with no other change points to an interrupted or disconnected pressor. Restoring flow fixes the cause; adding drugs before checking the line treats the wrong problem.
w: Give a 1-liter fluid bolus over 10 minutes
Add vasopressin at the septic shock dose
Push 1 mg of epinephrine IV for a presumed pulseless arrest

qs.q: A 64-year-old has ROSC after VF arrest. He is intubated and unresponsive with BP 78/48 (MAP 58) and HR 96. What is the best hemodynamic plan?
qs.a: Start a norepinephrine infusion and titrate to MAP 65 or greater
qs.x: Post-arrest hypotension worsens brain injury; a titrated vasopressor infusion to MAP 65 or greater is standard. Arrest-dose epinephrine pushes are for pulseless patients and cause wild swings, and permissive hypotension applies to bleeding trauma, not post-arrest care.
w: Give 1 mg epinephrine IV push every 3-5 minutes
Allow permissive hypotension to limit any reperfusion injury
Give atropine and recheck BP in 5 minutes

qs.q: A septic patient remains at MAP 58 on high-dose norepinephrine plus vasopressin. Bedside echo shows a poorly contracting left ventricle, and her extremities are cold. Which addition best fits?
qs.a: Add an epinephrine infusion titrated to MAP
qs.x: She needs both more pressure and more contractility, which epinephrine provides (labeled for septic shock). Dobutamine adds inotropy but often lowers BP further when the MAP is already below goal.
w: Add dobutamine and titrate to cardiac output
Add phenylephrine for more alpha tone
Start a nitroglycerin infusion to lower afterload

qs.q: A patient on an epinephrine infusion for septic shock develops frequent multifocal PVCs during transport. MAP is 72. A point-of-care potassium is 2.9 mEq/L. What is the most likely contributor?
qs.a: Epinephrine-driven shift of potassium into cells
qs.x: Hypokalemia and dysrhythmias are listed serious effects of epinephrine through beta-2 driven cellular potassium uptake. Replace potassium per protocol and reassess whether the dose can come down.
w: Hyperkalemia from a hemolyzed sample drawn from the line
Vasopressin-induced hyponatremia
Expected sinus tachycardia from sepsis alone

qs.q: Two minutes after intubation with propofol, a 70-year-old's BP falls from 104/62 to 68/40. HR is 108 and the tube position is confirmed. What is the best immediate treatment while an infusion is being prepared?
qs.a: Push-dose epinephrine 10-20 mcg IV, repeated per protocol
qs.x: Post-induction hypotension needs prompt vasoactive support; push-dose epinephrine per protocol bridges until an infusion runs. More propofol worsens the vasodilation that caused the drop.
w: Furosemide IV to reduce the after-intubation fluid shift
A second propofol dose to deepen the anesthetic plane
Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes for the hypotension

qs.q: A 4-year-old with septic shock has had repeated fluid boluses. He is still lethargic with HR 168, cool mottled legs, capillary refill 5 seconds and a narrow pulse pressure. Which vasoactive agent fits this cold-shock picture best?
qs.a: An epinephrine infusion
qs.x: Fluid-refractory cold shock in children reflects low cardiac output with high resistance, and epinephrine adds inotropy plus pressure. A pure vasoconstrictor such as phenylephrine or vasopressin raises afterload on a struggling heart.
w: A phenylephrine infusion
A vasopressin infusion alone
A nitroprusside infusion

qs.q: A septic patient is on norepinephrine and vasopressin. After source control and fluids, MAP is now 88 and rising. Which drip should be weaned first?
qs.a: Norepinephrine
qs.x: When MAP is well above goal, catecholamines are tapered first, and vasopressin is usually weaned last. Stopping both at once risks rebound hypotension.
w: Vasopressin
Both stopped at once
Neither until arrival

qs.q: During a 3-hour transfer, a patient on norepinephrine and vasopressin develops several new findings. Which one is most concerning?
qs.a: New severe abdominal pain with a rising lactate
qs.x: Mesenteric ischemia is a serious effect of vasopressin (and catecholamines), and pain with a climbing lactate is an early warning. A mild sodium change or slightly slower HR does not change the plan right now.
w: A drop in HR from 104 to 92
Sodium falling from 139 to 136 mEq/L
Mild headache with a stable MAP of 70 and good urine output

qs.q: Four patients need vasoactive support during interfacility transfer. In which patient is vasopressin LEAST suited as the only vasoactive agent?
qs.a: Cardiogenic shock with a low ejection fraction
qs.x: Vasopressin is a pure vasoconstrictor that can decrease cardiac output; without inotropy it can lower output in a failing heart and worsen cardiogenic shock. In vasodilatory states, which are labeled indications, it restores tone without that drawback.
w: Septic shock already on norepinephrine
Post-cardiotomy vasoplegia with good LV function
Vasodilatory shock with warm, flushed skin

qs.q: A 77-year-old with known severe aortic stenosis is intubated. Afterward, BP is 78/44 and HR 92 in sinus rhythm. Which drug best fits her physiology right now?
qs.a: Phenylephrine
qs.x: With fixed outflow obstruction, she needs diastolic pressure for coronary flow and a slower HR for filling, and pure alpha agonism with reflex slowing does both. Inotropes and chronotropes shorten filling time, and vasodilators can cause collapse.
w: Nitroglycerin
Dobutamine
Ketamine

qs.q: A patient with an EF of 15% gets several phenylephrine boluses for post-intubation hypotension. BP rises to 112/70, but HR falls to 48, SpO2 drops and new crackles appear. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Afterload rose and cardiac output fell; change to an inotropic pressor
qs.x: Phenylephrine can lower cardiac output (a listed serious effect) and causes reflex bradycardia. In a weak heart the BP looks better while forward flow and oxygenation worsen, so an agent with inotropy fits better.
w: Phenylephrine worked well; continue boluses as needed
This is aspiration from the intubation and is unrelated to the drug
The patient needs more phenylephrine to keep up with the HR

qs.q: A septic patient was started on dopamine at the referring hospital. During packaging she develops atrial fibrillation at 164 with frequent PVCs. MAP is 64. What is the best change?
qs.a: Switch from dopamine to norepinephrine
qs.x: Tachydysrhythmias are a stop criterion for dopamine, which causes more arrhythmias than norepinephrine, the first-line agent in septic shock. Beta-blocking a septic patient on a failing pressor risks collapse.
w: Increase dopamine to improve the MAP
Add an esmolol infusion for rate control
Give adenosine to break the arrhythmia

qs.q: A 72-year-old has symptomatic bradycardia at 36 with BP 76/40 and confusion. Atropine has failed, and transcutaneous pacing gives only intermittent capture despite pad and output changes. What is the best next drug per ACLS?
qs.a: A dopamine infusion titrated to HR and BP
qs.x: ACLS lists dopamine (or epinephrine) infusion when atropine fails and pacing is not effective. More atropine past the max adds little, and amiodarone or diltiazem would slow conduction further.
w: Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes
Another 3 mg of atropine as a single bolus
Diltiazem to stabilize the conduction system

qs.q: Three days after an MI, a 67-year-old has BP 98/64, HR 102, cool clammy skin, falling urine output and bibasilar crackles. MAP is 75. Which agent best addresses the main problem?
qs.a: Dobutamine
qs.x: This is low-output cardiogenic shock with acceptable BP, so contractility is the target. Pure vasoconstrictors raise afterload on a failing ventricle, and nitroprusside with a borderline BP risks hypotension.
w: Phenylephrine
Vasopressin
Nitroprusside

qs.q: Dobutamine is started for cardiogenic shock with an initial BP of 92/60. Ten minutes later, BP is 76/42 and HR 128. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Add norepinephrine and reassess the dobutamine dose
qs.x: Dobutamine can cause hypotension through beta-2 vasodilation, a stop criterion, so its dose is reassessed while a vasopressor such as norepinephrine restores MAP. Raising dobutamine worsens both the tachycardia and the vasodilation.
w: Increase dobutamine to raise cardiac output
Give a fast 2-liter crystalloid bolus
Stop all vasoactive drugs and observe the BP response for 10 minutes

qs.q: A septic patient has reached MAP 68 on norepinephrine after adequate fluids. Lactate keeps rising, the skin stays mottled, and echo shows a severely depressed LV. Which addition best fits?
qs.a: Add dobutamine to improve cardiac output
qs.x: With the MAP at goal but low output, an inotrope addresses the real deficit. Pushing the MAP higher or adding pure vasoconstriction does not fix a weak pump.
w: Raise norepinephrine until the MAP reaches about 85
Add vasopressin for more vascular tone
Give another large fluid bolus

qs.q: A 59-year-old with ischemic cardiomyopathy on high-dose home carvedilol is in low-output cardiogenic shock with BP 94/58. Dobutamine has had little effect. Which agent is most likely to work?
qs.a: Milrinone
qs.x: Milrinone raises contractility through PDE-3 inhibition, which bypasses beta receptors blocked by carvedilol. Increasing a beta agonist against a full blockade adds little inotropy.
w: Isoproterenol
Higher-dose dobutamine
Phenylephrine

qs.q: During an interfacility transfer, a patient on milrinone becomes hypotensive at 80/44 with new runs of ventricular ectopy. What is the best response?
qs.a: Reduce or stop milrinone per orders and support MAP with a pressor
qs.x: Hypotension and ventricular dysrhythmias are stop criteria for milrinone. A vasopressor supports MAP while the effect fades; a repeat load or a higher rate makes both problems worse.
w: Increase milrinone to improve cardiac output
Give the loading dose again so the drug reaches steady state faster
Continue unchanged since ectopy is expected

qs.q: A 66-year-old with pneumonia and septic shock needs RSI. BP is 86/52 and HR 124 (shock index about 1.4) on low-dose norepinephrine. Ketamine is chosen. What is the best dosing approach?
qs.a: Reduce the induction dose and give a full paralytic dose
qs.x: In shock, a lower induction dose limits hemodynamic collapse, while a full (or higher) paralytic dose ensures good conditions because slow circulation delays onset. Cutting the paralytic invites a failed first pass.
w: Give the full induction dose and reduce the paralytic
Give a full induction dose and skip the paralytic to avoid apnea
Reduce both drugs to half their usual dose

qs.q: A 52-year-old with a type A aortic dissection is in severe distress, hypoxic and needs intubation. BP is 192/110 and HR 112 despite an esmolol infusion. Which induction agent is LEAST appropriate?
qs.a: Ketamine
qs.x: Ketamine's sympathetic surge raises BP and HR, and severe hypertension is a stop criterion, which can extend a dissection. Agents that blunt or do not raise sympathetic tone fit better here.
w: Etomidate
Propofol at a reduced dose
Midazolam with fentanyl

qs.q: An intubated trauma patient on norepinephrine has BP 92/56 and needs sedation for a 90-minute flight. He was induced with ketamine and paralyzed with rocuronium. Which sedation plan best fits his hemodynamics?
qs.a: A ketamine infusion with fentanyl as needed
qs.x: Ketamine (per protocol infusion range) keeps sympathetic tone, so it suits a pressor-dependent patient. Propofol and large benzodiazepine boluses deepen hypotension, and a paralyzed patient always needs sedation and analgesia.
w: A propofol infusion at standard dose
Repeated large midazolam boluses
No sedation is needed because he is already paralyzed

qs.q: A septic patient has been on a propofol infusion at the referring facility. While on the transport ventilator, BP drifts from 104/60 to 82/48 and HR is 112. Sedation is deep (RASS -5). What is the best adjustment?
qs.a: Lower the propofol and shift to analgesia-first sedation
qs.x: Hypotension and oversedation are stop criteria for propofol. Lowering it and using an analgesia-first approach (with pressor support as needed) protects BP; large benzodiazepine boluses also drop BP.
w: Increase the propofol rate to blunt any sympathetic surges
Give furosemide to treat third-spacing
Switch to midazolam boluses at a high dose

qs.q: Propofol is the only induction agent available for a 74-year-old with GI bleeding who needs intubation. BP is 88/56 after 2 units of blood. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Give a reduced dose of 0.5-1 mg/kg with a pressor ready
qs.x: Propofol's labeled induction dose for unstable patients is 0.5-1 mg/kg, with vasopressor support at hand. A full dose risks arrest, and paralysis without sedation risks awareness.
w: Give the full 2.5 mg/kg dose for a smooth intubation
Avoid any induction agent and use paralytic only
Give propofol as a fast push followed by a fluid bolus

qs.q: A 41-year-old with hypertriglyceridemia-induced acute pancreatitis is intubated for respiratory failure before transfer. Which sedation agent should be avoided for the infusion?
qs.a: Propofol
qs.x: Propofol is a lipid emulsion that can raise triglycerides and cause pancreatitis (listed serious effects), so it is a poor choice in triglyceride-driven pancreatitis. The other agents lack that lipid load.
w: Fentanyl
Ketamine
Dexmedetomidine

qs.q: A 69-year-old in cardiogenic shock (BP 82/50, HR 108, crackles) needs RSI. Which induction choice best preserves hemodynamics?
qs.a: Etomidate at the standard weight-based dose
qs.x: Etomidate has little effect on contractility or vascular tone, which suits a patient with a failing heart. Propofol, induction-dose midazolam and fentanyl pretreatment all lower BP in a patient with no reserve.
w: Propofol at the full induction dose
Midazolam at an induction dose
Propofol with a full-dose fentanyl pretreatment for blunting

qs.q: Seconds after etomidate is pushed and before rocuronium takes effect, the patient has jerking movements of the arms. SpO2 is 96%. What is the most likely explanation and response?
qs.a: Myoclonus from etomidate; proceed with the intubation
qs.x: Myoclonus is a common effect of etomidate and resolves with paralysis. Treating it as a seizure delays the airway, and malignant hyperthermia is linked to succinylcholine and volatile agents, not etomidate.
w: A seizure; give lorazepam and delay intubation
Malignant hyperthermia from etomidate; give dantrolene now
Allergic reaction; give epinephrine IM

qs.q: A 100-kg patient in cardiogenic shock with a low cardiac output needs RSI. Which rocuronium dose best ensures fast intubating conditions?
qs.a: 1.2 mg/kg IV
qs.x: Low output slows drug delivery to muscles, so the upper RSI dose (1.2 mg/kg) gives faster onset. The lower doses are labeled for intubation but onset is slower, which matters most in a patient with little reserve.
w: 0.45 mg/kg IV
0.6 mg/kg IV
0.1 mg/kg IV

qs.q: A 63-year-old dialysis patient with sepsis missed two sessions. He needs RSI for hypoxic respiratory failure. K is 6.6 mEq/L with peaked T waves. Which paralytic plan is best?
qs.a: Avoid succinylcholine and use rocuronium
qs.x: Known hyperkalemia is a contraindication to succinylcholine, which raises potassium further and can cause arrest. Rocuronium avoids that risk; calcium or a lower dose does not make succinylcholine safe here.
w: Use succinylcholine at a reduced dose
Use succinylcholine after calcium pretreatment
Use succinylcholine with atropine first

qs.q: A 48-year-old has been bedbound in an ICU for 3 weeks after a stroke and now needs reintubation before transfer. Which paralytic consideration matters most?
qs.a: Prolonged immobilization and stroke make succinylcholine unsafe
qs.x: Stroke and immobilization over 48-72 hours upregulate receptors and can cause a severe potassium surge with succinylcholine, even with a normal baseline K. A nondepolarizing agent such as rocuronium avoids that.
w: Succinylcholine is preferred for its short duration here
Rocuronium is unsafe after prolonged ICU stays
Either agent is fine as long as the K is normal on arrival

qs.q: After intubation for ARDS, a 45-year-old is fighting the vent with HR 124 and BP 156/92. He is on a midazolam infusion only. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Add analgesia with fentanyl, then reassess sedation
qs.x: An endotracheal tube is painful, and analgesia-first sedation treats the cause of the distress. Paralyzing him or raising only the benzodiazepine leaves pain untreated, and labetalol hides the signs.
w: Add vecuronium to stop ventilator dyssynchrony
Increase midazolam until he stops moving
Give labetalol to control the HR and BP before anything else

qs.q: A 71-year-old with septic shock has BP 84/50 and HR 126 before RSI. Your protocol lists fentanyl pretreatment as an option. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Omit fentanyl pretreatment in this hypotensive patient
qs.x: Fentanyl pretreatment blunts sympathetic tone, which this shock patient depends on; hypotension is a stop criterion. It suits hypertensive patients such as TBI or dissection, not septic shock.
w: Give fentanyl pretreatment at the full dose
Give fentanyl pretreatment by rapid IV push
Give fentanyl and skip the induction agent to protect the BP

qs.q: An intubated patient in cardiogenic shock on norepinephrine becomes agitated during the flight. BP is 88/54. Which sedation choice is most likely to worsen his hemodynamics?
qs.a: Repeated large midazolam boluses
qs.x: Shock is a relative contraindication to midazolam, and large boluses cause hypotension in a patient without reserve. Small, titrated analgesic doses or ketamine better protect BP.
w: Small fentanyl doses titrated to effect
A low-dose ketamine infusion
Checking tube position and analgesia first

qs.q: A post-arrest patient on norepinephrine (MAP 72) has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure on the transport ventilator. He has not received a paralytic since intubation. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give midazolam IV titrated while watching BP
qs.x: Post-arrest seizures worsen brain injury and need treatment; a benzodiazepine is first-line, with close BP monitoring because of hypotension risk. A paralytic stops movement but not seizure activity in the brain.
w: Give rocuronium to stop the motor activity
Withhold treatment since post-arrest seizures are expected
Give phenylephrine to protect cerebral pressure

qs.q: A post-arrest patient on a dexmedetomidine infusion during transfer develops HR 42 in sinus rhythm with BP 82/50. What is the best first action?
qs.a: Stop the dexmedetomidine infusion
qs.x: Bradycardia under 50 with hypotension is a stop criterion for dexmedetomidine. Raising the rate or giving a load (which can cause sinus arrest or hypertension then hypotension) worsens the problem.
w: Increase the dexmedetomidine rate
Give a dexmedetomidine loading dose
Add a propofol infusion for deeper sedation

qs.q: A patient with ARDS is on a rocuronium infusion for a long flight. The only sedation running is dexmedetomidine at a low rate. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Sedation may be too light, risking awareness under paralysis
qs.x: Dexmedetomidine gives light, rousable sedation and does not reliably provide the deep sedation a paralyzed patient needs. Awareness under paralysis is a listed serious risk of rocuronium, so deep sedation and analgesia must be in place.
w: Dexmedetomidine reverses the rocuronium blockade
Dexmedetomidine causes malignant hyperthermia with rocuronium
There is no concern because dexmedetomidine is a complete anesthetic

qs.q: After ROSC from VF, a 70-year-old is in complete heart block with a ventricular rate of 38, BP 78/40 and occasional PVCs. The referring team asks about an amiodarone infusion. What is the best response?
qs.a: Withhold amiodarone and treat the bradycardia with pacing
qs.x: Third-degree AV block without a pacemaker is a contraindication to amiodarone, which could suppress the escape rhythm. The priority is rate support with pacing or a chronotrope.
w: Start amiodarone to suppress the PVCs
Give amiodarone 150 mg as a slow bolus only
Give amiodarone together with atropine to offset any slowing

qs.q: A patient on an amiodarone infusion for recurrent VT has BP 82/50 and sinus rhythm at 50 during transport. Before the infusion, BP was 118/70 and HR 82. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Stop the amiodarone and notify medical control
qs.x: Hypotension and bradycardia are stop criteria for amiodarone. Continuing or re-bolusing makes both worse; stop the drip and discuss next steps.
w: Speed up the infusion to finish the dose
Give another 150 mg amiodarone bolus
Continue unchanged since the VT is now suppressed

qs.q: An 82-year-old with heart failure has been on a lidocaine infusion for 12 hours after VT. During transfer he reports perioral numbness and ringing in the ears, then becomes confused with muscle twitching. What is the best action?
qs.a: Stop the lidocaine and prepare to treat seizures
qs.x: These are lidocaine toxicity signs, and heart failure plus older age reduce clearance. Stopping the drug and being ready for seizures is correct; more lidocaine would worsen CNS toxicity.
w: Give a lidocaine bolus to treat the twitching
Continue the infusion and recheck in an hour
Switch to a higher lidocaine infusion rate

qs.q: An intubated septic patient has pH 7.08, PaCO2 64 and HCO3 18. The ventilator is set to a low minute ventilation from the referring hospital. The referring physician suggests sodium bicarbonate. What should happen first?
qs.a: Increase minute ventilation to clear CO2
qs.x: Inadequate ventilation is a contraindication to bicarbonate, which makes CO2 that must be exhaled. The acidosis here is largely respiratory, so fixing ventilation comes first.
w: Give bicarbonate now and leave the vent alone
Give bicarbonate and lower the respiratory rate
Give calcium before the bicarbonate

qs.q: A patient with acute pulmonary edema is on a nitroglycerin infusion. During transport, BP falls from 168/96 to 86/50, HR rises to 118, the skin becomes cool and mottled, and crackles persist. What is the best change?
qs.a: Stop the nitroglycerin and start inotropic or pressor support
qs.x: An SBP under 90 is a stop criterion for nitroglycerin. With poor perfusion and crackles, this has turned into cardiogenic shock and needs support of BP and output, not more preload reduction.
w: Keep the nitroglycerin and give furosemide
Increase the nitroglycerin to reduce preload and congestion further
Switch to sublingual nitroglycerin tablets

qs.q: A septic patient has received several liters of fluid. MAP is 58 on low-dose norepinephrine, SpO2 is 90% and new crackles are present. The referring team suggests furosemide. What is the best response?
qs.a: Hold furosemide and titrate the vasopressor up
qs.x: Furosemide is held in hypotension because diuresis worsens perfusion. Raising the pressor supports MAP without more fluid; any diuresis can wait until the shock improves.
w: Give furosemide now to treat the crackles
Give furosemide and another fluid bolus together
Give furosemide and stop the norepinephrine

qs.q: A septic patient has sinus tachycardia at 138 with MAP 62 on norepinephrine and a lactate of 5. A crewmember suggests esmolol to slow the HR. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Withhold esmolol; the tachycardia is compensatory
qs.x: Sinus tachycardia in shock maintains cardiac output, and esmolol causes hypotension, a stop criterion. Treat the shock, not the heart rate.
w: Start esmolol to reduce myocardial oxygen use
Give esmolol as a bolus only with no infusion
Start esmolol and add phenylephrine to cover any BP drop

qs.q: A 76-year-old with a spontaneous ICH has SBP 186. The transfer orders call for a nicardipine infusion. Her chart shows advanced aortic stenosis. What is the best action?
qs.a: Clarify the order since advanced AS is a contraindication
qs.x: Advanced aortic stenosis is a listed contraindication to nicardipine because fixed outflow cannot compensate for the drop in afterload. Clarify and pick an agent that fits her physiology.
w: Start nicardipine at the maximum rate
Start nicardipine with a fluid bolus
Give nicardipine and add phenylephrine if the BP drops too low

qs.q: A 66-year-old with NSTEMI is on a heparin infusion during transfer. Mid-flight he reports a sudden severe headache and then develops left arm weakness. What is the best first action?
qs.a: Stop the heparin and notify the receiving team
qs.x: A new neuro change on heparin suggests intracranial bleeding, which is a stop criterion. More anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy could be fatal.
w: Bolus heparin to treat a possible new clot
Lower heparin by half and keep watching
Give aspirin for a possible embolic stroke and continue heparin

qs.q: A teenager in DKA is on an insulin infusion during transfer. A repeat potassium mid-flight is 3.1 mEq/L, and the patient has new PVCs. What is the best action?
qs.a: Hold insulin and replace potassium per protocol
qs.x: Potassium under 3.3 is a stop criterion for insulin, which drives potassium into cells and can cause dysrhythmias. Replace potassium first, then resume insulin.
w: Keep insulin running and recheck in 2 hours
Double the insulin to close the gap faster
Give sodium bicarbonate to raise potassium

qs.q: A post-arrest patient with GCS 3 starts bucking the ventilator with HR 132 and BP 172/96. The crew gives vecuronium only, saying he is comatose and needs no sedation. What is the main problem?
qs.a: He may be aware under paralysis without sedation
qs.x: A rising HR and BP while bucking suggest arousal, and paralysis hides both comfort and seizure signs. Awareness under paralysis is a listed serious risk, so sedation and analgesia must be given.
w: Vecuronium is unsafe in post-arrest patients
Vecuronium will raise his potassium sharply
Bucking proves he has no meaningful brain function left

qs.q: A dialysis patient has ROSC after a brief arrest. During transfer, the QRS widens to 160 ms with peaked T waves. K is 7.4 mEq/L, and a central line is in place. What is the best first drug?
qs.a: Calcium chloride slowly via the central line
qs.x: Calcium stabilizes the heart in hyperkalemia within minutes, and a central line suits calcium chloride, which can cause necrosis if it leaks. Antiarrhythmics do not address the cause.
w: Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes
Lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg IV push
Sodium bicarbonate alone with no calcium given first

qs.q: A 4-year-old with septic shock gets a second dose of succinylcholine after a failed first attempt. HR drops from 140 to 66 with delayed capillary refill. SpO2 is 97% with good BVM ventilation. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Give atropine IV per PALS dosing
qs.x: A repeat succinylcholine dose in a child commonly causes vagal bradycardia, and with oxygenation and ventilation confirmed, atropine treats it. Compressions are indicated only if HR falls below 60 with poor perfusion despite effective ventilation.
w: Give amiodarone for the slow rhythm
Give more succinylcholine to finish the attempt
Start chest compressions right away

qs.q: A 32-year-old ejected from a vehicle 50 minutes ago has HR 128, BP 84/52 and a positive FAST. The ground crew gave TXA 1 g IV over 10 minutes just before handoff. What should the flight crew do with TXA now?
qs.a: Start the second 1 g as an infusion over 8 hours
qs.x: Per CRASH-2 based protocols the 1 g load over 10 minutes is followed by 1 g over 8 hours. TXA is antifibrinolytic, not a pressor, so persistent hypotension is not a reason to stop it or to push another rapid bolus (rapid push causes hypotension).
w: Push a second 1 g bolus now because he is still hypotensive
Stop TXA because the BP did not improve after the bolus
Hold further TXA until a fibrinogen level is available

qs.q: A 54-year-old with a sudden worst-ever headache has GCS 13 and BP 168/94. CT at the sending hospital shows a nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage. A resident asks the crew to start TXA in flight to prevent rebleeding. What is the best response?
qs.a: Withhold TXA; SAH is a contraindication
qs.x: Subarachnoid hemorrhage is a contraindication to TXA, and the 3-hour window applies to trauma, not to this indication. BP control and rapid transport to neurosurgery are the priorities.
w: Give 1 g over 10 minutes since he is within 3 hours of onset
Give 2 g as a single bolus per the trauma protocol
Give TXA only if the BP rises above 180 systolic

qs.q: A 25-kg 7-year-old struck by a car 40 minutes ago has HR 150, BP 78/40 and capillary refill of 4 seconds. Your pediatric trauma protocol includes TXA. Which loading dose fits?
qs.a: 375 mg IV over 10 minutes, then 2 mg/kg/h
qs.x: Pediatric trauma protocols use 15 mg/kg over 10 minutes (max 1 g), here 375 mg, followed by 2 mg/kg/h. The adult 1 g or 2 g doses overshoot a 25-kg child, and a rapid push risks hypotension.
w: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, the same as an adult
250 mg IV push over 1 minute, then stop
2 g IV single bolus per the adult alternative

qs.q: Forty-five minutes into a TXA maintenance infusion, a trauma patient without head injury has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Glucose is 112 and SpO2 is 97%. What is the best interpretation and action?
qs.a: A known TXA adverse effect; stop it and treat the seizure
qs.x: Seizures are a listed serious adverse effect of TXA, so the infusion is stopped, the seizure treated, and medical control informed. Assuming it is unrelated and continuing, or giving more TXA, ignores a known drug toxicity.
w: This is expected with TXA; continue the infusion and observe
The seizure means occult head injury; double the TXA rate
Seizures signal under-dosing; give an extra 1 g bolus

qs.q: A dialysis patient with K 7.2 had a QRS of 160 ms. After calcium gluconate the QRS narrows to 110 ms and peaked T waves persist. What is the most important next step?
qs.a: Shift potassium into cells with insulin and dextrose
qs.x: Calcium only stabilizes the cardiac membrane for a short time and does not lower potassium, so a shifting agent such as insulin with dextrose is next. Furosemide is not useful in an anuric dialysis patient.
w: Stop treatment because the ECG has improved
Repeat calcium until the T waves normalize
Give furosemide to remove the potassium through the kidneys

qs.q: A 20-kg child with renal failure has K 7.4, peaked T waves and a widening QRS. Per PALS, which calcium gluconate dose is appropriate?
qs.a: 1.2 g (60 mg/kg) IV/IO given slowly
qs.x: PALS calcium gluconate for hyperkalemia is 60 mg/kg (max 3 g), 1.2 g for 20 kg. The tempting 20 mg/kg figure is the calcium chloride dose, which contains about three times more elemental calcium per gram.
w: 400 mg (20 mg/kg) IV/IO given slowly
3 g IV push regardless of weight
100 mg (5 mg/kg) IV/IO over 1 hour

qs.q: A 41-year-old industrial worker splashed hydrofluoric acid on two fingers. The skin looks almost normal, but he reports severe pain out of proportion to the findings. After copious irrigation, what is the best next treatment?
qs.a: Apply calcium gluconate topically to the burn
qs.x: Fluoride ions bind calcium and cause deep tissue injury with pain out of proportion; topical calcium gluconate binds fluoride. Opioids alone treat the symptom but not the ongoing chemical injury.
w: Apply silver-based burn dressing and reassess later
Give morphine only, since the skin is intact
Neutralize the area with sodium bicarbonate

qs.q: A 66-year-old with K 7.3 and a QRS of 150 ms is getting calcium chloride 1 g by slow push through a forearm IV. Halfway through, the site becomes swollen, pale and painful. The QRS has narrowed to 124 ms. What is the best action?
qs.a: Stop the push at that site and give the rest through new access
qs.x: Extravasation is a stop point for calcium chloride, which causes tissue necrosis, but the hyperkalemia still needs membrane stabilization, so the dose is completed through a new, reliable large vein. Pushing more drug or fluid into the infiltrated site worsens the injury, and calcium chloride is not given IM.
w: Finish the push quickly since the QRS is improving
Flush the IV briskly with saline to dilute the calcium
Give the remaining calcium chloride IM in the thigh

qs.q: A 60-year-old with a verapamil overdose has HR 40 and BP 72/40. After calcium chloride 1 g IV the BP rises to 90/56, then falls back to 74/42 fifteen minutes later. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Repeat calcium chloride; its effect is often brief
qs.x: In calcium channel blocker overdose, calcium is given as 1-2 g every 10-20 minutes because the response is often transient. A temporary response shows benefit, not failure, and switching salts adds nothing.
w: Conclude calcium has failed and do not give more
Give a fluid bolus only and recheck in 30 minutes
Switch to calcium gluconate because chloride failed

qs.q: A 34-week preeclamptic patient is on magnesium 2 g/h for transfer. Which new finding should prompt the crew to stop the infusion first?
qs.a: Patellar reflexes that were present are now absent
qs.x: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is an early sign of magnesium toxicity and appears before respiratory depression; it is a listed stop point. Flushing, warmth and nausea are common expected effects.
w: Facial flushing and a sensation of warmth after the bolus
BP 152/98, unchanged from the last reading
Mild nausea without vomiting

qs.q: A 30-week patient with severe preeclampsia has been on magnesium 2 g/h for 3 hours after a full load. Mid-flight she has a second eclamptic seizure. Reflexes were present and RR was 16 just before. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Protect the airway; give another magnesium bolus per protocol
qs.x: Recurrent eclamptic seizures on maintenance therapy are treated with an additional magnesium bolus per protocol while supporting the airway, with toxicity checks afterward. Magnesium is not abandoned for phenytoin, and an antihypertensive does not stop a seizure.
w: Stop magnesium since it has clearly failed, and give phenytoin instead
Give hydralazine first, then reassess the seizure
Double the magnesium infusion and wait 1 hour

qs.q: A 30-kg 9-year-old with severe asthma has poor air movement and SpO2 89% despite continuous albuterol, ipratropium and steroids. Which magnesium dose is appropriate?
qs.a: 750-1,500 mg IV over 15-30 minutes
qs.x: Pediatric magnesium for asthma is 25-50 mg/kg IV over 15-30 minutes (max 2 g), here 750-1,500 mg. The 4 g dose is an eclampsia load, and a rapid push risks hypotension and bradycardia.
w: 2 g IV push over 1 minute
4 g IV over 20 minutes
150 mg IM, repeated every 5 minutes

qs.q: A 36-week patient with severe preeclampsia is about to receive magnesium for seizure prophylaxis. Which history finding most changes the plan?
qs.a: Known third-degree heart block without a pacemaker
qs.x: Heart block is a listed contraindication to magnesium, which slows AV conduction, so this needs a different plan with medical control. Diabetes, prior surgery and asthma do not contraindicate magnesium.
w: Gestational diabetes treated with insulin
Prior cesarean section two years ago
Mild intermittent asthma with no attacks in the last several years

qs.q: After a field delivery of one infant, the mother's abdomen stays distended, the fundus is well above the umbilicus and fetal parts are palpable. Bleeding is moderate and the placenta has not delivered. A partner draws up oxytocin 10 units IM. What is the best action?
qs.a: Withhold oxytocin until a second fetus is ruled out
qs.x: A possible second twin is a listed contraindication; oxytocin could contract the uterus around an undelivered infant. A fundus well above the umbilicus with palpable fetal parts after one birth suggests another fetus, so it must be excluded first.
w: Give it now since bleeding is the top priority
Give it IV instead of IM for a faster effect
Give half the dose to reduce the uterine response and the bleeding

qs.q: A patient with postpartum hemorrhage has a boggy uterus after placental delivery. HR is 122 and BP 92/58. Two IV attempts have failed and the IO is not yet placed. What is the best oxytocin decision?
qs.a: Give 10 units IM now while vascular access continues
qs.x: Oxytocin 10 units IM is an accepted PPH route and should not be delayed for access. An IV push risks hypotension and tachycardia, and 40 units is the amount mixed into an infusion bag, not an IM dose.
w: Wait for IO access and then push 10 units IV
Hold oxytocin until a second IV line is placed
Give 40 units IM so it matches the amount placed in an IV infusion bag

qs.q: Ten minutes after carboprost 250 mcg IM for atony, a patient with no known asthma develops wheezing, RR 30 and SpO2 dropping from 97% to 88%. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Stop further carboprost and treat the bronchospasm
qs.x: Bronchospasm and hypoxemia are listed stop points for carboprost, even without an asthma history. Treating the airway takes priority over repeating a drug that is causing it.
w: Give the next carboprost dose now since bleeding control comes first
Give oxytocin IV push to replace carboprost
Assume amniotic fluid embolism and start CPR

qs.q: Twenty minutes after methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM for atony, a postpartum patient has crushing chest pain and BP 174/110. HR is 96. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Stop further doses; treat as coronary vasospasm
qs.x: Chest pain and severe hypertension are listed stop criteria; methylergonovine can cause coronary vasospasm. Repeating the dose or dismissing the pain as cramping misses a serious adverse effect.
w: Repeat the dose because bleeding has slowed
Give oxytocin IV push to reverse the effect
Reassure her; this is expected uterine cramping

qs.q: A patient with PPH from atony is vomiting repeatedly and cannot hold anything in her mouth. Oxytocin is running. Which misoprostol route fits best per ACOG/WHO?
qs.a: 800-1,000 mcg rectally, once
qs.x: Rectal misoprostol 800-1,000 mcg avoids the oral route in a vomiting patient. Misoprostol has no IV form, 200 mcg QID is the ulcer dose, and 250 mcg IM is carboprost.
w: 200 mcg PO four times daily
600 mcg IV over 10 minutes
250 mcg deep IM, repeat in 15 minutes

qs.q: A 66-year-old being transferred for a large PE has HR 112 and BP 118/76. The chart notes heparin-induced thrombocytopenia 18 months ago. The sending order is a heparin bolus and infusion. What is the best action?
qs.a: Withhold heparin and request a non-heparin anticoagulant
qs.x: A history of HIT is a listed contraindication to heparin, and a lower dose or a different route does not remove that risk. Medical control should order an alternative anticoagulant.
w: Give heparin since HIT more than a year ago no longer matters
Give a half-dose heparin bolus and watch platelets
Give heparin SQ instead of IV to lower the risk

qs.q: Two hours after a femoral cardiac catheterization, a patient on a heparin infusion during transfer develops a firm, enlarging groin swelling. HR has risen from 78 to 112 and BP has fallen from 132/80 to 96/60. What is the best first action?
qs.a: Stop the heparin and hold firm pressure above the puncture site
qs.x: An expanding hematoma with rising HR and falling BP is active bleeding, a stop point for heparin, and manual pressure just above the arterial puncture controls the source. Giving fluid while the anticoagulant keeps running treats the numbers, not the bleed.
w: Increase the heparin to prevent a clot at the puncture site
Give a fluid bolus and keep the heparin running unchanged
Apply ice to the groin and recheck the vitals in 30 minutes

qs.q: A 90-kg patient with NSTEMI needs heparin started for transfer per the ACC/AHA ACS regimen. What initial dosing is correct?
qs.a: 4,000-unit bolus, then 1,000 units/h
qs.x: The ACS regimen is 60 units/kg (max 4,000) then 12 units/kg/h (max 1,000/h), so both values are capped for a 90-kg patient. 5,400 units ignores the caps, and 7,200 units uses the VTE nomogram.
w: 5,400-unit bolus, then 1,080 units/h
7,200-unit bolus, then 1,620 units/h
10,000-unit bolus, then 2,000 units/h

qs.q: Forty minutes into an alteplase infusion for ischemic stroke, the patient reports a sudden severe headache, vomits, and her NIHSS rises by 6 points. What is the best immediate action?
qs.a: Stop the infusion; treat as intracranial hemorrhage
qs.x: New headache, vomiting and neurologic decline are listed stop criteria for alteplase and suggest hemorrhage. Treating the nausea or slowing the drip leaves a thrombolytic running into a possible bleed.
w: Give ondansetron and continue the infusion
Slow the infusion rate by half and recheck in 15 minutes
Finish the infusion since only 20 minutes remain

qs.q: A 71-year-old with sudden right-sided weakness and aphasia 1 hour ago is a possible alteplase candidate. Glucose is 42 mg/dL. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Treat the hypoglycemia and reassess the neuro exam
qs.x: Glucose under 50 is listed as a stroke thrombolytic exclusion because hypoglycemia can mimic stroke. Treat it and reassess; if deficits persist with normal glucose, the stroke pathway continues.
w: Start alteplase now and give dextrose afterward
Give alteplase since glucose does not affect stroke
Cancel all stroke care since this is not a stroke

qs.q: An acute ischemic stroke patient within 2 hours of onset has BP 170/92, glucose 130, and platelets 82,000 on labs. What is the alteplase decision?
qs.a: Withhold alteplase; the platelet count excludes it
qs.x: Platelets under 100,000 are a listed contraindication. Meeting the BP goal does not override it, and a reduced dose does not make a contraindicated thrombolytic safe.
w: Give alteplase since the BP is under 185/110
Give a reduced 0.6 mg/kg dose to offset the risk
Give alteplase and transfuse platelets if bleeding starts

qs.q: A 74-kg patient with an anterior STEMI is 3 hours from the nearest PCI center, and the decision is made to give TNKase. What is the correct dose?
qs.a: 40 mg IV bolus over 5 seconds
qs.x: The STEMI dose is weight-banded: 70-79 kg receives 40 mg as a single bolus. 20 mg is the stroke dose for that weight band, and 0.9 mg/kg over 60 minutes is the alteplase stroke regimen.
w: 50 mg IV bolus over 5 seconds
20 mg IV bolus over 5 seconds
0.9 mg/kg IV, 10% as a bolus and the rest over 60 minutes

qs.q: A 58-year-old with inferior ST elevation has tearing chest pain radiating to the back, BP 168/90 in the right arm and 128/70 in the left. PCI is 3 hours away. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Withhold it and treat as suspected aortic dissection
qs.x: Suspected aortic dissection is a listed contraindication; a dissection can extend into a coronary ostium and mimic STEMI. Lowering the BP does not make a thrombolytic safe.
w: Give tenecteplase since PCI is more than 120 minutes away
Give half-dose tenecteplase because of the BP difference
Give tenecteplase after lowering the BP below 140 systolic

qs.q: Twenty minutes after tenecteplase for STEMI, the chest pain eases, ST elevation falls by more than half, and a wide regular rhythm at 82 appears. BP is 128/76 and the patient is alert. What is the best interpretation?
qs.a: Probable reperfusion rhythm; monitor closely without treating
qs.x: An accelerated idioventricular rhythm with pain relief and ST resolution suggests reperfusion; it is usually benign in a stable patient. A rate of 82 is not VT, and tenecteplase is a single-bolus drug that is not repeated.
w: Ventricular tachycardia needing immediate cardioversion
Failed reperfusion needing a second tenecteplase dose
Hyperkalemia needing calcium chloride at once

qs.q: A 6-week-old infant with bronchiolitis is being intubated for transport. A crew member suggests ketamine as the induction agent. What is the main concern with this choice?
qs.a: Ketamine is contraindicated under 3 months of age
qs.x: Age under 3 months is a ketamine contraindication, so another agent should be chosen per protocol. The ICP concern is outdated, and IV dosing is not the issue.
w: Ketamine raises ICP too much in all infants, so it is always avoided
Ketamine cannot be given IV to infants
The infant must weigh 10 kg before ketamine

qs.q: A 5-year-old receiving ketamine for burn dressing sedation develops a high-pitched inspiratory noise, then silent chest movement and SpO2 falling from 98% to 86%. What is the best immediate action?
qs.a: Stop ketamine; jaw thrust and positive-pressure ventilation
qs.x: Laryngospasm is a listed ketamine stop point. It is managed first with airway positioning and positive pressure, then further steps per protocol. Naloxone does not reverse ketamine, and albuterol does not treat laryngospasm.
w: Give another ketamine dose to deepen the sedation
Give naloxone to reverse the ketamine
Give nebulized albuterol and wait several minutes for improvement

qs.q: A 58-year-old in atrial flutter at 150 with BP 86/52 receives a reduced propofol dose and is cardioverted to sinus rhythm at 84. Two minutes later she is apneic, SpO2 is falling from 98% to 89% and the capnography waveform is flat. BP is 102/64. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Ventilate with a bag-valve mask until breathing returns
qs.x: Apnea is a common effect of propofol and there is no reversal agent; because the drug is short-acting, assisted ventilation bridges her until spontaneous breathing returns. Oxygen without ventilation does not treat apnea, and naloxone and flumazenil do not act on propofol.
w: Give naloxone IV to reverse the propofol
Apply a non-rebreather mask and watch the SpO2
Give flumazenil IV to reverse the sedation

qs.q: A 20-kg 6-year-old has scald burns to both legs and severe pain. IV access has failed twice, and the IO is reserved for resuscitation. Which analgesic plan fits?
qs.a: Fentanyl 30-40 mcg intranasally
qs.x: Intranasal fentanyl 1.5-2 mcg/kg (30-40 mcg for 20 kg) gives fast analgesia without IV access. 100 mcg is an adult-sized dose, and delaying analgesia in a burned child is not appropriate.
w: Fentanyl 100 mcg intranasally
Morphine 10 mg IM in the thigh
Wait to medicate until IV access is obtained

qs.q: A non-intubated 45-year-old with rib fractures received fentanyl 50 mcg twice during the flight. He is now hard to rouse with RR 8, SpO2 89% and EtCO2 58. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Stop fentanyl, support ventilation, and give naloxone
qs.x: RR under 10-12 with falling SpO2 and rising EtCO2 are fentanyl stop points. Ventilate and reverse; more oxygen does not fix hypoventilation, and a benzodiazepine would deepen respiratory depression.
w: Give the next fentanyl dose since the pain is untreated
Raise oxygen flow and continue fentanyl at a lower dose
Give midazolam to help him breathe more calmly

qs.q: A 67-year-old with a COPD flare is on BiPAP for transfer. His PaCO2 is improving, but he is agitated and keeps pulling at the mask. HR is 96, BP 142/84 and SpO2 91%. Which sedation plan best fits?
qs.a: A low-dose dexmedetomidine infusion without a load
qs.x: Dexmedetomidine calms with little respiratory depression, so it suits a non-intubated hypercapnic patient, and skipping the load limits bradycardia and transient hypertension. Benzodiazepine boluses, propofol and stacked opioid doses can suppress the respiratory drive he depends on.
w: Repeated midazolam boluses until he is calm
A propofol infusion at an ICU sedation dose
Fentanyl 100 mcg IV boluses repeated every 5 minutes

qs.q: A 24-year-old with a severe TBI has a dilated right pupil, BP 192/104, HR 48 and irregular respirations. A partner draws up labetalol for the BP. What is the best response?
qs.a: Withhold it; treat the herniation, not the BP
qs.x: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing (Cushing triad) with a blown pupil mean herniation. Lowering the BP would cut cerebral perfusion, and bradycardia is a listed labetalol stop point.
w: Give 20 mg IV now since the BP is well over the 180 systolic threshold
Give labetalol and then atropine to correct the slow heart rate
Give labetalol and start a nicardipine drip

qs.q: A 64-year-old with a spontaneous ICH is on nicardipine at 12.5 mg/h with a target SBP of 130-150. During the flight SBP falls to 108, HR is 104 and she is newly more drowsy. What is the best action?
qs.a: Reduce or pause the nicardipine and recheck the BP and neuro exam
qs.x: A BP below target is a stop point for nicardipine, and overshooting in ICH can reduce cerebral perfusion, which may explain the new drowsiness (expansion of the bleed must also be considered). Lower is not better once below goal, and a second antihypertensive drops the BP further.
w: Continue the same rate since a lower BP limits bleeding
Increase the rate to control the reflex tachycardia
Add labetalol to slow the HR while nicardipine continues

qs.q: A 30-year-old with an isolated TBI was just intubated. BP falls from 118/70 to 82/48 with HR 96, attributed to induction drugs and positive pressure. What is the best immediate step while the cause is addressed?
qs.a: Give push-dose phenylephrine per protocol to restore MAP
qs.x: Even one hypotensive episode worsens TBI outcomes, so post-intubation hypotension is corrected quickly; push-dose phenylephrine is used per protocol. Permissive hypotension is for penetrating torso trauma, not TBI.
w: Accept the BP since permissive hypotension limits bleeding
Give labetalol to slow the HR and improve filling
Increase the sedation to blunt the stress response

qs.q: A 100-kg patient with a TBI is still seizing after two doses of midazolam. The physician orders a levetiracetam load for benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus. Which dose matches the ESETT approach?
qs.a: 4,500 mg IV over 10-15 minutes
qs.x: ESETT dosing is 60 mg/kg with a 4,500 mg maximum, so a 100-kg patient receives 4,500 mg. 6,000 mg ignores the cap, and 500 mg is the routine maintenance dose.
w: 6,000 mg IV over 10-15 minutes
500 mg IV over 15 minutes
1,000 mg IV push over 1 minute

qs.q: A 12-kg toddler with croup has stridor at rest and retractions. Racemic epinephrine is not stocked, so the crew uses 1 mg/mL epinephrine by nebulizer per croup guidelines. What volume is correct?
qs.a: 5 mL nebulized
qs.x: The croup dose is 0.5 mL/kg of 1 mg/mL (max 5 mL). For 12 kg this would be 6 mL, so the 5 mL cap applies. 0.12 mL is the IM anaphylaxis dose, and 0.5 mL is the racemic dose.
w: 6 mL nebulized
0.12 mL nebulized
0.5 mL nebulized

qs.q: Thirty minutes after nebulized racemic epinephrine, a 3-year-old with croup has no stridor at rest and SpO2 98%. No steroid has been given. What is the best plan?
qs.a: Give dexamethasone and keep watching for rebound stridor
qs.x: Racemic epinephrine wears off and stridor can return, so the child needs observation and a corticosteroid for longer-lasting relief. Scheduled repeat nebs and albuterol do not address the airway edema.
w: Cancel the transfer because the croup has resolved
Repeat racemic epinephrine every 20 minutes on schedule
Give albuterol to prevent the stridor from returning

qs.q: A 12-kg toddler found with a relative's methadone had RR 4 and pinpoint pupils. After naloxone 1.2 mg IV he woke and cried. Forty minutes into the flight he is drowsy again with RR 8. What is the best explanation and action?
qs.a: Methadone outlasts naloxone; redose per protocol
qs.x: Methadone has a much longer duration than naloxone, so resedation is expected and needs repeat dosing or an infusion. Improvement after the first dose confirms the opioid effect.
w: The first dose caused withdrawal; give no more naloxone
Naloxone failed, so this is not an opioid ingestion
The child is tired from crying; reassess on landing

qs.q: A 15-kg 3-year-old has seized for 7 minutes during an interfacility transfer, and the peripheral IV has infiltrated. Per protocol, which first anticonvulsant is best?
qs.a: Midazolam 3 mg intranasally
qs.x: Intranasal midazolam 0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg) is fast and needs no IV; for 15 kg that is 3 mg. 10 mg is the adult maximum, and waiting for IV access prolongs the seizure.
w: Midazolam 10 mg intranasally
Lorazepam 4 mg IV once access returns
Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV infusion

qs.q: A 24-year-old took amitriptyline 40 minutes ago. GCS has fallen from 15 to 11 during transport preparation and the gag reflex is weak. She is not intubated. What is the charcoal decision?
qs.a: Withhold it; her airway is not protected
qs.x: Altered mental status without a protected airway is a listed contraindication because of aspiration risk. A TCA patient can deteriorate quickly, so the airway and sodium bicarbonate readiness come first.
w: Give 1 g/kg PO now because she is within 1 hour
Give charcoal by nasogastric tube without intubation
Give a half dose so the volume is smaller

qs.q: A 20-kg 5-year-old pulled from a house fire has GCS 9, BP 70/40, and suspected cyanide toxicity. What is the hydroxocobalamin dose?
qs.a: 1.4 g IV over 15 minutes
qs.x: Pediatric dosing is 70 mg/kg (max 5 g) over 15 minutes, 1.4 g for 20 kg. 5 g is the adult dose, and a push over 1 minute does not match the labeled infusion time.
w: 5 g IV over 15 minutes
700 mg IV push over 1 minute
2.5 g IV over 2 hours

qs.q: Twenty minutes into the IV NAC loading dose for acetaminophen overdose, a patient develops flushing, hives and mild wheezing. BP is 118/72. What is the best action?
qs.a: Pause, treat the reaction, then restart slower
qs.x: Anaphylactoid reactions are rate-related; the standard approach is to pause, treat and restart slower. Stopping permanently leaves the overdose untreated, and charcoal will not replace NAC.
w: Stop NAC permanently and switch to activated charcoal
Continue NAC at the same rate since this is expected
Increase the rate to finish the load sooner

qs.q: After physostigmine for anticholinergic delirium, a patient becomes calm, then develops HR 46, drooling, vomiting and new wheezing. What is the best interpretation?
qs.a: Cholinergic excess from physostigmine; stop it and treat
qs.x: Bradycardia, salivation, vomiting and bronchospasm are cholinergic effects and listed physostigmine stop points. Anticholinergic toxicity causes tachycardia and dry skin, the opposite picture.
w: Return of the anticholinergic toxidrome; redose it
An allergic reaction; give epinephrine IM
Expected recovery; no action is needed

qs.q: A farmer with organophosphate poisoning received atropine until his secretions dried and his lungs cleared. He now has muscle fasciculations and weak respiratory effort. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Give pralidoxime and prepare ventilatory support
qs.x: Atropine blocks muscarinic effects but not nicotinic weakness and fasciculations, which pralidoxime targets. More atropine will not restore muscle strength once secretions are dry.
w: Give more atropine until the twitching stops
Give succinylcholine to stop the fasciculations
Give naloxone for the respiratory depression

qs.q: An intubated TCA overdose patient has received several sodium bicarbonate boluses and is on a bicarbonate infusion. The QRS has narrowed from 146 to 104 ms, and the arterial pH is now 7.58. What is the best plan for the bicarbonate?
qs.a: Stop further bicarbonate and keep monitoring the QRS
qs.x: A narrowed QRS and a pH above the 7.45-7.55 goal are stop points for bicarbonate; more alkalosis lowers potassium and ionized calcium and can provoke dysrhythmias. Bicarbonate resumes if the QRS widens again once pH allows, and hypoventilating the patient to make room for more is not standard care.
w: Give another bolus to narrow the QRS below 100 ms
Double the infusion to prevent the QRS from widening again
Lower the vent rate to raise CO2 so more bicarbonate can be given

qs.q: A dialysis patient with K 7.0 and peaked T waves has received calcium. The plan is insulin with dextrose to shift potassium. Which insulin dose fits for renal failure?
qs.a: 5 units IV with 25 g dextrose
qs.x: In renal failure the hyperkalemia dose is reduced to 5 units with 25 g dextrose because insulin clears slowly. Insulin without dextrose risks hypoglycemia, and 1 unit/kg is the HIET dose for toxicology.
w: 10 units IV without dextrose
0.1 unit/kg/h infusion with no bolus
1 unit/kg bolus with 25 g dextrose

qs.q: A dialysis patient who makes no urine has K 6.9 and mild crackles. A crew member suggests furosemide 80 mg IV to remove potassium. What is the best response?
qs.a: Withhold it; anuria is a contraindication
qs.x: Anuria is a listed contraindication; a loop diuretic needs functioning kidneys to work. This patient needs potassium shifting and urgent dialysis instead.
w: Give it as ordered since the crackles show fluid overload
Give a double dose since the kidneys respond poorly
Give it IM because the IV may be needed for calcium

qs.q: A 22-year-old runner collapsed in a marathon. He is confused with core temp 41.4 C (106.5 F), HR 150 and BP 98/58. A partner suggests IV acetaminophen 1,000 mg for the fever. What is the best response?
qs.a: Rapid cooling; antipyretics do not work here
qs.x: Heat stroke is not a fever driven by the hypothalamic set point, so antipyretics do not work; rapid cooling is the treatment. Liver injury is also common in heat stroke and adds acetaminophen risk.
w: Give acetaminophen now and cool if it fails in 30 minutes
Give ibuprofen instead, since it works faster
Give acetaminophen with the cooling to reach a target sooner

qs.q: A 38-year-old motorcyclist has GCS 5, a fixed dilated left pupil and an open femur fracture. After intubation, BP is 74/40 and HR 138. Medical control asks about hyperosmolar therapy for suspected herniation. Which plan is best?
qs.a: Avoid mannitol; restore perfusion and use hypertonic saline per protocol
