qs.x: Mannitol is contraindicated in severe hypovolemia and its diuresis worsens hypotension, which itself injures the brain; hypertonic saline per protocol lowers ICP without the diuretic volume loss. Herniation is urgent, but giving mannitol in hemorrhagic shock compounds secondary brain injury.
w: Give mannitol now, since herniation outweighs the low blood pressure
Give mannitol along with a furosemide dose to strengthen the ICP effect
Delay all ICP treatment until the femur fracture has been splinted

qs.q: A 70-kg intubated TBI patient is finishing a mannitol dose started 30 minutes ago at the sending facility. Since it began, the Foley has drained 900 mL, BP has fallen from 134/82 to 92/58 and HR has risen from 88 to 116. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Stop the mannitol, replace volume with isotonic fluid and reassess
qs.x: Mannitol's osmotic diuresis can cause dehydration and hypotension, and hypotension is a stop criterion; the lost volume must be replaced to protect cerebral perfusion. Clamping the catheter does not stop the diuresis, and a vasopressor does not make continuing the drug safe.
w: Give a repeat mannitol dose because the pupils are still unequal
Clamp the Foley catheter to limit any further fluid losses during flight
Start a vasopressor and continue the mannitol at the same rate

qs.q: During an interfacility transfer of a TBI patient who has had several mannitol doses, the latest labs show serum osmolality 326 mOsm/kg and sodium 151. The sending physician asks whether the next scheduled dose should be given in flight. What is the best response?
qs.a: Hold the dose and notify medical control, since osmolality is above 320
qs.x: Serum osmolality above 320 is a stop criterion for mannitol because of the risk of dehydration and renal injury. Slowing the infusion or adding water still delivers the osmotic load the threshold is meant to prevent.
w: Give the dose, since osmolality matters only when sodium is above 160
Give the dose at half the usual rate to limit the further rise in osmolality
Give the dose and add a free-water flush to offset the osmolality

qs.q: A 74-year-old with severe heart failure fell and now has GCS 7 with a new dilated right pupil. After intubation, pink frothy secretions fill the ETT, crackles are heard bilaterally and SpO2 is 86% on FiO2 1.0. Which finding most changes the hyperosmolar plan?
qs.a: The pulmonary edema, which contraindicates mannitol
qs.x: Mannitol is contraindicated in pulmonary edema or severe heart failure because its osmotic shift first expands intravascular volume; withhold it and discuss alternatives with medical control. Age alone does not change the dose in the drug data.
w: The age, which requires a reduced mannitol dose
The GCS of 7, which makes mannitol ineffective
The new pupil change, which calls for a doubled mannitol dose

qs.q: An intubated TBI patient is receiving mannitol every 6 hours during a long transfer. Which new finding is most concerning and calls for stopping the drug and notifying medical control?
qs.a: No urine output for the past hour despite a patent catheter
qs.x: Anuria is a contraindication and a stop criterion: mannitol is cleared by the kidneys, so it accumulates and can cause volume overload and renal injury. Brisk urine output is the expected effect, and an osmolality of 306 is below the 320 stop threshold.
w: Urine output of 350 mL in the first hour after the most recent dose
Serum osmolality of 306 mOsm/kg on the most recent lab
Serum sodium of 146 mEq/L on the most recent lab draw

qs.q: A TBI patient with signs of herniation is receiving 3% saline per protocol through a 20-gauge hand IV. Ten minutes later the site is swollen, pale and painful, and the infusion is slowing. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Stop the infusion at that site, notify the provider and get new access
qs.x: IV infiltration ends a 3% saline infusion because hypertonic fluid in the tissues causes pain and tissue injury; therapy resumes through new reliable IV or IO access per protocol. Flushing and resuming at an infiltrated site pushes more hypertonic fluid into the tissue.
w: Flush the IV with normal saline and resume the 3% at the same site
Slow the infusion rate and apply a warm pack to the swollen hand and wrist
Continue the infusion, since ICP control outweighs a local injury

qs.q: A 52-year-old with TBI is on a 3% saline infusion per protocol with an ordered sodium goal. Baseline sodium was 139. A repeat sodium 2 hours later is well above the ordered goal, and the intubated patient has stable vital signs. What is the best action?
qs.a: Hold the infusion and notify the provider of the sodium result
qs.x: A sodium rise faster than the planned correction is a hold criterion for 3% saline because of the risk of hypernatremia. Stable vital signs do not make an overshoot safe, and adding a diuretic does not address the excess sodium load.
w: Continue at the same rate, since the vital signs are stable
Increase the rate, since a higher sodium lowers ICP further
Give a furosemide dose and continue the 3% infusion as ordered

qs.q: A 4-hour interfacility transfer is arranged for a TBI patient on a 3% saline infusion per protocol. Point-of-care testing is available on the aircraft. Which value is most important to recheck during the flight?
qs.a: Serum sodium, every 2 to 4 hours during the infusion
qs.x: Serum sodium is checked every 2 to 4 hours during 3% saline to catch hypernatremia or an overly fast rise. Glucose matters in TBI, but it does not track the main risk of this drug.
w: Blood glucose, every 30 minutes during the infusion
INR, once before landing at the receiving facility
Troponin, once every hour while the infusion runs

qs.q: An 81-year-old with a subdural hematoma and a history of heart failure is receiving 3% saline per protocol. Twenty minutes in, RR rises to 32, crackles appear in both bases and SpO2 falls from 95% to 88%. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Stop the infusion, support oxygenation and notify the provider
qs.x: New pulmonary edema ends a 3% saline infusion; hypertonic saline expands intravascular volume and can cause fluid overload, especially in heart failure. Switching to normal saline would add even more volume.
w: Speed up the infusion to finish the dose before the aircraft lands
Continue the infusion and give a nebulized bronchodilator
Switch to normal saline at the same rate to dilute the sodium

qs.q: A TBI patient with a blown pupil has a serum sodium of 140. A new crew member objects to 3% saline because its label lists normal sodium as a contraindication. What is the best response?
qs.a: Its ICP use is off-label; give it per protocol and medical direction
qs.x: The label covers sodium depletion; using 3% saline to lower ICP is an established off-label use, so dosing follows protocol and medical direction. Applying the sodium-depletion label limits or waiting for hyponatremia would delay needed ICP treatment.
w: Agree and withhold it, since the label contraindication is absolute
Give it only at the label limit of 100 mL per hour for sodium loss
Give it only after the sodium has fallen below the normal range

qs.q: A 76-year-old on warfarin with a large intracerebral hemorrhage is ready for transfer. The 4F-PCC infusion finished 10 minutes ago, but no vitamin K appears on the medication record. What is the best action before departure?
qs.a: Ensure IV vitamin K is given, as the label pairs it with PCC
qs.x: The label pairs 4F-PCC with concurrent vitamin K: PCC replaces factors quickly, but that effect is temporary while warfarin persists, so vitamin K is needed to sustain reversal. Repeating PCC adds thrombotic risk without addressing the ongoing warfarin effect.
w: Give a second full PCC dose to cover the missing vitamin K
Take no action, since PCC fully replaces the vitamin K step
Give protamine to prolong the effect of the PCC during flight

qs.q: A 68-year-old on warfarin with septic shock has an INR of 4.8, oozing from every line site, platelets 38,000, a low fibrinogen and schistocytes on the smear. The sending team asks about 4F-PCC before transport. Which finding most argues against it?
qs.a: The picture of DIC, a label contraindication to PCC
qs.x: DIC is a label contraindication to 4F-PCC because concentrated clotting factors can worsen thrombosis, so the decision goes to medical control. An INR of 4 to 6 is within the labeled dosing range.
w: The INR of 4.8, which is too high for PCC to correct
The septic shock, which calls for vitamin K alone
The low platelet count, which calls for protamine first

qs.q: A 79-year-old on warfarin with a major GI bleed is receiving 4F-PCC with vitamin K. Near the end of the infusion he develops new right-sided weakness and slurred speech. BP is 148/86. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Stop the infusion, assess for stroke and notify medical control
qs.x: New neurologic deficits during PCC suggest thromboembolism such as stroke, a known serious effect, so the infusion is stopped and the provider notified. Protamine reverses heparin and does not reverse PCC.
w: Finish the infusion, since the bleeding is the bigger threat
Give more PCC, since the new weakness reflects ongoing blood loss
Give protamine to reverse the PCC and limit clot formation

qs.q: A warfarin patient with a traumatic subdural hematoma received 4F-PCC and IV vitamin K before a 90-minute transfer. Point-of-care INR testing is available on the aircraft. When is a repeat INR most useful to judge the response?
qs.a: About 30 minutes after the PCC infusion is complete
qs.x: The label calls for an INR at baseline and about 30 minutes after the infusion to confirm reversal. Waiting 24 hours misses the window in which PCC's effect should be measured, and warfarin effect is tracked by INR, not aPTT.
w: Only after 24 hours, once vitamin K has fully acted
Every 5 minutes until the INR reaches the normal range
Never; the aPTT is the test that tracks this reversal

qs.q: A 130-kg patient on warfarin has a life-threatening retroperitoneal bleed with an INR of 4.5. A partner calculates 4,550 units of 4F-PCC. Per the 4F-PCC (Kcentra) label, what is the correct dose?
qs.a: 3,500 units, because dosing uses weight only up to 100 kg
qs.x: For an INR of 4 to 6, the label dose is 35 units/kg with weight counted only up to 100 kg, so the maximum is 3,500 units. Using actual body weight overdoses the patient and adds thrombotic risk.
w: 4,550 units, because the dose follows actual body weight
2,500 units, because the INR is still below 5
5,000 units, because the patient weighs over 100 kg

qs.q: A 74-year-old with atrial fibrillation fell and has an expanding epidural hematoma. His pill organizer holds dabigatran, metoprolol and atorvastatin. The sending ED stocks andexanet alfa, 4F-PCC and idarucizumab. Which is the targeted reversal?
qs.a: Idarucizumab 5 g IV
qs.x: Idarucizumab is the specific reversal agent for dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor. Andexanet reverses the factor Xa inhibitors apixaban and rivaroxaban and has no effect on dabigatran.
w: Andexanet alfa high-dose bolus
4F-PCC 50 units/kg IV
Protamine 50 mg slow IV

qs.q: A 66-year-old on dabigatran for atrial fibrillation received idarucizumab for a traumatic splenic bleed. Two hours into the transfer, bleeding is controlled, but she develops sudden pleuritic chest pain, HR 124, BP 132/78 and SpO2 falling from 97% to 88%. What should the crew suspect first?
qs.a: A thromboembolic event now that anticoagulation is reversed
qs.x: Reversal removes dabigatran's protection against clotting in a patient with atrial fibrillation, and thrombosis is a known serious effect; sudden pleuritic pain with hypoxia suggests PE. Rebleeding would cause hypotension, not sudden pleuritic pain and hypoxia with a stable BP.
w: An allergic reaction to the earlier idarucizumab dose
Recurrent splenic bleeding causing early hemorrhagic shock in flight
Fluid overload from the small idarucizumab volume

qs.q: After idarucizumab is given for dabigatran-associated bleeding, the receiving team asks which coagulation tests best reflect the reversal. What is the best answer?
qs.a: aPTT and thrombin time
qs.x: Dabigatran directly inhibits thrombin, so the aPTT and thrombin time track its effect and its reversal. INR tracks warfarin, and anti-Xa activity relates to heparin and factor Xa inhibitors.
w: INR and fibrinogen level
Anti-Xa level and platelet count
D-dimer and repeat INR

qs.q: A 70-year-old on apixaban has a large intracerebral hemorrhage. A partner, seeing anticoagulant reversal on the idarucizumab box, prepares the 5 g dose. What is the best response?
qs.a: Withhold it; use andexanet or PCC per protocol for apixaban
qs.x: Idarucizumab binds only dabigatran and has no effect on factor Xa inhibitors; apixaban reversal uses andexanet alfa or 4F-PCC per protocol. Pairing it with protamine adds risk without reversing apixaban.
w: Give it, since it reverses all direct oral anticoagulants
Give half the dose, since apixaban is a weaker anticoagulant
Give it together with protamine to cover factor Xa activity

qs.q: A dabigatran patient with a life-threatening GI bleed is ordered idarucizumab. During a hurried loading, the partner has given one 2.5 g vial and is preparing to depart. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give the second 2.5 g vial so the full 5 g dose is complete
qs.x: The labeled dose is 5 g, supplied as two 2.5 g vials; giving only one leaves reversal incomplete in a life-threatening bleed. Waiting for labs delays reversal, and PCC is not the targeted agent for dabigatran.
w: Depart now, since one vial is the complete labeled dose
Hold the second vial until an aPTT results at the receiving ED
Replace the second vial with a weight-based dose of 4F-PCC

qs.q: A 62-year-old on a heparin infusion after a cardiac procedure develops an expanding groin hematoma. During IV protamine, BP drops from 126/78 to 80/48, HR falls to 52 and his face is flushed. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Stop the protamine, support BP and notify the provider
qs.x: Hypotension, bradycardia and flushing are recognized protamine reactions and hold criteria; stopping the drug, supporting perfusion and notifying the provider comes first. That these effects are common does not make continuing safe once the patient is unstable.
w: Push the remaining protamine faster to finish the reversal
Continue at the same rate, since these effects are common
Restart the heparin to counteract the protamine effect

qs.q: A 58-year-old with an NSTEMI is being flown on a heparin infusion. Midway through the flight he becomes confused, vomits and develops a new dilated left pupil with BP 196/104. What is the best first action?
qs.a: Stop the heparin infusion and notify medical control
qs.x: Suspected intracranial hemorrhage on heparin calls for stopping the source first, with protamine reversal to follow per order. Giving protamine while heparin keeps infusing works against itself.
w: Give protamine and keep the heparin running for the ACS
Give a heparin bolus for a possible new embolic stroke
Increase the heparin rate to protect the coronary arteries

qs.q: A 66-year-old man with diabetes treated with NPH insulin is receiving protamine for heparin reversal. Within minutes he develops diffuse hives, wheezing and BP 74/40. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Stop the protamine and treat anaphylaxis with IM epinephrine
qs.x: Anaphylaxis is the serious adverse effect of protamine, so the drug is stopped and epinephrine given. An antihistamine alone does not treat the hypotension or bronchospasm.
w: Slow the protamine and give diphenhydramine alone
Finish the protamine dose first, then give a fluid bolus for the BP
Give more protamine to complete the heparin reversal

qs.q: An 83-year-old on warfarin has a subdural hematoma with an INR of 3.6. A crew member suggests protamine because it is the reversal agent carried on the aircraft. What is the best response?
qs.a: Withhold it; protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin
qs.x: Protamine reverses heparin and partially reverses enoxaparin; warfarin reversal uses 4F-PCC with vitamin K. Giving protamine here adds hypotension and anaphylaxis risk with no benefit.
w: Give it, since it reverses most anticoagulants
Give it at half dose because of the patient's age
Give it first, then add vitamin K at the receiving ED

qs.q: A patient on a heparin infusion received protamine for bleeding at a femoral sheath site, and the bleeding has slowed. Which test best confirms the reversal at the transfer handoff?
qs.a: aPTT
qs.x: The aPTT reflects unfractionated heparin effect and is the lab used to follow protamine reversal. The INR tracks warfarin and does not confirm heparin reversal.
w: INR
Platelet count
Fibrinogen level

qs.q: A 69-year-old on rivaroxaban is being flown for an unrelated cardiac workup. She develops a nosebleed that stops after 10 minutes of direct pressure, with stable vital signs and normal mentation. What is the best plan for andexanet alfa?
qs.a: Do not give it; the bleed is neither life-threatening nor uncontrolled
qs.x: Andexanet is indicated for life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding; a controlled nosebleed does not justify its thromboembolic risk. Being on a factor Xa inhibitor is not by itself an indication.
w: Give the low-dose regimen to keep the bleed from recurring
Give the high-dose regimen because rivaroxaban is a factor Xa inhibitor
Give it only if the receiving team plans any procedure

qs.q: A patient on apixaban with an intracerebral hemorrhage received andexanet alfa before transfer. The receiving team plans to order a commercial anti-Xa level to judge the reversal. What is the best handoff point?
qs.a: Commercial anti-Xa assays are unreliable after andexanet
qs.x: Commercial anti-Xa assays are unreliable after andexanet, so reversal is judged by hemostasis, the clinical picture and hemoglobin. Acting on those results could lead to inappropriate redosing or early restarting of anticoagulation.
w: A near-zero anti-Xa level means apixaban can be restarted
A high anti-Xa level means a second full dose is required
The anti-Xa level should be repeated every 15 minutes

qs.q: A 77-year-old on rivaroxaban with a life-threatening GI bleed is on the andexanet infusion after the bolus. Forty minutes later he reports crushing chest pain, and the monitor shows new ST elevation in II, III and aVF. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Stop the infusion and notify the provider of a possible MI
qs.x: MI is a known serious thromboembolic effect of andexanet and a stop criterion. Anticoagulating a patient with an active major bleed is a medical control decision, not a reflex, and continuing the infusion ignores the stop criterion.
w: Continue the infusion, since chest pain is a known infusion effect
Give a heparin bolus while continuing the andexanet infusion
Increase to the high-dose rate to finish the course sooner

qs.q: A 64-year-old on apixaban with a traumatic intracranial bleed received the low-dose andexanet bolus at the sending hospital, and the 4 mg/min infusion has run for 20 minutes when the aircraft arrives. What is the best plan?
qs.a: Continue the infusion in flight for up to 120 minutes total
qs.x: The bolus is followed by an infusion for up to 120 minutes to sustain reversal; stopping or pausing it lets anticoagulant activity return. Switching to the high-dose rate changes the ordered regimen without an indication.
w: Stop the infusion, since the bolus provides the full reversal
Switch to the 8 mg/min rate to finish before landing
Pause the infusion for transport and restart it at the receiving ED

qs.q: An 82-year-old on rivaroxaban has a life-threatening bleed, and the low-dose andexanet regimen is ordered. A partner plans to push the 400 mg bolus over 2 minutes to save time. What is the best response?
qs.a: Give the bolus at 30 mg/min, then start the 4 mg/min infusion
qs.x: The labeled low-dose regimen is a 400 mg bolus at 30 mg/min (about 13 minutes) followed by 4 mg/min for up to 120 minutes. Skipping the bolus or stretching it over 2 hours delays reversal in a life-threatening bleed.
w: Push it over 2 minutes, since the rate does not matter for a bolus
Give the full 400 mg as a slow infusion over 2 hours instead
Skip the bolus and start the 8 mg/min infusion directly

qs.q: At 1500 you are dispatched to a two-car crash on a four-lane interstate. A fire engine is already parked angled across the left lane just upstream of the wrecked vehicles. Where should you position the ambulance?
qs.a: Beyond the crash, downstream of the engine, so it is shielded
qs.x: The fire apparatus acts as the upstream block, so the ambulance parks downstream of the scene where loading is protected. Parking upstream or beside the wreck in an open lane puts the crew and patient in the path of traffic.
w: Upstream of the fire engine to add a second barrier to traffic
In the open right lane alongside the wreck for faster loading
On the grass median directly across from the crash site

qs.q: At 2200 you arrive at a single-vehicle crash on an unlit two-lane highway. Traffic is still moving past the scene in both directions. Before stepping out of the ambulance, what is the most important personal protective step?
qs.a: Put on a high-visibility safety vest
qs.x: Being struck by traffic is a leading cause of EMS roadway deaths, so high-visibility apparel is required before working near moving traffic. Gloves and eye protection are needed before patient contact but do not address the traffic hazard.
w: Put on a pair of exam gloves and safety glasses
Turn on the interior dome light of the cab
Put on a structural firefighting helmet

qs.q: You arrive at a car that struck a utility pole in a rural area at night. A power line is lying across the hood, and the alert driver says his leg hurts. What is the best action?
qs.a: Tell him to stay in the car, stay back, and request the utility company
qs.x: A downed line can energize the car and the ground around it; the occupant is safest inside while the crew stays outside the hazard zone until the utility company de-energizes it. EMS gear is not rated electrical protection, and moving the line is never an EMS task.
w: Have him open the door and jump clear of the car with both feet together
Use a dry wooden pike pole to move the line off of the hood
Approach the car in rubber boots and gloves to assess his leg

qs.q: You are first on scene at a rollover of a tanker truck on a state highway. A liquid is pooling under the trailer and the driver is slumped in the cab. You can see an orange-bordered diamond placard but cannot read it from your position. What should you do first?
qs.a: Stop uphill and upwind, read it with binoculars, use the ERG
qs.x: Hazardous materials scenes are approached from uphill and upwind at a distance; binoculars allow identification so the Emergency Response Guidebook can set isolation distances. Moving closer or sending anyone toward the leak risks more victims.
w: Drive closer so the placard number can be read and reported to dispatch
Walk to the cab to check the driver while holding your breath
Have a bystander read the placard while you get the stretcher

qs.q: You are dispatched to a farm for a man who collapsed inside a manure pit. On arrival, a family member says a second man went in to help him and also collapsed. Both are visible at the bottom and are not moving. What is the best action?
qs.a: Do not enter; request fire and technical rescue with SCBA
qs.x: Confined spaces like manure pits can contain toxic gases and low oxygen; a second collapsed rescuer confirms a deadly atmosphere. Only rescuers with supplied air and confined-space training enter; a surgical mask gives no protection.
w: Enter quickly with a surgical mask to drag out the nearer man
Lower a crew member on a rope to check both men's breathing
Have the family member lower a ladder so you can climb down

qs.q: You enter a home for a 66-year-old man with COPD who is short of breath. He is wearing a nasal cannula from his home oxygen concentrator and is lighting a cigarette. What should you do first?
qs.a: Have him put out the cigarette before anything else
qs.x: Oxygen strongly supports combustion, and an open flame near a cannula can cause facial burns or a fire. Eliminating the ignition source is a scene safety step that comes before patient assessment.
w: Turn the oxygen flow up so he is less short of breath while smoking
Begin your primary assessment while he finishes the cigarette
Remove his cannula and leave the concentrator running nearby

qs.q: You are assigned to the rehab and treatment area at a working house fire. A firefighter tells you a resident may still be inside a back bedroom. You are wearing standard EMS gear. What is your role?
qs.a: Stay in the treatment area and prepare to receive the patient
qs.x: Interior search and rescue in a burning structure requires turnout gear, SCBA, and fire training. The EMT's role is to be ready in a safe treatment area to receive the patient once firefighters remove them.
w: Enter through a back window to search the bedroom quickly
Go in behind the attack crew to help carry the resident out
Break a back window to ventilate the bedroom for the resident

qs.q: You are dispatched to a home for a 34-year-old woman with a headache. As you step through the front door, the carbon monoxide monitor clipped to your bag starts alarming. What is the best action?
qs.a: Leave the home, help occupants out, and request fire
qs.x: A personal CO alarm means the environment is unsafe. The crew exits, helping occupants out if it can be done quickly, and requests the fire department to meter and ventilate; staying inside to treat exposes the crew.
w: Silence the monitor and continue to the patient while watching it
Open a window in the living room and then assess the patient there
Place oxygen on the patient and treat her inside the home

qs.q: You are dispatched to a warehouse for a worker who is "stuck" to an electrical panel. On arrival, a coworker says he is still in contact with the panel and shaking. What is the best action?
qs.a: Have qualified staff shut off the power first
qs.x: Rescuers must not touch a patient in contact with an energized source. Power is shut off by qualified personnel first; improvised insulators and medical gloves do not protect against industrial voltages.
w: Push him away from the panel using a dry wooden broom handle
Pull him off by his clothing while wearing exam gloves
Grab his ankle quickly and pull him away from the panel

qs.q: You are dispatched to a golf course. A group of four golfers was struck by lightning; the storm is still overhead. Two are moaning, and two are motionless and not breathing. After moving everyone to a safe location, who should receive care first?
qs.a: The two motionless, apneic golfers
qs.x: In lightning strikes, reverse triage applies: patients in respiratory or cardiac arrest often respond to prompt care, while those moaning are breathing and less likely to die. Crew safety from the ongoing storm comes first.
w: The two moaning golfers with burns
The golfer who appears most injured
Whoever is closest to the ambulance

qs.q: You arrive at a home for a 40-year-old woman with a nosebleed. While you are assessing her, her husband walks in holding a kitchen knife and shouts at you to leave. What is the best action?
qs.a: Leave with your partner and request law enforcement
qs.x: When the scene becomes unsafe mid-call, the crew retreats to a safe location and requests law enforcement. Disarming a person is not an EMS task, and continuing care with a weapon present risks the crew.
w: Try to take the knife from him while your partner holds the patient
Keep treating and calmly explain that you are there to help
Move the patient to the bathroom and lock the door

qs.q: You are dispatched to a reported shooting outside a nightclub. Dispatch states police are en route and the scene is not yet secure. What should you do?
qs.a: Stage out of sight nearby until police report the scene secure
qs.x: Responders stage a safe distance away and out of view until law enforcement secures the scene. Arriving early, even quietly, risks injury or creating more patients.
w: Drive to the front door with lights off to avoid drawing attention
Park at the scene and wait in the ambulance with the doors locked
Go to the scene because a shooting victim needs care immediately

qs.q: Police secure an apartment and you enter for a man who is pulseless and apneic with obvious signs of death and a gunshot wound to the head. How should you manage the scene?
qs.a: Use one path in and out and disturb as little as you can
qs.x: At a crime scene with obvious death, EMS confirms death, limits personnel, and disturbs nothing beyond what care requires. Touching the weapon or moving the body can destroy evidence; anything moved should be reported to police.
w: Move the body to the bed so you can examine it more fully
Pick up the handgun on the floor to make the scene safe
Cover the body with a sheet from the bedroom closet

qs.q: You are treating a 24-year-old man with a stab wound to the chest. Police say this is a crime scene. You need to expose the wound. How should you remove his shirt?
qs.a: Cut around, not through, the hole in the fabric
qs.x: Cutting around a stab or bullet hole preserves evidence while still allowing full exposure. Patient care still comes first, but avoiding the defect is easy and protects the investigation.
w: Cut straight through the hole to save time
Pull the shirt off over his head to keep it whole
Leave the shirt on and assess only by palpation

qs.q: A 22-year-old woman reports being sexually assaulted 1 hour ago and is calm. She asks if she can shower before going to the hospital. What is the best response?
qs.a: Ask her not to shower, change, or wash before the exam
qs.x: Showering, changing, or using the bathroom can destroy evidence, so the EMT gently asks her to avoid this. Clothing is placed in separate paper bags because plastic traps moisture and degrades evidence.
w: Let her shower but place her clothes in a plastic trash bag
Let her shower because her comfort comes before evidence
Ask her to wash her hands only and then change her clothes

qs.q: You are dispatched to a rural home for a man with a dog bite to the arm. As you pull into the driveway, the caller yells that the dog is still loose in the yard. What should you do?
qs.a: Stay in the ambulance and request animal control or police
qs.x: An uncontrolled aggressive animal makes the scene unsafe. The crew stays in the vehicle until the animal is secured, asking the patient to come out only if that can be done safely.
w: Walk quickly from the ambulance to the porch with your jump kit
Use your stretcher as a shield while you move toward the house
Have your partner distract the dog while you go into the house

qs.q: You are dispatched to a campground for a 14-year-old bitten on the ankle by a snake. The father says the snake is still under the picnic table next to the boy. What is the best action?
qs.a: Move the boy away from the table, then assess him
qs.x: The snake is a continuing hazard, so the patient is moved away before care. Killing or capturing it risks more bites; a photo from a safe distance is enough if identification is needed.
w: Kill the snake so it can be brought to the hospital
Capture the snake in a cooler for identification
Assess the boy where he is while watching the snake

qs.q: You are first on scene where a school bus collided with a pickup truck. Many children are crying, several are walking around, and the pickup driver is not moving. What is your first priority as the first arriving unit?
qs.a: Size up, request more units, and begin triage
qs.x: At a multiple-casualty incident, the first unit establishes command, estimates the number of patients, requests resources early, and begins triage. Stopping to treat one patient leaves everyone else unassessed.
w: Start care on the unmoving pickup truck driver
Load the most injured child and transport
Call each child's parents to come to the scene

qs.q: At an MCI, you ask everyone who can walk to move to a marked area by the fire engine. Twelve patients walk there. Using START triage, how are they categorized?
qs.a: Minor (green), with reassessment later
qs.x: In START, patients who can walk are initially triaged as minor (green) and moved to one place, but they must be reassessed because some may deteriorate.
w: Delayed (yellow), pending secondary triage
Immediate (red), since they may worsen
Their category is not assigned until all are assessed

qs.q: During START triage, an adult is breathing at 36 breaths per minute. Radial pulse is present and he follows commands. What is his triage category?
qs.a: Immediate (red)
qs.x: In START, a respiratory rate over 30 in an adult places the patient in the immediate category without further assessment.
w: Delayed (yellow)
Minor (green)
Expectant (black)

qs.q: During START triage, a woman is breathing 24 times per minute, follows commands, and cannot walk. Her radial pulse is absent. What is her triage category?
qs.a: Immediate (red)
qs.x: In START, an absent radial pulse (or capillary refill over 2 seconds) indicates poor perfusion and makes the patient immediate, even if breathing and mental status are acceptable.
w: Delayed (yellow)
Minor (green)
Expectant (black)

qs.q: During START triage, a man with a leg injury cannot walk. He breathes 20 times per minute, has a radial pulse, and correctly follows commands. What is his triage category?
qs.a: Delayed (yellow)
qs.x: A non-ambulatory patient with a respiratory rate of 30 or less, a radial pulse, and the ability to follow commands is delayed in START.
w: Immediate (red)
Minor (green)
Expectant (black)

qs.q: During START triage, an unresponsive adult is not breathing. You reposition the airway and she begins breathing at 12 per minute. What should you do?
qs.a: Tag her immediate (red) and move on
qs.x: In START, a patient who begins breathing after airway repositioning is immediate. The triager tags and moves on rather than staying to provide prolonged care.
w: Tag her expectant (black) and move on
Stay with her and assist ventilations
Tag her delayed (yellow) and move on

qs.q: During JumpSTART triage at a daycare fire, a 3-year-old is not breathing after airway positioning but has a palpable pulse. What should you do next?
qs.a: Give 5 rescue breaths, then reassess breathing
qs.x: JumpSTART recognizes that apnea in children is often respiratory. An apneic child with a pulse receives 5 rescue breaths; if breathing resumes, the child is immediate, and if not, expectant.
w: Tag her expectant (black) and move to the next child
Begin CPR and stay with her until she is transported
Tag her immediate (red) without any breaths

qs.q: You arrive at a two-car crash. The driver of one car says she was alone, but you see an empty child safety seat in the back with a sippy cup on the floor. What should you do?
qs.a: Ask about a child and search for another patient
qs.x: Determining the number of patients is part of scene size-up. An empty car seat with signs of recent use suggests a possibly ejected or wandering child who must be searched for promptly.
w: Assume the seat was empty and focus on the driver only
Document the empty seat and look for a child later
Ask a bystander to check whether anyone else was there

qs.q: You are dispatched to a crash on a rural two-lane road. A pickup rolled several times, and the unrestrained driver was ejected. He is confused, and the nearest trauma center is a 60-minute drive away. Which resource should you request early?
qs.a: Air medical transport
qs.x: An ejection with altered mental status is a high-risk mechanism. With a long ground transport, early air medical activation shortens time to definitive trauma care.
w: A supervisor for documentation
A second BLS ambulance
A tow truck for the pickup

qs.q: You are guiding an air medical helicopter to a landing zone in a field. The aircraft has landed and the rotors are still turning. How should you approach the aircraft?
qs.a: From the front, in view of the pilot, only when signaled
qs.x: The tail rotor and the downhill side are danger zones. Approach only when the flight crew signals, from the front in the pilot's view, and keep equipment low.
w: From the rear, so you do not distract the pilot
From the uphill side with the stretcher raised
Any time, as long as you crouch below the rotors

qs.q: You arrive at a car that struck a tree. The driver is trapped with her legs pinned under the dashboard, and the front airbags did not deploy. Which action improves crew safety?
qs.a: Avoid the airbag deployment path and request fire/rescue
qs.x: Undeployed airbags can deploy unexpectedly and injure anyone in their path. Rescuers stay out of the deployment zone and request fire/rescue for extrication and vehicle stabilization.
w: Lean across the steering wheel to reach her head
Cut the steering wheel cover to see the airbag
Ask her to pull her legs free while you hold her

qs.q: You are assessing a driver with neck pain who is still seated in his car, not trapped, when you notice smoke and then flames coming from the engine compartment. Fire is still 5 minutes out. What is the best action?
qs.a: Perform an emergency move and get him out now
qs.x: When an immediate threat such as fire develops, an emergency move takes priority over full spinal precautions. Waiting or using time-consuming devices could cost the patient and crew their lives.
w: Apply a collar before moving him from the car
Continue assessment until fire arrives
Use a short spine board to remove him slowly

qs.q: You are dispatched to a farm for a 52-year-old man pinned under an overturned tractor. He is conscious and in pain. Bystanders are trying to lift the tractor with a farm jack. What is the best size-up action?
qs.a: Request fire/rescue and have bystanders stop
qs.x: An unstable vehicle can shift and crush rescuers or the patient. Lifting requires trained crews with proper cribbing and equipment, so EMS stops unsafe efforts and requests fire/rescue.
w: Help the bystanders lift the tractor quickly
Crawl under to assess him while they lift
Pull him out while they raise the tractor

qs.q: At a construction site, a worker is buried to his waist after a trench wall collapsed. Coworkers are digging him out by hand from inside the trench. What is the best action?
qs.a: Get everyone out and request trench rescue
qs.x: Trenches often collapse again, and machinery vibration increases the risk. Rescuers stay out, nearby equipment is shut down, and a trench rescue team is requested to shore the walls.
w: Climb into the trench to help dig and assess him
Have an excavator remove the soil around him
Throw a rope to him and pull him out of the soil

qs.q: You arrive at a city park in winter. A 9-year-old boy has fallen through the ice of a pond about 30 feet from shore and is clinging to the edge. What is the best action?
qs.a: Reach or throw from shore and request water rescue
qs.x: The rescue sequence is reach, throw, row, go. Rescuers without ice rescue training and equipment stay on shore and request a specialized team; walking or crawling onto ice risks a second victim.
w: Walk out on the ice slowly and carefully toward him
Crawl out on the ice to grab his arms
Wade into the pond to break a path to him

qs.q: During a heavy rainstorm, you see a car stalled in fast-moving water over a low-water crossing. The driver is on the roof waving. What should you do?
qs.a: Stay out of the water and request swift water rescue
qs.x: Moving water just a few inches deep can knock a person down, and a little more can float a vehicle. Responders without swift water training stay out and request a specialized team.
w: Wade in tethered to your partner to reach the car
Drive the ambulance through the water to reach him
Tell him to swim to you while you hold a rope

qs.q: You are dispatched to a clinic for a 45-year-old man with a 3-week cough, night sweats, weight loss, and blood in his sputum. What PPE is most appropriate?
qs.a: An N95 respirator for you, and a surgical mask on him
qs.x: These findings suggest tuberculosis, an airborne disease. Providers wear a fit-tested N95 respirator, and the patient wears a surgical mask if tolerated to reduce spread.
w: A surgical mask for you, and an N95 respirator on him
Gloves only, since he is not actively bleeding
A gown and gloves, without any mask or respirator

qs.q: You are dispatched to a home for a 58-year-old man vomiting large amounts of bright red blood. What PPE should you put on before contact?
qs.a: Gloves plus eye and face protection
qs.x: Splashing body fluids require gloves and eye and face protection, with a gown if heavy soiling is likely. An N95 is for airborne pathogens and does not protect against splashes to the eyes.
w: Gloves only, removed after care
An N95 respirator and gloves
A gown only, since gloves are not needed

qs.q: You are dispatched to a home for a woman in active labor. She is crowning on arrival. What is the most appropriate PPE?
qs.a: Gloves, gown, mask, and eye protection
qs.x: Childbirth involves large amounts of blood and amniotic fluid that can splash, so full standard precautions with gloves, gown, mask, and eye protection are appropriate.
w: Gloves only, since birth is not an exposure
A mask and gloves, without eye protection
An N95 respirator and gown, without gloves

qs.q: You are dispatched to a bank mailroom. A worker opened an envelope containing white powder, and three workers nearby have mild cough. What is the best action?
qs.a: Isolate the area, keep people in place, and request hazmat
qs.x: An unknown powder is a possible hazardous or biological agent. Exposed people are isolated to prevent spread, and hazmat manages decontamination; EMS should not handle the substance or contaminate its unit.
w: Enter in gloves and mask to bag the envelope and powder
Have the workers walk out to your ambulance for care
Sweep the powder into a bag and bring it to the ER

qs.q: You arrive at a rental house for a 30-year-old man with a burn on his hand. Inside you smell a strong chemical odor and see glass jars, tubing, and camp stove fuel on the kitchen table. What is the best action?
qs.a: Leave with the patient if possible and request police and hazmat
qs.x: These findings suggest a clandestine drug lab, which can contain toxic, flammable, or explosive chemicals. The crew withdraws, removes the patient if it can be done safely, and requests law enforcement and hazmat without touching anything.
w: Treat him in the kitchen while your partner opens the windows
Move the jars to the sink so no one knocks them over
Turn off the stove and remove the tubing before assessing him

qs.q: You are dispatched to a farm for a 28-year-old field worker with vomiting and excessive drooling. His clothing is wet with a pesticide sprayed an hour ago. What should happen before he is loaded into the ambulance?
qs.a: Remove his clothing and decontaminate him
qs.x: A contaminated patient can expose the crew and ambulance. Gross decontamination by removing clothing and washing the skin, done with proper PPE, comes before transport.
w: Place oxygen on him and load him quickly
Cover him with a blanket to prevent cooling
Have him change into dry clothes himself

qs.q: You are treating a 19-year-old man with a seizure at an outdoor concert. A crowd gathers, and several people begin shouting and shoving toward your crew. What is the best action?
qs.a: Move him to the ambulance quickly and request police
qs.x: When a crowd becomes hostile, the scene is no longer safe. Moving quickly to the ambulance and leaving the area while requesting law enforcement protects both the crew and the patient.
w: Stay in place and ask the crowd to calm down
Give the crowd a full update on his condition
Finish the full secondary exam where he lies

qs.q: You are dispatched to a high school football game for a player who was hit and is now lying motionless on the field. His teammates say he hit the other player helmet first. What does the mechanism suggest?
qs.a: Possible spinal injury needing motion restriction
qs.x: A helmet-first collision transmits axial load to the cervical spine. The mechanism alone raises suspicion for spinal injury, guiding precautions before moving him.
w: A muscle strain, as he is a fit young athlete
A minor bump, since his helmet absorbed all of the hit
Dehydration, requiring oral fluids on the field

qs.q: You are dispatched for an 81-year-old woman found at the bottom of her stairs. She says she "got dizzy and then fell." How should you approach her care?
qs.a: Assess both the injuries and the cause of the dizziness
qs.x: In older adults, a fall may be caused by a medical problem such as an arrhythmia or stroke. Both the mechanism of injury and the nature of illness must be evaluated.
w: Treat only the fall, since trauma is the obvious problem
Treat only the dizziness, as falls are minor in older adults
Focus on the stairs to see if a rug made her trip

qs.q: You are dispatched to an apartment for a 6-year-old with a broken arm. The parents give different stories about how it happened, and you notice bruises in different stages of healing on his back. Which action is most appropriate?
qs.a: Treat him, document objectively, and report per local law
qs.x: Inconsistent stories and multiple bruises in different stages suggest abuse. The EMT provides care, documents facts without accusing, and reports as required by law; confronting caregivers can make the scene unsafe.
w: Confront the parents about abuse before treating him
Call the police and wait for them before giving any care
Leave the child with the parents if they refuse care

qs.q: You are dispatched to a public pool for a lifeguard who collapsed in the pump room. Other staff report a strong chlorine smell and coughing near that room. What is the best action?
qs.a: Keep everyone away and request fire and hazmat
qs.x: Chlorine gas is a respiratory hazard, and a collapsed person in the room confirms dangerous levels. EMS stays out and requests responders with SCBA; a surgical mask provides no protection against gas.
w: Enter the pump room with a surgical mask to remove him
Open the pump room door wide to vent the gas out
Turn off the chlorinator and then remove the lifeguard

qs.q: You are dispatched to a two-story home that partially collapsed after a gas explosion. A woman is calling for help from under debris inside. What is the best action?
qs.a: Stay out and request fire, the gas utility, and collapse rescue
qs.x: A partly collapsed structure with a gas leak risks further collapse and explosion. EMS stays out and requests fire, the gas utility, and structural collapse rescue; shutting off the gas does not make the structure stable.
w: Enter carefully to reach her and assess her airway first
Shut off the gas meter and then go in to get her out
Clear debris from the doorway to make a path in to her

qs.q: A CNA is helping four residents who all take warfarin. Which finding should be described to the nurse first?
qs.a: Dark, tarry stool in the bedpan
qs.x: Dark tarry stool suggests bleeding into the gut, which is a much larger bleed than the bruising and gum oozing that are common on warfarin. The CNA describes what was seen; the nurse decides what happens next.
w: A small bruise on the shin from a walker
Pink gums after brushing with a soft brush
A paper cut that stopped bleeding in a minute

qs.q: A resident on warfarin has started eating a large spinach salad every day. Which part of this does the nurse need to know about?
qs.a: The large daily amount of a vitamin K food
qs.x: Warfarin works by blocking vitamin K, so a steady vitamin K intake keeps the INR steady. It is a sudden large change in intake, not greens themselves, that shifts the level.
w: The calories in the dressing she adds to it
The fiber content of the raw greens
The iron in the dark green leaves

qs.q: While shaving a resident who takes warfarin, the CNA should use:
qs.a: An electric razor
qs.x: Electric razors lower the risk of cuts and bleeding in residents on blood thinners.
w: A sharp disposable blade razor
The resident's old straight razor
Any razor, as long as it is pressed down firmly

qs.q: A resident on apixaban has gums that bleed heavily during mouth care. The CNA should:
qs.a: Stop, use a soft brush, and tell the nurse
qs.x: Apixaban (Eliquis) is a blood thinner. Bleeding gums should be reported, and a soft toothbrush should be used.
w: Brush harder to remove the plaque causing it
Skip mouth care for the rest of the week
Rinse with hot salt water and not report it

qs.q: A resident on apixaban fell and hit her head two hours ago and says she feels fine. Which new finding should the CNA describe to the nurse first?
qs.a: She is harder to wake than she was at lunch
qs.x: A rising level of drowsiness points to bleeding inside the skull, which an anticoagulant such as apixaban makes more likely and which can appear hours after a fall that looked minor.
w: She has a small bruise forming on her forehead
She says her neck feels stiff after the fall
She asks for acetaminophen for a headache

qs.q: Two residents have black stools. One takes daily aspirin and one takes a ferrous sulfate tablet. What should the CNA tell the nurse?
qs.a: Both stools, because color alone does not sort out the cause
qs.x: Iron can darken stool harmlessly, but aspirin can cause stomach bleeding, which also looks black and tarry. The CNA cannot tell them apart at the bedside, so both get described to the nurse.
w: Only the aspirin resident, since iron always darkens the stool
Only the iron resident, since aspirin does not affect stool
Neither, because black stool is expected with both pills

qs.q: Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is commonly used to:
qs.a: Relieve mild pain and reduce fever
qs.x: Acetaminophen is a pain reliever and fever reducer.
w: Thin the blood and prevent stroke
Lower blood pressure and heart rate
Treat infections caused by bacteria in the bladder

qs.q: A resident is scheduled for acetaminophen and also takes hydrocodone-acetaminophen for pain. Why does the nurse want to know about every dose the resident gets?
qs.a: The two products add up toward a daily acetaminophen limit
qs.x: Many combination pain pills contain acetaminophen, and the total from all sources is capped at about 3000 to 4000 mg a day in adults because higher totals injure the liver.
w: Acetaminophen cancels out the pain relief from the hydrocodone
Taking both at once raises the risk of stomach bleeding
Acetaminophen makes hydrocodone leave the body faster

qs.q: Metformin is used to treat:
qs.a: Type 2 diabetes
qs.x: Metformin lowers blood sugar in people with type 2 diabetes.
w: High cholesterol
Pain from arthritis
Seasonal allergies

qs.q: A resident who started metformin has loose stools and an upset stomach. The CNA should:
qs.a: Report the symptoms to the nurse
qs.x: Stomach upset and diarrhea are common metformin side effects and should be reported. The CNA does not change medicines.
w: Stop giving the resident any food
Tell the resident to skip the next pill
Give the resident an anti-diarrhea pill from the cart

qs.q: A resident on insulin is shaky, sweaty, and confused before lunch. The CNA should first:
qs.a: Stay with the resident and call the nurse
qs.x: These are signs of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). The CNA should get the nurse right away and follow the care plan.
w: Have the resident lie down for a nap
Give the resident a glass of water
Leave to find the resident's family

qs.q: The care plan for a resident on insulin says to give 4 ounces of juice for signs of low blood sugar. The resident is sweaty and shaky but alert. The CNA should:
qs.a: Give the juice per the care plan and tell the nurse
qs.x: The CNA follows the care plan for a hypoglycemia snack and reports to the nurse. The CNA never gives insulin.
w: Give a full meal and wait an hour before telling anyone
Withhold all food and fluids until the doctor arrives
Give the juice and then the resident's next insulin dose

qs.q: A resident was given lispro insulin and then ate none of lunch. About how soon would the CNA expect signs of low blood sugar?
qs.a: Within about 15 to 60 minutes
qs.x: Lispro is rapid-acting: it starts working in roughly 15 minutes and peaks about 1 hour after the injection, so a skipped meal shows up quickly, unlike long-acting insulins that peak many hours later.
w: Not until about 8 hours later
Only after the next morning dose
Within about 10 to 12 hours

qs.q: A resident who gets NPH insulin is very hard to wake at 3 a.m. and is sweating. The CNA should:
qs.a: Call the nurse right away
qs.x: Low blood sugar can happen overnight with intermediate-acting insulin. Trouble waking is an emergency.
w: Let the resident sleep until morning
Change the damp sheets and leave the room
Give the resident a sleeping pill so they rest better

qs.q: Glipizide is a diabetes pill that can cause:
qs.a: Low blood sugar
qs.x: Glipizide makes the pancreas release more insulin, so low blood sugar is a key risk, especially if meals are missed.
w: Hair loss
High blood sugar
Ringing in the ears from too much fluid

qs.q: A resident who ate only a few bites of breakfast takes glipizide, and her roommate who also ate little takes metformin. Which resident should the CNA mention to the nurse first, and why?
qs.a: The glipizide resident, because that pill can drop blood sugar on its own
qs.x: Glipizide makes the pancreas release insulin whether or not food was eaten, so a missed meal can cause hypoglycemia. Metformin rarely causes low blood sugar by itself.
w: The metformin resident, because metformin also lowers blood sugar on its own
The glipizide resident, because glipizide needs food to be absorbed
Neither, because both pills are safe when a meal is skipped

qs.q: The CNA checks a resident's blood sugar as delegated and gets a reading of 52. The CNA should:
qs.a: Report the result to the nurse at once
qs.x: A low reading must be reported right away. Only trained, delegated CNAs check glucose, and they always report results.
w: Write it down and report it at shift change
Recheck it in two hours before telling anyone
Give the resident's scheduled insulin to bring it down

qs.q: A resident on lisinopril says the room spins when she first stands. What should the CNA measure and report to make this useful to the nurse?
qs.a: Blood pressure and pulse lying down and then standing
qs.x: Orthostatic readings show the drop that happens on standing. A fall of about 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic on standing is the finding the nurse is looking for.
w: Blood pressure in both arms while she is sitting quietly
Pulse before and after she walks down the hall
Temperature and pulse once she is back in bed

qs.q: Lisinopril is used to treat:
qs.a: High blood pressure
qs.x: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor that lowers blood pressure and protects the heart and kidneys.
w: Low thyroid
Constipation
Bladder spasms caused by an overactive bladder

qs.q: A resident on lisinopril has sudden swelling of the lips and tongue. The CNA should:
qs.a: Call for the nurse immediately
qs.x: Swelling of the face, lips, or tongue (angioedema) is a rare but dangerous lisinopril reaction that can block the airway.
w: Offer the resident ice chips and wait
Apply lotion to the lips and recheck later
Lay the resident flat and give a glass of water

qs.q: Amlodipine is a medicine for:
qs.a: High blood pressure
qs.x: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker that relaxes blood vessels to lower blood pressure.
w: Heartburn
Depression
Fungal infections of the skin and mouth

qs.q: A resident on amlodipine has swelling in both ankles. Which additional observation would make the nurse most concerned about something beyond the amlodipine?
qs.a: New shortness of breath when lying flat
qs.x: Amlodipine commonly causes ankle edema by dilating blood vessels in the legs, without fluid in the lungs. Breathlessness lying flat points to fluid overload from the heart instead.
w: Shoes feeling snug by the end of the day
Sock marks on both lower legs at bedtime
Swelling that is equal on the right and left

qs.q: A CNA takes vital signs before the morning metoprolol. Which set should be reported to the nurse before the dose is given?
qs.a: Pulse 48 and regular, blood pressure 118/70
qs.x: Metoprolol slows conduction through the heart, and doses are commonly held for a rate under 60. A rate of 48 crosses that line even though the blood pressure looks fine.
w: Pulse 72 and regular, blood pressure 128/78
Pulse 88 and regular, blood pressure 140/86
Pulse 64 and regular, blood pressure 110/68

qs.q: A resident on furosemide will likely need to:
qs.a: Use the bathroom more often
qs.x: Furosemide (Lasix) is a water pill that increases urine output, so toileting help is often needed.
w: Eat a high-salt diet each day
Stay in bed most of the day
Avoid drinking any fluids at all for the whole day

qs.q: The care plan for a resident on furosemide says daily weights. The CNA should weigh the resident:
qs.a: At the same time each day on the same scale
qs.x: Daily weights must be consistent (same time, scale, and clothing) so changes in fluid can be seen.
w: At any time of day on any available scale
Only when the resident looks swollen
After meals, wearing as many layers as possible

qs.q: A resident on daily weights for furosemide weighed 162 pounds yesterday. Which weight today should the CNA report to the nurse?
qs.a: 165 pounds
qs.x: A gain of about 2 to 3 pounds in a day is roughly 1 to 1.5 liters of retained fluid, which is the usual threshold for reporting. Small up-and-down changes of a pound are ordinary.
w: 161 pounds
162 pounds
160 pounds

qs.q: A resident on furosemide is on intake and output (I&O). The CNA should:
qs.a: Measure and record all fluids taken in and urine passed
qs.x: Accurate I&O helps the nurse see whether the water pill is working and if the resident is dehydrated.
w: Record only the water the resident drinks at meals
Estimate the totals at the end of the shift
Measure urine only if it looks dark

qs.q: Bumetanide, like furosemide, is a:
qs.a: Water pill (diuretic)
qs.x: Bumetanide is a loop diuretic that removes extra fluid, so I&O and daily weights matter.
w: Sleeping pill
Thyroid hormone
Pain reliever used for arthritis

qs.q: A resident with heart failure is on daily weights. Which finding tells the nurse the most about fluid building up?
qs.a: A 4 pound weight gain over two days
qs.x: Daily weight is the most sensitive measure of fluid gain and changes before swelling or breathlessness is obvious; 4 pounds is about 2 liters of fluid.
w: Reporting feeling tired in the afternoon
Needing two pillows instead of one at night
Ankles that look puffy after sitting up

qs.q: Spironolactone is a water pill that can raise potassium. A CNA should report:
qs.a: Muscle weakness or an irregular pulse
qs.x: High potassium can cause weakness and heart rhythm problems. Report these signs.
w: An increase in appetite at breakfast
Hair that looks shinier than usual
A preference for sitting by the window

qs.q: Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) is a water pill. It is best for residents to take it in the morning so that:
qs.a: They are not up at night to urinate
qs.x: Diuretics increase urination, so morning dosing helps prevent nighttime trips to the bathroom and falls.
w: Their meals taste better at lunch
It works better on an empty stomach at night
Their blood sugar stays high all day long

qs.q: Digoxin is a heart medicine. A CNA should report if the resident has:
qs.a: Nausea, poor appetite, or seeing yellow-green halos
qs.x: Nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, and vision changes can be signs of digoxin toxicity.
w: A good appetite and steady weight
A normal pulse of 72 and no complaints
Better sleep than usual over the last week

qs.q: The nurse asks the CNA to count an apical or radial pulse before the resident's digoxin. The CNA should:
qs.a: Count for one full minute and report it
qs.x: Counting a full minute is accurate and important because digoxin can slow or change the heart rhythm.
w: Count for 10 seconds and multiply by six
Guess based on how the resident looks
Count for 15 seconds and only report if high

qs.q: Potassium chloride is given to residents who:
qs.a: Have low potassium, often from water pills
qs.x: Diuretics like furosemide can lower potassium, so a potassium supplement is often added.
w: Have high blood sugar after meals
Need help falling asleep at night
Have a yeast infection in the mouth

qs.q: A resident says the potassium chloride tablet is too large to swallow. What should the CNA tell the nurse about why this matters?
qs.a: The tablet is extended release and cannot simply be crushed
qs.x: Most oral potassium chloride is extended release, and crushing it dumps the whole dose onto the stomach lining and can cause ulceration. The nurse or pharmacy can switch to a liquid or powder form.
w: Potassium tablets lose all strength when they get wet
The tablet has to be given on a completely empty stomach each day
Potassium tablets must be taken without any liquid

qs.q: Four residents on atorvastatin report aches. Which complaint should the CNA describe to the nurse first?
qs.a: Aching weakness in both thighs with dark brown urine
qs.x: Statin muscle injury is symmetrical and affects the large muscles, and dark urine suggests myoglobin from breaking down muscle, which can damage the kidneys. One-sided aches after activity point to strain.
w: Soreness in one shoulder after a physical therapy session
Stiff knees that loosen up after walking in the morning
A sore calf the day after a long walk outdoors

qs.q: A resident asks for grapefruit juice at breakfast. She takes simvastatin and her roommate takes pravastatin. Which should the CNA raise with the nurse?
qs.a: The simvastatin resident, because grapefruit raises its blood level
qs.x: Grapefruit blocks the CYP3A4 enzyme that clears simvastatin, so levels rise and muscle injury becomes more likely. Pravastatin is not cleared by that enzyme.
w: Both residents, because grapefruit blocks every statin in the same way
The pravastatin resident, because grapefruit weakens that drug
Neither, because grapefruit only matters with blood thinners

qs.q: Levothyroxine is used to treat:
qs.a: An underactive thyroid
qs.x: Levothyroxine (Synthroid) replaces thyroid hormone when the thyroid is underactive.
w: An overactive bladder
High blood pressure
Swelling caused by too much fluid in the legs

qs.q: After meals, a resident with heartburn should be positioned:
qs.a: Sitting upright for at least 30 minutes
qs.x: Staying upright after meals helps keep stomach acid from coming back up.
w: Lying flat on the back right after eating
Lying on the stomach with no pillow
In any position the CNA finds easiest

qs.q: Pantoprazole is in the same group as omeprazole and is used to:
qs.a: Reduce stomach acid
qs.x: Pantoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that lowers stomach acid.
w: Raise blood pressure
Thin the blood
Help the resident make more urine

qs.q: Famotidine (Pepcid) is used to:
qs.a: Lower stomach acid
qs.x: Famotidine blocks acid production and treats heartburn and ulcers.
w: Treat an infection of the toenails
Raise potassium levels
Stop seizures in residents with epilepsy

qs.q: Docusate is a stool softener. The CNA can help it work by:
qs.a: Offering fluids as allowed by the care plan
qs.x: Stool softeners pull water into stool; enough fluid makes them work better.
w: Limiting water so stools stay firm
Keeping the resident in bed all day
Serving mostly white bread and cheese

qs.q: A resident on docusate has not had a bowel movement in 4 days. The CNA should:
qs.a: Report it to the nurse
qs.x: The CNA tracks and reports bowel movements. Treatment is decided by the nurse.
w: Give an enema from the supply closet
Give the resident a laxative from home
Wait until the end of the week to report

qs.q: A resident on senna has cramping and many watery stools today. The CNA should:
qs.a: Report the diarrhea to the nurse
qs.x: Too many loose stools can lead to dehydration. The CNA reports it so the nurse can review the laxative.
w: Give the senna dose anyway at bedtime
Stop offering fluids so stools firm up
Do nothing since laxatives always cause this

qs.q: Polyethylene glycol (MiraLAX) is a powder that is:
qs.a: Mixed in a drink to treat constipation
qs.x: MiraLAX is mixed with liquid and draws water into the bowel to soften stool.
w: Rubbed on the skin to treat a rash
Inhaled to open the airways
Sprinkled on food to raise the blood sugar

qs.q: Milk of Magnesia (magnesium hydroxide) is commonly used for:
qs.a: Constipation or upset stomach
qs.x: Magnesium hydroxide is a laxative and antacid.
w: Seasonal allergies
Dry eyes
Low thyroid hormone

qs.q: Bisacodyl is a laxative that may come as a suppository. A CNA should:
qs.a: Not insert it unless state rules and training allow
qs.x: Inserting medicated suppositories is medication administration and is usually outside the CNA role.
w: Insert it whenever the resident is constipated
Cut it in half to make it work more slowly
Store it in the resident's drawer for later

qs.q: A resident on lactulose has frequent soft stools. The CNA should especially:
qs.a: Give good perineal care and watch the skin
qs.x: Frequent stools can break down skin. Good perineal care and reporting skin changes help prevent pressure sores.
w: Limit fluids so the stools firm up
Keep the resident in the same brief all shift
Ask the resident to hold the stool in

qs.q: A resident who takes oxycodone often has which bowel problem?
qs.a: Constipation
qs.x: Opioids slow the bowels and commonly cause constipation. Track and report bowel movements.
w: Diarrhea
Bright red bleeding
Very pale stools from liver failure

qs.q: A resident on oxycodone is very sleepy, hard to wake, and breathing 8 times a minute. The CNA should:
qs.a: Call the nurse immediately and stay
qs.x: Slow breathing and trouble waking are signs of opioid overdose, a medical emergency.
w: Let the resident sleep it off quietly
Recheck the breathing in an hour
Give the resident coffee to wake them up

qs.q: A resident on hydrocodone-acetaminophen (Norco) should be watched for:
qs.a: Drowsiness, dizziness, and constipation
qs.x: Hydrocodone is an opioid. Sleepiness, dizziness, falls, and constipation are common concerns.
w: Increased energy and trouble sleeping
Dark spots appearing on the fingernails
A faster heartbeat and a much higher blood sugar

qs.q: A resident waiting for a dose of hydrocodone says the pain is 8 out of 10. Which description would be most useful to the nurse?
qs.a: Where the pain is, what it feels like, and when it started
qs.x: A location, a quality and a time course let the nurse judge whether this is the expected pain or something new, such as a fracture or an abdomen that has become rigid. A number alone does not.
w: That the resident seems to be in a great deal of discomfort
That the resident has asked about pain twice today
That the resident rates the pain higher than yesterday

qs.q: A resident on morphine has pinpoint pupils and shallow breathing. The CNA should:
qs.a: Get the nurse right away
qs.x: Small pupils, slow or shallow breathing, and sleepiness are signs of opioid overdose.
w: Raise the head of the bed and leave
Offer a snack and fluids
Write it down to tell the doctor next week

qs.q: A resident wears a fentanyl patch. Which thing noticed during the bath should be mentioned to the nurse because it can raise the amount of drug absorbed?
qs.a: A heating pad has been left on over the patch site
qs.x: Heat increases blood flow and the rate drug crosses the skin, so a heating pad over a fentanyl patch can cause a dangerous rise in absorption. Normal bathing and a 72 hour wear time are expected.
w: The patch has been in place for about two days
The patch is on the upper back rather than the chest
The resident showered with warm water this morning

qs.q: A CNA finds a used fentanyl patch on the bed linen. Why does the CNA handle it with gloves rather than bare fingers?
qs.a: A used patch still holds drug that absorbs through skin
qs.x: A patch is built as a drug reservoir and a good deal of fentanyl remains when it comes off, so skin contact can dose the person handling it. The nurse witnesses disposal.
w: A used patch is sharp and can cut the fingers
A used patch grows bacteria once it leaves the skin
A used patch loses its backing and leaks drug into the air

qs.q: A resident has chest pain and asks the CNA to hand over the nitroglycerin bottle on the nightstand. The CNA should:
qs.a: Stay and call the nurse right away
qs.x: Chest pain is an emergency. The CNA stays with the resident and gets the nurse, who handles the medicine.
w: Hand over the bottle since it belongs to them
Place a tablet under the resident's tongue
Tell the resident to rest and come back later

qs.q: After a resident gets nitroglycerin, the CNA should watch for:
qs.a: Dizziness, headache, or low blood pressure
qs.x: Nitroglycerin can drop blood pressure and cause headache and dizziness, so help prevent falls.
w: Increased appetite and weight gain
Itchy eyes and a runny nose
A rise in blood sugar after the resident eats

qs.q: Isosorbide mononitrate is taken daily to:
qs.a: Prevent chest pain
qs.x: Long-acting nitrates like isosorbide help prevent angina episodes.
w: Prevent seizures
Treat a cold
Prevent blood clots after surgery on the hip

qs.q: After an albuterol treatment, a resident says his heart is racing and his hands are shaky. The CNA should:
qs.a: Report it to the nurse
qs.x: A fast heart rate and shakiness are common albuterol side effects. Report them to the nurse.
w: Give the resident another puff to calm him
Tell him to stop using the inhaler for good
Ignore it since it will pass on its own

qs.q: A resident with COPD uses tiotropium every morning and also has an albuterol inhaler. He is more short of breath than usual. What is true about the tiotropium?
qs.a: It is a daily maintenance inhaler, not a rescue inhaler
qs.x: Tiotropium is a long-acting bronchodilator taken once a day to prevent symptoms; albuterol is the rescue inhaler that works in minutes. Knowing which is which tells the nurse what the resident needs now.
w: It should be given a second time whenever breathing worsens
It works within a minute or two of being inhaled
It replaces the albuterol inhaler once started

qs.q: A resident uses a steroid inhaler (fluticasone). Afterward, the resident should usually:
qs.a: Rinse the mouth and spit
qs.x: Rinsing after inhaled steroids helps prevent thrush (a yeast infection of the mouth).
w: Eat a snack right away
Lie flat for 20 minutes
Drink milk to coat the throat

qs.q: Which is the most important oxygen safety rule?
qs.a: No smoking or open flames near oxygen
qs.x: Oxygen feeds fire. No smoking, candles, or flames near oxygen, and secure tanks upright.
w: Store tanks lying loose on the floor
Use petroleum jelly on the nose for dryness
Turn the flow up whenever the resident is short of breath

qs.q: A resident on 2 liters of oxygen by nasal cannula is more short of breath. Which observation should the CNA report along with the breathlessness?
qs.a: The tubing is kinked under the wheel of the recliner
qs.x: A kink stops flow no matter what the flowmeter reads, and checking the delivery path is within the CNA role. Prongs curve down by design, and a raised head of the bed helps rather than hurts.
w: The resident wears the cannula with the prongs curved down
The concentrator has been running since early this morning
The head of the bed is raised about 30 degrees

qs.q: A resident's family member lights a candle in a room where oxygen is in use. The CNA should:
qs.a: Ask them to put it out right away and explain why
qs.x: Open flames near oxygen can cause a fire. The candle must be put out.
w: Move the candle to the other side of the bed
Let it burn since the oxygen tank is closed
Turn off the oxygen so the candle is safe

qs.q: Where should a portable oxygen tank be kept?
qs.a: Secured upright in a holder or cart
qs.x: Tanks should be secured so they cannot fall and be damaged.
w: Lying on the floor under the bed
Next to the space heater to keep it warm
Leaning against the wall by the door

qs.q: A resident on donepezil has nausea, diarrhea, and a slow pulse. The CNA should:
qs.a: Report these signs to the nurse
qs.x: Donepezil can cause stomach upset and a slow heart rate. These signs should be reported.
w: Stop all of the resident's meals for the day
Give the resident extra fiber and fluids
Encourage the resident to walk around more

qs.q: Memantine (Namenda) is used to treat:
qs.a: Alzheimer's dementia
qs.x: Memantine is given for moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease.
w: Heartburn
Diabetes
Infections caused by fungus on the skin

qs.q: A resident with Parkinson's disease is very shaky and stiff late in the afternoon. The CNA should:
qs.a: Report the change to the nurse
qs.x: Symptoms can return when the medicine wears off. The nurse needs to know so timing can be reviewed.
w: Give the resident's next dose early
Tie the resident's hands to stop shaking
Tell the resident to try harder to move

qs.q: A resident on carbidopa-levodopa gets dizzy when standing. The CNA should:
qs.a: Have the resident stand up slowly
qs.x: This medicine can cause low blood pressure when standing. The resident should rise slowly, and fall precautions should be used.
w: Have the resident jump up quickly
Keep the resident in bed all day
Walk the resident without a gait belt

qs.q: A resident on sertraline says she wants to end her life. The CNA should:
qs.a: Stay with her and tell the nurse right away
qs.x: Any talk of suicide must be reported immediately. The CNA should not leave the resident alone.
w: Promise to keep it a secret
Tell her to cheer up and leave the room
Wait to report it at the end of the shift

qs.q: A resident recently started an antidepressant (escitalopram). The CNA should report:
qs.a: New confusion, falls, or mood changes
qs.x: Changes in mood, behavior, or new confusion should be reported, especially when a medicine is new.
w: That the resident ate all of lunch
That the resident watched TV today
That the resident wants to call a friend

qs.q: Mirtazapine may be given to an older resident for depression. A common side effect is:
qs.a: Sleepiness and increased appetite
qs.x: Mirtazapine often causes drowsiness and weight gain, so watch for falls.
w: Severe weight loss
Black stools
Very fast breathing and a high fever

qs.q: A resident takes trazodone at bedtime for sleep. The CNA should:
qs.a: Use fall precautions if the resident gets up at night
qs.x: Trazodone can cause drowsiness and dizziness, raising the fall risk at night.
w: Wake the resident every hour to check alertness
Walk the resident alone with no gait belt
Raise all bed rails without an order

qs.q: An 84 year old resident was started on lorazepam yesterday. Which change should the CNA describe to the nurse first?
qs.a: Unsteady walking with two near falls today
qs.x: New unsteadiness is the finding that predicts a hip fracture, and benzodiazepine effects are stronger and last longer in older adults. Sleeping a little longer and less anxiety are expected effects.
w: Sleeping about an hour longer this morning
Asking for help to the bathroom at night
Feeling less worried than she did last week

qs.q: A resident who takes alprazolam is drowsy at breakfast and keeps nodding off with food in her mouth. Which risk should the CNA act on first?
qs.a: Choking and aspiration while she is being fed
qs.x: A sedated resident cannot protect her airway, so aspiration is the immediate danger. Feeding stops and she is positioned upright while the nurse is told about the sedation.
w: Dry mouth from the medicine at breakfast
Losing weight from a poor appetite over several weeks
Spilling hot coffee on her lap at the table

qs.q: A resident takes zolpidem at bedtime. Which observation from the night shift is most important for the CNA to pass on?
qs.a: Walking in the hall at 2 a.m. with no memory of it
qs.x: Zolpidem can cause complex sleep behaviors such as walking or eating with no recall, which carry a real injury risk and are a reason the drug is reconsidered. Falling asleep in about 20 minutes is the expected effect.
w: Fell asleep about 20 minutes after taking the pill
Slept through the night without getting up
Woke once to use the bathroom and went back to sleep

qs.q: Temazepam is a sleeping pill. Because of this medicine, the CNA should:
qs.a: Keep the call light within reach at night
qs.x: Sleeping pills raise fall risk. Keep the bed low, the call light close, and the path lit.
w: Leave the bed in the highest position
Turn off the night light to help sleep
Put the walker in the closet overnight

qs.q: Quetiapine (Seroquel) is an antipsychotic. The CNA should watch for:
qs.a: Sleepiness and dizziness when standing
qs.x: Quetiapine causes sedation and low blood pressure on standing, increasing fall risk.
w: Increased energy and fast weight loss
Bleeding gums when brushing the teeth
Coughing up thick, yellow mucus each morning

qs.q: A resident on haloperidol has new stiffness, shuffling, and lip smacking. The CNA should:
qs.a: Report the movements to the nurse
qs.x: Antipsychotics can cause movement side effects. These must be reported.
w: Tell the resident to stop making faces
Ignore it since it is part of dementia
Massage the muscles until they loosen

qs.q: Antipsychotics such as risperidone should never be used in a nursing home to:
qs.a: Keep a resident quiet for staff convenience
qs.x: Using medicines to control behavior for staff convenience is a chemical restraint and is not allowed.
w: Treat a diagnosed mental illness as ordered
Help with hallucinations that frighten the resident
Treat symptoms that put the resident or others at risk

qs.q: Gabapentin is often used for nerve pain. A common side effect is:
qs.a: Dizziness and sleepiness
qs.x: Gabapentin can cause dizziness and drowsiness, raising fall risk in older adults.
w: Sudden hair growth
Purple urine
A dry cough and a sore throat that lasts for weeks

qs.q: A resident on tamsulosin gets dizzy getting out of bed. The CNA should:
qs.a: Have him sit on the edge of the bed first
qs.x: Tamsulosin can cause low blood pressure on standing. The resident should dangle first and rise slowly.
w: Help him stand up as fast as possible
Tell him to skip his next dose
Leave him alone to walk to the bathroom

qs.q: Oxybutynin is used for an overactive bladder. A CNA might notice:
qs.a: Dry mouth and constipation
qs.x: Oxybutynin is anticholinergic and often causes dry mouth, constipation, and confusion in older adults.
w: Very watery eyes
Excess saliva
Frequent loose stools and a large appetite

qs.q: A resident on prednisone should be watched for:
qs.a: Higher blood sugar and infection
qs.x: Steroids raise blood sugar, weaken the immune system, and can thin the skin.
w: Lower blood sugar and weight loss
Very slow pulse
Dark brown teeth

qs.q: A resident started on cephalexin today has a new red, itchy rash on the chest. The CNA should:
qs.a: Report the rash to the nurse right away
qs.x: A new rash after starting an antibiotic may be an allergic reaction and must be reported.
w: Apply lotion and check again tomorrow
Tell the resident to stop the antibiotic
Cover the rash so others do not see it

qs.q: A resident on nitrofurantoin has dark brown urine. The CNA should:
qs.a: Report it to the nurse
qs.x: Nitrofurantoin can darken urine, but any color change should be reported so the nurse can check.
w: Throw away the urine without recording it
Give cranberry juice and not report
Change the catheter without asking
