qs.x: Bile acid sequestrants can raise triglycerides; they also cause GI upset and reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and many drugs.
w: Cholesterol gallstone formation
Facial flushing after each dose
Elevated creatine kinase

qs.q: A 38-year-old man with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia remains above his LDL goal on a statin and ezetimibe. He starts a subcutaneous monoclonal antibody every 2 weeks. What is its target?
qs.a: PCSK9
qs.x: Evolocumab binds PCSK9, preventing LDL receptor degradation and increasing LDL clearance.
w: HMG-CoA reductase
NPC1L1
Apolipoprotein B-100 mRNA

qs.q: A 22-year-old man with secondary syphilis receives IM benzathine penicillin G. Which bacterial process does this drug inhibit?
qs.a: Peptidoglycan cross-linking by transpeptidases
qs.x: Penicillins bind penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases), blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking.
w: Polymerization of peptidoglycan by binding D-Ala-D-Ala
Synthesis of mycolic acids in the cell envelope
Formation of the 30S initiation complex

qs.q: A 30-year-old man who injects drugs has methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia, and the isolate produces penicillinase. Why is nafcillin effective against this organism?
qs.a: Its bulky side chain blocks beta-lactamase access
qs.x: Nafcillin and oxacillin have bulky R groups that protect the beta-lactam ring from penicillinase; they do not cover MRSA.
w: It irreversibly inactivates bacterial beta-lactamase
It binds altered PBP2a with high affinity
It binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini of cell wall precursors

qs.q: A 6-year-old boy with acute otitis media fails amoxicillin therapy because of a beta-lactamase-producing Moraxella. He is switched to amoxicillin-clavulanate. What is the role of clavulanate?
qs.a: Inhibits beta-lactamase enzymes
qs.x: Clavulanate is a suicide inhibitor of many beta-lactamases, protecting amoxicillin; probenecid is the drug that blocks tubular secretion.
w: Increases penetration through porins
Binds additional penicillin-binding proteins
Blocks renal tubular secretion of amoxicillin

qs.q: A 70-year-old man has enterococcal bacteremia that is resistant to vancomycin. What is the molecular basis of this resistance?
qs.a: Terminal D-Ala-D-Ala changed to D-Ala-D-Lac
qs.x: Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala; VRE replaces it with D-Ala-D-Lac, which vancomycin binds poorly.
w: Production of an altered PBP2a transpeptidase
Methylation of the 23S ribosomal RNA
Plasmid-encoded vancomycin acetyltransferase

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman receiving her first dose of IV vancomycin develops flushing and pruritus of the face, neck and upper chest. Her blood pressure is stable. Which measure is most appropriate?
qs.a: Slow the infusion and give an antihistamine
qs.x: The vancomycin infusion reaction is caused by non-IgE histamine release from mast cells; it is not a true allergy and responds to slower infusion and antihistamines.
w: Stop the drug permanently and give epinephrine
Switch to IV nafcillin for the full course
Give IV methylprednisolone and continue

qs.q: A 5-day-old neonate with suspected bacterial sepsis has significant jaundice. The team chooses cefotaxime rather than ceftriaxone. What is the main reason?
qs.a: Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin
qs.x: Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin (risk of kernicterus) and precipitates with IV calcium in neonates.
w: Ceftriaxone does not cross the blood-brain barrier
Ceftriaxone lacks activity against group B streptococci
Ceftriaxone causes gray baby syndrome

qs.q: A 64-year-old woman has a skin and soft tissue infection with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. She receives the only cephalosporin with reliable MRSA activity. Why does it work?
qs.a: It binds PBP2a with high affinity
qs.x: Ceftaroline, a fifth-generation cephalosporin, binds the altered PBP2a of MRSA.
w: It resists hydrolysis by penicillinase
It binds the D-Ala-D-Ala cell wall terminus
It inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit

qs.q: A 54-year-old man with a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin has Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia. Which beta-lactam can most safely be given?
qs.a: Aztreonam
qs.x: Aztreonam is a monobactam with minimal cross-reactivity with penicillins; it covers only gram-negative rods, including Pseudomonas.
w: Cefepime
Meropenem
Piperacillin

qs.q: A 72-year-old man with renal impairment is treated for a polymicrobial abdominal abscess with imipenem-cilastatin and has a generalized seizure. What is the role of cilastatin?
qs.a: Inhibits renal dehydropeptidase I
qs.x: Cilastatin inhibits renal dehydropeptidase I, preventing imipenem inactivation; carbapenems lower the seizure threshold.
w: Inhibits bacterial beta-lactamases
Blocks renal tubular secretion of imipenem
Prevents the seizures caused by imipenem

qs.q: A 52-year-old woman has a liver abscess with Bacteroides fragilis. Why would gentamicin alone be ineffective?
qs.a: Its uptake into bacteria requires oxygen
qs.x: Aminoglycoside uptake requires oxygen-dependent transport, so anaerobes are intrinsically resistant.
w: Anaerobes lack a 30S ribosomal subunit
Anaerobes inactivate it by acetylation
It cannot penetrate the abscess capsule

qs.q: A 76-year-old man with enterococcal endocarditis receives ampicillin and gentamicin. During treatment he is also given high-dose IV furosemide. Which toxicity is now of greatest concern?
qs.a: Ototoxicity
qs.x: Aminoglycosides and loop diuretics both damage the inner ear; combined use increases ototoxicity and also nephrotoxicity.
w: Hepatotoxicity
Optic neuritis
Pancreatitis

qs.q: A 24-year-old woman with Lyme disease takes doxycycline with her daily calcium carbonate and iron supplement, and her infection responds poorly. What is the mechanism of this interaction?
qs.a: Chelation by divalent cations reducing absorption
qs.x: Tetracyclines chelate calcium, magnesium, aluminum and iron, sharply reducing oral absorption.
w: Induction of CYP3A4 increasing drug clearance
Raised gastric pH preventing tablet dissolution
Increased renal tubular secretion of the drug

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman with Rocky Mountain spotted fever is treated with doxycycline. How does this drug stop bacterial protein synthesis?
qs.a: Blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding at the 30S A site
qs.x: Tetracyclines bind the 30S subunit and prevent aminoacyl-tRNA from attaching to the acceptor (A) site.
w: Blocks peptidyl transferase on the 50S subunit
Causes misreading of mRNA codons at the 30S
Prevents translocation along the 50S subunit

qs.q: A 68-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia is given azithromycin. Which molecular target does this drug bind?
qs.a: 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit
qs.x: Macrolides bind 23S rRNA on the 50S subunit and block translocation; they can prolong the QT interval.
w: 16S rRNA of the 30S subunit
DNA gyrase subunit A
Penicillin-binding protein 3

qs.q: A 52-year-old woman with diabetic gastroparesis is given low-dose erythromycin to improve gastric emptying. Which mechanism explains this effect?
qs.a: Agonism at motilin receptors
qs.x: Macrolides, especially erythromycin, stimulate motilin receptors and increase GI motility.
w: Antagonism at dopamine D2 receptors
Agonism at serotonin 5-HT4 receptors
Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase

qs.q: A 66-year-old woman treated with an antibiotic for an aspiration lung abscess develops profuse watery diarrhea and a positive toxin assay. The antibiotic binds the 50S subunit and has good anaerobic coverage. Which drug was it?
qs.a: Clindamycin
qs.x: Clindamycin binds the 50S subunit, covers anaerobes above the diaphragm and is strongly associated with C. difficile infection.
w: Gentamicin
Doxycycline
Aztreonam

qs.q: A 45-year-old man taking sertraline is given linezolid for vancomycin-resistant enterococcal bacteremia. Two days later he has agitation, hyperthermia, clonus and diarrhea. What property of linezolid explains this?
qs.a: Weak monoamine oxidase inhibition
qs.x: Linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor and can cause serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs; it also causes thrombocytopenia.
w: Inhibition of CYP2D6 raising sertraline levels
Agonism at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors
Blockade of serotonin reuptake transporters

qs.q: A premature infant treated with an antibiotic for meningitis develops vomiting, an ashen-gray color, hypotension and cardiovascular collapse. The infant lacks adequate UDP-glucuronyltransferase. Which drug was given?
qs.a: Chloramphenicol
qs.x: Gray baby syndrome results when neonates cannot glucuronidate chloramphenicol, a 50S peptidyltransferase inhibitor.
w: Ceftriaxone
Gentamicin
Ampicillin

qs.q: A 70-year-old man with MRSA bacteremia improves on daptomycin, but he later develops MRSA pneumonia that does not respond to this drug. Why is daptomycin ineffective here?
qs.a: It is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant
qs.x: Daptomycin, a lipopeptide that depolarizes the bacterial membrane, is inactivated by surfactant; monitor CK for myopathy.
w: It does not penetrate into lung tissue
MRSA in the lung loses its lipid membrane
It is rapidly cleared by alveolar macrophages

qs.q: A 72-year-old woman taking prednisone for COPD is treated with ciprofloxacin for pyelonephritis and feels a pop with sudden pain at the back of her ankle. What is the mechanism of the drug, and what happened?
qs.a: DNA gyrase inhibitor causing tendon rupture
qs.x: Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; tendon rupture risk rises with age and corticosteroids.
w: Cell wall synthesis inhibitor causing tendinitis
30S ribosomal inhibitor causing myopathy
Folate synthesis inhibitor causing a fracture

qs.q: A 66-year-old man taking theophylline for COPD is treated with ciprofloxacin. Four days later he has nausea, tachycardia and a seizure. What explains this interaction?
qs.a: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2
qs.x: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, the main enzyme metabolizing theophylline and tizanidine, raising their levels.
w: Ciprofloxacin induces CYP3A4
Ciprofloxacin displaces theophylline from albumin
Ciprofloxacin blocks renal theophylline excretion

qs.q: A 40-year-old man with HIV takes TMP-SMX for Pneumocystis prophylaxis. Which pair of enzymes in folate synthesis does this combination block?
qs.a: Dihydropteroate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase
qs.x: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase and trimethoprim inhibits bacterial DHFR, a sequential blockade.
w: Thymidylate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase
Dihydropteroate synthase and thymidylate synthase
Ribonucleotide reductase and dihydrofolate reductase

qs.q: A 70-year-old man taking lisinopril is treated with TMP-SMX for a urinary tract infection. His potassium rises from 4.6 to 6.2 mEq/L. Which mechanism of trimethoprim explains this?
qs.a: Blockade of ENaC in the collecting duct
qs.x: Trimethoprim blocks the epithelial sodium channel like amiloride, reducing potassium secretion.
w: Inhibition of renin release from the kidney
Inhibition of aldosterone synthesis
Shift of potassium out of cells

qs.q: A 36-year-old woman treated for bacterial vaginosis drinks wine at a party and develops flushing, headache, nausea and palpitations. Which enzyme does the drug inhibit to cause this?
qs.a: Aldehyde dehydrogenase
qs.x: Metronidazole causes a disulfiram-like reaction by inhibiting aldehyde dehydrogenase, allowing acetaldehyde to build up.
w: Alcohol dehydrogenase
Monoamine oxidase type A
Cytochrome P450 2E1

qs.q: An 82-year-old woman has taken nitrofurantoin for recurrent urinary tract infections for 2 years. She now has progressive dyspnea and bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Which drug toxicity is most likely?
qs.a: Pulmonary fibrosis
qs.x: Long-term nitrofurantoin can cause chronic pulmonary fibrosis; acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis also occurs.
w: Pulmonary embolism
Lung adenocarcinoma
Eosinophilic asthma

qs.q: A 38-year-old man with HIV starts dapsone for Pneumocystis prophylaxis. He becomes cyanotic with a pulse oximetry reading of 85 percent that does not improve with oxygen, and his blood is chocolate-brown. What is the treatment?
qs.a: Methylene blue
qs.x: Dapsone causes methemoglobinemia; methylene blue reduces ferric to ferrous iron (avoid in G6PD deficiency).
w: Hydroxocobalamin
Sodium bicarbonate
Hyperbaric oxygen

qs.q: A 34-year-old man has active tuberculosis resistant to isoniazid. Sequencing shows a mutation in katG. How does this mutation cause resistance?
qs.a: Loss of the enzyme that activates the prodrug
qs.x: Isoniazid is a prodrug activated by catalase-peroxidase (KatG); it then inhibits mycolic acid synthesis (InhA).
w: Increased drug efflux from the bacterial cell
Overexpression of the mycolic acid synthase
Altered RNA polymerase beta subunit binding

qs.q: A 26-year-old woman taking combined oral contraceptives starts treatment for latent tuberculosis and becomes pregnant 3 months later. She also noticed orange urine. Which mechanism explains the contraceptive failure?
qs.a: Induction of hepatic CYP3A4
qs.x: Rifampin is a potent CYP450 inducer that lowers levels of estrogens, warfarin, protease inhibitors and many other drugs.
w: Inhibition of hepatic CYP3A4
Chelation of estrogen in the gut
Blockade of estrogen receptors

qs.q: A 50-year-old man with active tuberculosis is treated with a 4-drug regimen. One drug inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Which mutation causes resistance to it?
qs.a: rpoB mutation altering the RNA polymerase
qs.x: Rifampin binds the beta subunit of RNA polymerase encoded by rpoB; resistance develops quickly if used alone.
w: katG mutation preventing prodrug activation
embB mutation altering arabinosyltransferase
pncA mutation preventing activation to pyrazinoic acid

qs.q: A 45-year-old man receiving 4-drug therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis develops a painful, swollen great toe in the second month. Which drug is most likely responsible?
qs.a: Pyrazinamide
qs.x: Pyrazinamide decreases renal urate excretion, causing hyperuricemia and gout; it is also hepatotoxic.
w: Rifampin
Isoniazid
Ethambutol

qs.q: A 52-year-old man on treatment for tuberculosis has blurred vision and cannot distinguish red from green. Which enzyme does the responsible drug inhibit?
qs.a: Arabinosyltransferase
qs.x: Ethambutol inhibits arabinosyltransferase (arabinogalactan synthesis) and causes optic neuritis with red-green color blindness.
w: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
Mycolic acid synthase (InhA)
Mycobacterial ATP synthase

qs.q: A 40-year-old man with cryptococcal meningitis is treated with amphotericin B. Which mechanism and laboratory toxicity are expected?
qs.a: Binds ergosterol forming pores; hypokalemia
qs.x: Amphotericin binds ergosterol and forms membrane pores; it causes nephrotoxicity with potassium and magnesium wasting.
w: Inhibits ergosterol synthesis; hyperkalemia
Inhibits glucan synthesis; hypercalcemia
Disrupts microtubules; hypernatremia

qs.q: A 65-year-old woman stable on warfarin is prescribed fluconazole for esophageal candidiasis. Her INR rises from 2.5 to 6.1. What is the mechanism?
qs.a: Inhibition of CYP2C9 by fluconazole
qs.x: Azoles inhibit fungal 14-alpha-demethylase and human CYP enzymes; fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9, which clears S-warfarin.
w: Induction of CYP2C9 by fluconazole
Displacement of warfarin from albumin
Reduced synthesis of vitamin K by gut flora

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman in the ICU has candidemia with Candida glabrata. She is treated with caspofungin. What is its target?
qs.a: Beta-1,3-glucan synthase
qs.x: Echinocandins inhibit beta-1,3-D-glucan synthesis in the fungal cell wall; they cause little toxicity.
w: Lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase
Squalene epoxidase
Fungal thymidylate synthase

qs.q: A 50-year-old man has thick, discolored toenails with dermatophytes on culture. He starts a 12-week oral course of terbinafine. Which enzyme does it inhibit?
qs.a: Squalene epoxidase
qs.x: Terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase, causing toxic squalene to build up; monitor for hepatotoxicity.
w: 14-alpha-demethylase
Beta-1,3-glucan synthase
Thymidylate synthase

qs.q: A 35-year-old man with cryptococcal meningitis receives amphotericin B with a second agent. He later develops pancytopenia. The second agent is converted within fungi by which enzyme?
qs.a: Cytosine deaminase
qs.x: Flucytosine is converted to 5-fluorouracil by fungal cytosine deaminase, inhibiting DNA and RNA synthesis; bone marrow suppression occurs.
w: Thymidine kinase
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase
Squalene epoxidase

qs.q: A 55-year-old man with leukemia and invasive aspergillosis starts voriconazole. Two days later he reports altered color perception and blurry vision. Which statement about this effect is most accurate?
qs.a: It is a common and usually transient effect
qs.x: Transient visual disturbances are common with voriconazole; photosensitivity and hepatotoxicity also occur.
w: It signals irreversible retinal damage
It reflects optic neuritis from the drug
It indicates fungal spread to the eye

qs.q: A 66-year-old woman receiving unfractionated heparin after knee replacement has a platelet count that falls from 250,000 to 90,000 on day 7, with a new leg DVT. What is the most appropriate anticoagulant?
qs.a: Argatroban
qs.x: HIT is caused by antibodies to heparin-platelet factor 4; stop all heparins and use a direct thrombin inhibitor such as argatroban.
w: Enoxaparin
Warfarin alone
Protamine sulfate

qs.q: A 55-year-old man develops bleeding after receiving too much unfractionated heparin during cardiac catheterization. Which antidote is most appropriate, and how does it act?
qs.a: Protamine, a basic protein binding heparin
qs.x: Protamine is positively charged and binds negatively charged heparin, neutralizing it.
w: Vitamin K, restoring clotting factor synthesis
Idarucizumab, an antibody binding heparin
Andexanet, a decoy factor Xa protein

qs.q: A 70-year-old man on warfarin has an INR of 9.5 and active GI bleeding. Which treatment provides the fastest reversal?
qs.a: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
qs.x: Four-factor PCC replaces factors II, VII, IX and X immediately; IV vitamin K is also given for sustained reversal.
w: Holding warfarin and giving oral vitamin K
Protamine sulfate given intravenously
Desmopressin given intravenously

qs.q: A 76-year-old woman taking dabigatran for atrial fibrillation has a subdural hematoma needing emergency surgery. Which agent specifically reverses this drug?
qs.a: Idarucizumab
qs.x: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor.
w: Protamine sulfate
Andexanet alfa
Phytonadione

qs.q: A 58-year-old man has a stent thrombosis despite taking clopidogrel. Genetic testing shows he is a CYP2C19 poor metabolizer. Why did the drug fail?
qs.a: It is a prodrug needing CYP2C19 activation
qs.x: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19 to irreversibly block the P2Y12 ADP receptor; ticagrelor does not need activation.
w: It is inactivated faster by CYP2C19
CYP2C19 metabolism creates an antagonist
It requires CYP2C19 for intestinal uptake

qs.q: A 62-year-old man takes low-dose aspirin daily to prevent heart attacks. Why does a single dose inhibit platelet function for the life of the platelet?
qs.a: It irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1
qs.x: Platelets lack a nucleus and cannot make new COX-1, so irreversible acetylation lasts 7 to 10 days.
w: It irreversibly blocks platelet P2Y12 receptors
It reversibly inhibits thromboxane synthase
It irreversibly blocks glycoprotein IIb/IIIa

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman with an acute ischemic stroke arrives 2 hours after symptom onset and receives alteplase. Which mechanism and major risk does this drug have?
qs.a: Converts plasminogen to plasmin; hemorrhage
qs.x: Tissue plasminogen activators convert plasminogen to plasmin to lyse fibrin; intracranial bleeding is the major risk.
w: Inhibits thrombin directly; thrombocytopenia
Blocks factor Xa; hyperkalemia
Blocks glycoprotein IIb/IIIa; hypotension

qs.q: A drug is given by continuous IV infusion. It has first-order elimination and a half-life of 6 hours. How long will it take to reach approximately 94 percent of steady-state concentration?
qs.a: 24 hours
qs.x: Time to steady state depends only on half-life: about 50, 75, 88 and 94 percent are reached after 1, 2, 3 and 4 half-lives.
w: 12 hours
36 hours
48 hours

qs.q: A drug has a volume of distribution of 40 L and bioavailability of 1. The target plasma concentration is 10 mg/L. What loading dose is needed?
qs.a: 400 mg
qs.x: Loading dose equals target concentration times volume of distribution divided by bioavailability: 10 times 40 = 400 mg.
w: 40 mg
4 mg

qs.q: A drug has a clearance of 5 L/h and an oral bioavailability of 0.5. The target steady-state concentration is 2 mg/L, given every 12 hours. What maintenance dose is needed?
qs.a: 240 mg
qs.x: Maintenance dose equals Css times CL times dosing interval divided by F: 2 times 5 times 12 divided by 0.5 = 240 mg.
w: 120 mg
60 mg
480 mg

qs.q: A drug has a volume of distribution of 70 L and a clearance of 7 L/h. What is its approximate elimination half-life?
qs.a: 7 hours
qs.x: Half-life equals 0.7 times Vd divided by CL: 0.7 times 70 divided by 7 = 7 hours.
w: 10 hours
0.7 hours
49 hours

qs.q: A 500 mg IV dose of a drug produces an initial plasma concentration of 2 mg/L. Which statement best describes this drug?
qs.a: It distributes extensively into tissues
qs.x: Vd equals dose divided by concentration (250 L), far above total body water, so the drug is sequestered in tissues.
w: It is confined mostly to the plasma
It distributes mainly in extracellular fluid
It is highly bound to plasma proteins

qs.q: In a phase 1 study, a drug has an ED50 of 10 mg and a TD50 of 200 mg. What is its therapeutic index?
qs.x: Therapeutic index equals TD50 divided by ED50; a higher value means a safer drug.

qs.q: In an isolated tissue experiment, adding a fixed concentration of an antagonist shifts the agonist dose-response curve to the right, but the maximal response is still reached at high agonist doses. What type of antagonist is this?
qs.a: Competitive antagonist
qs.x: A competitive (surmountable) antagonist raises EC50 without lowering Emax; potency falls but efficacy does not.
w: Noncompetitive antagonist
Partial agonist
Irreversible antagonist

qs.q: Two opioids are compared. Drug A produces a maximal analgesic effect of 100 percent at 10 mg. Drug B produces a maximal effect of 60 percent at 1 mg. Which statement is correct?
qs.a: Drug A has greater efficacy
qs.x: Efficacy is the maximal effect (Emax); potency relates to the dose needed (EC50). Drug A is more efficacious, and Drug B is more potent.
w: Drug B has greater efficacy
Drug A has greater potency
The two drugs have equal efficacy

qs.q: A 34-year-old man with HSV encephalitis receives high-dose IV acyclovir as a rapid infusion. On day 3 his creatinine rises from 0.9 to 2.4 mg/dL and urine microscopy shows needle-shaped crystals. What is the mechanism of his kidney injury?
qs.a: Drug precipitation within the renal tubules
qs.x: Acyclovir is poorly soluble in urine and can crystallize in tubules, causing obstructive nephropathy; IV hydration and slower infusion prevent it.
w: Immune-mediated acute interstitial nephritis
Direct toxicity to glomerular podocytes
Afferent arteriolar constriction from loss of prostaglandins

qs.q: A 38-year-old man with AIDS has HSV lesions that progress despite acyclovir, and the isolate lacks thymidine kinase activity. He is switched to a drug that does not need viral phosphorylation. Which laboratory abnormalities should be monitored most closely?
qs.a: Hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia
qs.x: Foscarnet is a pyrophosphate analog that binds viral DNA polymerase directly; it chelates divalent cations (risk of seizures) and is nephrotoxic.
w: Hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia
Hypernatremia and hypochloremia
Hypercalcemia and metabolic alkalosis

qs.q: A 52-year-old kidney transplant recipient develops CMV colitis and is treated with IV ganciclovir. Two weeks later his absolute neutrophil count is 600/uL. Which statement best explains the drug's activation and main toxicity?
qs.a: Activated by viral UL97 kinase; suppresses bone marrow
qs.x: Ganciclovir is monophosphorylated by the CMV UL97 kinase and then inhibits viral DNA polymerase; myelosuppression is its dose-limiting toxicity.
w: Pyrophosphate analog; chelates calcium and magnesium
Activated by host thymidine kinase; causes nephrolithiasis
Blocks viral uncoating; directly destroys neutrophils

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman develops fever, myalgia and cough during a winter outbreak, and a rapid test is positive for influenza A. She starts an oral drug within 48 hours of symptom onset. Which viral step does it inhibit?
qs.a: Release of new virions from infected cells
qs.x: Oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase, so progeny virions cannot cleave sialic acid and be released; baloxavir inhibits the cap-dependent endonuclease.
w: Fusion of the viral envelope with the endosome
Uncoating of the virus through the M2 channel
Cap-snatching by the polymerase acidic endonuclease

qs.q: A 29-year-old woman with HIV takes a regimen that includes zidovudine. Routine labs show hemoglobin of 8.9 g/dL with an MCV of 112 fL. Which mechanism underlies the antiviral effect of this drug?
qs.a: Chain termination of viral DNA after phosphorylation
qs.x: NRTIs such as zidovudine are phosphorylated by host kinases and lack a 3' hydroxyl, terminating DNA chains; zidovudine causes macrocytic anemia and marrow suppression.
w: Allosteric inhibition of reverse transcriptase without activation
Blockade of strand transfer by the viral integrase
Inhibition of the protease that cleaves the gag-pol protein

qs.q: A 26-year-old man starting HIV therapy has vivid dreams, insomnia and dizziness in the first weeks. The responsible drug binds reverse transcriptase at a pocket distant from the active site. How does it differ from nucleoside analogs?
qs.a: It does not require intracellular phosphorylation
qs.x: NNRTIs such as efavirenz bind an allosteric site and need no phosphorylation; CNS effects are characteristic.
w: It requires activation by a viral thymidine kinase
It competes with natural nucleotides at the catalytic site
It acts only after viral DNA has integrated into the host genome

qs.q: A 33-year-old woman with well-controlled HIV takes dolutegravir. Her viral load rises after she begins taking an aluminum-magnesium antacid at the same time as her morning pills. What explains the treatment failure?
qs.a: Chelation by polyvalent cations lowering absorption
qs.x: Integrase inhibitors bind metal ions in the integrase active site and also chelate Mg, Al, Ca and Fe in the gut; doses must be separated.
w: Induction of hepatic CYP3A4 increasing drug clearance
Higher gastric pH preventing tablet dissolution
Competition for renal tubular secretion of the drug

qs.q: A 36-year-old man's HIV regimen includes darunavir with a low dose of ritonavir. The ritonavir dose is too low to have meaningful antiviral activity on its own. What is its purpose?
qs.a: Inhibition of CYP3A4 to raise darunavir levels
qs.x: Low-dose ritonavir strongly inhibits CYP3A4, boosting levels of other protease inhibitors; this causes many drug interactions.
w: Induction of P-glycoprotein to improve CNS penetration
Inhibition of renal secretion to prolong darunavir action
Blockade of a second binding site on HIV protease

qs.q: Before starting a new HIV regimen, a 30-year-old man is tested for HLA-B*57:01 and the result is positive. Which drug must be avoided because of the risk of a severe hypersensitivity reaction?
qs.a: Abacavir
qs.x: Abacavir hypersensitivity (fever, rash, GI and respiratory symptoms) is strongly linked to HLA-B*57:01, and rechallenge can be fatal.
w: Lamivudine
Tenofovir
Raltegravir

qs.q: A 45-year-old treatment-experienced man with HIV has a tropism assay showing only CCR5-using virus. He starts a drug that blocks viral entry by binding a host cell protein. What is the drug's target?
qs.a: Host CCR5 chemokine coreceptor
qs.x: Maraviroc binds host CCR5 and prevents its interaction with gp120; enfuvirtide binds gp41 and blocks membrane fusion.
w: Viral gp41 transmembrane protein
Host CD4 receptor on helper T cells
Viral gp120 envelope glycoprotein

qs.q: A 50-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C genotype 1 is cured after 12 weeks of an oral combination that contains sofosbuvir. Which viral protein does sofosbuvir inhibit?
qs.a: NS5B RNA-dependent RNA polymerase
qs.x: Sofosbuvir is a nucleotide analog inhibitor of NS5B; drugs ending in -previr inhibit NS3/4A and those ending in -asvir inhibit NS5A.
w: NS3/4A serine protease complex
NS5A replication complex protein
E2 envelope glycoprotein receptor

qs.q: A 24-year-old soldier returning from Southeast Asia is treated for Plasmodium vivax malaria. Before a second drug is added to prevent relapse, his G6PD activity is measured. What does that second drug target, and what is the risk?
qs.a: Liver hypnozoites; hemolysis
qs.x: Primaquine eradicates dormant liver hypnozoites of P. vivax and P. ovale but causes oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
w: Blood schizonts; retinopathy
Gametocytes; QT prolongation
Liver hypnozoites; agranulocytosis

qs.q: A 35-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has taken hydroxychloroquine for 6 years. Which screening test should she have regularly because of this drug?
qs.a: Retinal examination
qs.x: Hydroxychloroquine can cause irreversible bull's-eye maculopathy, so annual retinal screening is recommended after 5 years of use.
w: Pulmonary function tests
Audiometry
Bone density scan

qs.q: A 6-year-old girl has perianal itching at night, and a tape test shows Enterobius eggs. She receives a single oral dose that is repeated in 2 weeks. What is the mechanism of this drug?
qs.a: Inhibits parasite microtubule polymerization
qs.x: Mebendazole binds parasite beta-tubulin and blocks microtubule formation, impairing glucose uptake; pyrantel is a depolarizing nicotinic agonist.
w: Opens glutamate-gated chloride channels
Increases tegument calcium permeability
Depolarizing nicotinic receptor agonism

qs.q: A 40-year-old man from Sierra Leone has itchy skin nodules and microfilariae in skin snips, consistent with onchocerciasis. Which drug and mechanism are most appropriate?
qs.a: Ivermectin; opens glutamate-gated chloride channels
qs.x: Ivermectin activates invertebrate glutamate-gated chloride channels, causing hyperpolarization and paralysis of microfilariae.
w: Praziquantel; raises tegument calcium permeability
Mebendazole; blocks beta-tubulin polymerization
Pyrantel; causes spastic paralysis via nicotinic agonism

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman returns from Nigeria with fever and uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria and receives artemether-lumefantrine. How does the artemisinin component kill the parasite?
qs.a: Endoperoxide-derived free radicals
qs.x: Heme iron cleaves the endoperoxide bridge of artemisinins, producing free radicals that damage parasite proteins.
w: Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase
Blockade of mitochondrial cytochrome b
Prevention of heme polymerization to hemozoin

qs.q: A 9-year-old boy has tinea capitis and starts oral griseofulvin, which his mother is told to give with a fatty meal. Which mechanism and drug interaction are characteristic of this drug?
qs.a: Disrupts microtubules; induces CYP450
qs.x: Griseofulvin deposits in keratin and disrupts the mitotic spindle; it induces CYP450, lowering warfarin and oral contraceptive levels, and is teratogenic.
w: Inhibits ergosterol synthesis; inhibits CYP3A4
Binds ergosterol; causes potassium wasting
Inhibits squalene epoxidase; induces CYP2D6

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman from rural Mexico has new-onset seizures, and MRI shows multiple cystic brain lesions containing scolices. In addition to corticosteroids, which drug is given?
qs.a: Albendazole
qs.x: Neurocysticercosis is treated with albendazole (sometimes with praziquantel), with steroids to limit inflammation as cysts die.
w: Ivermectin
Pyrantel pamoate
Nitazoxanide

qs.q: A 19-year-old student with pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly is given ampicillin. Three days later she develops a diffuse maculopapular rash. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: Nonallergic rash associated with EBV infection
qs.x: Aminopenicillins given during infectious mononucleosis commonly cause a nonallergic morbilliform rash that does not predict true penicillin allergy.
w: IgE-mediated type I penicillin hypersensitivity
Toxin-mediated scarlet fever from group A streptococci
Serum sickness from immune complex deposition

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman with epilepsy controlled on valproic acid is treated with meropenem for a resistant gram-negative infection. Two days later she has a generalized seizure. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Carbapenem-induced fall in valproate levels
qs.x: Carbapenems block hydrolysis of valproate glucuronide, so valproate levels drop sharply within days; the combination should be avoided.
w: Direct carbapenem agonism at GABA-A receptors
Valproate inhibition of meropenem clearance
Hyponatremia from carbapenem-induced SIADH

qs.q: A 78-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease receives full-dose cefepime for Pseudomonas pneumonia. Three days later she is confused with myoclonus, and EEG shows nonconvulsive status epilepticus. What best explains this toxicity?
qs.a: Drug accumulation with central GABA-A antagonism
qs.x: Cefepime accumulates when renal dosing is not adjusted and antagonizes GABA-A receptors, causing encephalopathy and seizures.
w: Thiamine depletion from altered gut flora
Hypoprothrombinemia from its N-methylthiotetrazole side chain
Disulfiram-like reaction to its side chain group

qs.q: A 60-year-old man has pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae that is resistant to levofloxacin. Which mechanism most likely produced this resistance?
qs.a: Mutations in DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
qs.x: Fluoroquinolone resistance arises mainly from chromosomal mutations in gyrA and parC, plus efflux pumps.
w: Methylation of the 23S ribosomal RNA
Production of an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase
Altered penicillin-binding protein 2a

qs.q: A 55-year-old man in the ICU has pneumonia caused by carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter and is treated with colistin. Which toxicity profile is most characteristic of this drug class?
qs.a: Nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity
qs.x: Polymyxins act as cationic detergents on bacterial membranes and cause dose-related nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity, including neuromuscular blockade.
w: Ototoxicity and red man syndrome
Hepatotoxicity and optic neuritis
Tendinopathy and QT prolongation

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman has a second recurrence of Clostridioides difficile colitis. She is treated with a narrow-spectrum macrocyclic antibiotic that is minimally absorbed and spares normal colonic flora. What is its target?
qs.a: Bacterial RNA polymerase sigma subunit
qs.x: Fidaxomicin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase and has lower recurrence rates than vancomycin.
w: Peptidyl transferase of the 50S ribosome
Cell wall D-Ala-D-Ala peptide terminus
Bacterial DNA gyrase A subunit

qs.q: A 30-year-old man with neurosyphilis declines IV therapy and is treated with IM procaine penicillin G plus oral probenecid. How does probenecid improve therapy?
qs.a: Inhibits renal tubular secretion of penicillin
qs.x: Probenecid blocks organic anion transporters in the proximal tubule, raising and prolonging penicillin levels.
w: Inhibits bacterial beta-lactamase enzymes
Increases penicillin entry across the blood-brain barrier
Slows hepatic glucuronidation of penicillin

qs.q: A 12-year-old boy with osteosarcoma receives high-dose methotrexate. Twenty-four hours later he is given a reduced folate that rescues normal cells without needing the enzyme that methotrexate blocks. Which enzyme does methotrexate inhibit?
qs.a: Dihydrofolate reductase
qs.x: Methotrexate inhibits DHFR; leucovorin (folinic acid) bypasses the block and rescues normal cells.
w: Thymidylate synthase
Ribonucleotide reductase
IMP dehydrogenase

qs.q: A 60-year-old man with colon cancer receives fluorouracil with leucovorin. Here leucovorin is given to increase cytotoxicity rather than to rescue normal cells. What is the target of fluorouracil?
qs.a: Thymidylate synthase
qs.x: 5-FdUMP forms a covalent complex with thymidylate synthase and methylene-THF; leucovorin stabilizes this complex.
w: Dihydrofolate reductase
Topoisomerase I
Ribonucleotide reductase

qs.q: A 42-year-old woman with lupus nephritis receives IV cyclophosphamide and is given mesna with each dose. Which toxicity is mesna preventing?
qs.a: Hemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein
qs.x: The metabolite acrolein injures bladder urothelium; mesna is a thiol that binds and inactivates acrolein in the urine.
w: Cardiomyopathy from free radicals
Pulmonary fibrosis from oxidative injury
Acute tubular necrosis from cast formation

qs.q: A 58-year-old man receiving cisplatin for bladder cancer develops high-frequency hearing loss, a rising creatinine and hypomagnesemia. How does cisplatin kill tumor cells?
qs.a: Crosslinks DNA by forming platinum adducts
qs.x: Cisplatin forms intrastrand and interstrand DNA crosslinks; it causes nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity and neuropathy, reduced by hydration and amifostine.
w: Stabilizes microtubules and blocks mitotic exit
Inhibits topoisomerase II and causes DNA breaks
Intercalates in DNA and generates oxygen free radicals

qs.q: A 50-year-old woman develops dyspnea, edema and an ejection fraction of 30 percent a year after breast cancer chemotherapy. Her cumulative dose of one agent exceeded recommended limits. Which drug could have been given with it to reduce this toxicity?
qs.a: Dexrazoxane
qs.x: Doxorubicin causes cumulative dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy through free radicals; the iron chelator dexrazoxane is protective.
w: Amifostine
Mesna
Leucovorin

qs.q: A 28-year-old man treated for testicular cancer with a three-drug regimen develops progressive dyspnea and bibasilar crackles, with a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing. Which drug most likely caused this?
qs.a: Bleomycin
qs.x: Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis because the lung lacks bleomycin hydrolase; it acts by generating free radicals that break DNA.
w: Etoposide
Cisplatin
Ifosfamide

qs.q: A 6-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukemia develops constipation, tingling in his hands and foot drop during induction chemotherapy. Which mechanism explains the responsible drug's activity?
qs.a: Prevents tubulin polymerization into microtubules
qs.x: Vincristine binds tubulin and blocks microtubule assembly, arresting cells in M phase; peripheral and autonomic neuropathy are dose-limiting.
w: Stabilizes microtubules and prevents disassembly
Depletes asparagine needed by leukemic cells
Inhibits topoisomerase II during the S and G2 phases

qs.q: A 25-year-old man with testicular cancer receives a podophyllotoxin derivative. Years later he develops acute myeloid leukemia with an 11q23 rearrangement. What is this drug's mechanism?
qs.a: Inhibition of topoisomerase II
qs.x: Etoposide stabilizes the topoisomerase II-DNA complex, causing double-strand breaks; secondary leukemias with MLL rearrangement can follow.
w: Inhibition of topoisomerase I
Alkylation of guanine at N7
Inhibition of DNA polymerase alpha

qs.q: A 48-year-old man with fatigue, splenomegaly and a WBC of 120,000/uL has a t(9;22) translocation. He starts an oral drug and achieves remission. What does the drug inhibit?
qs.a: BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase
qs.x: Imatinib blocks the ATP-binding site of the constitutively active BCR-ABL kinase in chronic myeloid leukemia.
w: JAK2 tyrosine kinase
EGFR tyrosine kinase
Bruton tyrosine kinase

qs.q: A 47-year-old woman with HER2-positive breast cancer receives trastuzumab, and echocardiograms are scheduled every 3 months. Which statement best describes its cardiotoxicity compared with that of anthracyclines?
qs.a: Usually reversible and not dose-dependent
qs.x: Trastuzumab cardiac dysfunction is usually reversible after stopping the drug and is not related to cumulative dose, unlike anthracycline cardiomyopathy.
w: Irreversible and cumulative dose-dependent
Mainly a restrictive cardiomyopathy
Fully prevented by dexrazoxane pretreatment

qs.q: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman has taken tamoxifen for 3 years for estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer and now has vaginal bleeding. Which property of the drug explains this finding?
qs.a: Partial estrogen agonism in the endometrium
qs.x: Tamoxifen is a SERM that blocks estrogen in breast tissue but acts as an agonist in the endometrium (hyperplasia, cancer) and raises VTE risk.
w: Complete estrogen antagonism in the uterus
Inhibition of peripheral aromatase activity
Suppression of pituitary gonadotropin release

qs.q: A 9-year-old boy on maintenance mercaptopurine for ALL is started on allopurinol for hyperuricemia without a dose change, and he develops severe pancytopenia. What explains this?
qs.a: Xanthine oxidase inhibition raises drug levels
qs.x: Xanthine oxidase inactivates mercaptopurine and azathioprine; with allopurinol or febuxostat their doses must be reduced by about 75 percent.
w: Allopurinol induces thiopurine methyltransferase
Allopurinol directly suppresses the bone marrow
Competition for renal secretion of the drug

qs.q: A 62-year-old man treated for metastatic melanoma develops fatigue, weight gain and a TSH of 24 mU/L after 3 months of an intravenous antibody. Which target of this drug best explains the adverse effect?
qs.a: Programmed cell death protein 1
qs.x: PD-1 inhibitors release T-cell checkpoints and can cause immune-related thyroiditis, colitis, hepatitis and pneumonitis.
w: Vascular endothelial growth factor A
BRAF V600E serine-threonine kinase
Epidermal growth factor receptor

qs.q: A 45-year-old kidney transplant recipient has gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism and hypertension, and his creatinine has risen slowly. By which mechanism does his immunosuppressant work?
qs.a: Inhibits calcineurin and lowers IL-2 transcription
qs.x: Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin, and the complex inhibits calcineurin, preventing NFAT activation and IL-2 transcription.
w: Inhibits mTOR and blocks IL-2 signal transduction
Inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase
Blocks the alpha chain of the IL-2 receptor on T cells

qs.q: A 38-year-old liver transplant recipient taking tacrolimus develops new-onset diabetes and a fine tremor. To which intracellular protein does tacrolimus bind before inhibiting its target?
qs.a: FK-binding protein 12
qs.x: Tacrolimus binds FKBP12, and the complex inhibits calcineurin; it is more diabetogenic and neurotoxic than cyclosporine.
w: Cyclophilin A
Calmodulin
Glucocorticoid receptor

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman with lupus nephritis is maintained on mycophenolate mofetil. Which enzyme does it inhibit, and why are lymphocytes most affected?
qs.a: IMP dehydrogenase; lymphocytes lack a salvage pathway
qs.x: Mycophenolate inhibits IMP dehydrogenase in de novo guanine synthesis, which lymphocytes rely on because they lack a purine salvage pathway.
w: Dihydrofolate reductase; lymphocytes divide fastest
Calcineurin; lymphocytes depend on IL-2 transcription
Xanthine oxidase; lymphocytes accumulate toxic purine bases

qs.q: A 34-year-old man with Crohn disease is about to start azathioprine. Which test should be done first to estimate his risk of severe myelosuppression?
qs.a: Thiopurine methyltransferase activity
qs.x: Low TPMT activity shunts azathioprine toward toxic thioguanine nucleotides and severe marrow suppression.
w: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase activity
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase level
HLA-B*58:01 genotyping

qs.q: A 40-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is about to start infliximab. Which test must be completed before the first dose?
qs.a: Interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis
qs.x: TNF-alpha maintains granulomas, so TNF inhibitors can reactivate latent tuberculosis; screening is required first.
w: Serum IgA level for anaphylaxis risk
Thiopurine methyltransferase genotype
Antinuclear antibody titer to predict drug-induced lupus

qs.q: A 25-year-old woman with severe allergic asthma and a high serum IgE has exacerbations despite high-dose inhaled steroids and a LABA. She starts a monthly injection. What does the drug bind?
qs.a: Free IgE at its Fc region
qs.x: Omalizumab binds the Fc portion of free IgE, preventing it from binding FcER1 on mast cells and basophils.
w: Interleukin-5 cytokine
IL-4 receptor alpha subunit
Thymic stromal lymphopoietin

qs.q: A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and an eGFR of 25 mL/min has his metformin stopped. Which adverse effect is being avoided, and what is the drug's main action?
qs.a: Lactic acidosis; decreased hepatic gluconeogenesis
qs.x: Metformin reduces hepatic glucose output (in part via AMPK); accumulation in renal failure can cause lactic acidosis, and it rarely causes hypoglycemia alone.
w: Hypoglycemia; increased pancreatic insulin release
Lactic acidosis; increased insulin secretion
Pancreatitis; slower gastric emptying

qs.q: A 78-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and reduced kidney function is found confused with a glucose of 38 mg/dL. Her drug closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels on beta cells and has active metabolites cleared by the kidney. Which drug is she taking?
qs.a: Glyburide
qs.x: Sulfonylureas depolarize beta cells to release insulin; long-acting glyburide is especially likely to cause prolonged hypoglycemia in older adults with CKD.
w: Sitagliptin
Metformin
Pioglitazone

qs.q: A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes develops weight gain, ankle edema and worsening dyspnea after a new drug is added. The drug acts on a nuclear receptor that is highly expressed in adipose tissue. What is its mechanism?
qs.a: PPAR-gamma agonist
qs.x: Thiazolidinediones activate PPAR-gamma to improve insulin sensitivity but cause fluid retention and can worsen heart failure.
w: PPAR-alpha agonist
SGLT2 inhibitor
DPP-4 inhibitor

qs.q: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes presents with nausea, a glucose of 190 mg/dL and an anion gap metabolic acidosis with positive serum ketones. Where does her diabetes drug act?
qs.a: Proximal tubule sodium-glucose cotransporter
qs.x: SGLT2 inhibitors cause glucosuria and can produce euglycemic DKA; they also increase the risk of genital mycotic infections.
w: Intestinal alpha-glucosidase in the brush border
Pancreatic beta cell sulfonylurea receptor
Hepatic peroxisome proliferator receptor

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman with obesity and type 2 diabetes wants to start weekly semaglutide injections. Which history would be a contraindication?
qs.a: Medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2
qs.x: GLP-1 agonists caused thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents and are contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2.
w: Papillary thyroid carcinoma or MEN1
Hashimoto thyroiditis or Graves disease
Pheochromocytoma or neurofibromatosis

qs.q: A 26-year-old woman at 8 weeks of gestation has Graves disease and is given an antithyroid drug for the first trimester only. Which property is unique to this drug compared with the alternative thionamide?
qs.a: Inhibits peripheral T4 to T3 conversion
qs.x: PTU inhibits thyroid peroxidase and peripheral 5'-deiodinase; it is used in the first trimester because methimazole is teratogenic, but it carries more hepatotoxicity.
w: Blocks iodide uptake through the NIS symporter
Carries no risk of agranulocytosis
Carries a lower risk of liver failure

qs.q: A 40-year-old woman with Graves disease started methimazole 6 weeks ago and now has a fever and severe sore throat. What should be checked immediately?
qs.a: Absolute neutrophil count
qs.x: Thionamides can cause agranulocytosis; the drug should be stopped and the neutrophil count checked when fever or sore throat develops.
w: Serum free T4 level
Liver transaminase levels
Throat culture for streptococci

qs.q: A 55-year-old man who has taken prednisone 20 mg daily for 6 months for polymyalgia rheumatica stops it abruptly. He develops weakness, vomiting, hypotension and hypoglycemia. What best explains this?
qs.a: Suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis
qs.x: Exogenous glucocorticoids suppress CRH and ACTH, causing adrenal atrophy; stopping abruptly causes secondary adrenal insufficiency.
w: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex
Rebound hypersecretion of pituitary ACTH
Hemorrhagic infarction of both adrenal glands

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency takes hydrocortisone but still has salt craving, orthostatic hypotension and hyperkalemia. Which drug and receptor would correct these findings?
qs.a: Fludrocortisone at the mineralocorticoid receptor
qs.x: Primary adrenal insufficiency causes aldosterone deficiency; fludrocortisone replaces mineralocorticoid activity.
w: Dexamethasone at the glucocorticoid receptor
Desmopressin at the vasopressin V2 receptor
Midodrine at the alpha-1 adrenergic receptor

qs.q: A 25-year-old man has polyuria after a head injury. His urine osmolality rises from 150 to 600 mOsm/kg after he receives a synthetic hormone. Which receptor and second messenger does this drug use?
qs.a: V2 receptor via Gs and cAMP
qs.x: Desmopressin is a selective V2 agonist; Gs-cAMP signaling inserts aquaporin-2 into collecting duct membranes in central diabetes insipidus.
w: V1 receptor via Gq and IP3
V2 receptor via Gi and lower cAMP
Oxytocin receptor via Gq and calcium

qs.q: A 29-year-old woman with amenorrhea, galactorrhea and a prolactin of 180 ng/mL has a 7-mm pituitary adenoma. What is the mechanism of the preferred drug?
qs.a: Dopamine D2 receptor agonism
qs.x: Dopamine tonically inhibits lactotrophs; D2 agonists such as cabergoline lower prolactin and shrink prolactinomas.
w: Somatostatin receptor agonism
Dopamine D2 receptor antagonism
GnRH receptor agonism

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome wants to conceive and is treated with clomiphene. How does this drug induce ovulation?
qs.a: Blocks estrogen negative feedback on the hypothalamus
qs.x: Clomiphene is a SERM that blocks hypothalamic estrogen receptors, raising GnRH, FSH and LH release.
w: Inhibits ovarian aromatase and lowers estradiol
Mimics LH to trigger rupture of the dominant follicle
Directly stimulates FSH receptors on granulosa cells

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman with severe osteoporosis and vertebral fractures starts daily subcutaneous teriparatide. Why does intermittent dosing build bone?
qs.a: Pulsatile PTH preferentially stimulates osteoblasts
qs.x: Intermittent PTH analogs favor osteoblast bone formation, whereas continuous PTH promotes resorption; osteosarcoma was seen in rats.
w: Pulsatile PTH directly inhibits osteoclast activity
Pulsatile PTH blocks RANKL binding to RANK
Pulsatile PTH increases calcitonin secretion

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman receives a prolonged high-dose oxytocin infusion in dilute dextrose during labor and later has a seizure with a serum sodium of 118 mEq/L. Which property of oxytocin explains this?
qs.a: Structural similarity to ADH causing antidiuresis
qs.x: Oxytocin resembles vasopressin and at high doses activates V2 receptors, causing water retention and hyponatremia.
w: Direct stimulation of adrenal aldosterone release
Inhibition of atrial natriuretic peptide secretion
Activation of renal sodium-wasting channels

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman who has taken omeprazole for 5 years develops muscle cramps, tremor and a prolonged QT interval. Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely?
qs.a: Hypomagnesemia
qs.x: Long-term PPI use impairs intestinal magnesium absorption; other risks include C. difficile, B12 deficiency and fractures.
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypernatremia
Hyperphosphatemia

qs.q: A 50-year-old man taking warfarin and phenytoin starts an over-the-counter H2 blocker for dyspepsia, and his INR rises. Which H2 blocker most likely caused this, and how?
qs.a: Cimetidine, by inhibiting CYP450 enzymes
qs.x: Cimetidine inhibits several CYP450 enzymes and has antiandrogenic effects; famotidine has few interactions.
w: Famotidine, by inhibiting CYP450 enzymes
Cimetidine, by displacing warfarin from albumin
Nizatidine, by blocking vitamin K absorption

qs.q: A 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis taking long-term NSAIDs is given a drug to prevent gastric ulcers that increases bicarbonate and mucus secretion. What is the drug, and which warning applies?
qs.a: PGE1 analog; contraindicated in pregnancy
qs.x: Misoprostol replaces protective prostaglandins; it stimulates uterine contraction and is an abortifacient, and diarrhea is common.
w: H2 antagonist; contraindicated in pregnancy
PGE1 analog; frequently causes constipation
Proton pump inhibitor; frequently causes diarrhea

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman receiving cisplatin is given ondansetron to prevent nausea. Which receptor does it block, and which ECG change can it cause?
qs.a: 5-HT3 receptor; QT prolongation
qs.x: Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and vagal afferents; it can prolong QT and cause constipation and headache.
w: D2 receptor; PR prolongation
NK1 receptor; QRS widening
H1 receptor; ST depression

qs.q: A 74-year-old man with diabetic gastroparesis has taken metoclopramide for 2 years and develops involuntary lip-smacking and tongue movements. Which mechanism caused this?
qs.a: Chronic dopamine D2 receptor blockade
qs.x: Metoclopramide is a D2 antagonist that crosses the blood-brain barrier; long-term use can cause irreversible tardive dyskinesia.
w: Serotonin 5-HT4 receptor agonism
Muscarinic receptor antagonism in the gut
Motilin receptor agonism in the gastric antrum

qs.q: A 35-year-old man with chronic diarrhea takes loperamide. Why does this mu-opioid agonist have little central effect at usual doses?
qs.a: P-glycoprotein efflux at the blood-brain barrier
qs.x: Loperamide is pumped out of the CNS by P-glycoprotein; massive doses or P-gp inhibitors can cause QT prolongation and CNS effects.
w: Selective agonism of kappa receptors in the gut
Complete first-pass sulfation in the liver
Inability to bind central mu receptors

qs.q: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis is confused and has asterixis. He is started on lactulose. How does this drug lower blood ammonia?
qs.a: Colonic acidification traps ammonia as ammonium
qs.x: Colonic bacteria metabolize lactulose to acids, converting NH3 to NH4+, which is trapped and excreted; it also acts as an osmotic laxative.
w: Increased activity of hepatic urea cycle enzymes
Inhibition of renal ammonia production
Direct killing of urease-producing bacteria

qs.q: A 22-year-old woman with an asthma exacerbation receives repeated albuterol nebulizer treatments and develops tremor and palpitations. Which laboratory change is expected?
qs.a: Decreased serum potassium
qs.x: Beta-2 stimulation activates Na/K-ATPase and shifts potassium into cells; it also raises glucose and lactate.
w: Increased serum potassium
Decreased serum glucose
Increased serum calcium

qs.q: A 66-year-old man with COPD starts a once-daily inhaled bronchodilator whose long duration comes from slow dissociation from its receptor. Which receptor does it act on, and how?
qs.a: Antagonist at muscarinic M3 receptors
qs.x: Tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist that blocks M3-mediated bronchoconstriction; dry mouth is common.
w: Agonist at beta-2 adrenergic receptors
Antagonist at leukotriene CysLT1 receptors
Antagonist at adenosine A1 receptors

qs.q: A 14-year-old boy with asthma and allergic rhinitis takes a nightly oral tablet. His parents notice nightmares and mood changes. What is the drug's mechanism?
qs.a: Leukotriene CysLT1 receptor antagonism
qs.x: Montelukast blocks CysLT1 receptors; it carries a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events. Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase.
w: 5-lipoxygenase enzyme inhibition
Mast cell degranulation inhibition
Phosphodiesterase-4 enzyme inhibition

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman with persistent asthma starts an inhaled corticosteroid and develops white plaques on her tongue and palate. Which measure most effectively prevents this?
qs.a: Rinsing the mouth after each use
qs.x: Oropharyngeal candidiasis from steroid deposition is reduced by rinsing and spitting after each dose and by using a spacer.
w: Taking the inhaler only at bedtime
Adding a long-acting beta agonist
Inhaling more slowly and deeply

qs.q: A 19-year-old man with moderate persistent asthma is prescribed salmeterol as his only controller medication. Why is this regimen unsafe?
qs.a: LABA monotherapy raises asthma-related deaths
qs.x: LABAs do not treat airway inflammation; used without an inhaled corticosteroid they increase severe exacerbations and asthma deaths.
w: LABAs cause bronchospasm via M3 stimulation
LABAs act too briefly to control persistent asthma
LABAs cause adrenal suppression unless paired with steroids

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman stable on lithium starts hydrochlorothiazide and develops coarse tremor, confusion and ataxia. What is the mechanism of this interaction?
qs.a: Increased proximal tubular lithium reabsorption
qs.x: Thiazides cause volume contraction, increasing proximal reabsorption of sodium and lithium; ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs also raise levels.
w: Inhibition of hepatic lithium metabolism
Displacement of lithium from plasma proteins
Reduced lithium distribution into the brain

qs.q: A 35-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia starts clozapine. Which laboratory value must be monitored regularly?
qs.a: Absolute neutrophil count
qs.x: Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis, so ANC is monitored; it also causes seizures, myocarditis and weight gain.
w: Serum prolactin level
Thyroid function tests
Serum creatine kinase

qs.q: A 28-year-old man given IM haloperidol develops a temperature of 40.5 C (104.9 F), lead-pipe rigidity, labile blood pressure and a CK of 18,000 U/L. Besides stopping haloperidol, which drug acting as a dopamine agonist can treat this?
qs.a: Bromocriptine
qs.x: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome results from D2 blockade; treatment includes supportive care, dantrolene and the D2 agonist bromocriptine.
w: Benztropine
Cyproheptadine
Physostigmine

qs.q: A 26-year-old man with schizophrenia gains 12 kg and develops hypertriglyceridemia and hyperglycemia within 6 months of starting a new drug. Which antipsychotic is most likely?
qs.a: Olanzapine
qs.x: Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest risk of weight gain and metabolic syndrome; aripiprazole and ziprasidone carry the least.
w: Aripiprazole
Ziprasidone
Haloperidol

qs.q: A 32-year-old woman is brought in after an amitriptyline overdose. She is tachycardic and hypotensive, and her QRS duration is 140 ms. Which treatment is first line, and why?
qs.a: Sodium bicarbonate to overcome sodium channel blockade
qs.x: Bicarbonate adds sodium and alkalinizes the blood, overcoming TCA fast sodium channel blockade; physostigmine is avoided because of seizures and asystole.
w: Physostigmine to reverse its anticholinergic toxicity
Flumazenil to reverse its CNS depression
Amiodarone to suppress ventricular ectopy

qs.q: A 20-year-old woman with bulimia nervosa wants medication to help her quit smoking. Which drug is contraindicated for her, and why?
qs.a: Bupropion; lowered seizure threshold
qs.x: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold, and patients with bulimia or anorexia have a higher seizure risk from electrolyte disturbances.
w: Varenicline; risk of severe nausea
Nicotine patch; risk of arrhythmia
Fluoxetine; worsening of purging behavior

qs.q: A 35-year-old woman with generalized anxiety disorder wants a nonsedating drug with no risk of dependence and starts buspirone. What is its mechanism and onset?
qs.a: 5-HT1A partial agonism; takes 1-2 weeks
qs.x: Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist without sedation or dependence. Some benefit may appear in 1-2 weeks, but the full anxiolytic effect often takes 4-6 weeks.
w: GABA-A modulation; works within an hour
Alpha-2 agonism; works within an hour
5-HT2A antagonism; takes 1-2 weeks

qs.q: A 50-year-old man with severe alcohol withdrawal is given phenobarbital. How does its action at the GABA-A receptor differ from that of benzodiazepines?
qs.a: Increases duration of chloride channel opening
qs.x: Barbiturates prolong channel opening and can open it directly at high doses; benzodiazepines increase opening frequency.
w: Increases frequency of chloride channel opening
Directly blocks NMDA glutamate receptors
Opens glycine-gated chloride channels in the cord

qs.q: A 30-year-old man has a phenytoin level of 15 mcg/mL. His dose is raised by 20 percent, and the level rises to 35 mcg/mL with nystagmus and ataxia. Which pharmacokinetic concept explains this?
qs.a: Saturation of metabolism causing zero-order kinetics
qs.x: Phenytoin metabolism saturates in the therapeutic range, so small dose increases cause disproportionate rises in level.
w: Autoinduction of its own hepatic metabolism
Displacement from albumin by a second drug
Rapid redistribution from fat stores

qs.q: A 7-year-old girl has brief staring spells many times a day, and EEG shows 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges. What is the mechanism of the first-line drug?
qs.a: Blocks thalamic T-type calcium channels
qs.x: Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons and treats absence seizures only.
w: Prolongs inactivation of sodium channels
Binds synaptic vesicle protein SV2A
Inhibits GABA transaminase in neurons

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman taking valproate has lamotrigine added at the usual starting dose and develops a widespread blistering rash with mucosal involvement. Why did valproate increase her risk?
qs.a: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation
qs.x: Valproate inhibits UGT-mediated lamotrigine clearance, roughly doubling levels; the lamotrigine dose and titration must be reduced to lower SJS risk.
w: Valproate induces lamotrigine CYP3A4 metabolism
Valproate displaces lamotrigine from its receptors
Valproate increases lamotrigine renal excretion

qs.q: A 68-year-old man with Parkinson disease takes levodopa combined with carbidopa. What does carbidopa contribute?
qs.a: Inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase
qs.x: Carbidopa does not cross the blood-brain barrier and blocks peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine, lowering nausea and increasing CNS delivery.
w: Inhibits central DOPA decarboxylase
Inhibits peripheral COMT activity
Inhibits central monoamine oxidase B

qs.q: A 35-year-old man who uses heroin daily takes his first dose of buprenorphine 4 hours after his last heroin use. He soon develops yawning, diarrhea, piloerection and agitation. What explains this?
qs.a: Partial agonist displacing a full agonist
qs.x: Buprenorphine binds mu receptors with high affinity but low intrinsic activity, displacing heroin and precipitating withdrawal.
w: Full agonist with very high receptor affinity
Antagonist with weak kappa agonist activity
Partial agonist with a very short half-life

qs.q: A 30-year-old man with 40 percent burns sustained 10 days ago receives succinylcholine for intubation and develops peaked T waves followed by cardiac arrest. What explains this reaction?
qs.a: Upregulated extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors
qs.x: Burns, crush injury and denervation upregulate extrajunctional receptors, so depolarization releases large amounts of potassium.
w: Decreased plasma cholinesterase from liver injury
Ryanodine receptor mutation releasing calcium
Direct inhibition of cardiac sodium-potassium ATPase

qs.q: During sevoflurane anesthesia, a 22-year-old man develops rising end-tidal CO2, masseter rigidity, tachycardia and a temperature of 40 C (104 F). What is the mechanism of the drug used to treat this?
qs.a: Blocks ryanodine receptor calcium release
qs.x: Malignant hyperthermia stems from RYR1 mutations; dantrolene blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
w: Blocks voltage-gated L-type calcium channels
Antagonizes nicotinic receptors at the endplate
Inhibits hypothalamic prostaglandin synthesis

qs.q: After induction with rocuronium, a 48-year-old woman cannot be intubated or ventilated, and the neuromuscular block must be reversed immediately. How does the reversal drug act?
qs.a: Encapsulates the steroidal blocker molecule
qs.x: Sugammadex is a modified cyclodextrin that binds rocuronium and vecuronium, reversing even deep block without muscarinic effects.
w: Inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the synapse
Competes with acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors
Increases presynaptic acetylcholine release

qs.q: A 40-year-old woman receives a single IV bolus of propofol for a short procedure and is awake within 10 minutes. What mainly explains her rapid awakening?
qs.a: Redistribution from brain to muscle and fat
qs.x: Lipid-soluble induction agents end their effect mainly by redistribution out of the brain, not by elimination.
w: Rapid hepatic metabolism to inactive products
Rapid renal excretion of the unchanged drug
Hydrolysis by plasma esterases in the blood

qs.q: A 25-year-old trauma patient in hemorrhagic shock is induced with a drug that maintains blood pressure and airway reflexes. On waking he has vivid hallucinations. What is the drug's mechanism?
qs.a: NMDA receptor antagonism
qs.x: Ketamine is a dissociative NMDA antagonist that increases sympathetic tone and causes emergence reactions.
w: GABA-A receptor potentiation
Alpha-2 receptor agonism
Mu opioid receptor agonism

qs.q: A 72-year-old man with septic shock is intubated after induction with a hemodynamically neutral agent. The next day he has refractory hypotension, and cortisol levels are low. Which enzyme did the induction agent inhibit?
qs.a: 11-beta hydroxylase
qs.x: Etomidate inhibits adrenal 11-beta hydroxylase, suppressing cortisol synthesis even after a single dose.
w: 21-alpha hydroxylase
17-alpha hydroxylase
Cholesterol desmolase

qs.q: A 30-year-old man who often inhales whipped-cream chargers develops paresthesias, gait ataxia and loss of vibration sense; MRI shows dorsal column changes. What is the mechanism?
qs.a: Oxidation of cobalamin inactivating methionine synthase
qs.x: Nitrous oxide oxidizes the cobalt in B12, inactivating methionine synthase and causing subacute combined degeneration.
w: Direct demyelination by nitrous oxide metabolites
Blockade of intestinal B12 absorption
Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase in neurons

qs.q: A 19-year-old woman ingests 20 g of acetaminophen, and her 4-hour level is above the treatment line. By which mechanism does the antidote prevent liver injury?
qs.a: Replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI
qs.x: NAC is a glutathione precursor and sulfhydryl donor that conjugates the toxic metabolite NAPQI.
w: Inhibits CYP2E1 to block NAPQI formation
Binds acetaminophen in the gut lumen
Enhances renal excretion of acetaminophen

qs.q: A 45-year-old man is found intoxicated with an anion gap metabolic acidosis, a high osmolal gap and calcium oxalate crystals in his urine. What is the mechanism of the preferred antidote?
qs.a: Inhibition of alcohol dehydrogenase
qs.x: Fomepizole blocks ADH, preventing conversion of ethylene glycol to toxic glycolic and oxalic acids.
w: Inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase
Chelation of oxalate in renal tubules
Enhanced metabolism of glycolic acid

qs.q: A 2-year-old boy ate his mother's prenatal vitamins. He has hematemesis, metabolic acidosis and radiopaque tablets on an abdominal radiograph. Which antidote is indicated?
qs.a: Deferoxamine
qs.x: Deferoxamine chelates free iron; the complex is renally excreted and can turn urine reddish.
w: Dimercaprol
Penicillamine
Succimer

qs.q: A 40-year-old man is rescued from a house fire. He has a lactate of 12 mmol/L, hypotension and a high venous oxygen saturation. What is the mechanism of the preferred antidote?
qs.a: Binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin
qs.x: Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide directly; nitrites induce methemoglobin and thiosulfate supplies sulfur to rhodanese.
w: Converts hemoglobin to methemoglobin
Displaces carbon monoxide from hemoglobin
Donates sulfur for the rhodanese reaction

qs.q: After a benzocaine throat spray for endoscopy, a 50-year-old woman is cyanotic with chocolate-brown blood and an SpO2 of 85 percent despite oxygen. How does the antidote work?
qs.a: Acts as a cofactor that reduces methemoglobin
qs.x: Methylene blue is reduced by NADPH-methemoglobin reductase to leukomethylene blue, which reduces ferric iron back to ferrous; it is ineffective in G6PD deficiency.
w: Chelates the ferric iron within hemoglobin
Competitively inhibits benzocaine oxidation
Increases oxygen dissolved in the plasma

qs.q: After an aspirin overdose, a 35-year-old woman has tinnitus, vomiting, and a mixed respiratory alkalosis and anion gap acidosis. She is given sodium bicarbonate. What is its main purpose?
qs.a: Ion trapping of salicylate in alkaline urine
qs.x: Alkalinization ionizes salicylate, trapping it in urine and keeping it out of the brain.
w: Neutralizing salicylic acid in the stomach
Inhibiting salicylate absorption in the gut
Increasing hepatic conjugation of salicylate

qs.q: A 50-year-old man overdoses on propranolol and has bradycardia and hypotension that do not respond to atropine. Glucagon is given. Why can glucagon help?
qs.a: Raises cardiac cAMP independent of beta receptors
qs.x: Glucagon receptors on cardiac myocytes activate Gs and adenylyl cyclase, bypassing the blocked beta receptor.
w: Directly blocks cardiac potassium channels
Displaces propranolol from beta-1 receptors
Increases hepatic metabolism of propranolol

qs.q: A 60-year-old man started on ticagrelor after an acute coronary syndrome reports new mild dyspnea. How does ticagrelor differ from clopidogrel?
qs.a: Reversibly binds P2Y12 and needs no activation
qs.x: Ticagrelor is a direct reversible P2Y12 antagonist; dyspnea may relate to increased adenosine levels.
w: Irreversibly binds P2Y12 after CYP2C19 activation
Blocks GP IIb/IIIa and needs no hepatic activation
Inhibits platelet PDE3 and needs CYP3A4 activation

qs.q: A 79-year-old woman taking apixaban for atrial fibrillation presents with a large intracerebral hemorrhage. In the US today, what is used to reverse this anticoagulant?
qs.a: 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
qs.x: Andexanet alfa, the decoy factor Xa, was withdrawn from the US market in 2025, so 4-factor PCC is used for factor Xa inhibitor bleeding; idarucizumab reverses only dabigatran.
w: Idarucizumab (Praxbind) 5 g IV
Protamine sulfate by slow IV push
Phytonadione (vitamin K) IV infusion

qs.q: A 58-year-old man taking sildenafil for erectile dysfunction reports a transient blue tint to his vision. What mechanism explains this effect?
qs.a: Cross-inhibition of retinal phosphodiesterase-6
qs.x: Sildenafil inhibits PDE5 but also partly inhibits PDE6 in photoreceptors, causing blue-tinged vision.
w: Inhibition of retinal carbonic anhydrase
Blockade of muscarinic receptors in retinal cones
Toxic accumulation of the drug in the macula

qs.q: A 58-year-old man has 40 minutes of crushing substernal chest pain. BP is 148/90 mm Hg and pulse 92/min. ECG shows 3-mm ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. He has no drug allergies. While the cath lab is activated, which medication should be given immediately?
qs.a: Non-enteric-coated aspirin 162 to 325 mg chewed
qs.x: Chewed non-enteric-coated aspirin gives rapid platelet inhibition and lowers mortality in STEMI. Routine IV beta blockade is not recommended early, and warfarin has no acute role.
w: Enteric-coated aspirin 81 mg swallowed whole with water
Intravenous metoprolol 5 mg every 5 minutes for 3 doses
Oral warfarin 10 mg as a loading dose

qs.q: A 64-year-old man has an inferior STEMI. BP is 86/54 mm Hg, pulse 58/min, jugular veins are distended, and lungs are clear. Right-sided leads show ST elevation in V4R. Which medication should be avoided?
qs.a: Sublingual nitroglycerin
qs.x: Right ventricular infarction is preload dependent; nitrates and other venodilators can cause profound hypotension. Treat with IV fluids.
w: Chewed aspirin 325 mg
Intravenous unfractionated heparin
Ticagrelor 180 mg loading dose

qs.q: A 61-year-old woman with NSTEMI undergoes PCI with a drug-eluting stent. She has no bleeding history and no prior stroke. Which antiplatelet regimen is most appropriate at discharge?
qs.a: Aspirin plus ticagrelor for 12 months
qs.x: After ACS with stent placement, DAPT with aspirin plus a potent P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or prasugrel) for 12 months is recommended when bleeding risk is acceptable.
w: Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 1 month only
Ticagrelor plus warfarin indefinitely
Aspirin monotherapy starting at discharge

qs.q: A 72-year-old man with a transient ischemic attack 2 years ago presents with NSTEMI and is taken for PCI. Which P2Y12 inhibitor is contraindicated in this patient?
qs.a: Prasugrel
qs.x: Prasugrel is contraindicated with prior stroke or TIA because of net harm from intracranial bleeding; it is also generally avoided at age 75 or older.
w: Clopidogrel
Ticagrelor
Cangrelor

qs.q: A 52-year-old man is recovering from an anterior STEMI treated with PCI. Fasting LDL cholesterol is 128 mg/dL. He has never taken lipid-lowering therapy. Which is the most appropriate lipid therapy?
qs.a: Atorvastatin 80 mg daily
qs.x: All patients with clinical ASCVD up to age 75 should receive high-intensity statin therapy such as atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg or rosuvastatin 20 to 40 mg.
w: Pravastatin 20 mg daily
Fenofibrate 145 mg daily
Diet and exercise alone for 3 months, then recheck

qs.q: A 60-year-old man with an MI 1 year ago and type 2 diabetes takes atorvastatin 80 mg daily with good adherence. LDL cholesterol is 88 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate next step?
qs.a: Add ezetimibe 10 mg daily
qs.x: In very high-risk ASCVD with LDL 70 mg/dL or higher on maximal statin, adding ezetimibe is a reasonable first step; niacin and high-dose simvastatin are not recommended.
w: Switch to simvastatin 80 mg daily
Add niacin extended-release
Add fish oil 1 g daily and recheck in a year

qs.q: A 57-year-old woman with prior MI and peripheral artery disease takes atorvastatin 80 mg and ezetimibe 10 mg daily. LDL cholesterol remains 96 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate addition?
qs.a: Evolocumab subcutaneously every 2 weeks
qs.x: A PCSK9 monoclonal antibody is reasonable for very high-risk ASCVD with LDL 70 mg/dL or higher despite maximal statin plus ezetimibe; it lowers LDL about 60 percent and reduces events.
w: Colestipol plus extended-release niacin twice daily
Gemfibrozil 600 mg twice daily
Omega-3 fatty acid 1 g once daily

qs.q: A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is discharged after an anterior MI. Echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 38 percent. BP is 128/78 mm Hg and creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. Which medication is most appropriate to add for long-term mortality reduction?
qs.a: An ACE inhibitor such as lisinopril
qs.x: ACE inhibitors reduce remodeling and mortality after MI, particularly with reduced EF, diabetes, or anterior infarction. Nondihydropyridine CCBs are harmful with reduced EF.
w: A nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem
Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily
Long-acting nifedipine

qs.q: A 63-year-old man has HFrEF with an ejection fraction of 30 percent and NYHA class II symptoms on lisinopril 20 mg, carvedilol, and furosemide. BP is 118/72 mm Hg and potassium is 4.3 mEq/L. His physician plans to switch him to an ARNI. Which is the correct approach?
qs.a: Stop lisinopril, wait 36 hours, then start sacubitril-valsartan
qs.x: A 36-hour washout after the last ACE inhibitor dose is required before starting sacubitril-valsartan to avoid angioedema from combined neprilysin and ACE inhibition.
w: Start sacubitril-valsartan today and continue lisinopril
Stop lisinopril and start sacubitril-valsartan the same evening
Halve the lisinopril dose and add sacubitril-valsartan

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman with HFrEF is switched to sacubitril-valsartan after an appropriate ACE inhibitor washout. Which adverse effect is most common after starting this drug?
qs.a: Symptomatic hypotension
qs.x: Hypotension is the most common adverse effect of sacubitril-valsartan. It causes less cough than ACE inhibitors and tends to raise, not lower, potassium.
w: Dry persistent cough
Hypokalemia with muscle cramps
Bradycardia with first-degree AV block

qs.q: A 59-year-old man with HFrEF (EF 28 percent) and NYHA class II symptoms takes sacubitril-valsartan, carvedilol, and dapagliflozin. BP is 112/70 mm Hg, potassium is 4.2 mEq/L, and eGFR is 55 mL/min. Which medication should be added next?
qs.a: Spironolactone 25 mg daily
qs.x: A mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist is one of the four pillars of HFrEF therapy and is indicated when eGFR is above 30 mL/min and potassium is below 5.0 mEq/L.
w: Diltiazem extended-release 120 mg daily
Amlodipine 5 mg daily
Cilostazol 100 mg twice daily

qs.q: A 66-year-old man with HFrEF has taken spironolactone for 8 months and now has painful bilateral breast enlargement. Potassium is 4.6 mEq/L. Which is the most appropriate change?
qs.a: Replace spironolactone with eplerenone
qs.x: Eplerenone is a selective MRA without antiandrogenic effects, so it preserves the mortality benefit while avoiding gynecomastia.
w: Replace spironolactone with hydrochlorothiazide and potassium
Stop spironolactone and add amiloride
Continue spironolactone and add tamoxifen

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman without diabetes has HFrEF (EF 32 percent) and persistent NYHA class II symptoms on sacubitril-valsartan, metoprolol succinate, and spironolactone. eGFR is 45 mL/min. Which medication will most likely reduce her risk of HF hospitalization and death?
qs.a: Dapagliflozin 10 mg daily
qs.x: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce cardiovascular death and HF hospitalization in HFrEF regardless of diabetes status. Pioglitazone and verapamil worsen heart failure.
w: Digoxin 0.125 mg daily
Verapamil 120 mg daily
Pioglitazone 15 mg daily

qs.q: A 55-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HFrEF (EF 25 percent). He is euvolemic on furosemide and an ARNI. Pulse is 88/min and BP is 124/76 mm Hg. Which beta blocker has proven mortality benefit and is most appropriate?
qs.a: Carvedilol
qs.x: Only carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, and bisoprolol have shown mortality benefit in HFrEF; start at a low dose once the patient is euvolemic.
w: Atenolol
Propranolol
Labetalol

qs.q: A 62-year-old Black man with HFrEF (EF 30 percent) remains NYHA class III despite optimal doses of sacubitril-valsartan, carvedilol, spironolactone, and empagliflozin. BP is 128/80 mm Hg. Which addition is most likely to improve survival?
qs.a: Hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate
qs.x: In self-identified Black patients with persistent NYHA class III to IV symptoms on optimal GDMT, adding hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate reduces mortality (A-HeFT).
w: Amlodipine plus chlorthalidone
Diltiazem plus digoxin
Clonidine patch weekly

qs.q: A 74-year-old woman with known HFrEF has 1 week of orthopnea and leg swelling. BP is 146/88 mm Hg and SpO2 is 90 percent on room air. She has crackles to the mid-lung fields and 3+ pitting edema. Creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL. Which is the best initial treatment?
qs.a: Intravenous furosemide
qs.x: Patients with acute decompensated HF who are congested but warm and well perfused need IV loop diuretics; inotropes are reserved for low-output states.
w: Oral metolazone alone
Intravenous metoprolol
Intravenous milrinone infusion

qs.q: A 57-year-old man with HFrEF (EF 30 percent) on maximally tolerated metoprolol succinate, sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone, and dapagliflozin is in sinus rhythm with a resting heart rate of 80/min. Which medication would further reduce HF hospitalization?
qs.a: Ivabradine
