qs.q: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis has hematemesis. BP is 92/58 mm Hg and pulse 116/min. He is given blood transfusions with a hemoglobin target of 7 g/dL. Which is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy before endoscopy?
qs.a: Octreotide infusion and IV ceftriaxone
qs.x: Suspected variceal bleeding is treated with a vasoactive agent such as octreotide and antibiotic prophylaxis with ceftriaxone, followed by endoscopy within 12 hours. Nonselective beta blockers are avoided acutely.
w: IV pantoprazole alone
IV propranolol infusion
Vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR

qs.q: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis has a second episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy despite adherence to lactulose with 2 to 3 soft stools daily. Which is the most appropriate addition?
qs.a: Add rifaximin
qs.x: Rifaximin added to lactulose reduces recurrent hepatic encephalopathy and hospitalization. Long-term metronidazole is neurotoxic, protein restriction is not recommended, and benzodiazepines precipitate encephalopathy.
w: Add long-term metronidazole three times daily
Restrict dietary protein to 0.5 g/kg/day
Add lorazepam at night for agitation

qs.q: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites has abdominal pain and fever. Ascitic fluid has 640 neutrophils/mm3. Creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL and bilirubin is 4.2 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: IV cefotaxime plus albumin on days 1 and 3
qs.x: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is treated with a third-generation cephalosporin. With creatinine above 1 mg/dL or bilirubin above 4 mg/dL, albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 reduces kidney failure and death.
w: IV cefotaxime alone
Oral norfloxacin daily
Large-volume paracentesis and IV furosemide

qs.q: A 32-year-old woman has mildly to moderately active ulcerative colitis extending to the splenic flexure with 4 bloody stools daily. Which is the most appropriate initial therapy?
qs.a: Oral mesalamine with rectal mesalamine
qs.x: Oral 5-ASA (2 g or more daily) combined with rectal mesalamine is first-line for mild to moderate left-sided ulcerative colitis. Steroids are for induction only and antibiotics have no role.
w: Oral prednisone 40 mg daily for 3 months
Infliximab infusion every 8 weeks
Oral ciprofloxacin and metronidazole

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman with heavy alcohol use has jaundice, fever, and tender hepatomegaly. Bilirubin is 14 mg/dL, AST 220 U/L, and ALT 90 U/L. Maddrey discriminant function is 48. Infection and GI bleeding are excluded. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days
qs.x: Prednisolone improves short-term survival in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (discriminant function 32 or more or MELD above 20). Prednisolone is used rather than prednisone because it does not require hepatic activation.
w: Pentoxifylline 400 mg three times daily
N-acetylcysteine alone
Infliximab infusion

qs.q: A woman on metoclopramide for 18 months develops lip smacking and tongue movements. Which mechanism underlies this?
qs.a: Upregulated D2 receptors after chronic blockade
qs.x: Tardive dyskinesia is attributed to supersensitivity of striatal D2 receptors upregulated during months of blockade, which is why risk climbs after about 12 weeks and why anticholinergics do not relieve it. The 5-HT4 agonism is what gives metoclopramide its prokinetic action.
w: Peripheral 5-HT4 receptor agonism in the gut wall
Depletion of presynaptic dopamine stores
Direct toxicity to cerebellar Purkinje cells

qs.q: A 70-year-old man with CKD has weakness. Potassium is 7.4 mEq/L and ECG shows peaked T waves and a widened QRS. Which is the most appropriate first medication?
qs.a: Intravenous calcium gluconate
qs.x: Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes in hyperkalemia with ECG changes. Insulin with glucose and albuterol shift potassium into cells, and binders, diuretics, or dialysis remove it.
w: Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate orally
Intravenous furosemide 80 mg
Patiromer orally with a recheck in 6 hours

qs.q: A 66-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is confused and dehydrated. Calcium is 14.6 mg/dL, PTH is suppressed, and creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: IV saline, calcitonin, and zoledronic acid
qs.x: Severe hypercalcemia of malignancy is treated with IV isotonic saline, calcitonin for rapid effect, and a bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid or denosumab for sustained control. Thiazides raise calcium.
w: IV furosemide 80 mg before any fluids
Oral alendronate and increased fluid intake
Hydrochlorothiazide and oral fluids

qs.q: A 62-year-old man on long-term omeprazole and furosemide has potassium 2.9 mEq/L despite 3 days of oral potassium chloride. Magnesium is 1.0 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate next step?
qs.a: Intravenous magnesium sulfate
qs.x: Hypomagnesemia causes renal potassium wasting through ROMK, making hypokalemia refractory until magnesium is replaced. PPIs and loop diuretics both cause hypomagnesemia.
w: Increase oral potassium chloride
Add spironolactone
Add sodium bicarbonate

qs.q: A 58-year-old man on hemodialysis has phosphate 7.2 mg/dL and calcium 10.4 mg/dL despite dietary counseling. Which is the most appropriate phosphate binder?
qs.a: Sevelamer carbonate
qs.x: Non-calcium binders such as sevelamer or lanthanum are preferred when calcium is high. Aluminum is avoided long term because of bone disease and encephalopathy.
w: Calcium acetate
Calcium carbonate
Aluminum hydroxide long term

qs.q: A 64-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 has fatigue. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, ferritin 60 ng/mL, and transferrin saturation 12 percent. Which is the most appropriate next step?
qs.a: Iron repletion before considering an ESA
qs.x: Iron deficiency should be corrected first in CKD anemia; ESAs are less effective without adequate iron. Hemoglobin targets above 11.5 g/dL with ESAs increase stroke and cardiovascular events.
w: Epoetin alfa targeting hemoglobin above 13 g/dL
Blood transfusion of 2 units
Oral folic acid alone

qs.q: A 45-year-old man has recurrent calcium oxalate stones. A 24-hour urine collection shows high urinary calcium with normal serum calcium and PTH. He drinks 3 L of fluid daily. Which is the most appropriate medication?
qs.a: Chlorthalidone
qs.x: Thiazide diuretics increase distal calcium reabsorption and reduce hypercalciuria and stone recurrence. Loop diuretics increase urinary calcium, and dietary calcium restriction increases oxalate absorption.
w: Furosemide
Allopurinol
Calcium restriction to 400 mg/day

qs.q: A 74-year-old woman with untreated hypothyroidism is found lethargic. Temperature is 34.2 C (93.6 F), BP 84/50 mm Hg, pulse 48/min, and sodium 124 mEq/L. TSH is 85 mU/L and free T4 is undetectable. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: IV hydrocortisone and IV levothyroxine
qs.x: Myxedema coma requires IV levothyroxine, with stress-dose hydrocortisone given first until adrenal insufficiency is excluded. Active rewarming can cause vasodilation and shock.
w: Oral levothyroxine 25 mcg daily, recheck TSH in 6 weeks
Active external rewarming with heating blankets only
IV liothyronine alone

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman has received denosumab every 6 months for 5 years for osteoporosis. She wants to stop treatment. Which is the most appropriate plan?
qs.a: Follow denosumab with a bisphosphonate
qs.x: Stopping denosumab causes rapid bone loss and rebound multiple vertebral fractures. Doses should not be delayed, and a bisphosphonate should follow discontinuation.
w: Stop denosumab with no further therapy
Delay the next dose by 1 year as a drug holiday
Switch to calcium and vitamin D supplements only

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman has amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Prolactin is 180 ng/mL, pregnancy test is negative, and MRI shows an 8-mm pituitary adenoma without visual field defects. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Cabergoline
qs.x: Dopamine agonists are first-line for prolactinomas; cabergoline is more effective and better tolerated than bromocriptine. Surgery is for intolerance or resistance.
w: Bromocriptine
Transsphenoidal surgery
Radiation therapy

qs.q: A 42-year-old woman has episodic headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis. BP is 172/104 mm Hg. Plasma metanephrines are markedly elevated and CT shows a 4-cm adrenal mass. Surgery is planned. Which medication should be started first?
qs.a: Phenoxybenzamine
qs.x: Preoperative alpha blockade for 10 to 14 days precedes beta blockade in pheochromocytoma. Starting a beta blocker first leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can cause hypertensive crisis.
w: Propranolol
Labetalol
Hydrochlorothiazide

qs.q: A 60-year-old man has taken prednisone 20 mg daily for 6 months for interstitial lung disease. He is scheduled for an open colectomy. Which is the most appropriate perioperative steroid plan?
qs.a: Stress-dose IV hydrocortisone, then taper
qs.x: Long-term glucocorticoid use at 20 mg or more for 3 weeks or more suppresses the HPA axis. Major surgery warrants stress-dose hydrocortisone (100 mg IV then 50 mg every 8 hours) with a taper.
w: Stop prednisone 1 week before surgery
Continue prednisone 20 mg orally alone
Give dexamethasone only if hypotension develops

qs.q: A 38-year-old woman has 2 weeks of anterior neck pain, palpitations, and tremor after a viral illness. The thyroid is tender. TSH is suppressed, free T4 is high, ESR is 70 mm/h, and radioactive iodine uptake is low. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Propranolol plus an NSAID
qs.x: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is self-limited thyrotoxicosis from hormone release, not synthesis. Treatment is beta blockade and NSAIDs, with prednisone if severe. Thionamides and RAI are ineffective.
w: Methimazole 20 mg daily
Radioactive iodine ablation
Total thyroidectomy

qs.q: A 19-year-old woman ingested an unknown amount of acetaminophen 4 hours ago. She is asymptomatic. The 4-hour acetaminophen level is 220 mcg/mL, above the treatment line. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: N-acetylcysteine
qs.x: An acetaminophen level above the treatment line on the nomogram requires NAC, which replenishes glutathione. It is most effective within 8 hours of ingestion.
w: Activated charcoal alone
Fomepizole
Hemodialysis

qs.q: A 45-year-old man ingested a large amount of aspirin. He is confused and has tinnitus. Salicylate level is 105 mg/dL, pH 7.30, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Sodium bicarbonate is infusing. Which is the most appropriate next step?
qs.a: Hemodialysis
qs.x: Hemodialysis is indicated for salicylate poisoning with altered mental status, a level above 90 to 100 mg/dL, kidney failure, or pulmonary edema. Intubation is dangerous because loss of respiratory compensation worsens acidosis.
w: Intubation with low minute ventilation
Activated charcoal alone
Intravenous acetazolamide

qs.q: A 40-year-old man is confused after drinking antifreeze. pH is 7.12, anion gap 28, and osmolal gap 30 mOsm/kg. Urine shows calcium oxalate crystals. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Fomepizole
qs.x: Fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase to block formation of toxic metabolites of ethylene glycol and methanol. Hemodialysis is added for severe acidosis or kidney failure.
w: N-acetylcysteine
Physostigmine
Deferoxamine

qs.q: A 78-year-old woman on digoxin for AF has nausea and yellow-tinted vision. Pulse is 40/min with runs of bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. Potassium is 6.1 mEq/L and the digoxin level is 4.2 ng/mL. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Digoxin immune Fab
qs.x: Life-threatening dysrhythmias, potassium above 5 to 6 mEq/L, or end-organ toxicity are indications for digoxin-specific antibody fragments. Dialysis does not remove digoxin.
w: Intravenous calcium gluconate
Intravenous amiodarone
Hemodialysis

qs.q: A 35-year-old farmer has vomiting, diarrhea, miosis, bronchorrhea, wheezing, bradycardia, and fasciculations after spraying pesticide. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Atropine plus pralidoxime
qs.x: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Atropine treats muscarinic effects, titrated to drying of secretions, and pralidoxime regenerates the enzyme to reverse nicotinic weakness before aging.
w: Physostigmine plus atropine
Atropine alone without any other antidote
Neostigmine plus glycopyrrolate

qs.q: A 40-year-old man is rescued from a house fire. He is confused and hypotensive with soot in the oropharynx. Lactate is 12 mmol/L and SpO2 is normal. Which is the most appropriate antidote in addition to 100 percent oxygen?
qs.a: Hydroxocobalamin
qs.x: Smoke inhalation with lactate above 8 suggests cyanide poisoning. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin. Nitrites induce methemoglobinemia, worsening oxygen delivery with coexisting carbon monoxide.
w: Methylene blue
Sodium nitrite plus amyl nitrite
Pralidoxime

qs.q: A 24-year-old man has cyanosis and dyspnea after receiving topical benzocaine spray before endoscopy. SpO2 is 85 percent despite oxygen, and PaO2 is 210 mm Hg. Methemoglobin is 32 percent. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Methylene blue
qs.x: Methylene blue reduces methemoglobin to hemoglobin via NADPH methemoglobin reductase. It is ineffective and may cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, and it can cause serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs.
w: Hydroxocobalamin
Hyperbaric oxygen
Ascorbic acid only

qs.q: A 55-year-old woman who has taken alprazolam daily for years is found unresponsive next to empty bottles of alprazolam and amitriptyline. Respiratory rate is 8/min and ECG shows a QRS duration of 120 ms. Which medication should be avoided?
qs.a: Flumazenil
qs.x: Flumazenil can precipitate seizures in chronic benzodiazepine users and in coingestion of proconvulsants such as TCAs. Airway support is preferred.
w: Naloxone
Sodium bicarbonate
Intravenous fluids

qs.q: A 22-year-old woman who recently started treatment for latent TB took an overdose of her medication. She has recurrent seizures not responding to lorazepam and a severe anion gap metabolic acidosis. Which is the most appropriate antidote?
qs.a: Intravenous pyridoxine
qs.x: Isoniazid overdose depletes pyridoxine and GABA, causing refractory seizures and lactic acidosis. IV pyridoxine, 1 g per g of isoniazid or 5 g empirically, is the antidote; phenytoin is ineffective.
w: Intravenous phenytoin
N-acetylcysteine
Fomepizole

qs.q: A 17-year-old boy has inflammatory papules and pustules on the face, chest, and back with scattered comedones, unresponsive to topical benzoyl peroxide. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Topical retinoid, benzoyl peroxide, and oral doxycycline
qs.x: Moderate inflammatory acne is treated with a topical retinoid and benzoyl peroxide plus an oral tetracycline for about 3 months. Benzoyl peroxide limits resistance and antibiotics should not be used alone.
w: Oral doxycycline monotherapy for 12 months
Oral isotretinoin as first-line without other trials
Topical clindamycin alone

qs.q: A 7-year-old boy has a scaly patch of alopecia with broken hairs and posterior cervical adenopathy. KOH prep shows hyphae within the hair shaft. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Oral terbinafine or griseofulvin
qs.x: Tinea capitis requires systemic therapy because topical agents do not penetrate hair follicles. Terbinafine and griseofulvin are first-line; selenium sulfide shampoo reduces spread.
w: Topical clotrimazole cream
Topical hydrocortisone cream
Oral fluconazole for 3 days only

qs.q: An 84-year-old nursing home resident has thick, crusted, scaling plaques on the hands and trunk. Several staff members have itching. Scraping shows numerous mites. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Oral ivermectin plus topical permethrin
qs.x: Crusted scabies has a very high mite burden and requires combined oral ivermectin with topical permethrin. Contacts and staff are treated simultaneously.
w: Topical permethrin once only
Topical hydrocortisone and oral cetirizine
Oral fluconazole and topical clotrimazole

qs.q: You are cross-covering an 80-year-old man on warfarin with a stable INR of 2.4. He is started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for cystitis. Which is the most appropriate plan?
qs.a: Choose a different antibiotic or recheck the INR within 3-5 days
qs.x: TMP-SMX inhibits CYP2C9 and markedly raises the INR; avoid it or monitor closely.
w: Double the warfarin dose for the full length of the antibiotic course
Stop warfarin until the antibiotic course is fully finished
Continue both drugs unchanged and recheck the INR in 1 month

qs.q: A 92-kg man with MRSA bacteremia is admitted. Which approach to vancomycin monitoring do current national guidelines recommend?
qs.a: Adjust dosing to an AUC/MIC target of about 400-600
qs.x: The 2020 ASHP/IDSA consensus favors AUC-guided dosing (AUC/MIC 400-600) over trough-only monitoring to limit nephrotoxicity.
w: Adjust dosing to keep every trough between 25 and 30
Give a fixed dose of 1 g every 12 hours without drug levels
Check a peak level after the first dose and target 40

qs.q: A 100-kg woman with septic shock and suspected MRSA pneumonia has normal renal function. Which initial vancomycin order is most appropriate?
qs.a: Loading dose of about 20-35 mg/kg of actual body weight, maximum 3 g
qs.x: Per ASHP/IDSA guidelines (off-label; the label lists 2 g/day), critically ill patients get a 20-35 mg/kg loading dose capped near 3 g.
w: Loading dose of 5 mg/kg of ideal body weight, then check levels
Flat dose of 500 mg IV every 6 hours without any loading dose
Loading dose of 50 mg/kg of actual body weight with no maximum

qs.q: A patient on once-daily (extended-interval) gentamicin 7 mg/kg has a random level drawn 10 hours after the dose. How is this level used?
qs.a: Plotted on a nomogram to choose the dosing interval
qs.x: With extended-interval dosing, a single random level (6-14 hours post-dose) is plotted on a nomogram such as the Hartford nomogram to set a q24h, q36h, or q48h interval.
w: Compared with a target peak of 20-30 mcg/mL for efficacy
Ignored, since only troughs matter for extended dosing
Used to calculate a new loading dose for the next day

qs.q: A patient is on gentamicin 1 mg/kg q8h for enterococcal synergy. Which peak and trough pair is the target for that indication?
qs.a: Peak 3 to 4 mcg/mL with a trough under 1 mcg/mL
qs.x: Synergy dosing aims only for a peak near 3 to 4 mcg/mL, because the role is to help a cell-wall agent rather than to kill on its own. Troughs are kept under 1 mcg/mL since sustained exposure drives nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity; peaks of 16 to 24 belong to extended-interval dosing for gram-negative infection.
w: Peak 16 to 24 mcg/mL with a trough under 1 mcg/mL
Peak 3 to 4 mcg/mL with a trough of 5 to 10 mcg/mL
Peak 8 to 10 mcg/mL with a trough of 2 to 4 mcg/mL

qs.q: A 70-kg man with type 2 diabetes on metformin is admitted for cellulitis. He is eating normally, and his glucose readings are 220-280 mg/dL. Which regimen is preferred?
qs.a: Basal-bolus insulin of about 0.4-0.5 units/kg/day total
qs.x: ADA guidance favors basal-bolus (or basal plus correction) insulin over sliding-scale insulin alone, with half of the total daily dose given as basal and half as prandial insulin.
w: Sliding-scale regular insulin alone before each meal
Continue metformin and add glipizide for the stay
Glargine 1 unit/kg once daily with no prandial or correction insulin

qs.q: An 84-year-old woman with an eGFR of 25 mL/min is starting inpatient insulin. How should the weight-based total daily dose be chosen?
qs.a: Use a lower dose, about 0.2-0.3 units/kg/day
qs.x: Older adults and those with renal impairment are at higher hypoglycemia risk, so start insulin at about 0.2-0.3 units/kg/day.
w: Use the standard dose of 0.5 units/kg/day
Use a higher dose, about 0.8 units/kg/day, to avoid DKA
Use 1 unit/kg/day split into four injections

qs.q: What is the generally recommended glucose target for most non-critically ill hospitalized patients on insulin?
qs.x: ADA recommends 140-180 mg/dL for most hospitalized patients; tighter targets of 80-110 mg/dL increase hypoglycemia without benefit.
w: 80-110 mg/dL (tight control)

qs.q: A woman with type 1 diabetes is made NPO for a morning procedure. The night-float nurse asks whether to hold her bedtime glargine. What do you order?
qs.a: Give glargine at about 75-80% of the usual dose
qs.x: Patients with type 1 diabetes always need basal insulin to prevent DKA; a modest dose reduction (about 20-25%) limits fasting hypoglycemia.
w: Hold all glargine until she is eating again
Give the full glargine dose plus extra prandial insulin
Replace glargine with sliding-scale insulin only

qs.q: A 75-kg patient with a new pulmonary embolism is started on an unfractionated heparin weight-based nomogram. What is the usual initial order?
qs.a: 80 units/kg bolus, then 18 units/kg/hr
qs.x: The standard VTE nomogram is an 80 units/kg bolus and 18 units/kg/hr; 60/12 is the lower-dose ACS nomogram.
w: 60 units/kg bolus, then 12 units/kg/hr with a 1000 units/hr cap
5000 units subcutaneously every 8 hours
1 mg/kg bolus, then 1 mg/kg/hr

qs.q: After a heparin infusion rate change, when should the next aPTT or anti-Xa level be drawn?
qs.a: About 6 hours after the change
qs.x: Heparin reaches a new steady state in about 6 hours, so levels are checked about 6 hours after each change.

Only at the next morning labs
After 3 full days at the new rate

qs.q: On day 7 of heparin therapy, a patient's platelet count has fallen from 240,000 to 95,000/mm3, and a new DVT is found. The 4T score is high. What is the next step?

Stop heparin and start warfarin immediately at full dose
Transfuse platelets and continue the heparin infusion

qs.q: A patient on telemetry has a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L and has only a peripheral IV. What is a safe maximum infusion rate for IV potassium chloride?

About 60 mEq/hr by IV push
About 100 mEq/hr

qs.q: Roughly how much will 40 mEq of potassium chloride raise serum potassium in a patient with normal renal function?
qs.a: About 0.4 mEq/L
qs.x: A common rule is that each 10 mEq raises serum potassium by about 0.1 mEq/L, though total body deficits vary.

About 1.5 mEq/L
About 0.04 mEq/L

qs.q: A patient with diarrhea has received 120 mEq of potassium over 2 days, but potassium remains 3.1 mEq/L. Which laboratory test is most useful to check next?

Serum uric acid and lactate

qs.q: A patient on telemetry develops polymorphic VT with a prolonged QT but still has a pulse and a normal blood pressure. Which drug should be given first?

qs.q: A malnourished patient restarted on tube feeds has muscle weakness and a phosphorus level of 0.9 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate step?

Give IV calcium chloride to raise the phosphorus

qs.q: A patient has ionized hypocalcemia with perioral tingling after thyroidectomy and has only a peripheral IV. Which order is preferred?

qs.x: Calcium gluconate is preferred peripherally; calcium chloride has three times the elemental calcium but causes severe tissue injury if it extravasates.

Oral calcium carbonate alone
IV sodium bicarbonate

qs.q: A patient has total calcium 7.6 mg/dL and albumin 2.0 g/dL. What is the corrected calcium?
qs.a: 9.2 mg/dL
qs.x: Corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.8 x (4 - albumin) = 7.6 + 1.6 = 9.2 mg/dL.
w: 7.6 mg/dL
8.4 mg/dL
10.8 mg/dL

qs.q: A patient with chronic hyponatremia (sodium 112 mEq/L) is mildly confused. What is a generally accepted maximum correction in the first 24 hours?
qs.a: About 8 mEq/L
qs.x: Limit correction to about 8 mEq/L per 24 hours in high-risk chronic hyponatremia to avoid osmotic demyelination.
w: About 20 mEq/L
About 15 mEq/L
About 25 mEq/L

qs.q: A woman with a sodium of 116 mEq/L is now having a seizure. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
qs.a: 100 mL of 3% saline IV, repeated if symptoms persist
qs.x: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia is treated with 100-mL boluses of 3% saline (up to three), aiming for a 4-6 mEq/L rise.
w: 1 L of 0.9% saline wide open over 30 minutes
Fluid restriction to 800 mL per day and recheck sodium in the morning
Oral tolvaptan 15 mg and recheck in 24 hours

qs.q: Twelve hours into treatment of hyponatremia, the sodium has risen from 114 to 125 mEq/L. Which action is appropriate?
qs.a: Give D5W and consider desmopressin to re-lower sodium
qs.x: An 11 mEq/L rise in 12 hours exceeds limits; re-lowering with free water and desmopressin reduces osmotic demyelination risk.
w: Continue the 3% saline at the same infusion rate
Switch to 0.9% saline at a higher rate to slow the rise in sodium
Add oral salt tablets and fluid restriction

qs.q: Which patient is the least appropriate candidate for tolvaptan for hyponatremia?
qs.a: A patient with cirrhosis and SIADH-range sodium
qs.x: Tolvaptan can cause serious liver injury and should be avoided in liver disease; it must also be started in the hospital.

A patient with euvolemic SIADH and normal liver tests
A patient with heart failure and Na 124 mEq/L

qs.q: An 82-year-old woman has taken omeprazole for 6 years after a single episode of dyspepsia and has no history of Barrett esophagus, ulcer, or GI bleeding. What is the best plan?

Stop omeprazole and start sucralfate four times daily
Double the omeprazole dose to prevent rebound symptoms

qs.q: A 79-year-old woman has taken lorazepam 1 mg nightly for 10 years and has fallen twice. What is the best deprescribing approach?
qs.a: Taper gradually by about 10-25% every 2-4 weeks

Switch to diazepam 10 mg nightly for long-term use
Continue it, since stopping at her age is unsafe

qs.q: Which sleep aid is the most appropriate to remove from the medication list of an 85-year-old man with BPH and mild cognitive impairment?

Sleep hygiene education handout
Acetaminophen 500 mg as needed

qs.q: A 78-year-old man with an eGFR of 40 mL/min has recurrent morning hypoglycemia. Which home medication is the most likely culprit and should be stopped?
qs.a: Glyburide
qs.x: Glyburide has active renally cleared metabolites and a long duration; Beers advises avoiding it in older adults.
w: Sitagliptin
Metformin
Empagliflozin

qs.q: An 81-year-old woman with no vascular disease takes aspirin 81 mg daily for primary prevention. What is the best recommendation?
qs.a: Discuss stopping it, since bleeding risk outweighs benefit
qs.x: Beers and USPSTF guidance advise against starting aspirin for primary prevention in older adults; consider deprescribing.
w: Increase aspirin to 325 mg for better protection
Add clopidogrel for dual antiplatelet prevention
Continue aspirin and add a daily NSAID for her arthritis pain

qs.q: An 88-year-old woman with CrCl 22 mL/min has uncomplicated cystitis. Which agent is least appropriate?

qs.q: A man on simvastatin 40 mg is prescribed clarithromycin for pneumonia. Two days later he has myalgias and dark urine. What is the mechanism?

Stop simvastatin for the duration
Make no change to the simvastatin

80 mg daily
10 mg twice daily

qs.q: A kidney transplant patient on tacrolimus is started on voriconazole for invasive aspergillosis. What is the expected adjustment?

qs.q: A patient on warfarin with an INR of 2.5 is started on fluconazole for esophageal candidiasis. What is the expected effect?

The INR will fall, so increase the warfarin dose by half for the course

Bleeding that requires immediate vitamin K

qs.q: An inpatient on methadone, IV haloperidol, and levofloxacin has a QTc of 520 ms. Nausea develops. Which antiemetic plan is best?

Give ondansetron with promethazine and no ECG monitoring

qs.a: A 12-lead ECG for the QTc
qs.x: IV haloperidol prolongs the QTc and can cause torsades; check a baseline ECG and electrolytes.

qs.q: A patient on sertraline is started on linezolid for VRE. Two days later he has tremor, clonus, diarrhea, and fever. What is the most likely cause?

Anticholinergic toxicity from high-dose sertraline

qs.a: Benzodiazepines, supportive care, and cyproheptadine
qs.x: Management is stopping serotonergic drugs, benzodiazepines, supportive care, and the 5-HT2A antagonist cyproheptadine.

Haloperidol for agitation and a cooling blanket
Physostigmine and a repeat dose of the SSRI

qs.q: A patient on high-dose venlafaxine needs post-op pain control. Which opioid is most important to avoid?

Oxycodone
Morphine

qs.q: A patient on fluoxetine develops vasoplegia after cardiac surgery and the team considers methylene blue. What is the main concern?

Anaphylaxis from cross-reacting sulfa groups
Prolonged neuromuscular blockade

qs.q: A 29-year-old woman on lisinopril for chronic hypertension tells you she is 7 weeks pregnant. What is the best plan?

w: Continue lisinopril, since risk is in the first trimester
Switch to losartan for safer blood pressure control
Stop all antihypertensives for the rest of pregnancy

qs.q: A woman on warfarin for recurrent DVT learns that she is 6 weeks pregnant. Which anticoagulant should replace warfarin?

Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily with the evening meal
Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily

Hydromorphone
Morphine

qs.q: A patient with compensated cirrhosis who does not drink asks about acetaminophen. What is a commonly recommended daily maximum?

About 4 g every 12 hours

qs.q: A 70-kg patient with CrCl 22 mL/min has a new DVT. Which enoxaparin dose is appropriate?

qs.q: A patient on dabigatran with severe GI bleeding needs reversal. Which agent is specific for dabigatran?
