qs.q: A 78-year-old woman with diabetes reports weakness, nausea, and mild shortness of breath for 2 hours. She denies chest pain. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
qs.a: Suspect a possible heart attack and treat accordingly
qs.x: Older adults, women, and diabetics often have atypical ACS presentations without chest pain, so these symptoms should be treated as a possible heart attack.
w: Chest pain is absent, so a heart problem is ruled out
These are common age-related symptoms needing no treatment
This is most likely a stomach virus with dehydration

qs.q: A 69-year-old man has new right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Which piece of history is most important to obtain?
qs.a: The time he was last known well
qs.x: Stroke treatment eligibility depends on time from onset, which is defined as the last time the patient was known to be at baseline.
w: Whether he has had a recent flu shot
His typical daily fluid intake
The name of his primary care doctor

qs.q: Which components make up the Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Facial droop; Arm drift; Abnormal speech
qs.x: The Cincinnati scale checks for facial droop, arm drift, and speech abnormality; any one abnormal finding raises suspicion of stroke.
opts: Facial droop
Arm drift
Abnormal speech
Pupil size and reactivity
Blood pressure difference between arms
ok: Facial droop
Arm drift
Abnormal speech

qs.q: An 80-year-old man has confusion and weakness on one side of his body. Which assessment should you perform because its result can mimic a stroke?
qs.a: Blood glucose level
qs.x: Hypoglycemia can produce stroke-like deficits, so the blood glucose should be checked in any patient with suspected stroke.
w: Pupil response to light
Capillary refill time
Lung sounds

qs.q: A patient with suspected stroke asks for a glass of water. What should you do?
qs.a: Withhold food and drink because swallowing may be impaired
qs.x: Stroke patients frequently have difficulty swallowing, so they should receive nothing by mouth to prevent aspiration.
w: Give small sips of water to keep her mouth moist
Allow water but not food until the hospital
Give a sugary drink to protect her brain

qs.q: A 72-year-old man has sudden severe abdominal pain radiating to his back, a pulsating mass near the umbilicus, and pale skin. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Abdominal aortic aneurysm
qs.x: Sudden abdominal or back pain with a pulsatile mass in an older man suggests an AAA; handle the abdomen gently, treat for shock, and transport rapidly.
w: Kidney stone
Acute appendicitis
Gastroenteritis with severe cramping

qs.q: A 1-year-old has a heart rate of 52/min, pale mottled skin, and poor responsiveness despite effective BVM ventilation with oxygen. What should you do?
qs.a: Begin chest compressions
qs.x: In infants and children, a heart rate below 60/min with poor perfusion despite adequate oxygenation and ventilation requires CPR.
w: Continue ventilations only
Recheck the pulse in 5 minutes
Place the child in a car seat for transport

qs.q: After defibrillation, an adult regains a pulse but remains unresponsive and is not breathing adequately. How should you ventilate?
qs.a: 1 breath every 6 seconds
qs.x: After ROSC, ventilate at about 10 breaths/min and avoid hyperventilation, which raises intrathoracic pressure and lowers cardiac output.
w: 1 breath every 2 seconds
As fast as possible to clear CO2
Only when SpO2 drops below 80%

qs.q: A 28-year-old with a suspected opioid overdose is unresponsive, apneic, and pulseless. What is your priority?
qs.a: High-quality CPR and AED use
qs.x: A pulseless patient is in cardiac arrest; CPR and defibrillation take priority, and naloxone, if given, must not delay them.
w: Giving naloxone before any compressions
Searching the scene for the drug used
Placing a nonrebreather mask

qs.q: Which findings are considered obvious signs of death that allow you to withhold resuscitation? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Dependent lividity; Decomposition of tissue; Decapitation
qs.x: Dependent lividity, decomposition, decapitation, and rigor mortis are definitive signs; fixed pupils, pulselessness, and cool skin also occur in patients who may still be resuscitated.
opts: Dependent lividity
Decomposition of tissue
Decapitation
Fixed and dilated pupils
Absence of a pulse and breathing
Skin that feels cool to the touch
ok: Dependent lividity
Decomposition of tissue
Decapitation

qs.q: A woman who is 34 weeks pregnant is in cardiac arrest. Along with high-quality CPR, what should be done?
qs.a: Manual left uterine displacement
qs.x: Manually displacing the uterus to the left relieves compression of the vena cava and improves blood return during CPR.
w: Elevate both legs 12 inches
Compress lower on the abdomen
Place her on her right side for CPR

qs.q: You are applying AED pads to an adult in cardiac arrest. Which steps are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Wipe a wet chest dry before placing pads; Remove a medication patch and wipe the skin; Avoid placing a pad directly over an implanted device
qs.x: Water and medication patches can divert current or cause burns, and pads should be placed away from implanted devices; defibrillation should never be delayed for ALS.
opts: Wipe a wet chest dry before placing pads
Remove a medication patch and wipe the skin
Avoid placing a pad directly over an implanted device
Place one pad directly over the pacemaker to improve contact
Delay defibrillation until ALS confirms the rhythm
ok: Wipe a wet chest dry before placing pads
Remove a medication patch and wipe the skin
Avoid placing a pad directly over an implanted device

qs.q: A 59-year-old man had chest pressure begin while shoveling snow. It has continued for 30 minutes despite rest. How should this be interpreted?
qs.a: Possible heart attack, because the pain is not relieved by rest
qs.x: Angina typically resolves within minutes of rest; chest pain persisting despite rest suggests an acute MI and should be treated as ACS.
w: Stable angina that will resolve if he keeps resting
Muscle strain because it started during physical work
Indigestion because it has lasted longer than 15 minutes

qs.q: An 81-year-old woman fainted while sitting at the dinner table and is now alert. What is the most concerning possible cause?
qs.a: A cardiac dysrhythmia
qs.x: Syncope that occurs while seated or without warning in an older adult raises concern for a cardiac rhythm problem and needs evaluation.
w: Simple dehydration from heat
Standing up too quickly
An emotional fainting reaction

qs.q: Two EMTs are performing CPR on an infant. Which compression technique is preferred?
qs.a: Two thumbs with hands encircling the chest
qs.x: For two-rescuer infant CPR, the two thumb-encircling hands technique is recommended because it produces better depth and blood pressure.
w: Heel of both hands stacked on the sternum
Three fingers placed below the nipple line
One thumb pressing on the lower sternum

qs.q: A man has bright red blood spurting from a deep wound to his mid-thigh. What should you do?
qs.a: Apply a tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound
qs.x: Life-threatening extremity bleeding is controlled with a tourniquet placed 2-3 inches proximal to the wound, not over a joint, and tightened until bleeding stops.
w: Elevate the leg and apply a cold pack
Apply a loose dressing and check distal pulses
Apply a tourniquet directly over the knee joint

qs.q: A tourniquet has been tightened fully on a patient's thigh, but bright red bleeding continues. What should you do next?
qs.a: Apply a second tourniquet just above the first
qs.x: If one correctly applied tourniquet does not stop the bleeding, a second tourniquet is placed proximal to the first.
w: Remove the tourniquet and use direct pressure
Loosen the tourniquet to let the limb reperfuse
Place it lower, directly over the wound

qs.q: A stab wound to the groin is bleeding heavily. A tourniquet cannot be applied. What should you do?
qs.a: Pack the wound and hold firm direct pressure
qs.x: Junctional wounds such as the groin are controlled by packing the wound tightly with gauze, ideally hemostatic, and holding firm direct pressure.
w: Elevate the legs and apply an ice pack
Apply a loose bandage and transport quickly
Wait for ALS to arrive and place a tourniquet at the hip

qs.q: A patient with a gunshot wound to the chest is deteriorating. Which findings suggest a tension pneumothorax? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Severe and increasing shortness of breath; Absent breath sounds on one side; Hypotension with distended neck veins
qs.x: Tension pneumothorax causes worsening respiratory distress, unilateral absent breath sounds, and signs of obstructive shock such as hypotension and JVD.
opts: Severe and increasing shortness of breath
Absent breath sounds on one side
Hypotension with distended neck veins
Equal breath sounds bilaterally
Slow, deep respirations of 10 per minute
ok: Severe and increasing shortness of breath
Absent breath sounds on one side
Hypotension with distended neck veins

qs.q: After you seal an open chest wound with an occlusive dressing, the patient becomes more short of breath and hypotensive. What should you do?
qs.a: Briefly lift a corner of the dressing to release air
qs.x: Worsening distress after sealing a chest wound suggests developing tension pneumothorax; briefly lifting the dressing lets trapped air escape.
w: Add a second occlusive dressing over the first
Pack the chest wound with gauze
Increase BVM pressure to force the lung open

qs.q: A man has a knife impaled in his abdomen. He is alert and his airway is clear. How should you manage the knife?
qs.a: Stabilize it in place with bulky dressings
qs.x: Impaled objects are stabilized in place because removal can cause uncontrolled bleeding; they are removed only if they obstruct the airway or prevent CPR.
w: Remove it and apply direct pressure
Pull it out partway to reduce bleeding
Cut it off at skin level so it fits under a dressing

qs.q: A patient has abdominal organs protruding through a laceration. How should you treat the wound?
qs.a: Cover it with a moist sterile dressing and then an occlusive layer
qs.x: Eviscerated organs are covered with a moist sterile dressing and occlusive layer to keep them moist and warm; never try to replace them.
w: Gently push the organs back into the abdomen
Apply a dry gauze dressing held with firm pressure
Leave the organs uncovered so they can be watched

qs.q: After a car crash, which findings indicate the need for spinal motion restriction? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Tenderness over the midline of the neck; Numbness and tingling in both hands; Intoxication that prevents a reliable exam
qs.x: Midline tenderness, neurologic deficits, and an unreliable exam from intoxication or altered mental status indicate spinal motion restriction; the other findings support clearing it.
opts: Tenderness over the midline of the neck
Numbness and tingling in both hands
Intoxication that prevents a reliable exam
Alert patient with only a forearm laceration
Normal motor and sensory function in all limbs
Able to turn head 45 degrees each way without pain
ok: Tenderness over the midline of the neck
Numbness and tingling in both hands
Intoxication that prevents a reliable exam

qs.q: A 40-year-old man has lost a large amount of blood. Which sign indicates his shock has become decompensated?
qs.a: Falling blood pressure
qs.x: Hypotension is a late sign of shock that appears after compensatory mechanisms fail; anxiety, tachycardia, and pale cool skin are earlier signs.
w: Anxiety and restlessness
Mild tachycardia
Pale, cool skin

qs.q: A 6-year-old struck by a bicycle has a heart rate of 150, capillary refill of 4 seconds, cool skin, and a normal blood pressure. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Compensated shock
qs.x: Children maintain blood pressure until late; tachycardia and poor perfusion with a normal BP indicate compensated shock needing rapid treatment and transport.
w: No shock because blood pressure is normal
Anxiety from the accident
Normal vital signs for this age

qs.q: Using the rule of nines, estimate the burned area for an adult with full-thickness burns to the entire right arm and the entire front of the torso.
qs.x: In an adult each arm is 9% and the anterior trunk is 18%, totaling 27% of body surface area.

qs.q: A worker is covered with a dry chemical powder that is burning his skin. What should you do first?
qs.a: Brush off the powder, then flush with large amounts of water
qs.x: Dry chemicals should be brushed away before irrigation, because some react with water; then flush with copious water.
w: Immediately pour water over the powder
Cover the area with a dry sterile dressing
Apply a neutralizing chemical solution

qs.q: A man with a head injury has a blood pressure of 188/100, a pulse of 48, and irregular respirations. What do these findings suggest?
qs.a: Increasing pressure in the skull
qs.x: Rising blood pressure, falling pulse, and irregular breathing (Cushing's triad) indicate increasing intracranial pressure and possible brain herniation.
w: Hemorrhagic shock from a scalp wound
Spinal shock
An anxiety reaction to the crash and injury

qs.q: You are splinting an open fracture of the forearm. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Check pulse, motor, and sensation before and after splinting; Immobilize the joints above and below the injury; Cover the open wound with a sterile dressing
qs.x: Splinting includes neurovascular checks before and after, immobilizing adjacent joints, and dressing open wounds; never push bone ends back in.
opts: Check pulse, motor, and sensation before and after splinting
Immobilize the joints above and below the injury
Cover the open wound with a sterile dressing
Push the exposed bone end back under the skin
Straighten every deformity, even at the joints
ok: Check pulse, motor, and sensation before and after splinting
Immobilize the joints above and below the injury
Cover the open wound with a sterile dressing

qs.q: Which finding is a contraindication to using a traction splint for a suspected femur fracture?
qs.a: A suspected pelvic fracture
qs.x: Traction splints pull against the pelvis and are contraindicated with pelvic, hip, knee, or lower leg injuries on the same side; a closed midshaft femur fracture is the indication.
w: Severe pain in the thigh
A closed midshaft femur fracture
An intact distal pulse

qs.q: A woman struck by a car has pelvic pain, instability, and signs of shock. What is the best action?
qs.a: Apply a pelvic binder and avoid rocking the pelvis
qs.x: An unstable pelvis can bleed heavily; a pelvic binder or sheet wrap stabilizes it, and repeated manipulation may worsen bleeding.
w: Compress and rock the pelvis to confirm instability
Elevate her legs and roll her to check her back
Apply a traction splint to both legs

qs.q: How should you care for a finger that was completely amputated?
qs.a: Wrap it in moist sterile gauze, seal it in a bag, and keep it cool
qs.x: The part should be wrapped in moist sterile gauze, placed in a sealed bag, and kept cool without direct contact with ice to avoid tissue damage.
w: Submerge the finger directly in a cup of ice water
Pack the finger in dry ice for the trip
Rinse it in tap water and wrap it in a towel

qs.q: An 82-year-old woman on a blood thinner fell from standing and bumped her head. She is alert with a small bruise on her forehead. What is your main concern?
qs.a: Delayed bleeding inside the skull
qs.x: Older adults on anticoagulants have a high risk of intracranial bleeding even after minor head trauma, and symptoms may be delayed, so they should be transported.
w: A minor bruise that only needs an ice pack
Hip fracture from the fall
Dehydration that caused her to fall

qs.q: Which findings meet criteria for transport to the highest level of trauma center? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Amputation above the wrist; Penetrating wound to the chest; Unable to follow commands
qs.x: National field triage guidelines direct patients with proximal amputations, penetrating torso injuries, or altered mental status to the highest-level trauma center.
opts: Amputation above the wrist
Penetrating wound to the chest
Unable to follow commands
Isolated closed wrist fracture
Scalp cut controlled with pressure
Age of 40 years
ok: Amputation above the wrist
Penetrating wound to the chest
Unable to follow commands

qs.q: A 52-year-old diabetic is confused but can follow commands and swallow. Her blood glucose is 48 mg/dL. What should you do?
qs.a: Give oral glucose
qs.x: A hypoglycemic patient who can swallow and protect the airway should receive oral glucose, then be reassessed.
w: Withhold all treatment
Give her insulin
Have her lie flat and rest

qs.q: A diabetic man is unresponsive with snoring respirations and a glucose of 32 mg/dL. Which action is inappropriate?
qs.a: Placing oral glucose between his cheek and gum
qs.x: Oral glucose should not be given to a patient who cannot swallow or protect the airway because of aspiration risk; manage the airway and request ALS.
w: Opening the airway and providing ventilation as needed
Requesting ALS for IV dextrose
Positioning him to protect the airway

qs.q: Which findings are consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Deep, rapid respirations; Fruity odor on the breath; Excessive thirst and urination
qs.x: DKA develops over hours to days with Kussmaul respirations, fruity breath, and polyuria; sudden onset with cool, clammy skin suggests hypoglycemia.
opts: Deep, rapid respirations
Fruity odor on the breath
Excessive thirst and urination
Onset over a few minutes
Cool, clammy, sweaty skin
ok: Deep, rapid respirations
Fruity odor on the breath
Excessive thirst and urination

qs.q: A 19-year-old was stung by a bee. Which findings indicate anaphylaxis? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hives with wheezing; Blood pressure of 78/40; Swelling of the lips and tongue
qs.x: Anaphylaxis involves multiple body systems or airway, breathing, or circulatory compromise; local reactions and mild allergy symptoms alone are not anaphylaxis.
opts: Hives with wheezing
Blood pressure of 78/40
Swelling of the lips and tongue
Redness at the sting site only
Sneezing and watery eyes only
ok: Hives with wheezing
Blood pressure of 78/40
Swelling of the lips and tongue

qs.q: An 18-month-old with a fever had a seizure that stopped after 1 minute. He is now drowsy but breathing adequately. What is appropriate?
qs.a: Remove excess clothing and transport
qs.x: Febrile seizures are managed by protecting the airway, removing excess clothing, and transport; cold baths and alcohol can cause hypothermia or toxicity.
w: Place him in a cold-water bath to lower the fever quickly
Sponge him with rubbing alcohol
Place a bite block in his mouth in case of another seizure

qs.q: A 2-year-old may have swallowed some of her grandmother's pills. What information is most important to obtain?
qs.a: What was taken, how much, and when
qs.x: The substance, amount, and time of ingestion guide treatment; bring the containers and contact poison control per protocol.
w: Whether the child has been vaccinated
The grandmother's medical history
The color of the child's last stool

qs.q: On a cold winter night, a family of four has headaches, nausea, and dizziness. Their furnace was recently repaired. What should you do?
qs.a: Remove them from the home and give high-flow oxygen
qs.x: Multiple people with the same symptoms indoors suggests carbon monoxide poisoning; remove them from the environment and give high-flow oxygen, as pulse oximetry can be falsely normal.
w: Have them rest in bed and recheck in an hour
Give oxygen only if their SpO2 is below 94%
Open one window and treat them inside

qs.q: A farm worker was exposed to an organophosphate pesticide. Which signs would you expect? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Excessive salivation; Pinpoint pupils; Vomiting and diarrhea
qs.x: Organophosphates cause excessive secretions (SLUDGEM), small pupils, and GI symptoms; hot dry skin and dilated pupils are anticholinergic signs.
opts: Excessive salivation
Pinpoint pupils
Vomiting and diarrhea
Hot, dry skin
Dilated pupils
ok: Excessive salivation
Pinpoint pupils
Vomiting and diarrhea

qs.q: A marathon runner collapsed on a hot day. He is confused with hot skin and a rapid pulse. What is the priority?
qs.a: Begin rapid cooling
qs.x: Heat stroke is life-threatening; altered mental status with hyperthermia requires immediate, aggressive cooling and rapid transport.
w: Give a sports drink
Let him rest in the shade
Wrap him in a blanket

qs.q: Which finding most reliably separates heat stroke from heat exhaustion?
qs.a: Altered mental status
qs.x: Heat stroke is defined by central nervous system dysfunction such as confusion or seizures; sweating may be present in either condition.
w: Heavy sweating
Painful muscle cramps in the legs
Nausea

qs.q: A severely hypothermic patient is found outdoors with a slow pulse. Why should you handle him gently?
qs.a: Rough movement can trigger ventricular fibrillation
qs.x: The cold heart is very irritable, and rough handling can cause ventricular fibrillation; move patients gently and prevent further heat loss.
w: Rough movement will make him shiver less
His skin is too cold to feel pain
Fast movement improves blood flow to the heart

qs.q: A hiker has frozen, hard, white toes. Transport will take 2 hours over snowy terrain. What should you do?
qs.a: Protect the area and avoid rewarming if refreezing is possible
qs.x: Frostbitten tissue should not be rubbed and should not be thawed if refreezing could occur; protect the area and transport.
w: Rub the toes vigorously with snow
Massage the toes until color returns
Apply a heating pad set to high

qs.q: A child is pulled from a pool. She is apneic but has a pulse. What should you do first?
qs.a: Begin BVM ventilation with oxygen
qs.x: Hypoxia is the main problem in drowning; ventilation with oxygen is the priority, and abdominal thrusts to remove water are not recommended.
w: Perform abdominal thrusts to remove water
Turn her on her side to drain water
Wrap her in blankets and recheck

qs.q: A man was bitten on the leg by a rattlesnake. What is appropriate care?
qs.a: Keep him calm, limit movement, and remove tight items
qs.x: Keep the patient calm, immobilize the limb, and remove rings or constricting items before swelling; ice, tourniquets, and cutting can cause harm.
w: Apply ice directly to the bite
Apply a tight tourniquet above the bite
Cut the wound and suction the venom

qs.q: A woman in labor has the urge to push and you see the baby's head at the vaginal opening during contractions. What should you do?
qs.a: Prepare to deliver the baby on scene
qs.x: Crowning with the urge to push indicates imminent delivery; prepare for birth on scene rather than attempting transport.
w: Transport immediately with legs crossed
Tell her to hold her breath
Push the head back to slow labor

qs.q: During delivery, you find the umbilical cord wrapped loosely around the infant's neck. What should you do?
qs.a: Gently slip the cord over the head
qs.x: A loose nuchal cord should be slipped over the head; if it is too tight, clamp it in two places and cut between the clamps.
w: Pull hard on the cord to free it
Cut the cord immediately
Push the baby back into the birth canal

qs.q: During labor, you see the umbilical cord protruding from the vagina before the baby. What should you do?
qs.a: Raise her hips and lift the baby's head off the cord
qs.x: A prolapsed cord is compressed by the presenting part; elevate the hips, lift the presenting part off the cord with gloved fingers, keep the cord moist, and transport rapidly.
w: Gently push the cord back into the vagina
Pull the cord to speed up delivery
Have her push hard with each contraction

qs.q: During delivery, a single arm protrudes from the vagina. What should you do?
qs.a: Transport immediately
qs.x: A limb presentation cannot be delivered in the field; place the mother in a position of comfort, give oxygen, and transport immediately.
w: Pull on the arm
Push the arm back in
Wait for contractions to deliver the baby

qs.q: After delivery, a mother is bleeding heavily and her uterus feels soft. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Massage the top of the uterus firmly; Encourage her to breastfeed; Treat for shock and transport
qs.x: Fundal massage and breastfeeding help the uterus contract; treat for shock and transport. Never pack the vagina or pull on the cord.
opts: Massage the top of the uterus firmly
Encourage her to breastfeed
Treat for shock and transport
Pack the vagina with gauze
Pull on the cord to deliver the placenta
ok: Massage the top of the uterus firmly
Encourage her to breastfeed
Treat for shock and transport

qs.q: After 30 seconds of effective BVM ventilation, a newborn's heart rate remains 50/min. What should you do?
qs.a: Begin chest compressions at a 3:1 ratio
qs.x: A newborn heart rate below 60 despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation requires compressions coordinated with ventilations at a 3:1 ratio.
w: Continue ventilation only and recheck in 5 minutes
Stimulate the baby
Check blood glucose

qs.q: A newborn is apneic with a heart rate of 80/min after drying and stimulation. What should you do?
qs.a: Begin BVM ventilation with room air or oxygen
qs.x: Apnea or a heart rate below 100 after initial steps requires positive pressure ventilation.
w: Start chest compressions
Continue drying and rubbing the back for 2 more minutes
Suction the stomach

qs.q: A baby has just been born. What are the first steps in caring for the newborn?
qs.a: Dry, warm, position, and stimulate
qs.x: Initial newborn care includes drying, warming, positioning the airway, clearing secretions as needed, and stimulating breathing.
w: Suction the stomach and give oxygen
Give 2 breaths and check a pulse
Clamp the cord and weigh the baby

qs.q: A woman 36 weeks pregnant becomes dizzy and hypotensive while lying flat on her back. What should you do?
qs.a: Place her on her left side
qs.x: Supine hypotensive syndrome occurs when the uterus compresses the vena cava; placing her on her left side relieves it.
w: Have her sit upright
Raise her legs
Keep her supine and raise the head of the stretcher

qs.q: A woman 34 weeks pregnant has a severe headache, blurred vision, swelling of her hands and face, and a BP of 168/110. What complication is she at risk for?
qs.a: Seizures
qs.x: These findings suggest preeclampsia, which can progress to eclampsia with seizures; keep her calm, minimize stimulation, and transport.
w: Hypoglycemia
Ruptured appendix
Asthma attack

qs.q: A 26-year-old woman has sudden lower abdominal pain, a missed period, dizziness, and a rapid pulse. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
qs.x: Abdominal pain with a missed period and signs of shock in a woman of childbearing age suggests a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise.
w: Urinary tract infection
Normal early pregnancy symptoms
Constipation

qs.q: You arrive at a scene where a patient says he wants to die and is holding a knife. What should you do first?
qs.a: Retreat to safety and wait for police
qs.x: Scene safety comes first; retreat and wait for law enforcement to secure the scene.
w: Approach and take the knife
Leave and clear the call
Restrain him without help

qs.q: A combative patient must be physically restrained for transport. How should he be positioned?
qs.a: Supine or on his side with continuous monitoring
qs.x: Restraining a patient face down can cause positional asphyxia and death; restrain supine or on the side and monitor airway and breathing continuously.
w: Face down with his wrists tied to his ankles
Face down with a responder kneeling on his back
Seated upright with a towel over his face

qs.q: A patient has new bizarre behavior. Which medical conditions can cause this? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hypoglycemia; Hypoxia; Head injury
qs.x: Hypoglycemia, hypoxia, head injury, and other medical problems can mimic psychiatric emergencies, so they must be considered before assuming a behavioral cause.
opts: Hypoglycemia
Hypoxia
Head injury
Seasonal allergies
Tension headache
ok: Hypoglycemia
Hypoxia
Head injury

qs.q: A 9-month-old has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days. Which findings suggest dehydration? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Sunken fontanelle; No tears when crying; Few wet diapers
qs.x: Signs of infant dehydration include a sunken fontanelle, absent tears, and decreased urine output; a bulging fontanelle suggests increased intracranial pressure.
opts: Sunken fontanelle
No tears when crying
Few wet diapers
Bulging fontanelle
Moist mucous membranes
ok: Sunken fontanelle
No tears when crying
Few wet diapers

qs.q: A patient is having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Move nearby objects away; Time the seizure; Place in recovery position afterward if no trauma
qs.x: Protect the patient from injury, note the duration, and position for airway protection after the seizure; restraint and objects in the mouth can cause injury.
opts: Move nearby objects away
Time the seizure
Place in recovery position afterward if no trauma
Restrain the arms and legs
Place a bite block between the teeth
ok: Move nearby objects away
Time the seizure
Place in recovery position afterward if no trauma

qs.q: A 64-year-old man vomited dark material resembling coffee grounds. What does this suggest?
qs.a: Upper GI bleeding
qs.x: Coffee-ground emesis indicates partially digested blood from the upper GI tract, such as from an ulcer.
w: Food poisoning
Bleeding from hemorrhoids in the rectum
Appendicitis

qs.q: A 76-year-old man taking a beta blocker has a GI bleed. His heart rate is 68. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: The beta blocker may be hiding a fast heart rate
qs.x: Beta blockers can blunt the expected tachycardia of shock, so older adults may be in shock despite a normal heart rate.
w: His bleeding is minor because his heart rate is normal
The heart rate shows he is not in shock
He needs no further evaluation

qs.q: What are the three components of the Pediatric Assessment Triangle?
qs.a: Appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin
qs.x: The Pediatric Assessment Triangle is a quick visual assessment of appearance, work of breathing, and skin circulation.
w: Airway, breathing, circulation
Pulse, blood pressure, temperature
Pupils, motor, sensation

qs.q: A dialysis patient has an AV fistula in the left arm. Where should you take a blood pressure?
qs.a: The right arm
qs.x: Blood pressure should not be taken on an arm with a fistula because cuff pressure can damage it.
w: The left arm
Either arm
Over the fistula

qs.q: A college student has fever, headache, a stiff neck, and a purple rash. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Meningitis
qs.x: Fever, headache, stiff neck, and petechial rash suggest meningitis; use droplet precautions including a mask.
w: Migraine
Allergic reaction
Sunburn

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman suddenly develops the worst headache of her life and vomits. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Bleeding in the brain
qs.x: A sudden, severe headache suggests a subarachnoid hemorrhage, a type of hemorrhagic stroke requiring rapid transport.
w: Tension headache
Food poisoning
A sinus infection with pressure behind the eyes

qs.q: You are dispatched to a shooting. Police have not yet arrived. What should you do?
qs.a: Stage nearby until the scene is secured
qs.x: Responders should stage at a safe distance until law enforcement secures a violent scene.
w: Enter quickly to treat the patient
Park in front of the house
Ask bystanders whether the shooter has left, then enter

qs.q: At an MCI using START triage, an adult is breathing 34 times per minute. How should this patient be triaged?
qs.a: Immediate
qs.x: In START, a respiratory rate over 30 indicates immediate (red) priority.
w: Delayed, because the patient is still breathing
Minor
Expectant

qs.q: At an MCI, a 5-year-old is apneic but has a pulse. Using JumpSTART, what should you do?
qs.a: Give 5 rescue breaths
qs.x: JumpSTART calls for 5 rescue breaths for an apneic child with a pulse; if breathing resumes, the child is tagged immediate.
w: Tag the child as expectant
Begin CPR
Move to the next patient

qs.q: Using SALT triage, which lifesaving interventions may be done during individual assessment? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Control major bleeding; Open the airway; Give an antidote auto-injector
qs.x: SALT lifesaving interventions are quick actions such as hemorrhage control, airway opening, chest decompression, and antidote auto-injectors; CPR and splinting are not done during triage.
opts: Control major bleeding
Open the airway
Give an antidote auto-injector
Start CPR
Apply a traction splint
Obtain full vital signs
ok: Control major bleeding
Open the airway
Give an antidote auto-injector

qs.q: When lifting a stretcher, what is the correct technique?
qs.a: Keep the weight close and lift with your legs
qs.x: The power lift keeps the back straight and the weight close, using the legs to lift and reducing back injury.
w: Bend at the waist and lift with your back
Twist your torso while lifting to face the ambulance
Hold the weight far from your body

qs.q: A patient is in a car that is on fire. What type of move should you use?
qs.a: An emergency move along the long axis of the body
qs.x: An emergency move is used when there is immediate danger; pull along the long axis of the body to limit spinal movement.
w: A full spinal immobilization before moving
A standard stretcher move
A slow, careful extrication

qs.q: A physician gives you an order over the radio. What should you do?
qs.a: Repeat the order back to confirm it
qs.x: The echo technique confirms the order and prevents errors.
w: Carry out the order immediately
Ask your partner to write it down for the report later
Ignore it if you disagree

qs.q: You discover an error in a patient care report. How should you correct it?
qs.a: Draw a single line through it, initial, and date
qs.x: Errors are corrected with a single line, initials, and date so the original remains readable; never erase or obliterate.
w: Erase or white out the error
Rewrite the entire report and throw away the original copy
Ignore the error

qs.q: An adult patient wants to refuse transport. Which elements are required for a valid refusal? Select all that apply.
qs.a: The patient has decision-making capacity; The patient is informed of the risks, including death; The refusal is documented and signed
qs.x: A valid refusal requires capacity, informed understanding of the risks, and documentation; family agreement, age over 21, or police witness are not required.
opts: The patient has decision-making capacity
The patient is informed of the risks, including death
The refusal is documented and signed
A family member agrees
The patient is over 21
A police officer witnesses it
ok: The patient has decision-making capacity
The patient is informed of the risks, including death
The refusal is documented and signed

qs.q: Which action would be considered abandonment?
qs.a: Transferring care to a lower-level provider
qs.x: Abandonment is terminating care without ensuring continued care at an equal or higher level.
w: Transferring care to a paramedic
Giving a report to a nurse
Waiting for ALS to arrive

qs.q: A hospice patient with a valid DNR is short of breath but has a pulse. What should you do?
qs.a: Give comfort care such as oxygen and positioning
qs.x: A DNR applies to resuscitation, not to comfort care; patients with a pulse should still receive appropriate treatment.
w: Start CPR
Withhold all treatment
Call the police

qs.q: You suspect a patient has tuberculosis. What PPE should you use?
qs.a: An N95 respirator
qs.x: Tuberculosis is airborne; responders should wear an N95 respirator and place a surgical mask on the patient if tolerated.
w: A surgical mask only
Gloves only
No PPE

qs.q: You approach an overturned tanker with a hazmat placard. Where should you stage?
qs.a: Upwind and uphill at a safe distance
qs.x: Stage upwind and uphill at a safe distance, identify the hazard with binoculars and the ERG, and wait for a hazmat team.
w: Downwind and close
Downhill near the spill so you can see the product
Directly beside the truck

qs.q: Where do most ambulance crashes occur?
qs.a: Intersections
qs.x: Intersections are the most common location of ambulance crashes; slow down and ensure all lanes have stopped.
w: Highways
Parking lots
Long straight rural roads

qs.q: Which findings may indicate elder abuse? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Bruises in different stages of healing; Injuries that do not match the explanation; A caregiver refuses to let the patient speak
qs.x: Multiple injuries in various stages, injuries inconsistent with the story, and a controlling caregiver suggest abuse; report suspected abuse per law.
opts: Bruises in different stages of healing
Injuries that do not match the explanation
A caregiver refuses to let the patient speak
Taking several medications
A single bruise consistent with a reported fall
ok: Bruises in different stages of healing
Injuries that do not match the explanation
A caregiver refuses to let the patient speak

qs.q: You placed a supraglottic airway in a 55-year-old apneic man who still has a strong carotid pulse. How often should you deliver ventilations through the device?
qs.a: One breath every 6 seconds
qs.x: An adult who is apneic but has a pulse receives about 10 breaths per minute, one every 6 seconds, whether ventilated by mask or advanced airway. Faster rates cause hyperventilation, raise intrathoracic pressure and reduce venous return.
w: One breath every 2 to 3 seconds as fast as the bag refills
One breath every 12 to 15 seconds to limit gastric inflation
Two breaths after every 30 chest compressions

qs.q: After inserting a supraglottic airway and making one attempt to reposition it, you see no chest rise, hear no lung sounds and get no capnography waveform. What should you do?
qs.a: Remove it and ventilate with a BVM and basic adjunct
qs.x: A device that still cannot ventilate after adjustment must be removed so oxygenation is not delayed. BVM ventilation with an oral or nasal airway is the fallback while you prepare a further attempt or transport.
w: Inflate the cuff with an additional 30 mL of air and keep ventilating
Increase the ventilation rate until lung sounds become audible
Leave it in place and let the hospital team confirm placement

qs.q: Which patient is the most appropriate candidate for a supraglottic airway?
qs.a: Adult in cardiac arrest with no gag reflex
qs.x: Supraglottic airways are for unresponsive patients without a gag reflex who need ventilation. An intact gag reflex, caustic ingestion and known esophageal disease are contraindications.
w: Responsive overdose patient who gags when an oral airway is inserted
Adult who drank drain cleaner and is now drooling and anxious
Alert asthmatic who is tiring but still speaking in short phrases

qs.q: A 30-year-old motorcyclist is unresponsive with snoring respirations after striking a guardrail. What is the best way to open the airway?
qs.a: Jaw-thrust maneuver with manual spinal stabilization
qs.x: Snoring signals partial obstruction by the tongue, and the jaw-thrust opens the airway without moving the cervical spine. If the jaw-thrust fails to open the airway, a head-tilt chin-lift is still used because the airway takes priority.
w: Head-tilt chin-lift maneuver with the head turned to the side
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway before any manual maneuver
Place the patient in the recovery position and observe

qs.q: You hear gurgling while ventilating an unresponsive adult. What is the longest you should apply suction in a single attempt?
qs.a: 15 seconds
qs.x: Adult suctioning is limited to 15 seconds per attempt because suction removes oxygen along with secretions. Shorter limits apply to children and infants, and the patient is reoxygenated between attempts.
w: 5 seconds in adults and 15 seconds in infants
30 seconds or until the airway is clear
Until the oxygen saturation drops below 90 percent

qs.q: A 4-year-old is sitting upright and leaning forward, drooling, with a muffled voice, high fever and soft stridor. What is the most appropriate management?
qs.a: Keep her calm in a position of comfort and transport
qs.x: This picture suggests epiglottitis, where agitation or throat manipulation can trigger complete obstruction. Give oxygen as tolerated, avoid examining the pharynx, keep the child with a caregiver and transport.
w: Lay her supine and inspect the throat with a tongue depressor
Insert an oral airway to prevent the tongue from obstructing
Have her lie flat so you can start an IV before moving her

qs.q: A firefighter removed a 40-year-old woman from a house fire. She has a headache and nausea, and her pulse oximeter reads 99 percent. Which action is most appropriate?
qs.a: High-flow oxygen by nonrebreather mask
qs.x: Standard pulse oximeters cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so readings stay falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning. High-concentration oxygen shortens the half-life of carbon monoxide.
w: Nasal cannula at 2 L/min because the saturation is normal
No oxygen, since a normal reading rules out poisoning
Room air with a repeat pulse oximetry reading in 15 minutes

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman is breathing 6 times per minute with shallow breaths, and her waveform capnography reads 62 mmHg. What does this reading most likely indicate?
qs.a: Hypoventilation with carbon dioxide retention
qs.x: A normal ETCO2 is roughly 35 to 45 mmHg, and a high value with slow shallow breathing shows the patient is retaining carbon dioxide. She needs assisted ventilation.
w: Hyperventilation with excessive carbon dioxide loss
Normal ventilation for a patient of her age
Poor pulmonary blood flow from a large pulmonary embolism

qs.q: A 19-year-old with a history of asthma has a capnography waveform with a slanted, shark-fin upstroke. What does this pattern suggest?
qs.a: Bronchospasm
qs.x: A sloped upstroke shows slow, obstructed exhalation from narrowed lower airways, as in asthma or COPD. The shape often improves as the bronchospasm is treated.
w: An esophageal placement of the sensor tubing
Cardiac arrest with absent pulmonary perfusion
Normal respiratory pattern in a young adult

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman found on the floor next to opioid pills is breathing 6 times per minute with pinpoint pupils and an SpO2 of 82 percent. What should you do first?
qs.a: Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen
qs.x: Inadequate breathing is corrected right away with assisted ventilation, which treats the hypoxia while naloxone is being prepared. Naloxone is then titrated to restore adequate breathing.
w: Give naloxone and wait to see whether her breathing improves
Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min and reassess
Insert a supraglottic airway while she still has a gag reflex

qs.q: You are considering CPAP for a patient in respiratory distress. Which finding is a contraindication?
qs.a: Systolic blood pressure of 82 mmHg
qs.x: CPAP raises intrathoracic pressure and lowers venous return, so it can worsen hypotension. Other contraindications include an inability to protect the airway, unresponsiveness, suspected pneumothorax and vomiting.
w: Crackles in both lung bases with an SpO2 of 88 percent
Respiratory rate of 28 with accessory muscle use
An alert patient who can follow commands and hold the mask

qs.q: While you ventilate a patient with a BVM, the abdomen becomes increasingly distended. Which change in technique best reduces this problem?
qs.a: Give each breath over 1 second with just enough volume to make the chest rise
qs.x: Gastric inflation happens when ventilation pressure exceeds esophageal opening pressure, usually from breaths that are too large or too fast. Slow, modest breaths lower the risk of regurgitation and aspiration.
w: Squeeze the bag faster and harder so the air reaches the lungs first
Stop ventilating and switch to a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Push firmly on the upper abdomen during each ventilation

qs.q: You are opening the airway of an unresponsive 3-month-old infant on a flat surface. What helps keep the airway in a neutral position?
qs.a: A folded towel under the shoulders
qs.x: An infant's large occiput bends the neck forward when the infant lies flat, which can close off the airway. Padding under the shoulders aligns the airway in a neutral or sniffing position.
w: A pillow under the back of the head
Hyperextending the neck as far as possible
Placing the infant face down with the head turned

qs.q: A 12-year-old with a tracheostomy has noisy breathing, retractions and a falling SpO2. His mother says the tube has not been cleaned today. What should you do first?
qs.a: Suction the tracheostomy tube
qs.x: Mucus plugging is the most common cause of distress in a tracheostomy patient, and suctioning the tube often fixes it right away. If suctioning fails, the tube may need to be replaced or the patient ventilated through the stoma.
w: Apply a nonrebreather mask over the mouth and nose
Insert a supraglottic airway through the mouth
Start an IV and give a fluid bolus

qs.q: A 9-year-old having an asthma attack has become drowsy, and her wheezing is getting quieter while her breath sounds fade. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Impending respiratory failure
qs.x: Quieter wheezing with fading breath sounds and drowsiness means little air is moving and the child is tiring. Prepare to assist ventilation and transport urgently.
w: Improving bronchospasm because the wheezing is resolving
An anxiety reaction that is ending
A normal response to the albuterol she took at home

qs.q: An adult is breathing but responds only to pain. Which findings indicate inadequate breathing that requires assisted ventilation? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Respiratory rate of 6 with shallow chest rise; Cyanosis with an SpO2 of 80 percent on oxygen; Irregular, gasping respirations
qs.x: Inadequate rate or depth, gasping and hypoxia despite oxygen all call for positive pressure ventilation. A normal rate with good chest rise and a normal ETCO2 shows adequate ventilation.
opts: Respiratory rate of 6 with shallow chest rise
Cyanosis with an SpO2 of 80 percent on oxygen
Irregular, gasping respirations
Rate of 16 with equal, full chest rise
Clear lung sounds with an ETCO2 of 38 mmHg
ok: Respiratory rate of 6 with shallow chest rise
Cyanosis with an SpO2 of 80 percent on oxygen
Irregular, gasping respirations

qs.q: Which conditions are contraindications to inserting a supraglottic airway? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Intact gag reflex; Recent ingestion of a caustic substance; Known esophageal disease such as varices
qs.x: Supraglottic airways sit in the esophagus or hypopharynx, so an intact gag reflex, caustic ingestion and esophageal disease make them unsafe. Unresponsive apneic patients without a gag reflex are typical candidates.
opts: Intact gag reflex
Recent ingestion of a caustic substance
Known esophageal disease such as varices
Cardiac arrest with no gag reflex
Apnea after an overdose with no gag reflex
ok: Intact gag reflex
Recent ingestion of a caustic substance
Known esophageal disease such as varices

qs.q: After inserting a supraglottic airway, which findings help confirm proper placement? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Visible, equal chest rise with ventilation; Breath sounds over both lungs and none over the epigastrium; A consistent waveform on capnography
qs.x: Placement is confirmed with chest rise, lung sounds and continuous waveform capnography together. Gagging means the patient has a gag reflex and does not tolerate the device, and epigastric sounds suggest air going into the stomach.
opts: Visible, equal chest rise with ventilation
Breath sounds over both lungs and none over the epigastrium
A consistent waveform on capnography
The patient begins to gag and cough on the device
Gurgling heard over the epigastrium with each breath
ok: Visible, equal chest rise with ventilation
Breath sounds over both lungs and none over the epigastrium
A consistent waveform on capnography

qs.q: A 2-year-old has had increasing respiratory distress for several hours. Which findings suggest progression to respiratory failure? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Heart rate falling from 170 to 80; Limp and responding only to painful stimuli; Slow, irregular respiratory effort
qs.x: Bradycardia, a decreased level of responsiveness and weakening respiratory effort show the child is tiring and hypoxic and needs ventilation. Flaring, retractions and tachypnea in an alert child indicate distress with compensation still intact.
opts: Heart rate falling from 170 to 80
Limp and responding only to painful stimuli
Slow, irregular respiratory effort
Nasal flaring while alert and crying
Tachypnea with intercostal retractions while watching you
ok: Heart rate falling from 170 to 80
Limp and responding only to painful stimuli
Slow, irregular respiratory effort

qs.q: At what rate should chest compressions be performed on an adult in cardiac arrest?
qs.a: 100 to 120 per minute
qs.x: Current AHA guidelines call for 100 to 120 compressions per minute. Slower rates decrease blood flow, and faster rates reduce depth and filling time.
w: 80 to 100 per minute
At least 140 per minute
60 per minute with long pauses for recoil

qs.q: How deep should chest compressions be for an average-sized adult?
qs.a: At least 2 inches but no more than 2.4 inches
qs.x: Adult compressions should be at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep and not more than 2.4 inches (6 cm). Compressions that are too shallow fail to circulate blood, and excessive depth increases injury.
w: About 1 inch, or one-quarter of the chest depth
At least 3 inches, regardless of patient size
One-half the anterior-posterior chest diameter

qs.q: Two rescuers are performing CPR on a pulseless 6-month-old infant without an advanced airway. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should they use?
qs.x: Two-rescuer CPR for infants and children uses 15 compressions to 2 breaths, with the two-thumb encircling-hands technique for infants. A single rescuer uses 30:2.

qs.q: The AED has just delivered a shock to a 60-year-old man in cardiac arrest. What should you do next?
qs.a: Resume CPR, starting with compressions
qs.x: Compressions resume immediately after a shock and continue for 2 minutes before the next rhythm check. Even when defibrillation works, the heart usually needs perfusion support before a pulse can be felt.
w: Check for a carotid pulse for up to 30 seconds
Press analyze again to confirm the rhythm
Give two rescue breaths and then check for breathing

qs.q: A supraglottic airway has been placed in an adult in cardiac arrest. How should compressions and ventilations now be coordinated?
qs.a: Continuous compressions and 1 breath every 6 seconds
qs.x: With an advanced airway in place, compressions are continuous and ventilations are given asynchronously at 10 per minute. This keeps compressions going while avoiding hyperventilation.
w: Pauses after every 30 compressions to give 2 breaths
Continuous compressions with a breath every 2 seconds
Compressions paused for 1 breath every 15 compressions

qs.q: You are about to use an AED on a pulseless 5-year-old, but only adult pads are available. What should you do?
qs.a: Use the adult pads, placing them front and back if they would touch
qs.x: If pediatric pads or an attenuator are unavailable, a standard AED with adult pads should be used. Pads must not touch or overlap, so anterior-posterior placement is used on a small chest.
w: Withhold defibrillation until pediatric pads arrive
Cut the adult pads in half to fit the small chest
Use one adult pad on the chest and skip the second pad

qs.q: A 66-year-old diabetic woman complains of sudden fatigue, nausea and shortness of breath but denies chest pain. Her skin is cool and diaphoretic. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Atypical acute coronary syndrome
qs.x: Women, older adults and diabetics often have ACS without classic chest pain, presenting instead with dyspnea, weakness or nausea. Treat as a possible cardiac event and transport to an appropriate facility.
w: Gastroenteritis, because she has no chest pain
A panic attack brought on by the stress of the call
Hyperglycemia from missing her morning insulin

qs.q: A 58-year-old man has substernal chest pressure and a BP of 146/90. He says he took sildenafil for erectile dysfunction about 12 hours ago. What is the correct approach to nitroglycerin?
qs.a: Withhold it
qs.x: Nitroglycerin given within 24 hours of sildenafil (48 hours for tadalafil) can cause profound hypotension. Continue other ACS care and tell the receiving facility.
w: Give half the usual dose and recheck the BP
Give it as normal since the BP is above 100
Give it only after a fluid bolus

qs.q: A 71-year-old man with crushing chest pain is pale and cool with a BP of 78/50, HR of 112 and crackles throughout both lungs. Which action is most appropriate?
qs.a: Expedite transport to a PCI center without nitroglycerin
qs.x: Hypotension with pulmonary edema after an MI suggests cardiogenic shock, where nitroglycerin and CPAP can worsen hypotension and large fluid boluses worsen pulmonary edema. Rapid transport for reperfusion is the priority.
w: Infuse 2 liters of normal saline wide open to raise the BP
Give nitroglycerin to relieve the chest pain and pulmonary edema
Apply CPAP at high pressure to clear the crackles quickly

qs.q: A 74-year-old woman has a new facial droop and slurred speech. Which piece of information is most important for the receiving stroke center?
qs.a: Time she was last known to be well
qs.x: Eligibility for clot-dissolving drugs and clot removal depends on the time since the patient was last known well. Get this time from witnesses and report it early.
w: Her blood pressure readings from last month
The name of her primary care physician
Whether she has had a flu vaccine this year

qs.q: A 62-year-old man has sudden confusion and weakness on one side. Before you call a stroke alert, which assessment helps rule out a common stroke mimic?
qs.a: Blood glucose level
qs.x: Hypoglycemia can cause focal weakness and confusion that look exactly like a stroke. A glucose check takes moments and changes management.
w: Pupil reaction to light
Capillary refill time
Temperature of the skin

qs.q: An 80-year-old woman is sitting bolt upright with severe dyspnea, crackles to the mid-lung fields, BP of 184/102 and an SpO2 of 86 percent. She is alert and following commands. Which intervention will most improve her oxygenation?
qs.a: Continuous positive airway pressure
qs.x: CPAP pushes fluid out of the alveoli, improves gas exchange and reduces the work of breathing in acute pulmonary edema. She is hypertensive and alert, so she is a good candidate.
w: A large isotonic fluid bolus
Oral glucose for possible hypoglycemia
Laying her flat to rest the heart

qs.q: A 67-year-old man with a history of hypertension has sudden, tearing chest pain that radiates to his back. His BP is 190/100 in the right arm and 140/84 in the left. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Aortic dissection
qs.x: Abrupt tearing pain radiating to the back with a significant BP difference between the arms suggests aortic dissection. Transport rapidly and notify the receiving facility.
w: Spontaneous pneumothorax
Stable angina
Acute pericarditis

qs.q: A 1-year-old has a heart rate of 50, mottled skin and poor responsiveness despite effective oxygenation and ventilation. What should you do next?
qs.a: Start chest compressions
qs.x: In children, a heart rate below 60 with signs of poor perfusion despite adequate ventilation calls for CPR. Bradycardia in children is usually caused by hypoxia and is a sign of arrest about to happen.
w: Continue ventilating and recheck in 10 minutes
Give oral glucose
Apply the AED and deliver a shock

qs.q: After defibrillation and 4 minutes of CPR, a 59-year-old man has a pulse. He remains unresponsive with a BP of 74/40 and clear lung sounds. Which intervention is appropriate?
qs.a: An isotonic crystalloid bolus
qs.x: After return of spontaneous circulation, hypotension is treated to keep systolic pressure at least 90 mmHg, and a crystalloid bolus is a first step when the lungs are clear. Keep the pads on in case of re-arrest.
w: Nitroglycerin to improve coronary flow
Ventilating at 30 breaths per minute
Removing the AED pads to prevent burns

qs.q: An AED analyzes the rhythm of a pulseless, apneic 70-year-old woman and advises no shock. What should you do?
qs.a: Resume CPR immediately
qs.x: A no-shock message means the rhythm is not shockable, such as asystole or PEA, but the patient is still in arrest. Resume high-quality CPR and reanalyze every 2 minutes.
w: Turn off the AED and start transport without CPR
Check for a pulse for 1 full minute
Reposition the pads and analyze again right away

qs.q: A bystander is doing CPR on a pulseless 25-year-old found with a syringe in his arm. What is your highest priority?
qs.a: High-quality CPR and early AED use
qs.x: Once an opioid overdose patient is pulseless, CPR and defibrillation take priority. Naloxone may be given but must not delay or interrupt compressions.
w: Naloxone before any other care
Placing an IV for drug administration
Searching the scene for the substance used

qs.q: Which actions are components of high-quality adult CPR? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Allowing full chest recoil after each compression; Keeping pauses in compressions under 10 seconds; Compressing at 100 to 120 per minute
qs.x: Full recoil lets the heart refill, short pauses maintain coronary perfusion, and the correct rate maximizes blood flow. Leaning on the chest and overventilating both reduce venous return.
opts: Allowing full chest recoil after each compression
Keeping pauses in compressions under 10 seconds
Compressing at 100 to 120 per minute
Leaning on the chest between compressions to keep pressure
Ventilating every 2 seconds once an advanced airway is placed
ok: Allowing full chest recoil after each compression
Keeping pauses in compressions under 10 seconds
Compressing at 100 to 120 per minute

qs.q: Which findings are part of the Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Facial droop; Arm drift; Abnormal speech
qs.x: The Cincinnati scale assesses a facial smile, arm drift with eyes closed and repeating a simple sentence. Any one abnormal finding raises the chance of stroke.
opts: Facial droop
Arm drift
Abnormal speech
Pupil size and reactivity
Blood pressure difference between arms
ok: Facial droop
Arm drift
Abnormal speech

qs.q: Which actions are appropriate when using an AED? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Ensuring no one touches the patient during analysis and shock; Removing a medication patch and wiping the skin before applying a pad; Moving the patient out of standing water and drying the chest
qs.x: Clearing the patient, removing patches and drying the chest prevent injury and help the shock work. Pads go at least 1 inch away from an implanted device, and compressions stop during analysis so motion does not interfere.
opts: Ensuring no one touches the patient during analysis and shock
Removing a medication patch and wiping the skin before applying a pad
Moving the patient out of standing water and drying the chest
Placing a pad directly over an implanted pacemaker
Continuing compressions while the AED analyzes the rhythm
ok: Ensuring no one touches the patient during analysis and shock
Removing a medication patch and wiping the skin before applying a pad
Moving the patient out of standing water and drying the chest

qs.q: A 76-year-old man reports worsening shortness of breath at night. Which findings support left-sided heart failure with pulmonary edema? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Crackles in both lung bases; Needing to sleep sitting up in a recliner; Pink, frothy sputum
qs.x: Left ventricular failure backs fluid into the lungs, causing crackles, orthopnea and frothy sputum. Pain relieved by leaning forward points to pericarditis, and clear lungs argue against pulmonary edema.
opts: Crackles in both lung bases
Needing to sleep sitting up in a recliner
Pink, frothy sputum
Clear and equal breath sounds throughout
Pain that improves when he leans forward
ok: Crackles in both lung bases
Needing to sleep sitting up in a recliner
Pink, frothy sputum

qs.q: A 22-year-old has bright red blood spurting from a deep laceration on his upper thigh that continues despite firm direct pressure. What should you do next?
qs.a: Apply a tourniquet proximal to the wound
qs.x: Life-threatening extremity bleeding that is not controlled by direct pressure requires a tourniquet placed 2 to 3 inches above the wound. Elevation and pressure points are not reliable for hemorrhage control.
w: Elevate the leg and add more gauze on top
Apply pressure to the femoral artery at the groin
Apply a cold pack and loosen the dressing

qs.q: A 28-year-old man was stabbed in the abdomen. He is anxious with a weak radial pulse and a BP of 80/50, and there is no head injury. Transport will take 20 minutes. What is the best fluid strategy?
qs.a: Small boluses to keep a radial pulse
qs.x: In penetrating torso trauma without head injury, permissive hypotension aims for a palpable radial pulse or a systolic pressure around 80 to 90 mmHg. Large volumes can raise pressure enough to disrupt clots and dilute clotting factors.
w: Two liters wide open through two large-bore lines
No IV access until arrival at the trauma center
Dextrose infusion to provide energy to tissues

qs.q: A 35-year-old has a severe head injury with a GCS of 7 and a BP of 84/50. What is the blood pressure goal for this patient?
qs.a: Systolic pressure of at least 90 mmHg
qs.x: Even one episode of hypotension worsens outcomes after a traumatic brain injury, so permissive hypotension is not used. Give fluids to keep the systolic pressure at or above 90 mmHg in adults.
w: Systolic pressure of 70 mmHg to limit brain swelling
The lowest pressure that keeps a radial pulse present
Systolic pressure above 200 mmHg to force perfusion

qs.q: A patient with a head injury develops a BP of 196/110, a pulse of 48 and irregular breathing. What do these findings indicate?
qs.a: Increasing intracranial pressure
qs.x: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respirations make up Cushing's triad, a late sign of rising intracranial pressure and possible herniation. Manage the airway, avoid hypoxia and transport rapidly.
w: Hypovolemic shock that is still compensated
Neurogenic shock from a spinal injury
Pain-induced anxiety

qs.q: You sealed a gunshot wound to the chest with an occlusive dressing. The patient now has worsening dyspnea, absent breath sounds on that side and a falling BP. What should you do?
qs.a: Briefly lift the dressing to release trapped air
qs.x: These signs suggest a developing tension pneumothorax, and briefly unsealing the dressing lets trapped air escape. Reseal it afterward and transport rapidly to ALS or a trauma center.
w: Add a second occlusive dressing over the first
Give a 2-liter fluid bolus
Place the patient supine with legs elevated

qs.q: A 45-year-old was ejected from a vehicle. She has pelvic pain, instability and signs of shock. Which intervention is most appropriate?
qs.a: Apply a pelvic binder over the greater trochanters
qs.x: A binder centered over the greater trochanters closes an open pelvic ring and reduces bleeding. Repeated manipulation can disrupt clots, and a binder placed too high is ineffective.
w: Rock the pelvis repeatedly to check for instability
Apply the binder around the waist at the iliac crests
Flex both hips and knees and tie the legs together

qs.q: An 82-year-old who takes a blood thinner fell from standing and hit her head. She is alert with a small forehead bruise and wants to stay home. What is your main concern?
qs.a: Delayed intracranial bleeding
qs.x: Anticoagulants and age-related brain atrophy raise the risk of a slowly expanding brain bleed after minor head trauma. These patients need hospital evaluation even when they appear well.
w: Hip fracture from a minor fall
Dehydration from poor oral intake
Infection of the forehead abrasion

qs.q: An adult has partial-thickness burns covering the entire anterior chest and abdomen and the entire right arm. Using the rule of nines, estimate the burned body surface area.
qs.a: 27 percent
qs.x: In adults, the anterior trunk is 18 percent and each arm is 9 percent, giving 27 percent. Superficial burns are not counted in this total.
w: 18 percent
36 percent
45 percent

qs.q: A 1-year-old has partial-thickness burns covering the entire head and the entire anterior trunk. Using the pediatric rule of nines, estimate the burned body surface area.
qs.a: 36 percent
qs.x: In infants, the head is about 18 percent because it is larger in proportion, and the anterior trunk is 18 percent. Children lose heat and fluid quickly from burns, so prevent hypothermia.
w: 27 percent
18 percent
45 percent

qs.q: A 24-year-old diver hit his head in shallow water. He cannot move his legs and has a BP of 78/48, pulse of 54, and warm, dry skin below the nipple line. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Neurogenic shock
qs.x: Spinal cord injury cuts off sympathetic tone, causing vasodilation, hypotension and a slow heart rate with warm, dry skin. Hemorrhagic shock usually produces tachycardia with cool, clammy skin.
w: Hemorrhagic shock
Septic shock
Cardiogenic shock

qs.q: You have made two unsuccessful IV attempts in a 30-year-old with hemorrhagic shock who has an altered mental status. What is the most appropriate next step for vascular access?
qs.a: Intraosseous access
qs.x: IO access is fast and reliable when peripheral IVs fail in a critically ill patient, and AEMTs can place it. An injured extremity should not be used for vascular access.
w: Keep attempting IVs in the hands until one succeeds
Abandon vascular access and give fluids orally
Place an IV in the foot of the injured leg

qs.q: A 34-year-old fell from a ladder and has a femur fracture. Which findings suggest compensated shock? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Heart rate of 122; Pale, cool, clammy skin; Restlessness and anxiety
qs.x: Tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction and anxiety are early compensatory signs while blood pressure is still maintained. Hypotension marks decompensation, and bradycardia is a late, ominous finding.
opts: Heart rate of 122
Pale, cool, clammy skin
Restlessness and anxiety
Systolic BP of 70 mmHg
Heart rate of 46
ok: Heart rate of 122
Pale, cool, clammy skin
Restlessness and anxiety

qs.q: Using national field triage guidelines, which injured adults meet high-risk criteria for transport to the highest level trauma center? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Gunshot wound to the torso; Systolic BP of 84 mmHg after a crash; Amputation proximal to the wrist
qs.x: Penetrating injuries to the torso, hypotension and amputations proximal to the wrist or ankle are high-risk criteria. Isolated minor injuries and ground-level falls in healthy young adults are not.
opts: Gunshot wound to the torso
Systolic BP of 84 mmHg after a crash
Amputation proximal to the wrist
Healthy 25-year-old who fell from standing
Isolated closed wrist fracture with good pulses
ok: Gunshot wound to the torso
Systolic BP of 84 mmHg after a crash
Amputation proximal to the wrist

qs.q: Which actions are correct when applying a tourniquet for severe extremity bleeding? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Place it 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over a joint; Tighten until bleeding stops and the distal pulse is absent; Record the time it was applied
qs.x: A tourniquet must be tight enough to stop arterial flow, placed above the wound and away from joints, and timed. Periodic loosening causes repeated blood loss and is not done in the field.
opts: Place it 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over a joint
Tighten until bleeding stops and the distal pulse is absent
Record the time it was applied
Loosen it every 10 minutes to restore circulation
Place it directly over the knee for a lower leg wound
ok: Place it 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over a joint
Tighten until bleeding stops and the distal pulse is absent
Record the time it was applied

qs.q: A 54-year-old diabetic man is unresponsive with a blood glucose of 36 mg/dL, and you have a patent IV. Which treatment is most appropriate?
qs.a: Intravenous dextrose
qs.x: An unresponsive hypoglycemic patient cannot protect the airway, so oral glucose is unsafe. IV dextrose, such as D10 titrated to response, raises the glucose quickly.
w: Oral glucose gel between the cheek and gum
A rapid bolus of normal saline only
Waiting for him to wake up enough to drink juice

qs.q: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has deep, rapid respirations, a fruity breath odor, a glucose reading of HI, a pulse of 124 and dry mucous membranes. Which intervention is most appropriate?
qs.a: Isotonic crystalloid bolus
qs.x: Diabetic ketoacidosis causes severe dehydration from osmotic diuresis, so isotonic fluid replacement is the key prehospital treatment. The deep, rapid breathing compensates for acidosis and should not be suppressed.
w: Oral glucose to correct the imbalance
Dextrose IV
Encouraging him to slow his breathing

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman is unresponsive with a blood glucose of 30 mg/dL. Two IV attempts have failed. What is a reasonable alternative within AEMT scope?
qs.a: Glucagon IM
qs.x: Glucagon given IM mobilizes stored glycogen when IV access cannot be obtained. It works more slowly than IV dextrose and depends on liver glycogen stores.
w: Oral glucose solution poured into the mouth
Nitroglycerin sublingually
Repeated IV attempts for 20 more minutes

qs.q: An 18-month-old had a 2-minute generalized seizure that has stopped. He has a temperature of 39.6 C (103.3 F) and is becoming more alert. What is appropriate care?
qs.a: Remove excess clothing and monitor during transport
qs.x: Simple febrile seizures are common in this age group and are managed with airway support, passive cooling and transport. Ice baths and alcohol can cause shivering, hypothermia or toxicity.
w: Put the child in an ice water bath
Sponge the child with rubbing alcohol to cool the skin
Restrain the child to prevent another seizure

qs.q: A 12-kg 2-year-old with vomiting and diarrhea is lethargic, with a capillary refill of 4 seconds and a heart rate of 180. Protocol calls for a 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus. What volume should you give?
qs.a: 240 mL
qs.x: 20 mL/kg multiplied by 12 kg equals 240 mL. Reassess perfusion, mental status and lung sounds after each bolus.
w: 120 mL
480 mL

qs.q: A woman who is 34 weeks pregnant becomes dizzy and pale while lying supine on a stretcher. What should you do?
qs.a: Position her on her left side
qs.x: In late pregnancy, the uterus can compress the inferior vena cava when the patient lies supine, decreasing venous return. Left lateral positioning or manually moving the uterus to the left restores blood flow.
w: Elevate her legs and keep her supine
Place her in a seated position with her legs dangling
Start CPR

qs.q: A woman who is 35 weeks pregnant has a severe headache, visual disturbances, swelling of the hands and face, and a BP of 172/112. What is the most likely condition?
qs.a: Preeclampsia
qs.x: Hypertension with headache and visual changes after 20 weeks of gestation suggests severe preeclampsia, which can progress to seizures (eclampsia). Keep the environment calm and transport.
w: Placenta previa
Supine hypotensive syndrome
Normal late pregnancy

qs.q: A newborn was dried and stimulated and has received 30 seconds of effective ventilation, but the heart rate is 50. What should you do?
qs.a: Start compressions with ventilations at 3:1
qs.x: Newborn resuscitation calls for chest compressions when the heart rate remains below 60 despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation. The ratio is 3 compressions to 1 breath.
w: Continue ventilations and recheck in 5 minutes
Stop ventilating and give blow-by oxygen
Increase stimulation by flicking the feet

qs.q: Ten minutes after delivering the placenta, a woman continues to bleed heavily and her uterus feels soft and boggy. What should you do first?
qs.a: Massage the fundus firmly
qs.x: Fundal massage stimulates uterine contraction, the main way bleeding is controlled after delivery. Breastfeeding also helps, and signs of shock call for IV fluids and rapid transport.
w: Pack the vagina with gauze
Have her sit upright
Pull gently on the umbilical cord

qs.q: A 24-year-old woman has sudden, severe lower abdominal pain, a missed period and dizziness. Her pulse is 128 and BP is 86/56. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
qs.x: A woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain, a missed period and shock should be assumed to have a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Treat for hemorrhagic shock and transport rapidly.
w: Gastroenteritis with mild dehydration
Urinary tract infection
Normal menstrual cramping

qs.q: After a small dose of naloxone, a patient who overdosed on opioids is breathing 14 times per minute with good tidal volume but remains drowsy. What should you do?
qs.a: Continue to monitor without additional naloxone
qs.x: Naloxone is titrated to adequate breathing, not to a full return of consciousness. Large doses can cause abrupt withdrawal, vomiting and agitation.
w: Give more naloxone until he is fully awake
Insert a supraglottic airway
Restrain him before giving another dose

qs.q: A 21-year-old runner collapsed in a race on a hot day. She is confused with hot skin and a rectal temperature of 41.2 C (106.2 F). What is the priority?
qs.a: Rapid active cooling
qs.x: Exertional heat stroke is a true emergency, and outcomes depend on how fast the core temperature drops. Cold water immersion or aggressive ice and water cooling should begin as soon as possible.
w: Oral rehydration while monitoring her
Transport without cooling to avoid delay
Warming blankets to prevent shivering

qs.q: A 7-year-old was pulled from a pool. She is unresponsive and apneic with a slow pulse. What is your first priority?
qs.a: Rescue breaths
qs.x: Drowning causes death by hypoxia, so ventilation is the priority. Abdominal thrusts delay ventilation and increase the risk of vomiting.
w: Abdominal thrusts to expel water
An AED
Rewarming before any other care

qs.q: After a bee sting, a 40-year-old has widespread hives, wheezing, a swollen tongue and a BP of 76/44. Which medication is the first-line treatment?
qs.a: Epinephrine 1 mg/mL IM
qs.x: Anaphylaxis with airway involvement and hypotension requires epinephrine IM in the lateral thigh. Albuterol can help with wheezing but does not reverse the systemic reaction.
w: Albuterol by nebulizer
Oral glucose
Nitroglycerin SL

qs.q: A 35-year-old man says he wants to kill himself and has a plan, but he refuses transport. He is calm and alert. What is the most appropriate action?
qs.a: Stay with him and involve law enforcement as needed
qs.x: A patient with active suicidal intent and a plan lacks the capacity to refuse care for this condition and must not be left alone. Follow local protocols, which often require law enforcement assistance.
w: Leave after he signs a refusal form
Agree to leave if he promises not to hurt himself
Leave him with a family member and depart

qs.q: A 64-year-old dialysis patient with an AV fistula in his left arm needs IV access and a blood pressure reading. Which arm should you use?
qs.a: The right arm
qs.x: Cuffs and IVs on the fistula arm can damage or clot the dialysis access. Use the opposite extremity.
w: The left arm, above the fistula
The left arm, below the fistula
Either arm

qs.q: An 84-year-old nursing home resident with a urinary catheter is newly confused, with a temperature of 38.9 C (102 F), a pulse of 118, a respiratory rate of 26 and a BP of 84/50. Lung sounds are clear. What is the most appropriate care?
qs.a: Isotonic crystalloid bolus
qs.x: This presentation suggests septic shock from a urinary source. Isotonic fluids are given while lung sounds are reassessed frequently, especially in older patients.
w: Nitroglycerin to support cardiac output
Oral glucose
Supine positioning with no IV

qs.q: During a fluid bolus, a 79-year-old with a history of heart failure develops crackles, worsening dyspnea and a falling SpO2. What should you do?
qs.a: Slow the infusion and raise the head
qs.x: New crackles and worsening oxygenation during fluid administration suggest fluid overload. Reduce the rate to keep the vein open, sit the patient up, give oxygen and notify medical direction.
w: Increase the flow rate to finish the bolus
Lay the patient flat
Switch to a second large-bore IV

qs.q: You notice cool, pale, swollen skin around an IV site, and the infusion has slowed. What is the most likely problem?
qs.a: Infiltration
qs.x: Infiltration occurs when fluid leaks into the surrounding tissue, causing swelling and coolness. Stop the infusion, remove the catheter and restart in another site.
w: Air embolism
Pyrogenic reaction
Circulatory overload

qs.q: You need to infuse 600 mL over 1 hour using a 10 gtt/mL set. What drip rate should you use?
qs.a: 100 gtt/min
qs.x: 600 mL over 60 minutes is 10 mL/min, and 10 mL/min times 10 gtt/mL equals 100 gtt/min. Check the drip chamber against a watch and reassess.
w: 60 gtt/min
10 gtt/min
600 gtt/min

qs.q: Which findings are consistent with hypoglycemia? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Diaphoresis; Confusion; Tachycardia
qs.x: Low glucose triggers an adrenergic response and brain dysfunction. Deep rapid breathing and a fruity breath odor suggest diabetic ketoacidosis.
opts: Diaphoresis
Confusion
Tachycardia
Deep, rapid breathing
Fruity breath odor
ok: Diaphoresis
Confusion
Tachycardia

qs.q: Which findings are consistent with anaphylaxis? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hives; Stridor or wheezing; Hypotension
qs.x: Anaphylaxis involves multiple systems and can include skin, airway and circulatory findings. Unilateral leg swelling suggests DVT, and focal weakness suggests stroke.
opts: Hives
Stridor or wheezing
Hypotension
Unilateral leg swelling
Focal weakness
ok: Hives
Stridor or wheezing
Hypotension

qs.q: Which findings distinguish heat stroke from heat exhaustion? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Altered mental status; Core temperature above 40 C (104 F)
qs.x: Altered mental status and a core temperature above 40 C (104 F) define heat stroke. Sweating may persist in exertional heat stroke, so its presence does not rule it out.
opts: Altered mental status
Core temperature above 40 C (104 F)
Heavy sweating
Muscle cramps
Headache with normal mental status
ok: Altered mental status
Core temperature above 40 C (104 F)

qs.q: Which findings suggest severe dehydration in an infant? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Sunken fontanelle; Absence of tears; Delayed capillary refill
qs.x: Severe dehydration causes a sunken fontanelle, decreased tear production and poor perfusion. A bulging fontanelle suggests increased intracranial pressure.
opts: Sunken fontanelle
Absence of tears
Delayed capillary refill
Bulging fontanelle
Frequent wet diapers
ok: Sunken fontanelle
Absence of tears
Delayed capillary refill

qs.q: Which findings suggest that delivery is imminent? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Crowning; Urge to push or have a bowel movement; Contractions 2 minutes apart lasting 60 seconds
qs.x: Crowning, a strong urge to push and frequent, long contractions mean birth is near and you should prepare for delivery on scene. Early labor signs alone allow time for transport.
opts: Crowning
Urge to push or have a bowel movement
Contractions 2 minutes apart lasting 60 seconds
Contractions 15 minutes apart
Bloody show alone in a first pregnancy
ok: Crowning
Urge to push or have a bowel movement
