Contractions 2 minutes apart lasting 60 seconds

qs.q: You arrive at a tanker rollover with a placard on the truck. Where should you stage?
qs.a: Upwind and uphill
qs.x: Staging upwind and uphill at a safe distance keeps responders away from vapors and runoff. Use the Emergency Response Guidebook to identify the hazard and set isolation distances.
w: Downwind to monitor vapors
Close to the vehicle to start care quickly
Downhill so runoff is easy to see

qs.q: Using START triage, how would you categorize an adult who cannot walk and has a respiratory rate of 36?
qs.a: Immediate
qs.x: In START triage, a respiratory rate above 30 places the patient in the immediate category. No further assessment is needed for categorization.
w: Delayed
Minor
Expectant

qs.q: Which intervention is one of the lifesaving interventions allowed during SALT triage?
qs.a: Opening the airway
qs.x: SALT allows only quick lifesaving interventions such as controlling major hemorrhage, opening the airway, chest decompression, antidote autoinjectors, and 2 rescue breaths for children. Longer treatments wait until triage is complete.
w: Splinting a fracture
Starting an IV
Applying a cervical collar

qs.q: A diabetic man is alert and oriented after receiving IV dextrose, and he refuses transport. What must happen before you leave?
qs.a: He makes an informed refusal and you document it
qs.x: A competent adult may refuse care after being told the risks, benefits and alternatives. Recommend that he eat and have someone with him, and document thoroughly.
w: He must accept transport because he received medication
You must leave immediately when he refuses
You must call the police to force transport

qs.q: You arrive to find a pulseless, apneic patient whose family shows you a valid, signed DNR order. What should you do?
qs.a: Withhold resuscitation per protocol
qs.x: A valid DNR order directs EMS not to start resuscitation. Follow local protocol for verifying the order and confirming death.
w: Start CPR until a physician arrives
Begin compressions but withhold ventilations
Ask the family to vote on care

qs.q: While you treat a 3-year-old, you notice bruises in different stages of healing and an explanation that does not match the injuries. What is your obligation?
qs.a: Report your concerns per mandatory reporting laws
qs.x: EMS providers are mandatory reporters of suspected child abuse in most states. Document objective findings and report to the appropriate authority.
w: Confront the parents about abuse
Ignore the bruises because they are old
Wait for the child to tell you what happened

qs.q: Your service's written protocols allow you to give certain treatments without calling a physician. What type of medical direction is this?
qs.a: Offline medical direction
qs.x: Offline (indirect) medical direction includes protocols and standing orders written ahead of time. Online medical direction is real-time contact with a physician.
w: Online medical direction
Direct medical control
Emergency medical dispatch

qs.q: You discover an error on a patient care report you have already completed. How should you correct it?
qs.a: Draw a single line through it and initial it
qs.x: A single line keeps the original entry readable and initialing it shows who made the correction. Follow agency policy for electronic reports.
w: Use correction fluid to cover it
Erase it
Create a new report and destroy the old one

qs.q: A patient has a chronic cough, night sweats, weight loss and blood-tinged sputum. What personal protection should you use?
qs.a: An N95 respirator
qs.x: These symptoms suggest tuberculosis, which spreads by airborne droplets. Wear an N95 respirator and put a surgical mask on the patient if possible.
w: A surgical mask only
Gloves only
No precautions

qs.q: Which actions are appropriate for the first-arriving unit at a mass-casualty incident? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Establish command; Perform a size-up and request resources; Begin triage
qs.x: The first unit establishes command, assesses the scene, requests resources and starts triage. Committing to one patient leaves no one to manage the incident.
opts: Establish command
Perform a size-up and request resources
Begin triage
Transport the first patient found
Treat the first critical patient until help arrives
ok: Establish command
Perform a size-up and request resources
Begin triage

qs.q: Which are proper lifting techniques? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Keep the load close to your body; Lift with your legs and keep your back straight; Communicate with your partner
qs.x: Good body mechanics reduce injury by keeping the load near your center of gravity and using your leg muscles. Twisting and reaching increase strain on the back.
opts: Keep the load close to your body
Lift with your legs and keep your back straight
Communicate with your partner
Twist at the waist while lifting
Reach far out in front
ok: Keep the load close to your body
Lift with your legs and keep your back straight
Communicate with your partner

qs.q: You are ventilating an intubated adult whose continuous capnography waveform has been normal at 38 mmHg. While moving him to the stretcher the waveform suddenly becomes a flat line at zero, although his SpO2 still reads 97 percent. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Displacement of the endotracheal tube
qs.x: A sudden loss of the waveform after patient movement means the tube is out of the trachea (or the circuit is disconnected) until proven otherwise. SpO2 lags behind, so it cannot be used to rule out displacement.
w: Hypoventilation from a slow bagging rate
Developing bronchospasm
Return of spontaneous circulation

qs.q: A 24-year-old with a severe asthma attack is being assisted with a bag-valve mask. The capnography waveform has a slanted, rounded upstroke with no flat plateau, giving a shark-fin shape. What does this pattern indicate?
qs.a: Lower airway obstruction
qs.x: A shark-fin waveform reflects slow, uneven emptying of narrowed lower airways, as in bronchospasm. Esophageal placement gives no sustained waveform at all.
w: Esophageal placement of the device
Hyperventilation with low CO2
Cardiogenic oscillations from the heartbeat

qs.q: A 30-year-old with an isolated severe head injury is intubated. BP 138/82, HR 88, SpO2 99 percent, ETCO2 27 mmHg with no signs of herniation. What should you do?
qs.a: Slow the ventilation rate
qs.x: Routine hyperventilation lowers cerebral blood flow and worsens outcomes in TBI. Ventilation should be slowed to bring ETCO2 back to 35 to 45 mmHg.
w: Increase the tidal volume
Increase the rate to 20 breaths per minute
Add 15 cm H2O of PEEP

qs.q: An adult in cardiac arrest now has an endotracheal tube in place and confirmed. How should ventilations be given during ongoing CPR?
qs.a: One breath every 6 seconds
qs.x: Once an advanced airway is placed, compressions are continuous and the adult is ventilated at about 10 breaths per minute. Faster rates raise intrathoracic pressure and reduce coronary perfusion.
w: Two breaths after every 30 compressions
One breath every 3 seconds with compressions paused
One breath every 10 seconds timed to pauses in compressions

qs.q: During an interfacility transfer, a ventilated 58-year-old abruptly becomes hypoxic with SpO2 dropping to 82 percent, and the high-pressure alarm sounds. What is your first step?
qs.a: Disconnect the ventilator and ventilate by bag-valve device
qs.x: Taking the patient off the ventilator and bagging by hand removes the machine as a cause and lets you feel compliance while you work through tube displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax and equipment failure.
w: Increase the FiO2 to 1.0 and continue to observe
Increase the PEEP setting to recruit alveoli
Give additional sedation and recheck in 5 minutes

qs.q: You are setting up a transport ventilator for a 70-inch adult male with no lung injury. What tidal volume is generally recommended for lung-protective ventilation?
qs.a: 6 to 8 mL/kg of ideal body weight
qs.x: Lung-protective ventilation uses about 6 to 8 mL/kg based on ideal body weight, which depends on height and sex rather than actual weight. Larger volumes risk barotrauma and volutrauma.
w: 10 to 12 mL/kg of actual body weight
4 mL/kg of actual body weight
15 mL/kg of ideal body weight

qs.q: A ventilated patient's blood pressure falls from 108/66 to 84/50 right after the PEEP is raised from 5 to 12 cm H2O. What best explains the change?
qs.a: Higher chest pressure reducing venous return
qs.x: PEEP raises intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return and preload, so cardiac output and blood pressure can drop, especially in volume-depleted patients.
w: Vasodilation caused by high oxygen concentration
Increased right ventricular preload
Hypercarbia from overventilation

qs.q: Before rapid sequence intubation, a 64-year-old with pneumonia remains at SpO2 88 percent despite a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min. He is breathing on his own. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Delay induction and improve oxygenation first
qs.x: Starting RSI in a patient who is not preoxygenated leaves almost no safe apnea time. Improve oxygenation first, for example with a bag-valve mask and PEEP valve or noninvasive ventilation plus nasal cannula oxygen.
w: Proceed with induction because the airway takes priority
Perform a surgical cricothyrotomy
Intubate quickly without further preoxygenation

qs.q: After two failed intubation attempts and a failed supraglottic airway, you cannot keep an adult's SpO2 above 80 percent with a two-person bag-valve mask and adjuncts. What is the next step?
qs.a: Surgical cricothyrotomy
qs.x: This is a cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate situation. Once the less invasive rescue options have failed, a surgical airway is required without delay.
w: A third intubation attempt with the same blade
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway and wait
Give another dose of the paralytic

qs.q: A 6-year-old with severe facial trauma cannot be intubated or oxygenated with any device. Which emergency airway is preferred for a child this age?
qs.a: Needle cricothyrotomy
qs.x: In young children the cricothyroid membrane is small and the larynx is funnel shaped, so needle cricothyrotomy is generally preferred over a surgical cricothyrotomy.
w: Open surgical cricothyrotomy
Blind nasotracheal intubation
Retrograde wire intubation

qs.q: Which method is the most reliable way to confirm and continuously monitor endotracheal tube placement in the field?
qs.a: Waveform capnography
qs.x: Continuous waveform capnography is the standard for confirming and monitoring tube placement. Fogging, breath sounds and skin color can all be misleading.
w: Condensation fogging inside the tube
Bilateral breath sounds alone
Improvement in the patient's skin color

qs.q: A 4-year-old with a tracheostomy is in respiratory distress with SpO2 82 percent, and you hear and feel little air moving through the tube. What should you do first?
qs.a: Suction the tracheostomy tube
qs.x: Mucus plugging is the most common cause of tracheostomy obstruction. Suction is the first step, and the tube is changed if suction fails.
w: Begin chest compressions
Attempt orotracheal intubation
Give blow-by oxygen over the face

qs.q: You are assessing a patient for a possible difficult laryngoscopy. Which finding predicts difficulty?
qs.a: Thyromental distance under three fingerbreadths
qs.x: In the LEMON assessment, a thyromental distance under three fingerbreadths suggests a cramped mandibular space and a difficult view. The other findings are reassuring.
w: Mouth opening of three fingerbreadths
Mallampati class I view
Neck flexion and extension without limit

qs.q: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes is breathing deeply and rapidly. Blood glucose reads HI and ETCO2 is 18 mmHg with a normal square waveform. How should you interpret the ETCO2?
qs.a: Compensation for metabolic acidosis
qs.x: In DKA, deep rapid Kussmaul breathing blows off CO2 to offset the metabolic acidosis, so a low ETCO2 is expected and is not a reason to slow the patient's breathing.
w: Hypoventilation with CO2 retention
A primary respiratory acidosis
A falsely low reading from equipment failure

qs.q: While you ventilate a 3-month-old by bag-valve mask, the abdomen becomes distended and it is getting harder to squeeze the bag. What is the best correction?
qs.a: Reposition the airway and use only enough volume for chest rise
qs.x: Overventilation pushes air into the stomach, which splints the diaphragm and makes ventilation harder. Use proper positioning and the smallest volume that produces visible chest rise.
w: Increase the rate to 60 breaths per minute
Squeeze harder to overcome the resistance
Stop ventilating and give blow-by oxygen

qs.q: An arterial blood gas from a drowsy COPD patient shows pH 7.28, PaCO2 58 mmHg and HCO3 26 mEq/L. How should it be interpreted?
qs.a: Acute respiratory acidosis
qs.x: A low pH with a high PaCO2 and a normal bicarbonate is an acute respiratory acidosis with no metabolic compensation yet.
w: Metabolic acidosis with full compensation
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis

qs.q: An intubated asthmatic is being bagged at 28 breaths per minute. BP falls to 72/40 and the bag gets stiffer with every breath. What should you do?
qs.a: Disconnect briefly to let the lungs empty, then ventilate slower
qs.x: Rapid ventilation in obstructive disease traps air (auto-PEEP), which raises intrathoracic pressure and cuts venous return. Allowing full exhalation and then using a slower rate with a long expiratory time reverses it.
w: Raise the rate to clear the retained CO2
Increase the tidal volume
Add 15 cm H2O of PEEP

qs.q: You have made two unsuccessful intubation attempts on an adult. SpO2 is falling to 85 percent and two-person bag-valve-mask ventilation is difficult. What is the next step?
qs.a: Insert a supraglottic airway
qs.x: A supraglottic airway is the rescue device after failed intubation when bag-mask ventilation is not working well. A surgical airway follows only if the SGA also fails to oxygenate.
w: A third attempt using the same technique
An immediate surgical cricothyrotomy
Stop ventilating and transport quickly

qs.q: A 72-year-old with a long history of COPD and CO2 retention is mildly short of breath. What SpO2 target is generally appropriate?
qs.a: 88 to 92 percent
qs.x: In chronic CO2 retainers a target of about 88 to 92 percent avoids worsening hypercapnia while preventing hypoxia. Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient.
w: 100 percent
80 to 84 percent
96 to 100 percent

qs.q: You find a 45-year-old after an overdose. Which findings indicate that ventilation is inadequate and needs assistance? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Respiratory rate of 6 with minimal chest rise; ETCO2 of 62 mmHg with a rising trend; Responsive only to pain with shallow, irregular breathing
qs.x: A slow or shallow pattern, a high or rising ETCO2 and a falling level of consciousness all show inadequate ventilation that needs positive pressure. A normal rate with good chest rise and a normal ETCO2 does not.
opts: Respiratory rate of 6 with minimal chest rise
ETCO2 of 62 mmHg with a rising trend
Respiratory rate of 16 with good chest rise
Responsive only to pain with shallow, irregular breathing
ETCO2 of 38 mmHg with a normal waveform
ok: Respiratory rate of 6 with minimal chest rise
ETCO2 of 62 mmHg with a rising trend
Responsive only to pain with shallow, irregular breathing

qs.q: An intubated patient suddenly deteriorates during transport. Which possible causes should you assess for? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Displacement of the tube; Obstruction of the tube by secretions; Tension pneumothorax
qs.x: The DOPE mnemonic (displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax, equipment failure) guides troubleshooting. A steady waveform and equal breath sounds are reassuring, not causes.
opts: Displacement of the tube
Obstruction of the tube by secretions
A steady ETCO2 waveform at 38 mmHg
Tension pneumothorax
Equal breath sounds on both sides
ok: Displacement of the tube
Obstruction of the tube by secretions
Tension pneumothorax

qs.q: You are planning an airway for a patient who may need RSI. Which findings predict difficult bag-valve-mask ventilation? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Full beard; Morbid obesity; No teeth
qs.x: The MOANS and BOOTS mnemonics list beards, obesity and missing teeth among the predictors of a poor mask seal or high airway resistance. Young age and normal neck mobility do not predict difficulty.
opts: Full beard
Morbid obesity
Age 25 years
No teeth
Normal neck mobility
ok: Full beard
Morbid obesity
No teeth

qs.q: In a spontaneously breathing patient with a good waveform, which conditions can cause a low ETCO2? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hyperventilation; Pulmonary embolism; Low cardiac output from shock
qs.x: Hyperventilation removes CO2, while poor pulmonary blood flow from PE or shock delivers less CO2 to the lungs. Hypoventilation and fever raise ETCO2.
opts: Hyperventilation
Pulmonary embolism
Respiratory depression from an opioid overdose
Low cardiac output from shock
Rising body temperature with fever
ok: Hyperventilation
Pulmonary embolism
Low cardiac output from shock

qs.q: You are considering CPAP for a patient in respiratory distress. Which findings are contraindications? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Systolic BP of 80 mmHg; Unable to follow commands; Suspected pneumothorax
qs.x: CPAP needs an awake patient who can protect the airway and a blood pressure that can tolerate higher intrathoracic pressure, and it can worsen a pneumothorax. Pulmonary edema with tachypnea is a typical indication.
opts: Systolic BP of 80 mmHg
Unable to follow commands
Crackles from acute pulmonary edema
Suspected pneumothorax
Respiratory rate of 28
ok: Systolic BP of 80 mmHg
Unable to follow commands
Suspected pneumothorax

qs.q: A 62-year-old has chest pain. The 12-lead shows ST elevation in II, III and aVF with ST depression in I and aVL. Which area of the heart is involved?
qs.a: Inferior wall
qs.x: ST elevation in II, III and aVF points to the inferior wall, usually supplied by the right coronary artery. Depression in I and aVL is the reciprocal change.
w: Anterior wall
Lateral wall
Interventricular septum

qs.q: A 66-year-old with an inferior STEMI has BP 82/50, clear lung sounds and distended neck veins. A right-sided lead V4R shows ST elevation. What is the most appropriate approach?
qs.a: Small fluid boluses and avoid nitrates
qs.x: These findings point to right ventricular infarction, which depends on preload. Fluid supports cardiac output, while nitrates can cause severe hypotension.
w: Nitroglycerin to relieve the chest pain
CPAP for the low blood pressure
Fluid restriction and diuresis

qs.q: A 12-lead ECG shows ST elevation in leads V1 through V4. Which coronary artery is most likely occluded?
qs.a: Left anterior descending artery
qs.x: Anterior and septal leads V1 to V4 view tissue supplied by the left anterior descending artery. RCA lesions usually show inferior changes and circumflex lesions show lateral changes.
w: Right coronary artery
Circumflex artery
Posterior descending artery

qs.q: A 58-year-old with crushing chest pain has ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves and no ST elevation elsewhere. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Obtain posterior leads V7 to V9
qs.x: Anterior ST depression with tall R waves can be a mirror image of a posterior STEMI. Posterior leads V7 to V9 can confirm it.
w: Treat this as unstable angina only
Repeat the same 12-lead in an hour
Treat for a pulmonary embolism

qs.q: A 28-year-old has palpitations. The monitor shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 186 with no visible P waves. BP 124/78, alert, no chest pain. What is the first treatment?
qs.a: Vagal maneuvers
qs.x: For a stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia, vagal maneuvers such as the modified Valsalva are tried first. Electrical therapy is for patients who are unstable.
w: Synchronized cardioversion
Defibrillation
Transcutaneous pacing

qs.q: A 70-year-old is confused and pale. The monitor shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 and BP 70/40. Which intervention is indicated?
qs.a: Synchronized cardioversion
qs.x: A tachycardia with hypotension and altered mental status is unstable and needs immediate synchronized cardioversion. Vagal maneuvers should not delay it.
w: Vagal maneuvers and reassessment
Unsynchronized defibrillation
Transcutaneous pacing

qs.q: An unresponsive 55-year-old has a weak carotid pulse, BP 60 by palpation, and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia on the monitor. Which electrical therapy is appropriate?
qs.a: Unsynchronized shock at defibrillation energy
qs.x: The irregular, changing QRS shapes of polymorphic VT keep the defibrillator from syncing reliably. An unstable patient gets an unsynchronized shock at defibrillation energy.
w: Synchronized cardioversion at low energy
Transcutaneous pacing
No shock until the pulse is lost

qs.q: A 78-year-old is diaphoretic with BP 72/40. The monitor shows third-degree AV block with a wide-complex escape rhythm at 32. Atropine has had no effect. What is the next step?
qs.a: Transcutaneous pacing
qs.x: An unstable bradycardia that does not respond to atropine needs pacing (or a chronotropic infusion). A wide escape rhythm from a third-degree block seldom responds to atropine.
w: Synchronized cardioversion
Defibrillation
Vagal maneuvers

qs.q: A rhythm strip shows the PR interval getting longer with each beat until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, and then the pattern repeats. What is the rhythm?
qs.a: Second-degree AV block type I
qs.x: A PR interval that lengthens until a beat is dropped, in a repeating cycle, is Mobitz I (Wenckebach). It is usually at the AV node and is often benign.
w: Second-degree AV block type II
Third-degree AV block
First-degree AV block

qs.q: A rhythm strip shows a constant PR interval with occasional P waves that are not followed by a QRS. The QRS is wide. What is the rhythm?
qs.a: Second-degree AV block type II
qs.x: Dropped beats with a constant PR interval are Mobitz II. It arises below the AV node and can suddenly progress to complete heart block.
w: Second-degree AV block type I
First-degree AV block
Sinus arrhythmia

qs.q: The monitor shows sawtooth atrial waves at about 300 per minute and a regular ventricular rate of 150. What is the most likely rhythm?
qs.a: Atrial flutter with 2 to 1 conduction
qs.x: Sawtooth flutter waves near 300 per minute with every second wave conducted give a regular ventricular rate of about 150, which is classic atrial flutter.
w: Atrial fibrillation with rapid response
Sinus tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia

qs.q: An unresponsive 60-year-old has sinus rhythm at 80 on the monitor but no palpable pulse. What should you do?
qs.a: Resume CPR and look for reversible causes
qs.x: An organized rhythm without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity, which is not shockable. Good-quality CPR plus a search for the H's and T's is the priority.
w: Defibrillate immediately
Perform synchronized cardioversion
Start transcutaneous pacing

qs.q: You have just delivered a shock for ventricular fibrillation in an adult. What should happen next?
qs.a: Resume compressions for 2 minutes
qs.x: Compressions restart immediately after the shock without a pulse or rhythm check. Even if the shock worked, the heart usually needs perfusion support at first.
w: Check the carotid pulse right away
Analyze the rhythm again right away
Deliver two more stacked shocks

qs.q: How deep should chest compressions be for an adult in cardiac arrest?
qs.a: At least 2 inches but not over 2.4 inches
qs.x: Adult compressions should be at least 2 inches (5 cm) and no more than about 2.4 inches (6 cm) deep, at 100 to 120 per minute with full recoil.
w: About 1 inch
About one-half the chest depth
At least 3 inches

qs.q: During CPR on an intubated adult the ETCO2 stays at 8 mmHg. What does this most likely mean?
qs.a: Compressions are not producing enough blood flow
qs.x: During CPR, ETCO2 mainly reflects the blood flow that compressions create. A value under 10 mmHg suggests poor compression quality, so check depth, rate and recoil and change compressors.
w: Return of spontaneous circulation has occurred
The tube is definitely in the esophagus
The patient is being hyperventilated

qs.q: After ROSC, a 64-year-old is intubated with SpO2 96 percent and BP 78/40. What is the priority?
qs.a: Bring the systolic BP to at least 90 mmHg
qs.x: Hypotension after cardiac arrest worsens brain and organ injury. Post-ROSC care targets a systolic BP of at least 90 mmHg and a MAP of at least 65 mmHg, using fluids and vasopressors.
w: Allow permissive hypotension
Increase ventilations to 30 per minute
Raise the head of the bed and observe

qs.q: Two paramedics are doing CPR on a 5-year-old with no advanced airway. Which compression-to-ventilation ratio should they use?
qs.a: 15 to 2
qs.x: Two-rescuer CPR for infants and children uses 15 compressions to 2 breaths. A lone rescuer uses 30 to 2, and newborns get 3 to 1.
w: 30 to 2 as for adults
5 to 1
3 to 1

qs.q: A 7-month-old is pale and mottled, with a heart rate of 52 despite effective ventilation with oxygen. What should you do next?
qs.a: Begin chest compressions
qs.x: In pediatric bradycardia, a heart rate under 60 with poor perfusion despite good oxygenation and ventilation calls for CPR.
w: Continue ventilations and reassess in 10 minutes
Perform synchronized cardioversion
Wait for a palpable pulse to disappear

qs.q: A 4-year-old in cardiac arrest has been intubated. What ventilation rate is recommended during continuous compressions?
qs.a: One breath every 2 to 3 seconds
qs.x: Current pediatric guidance recommends 20 to 30 breaths per minute (one every 2 to 3 seconds) once an advanced airway is in place, a faster rate than for adults.
w: One breath every 6 seconds
Two breaths after every 15 compressions
One breath every 10 seconds

qs.q: A 71-year-old woman woke at 06:30 with right-sided weakness and slurred speech. She went to bed feeling normal at 22:00. What is her last known well time?
qs.x: Last known well is the last time the patient was seen at baseline. For wake-up strokes, that is when she went to sleep, not when the symptoms were found.
w: The time EMS arrived
The time of the 911 call

qs.q: A 67-year-old with diabetes has new left-sided weakness and confusion. Before you call a stroke alert, which assessment is most important to rule out a common mimic?
qs.a: Blood glucose level
qs.x: Hypoglycemia can cause focal deficits that look exactly like a stroke. A glucose check is required before stroke triage.
w: Pupil size
Skin temperature
Rhythm strip

qs.q: A 59-year-old with hypertension has sudden tearing chest pain that radiates to his back. BP is 182/100 in the right arm and 140/80 in the left. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Aortic dissection
qs.x: Sudden ripping pain that radiates to the back, with a large blood pressure difference between the arms, strongly suggests aortic dissection.
w: Inferior STEMI
Pulmonary embolism
Spontaneous pneumothorax

qs.q: You achieve ROSC in a 58-year-old after a VF arrest. Which actions are part of post-arrest care? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Obtain a 12-lead ECG; Titrate oxygen to SpO2 92 to 98 percent; Ventilate to ETCO2 35 to 45 mmHg
qs.x: Post-ROSC care includes a 12-lead to look for STEMI, avoiding both hypoxia and hyperoxia, normal ventilation, and keeping systolic BP at 90 or higher. Hyperventilation and hypotension worsen outcomes.
opts: Obtain a 12-lead ECG
Titrate oxygen to SpO2 92 to 98 percent
Hyperventilate at 30 per minute to protect the brain
Ventilate to ETCO2 35 to 45 mmHg
Allow a systolic BP of 70 as permissive hypotension
ok: Obtain a 12-lead ECG
Titrate oxygen to SpO2 92 to 98 percent
Ventilate to ETCO2 35 to 45 mmHg

qs.q: Which of these are reversible causes of cardiac arrest included in the H's and T's? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hypovolemia; Tension pneumothorax; Hyperkalemia
qs.x: Hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo- or hyperkalemia, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins and thrombosis are the treatable causes to look for. Hypertension and tachycardia are not on the list.
opts: Hypovolemia
Tension pneumothorax
Hypertension
Hyperkalemia
Tachycardia
ok: Hypovolemia
Tension pneumothorax
Hyperkalemia

qs.q: A patient has a heart rate of 160. Which findings would make this tachycardia unstable and call for immediate electrical therapy? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hypotension with signs of shock; Acute change in mental status; Ischemic chest discomfort
qs.x: Instability means the rhythm is causing hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort or acute heart failure. Rate alone or palpitations with normal perfusion do not meet that standard.
opts: Hypotension with signs of shock
Acute change in mental status
Heart rate of 160 with no other findings
Ischemic chest discomfort
Palpitations with a normal blood pressure
ok: Hypotension with signs of shock
Acute change in mental status
Ischemic chest discomfort

qs.q: A 60-year-old has ST elevation in II, III and aVF. Which findings suggest the right ventricle is also involved? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hypotension with clear lung sounds; Jugular venous distention; ST elevation in lead V4R
qs.x: An RV infarct produces the triad of hypotension, distended neck veins and clear lungs, along with ST elevation in V4R. Crackles point to left ventricular failure.
opts: Hypotension with clear lung sounds
Jugular venous distention
Bilateral crackles in the lower lobes
ST elevation in lead V4R
ST depression in lead V4R
ok: Hypotension with clear lung sounds
Jugular venous distention
ST elevation in lead V4R

qs.q: A 74-year-old has an acute stroke. Which findings suggest a large vessel occlusion? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Gaze deviation toward one side; Aphasia; Neglect of one side of the body
qs.x: Cortical signs such as gaze deviation, aphasia and neglect suggest a large vessel occlusion that may need thrombectomy. Isolated dizziness or minor sensory changes do not.
opts: Gaze deviation toward one side
Aphasia
Isolated dizziness with a normal exam
Neglect of one side of the body
Tingling in one cheek only
ok: Gaze deviation toward one side
Aphasia
Neglect of one side of the body

qs.q: You are about to defibrillate an adult in VF. Which practices are correct? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Remove a medication patch from the pad site; Avoid placing a pad directly over an implanted pacemaker; Keep the pause in compressions under 10 seconds
qs.x: Patches can block current or cause burns, pads should not sit right on an implanted device, and pauses around the shock should be minimal. VF has no R wave to sync with, and compressions resume right after the shock.
opts: Remove a medication patch from the pad site
Avoid placing a pad directly over an implanted pacemaker
Keep the pause in compressions under 10 seconds
Check for a pulse right after each shock
Synchronize the shock to the R wave
ok: Remove a medication patch from the pad site
Avoid placing a pad directly over an implanted pacemaker
Keep the pause in compressions under 10 seconds

qs.q: You are about to perform needle decompression for a tension pneumothorax. Where should the needle enter in relation to the rib?
qs.a: Just over the superior border of the rib
qs.x: The intercostal artery, vein and nerve run along the inferior border of each rib, so the needle goes over the superior border of the rib below.
w: Just under the inferior border of the rib
Straight through the middle of the rib
Next to the sternum, medial to the nipple line

qs.q: An intubated motorcycle crash victim is getting harder to bag. Breath sounds are absent on the right, the neck veins are distended and BP is 70/40. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Tension pneumothorax
qs.x: Positive pressure can quickly turn a pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax. One-sided absent breath sounds, rising airway resistance, JVD and hypotension call for immediate decompression.
w: Pericardial tamponade
Simple pneumothorax
Massive hemothorax

qs.q: A 25-year-old has a stab wound to the left chest. He is hypotensive and has distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds, with equal breath sounds on both sides. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Pericardial tamponade
qs.x: Hypotension, JVD and muffled heart tones (Beck's triad) with equal breath sounds point to tamponade rather than tension pneumothorax.
w: Tension pneumothorax
Massive left hemothorax
Flail chest

qs.q: A 34-year-old with a thigh laceration has bright red blood spurting from the wound. He is talking, with RR 24. What is the first intervention?
qs.a: Control the bleeding with a tourniquet
qs.x: Severe external hemorrhage is controlled first (the X in XABCDE), because it can kill within minutes. The patient is talking, so his airway is open for now.
w: Apply a cervical collar
Start two large-bore IVs
Apply high-flow oxygen

qs.q: You applied a tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above a forearm amputation, but bright red bleeding continues. What should you do?
qs.a: Tighten it more or add a second one above it
qs.x: A tourniquet is tightened until the bleeding stops and the distal pulse is gone. If one is not enough, a second is applied just above the first.
w: Loosen it to let some blood return
Remove it and use direct pressure instead
Elevate the arm and wait for a clot

qs.q: A 22-year-old has a gunshot wound to the abdomen. He is alert with a radial pulse, BP 86/50 and HR 118. Your transport time is 12 minutes. What is the best fluid approach?
qs.a: Limit fluids and transport rapidly
qs.x: In penetrating torso trauma without a head injury, permissive hypotension (a palpable radial pulse, SBP around 80 to 90) limits clot disruption and dilution while you transport rapidly for surgery.
w: Infuse 3 liters of crystalloid to normalize BP
Withhold transport until BP reaches 120
Elevate the legs and start no IV

qs.q: A 40-year-old has an isolated severe head injury after a fall, GCS 8, BP 84/50. What is the blood pressure goal?
qs.a: Systolic BP of at least 90 mmHg
qs.x: Even one episode of hypotension doubles mortality in TBI. Keep systolic BP at 90 or higher (higher in some age groups) and avoid hypoxia, so permissive hypotension does not apply.
w: Permissive hypotension near 70 systolic
No fluids, to avoid cerebral edema
Mean arterial pressure near 50 mmHg

qs.q: A patient with a head injury now has BP 210/110, HR 48 and irregular respirations. What do these findings indicate?
qs.a: Rising intracranial pressure
qs.x: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respirations (Cushing's triad) are late signs of rising ICP and possible herniation.
w: Neurogenic shock
Compensated hypovolemic shock
Hypertensive emergency unrelated to the injury

qs.q: An adult has partial-thickness burns covering the entire front of the torso and the whole right arm. Using the rule of nines, what is the burned body surface area?
qs.a: 27 percent
qs.x: For adults, the front of the torso is 18 percent and each whole arm is 9 percent, which totals 27 percent.
w: 18 percent, torso only
36 percent
45 percent

qs.q: After a diving injury, a 30-year-old has BP 78/44, HR 52 and warm, dry skin below the nipple line. What type of shock is most likely?
qs.a: Neurogenic shock
qs.x: Losing sympathetic tone after a cervical or high thoracic cord injury causes hypotension without the expected tachycardia, along with warm, dry skin, which is neurogenic shock. Hidden bleeding must still be ruled out.
w: Hypovolemic shock
Cardiogenic shock
Obstructive shock

qs.q: Under the national field triage guidelines, which patient meets a high-risk injury criterion for transport to the highest-level trauma center?
qs.a: Penetrating wound to the upper thigh
qs.x: Penetrating injuries to the head, neck, torso or extremities proximal to the elbow or knee are high-risk criteria. The other injuries do not meet triage criteria by themselves.
w: Closed wrist fracture
Abrasions after a fall from standing
Neck soreness after a slow rear-end crash

qs.q: You suspect an unstable pelvic fracture in a hypotensive patient. Where should the pelvic binder be centered?
qs.a: Over the greater trochanters
qs.x: Centering the binder over the greater trochanters closes the pelvic ring most effectively. Placing it too high over the iliac crests can widen the fracture.
w: Over the iliac crests
At the level of the umbilicus
Over the middle of the thighs

qs.q: An 82-year-old on an anticoagulant tripped and hit her head. She is alert with GCS 15 and a small forehead bruise. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Transport for evaluation of a hidden head bleed
qs.x: Older adults on anticoagulants have a much higher risk of delayed intracranial bleeding after minor head trauma, so they need hospital evaluation even with a normal exam.
w: Release her because GCS is normal
Advise rest and an ice pack
Release her if she can walk

qs.q: A 4-year-old struck by a car has HR 160, cap refill of 4 seconds, cool hands and BP 98/60. How should you classify this?
qs.a: Compensated shock
qs.x: Children keep a normal blood pressure until very late in shock. Tachycardia and poor peripheral perfusion with a normal BP mean compensated shock that needs urgent care.
w: Decompensated shock
Normal findings for age
Neurogenic shock

qs.q: A firefighter was trapped in a burning room. Which findings suggest an inhalation injury? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Singed nasal hairs; Soot in the sputum; A hoarse voice
qs.x: Singed hairs, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness or stridor, and facial burns suggest airway injury that can swell quickly and may need early advanced airway management.
opts: Singed nasal hairs
Soot in the sputum
Partial-thickness burns to both lower legs
A hoarse voice
Pain at the burn sites
ok: Singed nasal hairs
Soot in the sputum
A hoarse voice

qs.q: After a fall, which findings indicate the need for spinal motion restriction? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Midline cervical spine tenderness; Intoxication with altered mental status; New numbness in both hands
qs.x: Midline tenderness, an unreliable exam from intoxication or altered mental status, and focal neurologic deficits all call for spinal motion restriction. A reliable patient with a normal exam does not need it.
opts: Midline cervical spine tenderness
Intoxication with altered mental status
New numbness in both hands
Alert and sober with a normal exam and no neck pain
An isolated forearm laceration
ok: Midline cervical spine tenderness
Intoxication with altered mental status
New numbness in both hands

qs.q: Under the national field triage guidelines, which findings meet high-risk criteria for the highest-level trauma center? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Systolic BP under 90 in an adult; Chest wall instability or deformity; Unable to follow commands after a head injury
qs.x: Hypotension, chest wall instability and an inability to follow commands are red criteria that call for transport to the highest-level trauma center. Isolated minor injuries do not.
opts: Systolic BP under 90 in an adult
Chest wall instability or deformity
Unable to follow commands after a head injury
An isolated ankle fracture
A scalp laceration with GCS 15
ok: Systolic BP under 90 in an adult
Chest wall instability or deformity
Unable to follow commands after a head injury

qs.q: A patient with a severe head injury is deteriorating. Which findings suggest herniation? Select all that apply.
qs.a: One dilated, nonreactive pupil; Extensor posturing; Hypertension with bradycardia
qs.x: A blown pupil, posturing and Cushing's response are signs of herniation. Tachycardia with hypotension suggests blood loss, not raised ICP.
opts: One dilated, nonreactive pupil
Extensor posturing
Tachycardia with hypotension
Hypertension with bradycardia
Equal, briskly reactive pupils
ok: One dilated, nonreactive pupil
Extensor posturing
Hypertension with bradycardia

qs.q: A term newborn is limp and apneic after you warm, dry, stimulate and position the airway. The heart rate is 80. What should you do next?
qs.a: Begin positive pressure ventilation
qs.x: An apneic newborn or one with a heart rate under 100 after the initial steps needs PPV within the first minute. Ventilation is the most important part of neonatal resuscitation.
w: Start chest compressions
Continue stimulation for another minute
Give blow-by oxygen only

qs.q: After 30 seconds of effective PPV with corrective steps, a newborn's heart rate is 50. Chest compressions are started. What ratio should you use?
qs.a: 3 compressions to 1 breath
qs.x: Neonatal compressions are coordinated with ventilation at 3 to 1, giving 90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen is increased to 100 percent.
w: 15 compressions to 2 breaths
30 compressions to 2 breaths
5 compressions to 1 breath

qs.q: A term newborn is breathing and crying at 3 minutes of age with a heart rate of 150. A pulse oximeter on the right hand reads 72 percent. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Normal for age, so oxygen need not be increased
qs.x: Preductal saturation rises slowly after birth, with a target of about 70 to 75 percent at 3 minutes and 85 to 95 percent by 10 minutes. Giving oxygen to reach adult levels risks hyperoxia.
w: Hypoxia requiring 100 percent oxygen
Hypoxia requiring intubation
A probe error because it should read 98 percent

qs.q: During a delivery, the baby's head delivers but then retracts against the perineum and the shoulders do not deliver. What should you do first?
qs.a: Hyperflex the mother's thighs and apply suprapubic pressure
qs.x: Shoulder dystocia is managed first with the McRoberts maneuver and suprapubic pressure, which widen the pelvic outlet. Fundal pressure and strong traction on the head can cause injury.
w: Pull firmly downward on the baby's head
Push on the top of the uterus
Have the mother stand and push

qs.q: During active labor, you see the umbilical cord protruding from the vagina before the baby. What should you do?
qs.a: Lift the presenting part off the cord with gloved fingers
qs.x: With a prolapsed cord, lifting the presenting part off the cord and placing the mother in knee-chest or Trendelenburg position keeps blood flowing to the baby during rapid transport.
w: Push the cord back into the vagina
Have the mother bear down to speed delivery
Clamp and cut the exposed cord

qs.q: A 26-year-old who is 34 weeks pregnant has a severe headache and blurred vision. BP 168/112 and she has new swelling in her hands and face. What is the most likely condition?
qs.a: Preeclampsia with severe features
qs.x: New hypertension after 20 weeks with headache and visual changes is preeclampsia with severe features, which puts her at high risk of seizures (eclampsia).
w: Gestational diabetes
Supine hypotensive syndrome
Placenta previa

qs.q: A 31-year-old at 36 weeks fell and now has constant abdominal pain, a rigid tender uterus and a small amount of dark vaginal bleeding. HR 118, BP 92/60. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Placental abruption
qs.x: Painful bleeding with a firm, tender uterus after trauma suggests abruption. Bleeding can be concealed, so shock may be worse than the visible blood suggests.
w: Placenta previa
Braxton Hicks contractions
Ectopic pregnancy

qs.q: A woman 35 weeks pregnant becomes dizzy and pale while lying flat on her back. BP falls from 118/72 to 88/50. What should you do first?
qs.a: Turn her onto her left side
qs.x: The uterus can compress the inferior vena cava in the supine position. Left lateral positioning, or manually displacing the uterus to the left, restores venous return.
w: Elevate her legs while she stays supine
Have her sit upright and bear down
Begin fast fluid boluses while she stays supine

qs.q: Ten minutes after a field delivery, the placenta has delivered but heavy vaginal bleeding continues and the uterus feels soft. What is the first intervention?
qs.a: Firm fundal massage
qs.x: Uterine atony is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Fundal massage, and breastfeeding if possible, helps the uterus contract.
w: Pack the vagina with gauze
Pull on the remaining cord
Have the mother walk to the stretcher

qs.q: A 24-year-old with a missed period seven weeks ago has sudden right lower abdominal pain, shoulder pain, HR 124 and BP 84/52. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
qs.x: Any woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain and shock should be treated as a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise. Shoulder pain suggests blood irritating the diaphragm.
w: Appendicitis
Kidney stone
Ovarian cyst without bleeding

qs.q: A 5-year-old is sitting upright and leaning forward, drooling, with a high fever, muffled voice and soft stridor. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Leave her in a position of comfort and keep her calm
qs.x: Epiglottitis can progress to complete obstruction if the child is upset or the throat is examined. Keep her calm and upright with the parent and be ready to manage the airway.
w: Look at the throat with a tongue blade
Lay her flat to examine the airway
Separate her from the parent to start an IV

qs.q: What are the three components of the Pediatric Assessment Triangle?
qs.a: Appearance, work of breathing, skin circulation
qs.x: The Pediatric Assessment Triangle is a quick visual check of appearance, work of breathing and circulation to the skin that identifies a sick child before any hands-on assessment.
w: Pulse, blood pressure, temperature
Airway, breathing, blood glucose
Mental status, pupils, motor function

qs.q: What is the lowest acceptable systolic blood pressure for a 5-year-old?
qs.a: 80 mmHg
qs.x: For children aged 1 to 10, the lower limit of systolic BP is about 70 plus twice the age in years, so a 5-year-old's limit is 80 mmHg.
w: 70 mmHg
60 mmHg
90 mmHg, as for adults

qs.q: An 84-year-old with type 2 diabetes has been confused for several days. Glucose is 1,100 mg/dL. She is profoundly dehydrated, breathing normally, and has no fruity odor. What is the most likely condition?
qs.a: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
qs.x: HHS develops over days in older type 2 diabetics, with extreme hyperglycemia and dehydration but little ketosis. That is why Kussmaul respirations and a fruity odor are absent.
w: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Hypoglycemia
Adrenal crisis

qs.q: A 78-year-old nursing home resident with a urinary catheter has a temperature of 39.2 C (102.6 F), HR 118, RR 26, BP 82/48 and new confusion. What is the most likely condition?
qs.a: Septic shock
qs.x: A likely source of infection plus hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea and altered mentation is septic shock, which needs early fluids and notification of the receiving hospital.
w: Hypovolemic shock from a GI bleed
Cardiogenic shock
Anaphylaxis

qs.q: A farm worker has pinpoint pupils, drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, wheezing with heavy secretions and HR 44. Which exposure is most likely?
qs.a: Organophosphate pesticide
qs.x: SLUDGE signs with bronchorrhea, bradycardia and miosis make up the cholinergic toxidrome typical of organophosphate poisoning.
w: Anticholinergic plant
Opioid
Stimulant

qs.q: A 17-year-old is agitated and picking at the air. He is hot, dry and flushed, with dilated pupils, HR 132 and a full bladder. Which toxidrome fits best?
qs.a: Anticholinergic
qs.x: Hot, dry, red skin, dilated pupils, delirium, tachycardia and urinary retention are the classic anticholinergic toxidrome, as seen with diphenhydramine overdose.
w: Cholinergic
Opioid
Sedative-hypnotic

qs.q: A 45-year-old with a suspected overdose has a seizure. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS of 140 ms and BP 80/50. Which overdose is most likely?
qs.a: Tricyclic antidepressant
qs.x: Tricyclics block sodium channels, which widens the QRS and causes seizures, hypotension and dysrhythmias.
w: Extended-release acetaminophen
Benzodiazepine
Opioid

qs.q: Everyone in a family has had headaches and nausea since the furnace was turned on. The mother is confused with SpO2 99 percent on a standard pulse oximeter. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Carbon monoxide poisoning
qs.x: Several people with symptoms from an indoor heat source suggest CO poisoning. Standard pulse oximeters read carboxyhemoglobin as oxygenated, so the SpO2 is falsely reassuring.
w: Viral gastroenteritis
Hypoglycemia
Migraine

qs.q: You find a 30-year-old unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, RR 6, SpO2 84 percent and a pulse. What is the first action?
qs.a: Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
qs.x: Ventilate and oxygenate first. Naloxone can follow, but supporting breathing is the immediate priority in opioid-induced respiratory depression.
w: Give naloxone before any other care
Place in recovery position and observe
Perform immediate intubation

qs.q: A 40-year-old with epilepsy has been having continuous generalized seizure activity for 7 minutes on your arrival. What is this called?
qs.a: Status epilepticus
qs.x: A seizure lasting more than about 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery in between, is status epilepticus and needs prompt treatment.
w: Simple partial seizure
Postictal state
Psychogenic nonepileptic event

qs.q: A 48-year-old had a sudden severe headache she calls the worst of her life while lifting weights. She is vomiting and has a stiff neck. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
qs.x: A sudden thunderclap headache that peaks within seconds, with vomiting and a stiff neck, is a classic sign of subarachnoid hemorrhage.
w: Tension headache
Migraine
Sinusitis

qs.q: A dialysis patient who missed two sessions is weak, with HR 48. The ECG shows tall, peaked T waves and a widening QRS. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Hyperkalemia
qs.x: Missed dialysis lets potassium build up. Peaked T waves, a widening QRS and bradycardia warn that hyperkalemia may lead to arrest.
w: Hypokalemia
Hypomagnesemia
Hypoglycemia

qs.q: Police have restrained a man with severe agitation, hyperthermia and extreme strength. How should he be positioned for transport?
qs.a: On his side or back with continuous monitoring
qs.x: Prone and hog-tie positions with weight on the back restrict breathing and are linked to sudden death. Keep restrained patients supine or on their side with continuous monitoring, including ETCO2.
w: Face down with his hands behind his back
Hobbled in a hog-tie position
Face down with an officer kneeling on his back

qs.q: A 35-year-old tells you he plans to kill himself with a gun he keeps at home. He is calm and cooperative. What is the most important action?
qs.a: Make sure the scene is safe and never leave him alone
qs.x: A patient with a suicidal plan is at high risk. Scene safety and constant supervision come first, and he does not have capacity to refuse care.
w: Accept his refusal if he declines transport
Let him go home to collect his belongings
Leave the room so he feels less pressured

qs.q: A 19-year-old collapsed while running a race in hot, humid weather. He is confused with a core temperature of 41.4 C (106.5 F). What is the priority?
qs.a: Rapid whole-body cooling
qs.x: Exertional heat stroke is time-dependent. Rapid cooling, ideally by cold-water immersion, should start before or during transport.
w: Immediate transport with no cooling
Oral fluids and rest in the shade
Warm blankets to prevent shivering

qs.q: A homeless man found outdoors in winter has a core temperature of 30 C (86 F), HR 42 and BP 90/60, and he responds to pain. What is especially important in his care?
qs.a: Handle him gently and keep him horizontal
qs.x: A cold myocardium is very irritable, and rough handling can trigger VF. Move him gently and horizontally, and use passive and active external rewarming.
w: Rub his arms and legs to warm them
Have him walk to the ambulance
Give him hot drinks by mouth

qs.q: An 80-year-old has become confused over the past day, with attention that comes and goes. Her family says she was sharp last week. How is this best described?
qs.a: Delirium
qs.x: An abrupt, fluctuating change in attention and awareness is delirium. It usually has a treatable cause such as infection, medications or hypoxia, so it must be investigated.
w: Dementia
Normal aging
Schizophrenia

qs.q: A 72-year-old smoker has sudden severe back pain, a pulsating abdominal mass, HR 122 and BP 78/46. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
qs.x: Sudden back or abdominal pain with a pulsating mass and shock in an older smoker suggests a ruptured AAA, which needs rapid transport to a surgical center.
w: Kidney stone
Lumbar strain
Pancreatitis

qs.q: Five days after knee surgery, a 52-year-old has sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing, HR 124 and SpO2 89 percent. Her lungs are clear. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Pulmonary embolism
qs.x: Recent surgery and immobility raise the risk of clots. Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia with clear lungs suggest PE.
w: Pneumonia
Congestive heart failure
Asthma exacerbation

qs.q: A term newborn is not crying. Which are part of the initial steps of newborn care? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Warm and dry the baby; Position the airway and clear secretions if needed; Stimulate the baby
qs.x: Warming, drying, positioning, clearing secretions only when needed, and stimulation are the first steps. Routine deep suctioning and routine tracheal suctioning for meconium are no longer recommended.
opts: Warm and dry the baby
Position the airway and clear secretions if needed
Stimulate the baby
Deep suction every newborn
Routine tracheal suction for meconium-stained fluid
ok: Warm and dry the baby
Position the airway and clear secretions if needed
Stimulate the baby

qs.q: You suspect sepsis in an adult. Which findings are qSOFA criteria? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Respiratory rate of 22 or more; Altered mentation; Systolic BP of 100 or less
qs.x: The qSOFA screen uses RR of 22 or more, altered mental status and SBP of 100 or less. Two or more positive criteria with suspected infection mean a higher risk of a poor outcome.
opts: Respiratory rate of 22 or more
Altered mentation
Systolic BP of 100 or less
Heart rate of 88
Temperature of 37.0 C (98.6 F)
ok: Respiratory rate of 22 or more
Altered mentation
Systolic BP of 100 or less

qs.q: Which findings are part of the cholinergic toxidrome? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Heavy bronchial secretions; Pinpoint pupils; Excessive salivation
qs.x: Cholinergic excess causes secretions (SLUDGE), bronchorrhea and miosis. Dry, flushed skin and dilated pupils are anticholinergic signs.
opts: Heavy bronchial secretions
Pinpoint pupils
Excessive salivation
Hot, dry, flushed skin
Dilated pupils
ok: Heavy bronchial secretions
Pinpoint pupils
Excessive salivation

qs.q: A 32-week pregnant patient is being assessed. Which findings suggest preeclampsia with severe features? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Headache with visual changes; Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain; BP of 166/112
qs.x: Severe-range BP, neurologic symptoms and RUQ or epigastric pain are severe features of preeclampsia. Painless bright red bleeding points to placenta previa.
opts: Headache with visual changes
Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain
Painless bright red vaginal bleeding
BP of 118/76
ok: Headache with visual changes
Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain

qs.q: A worker became ill in the heat. Which findings point to heat stroke rather than heat exhaustion? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Altered mental status; Core temperature of 41 C (105.8 F)
qs.x: Heat stroke is defined by central nervous system dysfunction with a core temperature usually above 40 C (104 F). A normal mental status with mild temperature elevation fits heat exhaustion or heat cramps.
opts: Altered mental status
Core temperature of 41 C (105.8 F)
Normal mentation with heavy sweating
Core temperature of 38 C (100.4 F)
Muscle cramps only
ok: Altered mental status
Core temperature of 41 C (105.8 F)

qs.q: A 6-year-old is having an asthma attack. Which findings indicate impending respiratory failure? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Decreasing level of consciousness; Bradycardia; Diminished breath sounds with little air movement
qs.x: Falling mental status, bradycardia and a quiet chest are ominous late signs that call for assisted ventilation. An alert, wheezing child who can talk is in distress but not yet in failure.
opts: Decreasing level of consciousness
Bradycardia
Diminished breath sounds with little air movement
Loud expiratory wheezing while alert
RR of 30 while talking in sentences
ok: Decreasing level of consciousness
Bradycardia
Diminished breath sounds with little air movement

qs.q: During START triage at a bus crash, an adult who cannot walk is breathing at 34 per minute. What category is assigned?
qs.a: Immediate (red)
qs.x: In START, an adult with a respiratory rate above 30 is tagged immediate without further assessment.
w: Delayed (yellow)
Minor (green)
Expectant (black)

qs.q: During JumpSTART triage, a 4-year-old is not breathing after you open the airway but has a palpable pulse. What should you do?
qs.a: Give five rescue breaths
qs.x: Children often stop breathing from respiratory causes, so JumpSTART calls for five rescue breaths when a pulse is present. If breathing resumes, the child is tagged immediate.
w: Tag expectant and move on
Tag immediate without other action
Begin full CPR

qs.q: An adult with decision-making capacity wants to refuse transport. Which is required for a valid informed refusal?
qs.a: He understands the risks, including possible death
qs.x: A valid refusal requires capacity and understanding of the risks, benefits and alternatives, including the possibility of death, and it should be documented.
w: A family member agrees with the decision
Medical direction signs the form at the scene
He has normal vital signs

qs.q: Under HIPAA, which disclosure of patient information is permitted without the patient's written authorization?
qs.a: Report to the receiving hospital staff
qs.x: Sharing protected health information with other providers for treatment is allowed. Disclosure to the public or the media is not.
w: Description of the call on social media
Details to a curious neighbor
Account of the call to a news reporter

qs.q: At a hazardous materials incident, in which zone should decontaminated patients receive full treatment?
qs.a: Cold zone
qs.x: The hot zone is for rescue only, decontamination happens in the warm zone, and full assessment and treatment take place in the cold zone.
w: Hot zone
Warm zone
Exclusion zone

qs.q: You find an error in a paper patient care report you just completed. How should you correct it?
qs.a: Draw one line through it, then initial and date it
qs.x: A single line keeps the original entry readable, and initialing and dating it show who changed it and when, which protects the record's integrity.
w: Erase it and write over it
Black out the error completely
Rewrite the whole report and discard the original

qs.q: While treating a 3-year-old, you notice burns in a stocking pattern on both feet and an explanation that does not fit the injury. What must you do?
qs.a: Report to the proper authority as required by law
qs.x: Paramedics are mandated reporters of suspected child abuse in every state. You report suspicion, and proof is not required.
w: Confront the caregivers about abuse
Do nothing unless the child confirms it
Report only if the hospital agrees

qs.q: You are treating a gunshot victim at a crime scene. How should you remove his clothing?
qs.a: Cut around the bullet holes
qs.x: Patient care comes first, but cutting around holes and limiting disturbance of the scene preserves evidence for law enforcement.
w: Cut straight through the bullet holes
Pull it off and leave it at the scene
Shake it out and fold it for police

qs.q: A hospice patient is found pulseless and apneic. The family shows you a valid DNR order that applies in your state. What should you do?
qs.a: Withhold resuscitation and support the family
qs.x: A valid out-of-hospital DNR order should be honored. Your role becomes confirming death per protocol and supporting the family.
w: Start CPR until medical direction is contacted
Do CPR but skip the advanced airway
Transport with lights and siren

qs.q: While running lights and siren, you come to a red light at an intersection. What is the safest practice?
qs.a: Stop and confirm every lane has yielded
qs.x: Intersections are where most ambulance crashes happen. Stop fully and check that each lane has yielded before crossing.
w: Slow slightly and proceed through
Rely on the siren to clear traffic
Pass on the right of stopped cars

qs.q: You leave a patient at the hospital entrance without handing off care to qualified staff. What legal problem have you created?
qs.a: Abandonment
qs.x: Ending care without transferring it to someone with equal or higher training is abandonment.
w: Assault
Libel
False imprisonment

qs.q: A patient is suing a paramedic for negligence. Which elements must the patient prove? Select all that apply.
qs.a: The paramedic had a duty to act; The paramedic breached the standard of care; The breach caused the injury
qs.x: Negligence requires duty, breach of duty, damages and proximate cause. Intent to harm is not required, and a signed refusal does not prove negligence.
opts: The paramedic had a duty to act
The paramedic breached the standard of care
The patient signed a refusal form
The breach caused the injury
The paramedic intended to cause harm
ok: The paramedic had a duty to act
The paramedic breached the standard of care
The breach caused the injury

qs.q: You are transporting a patient with suspected active tuberculosis. Which precautions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A fit-tested N95 respirator for the crew; A surgical mask on the patient if tolerated; The patient compartment exhaust fan on
qs.x: TB spreads by the airborne route, so the crew needs N95 or higher respirators, source control on the patient and good ventilation. Surgical masks do not protect the wearer against airborne particles.
opts: A fit-tested N95 respirator for the crew
A surgical mask on the patient if tolerated
The patient compartment exhaust fan on
A surgical mask on the crew alone is enough
No precautions if the patient is not coughing
ok: A fit-tested N95 respirator for the crew
A surgical mask on the patient if tolerated
The patient compartment exhaust fan on

qs.q: Under the Incident Command System, which positions belong to the command staff? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Safety officer; Public information officer; Liaison officer
qs.x: The command staff are the safety, public information and liaison officers. Triage and treatment unit leaders sit under the operations section in the general staff.
opts: Safety officer
Public information officer
Liaison officer
Triage unit leader
Treatment unit leader
ok: Safety officer
Public information officer
Liaison officer

qs.q: You are preparing to ventilate an unresponsive 8-month-old lying flat on a firm surface. His head is bent forward, chin toward the chest. What simple step will best help open his airway?
qs.a: Place a thin folded towel under his shoulders
qs.x: An infant's large occiput flexes the neck when supine; padding under the shoulders brings the head to a neutral position, while hyperextension can kink the soft trachea.
w: Place a thick pillow under the back of his head
Hyperextend his neck as far as it will go
Turn his head fully to one side

qs.q: Which structure closes over the glottic opening during swallowing to keep food out of the trachea?
qs.a: Epiglottis
qs.x: The epiglottis is a leaf-shaped flap that folds over the larynx during swallowing; when it fails or is bypassed, aspiration can occur.
w: Uvula
Cricoid cartilage
Vallecula

qs.q: A 2-month-old with a runny nose and low-grade fever is breathing 64 times per minute with nasal flaring and audible nasal congestion. SpO2 is 92%. What should you do first?
qs.a: Gently suction the nose with a bulb syringe
qs.x: Young infants breathe mainly through the nose, so clearing nasal secretions can significantly improve their breathing; this child is still breathing on his own and does not yet need ventilation.
w: Insert a nasopharyngeal airway
Begin BVM ventilation at 40 breaths per minute
Have the parent feed the infant a bottle

qs.q: How is a nasopharyngeal airway measured for an adult patient?
qs.a: From the tip of the nose to the earlobe
qs.x: An NPA is sized from the tip of the nose to the earlobe, and its diameter should fit comfortably in the nostril without blanching.
w: From the corner of the mouth to the chin
From the earlobe to the sternal notch
From the nostril to the corner of the eye

qs.q: You are inserting a nasopharyngeal airway into the right nostril. How should the bevel be oriented?
qs.a: Toward the nasal septum
qs.x: The bevel should face the septum (the midline) so the tip slides along it rather than catching on the turbinates; lubricate with a water-soluble gel first.
w: Toward the outside of the nose
Pointing up toward the eye
It does not matter in the right nostril

qs.q: You are placing an oropharyngeal airway in an unresponsive 4-year-old. Which insertion method is recommended?
qs.a: Depress the tongue and insert it right side up
qs.x: In children, use a tongue depressor and insert the OPA in its anatomic position; rotating it can injure the soft palate.
w: Insert it upside down and rotate it 180 degrees
Insert it sideways and turn it 90 degrees
Push it straight in without moving the tongue

qs.q: Shortly after you insert an OPA, a 40-year-old seizure patient begins gagging and coughing. What should you do?
qs.a: Remove the OPA and consider an NPA
qs.x: A gag reflex means the patient cannot tolerate an OPA and may vomit; remove it and use an NPA if an adjunct is still needed.
w: Push the OPA in farther to stop the gag
Tape the OPA in place and continue
Suction around the OPA and leave it in

qs.q: While you suction the mouth of a 6-week-old infant, her heart rate drops from 150 to 84/min. What should you do?
qs.a: Stop suctioning and oxygenate her
qs.x: Stimulating the back of the throat can trigger a vagal response and bradycardia in infants; stop, oxygenate or ventilate, and limit suction time.
w: Insert the catheter deeper to finish
Switch to a larger rigid catheter
Continue suctioning but at lower pressure

qs.q: You hear gurgling while ventilating an unresponsive 50-year-old woman with a BVM. What should you do?
qs.a: Suction the airway, then resume ventilating
qs.x: Gurgling means fluid is in the upper airway; ventilating through it pushes fluid into the lungs, so suction first.
w: Increase the force of each ventilation to push past it
Increase the oxygen flow rate
Switch to a nonrebreather mask

qs.q: An unresponsive man with no suspected spinal injury vomits a large volume, more than your suction unit can keep up with. What should you do?
qs.a: Roll him onto his side to drain the airway
qs.x: Turning the patient lets gravity clear large amounts of vomit quickly; then finish clearing with suction and resume ventilation.
w: Keep suctioning while ventilating over it
Insert an OPA to hold the airway open
Give abdominal thrusts to empty the stomach

qs.q: Two EMTs are available to ventilate an apneic adult with a BVM. What is the most effective division of tasks?
qs.a: One seals the mask with both hands while the other squeezes the bag
qs.x: Two-rescuer BVM ventilation gives a much better mask seal, the most common reason single-rescuer BVM fails.
w: One squeezes the bag while the other does chest compressions
Each EMT alternates mouth-to-mask and BVM every few breaths
One holds the bag and mask while the other only watches

qs.q: When a BVM with a reservoir is attached to oxygen for ventilating an adult, what flow rate should be used?
qs.a: 15 L/min
qs.x: A flow of 15 L/min keeps the reservoir full so each ventilation delivers oxygen concentrations near 100 percent.
w: 4 L/min
6 L/min to conserve the cylinder
8 L/min

qs.q: An apneic 62-year-old man with a pulse has a laryngectomy stoma in his neck. How should you ventilate him?
qs.a: Through the stoma using an infant or child mask
qs.x: A patient with a total laryngectomy breathes only through the stoma, so seal a small round mask over it and ventilate there.
w: Through the mouth with the stoma left uncovered
With a nonrebreather placed over his face
By mouth only after closing the stoma with gauze

qs.q: A 55-year-old woman with mild dyspnea and an SpO2 of 92% says she feels smothered by a face mask. What is an appropriate alternative?
qs.a: A nasal cannula at 1 to 6 L/min
qs.x: A nasal cannula is well tolerated and suits mild hypoxia; a nonrebreather needs 10-15 L/min or the patient will rebreathe exhaled air.
w: A nonrebreather at 4 L/min
A BVM held over her face
No oxygen at all

qs.q: Which device delivers the highest oxygen concentration to a patient who is breathing adequately on his own?
qs.a: Nonrebreather mask
qs.x: A nonrebreather at 10-15 L/min with a full reservoir delivers the highest concentration available to a spontaneously breathing patient.
w: Nasal cannula
Simple face mask
Venturi mask set at 28 percent

qs.q: You arrive at a home where a 78-year-old man on home oxygen is lighting a cigarette. What should you do first?
qs.a: Have him put out the cigarette and turn off the oxygen
qs.x: Oxygen strongly supports combustion, so an open flame near a flowing oxygen source is a fire and burn hazard; stop the hazard before patient care.
w: Increase his oxygen flow so he stays oxygenated
Move the oxygen tank to the next room and continue your exam
Ask him to finish quickly before you begin

qs.q: An unresponsive 30-year-old man who took an unknown amount of heroin has an SpO2 of 97% on a nonrebreather. His respirations are 6 per minute and shallow. What does this reading tell you?
qs.a: It does not show that he is ventilating adequately
qs.x: Pulse oximetry measures oxygen saturation, not ventilation; high-flow oxygen can keep saturation up while carbon dioxide builds, so a rate of 6 still needs BVM ventilation.
w: His breathing is adequate and needs no help
He has carbon monoxide poisoning
The probe is faulty and should be ignored

qs.q: Your paramedic partner points to the capnography display on a breathing adult. In a healthy person, what range of end-tidal CO2 is considered normal?
qs.a: 35 to 45 mmHg
qs.x: Normal ETCO2 is about 35-45 mmHg; a low value can mean hyperventilation or poor perfusion and a high value can mean hypoventilation.
w: 10 to 20 mmHg
60 to 80 mmHg
94 to 99 mmHg, matching the SpO2 target

qs.q: You are helping a 19-year-old with mild wheezing use her own metered-dose inhaler, which has no spacer. What should you coach her to do?
qs.a: Exhale fully, then breathe in deeply while pressing the inhaler
qs.x: Exhaling first and then inhaling deeply as the canister is pressed, followed by a breath hold, carries the medication deep into the lungs.
w: Breathe in and out rapidly while spraying several puffs
Hold the inhaler at arm's length and inhale slowly
Inhale through the nose while spraying into the mouth

qs.q: A thin 71-year-old man with a 50-year smoking history has a barrel-shaped chest and breathes out through pursed lips. Which chronic condition do these findings most suggest?
qs.a: Emphysema
qs.x: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and traps air, causing a barrel chest; pursed-lip breathing helps keep the small airways open during exhalation.
w: Asthma
Pneumonia
Pulmonary edema

qs.q: An 84-year-old nursing home resident has had a fever and cough with yellow sputum for 2 days. You hear crackles over the right lower lung only. Which condition is most likely?
qs.a: Pneumonia
qs.x: Fever, productive cough, and crackles localized to one area point to pneumonia; CHF usually causes crackles in both bases without fever.
w: Spontaneous pneumothorax
Asthma attack
Congestive heart failure

qs.q: A 31-year-old woman who gave birth 2 weeks ago has sudden shortness of breath and sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing. HR is 124, lungs are clear, SpO2 is 89%. Which condition should you suspect?
qs.a: Pulmonary embolism
qs.x: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, and hypoxia with clear lungs in a postpartum patient strongly suggest PE; give oxygen and transport promptly.
w: Asthma attack
Pneumonia
Anxiety attack

qs.q: A tall, thin 20-year-old man felt sudden sharp left chest pain and shortness of breath while sitting in class. Breath sounds are diminished on the left. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Spontaneous pneumothorax
qs.x: Spontaneous pneumothorax classically affects tall, thin young men when a small weak area of lung ruptures, causing sudden pain and unilateral decreased breath sounds.
w: Acute myocardial infarction
Pulmonary edema
Croup

qs.q: A 24-year-old with a known spontaneous pneumothorax becomes more short of breath during transport. His neck veins are now distended, BP has fallen to 82/50, and breath sounds are absent on the right. What should you do?
qs.a: Request ALS for decompression and expedite transport
qs.x: These are signs of a developing tension pneumothorax, which needs needle decompression beyond EMT scope; CPAP can make it worse.
w: Begin CPAP to re-expand the lung
Have him lie flat on his right side
Slow down so the ride is smoother

qs.q: A 2-year-old has had a cold for 2 days and tonight developed a seal-like barking cough and noisy breathing on inspiration. She has a low-grade fever and is not drooling. What is the most likely condition?
qs.a: Croup
qs.x: A barking cough and inspiratory stridor after a viral illness, typically worse at night, is classic croup, a swelling of the larynx and trachea.
w: Epiglottitis
Asthma
Bronchiolitis

qs.q: A 3-year-old was eating peanuts when he suddenly began coughing. He is now coughing forcefully, crying, and has pink skin. What should you do?
qs.a: Encourage him to keep coughing and monitor him closely
qs.x: A child who can cough forcefully and cry has a mild obstruction; do not interfere with an effective cough, but be ready to act if it becomes ineffective.
w: Give 5 back slaps and 5 chest thrusts
Perform abdominal thrusts until the coughing stops
Sweep his mouth with your finger to find the nut

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman clutches her throat at a restaurant. She has a weak, ineffective cough, a high-pitched noise when inhaling, and is becoming dusky. What should you do?
qs.a: Perform abdominal thrusts
qs.x: A weak cough with high-pitched sounds and cyanosis means poor air exchange and should be treated as a severe obstruction with abdominal thrusts.
w: Encourage her to keep coughing
Give her water to wash it down
Have her lie down and wait for ALS

qs.q: A 6-year-old is sitting calmly watching television and breathing 40 times per minute. How should you interpret this rate?
qs.a: It is faster than normal for her age
qs.x: A resting rate of about 18-30 is typical for a school-age child, so 40 at rest is tachypnea and warrants a search for a cause.
w: It is normal for a school-age child
It is slower than normal for her age
Rate alone cannot be interpreted in children

qs.q: You hear a high-pitched sound mainly on inspiration from a patient's neck. What does this most likely indicate?
qs.a: Partial upper airway obstruction
qs.x: Inspiratory stridor comes from narrowing of the upper airway, such as from swelling or a foreign body, and is a warning sign of possible complete obstruction.
w: Fluid in the alveoli
Narrowing of the small lower airways
Normal breath sounds

qs.q: You hear fine crackles at the bases of both lungs in a 76-year-old woman. What do crackles generally indicate?
qs.a: Fluid in the small airways and alveoli
qs.x: Crackles (rales) are popping sounds made as fluid-filled alveoli and small airways open, as in pulmonary edema or pneumonia.
w: Narrowing of the bronchioles from spasm
An object lodged in the upper airway
A collapsed lung

qs.q: A 23-year-old with type 1 diabetes is breathing very deeply and rapidly, and her breath has a fruity odor. What breathing pattern is this?
qs.a: Kussmaul respirations
qs.x: Deep, rapid Kussmaul breathing is the body's attempt to blow off acid in diabetic ketoacidosis.
w: Cheyne-Stokes respirations
Agonal respirations
Biot respirations

qs.q: A 7-year-old with a tracheostomy tube is in respiratory distress, and you hear gurgling from the tube. What should you do first?
qs.a: Suction the tracheostomy tube
qs.x: Secretions commonly obstruct tracheostomy tubes, so suctioning the tube is the first step; prepare to ventilate through it with a BVM.
w: Cover the tube and ventilate by mouth
Place a nonrebreather over the face
Remove the tube and wait for ALS

qs.q: A ventilator-dependent 9-year-old's home ventilator is alarming, and the child is pale and struggling to breathe. What should you do first?
qs.a: Disconnect the ventilator and ventilate through the tube with a BVM
qs.x: When a ventilated patient is in distress, take the machine out of the equation and ventilate manually with a BVM while looking for the cause.
w: Increase the ventilator settings
Wait for the parents to reset the machine
Place a nasal cannula under the ventilator tubing

qs.q: Your partner wants to press on the cricoid cartilage throughout BVM ventilation of every unresponsive patient to prevent vomiting. What is the current recommendation?
qs.a: Routine cricoid pressure is not recommended
qs.x: Routine cricoid pressure can impede ventilation and does not reliably prevent aspiration, so it is no longer routinely recommended.
w: It should be used on every patient during BVM ventilation
It should only be used in infants
It is required before suctioning

qs.q: A 35-year-old found unresponsive after drinking heavily is breathing 14 times per minute with good chest rise. There is no sign of trauma. How should you position her?
qs.a: Recovery position on her side
qs.x: An unresponsive patient who is breathing adequately and has no suspected spinal injury should be placed on the side to keep the airway clear if she vomits.
w: Supine with her head flat and arms at her sides
Sitting fully upright
Prone with her face down

qs.q: An alert 68-year-old man with COPD is leaning forward with his hands on his knees and refuses to lie down. How should he be transported?
qs.a: Sitting upright in his position of comfort
qs.x: A patient in respiratory distress who can protect his airway should stay upright, which eases the work of the breathing muscles.
w: Supine with his legs raised to improve blood return
Flat on his left side
Supine with his head lowered

qs.q: Twenty minutes after a bee sting, a 33-year-old woman's voice has become hoarse and she has a tight feeling in her throat. What do these findings most suggest?
qs.a: Swelling of the upper airway
qs.x: Hoarseness and throat tightness after an allergen exposure mean the larynx is swelling, a life-threatening sign of anaphylaxis requiring immediate treatment and transport.
w: Normal anxiety after a sting
A lower airway infection
Pulmonary edema from heart failure

qs.q: A 52-year-old man was in a house fire. He has soot around his mouth, singed nasal hairs, and a hoarse voice, but no distress yet. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Airway swelling that may progress quickly
qs.x: Signs of inhalation injury mean the airway may swell rapidly over minutes to hours; give high-flow oxygen and transport promptly, with early ALS.
w: A minor burn that needs no oxygen
Hypoglycemia from the stress of the fire
Dehydration from sweating

qs.q: A 14-year-old was pulled from a pool. He has a pulse but is breathing 4 times per minute. What should you do first?
qs.a: Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen
qs.x: Drowning causes hypoxia, so ventilation is the priority; abdominal thrusts to remove water delay care and risk vomiting.
