w: Give abdominal thrusts to remove water
Place him on a nonrebreather
Tilt his head down to drain the lungs

qs.q: An alert 2-year-old with croup has mild retractions and cries when you bring an oxygen mask near her face. She is in her mother's lap. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Have her mother hold blow-by oxygen near her face
qs.x: Upsetting a child with upper airway swelling can worsen the obstruction, so keep her calm with her parent and give oxygen by the least distressing method.
w: Restrain her and secure the mask tightly
Withhold oxygen and lay her on the stretcher
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway

qs.q: An alert 46-year-old man without lung disease has an SpO2 of 88% on room air. How should this be interpreted?
qs.a: He is hypoxic and should receive oxygen
qs.x: A healthy adult normally saturates about 95 percent or higher, so 88 percent indicates hypoxia that needs oxygen and a search for the cause.
w: This is normal for an adult at rest
The reading is high and oxygen should be avoided
It is only significant if he is cyanotic

qs.q: In a healthy person, what is the main stimulus that triggers the urge to breathe?
qs.a: A rising level of carbon dioxide in the blood
qs.x: Chemoreceptors in the brainstem respond mainly to rising carbon dioxide; low oxygen is a backup drive.
w: A falling level of oxygen in the blood
A falling level of carbon dioxide in the blood
A rising level of glucose in the blood

qs.q: You are ventilating a 3-year-old with a BVM. How should you judge how much volume to give with each squeeze?
qs.a: Squeeze only until you see the chest begin to rise
qs.x: Volume is guided by visible chest rise; more than that causes gastric distention and can injure the lungs.
w: Squeeze the bag fully every time
Give as much volume as you would to an adult
Squeeze about halfway regardless of chest rise

qs.q: A term newborn is limp and not breathing after warming, drying, and stimulation. What should you do next?
qs.a: Begin positive-pressure ventilation at 40 to 60 breaths per minute
qs.x: Under NRP, a newborn who is apneic or gasping, or has a heart rate under 100, after initial steps needs positive-pressure ventilation at 40-60 breaths per minute.
w: Begin chest compressions at a 3:1 ratio
Continue rubbing the back for 2 more minutes
Give blow-by oxygen and observe

qs.q: You need to ventilate a severely obese, unresponsive 39-year-old man who is breathing inadequately. How can you position him to make ventilation easier?
qs.a: Elevate his head and shoulders so his ear lines up with his sternum
qs.x: A ramped position, with the ear level with the sternal notch, improves airway alignment and lowers the weight of the chest and abdomen on the lungs.
w: Lay him completely flat with no padding
Place him in the Trendelenburg position
Roll him onto his stomach

qs.q: An unresponsive 80-year-old woman with snug-fitting dentures needs BVM ventilation. What should you do about the dentures?
qs.a: Leave them in to support a better mask seal
qs.x: Well-fitting dentures help maintain facial shape and mask seal; remove them only if they are loose or obstructing the airway.
w: Always remove them before ventilating
Push them farther back in the mouth
Remove only the lower denture and leave the upper one

qs.q: A 47-year-old man with pneumonia is anxious and breathing 34 times per minute with shallow breaths. His SpO2 is 85% on a nonrebreather. You decide to assist his ventilations with a BVM. How should you time the breaths?
qs.a: Squeeze as he begins each inhalation and gradually slow his rate
qs.x: Assisted ventilation should match the patient's own inhalations, then gradually adjust to a more effective rate and depth.
w: Squeeze as hard as possible when he exhales
Ignore his own breaths and ventilate at 30 per minute
Squeeze only every other time he exhales

qs.q: An alert 64-year-old man with CHF has been on CPAP for 5 minutes and is improving, but he suddenly becomes confused and can no longer follow commands. What should you do?
qs.a: Remove the CPAP and assist ventilations with a BVM
qs.x: CPAP requires an alert patient who can protect his airway; declining mental status signals failure, so switch to BVM ventilation.
w: Increase the oxygen and leave the CPAP on
Tighten the mask straps for a better seal
Sit him up and wait 10 minutes

qs.q: A 4-year-old has a sudden high fever and respiratory distress. Which findings suggest epiglottitis rather than croup? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Drooling and difficulty swallowing; Rapid onset over a few hours; Sitting forward in a tripod position
qs.x: Epiglottitis develops rapidly with high fever, drooling, and tripod positioning; a barking cough after a few days of cold symptoms is typical of croup.
opts: Drooling and difficulty swallowing
Rapid onset over a few hours
Sitting forward in a tripod position
A barking, seal-like cough
Several days of runny nose before the noisy breathing
ok: Drooling and difficulty swallowing
Rapid onset over a few hours
Sitting forward in a tripod position

qs.q: Which findings are consistent with a spontaneous pneumothorax? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Sudden onset of sharp chest pain; Decreased breath sounds on one side
qs.x: Spontaneous pneumothorax causes sudden sharp pain, dyspnea, and diminished breath sounds on the affected side; bilateral crackles and fever suggest other conditions.
opts: Sudden onset of sharp chest pain
Decreased breath sounds on one side
Crackles in both lung bases
Fever and productive cough for 3 days
A barking cough at night
ok: Sudden onset of sharp chest pain
Decreased breath sounds on one side

qs.q: Which steps are correct when inserting a nasopharyngeal airway? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Lubricate it with a water-soluble gel; Measure from the tip of the nose to the earlobe; Insert it gently along the floor of the nostril
qs.x: An NPA is sized from nose tip to earlobe, lubricated with water-soluble gel, and inserted gently; if resistance is met, try the other nostril rather than forcing it.
opts: Lubricate it with a water-soluble gel
Measure from the tip of the nose to the earlobe
Insert it gently along the floor of the nostril
Lubricate it with petroleum jelly
Insert it upside down and rotate it 180 degrees
Force it past resistance to secure the airway
ok: Lubricate it with a water-soluble gel
Measure from the tip of the nose to the earlobe
Insert it gently along the floor of the nostril

qs.q: A 38-year-old woman has sudden shortness of breath. Which history findings increase your suspicion of a pulmonary embolism? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Knee surgery 10 days ago; A recent 14-hour flight; Taking oral contraceptives and smoking
qs.x: Recent surgery, prolonged immobility, and estrogen use with smoking all increase clot risk; allergies and regular exercise do not.
opts: Knee surgery 10 days ago
A recent 14-hour flight
Taking oral contraceptives and smoking
A history of seasonal allergies
Running 3 miles a day
ok: Knee surgery 10 days ago
A recent 14-hour flight
Taking oral contraceptives and smoking

qs.q: A patient is receiving CPAP for respiratory distress. Which changes mean you should stop CPAP and prepare to ventilate with a BVM? Select all that apply.
qs.a: He becomes unresponsive; He begins vomiting
qs.x: Unresponsiveness or vomiting means the patient can no longer protect his airway under a sealed mask; rising saturation, a slowing rate, and patient relief show CPAP is working.
opts: He becomes unresponsive
He begins vomiting
His SpO2 rises from 86% to 93%
His respiratory rate falls from 32 to 24
He says his breathing feels easier
ok: He becomes unresponsive
He begins vomiting

qs.q: Which features of a child's airway differ from an adult's? Select all that apply.
qs.a: The tongue is larger in proportion to the mouth; The occiput is larger, flexing the neck when supine; The trachea is softer and more easily kinked
qs.x: Children have relatively large tongues and heads and soft, narrow tracheas; young infants breathe mainly through the nose.
opts: The tongue is larger in proportion to the mouth
The occiput is larger, flexing the neck when supine
The trachea is softer and more easily kinked
The airway is wider and less affected by swelling
Infants breathe mainly through the mouth
ok: The tongue is larger in proportion to the mouth
The occiput is larger, flexing the neck when supine
The trachea is softer and more easily kinked

qs.q: Which practices are appropriate for oxygen cylinder safety? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Secure cylinders so they cannot fall or roll; Keep cylinders away from open flames and smoking
qs.x: Cylinders must be secured and kept from heat and flame; oil, grease, and adhesive near high-pressure oxygen can ignite.
opts: Secure cylinders so they cannot fall or roll
Keep cylinders away from open flames and smoking
Lubricate a sticking regulator with oil or grease
Store cylinders in a hot vehicle trunk
Use adhesive tape to mark the cylinder valve
ok: Secure cylinders so they cannot fall or roll
Keep cylinders away from open flames and smoking

qs.q: A 22-year-old with asthma calls for help. Which findings indicate a severe attack? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Speaking only 2 or 3 words between breaths; Sitting forward braced on her arms; SpO2 of 88% on room air
qs.x: Short phrases, tripod positioning, and hypoxia show a severe attack; mild wheezes with a normal rate and full sentences indicate a mild one.
opts: Speaking only 2 or 3 words between breaths
Sitting forward braced on her arms
SpO2 of 88% on room air
Mild end-expiratory wheezes with RR of 18
Talking in full sentences while you assess her
ok: Speaking only 2 or 3 words between breaths
Sitting forward braced on her arms
SpO2 of 88% on room air

qs.q: Which techniques are appropriate when suctioning an adult's oropharynx with a rigid tip? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Insert the tip only as far as you can see; Oxygenate the patient before and after suctioning; Apply suction while withdrawing the tip
qs.x: Suction under direct vision, apply it on withdrawal, keep attempts brief, and oxygenate around each attempt to limit hypoxia.
opts: Insert the tip only as far as you can see
Oxygenate the patient before and after suctioning
Apply suction while withdrawing the tip
Apply suction while advancing the tip
Suction for as long as secretions remain
ok: Insert the tip only as far as you can see
Oxygenate the patient before and after suctioning
Apply suction while withdrawing the tip

qs.q: Which findings are EARLY signs of hypoxia in an adult? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Restlessness or anxiety; Increased heart rate; Increased respiratory rate
qs.x: Early hypoxia causes restlessness, tachycardia, and tachypnea; cyanosis, bradycardia, and unresponsiveness are late, ominous signs.
opts: Restlessness or anxiety
Increased heart rate
Increased respiratory rate
Cyanosis of the lips and nail beds
Slowing heart rate
Unresponsiveness
ok: Restlessness or anxiety
Increased heart rate
Increased respiratory rate

qs.q: A patient was in an enclosed-space fire. Which findings suggest an inhalation injury to the airway? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Singed eyebrows or nasal hairs; Soot in the mouth or sputum; Hoarseness or a change in voice
qs.x: Singed facial hair, soot in the airway, and hoarseness indicate heat or smoke injury that may lead to rapid airway swelling.
opts: Singed eyebrows or nasal hairs
Soot in the mouth or sputum
Hoarseness or a change in voice
A first-degree burn on the forearm
A heart rate of 88/min
ok: Singed eyebrows or nasal hairs
Soot in the mouth or sputum
Hoarseness or a change in voice

qs.q: Which actions are part of correct BVM technique for an unresponsive adult with inadequate breathing? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Use an E-C clamp to seal the mask; Insert an OPA or NPA if one is tolerated; Deliver each breath over about 1 second
qs.x: An E-C clamp seal, an airway adjunct, and 1-second breaths with visible chest rise give effective ventilation without gastric inflation; flexing the neck closes the airway.
opts: Use an E-C clamp to seal the mask
Insert an OPA or NPA if one is tolerated
Deliver each breath over about 1 second
Squeeze the bag as fast and hard as possible
Hold the head in full flexion to protect the airway
ok: Use an E-C clamp to seal the mask
Insert an OPA or NPA if one is tolerated
Deliver each breath over about 1 second

qs.q: A 58-year-old man has substernal chest pressure. He is alert, and his SpO2 is 98% on room air with no shortness of breath. What is the best approach to oxygen?
qs.a: Monitor; extra oxygen is not routinely needed with normal saturation
qs.x: Current guidance gives oxygen in suspected ACS for hypoxia or respiratory distress, not routinely when saturation is normal.
w: Give 15 L/min by nonrebreather to all chest pain patients
Ventilate with a BVM to protect the heart muscle
Withhold oxygen even if his saturation later drops

qs.q: A 52-year-old woman has had indigestion-like upper abdominal discomfort, sweating, and nausea for an hour. She has no chest pain and thinks it is something she ate. What is the most appropriate EMT action?
qs.a: Treat this as possible ACS and transport
qs.x: Women frequently have ACS without classic chest pain; epigastric discomfort with diaphoresis and nausea should be treated as a possible heart attack.
w: Advise her to take an antacid and stay home
Assume food poisoning and offer a sip of water
Recommend she follow up with her doctor tomorrow

qs.q: Why might a patient with long-standing diabetes have a heart attack without significant chest pain?
qs.a: Nerve damage can blunt the sensation of pain
qs.x: Diabetic neuropathy can dull the warning pain of ischemia, so these patients may present only with weakness, dyspnea, or nausea.
w: High blood sugar protects the heart muscle
Insulin blocks pain signals from the heart
Diabetes prevents coronary artery blockage

qs.q: A 67-year-old man had a heart attack 2 days ago. He is now confused, with cool clammy skin, crackles in both lungs, HR 118, and BP 76/50. What type of shock is most likely?
qs.a: Cardiogenic
qs.x: A damaged heart that cannot pump effectively causes low blood pressure with fluid backing into the lungs, the hallmark of cardiogenic shock.
w: Hypovolemic
Anaphylactic
Neurogenic

qs.q: An 8-year-old who has been vomiting for 2 days has a heart rate of 140, cool hands and feet, and capillary refill of 4 seconds. Her blood pressure is normal for her age. How should you interpret these findings?
qs.a: Compensated shock
qs.x: Children maintain their blood pressure until late in shock; tachycardia and poor peripheral perfusion with a normal BP indicate compensated shock.
w: Normal findings for a sick child
Irreversible shock
Decompensated shock

qs.q: In a child developing shock, which finding is a late sign that suggests decompensation?
qs.a: Falling blood pressure
qs.x: Hypotension in a child is a late sign that compensatory mechanisms are failing and cardiac arrest may be near.
w: Increased heart rate
Delayed capillary refill
Anxiety or restlessness

qs.q: An 81-year-old woman with a 2-day history of fever and urinary symptoms is confused. Her skin is flushed, HR is 122, RR is 28, and BP is 84/48. Which condition should you suspect?
qs.a: Septic shock
qs.x: Fever, confusion, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension with a likely infection source point to sepsis with shock, which needs early hospital notification.
w: Cardiogenic shock
Hypertensive emergency
Stable angina

qs.q: A 74-year-old man has had black tarry stools for 2 days and feels dizzy when standing. He is pale, HR 118, BP 92/60. After giving oxygen as needed, how should you position him?
qs.a: Supine and kept warm
qs.x: Signs of GI bleeding with tachycardia and dizziness suggest hypovolemic shock; keep him supine, prevent heat loss, and transport rapidly.
w: Sitting fully upright
Standing to recheck his vital signs
Head-down Trendelenburg

qs.q: A 79-year-old who takes a beta-blocker fell and has a large thigh bruise. She is pale and anxious with a BP of 88/54, but her heart rate is 70. What should you conclude about the heart rate?
qs.a: A normal heart rate does not rule out shock in this patient
qs.x: Beta-blockers can prevent the compensatory rise in heart rate, so older patients on these medications may be in shock without tachycardia.
w: It proves she is not bleeding significantly
It means the blood pressure reading is wrong
It means she is in cardiogenic shock

qs.q: Where should you place your hands to perform chest compressions on an adult?
qs.a: On the lower half of the sternum
qs.x: Compressions are delivered on the lower half of the breastbone in the center of the chest; pressing on the xiphoid can injure the liver.
w: On the xiphoid process
On the upper third of the sternum
Over the left nipple

qs.q: You are performing CPR on a 7-year-old child. What compression depth should you target?
qs.a: About 2 inches
qs.x: For children, compress at least one-third of the chest depth, which is about 2 inches (5 cm).
w: About 1 inch
About 3 inches
About one-half inch

qs.q: You are alone with a 4-month-old infant in cardiac arrest until your partner returns from the ambulance. Which compression technique should you use?
qs.a: Two-thumb encircling hands or the heel of one hand
qs.x: Current guidance for infant CPR uses the two-thumb encircling hands technique or, if the rescuer cannot encircle the chest, the heel of one hand.
w: Two fingers placed just below the nipple line
The heel of both hands stacked on the sternum
One thumb pressing on the xiphoid process

qs.q: You are the only rescuer performing CPR on an 18-month-old. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should you use?
qs.x: A single rescuer uses 30:2 for all ages beyond the newborn period; 15:2 is used when two rescuers perform infant or child CPR.
w: 5 compressions to 1 breath

qs.q: A term newborn's heart rate remains below 60/min despite 30 seconds of positive-pressure ventilation that moves the chest well. What should you do?
qs.a: Begin chest compressions coordinated with ventilations at 3:1
qs.x: Under NRP, a heart rate below 60 despite effective ventilation calls for compressions with a 3:1 ratio (90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute).
w: Continue ventilations alone and recheck in 5 minutes
Stop ventilating and dry the baby again
Begin compressions at a ratio of 15:2

qs.q: Where should you place AED pads on an adult in the standard anterolateral position?
qs.a: Below the right collarbone and on the left side below the armpit
qs.x: Anterolateral placement puts one pad below the right clavicle and the other on the left lateral chest, so current travels through the heart.
w: Both pads side by side on the center of the chest
On the left shoulder and the right hip
On the upper back and the right shoulder

qs.q: The AED analyzes the rhythm of a 63-year-old man in cardiac arrest and advises no shock. What should you do?
qs.a: Resume CPR immediately, starting with compressions
qs.x: No shock advised does not mean the patient has a pulse; resume CPR for about 2 minutes before the next analysis.
w: Turn off the AED and remove the pads
Check for a pulse for 30 seconds
Reanalyze right away to confirm

qs.q: You are transporting a patient in cardiac arrest, and it is time for the AED to analyze. What should be done?
qs.a: Stop the ambulance for analysis and any shock
qs.x: Vehicle motion can interfere with rhythm analysis, so the ambulance should be stopped during analysis and shock delivery.
w: Analyze while the vehicle is moving
Skip the analysis until arrival at the hospital
Analyze only if the road is smooth

qs.q: A 54-year-old man in cardiac arrest is lying in a puddle of rainwater on a sidewalk. What should you do before using the AED?
qs.a: Move him to a dry area and dry his chest
qs.x: Standing water can conduct current to rescuers and divert it from the heart; move the patient to a dry surface and dry the chest quickly.
w: Apply the pads and shock immediately where he lies
Skip the AED and perform CPR only
Place the pads on his back instead

qs.q: You place AED pads on a man with a very hairy chest, and the AED prompts that the pads are not making good contact. What should you do?
qs.a: Pull off the pads to remove hair and apply a new set
qs.x: Quickly removing the first pads, or shaving the area, removes hair so a second set can make good contact; do not delay defibrillation longer than necessary.
w: Push harder on the pads during the shock
Place the pads over his clothing
Continue CPR without the AED

qs.q: You are treating an alert 60-year-old man with an implanted defibrillator when it delivers a shock while your hand is on his chest. What is true?
qs.a: You may feel a tingle, but it is not dangerous to you
qs.x: Implanted defibrillators deliver low-energy shocks that a rescuer may feel but that do not harm rescuers.
w: You will likely receive a dangerous shock
The device will stop working permanently
You should immediately apply AED pads over the device

qs.q: A 26-year-old was pulled from a lake after being submerged and is pulseless and apneic. What is especially important in this arrest?
qs.a: Early effective ventilation along with compressions
qs.x: Drowning arrests are caused by hypoxia, so effective ventilations are a key part of CPR along with compressions and the AED.
w: Abdominal thrusts to remove water from the lungs
Delaying CPR until the patient is fully warmed
Compressions only, with no breaths

qs.q: A 22-year-old is found pulseless in the snow after a night outdoors, with a core temperature that feels very cold. There are no obvious signs of death. What should you do?
qs.a: Start CPR and apply the AED while preventing further heat loss
qs.x: Severely hypothermic patients may survive prolonged arrest, so begin resuscitation, protect from further cooling, and transport.
w: Pronounce death because he is too cold to resuscitate
Rewarm him for 30 minutes before starting CPR
Rub his arms and legs vigorously to warm him

qs.q: What is the most common cause of cardiac arrest in infants and children?
qs.a: Respiratory failure or shock
qs.x: Pediatric arrest is usually the end result of hypoxia from respiratory failure or shock, so supporting airway and breathing early can prevent it.
w: A sudden ventricular dysrhythmia
A heart attack
Pulmonary embolism

qs.q: During a cardiac arrest, the paramedic team leader says to you, Take over compressions at the next switch. Which response reflects good closed-loop communication?
qs.a: Taking over compressions at the next switch
qs.x: Closed-loop communication means repeating the order back so the leader knows it was heard and understood.

Nodding silently and moving toward the chest
Asking someone else to do it

qs.q: During a resuscitation you notice the person doing compressions is allowing the chest to recoil only partway. What should you do?
qs.a: Tell the compressor and team leader clearly and respectfully
qs.x: Effective teams encourage members to speak up about quality problems during the event so they can be corrected immediately.

Stop compressions yourself and take over without speaking
Report it only after the call is over

qs.q: You arrive at a home where an 89-year-old man is pulseless and apneic. His wife hands you a valid, signed out-of-hospital DNR order. What should you do?
qs.a: Verify the document and withhold resuscitation
qs.x: A valid out-of-hospital DNR or POLST order should be honored; confirm it belongs to the patient and follow local protocol.
w: Start CPR anyway until medical control arrives
Apply the AED and shock only once

qs.q: A 76-year-old woman with a valid DNR order has severe shortness of breath and a strong pulse. What care should you provide?
qs.a: Oxygen and comfort measures
qs.x: A DNR order addresses resuscitation from arrest, not other care; patients with DNR orders should still receive oxygen, comfort, and appropriate treatment.
w: No treatment of any kind
Only transport, with no assessment
Full CPR if she becomes worse

qs.q: A 70-year-old man is pulseless and apneic in his bed. His adult son says his father never wanted CPR, but there is no written order. There are no signs of obvious death. What should you do?
qs.a: Begin resuscitation
qs.x: Without a valid written order or obvious signs of death, resuscitation should be started; verbal wishes from family generally are not sufficient.
w: Withhold CPR based on the son's request
Wait for the family to find the paperwork
Call the patient's doctor before doing anything

qs.q: Under the widely used BLS termination of resuscitation rule, which finding means resuscitation should continue and the patient should be transported?
qs.a: The AED delivered a shock
qs.x: The BLS rule allows considering termination only if the arrest was not witnessed by EMS, no shock was given, and there was no ROSC; a delivered shock means continue.
w: The arrest was not witnessed by EMS
There was no return of pulse on scene
The patient is over 65 years old

qs.q: A 64-year-old man regained a pulse after AED shocks. During transport, he again becomes pulseless. What should you do?
qs.a: Resume CPR and use the AED
qs.x: Rearrest is common after ROSC; restart compressions immediately and follow AED prompts.
w: Continue ventilations only
Check his blood pressure first
Wait 2 minutes to see if the pulse returns

qs.q: A 15-year-old baseball catcher collapses after a pitch strikes him in the chest. He is unresponsive and pulseless. What should you do?
qs.a: Begin CPR and apply the AED immediately
qs.x: A blow to the chest at the wrong moment can trigger ventricular fibrillation (commotio cordis); early CPR and defibrillation are lifesaving.
w: Splint his chest and transport
Give oxygen and observe for 5 minutes
Stabilize the spine before any other care

qs.q: An adult in cardiac arrest is lying in a soft hospital-style bed at home. What should you do before starting compressions?
qs.a: Move him to the floor or a firm surface
qs.x: Compressions on a soft mattress lose depth; move the patient to a firm surface quickly or place a backboard beneath him.
w: Do compressions on the bed with extra force
Sit him up against the headboard
Place a pillow under his back

qs.q: Where should you check for a pulse in an unresponsive 5-month-old?
qs.a: Brachial artery
qs.x: The brachial pulse on the inside of the upper arm is the most reliable location in infants, whose short necks make carotid checks difficult.
w: Carotid artery
Radial artery
Dorsalis pedis artery

qs.q: You arrive to find a bystander performing good CPR on a 60-year-old man. What should you do first?
qs.a: Have the bystander continue while you apply the AED
qs.x: Keep compressions going while the AED is applied, minimizing interruptions, then take over CPR.
w: Stop the bystander and recheck for breathing for 30 seconds
Take over compressions and delay the AED until ALS arrives
Ask the bystander how long he has been doing CPR

qs.q: Which of these is added in BE-FAST that the basic FAST stroke screen does not include?
qs.a: Balance and eyes
qs.x: BE-FAST adds sudden loss of balance and vision changes to face, arm, and speech findings, catching posterior strokes that FAST can miss.
w: Face and arms
Speech and time
Blood pressure and glucose

qs.q: A 66-year-old woman went to bed at 10 p.m. feeling fine and woke at 6 a.m. unable to move her left arm. When was she last known well?
qs.x: For symptoms discovered on waking, the last known well time is when the patient was last seen normal, here at bedtime.
w: 6 a.m.
The time EMS was called
Midnight, the start of the new day

qs.q: You are treating a 73-year-old man with sudden facial droop, arm weakness, and slurred speech that began 30 minutes ago. Which action will most shorten his time to definitive treatment?
qs.a: Notify the receiving stroke-capable hospital early
qs.x: Early prehospital notification lets the hospital prepare its stroke team and imaging before the patient arrives.
w: Delay transport until his symptoms stabilize
Transport without lights and sirens to the closest clinic
Wait to see if his symptoms resolve

qs.q: A 69-year-old man had 20 minutes of slurred speech and right-hand weakness that completely resolved before you arrived. He feels fine and wants to stay home. What should you advise?
qs.a: He needs evaluation because this may be a TIA with high stroke risk
qs.x: A TIA is a warning that a stroke may follow soon, so the patient should be transported for urgent evaluation.
w: He is fine because his symptoms resolved
He can take an aspirin and go to bed
He should call his doctor next month

qs.q: A 48-year-old woman has a sudden, explosive headache she calls the worst of her life, followed by vomiting and a stiff neck. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Bleeding in or around the brain
qs.x: A sudden severe headache with vomiting suggests a hemorrhagic stroke such as a subarachnoid hemorrhage; monitor the airway and transport rapidly.
w: A tension headache
A sinus infection
Migraine with aura

qs.q: A 57-year-old man has a severe headache, blurred vision, and confusion. His BP is 232/138. What condition is most likely?
qs.a: Hypertensive emergency
qs.x: Severely elevated blood pressure with signs of organ damage such as confusion or vision changes is a hypertensive emergency requiring prompt transport.
w: Stable angina
Hypovolemic shock
Vasovagal syncope

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant has a severe headache, spots in her vision, and swollen hands and face. BP is 166/112. What should you do?
qs.a: Keep her calm in a quiet setting, position her on her left side, and transport
qs.x: These are signs of severe preeclampsia with a high risk of seizures; minimize stimulation, use left-side positioning, and transport while being ready to manage a seizure.
w: Have her walk to the ambulance to improve circulation
Turn on lights and sirens and keep the cabin bright so you can watch her
Lay her supine and elevate her legs

qs.q: A 77-year-old man has distended neck veins, swelling in both ankles, and an enlarged abdomen, but his lungs are clear. Which condition do these findings suggest?
qs.a: Right-sided heart failure
qs.x: Right-sided failure causes blood to back up into the body, producing JVD, peripheral edema, and abdominal swelling; left-sided failure causes pulmonary edema.
w: Left-sided heart failure
Asthma
Spontaneous pneumothorax

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman with CHF says she now has to sleep on three pillows and wakes up at night gasping for air. What does this history suggest?
qs.a: Worsening fluid in the lungs when lying flat
qs.x: Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea occur when lying flat lets fluid shift into the lungs, a sign of worsening heart failure.
w: Improving heart function
An upper airway obstruction
A normal sign of aging

qs.q: A 61-year-old man with high blood pressure has sudden severe chest pain he describes as tearing, radiating to his back. BP is 182/104 in the right arm and 140/82 in the left. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Aortic dissection
qs.x: Sudden tearing pain to the back with a blood pressure difference between arms is classic for aortic dissection; keep him calm and transport rapidly.
w: Stable angina
Spontaneous pneumothorax
Pericarditis

qs.q: A 20-year-old woman fainted after seeing blood at a clinic. She is now awake, lying supine, and reports feeling nauseated and warm. What should you do?
qs.a: Keep her lying down while you assess her
qs.x: Vasovagal syncope usually follows a trigger, but sitting or standing too soon can cause another faint; keep her supine while you assess.
w: Have her stand quickly to check her balance
Give her a large glass of water
Place her in a sitting position immediately

qs.q: A 16-year-old basketball player suddenly fainted while sprinting and recovered within a minute. He feels fine now. What is the most important concern?
qs.a: A possible underlying heart condition
qs.x: Syncope during exertion in a young athlete may indicate a structural or electrical heart problem that can cause sudden death; he needs evaluation.
w: Simple dehydration that needs no care
An anxiety reaction to the game
Low blood sugar from skipping breakfast

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman who is 36 weeks pregnant becomes dizzy and pale while lying flat on her back for your assessment. What should you do?
qs.a: Position her on her left side
qs.x: The heavy uterus can compress the vena cava when she lies supine, reducing blood return to the heart; left lateral positioning relieves it.
w: Elevate her legs while she stays supine
Have her sit up and drink water
Place her face down

qs.q: You are called for a 58-year-old man with an LVAD who feels weak. He is alert and talking, but you cannot feel a radial pulse or obtain a BP with your cuff. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: His continuous-flow pump often makes the pulse hard to feel
qs.x: Continuous-flow LVADs may produce little or no palpable pulse; assess perfusion by mental status, skin color, and capillary refill rather than pulse alone.
w: He is in cardiac arrest and needs compressions
Your equipment must be malfunctioning
He is in severe hypovolemic shock

qs.q: Which findings may be the presenting symptoms of ACS, even without chest pain? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Jaw or arm discomfort; Sudden unexplained shortness of breath; Sweating with nausea
qs.x: Jaw or arm discomfort, sudden dyspnea, and sweating with nausea can all be ACS, especially in women, older adults, and diabetics; cold symptoms and rashes are not.
opts: Jaw or arm discomfort
Sudden unexplained shortness of breath
Sweating with nausea
A sore throat with runny nose
An itchy rash on both arms
ok: Jaw or arm discomfort
Sudden unexplained shortness of breath
Sweating with nausea

qs.q: You are about to deliver an AED shock. Which actions promote safety? Select all that apply.
qs.a: State loudly that everyone is clear; Visually confirm no one is touching the patient; Move free-flowing oxygen away from the chest
qs.x: Announcing and confirming clear and moving oxygen away prevents injury and fire; touching the patient during analysis or shock is unsafe and interferes with the device.
opts: State loudly that everyone is clear
Visually confirm no one is touching the patient
Move free-flowing oxygen away from the chest
Continue compressions while the AED analyzes
Hold the patient's hand to feel for a pulse during the shock
ok: State loudly that everyone is clear
Visually confirm no one is touching the patient
Move free-flowing oxygen away from the chest

qs.q: Which findings are typical of hypovolemic shock in an adult? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Rapid heart rate; Cool, pale, clammy skin; Anxiety or restlessness
qs.x: Volume loss causes tachycardia, pale cool clammy skin, and anxiety; flat, not distended, neck veins and rapid shallow breathing are expected.
opts: Rapid heart rate
Cool, pale, clammy skin
Anxiety or restlessness
Warm, flushed, dry skin
Distended neck veins
Slow, deep respirations
ok: Rapid heart rate
Cool, pale, clammy skin
Anxiety or restlessness

qs.q: An adult has ROSC after defibrillation. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Leave the AED pads attached; Ventilate if needed without hyperventilating; Check blood pressure and prepare for rearrest
qs.x: After ROSC, keep the AED attached because rearrest is common, avoid hyperventilation, monitor vital signs, and transport to an appropriate facility.
opts: Leave the AED pads attached
Ventilate if needed without hyperventilating
Check blood pressure and prepare for rearrest
Remove the AED to prevent accidental shocks
Ventilate at 30 breaths per minute to remove CO2
ok: Leave the AED pads attached
Ventilate if needed without hyperventilating
Check blood pressure and prepare for rearrest

qs.q: Which conditions can mimic a stroke in the field? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hypoglycemia; A postictal state after a seizure
qs.x: Hypoglycemia and postictal weakness can produce stroke-like deficits; atrial fibrillation and high cholesterol are stroke risk factors, not mimics.
opts: Hypoglycemia
A postictal state after a seizure
High cholesterol
A history of atrial fibrillation
A sprained ankle
ok: Hypoglycemia
A postictal state after a seizure

qs.q: Which findings suggest an aortic dissection? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Sudden tearing pain radiating to the back; A large blood pressure difference between arms; A weak or absent pulse in one arm
qs.x: Dissection causes abrupt tearing pain and can block branch arteries, producing unequal arm pressures or pulses.
opts: Sudden tearing pain radiating to the back
A large blood pressure difference between arms
A weak or absent pulse in one arm
Pain that developed gradually over a week with fever
Pain only when swallowing
ok: Sudden tearing pain radiating to the back
A large blood pressure difference between arms
A weak or absent pulse in one arm

qs.q: Which findings are consistent with congestive heart failure? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Swelling in both ankles; Shortness of breath when lying flat; Jugular vein distention
qs.x: CHF causes bilateral edema, orthopnea, and JVD; a barking cough suggests croup and one-sided calf swelling suggests a DVT.
opts: Swelling in both ankles
Shortness of breath when lying flat
Jugular vein distention
A barking cough
Pain and swelling in one calf only
ok: Swelling in both ankles
Shortness of breath when lying flat
Jugular vein distention

qs.q: Which practices reflect effective teamwork during a resuscitation? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Repeating orders back to the leader; Having a leader assign clear roles; Speaking up when you see an error
qs.x: Clear roles, closed-loop communication, and speaking up improve resuscitation; multiple leaders and long pauses in compressions harm it.
opts: Repeating orders back to the leader
Having a leader assign clear roles
Speaking up when you see an error
Several people giving orders at once
Stopping compressions so everyone can check a pulse
ok: Repeating orders back to the leader
Having a leader assign clear roles
Speaking up when you see an error

qs.q: A patient with a valid DNR order is breathing and has a pulse. Which care can still be given? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Oxygen; Suctioning of the airway; Comfort positioning
qs.x: A DNR order limits resuscitation after arrest, but patients still receive oxygen, suctioning, comfort, and other supportive care.
opts: Oxygen
Suctioning of the airway
Comfort positioning
Chest compressions if he arrests
Defibrillation if he arrests
ok: Oxygen
Suctioning of the airway
Comfort positioning

qs.q: You are caring for a patient with an LVAD. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Call the VAD coordinator listed on the device; Bring the controller and spare batteries; Judge perfusion by mental status and skin
qs.x: LVAD patients need their equipment and the VAD team's guidance; perfusion is judged by mental status and skin, and a missing pulse alone does not mean arrest.
opts: Call the VAD coordinator listed on the device
Bring the controller and spare batteries
Judge perfusion by mental status and skin
Disconnect the pump to check for a pulse
Assume no palpable pulse means cardiac arrest
ok: Call the VAD coordinator listed on the device
Bring the controller and spare batteries

qs.q: A 59-year-old man has a BP of 224/132. Which findings indicate a hypertensive emergency rather than just high blood pressure? Select all that apply.
qs.a: New confusion; Blurred vision; Chest pain
qs.x: Severe hypertension becomes an emergency when it causes organ damage, shown by neurologic changes, vision problems, or chest pain.
opts: New confusion
Blurred vision
Chest pain
No symptoms at all
He missed one dose of his medication
ok: New confusion
Blurred vision
Chest pain

qs.q: Which features of a fainting episode suggest a dangerous cardiac cause? Select all that apply.
qs.a: It occurred during exercise; It happened without any warning; Palpitations just before fainting
qs.x: Exertional syncope, syncope without warning, and palpitations suggest a dysrhythmia or structural heart problem; triggered faints with warning signs are usually vasovagal.
opts: It occurred during exercise
It happened without any warning
Palpitations just before fainting
It followed the sight of a needle
It followed prolonged standing in the heat with nausea
ok: It occurred during exercise
It happened without any warning
Palpitations just before fainting

qs.q: A 30-year-old man fell 15 feet from a roof and is unresponsive. You hear gurgling with each breath, his right wrist is deformed, and there is no visible bleeding. After manually stabilizing his head, what should you do first?
qs.a: Suction the airway
qs.x: Gurgling means fluid in the airway, an immediate threat found in the primary survey; splinting, vital signs, and history all wait until airway, breathing, and circulation are managed.
w: Splint the deformed wrist before moving him onto the stretcher
Apply a cervical collar and secure him to a long backboard
Obtain a full set of baseline vital signs and a SAMPLE history

qs.q: During the assessment of a multisystem trauma patient, when should you perform a detailed secondary assessment and obtain a full SAMPLE history?
qs.a: After life threats from the primary survey are treated
qs.x: The primary survey finds and treats immediate life threats first; the secondary assessment and history follow, and in a critical patient they are often done en route.
w: Before any treatment, so care is based on complete information
Only after arrival at the receiving hospital
During scene size-up, before touching the patient

qs.q: A 22-year-old woman was thrown from a horse and is unresponsive with snoring respirations. You suspect a cervical spine injury. How should you open her airway?
qs.a: Jaw-thrust maneuver
qs.x: The jaw-thrust opens the airway while keeping the head and neck in line; if it fails to open the airway, a head-tilt may be needed because the airway takes priority.
w: Head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway before any manual maneuver
Turn her head to the side and sweep the mouth

qs.q: A 19-year-old cut his palm on broken glass while washing dishes. He is alert, the bleeding is controlled, and he has no other complaints. After the primary survey, what type of physical exam is most appropriate?
qs.a: A focused exam of the injured hand
qs.x: With no significant mechanism and an isolated injury, a focused exam of the affected area, including distal circulation, sensation, and movement, is appropriate.
w: A rapid head-to-toe trauma assessment with spinal motion restriction
A full detailed exam of every body region before transport
No physical exam, since the bleeding has stopped

qs.q: A 34-year-old man has heavy, life-threatening bleeding from a laceration in the middle of his lower leg. Where should the tourniquet be placed?
qs.a: 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over the knee
qs.x: When the wound location is clear, a tourniquet goes 2-3 inches above the wound and not over a joint; if the wound cannot be seen or located, place it high and tight on the limb.
w: Directly over the wound so it compresses the bleeding vessel
Over the knee joint to anchor it securely
On the upper thigh only, regardless of where the leg wound is

qs.q: A bystander applied a commercial tourniquet to a patient's arm 25 minutes before you arrived. The bleeding is controlled, but the patient complains of severe pain from the tourniquet. What should you do?
qs.a: Leave it in place and document the time it was applied
qs.x: A properly applied tourniquet that controls bleeding should not be loosened or removed in the field; tourniquet pain is expected, and the application time must be recorded.
w: Loosen it briefly to restore circulation and then retighten it
Remove it and replace it with a pressure dressing
Loosen it until the pain is tolerable to the patient

qs.q: A 26-year-old man has a deep laceration to the side of his neck with dark blood flowing from it. What is the most important dressing for this wound?
qs.a: An occlusive dressing held with direct pressure
qs.x: An open neck vein can draw in air and cause an air embolism, so cover it with an occlusive dressing and hold pressure; never wrap a bandage around the neck.
w: A circumferential pressure bandage wrapped snugly around the neck
A loose, moist sterile dressing taped on all sides
A tourniquet placed just below the wound

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman fell from a ladder and cannot move or feel her legs. Her blood pressure is 82/50, pulse 54, and her skin is warm, dry, and pink below the nipple line. What type of shock is most likely?
qs.a: Neurogenic shock
qs.x: A spinal cord injury can cause loss of sympathetic tone, producing hypotension with a normal or slow heart rate and warm, dry skin, unlike the tachycardia and pale, cool skin of hemorrhagic shock.
w: Hemorrhagic shock
Cardiogenic shock
Anaphylactic shock

qs.q: A 78-year-old man who takes a beta blocker fell down several stairs and complains of left upper abdominal pain. His pulse is 74, blood pressure 98/62, and his skin is pale and moist. How should you interpret his heart rate?
qs.a: It may not rise in shock because of his medication
qs.x: Beta blockers and aging blunt the normal tachycardia of shock, so an older adult can be bleeding significantly with a normal pulse; his pale, moist skin and low pressure point to shock.
w: It proves his blood loss is minimal
It indicates a heart attack rather than an injury
It is too slow and he needs CPR

qs.q: A 24-year-old man was stabbed in the left chest. He has distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, equal breath sounds, and a blood pressure of 76/58. What is the most appropriate EMT action?
qs.a: Rapid transport to a trauma center with ALS intercept if available
qs.x: Hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds with equal breath sounds suggest cardiac tamponade, which requires hospital treatment; EMTs treat it with rapid transport.
w: Seal the wound and wait on scene for a paramedic unit
Position him flat with legs raised and complete a full secondary exam on scene
Have him sit upright and breathe into a paper bag

qs.q: An unrestrained driver hit a tree head-on. The steering wheel is bent and the windshield has a starred spider-web break. Which injuries should you suspect? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Head and cervical spine injury; Blunt chest injury such as rib fractures or cardiac contusion; Knee, femur, or hip injury from striking the dash
qs.x: A frontal impact can send an unrestrained occupant up and over into the windshield (head and neck) and into the steering wheel (chest), or down and under into the dash (knees, femurs, hips); airbags do not rule out serious injury.
opts: Head and cervical spine injury
Blunt chest injury such as rib fractures or cardiac contusion
Knee, femur, or hip injury from striking the dash
No serious injury because the airbag deployed
Injuries limited to the side opposite the impact
ok: Head and cervical spine injury
Blunt chest injury such as rib fractures or cardiac contusion
Knee, femur, or hip injury from striking the dash

qs.q: A car was struck on the driver's door in a T-bone collision with significant intrusion. Which abdominal organ of the driver is most at risk?
qs.a: The spleen
qs.x: In a lateral impact, injuries occur on the side struck; for the driver in a left-side impact, the spleen, left ribs, and left pelvis are at highest risk.
w: The liver
The appendix
The bladder

qs.q: Under the 2021 National Guideline for Field Triage, which mechanisms of injury are considered high risk for serious injury? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Fall from a height greater than 10 feet; Partial or complete ejection from a vehicle; Pedestrian thrown or run over by a vehicle
qs.x: The 2021 guideline lists falls over 10 feet, ejection, and pedestrians or cyclists thrown, run over, or with significant impact as high-risk mechanisms that warrant trauma center transport.
opts: Fall from a height greater than 10 feet
Partial or complete ejection from a vehicle
Pedestrian thrown or run over by a vehicle
Fall from standing in an alert, healthy 30-year-old
Low-speed crash with a seat belt and no intrusion
ok: Fall from a height greater than 10 feet
Partial or complete ejection from a vehicle
Pedestrian thrown or run over by a vehicle

qs.q: A 35-year-old man with a head injury is becoming less responsive. Which findings suggest brain herniation? Select all that apply.
qs.a: One pupil dilated and not reactive to light; Extension posturing of the arms and legs; A falling Glasgow Coma Scale score
qs.x: A unilateral fixed, dilated pupil, posturing, and a declining GCS indicate rising pressure forcing the brain downward; bruising behind the ears and nasal fluid suggest a skull fracture but are not herniation signs.
opts: One pupil dilated and not reactive to light
Extension posturing of the arms and legs
A falling Glasgow Coma Scale score
Bruising behind the ears
Equal pupils that react briskly to light
Clear fluid draining from the nose
ok: One pupil dilated and not reactive to light
Extension posturing of the arms and legs
A falling Glasgow Coma Scale score

qs.q: A 40-year-old woman has a serious head injury after a fall. Which priority does the most to prevent further damage to her brain during your care?
qs.a: Preventing hypoxia and hypotension
qs.x: Even brief episodes of low oxygen or low blood pressure worsen outcomes after a brain injury; routine hyperventilation is harmful because it reduces blood flow to the brain.
w: Hyperventilating her at 30 breaths per minute as soon as possible
Keeping her flat with her legs elevated
Checking her blood glucose every 2 minutes

qs.q: Two hours after being struck in the head with a baseball bat, a 20-year-old man has bruising behind both ears. What does this finding suggest?
qs.a: A basilar skull fracture
qs.x: Bruising over the mastoid process behind the ear (Battle sign) is a delayed sign of a basilar skull fracture, often appearing hours after the injury.
w: An epidural hematoma
A cervical spine fracture
A fractured mandible

qs.q: A 17-year-old was hit in the side of the head by a baseball, briefly lost consciousness, then woke up talking normally. Twenty minutes later he becomes confused and drowsy. What injury does this pattern suggest?
qs.a: Epidural hematoma
qs.x: A brief loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval and then rapid decline is the classic pattern of an epidural hematoma, an arterial bleed that needs rapid transport.
w: Simple concussion with full recovery
Basilar skull fracture
Spinal cord injury

qs.q: After a crash, a 33-year-old man opens his eyes only to pain, makes incomprehensible sounds, and withdraws his hand from a painful stimulus. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
qs.x: Eye opening to pain is 2, incomprehensible sounds are 2, and withdrawal from pain is 4, for a total of 8.

qs.q: A 26-year-old was struck in the face with a nail gun. A nail passes completely through his cheek, and blood is draining into his mouth and threatening his airway. What should you do?
qs.a: Remove the nail and pack the inside of the cheek with gauze
qs.x: An object impaled in the cheek may be removed if it threatens the airway; then dress the outside and pack the inside of the cheek while managing the airway.
w: Stabilize the nail in place with bulky dressings on the outside only
Push the nail through into the mouth to clear the outside wound
Place him supine and suction only when he starts choking

qs.q: A 41-year-old carpenter has a small metal shard impaled in his right eye. How should you care for the eye?
qs.a: Stabilize the object with a cup and cover both eyes
qs.x: Impaled objects in the eye are stabilized, not removed; covering both eyes reduces sympathetic eye movement that could worsen the injury.
w: Remove the object gently and flush the eye with saline
Cover only the injured eye tightly with a pressure patch
Leave both eyes uncovered so he can see during transport

qs.q: A 36-year-old worker splashed a cleaning chemical into his left eye. How should you irrigate it?
qs.a: With water flowing from the inner corner outward
qs.x: Irrigate immediately and continuously, directing the flow from the inner corner outward so contaminated fluid does not wash into the other eye; do not delay to identify the chemical.
w: With water flowing from the outer corner toward the nose
With a few drops of saline every few minutes
Only after you identify the exact chemical

qs.q: A 23-year-old was struck across the front of the neck by a wire while riding a motorcycle. He is hoarse, and you feel a crackling sensation under the skin of his neck. What does this suggest?
qs.a: Possible laryngeal or tracheal injury that may compromise the airway
qs.x: Hoarseness and subcutaneous air after a blow to the neck suggest injury to the larynx or trachea, which can rapidly obstruct the airway.
w: A minor abrasion that needs only a dressing
A cervical spine injury with spinal cord damage
Normal swelling expected after any neck trauma

qs.q: A 31-year-old man was in a low-speed crash. He is alert, sober, has no neck pain or midline tenderness, no numbness or weakness, and no other painful injuries. Based on current national guidance, what is the most appropriate approach to spinal motion restriction?
qs.a: It is not needed for this patient
qs.x: Current joint guidance supports selective spinal motion restriction; an alert, sober patient with no spinal pain, tenderness, neurologic deficit, or distracting injury does not need it.
w: Apply a cervical collar and long backboard because he was in a crash
Apply a cervical collar only, since the mechanism alone requires it
Have him lie on the floor while you call for a backboard

qs.q: You are placing a 2-year-old on a firm, flat device for spinal motion restriction. What should you do to keep the spine in a neutral position?
qs.a: Pad beneath the shoulders and torso
qs.x: A young child's large head flexes the neck forward when lying flat, so padding under the shoulders and torso keeps the airway open and the spine neutral.
w: Place a folded towel under the back of the head
Tilt the head forward with the chin on the chest
Leave the child flat on the device with no padding

qs.q: A 29-year-old motorcyclist wearing a full-face helmet is vomiting and you cannot clear his airway with the helmet on. What should you do?
qs.a: Remove the helmet with two rescuers while keeping the head stable
qs.x: A helmet must be removed if it prevents airway management; two rescuers work together, one stabilizing the head and neck while the other removes the helmet.
w: Leave the helmet on and suction through the face opening only
Cut the chin strap and tilt the head back to drain the vomit
Have him remove the helmet himself while you hold suction ready

qs.q: An 86-year-old woman with a severely curved upper spine (kyphosis) needs spinal motion restriction after a fall. How should you position her?
qs.a: Pad behind her head and shoulders to support her natural curve
qs.x: Older adults with kyphosis cannot lie flat without forcing the spine out of its normal position, so padding fills the gaps and keeps them in a neutral, comfortable position.
w: Force her head back against the board so it lies flat
Place her prone on the stretcher to protect her airway
Secure her flat without padding to keep the spine straight

qs.q: A 21-year-old man dove into a shallow pool. His chest wall does not move as he breathes, but his abdomen rises and falls with each breath. What should you be prepared to do?
qs.a: Assist his ventilations
qs.x: Abdominal breathing without chest movement suggests a cervical spinal cord injury that paralyzes the intercostal muscles; breathing may quickly become inadequate.
w: Apply a pelvic binder
Place him in the recovery position
Give oral glucose

qs.q: A 64-year-old driver struck the steering wheel. A section of his right chest moves inward when he inhales and outward when he exhales. His breathing is shallow at 32 per minute with an SpO2 of 86 percent. What is the best treatment?
qs.a: Assist ventilations with a BVM and oxygen
qs.x: Paradoxical movement means a flail segment, and the underlying lung injury causes poor oxygenation; positive-pressure ventilation with a BVM supports breathing and stabilizes the segment from inside.
w: Tape a heavy sandbag over the moving segment
Wrap a bandage tightly around the entire chest
Place him on his left side and give oxygen by nasal cannula

qs.q: A 30-year-old man has a stab wound to the right chest. Air bubbles from the wound each time he breathes. What should you do first?
qs.a: Cover the wound with a gloved hand
qs.x: An open chest wound should be sealed immediately, first with a gloved hand and then with an occlusive dressing, to stop air from entering the chest.
w: Look for an exit wound on his back
Place him supine and elevate his legs
Apply a bulky gauze dressing with tape

qs.q: A 55-year-old man fell onto a railing and has no open wounds. He is increasingly short of breath with absent breath sounds on the left, distended neck veins, and falling blood pressure. What is the most appropriate EMT care?
qs.a: High-flow oxygen, assisted ventilations as needed, and rapid transport with ALS intercept
qs.x: These findings suggest a tension pneumothorax; needle decompression is outside EMT scope, so EMTs support oxygenation and ventilation and get the patient to definitive care quickly.
w: Insert a needle into the second intercostal space on the left side
Seal the left chest with an occlusive dressing
Keep him on scene until his breath sounds return

qs.q: After a fall, a 42-year-old man has diminished breath sounds on the right and signs of shock. Which finding suggests massive hemothorax rather than tension pneumothorax?
qs.a: Flat neck veins
qs.x: Both can cause decreased breath sounds and shock, but blood loss into the chest usually leaves the neck veins flat, while tension pneumothorax often distends them.
w: Absent breath sounds on the injured side
Rapid heart rate
Shortness of breath

qs.q: A 14-year-old baseball catcher is struck in the chest by a pitch and immediately collapses. He is unresponsive, not breathing, and pulseless. What should you do?
qs.a: Start CPR and apply an AED as soon as possible
qs.x: A blow directly over the heart at a vulnerable moment can trigger ventricular fibrillation (commotio cordis); immediate CPR and early defibrillation are lifesaving.
w: Apply high-flow oxygen and check for rib fractures
Assess for a tension pneumothorax and transport
Place him in the recovery position and monitor

qs.q: A 38-year-old man was pinned under a car for several minutes with heavy pressure on his chest. His face and neck are purple and swollen, with small red spots on the skin and bloodshot eyes. What injury does this suggest?
qs.a: Traumatic asphyxia
qs.x: Sudden severe chest compression forces blood back into the head and neck, producing the purple face, petechiae, and bloodshot eyes of traumatic asphyxia; associated chest injuries are common.
w: Smoke inhalation
An allergic reaction
A simple facial contusion

qs.q: A 33-year-old restrained driver has a red, bruised band across her lower abdomen from the lap belt. Her vital signs are normal and she says she feels fine. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Suspect an internal abdominal injury despite normal vital signs
qs.x: A seat belt sign is associated with injuries to the bowel, other abdominal organs, and the lumbar spine; patients can look stable early before shock develops.
w: A seat belt mark is expected and not concerning in a stable patient
Normal vital signs rule out internal bleeding
The injury is limited to the skin and needs only a cold pack

qs.q: Where should a pelvic binder be positioned to stabilize a suspected unstable pelvic fracture?
qs.a: Over the greater trochanters
qs.x: A pelvic binder centered over the greater trochanters (the bony points of the hips) best closes the pelvic ring; placing it too high is a common error.
w: Around the waist at the level of the navel
Just below the ribs
Around the upper thighs above the knees

qs.q: A 13-year-old fell off a skateboard and has a painful, deformed midshaft forearm. When splinting, which joints must be immobilized?
qs.a: The wrist and the elbow
qs.x: For a long bone fracture, splint the joint above and the joint below; for a midforearm fracture, that is the wrist and elbow.
w: The elbow and the shoulder
Only the wrist
Only the elbow

qs.q: A 25-year-old basketball player has a deformed, painful elbow after a fall. He has a strong radial pulse and normal sensation in his fingers. How should you splint it?
qs.a: In the position found
qs.x: Joint injuries with intact distal circulation are splinted in the position found because manipulation could injure nearby nerves and vessels.
w: Straighten the arm fully before splinting
Pull firmly on the forearm to reduce the joint
Apply a traction splint to the arm

qs.q: A 47-year-old man has a severely angulated midshaft fracture of the lower leg. His foot is cool and pale with no pulse. What should you do?
qs.a: Apply gentle manual traction to align the limb, then splint
qs.x: A long bone with absent distal circulation should be gently realigned to restore blood flow; stop if resistance or a large increase in pain occurs, then splint and reassess pulses.
w: Splint in the angulated position and transport immediately
Wrap the foot in a heat pack and recheck in 15 minutes
Elevate the leg and apply a tourniquet above the fracture

qs.q: A 24-year-old has a crushed lower leg from a motorcycle crash. Which findings suggest compartment syndrome? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Pain far greater than expected for the injury; Severe pain when the toes are passively stretched; A tense, firm swelling of the lower leg
qs.x: Compartment syndrome is rising pressure within a muscle compartment; early signs are pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, and tense swelling, while pulses may stay present until late.
opts: Pain far greater than expected for the injury
Severe pain when the toes are passively stretched
A tense, firm swelling of the lower leg
Crepitus at the fracture site
Bright red blood spurting from the wound
ok: Pain far greater than expected for the injury
Severe pain when the toes are passively stretched
A tense, firm swelling of the lower leg

qs.q: A 22-year-old fell on his outstretched arm. He holds his arm away from his body and will not let it move; the shoulder looks squared off. How should you splint it?
qs.a: Place a pillow between the arm and chest and secure with a sling and swathe
qs.x: An anterior shoulder dislocation is splinted in the position of comfort, often with a pillow filling the gap between arm and chest, then a sling and swathe.
w: Pull the arm down and in until it pops back into place
Straighten the arm against his side and tape it there
Apply a rigid splint from wrist to shoulder with the arm extended overhead

qs.q: You have applied a splint to a fractured forearm. Which steps are correct? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Check circulation, sensation, and movement before and after splinting; Pad the splint to fill gaps and protect the skin; Remove rings or watches from the injured limb
qs.x: Assess distal function before and after, pad the splint, and remove jewelry before swelling worsens; leave the fingertips exposed to monitor circulation.
opts: Check circulation, sensation, and movement before and after splinting
Pad the splint to fill gaps and protect the skin
Remove rings or watches from the injured limb
Apply the splint tightly enough to stop all finger movement
Leave the fingertips covered so they stay warm
ok: Check circulation, sensation, and movement before and after splinting
Pad the splint to fill gaps and protect the skin
Remove rings or watches from the injured limb

qs.q: A 10-month-old infant was scalded over the entire head and the entire front of the torso. Using the pediatric rule of nines, what percentage of body surface area is burned?
qs.a: 36 percent
qs.x: In infants the head is about 18 percent and the front of the torso is 18 percent, totaling 36 percent; the infant head is proportionally larger than an adult head.
w: 27 percent
18 percent
About 45 percent

qs.q: A 45-year-old man has partial- and full-thickness burns over 40 percent of his body. The burning process has been stopped. Which dressing is most appropriate?
qs.a: Dry, sterile dressings and blankets to keep him warm
qs.x: Large burns destroy the skin's ability to hold heat, so after cooling briefly, cover with dry sterile dressings and prevent hypothermia; ice and prolonged wet dressings over large areas cause harm.
w: Wet, cold towels over all burned areas for the entire transport
Burn ointment applied under occlusive plastic wrap
Ice packs placed directly on the burned skin

qs.q: A 52-year-old woman was rescued from a house fire. Which finding is most concerning for an airway burn that could rapidly obstruct her airway?
qs.a: Hoarse voice
qs.x: Hoarseness, along with soot in the mouth, singed nasal hair, and stridor, signals swelling of the upper airway that can progress quickly; early ALS and rapid transport are needed.
w: Burns to the backs of both hands
Pain in her lower legs
Smoke odor on her clothing

qs.q: A utility worker is still in contact with a downed power line and appears unresponsive. What should you do?
qs.a: Stay clear until the power company confirms the line is de-energized
qs.x: Never approach a patient in contact with an electrical source until trained personnel have confirmed it is safe; improvised tools and standard gloves do not protect from high voltage.
w: Use a dry wooden broom handle to push the wire away
Grab him by his clothing and pull him away quickly
Approach with rubber gloves and boots to assess his pulse

qs.q: A 30-year-old electrician received a high-voltage shock. He has small burns on his hand and foot and says he feels fine. What is your main concern?
qs.a: Hidden internal injury and abnormal heart rhythms
qs.x: Electrical current can damage deep tissues and the heart even when surface burns are small, so these patients need transport and monitoring for dysrhythmias.
w: Infection of the small skin burns
Dehydration from sweating
A sprained wrist from the fall

qs.q: Lightning strikes a group of hikers. Several are injured; one is pulseless and apneic while others are awake and moving. How should triage differ from a typical MCI?
qs.a: Treat the patient in cardiac arrest first
qs.x: Lightning victims in arrest often have a good chance of recovery with prompt CPR and ventilation, and those still conscious are likely to survive, so lightning triage reverses the usual priority.
w: Tag the pulseless patient as deceased and move on
Treat the awake and moving patients first
Wait for police before treating anyone

qs.q: A 2-year-old has sharply outlined burns covering both feet and ankles like socks, with no splash marks. The caregiver says the child stepped into a hot bath. What should you suspect?
qs.a: An intentional immersion burn
qs.x: Burns with sharp, uniform borders in a stocking or glove pattern without splash marks suggest forced immersion; document carefully and report suspected abuse as required.
w: An accidental scald from a spilled cup
A chemical burn from bath products
A contact burn from a heater

qs.q: A 44-year-old man has been stabbed in the back and is now in cardiac arrest. The knife is still in place and prevents you from placing him supine for compressions. What should you do?
qs.a: Remove the knife and begin CPR
qs.x: Impaled objects are normally stabilized, but one that prevents CPR may be removed, followed by bleeding control and high-quality compressions.
w: Perform CPR with him lying on his side
Stabilize the knife and delay CPR until arrival
Pad around the knife and compress with him prone

qs.q: A 37-year-old man caught his hand in a machine. The hand is nearly severed and remains attached only by a strip of skin. What should you do?
qs.a: Keep it attached, align it, and splint it
qs.x: A partial amputation should never be completed in the field; keep the part attached, align it in normal position, dress it, and splint it.
w: Complete the amputation and place the part on ice
Leave it hanging and apply a tourniquet to the forearm
Pull the hand into its normal position firmly

qs.q: A 50-year-old construction worker's leg has been pinned under a concrete slab for 5 hours. He is alert with stable vital signs. Before the slab is lifted, what should you do?
qs.a: Request ALS so treatment can begin before release
qs.x: Prolonged crush injury can release potassium and toxins into the circulation when pressure is removed, causing cardiac arrest; ALS care should begin before the release.
w: Lift the slab as quickly as possible and transport
Apply ice to the leg and wait another hour
Massage the leg to restore circulation

qs.q: Ten minutes after you applied a pressure bandage to a forearm laceration, the patient says his fingers are numb, cool, and tingling. What should you do?
qs.a: Loosen the bandage and reassess circulation
qs.x: New numbness, coolness, or tingling distal to a bandage suggests it is too tight; loosen it enough to restore circulation while maintaining bleeding control.
w: Tighten the bandage further to stop any residual bleeding
Apply a tourniquet above the bandage
Ignore it, since numbness is expected after a laceration

qs.q: A 34-week pregnant woman is secured supine to a long backboard after a crash. She becomes dizzy and her blood pressure falls to 86/54. What should you do?
qs.a: Tilt the board to her left or manually displace the uterus to the left
qs.x: The pregnant uterus can compress the inferior vena cava when the patient is supine, reducing blood return to the heart; tilting the board left or displacing the uterus relieves the pressure.
w: Raise her legs and lower her head
Remove her from the board and have her stand
Place her prone to take pressure off the uterus

qs.q: A 30-week pregnant woman was in a crash. She has a rigid, painful abdomen, dark vaginal bleeding, and signs of shock. What does this suggest?
qs.a: Placental abruption
qs.x: Separation of the placenta from the uterine wall causes abdominal pain, a rigid uterus, dark bleeding, and maternal shock; the fetus is at high risk.
w: Normal labor
Ectopic pregnancy
Urinary tract infection

qs.q: A 26-week pregnant woman was the restrained driver in a minor crash. She has no pain and normal vital signs and wants to go home. What is the most appropriate advice?
qs.a: She should be evaluated at the hospital because the fetus may be injured
qs.x: Pregnancy beyond 20 weeks is a special consideration in field triage; placental and fetal injury can occur without maternal symptoms, so she should be evaluated with fetal monitoring.
w: She can safely stay home since her vital signs are normal
She should only seek care if she notices bleeding in the next week
She should lie on her back at home and rest for 24 hours

qs.q: A 6-year-old was struck in the chest by a car's mirror. His ribs feel intact, but he is tachypneic and anxious. What is important to remember about children with chest trauma?
qs.a: Serious lung or heart injury can occur without rib fractures
qs.x: A child's ribs are flexible and transmit force to the organs beneath without breaking, so significant internal injury can be present with an intact chest wall.
w: Children rarely injure internal organs if the ribs are intact
Children compensate poorly, so vital signs drop immediately with injury
Rib fractures are more common in children than in adults

qs.q: What is the lowest acceptable systolic blood pressure for a 4-year-old child?
qs.a: 78 mmHg
qs.x: For children 1 to 10 years, the minimum systolic pressure is about 70 plus twice the age in years, which is 78 mmHg for a 4-year-old.
w: 70 mmHg
90 mmHg
100 mmHg

qs.q: A 74-year-old man was in a car crash. He is alert with a blood pressure of 104/70 and a pulse of 92. Under the 2021 field triage guideline, how should his blood pressure be interpreted?
qs.a: It meets high-risk criteria because it is below 110 in an older adult
qs.x: The 2021 guideline uses a systolic pressure below 110 mmHg as a high-risk criterion for adults 65 and older, since older adults may be in shock at pressures that look normal.
w: It is normal and does not affect destination
It only matters if his pulse is over 120
It meets criteria only if he becomes unresponsive

qs.q: Which factors are listed as special considerations that should lower your threshold for trauma center transport under the 2021 field triage guideline? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Taking an anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication; Pregnancy beyond 20 weeks; Burns combined with other trauma
qs.x: Anticoagulant use, pregnancy over 20 weeks, burns with trauma, low-level falls in older adults with head impact, and EMS provider judgment are among the special considerations; insurance and home location are not triage factors.
opts: Taking an anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication
Pregnancy beyond 20 weeks
Burns combined with other trauma
Patient insurance status
Distance from the patient's home
ok: Taking an anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication
Pregnancy beyond 20 weeks
Burns combined with other trauma

qs.q: A 31-year-old was near an explosion at a factory. He has no visible injuries but complains of ringing in his ears and shortness of breath. Which injury should you be most concerned about?
qs.a: Blast injury to the lungs
qs.x: The pressure wave of a blast damages air-filled organs such as the ears, lungs, and bowel; ear injury suggests the patient was exposed to enough pressure to injure the lungs.
w: Anxiety from witnessing the event
A minor ear infection
A simple muscle strain

qs.q: A 28-year-old was struck in the face with a bat. His left eye has been forced out of the socket and is hanging on the cheek. How should you manage it?
qs.a: Cover it with a moist dressing and a protective cup without pushing it back
qs.x: Never try to replace an extruded eye; protect it with a moist sterile dressing and a cup, and cover the other eye to reduce movement.
w: Gently push the eye back into the socket before covering it
Apply a firm pressure dressing over the eye
Leave it uncovered and have him keep both eyes open

qs.q: A 16-year-old was hit in the nose by a soccer ball. His nose is bleeding steadily, he is alert, and there is no concern for spinal injury. How should you position him?
qs.a: Sitting up and leaning forward while pinching the nostrils
qs.x: Leaning forward keeps blood from running down the throat, where it can be aspirated or cause vomiting; pinch the soft part of the nose with steady pressure.
w: Lying flat on his back with his head tilted back
Sitting with his head tilted back while pinching the bridge of the nose
Lying on his stomach with his face turned down

qs.q: A 72-year-old woman fell down stairs. Which statements about older trauma patients are true? Select all that apply.
qs.a: They may have serious injury from a relatively minor mechanism; Reduced pain perception can hide significant injuries; Brain atrophy increases the risk of bleeding inside the skull
qs.x: Fragile bones, reduced pain sensation, medications, and a shrinking brain that stretches bridging veins put older adults at higher risk, while blunted vital sign changes can hide shock.
opts: They may have serious injury from a relatively minor mechanism

Responsive to verbal stimulus

qs.q: A 56-year-old woman opens her eyes when you speak to her, answers questions but is confused about where she is, and follows your commands to squeeze your hand. What is her Glasgow Coma Scale score?
qs.x: Eye opening to voice scores 3, confused speech scores 4, and obeying commands scores 6, for a total of 13.

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman has vomited for 3 days. Lying down, her BP is 116/74 and pulse 86. When she sits up, she becomes lightheaded and her pulse rises to 118. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: She likely has significant volume loss
qs.x: A marked rise in heart rate with dizziness on sitting or standing suggests a low circulating volume, as seen with prolonged vomiting or bleeding.
w: This is a normal response to changing position
It shows that she is having an allergic reaction
It confirms that her dizziness is from an inner ear disorder

qs.q: From the doorway you see a 3-year-old boy who is limp and not interacting with his mother. His breathing appears quiet and unlabored, but his skin is pale and mottled. What does this general impression suggest?
qs.a: He is critically ill, likely in shock
qs.x: Abnormal appearance combined with abnormal circulation to the skin on the Pediatric Assessment Triangle indicates shock and a critically ill child.
w: He has respiratory distress that is well compensated
He has an isolated breathing problem from a partial airway obstruction
He is stable, so a slower, detailed assessment is acceptable

qs.q: A 4-year-old girl is drowsy and not tracking your movements. Her breathing is quiet and unlabored, and her skin color is normal. Using the Pediatric Assessment Triangle, which problem is most likely?
qs.a: A brain dysfunction such as a toxin, low glucose, or head injury
qs.x: Abnormal appearance with normal work of breathing and normal circulation points to a primary brain or metabolic problem, such as hypoglycemia, poisoning, or head injury.
w: Compensated shock from fluid loss
Upper airway obstruction from a foreign body
Lower airway disease such as asthma or bronchiolitis

qs.q: You are forming a general impression of a 2-year-old using the Pediatric Assessment Triangle. Which findings indicate increased work of breathing? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Nasal flaring; Retractions between the ribs; Head bobbing with each breath
qs.x: Nasal flaring, retractions, and head bobbing are signs of increased work of breathing; skin color reflects circulation and playfulness reflects normal appearance.
opts: Nasal flaring
Retractions between the ribs
Head bobbing with each breath
Pink skin with brisk capillary refill
Playing with a toy while sitting on a parent's lap
ok: Nasal flaring
Retractions between the ribs
Head bobbing with each breath

qs.q: A calm, content 6-month-old has a resting heart rate of 140/min and a respiratory rate of 40/min. How should you interpret these vital signs?
qs.a: They are within normal limits for an infant
qs.x: Normal infant heart rates are roughly 100-160/min and respiratory rates roughly 30-60/min, so these values are expected.
w: Both indicate early compensated shock
The heart rate is normal but the respiratory rate shows distress
Both are too slow and suggest hypoxia

qs.q: A 47-year-old woman with a medical complaint is awake and able to answer questions. After the primary assessment, what is usually the next step?
qs.a: Obtain the history of the present illness and SAMPLE history
qs.x: For a responsive medical patient, the history guides the exam, so the history of present illness and SAMPLE history come before the focused secondary assessment.
w: Perform a rapid head-to-toe trauma assessment before speaking with her
Obtain a full set of baseline vital signs before asking any questions
Transport immediately and defer all history to the hospital staff

qs.q: You find a 60-year-old man unresponsive on his kitchen floor with no signs of trauma. His airway is open and breathing is adequate. What is the most appropriate approach to the secondary assessment?
qs.a: Rapid full-body exam, then history from bystanders
qs.x: An unresponsive medical patient cannot give a history, so a rapid full-body exam is done first, followed by information from family, bystanders, and the scene.
