Begin ventilation if apneic or the heart rate is below 100

qs.q: Which sounds indicate a partial upper airway obstruction? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Snoring; Gurgling; Stridor
qs.x: Snoring suggests the tongue, gurgling suggests fluid and stridor suggests narrowing of the upper airway. Normal speech and quiet, easy breathing indicate an open airway.
opts: Snoring
Gurgling
Stridor
Clear speech in full sentences
Quiet, unlabored breathing
ok: Snoring
Gurgling
Stridor

qs.q: You have placed a supraglottic airway in an adult. Which actions help keep it working during care? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Secure the device and note its position marker; Monitor continuous waveform capnography; Reassess after every patient move
qs.x: Securing the device, continuous capnography and reassessment after moves catch displacement early. Overinflating the cuff and rapid ventilation cause harm.
opts: Secure the device and note its position marker
Monitor continuous waveform capnography
Reassess after every patient move
Add air to the cuff whenever breath sounds change
Ventilate as fast as possible to maintain oxygenation
ok: Secure the device and note its position marker
Monitor continuous waveform capnography
Reassess after every patient move

qs.q: Four rescuers are working an adult cardiac arrest. How often should the person doing compressions be changed?
qs.a: About every 2 minutes
qs.x: Compression quality declines with fatigue even before rescuers notice it, so compressors switch about every 2 minutes, usually during the rhythm analysis.
w: Every 30 seconds
Every 5 minutes
Only when the compressor says they are tired

qs.q: During CPR on an adult with a supraglottic airway, the ETCO2 reads 8 mmHg. What does this most likely mean?
qs.a: Compressions are not producing enough blood flow
qs.x: An ETCO2 below about 10 mmHg during CPR suggests poor cardiac output from compressions. Check depth, rate, recoil and rescuer fatigue, as well as airway placement.
w: The patient has return of spontaneous circulation
The ventilation rate is too slow
The supraglottic airway is in perfect position

qs.q: While you perform CPR on a 63-year-old man, the ETCO2 suddenly rises from 16 to 44 mmHg and stays there. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: Return of spontaneous circulation
qs.x: An abrupt, sustained rise in ETCO2 during CPR usually means return of circulation, as blood flow delivers more carbon dioxide to the lungs. Check for a pulse at the next planned pause.
w: The compressor is pushing too hard
The supraglottic airway is in the esophagus
The patient is being hyperventilated

qs.q: What chest compression fraction should a resuscitation team aim for at a minimum?
qs.a: At least 60 percent of the resuscitation
qs.x: Compressions should occur during at least 60 percent of the resuscitation, with higher fractions being better. Minimizing pauses for airway placement, rhythm analysis and moves raises the fraction.
w: At least 20 percent of the resuscitation
Exactly 50 percent so ventilations get equal time
At least 30 percent when an advanced airway is in place

qs.q: Your team is working a witnessed adult cardiac arrest. Which should take priority over placing a supraglottic airway?
qs.a: High-quality compressions and early defibrillation
qs.x: Compressions and defibrillation have the greatest effect on survival from cardiac arrest. An advanced airway can be placed when it will not interrupt or delay them.
w: Starting an IV before any other intervention
Obtaining and transmitting a 12-lead ECG to the receiving hospital
Moving the patient to the ambulance

qs.q: Which rhythm will an AED recognize as shockable?
qs.a: Ventricular fibrillation
qs.x: AEDs shock ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Asystole and PEA are not shockable and are treated with CPR and finding reversible causes.
w: Asystole
Pulseless electrical activity
Sinus bradycardia

qs.q: An AED advises no shock for a pulseless, apneic 74-year-old man. What does this tell you about his rhythm?
qs.a: It is a nonshockable rhythm such as asystole or PEA
qs.x: A no shock message in a pulseless patient means the AED did not detect VF or VT, so the rhythm is likely asystole or PEA. CPR continues immediately.
w: He has a perfusing rhythm and needs no further CPR
The AED is malfunctioning and should be replaced
He is in ventricular fibrillation that is too fine to shock

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman in cardiac arrest has a bulge under the skin below her left collarbone from an implanted pacemaker. How should you place the AED pads?
qs.a: Avoid placing a pad directly over the device
qs.x: Pads are placed at least about an inch away from an implanted device so the shock is not blocked and the device is not damaged. Defibrillation should not be delayed.
w: Place one pad directly over the device
Do not use the AED in patients with pacemakers
Place both pads on her back

qs.q: A woman who appears about 30 weeks pregnant is in cardiac arrest. What should one rescuer do while another performs compressions?
qs.a: Manually displace the uterus to her left
qs.x: Manual left uterine displacement relieves pressure on the inferior vena cava so compressions produce better blood flow. High-quality CPR continues uninterrupted on a firm, flat surface.
w: Tilt her head to the right to open the airway
Hold compressions until she is placed on her left side
Elevate her legs to improve venous return

qs.q: Two rescuers are performing CPR on a 4-month-old in cardiac arrest. Which compression technique is preferred?
qs.a: Two-thumb encircling hands
qs.x: For two-rescuer infant CPR, the two-thumb encircling hands technique is preferred because it produces better depth and blood flow. The two-finger method is no longer recommended.
w: Two fingers in the center of the chest
Heel of two hands stacked on the sternum
One finger on the lower sternum

qs.q: How deep should compressions be for a 5-year-old child in cardiac arrest?
qs.a: About 2 inches
qs.x: Child compressions should be at least one third of the chest depth, about 2 inches. Infants need about 1.5 inches.
w: About 1 inch
At least 3 inches
About half an inch

qs.q: After ROSC, a 64-year-old man remains unresponsive and is being ventilated through a supraglottic airway. What oxygen saturation should you target?
qs.a: 92 to 98 percent
qs.x: After cardiac arrest, both hypoxia and excessive oxygen are harmful, so oxygen is titrated to about 92 to 98 percent once a reliable reading is available.
w: 100 percent
85 to 90 percent
Any reading above 80 percent

qs.q: A 55-year-old has ROSC after a witnessed VF arrest. His BP is 112/70 and ventilation is controlled. Why should you obtain a 12-lead ECG?
qs.a: To identify a STEMI that needs an interventional center
qs.x: Many cardiac arrests are caused by coronary occlusion, and a 12-lead after ROSC can identify a STEMI so the patient goes to a center that can open the artery.
w: To confirm that he no longer needs ventilation
To decide whether to stop monitoring capnography
To determine whether he needs another shock from the AED in the next few minutes

qs.q: A 59-year-old man has chest pressure and diaphoresis. Within how many minutes of first contact should you acquire a 12-lead ECG?
qs.a: 10 minutes
qs.x: A 12-lead should be obtained within about 10 minutes of first contact in suspected ACS so a STEMI can be identified early and the receiving center notified.
w: 30 minutes
60 minutes
Only after arrival at the hospital

qs.q: Where should the V1 electrode be placed when acquiring a 12-lead ECG?
qs.a: Fourth intercostal space at the right edge of the sternum
qs.x: V1 is placed in the fourth intercostal space just to the right of the sternum, and V2 mirrors it on the left. Misplaced chest leads can mimic or hide ischemic changes.
w: Fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line
Second intercostal space at the left edge of the sternum, just below the collarbone
Fifth intercostal space at the left midaxillary line

qs.q: You have acquired a 12-lead ECG for a 62-year-old with chest pain that the monitor interprets as acute MI. What is the main benefit of transmitting it to the receiving hospital?
qs.a: The cardiac cath lab can be activated before arrival
qs.x: Transmitting the 12-lead lets the hospital activate the cath lab early, which shortens the time to reperfusion. You still give a radio report and keep reassessing the patient.
w: It allows you to give medications outside your scope
It removes the need for a radio report
It lets you skip reassessment of vital signs

qs.q: A 66-year-old has chest pain, and the receiving physician reports an inferior STEMI with likely right ventricular involvement. His BP is 94/62 and his lungs are clear. What is the correct approach to nitroglycerin?
qs.a: Withhold it
qs.x: Right ventricular infarction makes the heart dependent on preload, and nitroglycerin can cause sudden severe hypotension. With a borderline BP and suspected RV involvement, nitroglycerin is withheld.
w: Give it every 2 minutes until the pain resolves
Give a double dose to open the artery faster
Give it only if he becomes hypotensive

qs.q: A 71-year-old woman has sudden right-sided paralysis, inability to speak and her eyes deviated to the left. She was last known well 90 minutes ago. Which destination is generally preferred?
qs.a: A stroke center that can perform thrombectomy, per regional protocol
qs.x: Severe deficits such as dense weakness, aphasia and gaze deviation suggest a large vessel occlusion that may need clot removal. Regional protocols often route these patients to a thrombectomy-capable center when transport time allows.
w: The closest hospital regardless of its stroke capabilities
Any trauma center
A primary care clinic for a neurology referral

qs.q: A 69-year-old man has new left-sided weakness and a BP of 206/112. Which approach to his blood pressure is correct in the field?
qs.a: Monitor it and transport without trying to lower it
qs.x: Elevated blood pressure may be maintaining blood flow to the brain after a stroke. Prehospital providers monitor and report it rather than lowering it.
w: Lower it quickly with nitroglycerin to reduce the risk of bleeding into the brain
Give a fluid bolus to bring it down
Lay him flat with his legs raised to reduce it

qs.q: A 74-year-old woman with slurred speech and facial droop asks for a drink of water. What should you do?
qs.a: Give nothing by mouth
qs.x: Stroke often impairs swallowing, so patients are kept from eating or drinking until a swallow screen is done. This prevents aspiration.
w: Give small sips through a straw
Give water only if her glucose is normal
Give a full glass to prevent dehydration

qs.q: A 62-year-old man woke at 0600 with right arm weakness. He went to bed at 2300 the night before feeling normal. What is his last known well time?
qs.x: When symptoms are found on waking, the last known well time is when the patient was last seen normal, usually bedtime. This time drives treatment eligibility.
w: The time EMS was called
The time you arrived on scene

qs.q: Which stroke screening tool adds balance and eye findings to face, arm and speech checks?
qs.a: BE-FAST
qs.x: BE-FAST adds balance loss and vision changes to the face, arm, speech and time elements, which helps detect strokes in the back of the brain that can be missed by face, arm and speech checks alone.
w: Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale
Glasgow Coma Scale
SAMPLE history

qs.q: A 67-year-old had 20 minutes of left arm weakness and slurred speech that has completely resolved. He now feels fine and does not want to go to the hospital. What should you advise?
qs.a: He needs evaluation today because his stroke risk is high
qs.x: A transient ischemic attack is a warning sign, and the risk of stroke is highest in the hours and days that follow. Urge prompt evaluation and document an informed refusal if he still declines.
w: He can safely follow up with his primary care doctor in a few weeks if nothing recurs
No evaluation is needed because symptoms resolved
He should take a nap and call back if symptoms return

qs.q: An 80-year-old man who takes metoprolol has been vomiting blood. He is pale and diaphoretic with a BP of 82/50 and a pulse of 72. Why is his heart rate not elevated?
qs.a: His beta-blocker blunts the normal tachycardia of shock
qs.x: Beta-blockers prevent the expected compensatory tachycardia, so a normal heart rate can hide significant shock. Rely on blood pressure, skin signs and mental status.
w: He has lost too little blood to cause shock
Older adults always have slower heart rates in shock
Vomiting raises vagal tone and permanently slows the heart

qs.q: Which IV fluid is an isotonic crystalloid suitable for volume replacement?
qs.a: Lactated Ringer's solution
qs.x: Lactated Ringer's and normal saline are isotonic crystalloids that stay in the vascular space long enough for volume replacement. D5W behaves like free water once the sugar is used, and D50 is a concentrated glucose solution.
w: Dextrose 5 percent in water
0.45 percent sodium chloride
Dextrose 50 percent

qs.q: A 78-year-old has a cough with yellow sputum, a fever of 38.9 C (102 F), crackles only over the right lower lobe and no leg swelling. What is the most likely cause of his dyspnea?
qs.a: Pneumonia
qs.x: Fever, productive cough and localized crackles point to pneumonia. Heart failure more often produces bilateral crackles, orthopnea, edema and distended neck veins.
w: Left-sided heart failure
Pulmonary embolism
Asthma

qs.q: A 72-year-old has dyspnea and crackles. Which finding most strongly favors heart failure over pneumonia?
qs.a: Distended neck veins with pitting ankle edema
qs.x: Distended neck veins and pitting edema reflect fluid overload from heart failure. Fever, purulent sputum and localized crackles suggest infection.
w: A temperature of 38.6 C (101.5 F)
Productive cough with green sputum
Crackles heard only over one lobe

qs.q: A 51-year-old man has a severe headache, vomiting and confusion with a BP of 232/134. What makes this a hypertensive emergency?
qs.a: Signs of organ damage along with the high blood pressure
qs.x: A hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension with evidence of acute organ damage, such as confusion, chest pain or pulmonary edema. A high reading without symptoms is not an emergency in itself.
w: The systolic pressure being above 180 mmHg alone
The headache starting slowly over a few days
The patient having a long history of poorly controlled high blood pressure

qs.q: A woman who gave birth 6 days ago has a severe headache, blurred vision and a BP of 168/110. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Postpartum preeclampsia
qs.x: Preeclampsia can develop or worsen up to several weeks after delivery. Severe headache, visual changes and high blood pressure require prompt transport, and seizures may occur.
w: Normal postpartum recovery
Migraine caused by sleep loss
Postpartum depression

qs.q: A 24-year-old was stabbed in the left chest. He has a BP of 78/60, distended neck veins and heart sounds that are hard to hear. Breath sounds are equal. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Cardiac tamponade
qs.x: Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds form Beck's triad of tamponade. Equal breath sounds make tension pneumothorax less likely.
w: Tension pneumothorax
Hypovolemic shock from a liver injury
Neurogenic shock

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman with lung cancer has increasing dyspnea, a BP of 86/70, distended neck veins and a radial pulse that weakens noticeably each time she inhales. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Pericardial tamponade
qs.x: Cancer can cause fluid around the heart, and a narrow pulse pressure, distended neck veins and a pulse that weakens on inspiration point to tamponade. She needs rapid transport for drainage.
w: Community-acquired pneumonia
Anxiety attack
Asthma exacerbation

qs.q: A 76-year-old man is dizzy with a heart rate of 36, a BP of 74/40 and cool skin. Within AEMT scope, what is the most appropriate care?
qs.a: Oxygen if needed, supine positioning and rapid transport or ALS intercept
qs.x: An adult with symptomatic bradycardia and a pulse needs supportive care and rapid access to pacing or medications. Adult compressions are for pulseless patients.
w: Chest compressions because his heart rate is below 60 beats per minute
Have him bear down to increase the heart rate
Withhold any treatment until a 12-lead is reviewed

qs.q: A 70-year-old man has sudden severe back pain, a pulsating mass in his abdomen, a BP of 82/50 and pale, clammy skin. What is the most appropriate management?
qs.a: Rapid transport with small fluid boluses to keep a radial pulse
qs.x: A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm needs surgery quickly, and permissive hypotension avoids increasing the bleeding. Avoid deep palpation of the mass.
w: Palpate the mass firmly to estimate its size
Give large, rapid fluid boluses to bring the systolic BP above 140 mmHg before transport
Delay transport until the pain is controlled

qs.q: A 4-year-old with fever and vomiting has a capillary refill of 4 seconds, a heart rate of 164 and a BP of 70/40. How should you interpret the blood pressure?
qs.a: It indicates decompensated shock
qs.x: The lower limit of systolic pressure for a child aged 1 to 10 is about 70 plus twice the age in years, which is 78 for a 4-year-old. Hypotension in a child is a late sign of decompensated shock.
w: It is normal for a child of this age
It indicates compensated shock
It shows that the child is dehydrated but not in shock

qs.q: A 15-year-old baseball catcher is struck in the chest by a pitch and collapses. He is pulseless and apneic. What is the priority?
qs.a: Immediate CPR and use of an AED
qs.x: A blow to the chest at a critical moment of the cardiac cycle can trigger ventricular fibrillation. Immediate CPR and early defibrillation give the best chance of survival.
w: Spinal immobilization before any other care
Cold packs over the chest
A full secondary assessment

qs.q: A 63-year-old has a STEMI on the 12-lead, a BP of 132/84 and an SpO2 of 97 percent on room air. What is the correct approach to oxygen?
qs.a: Withhold supplemental oxygen and monitor saturation
qs.x: In ACS, oxygen is given when the saturation is below about 90 to 94 percent or the patient is short of breath. Routine oxygen for patients with normal saturation has no benefit.

Give oxygen by nasal cannula at 6 L/min
Give oxygen by BVM at a fast rate to improve coronary blood flow and limit infarct size

qs.q: Which actions are correct during team CPR on an adult with a supraglottic airway? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Switch compressors about every 2 minutes; Give 1 breath every 6 seconds without pausing compressions; Keep pauses for rhythm analysis under 10 seconds
qs.x: With an advanced airway, compressions continue nonstop and breaths are given every 6 seconds. Rescuers switch every 2 minutes and keep pauses brief and infrequent.
opts: Switch compressors about every 2 minutes
Give 1 breath every 6 seconds without pausing compressions
Keep pauses for rhythm analysis under 10 seconds
Pause compressions for each ventilation
Stop CPR to check for a pulse every minute
ok: Switch compressors about every 2 minutes
Give 1 breath every 6 seconds without pausing compressions
Keep pauses for rhythm analysis under 10 seconds

qs.q: Which actions are appropriate after return of spontaneous circulation? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Avoid hyperventilation; Obtain a 12-lead ECG; Treat hypotension with fluids per protocol
qs.x: Post-arrest care focuses on normal ventilation, adequate blood pressure, titrated oxygen and finding STEMI. Unresponsive patients still need their airway protected.
opts: Avoid hyperventilation
Obtain a 12-lead ECG
Treat hypotension with fluids per protocol
Keep the SpO2 at 100 percent at all times
Remove the supraglottic airway even if the patient remains unresponsive
ok: Avoid hyperventilation
Obtain a 12-lead ECG
Treat hypotension with fluids per protocol

qs.q: Which are classic findings of cardiac tamponade? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hypotension; Distended neck veins; Muffled heart sounds
qs.x: Beck's triad of hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds suggests tamponade. One-sided absent breath sounds suggest pneumothorax, and hypertension with bradycardia suggests rising intracranial pressure.

Distended neck veins
Muffled heart sounds
Absent breath sounds on one side
Hypertension with bradycardia
ok: Hypotension
Distended neck veins
Muffled heart sounds

Cardiac tamponade
Sepsis
Gastrointestinal bleeding
Spinal cord injury
ok: Tension pneumothorax
Massive pulmonary embolism

qs.q: A 56-year-old has a BP of 228/130. Which findings indicate a hypertensive emergency? Select all that apply.
qs.a: New confusion; Chest pain; Crackles with severe dyspnea
qs.x: Severe hypertension with signs of organ damage, such as altered mental status, chest pain or pulmonary edema, is an emergency. A high reading without symptoms is managed less urgently.

Crackles with severe dyspnea
No symptoms at all
Mild anxiety about the reading
ok: New confusion
Chest pain
Crackles with severe dyspnea

qs.q: Which practices improve the quality of a prehospital 12-lead ECG? Select all that apply.

Place electrodes over clothing to save time
Acquire the tracing during a bumpy ride
ok: Have the patient lie still and relaxed
Clean, dry and shave the skin as needed
Place chest leads by counting intercostal spaces

qs.q: Which findings favor pneumonia over heart failure as the cause of dyspnea? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Fever and chills; Productive cough; Localized crackles over one area
qs.x: Fever, productive cough and localized crackles suggest infection. Distended neck veins and bilateral leg edema reflect fluid overload from heart failure.
opts: Fever and chills
Productive cough
Localized crackles over one area
Distended neck veins
Pitting edema of both legs
ok: Fever and chills
Productive cough
Localized crackles over one area

qs.q: Which findings suggest a large vessel occlusion stroke? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Eyes deviated to one side; Inability to speak or understand speech; Dense weakness of one side of the body
qs.x: Gaze deviation, aphasia and dense hemiparesis suggest a large vessel blockage that may benefit from thrombectomy. Brief mild dizziness and localized fingertip numbness are not typical.
opts: Eyes deviated to one side

Dense weakness of one side of the body
Isolated mild dizziness that resolves with rest
Numbness of one fingertip after typing
ok: Eyes deviated to one side
Inability to speak or understand speech
Dense weakness of one side of the body

qs.q: Which actions are appropriate for a patient with suspected acute stroke? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Check the blood glucose; Determine the time last known well; Notify the receiving hospital early

Notify the receiving hospital early

Give food or drink to prevent hypoglycemia
ok: Check the blood glucose

qs.q: You are preparing to start an IV and have cleansed the site with chlorhexidine. What should you do before puncturing the skin?
qs.a: Let the antiseptic dry completely

Wipe the antiseptic off with sterile gauze
Palpate the vein again with an ungloved finger

qs.q: You have just withdrawn the needle after placing an IV catheter. What should you do with the needle?
qs.a: Place it in a sharps container immediately
qs.x: Used sharps go straight into a sharps container at the point of use. Recapping, setting needles down or passing them by hand causes needlestick injuries.
w: Recap it with two hands and dispose of it later
Lay it on the stretcher until the line is secured
Hand it to your partner to dispose of

qs.q: You stick yourself with a used IV needle while caring for a patient. Patient care has been handed off. What should you do first?
qs.a: Wash the area with soap and water
qs.x: Wash the site with soap and water right away and then report the exposure immediately so post-exposure evaluation can begin promptly. Some preventive treatments work best when started within hours.
w: Squeeze the wound and apply bleach
Finish your shift and report it if you feel sick
Ask the patient whether they have any infections and decide based on that

qs.q: You have trouble threading an IV catheter. Why must you never reinsert the needle into the catheter?
qs.a: The needle can shear off part of the catheter
qs.x: Pushing the needle back into the catheter can cut off a fragment that travels to the heart or lungs as an embolus. Withdraw both together and use a new catheter.
w: It will make the catheter too stiff to thread
It will cause the flash chamber to fill with air
It will make the catheter kink at the hub

qs.q: Which step is most important to prevent an air embolism when setting up an IV line?
qs.a: Flush all air out of the tubing before connecting it
qs.x: Air in the tubing can enter the vein and cause an embolism, so the line is primed fully before it is connected. The bag is hung above the patient to allow gravity flow.
w: Use the largest catheter available
Keep the bag below the level of the patient so air rises out of the line
Leave the roller clamp fully open during setup

qs.q: Your partner hands you a vial of dextrose to give an unresponsive hypoglycemic patient. What should you do before giving it?
qs.a: Check the name, concentration and expiration date aloud
qs.x: Checking the medication name, concentration and expiration date, and confirming them aloud with your partner, prevents medication errors. Errors are more likely when the situation is urgent.
w: Give it right away because time is critical
Smell the solution to confirm it is dextrose
Assume it is correct because your partner prepared it and is also a certified provider

qs.q: Online medical control orders 0.4 mg of naloxone IN for an opioid overdose. What should you do next?
qs.a: Repeat the order back to confirm it
qs.x: Repeating an order back confirms the drug, dose and route and allows the physician to correct any misunderstanding before the drug is given.
w: Give it and report afterward
Ask your partner to remember the order
Give twice the dose to make sure it works

qs.x: You are responsible for the medications you administer, so questionable orders must be clarified. Changing a dose without telling medical control is not acceptable.
w: Give the dose because the physician is responsible
Refuse to give any medications to this patient
Give half the ordered dose without telling the physician, then document the change

qs.q: A 58-year-old diabetic man has a blood glucose of 34 mg/dL and is confused and combative. He tells you to leave. What is the most appropriate approach?
qs.a: Treat him because he lacks decision-making capacity
qs.x: A patient whose confusion is caused by hypoglycemia cannot make an informed decision, so care proceeds under implied consent. Once alert, he can make his own decision about transport.
w: Leave because he has refused care
Get his refusal signature before treating
Call his family to obtain consent first

qs.q: At a bus crash, a 7-year-old cannot walk and is not breathing even after you reposition the airway. She has a palpable pulse. Using JumpSTART, what should you do?
qs.a: Give 5 rescue breaths and reassess
qs.x: In JumpSTART, a child who is apneic after repositioning but has a pulse gets 5 rescue breaths. If breathing starts, she is immediate, and if not, she is expectant or deceased.
w: Tag her as deceased and move on to the next patient without further intervention
Tag her as delayed
Begin CPR and stay with her

qs.q: Using START, how should you triage an adult who cannot walk, is breathing 24 times per minute, has a radial pulse and cannot follow simple commands?
qs.a: Immediate
qs.x: An adult who cannot follow simple commands is triaged as immediate even if breathing and perfusion are adequate.
w: Delayed
Minor
Expectant

qs.q: Using SALT triage, an adult does not breathe after you open the airway. How is he categorized?
qs.a: Dead
qs.x: In SALT, an adult who remains apneic after the airway is opened is categorized as dead. For children, 2 rescue breaths are considered before making this decision.
w: Immediate
Expectant
Delayed

qs.q: You see a placard with a four-digit number on an overturned tanker truck. What resource should you use to identify the hazard and initial safety distances?
qs.a: The Emergency Response Guidebook
qs.x: The Emergency Response Guidebook links the four-digit UN number to a guide page with hazards, isolation distances and first aid measures.
w: The patient care report
The local street map
Your service's drug reference

qs.q: At a hazardous materials incident, where should EMS provide patient care?
qs.a: In the cold zone after decontamination
qs.x: EMS personnel without specialized training and protective equipment treat patients in the cold zone after decontamination is completed in the warm zone.
w: In the hot zone where the release occurred
In the warm zone before decontamination
Wherever the patient was found

qs.q: You are dispatched to a radiation incident. Which principle best limits your exposure?
qs.a: Time, distance and shielding
qs.x: Reducing time near the source, increasing distance and using shielding all reduce radiation exposure. Respirators and gloves help with contamination but not with exposure.
w: Wearing an N95 respirator
Wearing two pairs of gloves
Working closer to finish faster

qs.q: You are giving a radio report to the receiving hospital. Which practice is correct?
qs.a: Use plain language and keep the report brief
qs.x: Plain language prevents confusion, and patient identifiers are not given over the radio. Pause a moment after pressing the button so the first words are not cut off.
w: Use the patient's full name and address
Start talking as soon as you press the button
Use your service's internal codes

qs.q: Which disclosure of patient information is permitted without the patient's written authorization?
qs.a: Giving report to the receiving nurse for treatment
qs.x: Privacy laws allow sharing of protected health information with other providers involved in the patient's treatment. Other disclosures need authorization or a specific legal exception.
w: Posting a photo of the scene on social media
Discussing the call with your neighbor by name
Telling the patient's employer about the injury

qs.q: You are driving to a call with lights and siren and approach a red light. What should you do?

qs.x: Laws allow emergency vehicles to proceed through red lights only with due regard for others. Stopping and making sure every lane has yielded prevents intersection crashes.

Slow slightly and go through without looking
Turn off the siren and proceed through the intersection at the posted speed limit

qs.q: You are first on scene at a crash on a busy highway, and a fire engine is positioned behind the wreck to block traffic. Where should you generally park the ambulance?
qs.a: Beyond the crash, protected by the blocking vehicle
qs.x: The fire engine shields the work area, and parking the ambulance beyond the scene keeps the loading area protected from traffic. Crews should also wear high-visibility vests.
w: In the lane behind the fire engine
Between the fire engine and the wrecked vehicles
In the opposite lane facing traffic

qs.q: You need to back the ambulance into a narrow driveway at night. What is the safest practice?
qs.a: Use a spotter at the rear of the vehicle
qs.x: A spotter standing behind the vehicle and in view of the driver's mirror prevents most backing collisions. Cameras have blind spots.
w: Rely on the backup camera alone
Back up quickly to limit time in the street
Turn on the siren to warn people

qs.q: You arrive at a domestic disturbance. As you start care, a man begins shouting threats and reaching into his pocket. What should you do?
qs.a: Leave the scene and wait for law enforcement
qs.x: Crew safety comes first. If the scene becomes unsafe, retreat to a safe location and request law enforcement before returning.
w: Continue treating the patient and ignore him
Calmly approach him and try to take whatever is in his pocket before he can use it
Restrain him with your partner

qs.q: You transported a patient with diarrhea caused by Clostridioides difficile. Which hand hygiene method is best?
qs.a: Washing with soap and water
qs.x: Alcohol-based sanitizers do not kill C. difficile spores, so hands are washed with soap and running water to remove them mechanically.
w: Alcohol-based hand sanitizer
Wiping hands with a disinfectant cloth
Rinsing gloved hands with water

qs.q: A bystander identifies himself as a physician and asks you to perform a procedure outside your scope of practice. What should you do?

w: Perform it because a physician asked
Perform it if he signs your report
Leave the patient with him and return to service

qs.q: You are using a glucometer on several patients at an event. Which practice prevents the spread of infection?

qs.x: Lancets are single use, and meters can carry blood between patients, so they are disinfected after each use.

Use the same lancet for patients in the same family, since they share household germs
Clean the meter only at the end of the shift

qs.q: Which conditions are contraindications to placing an intraosseous needle in a particular bone? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A fracture of that bone; An IO attempt in that bone earlier in the day; Infection at the insertion site
qs.x: A fracture, a previous attempt that leaves a hole, or infection at the site makes that bone unsafe. Shock and cardiac arrest without IV access are common indications for IO access.
opts: A fracture of that bone
An IO attempt in that bone earlier in the day
Infection at the insertion site
Shock with no IV access
Cardiac arrest
ok: A fracture of that bone
An IO attempt in that bone earlier in the day

qs.a: Drug name, dose and route; Time given; Patient's response

qs.q: Which practices reduce the risk of a needlestick injury? Select all that apply.

qs.q: Which actions are appropriate at a hazardous materials incident? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Stage upwind and uphill; Use the Emergency Response Guidebook; Wait for decontamination before treating patients

Remove contaminated clothing only after arrival at the hospital

Wait for decontamination before treating patients

qs.q: Using START, which adults who cannot walk should be tagged immediate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Respiratory rate of 34; No palpable radial pulse; Unable to follow simple commands
qs.x: In START, a respiratory rate over 30, absent radial pulse or delayed capillary refill, or inability to follow commands makes a patient immediate. A nonambulatory patient with adequate breathing, perfusion and mental status is tagged delayed.

qs.q: A 38-year-old driver with a suspected splenic injury had a BP of 70/40 and no radial pulse. After 500 mL of isotonic fluid he has a palpable radial pulse, a BP of 88/56 and is more alert. There is no head injury. What should you do with the fluids?
qs.a: Slow to a keep-open rate and reassess frequently
qs.x: In uncontrolled hemorrhage without head injury, fluids are titrated to a palpable radial pulse and improved mentation, roughly a systolic of 80 to 90 mmHg. Pushing the pressure higher can dislodge clots and dilute clotting factors, while keeping the line open allows rebolusing if he deteriorates.
w: Open both lines wide until the systolic BP is above 120 mmHg to build a reserve
Stop the infusion and remove the catheter because he has responded
Switch to a dextrose solution to give the clotting system energy

qs.q: Why should large volumes of crystalloid be avoided in a patient with ongoing internal hemorrhage?
qs.a: They dilute clotting factors and can disrupt forming clots
qs.x: Crystalloid carries no clotting factors or oxygen, so large volumes dilute the blood, cool the patient and raise pressure enough to blow out fragile clots. Definitive treatment is surgical control of the bleeding and blood products.
w: They draw water out of cells and cause severe dehydration of the brain
They cause an immediate allergic reaction in most trauma patients
They lower the blood glucose and cause confusion

qs.q: Which IV fluid is appropriate for volume replacement in a hypotensive trauma patient within AEMT scope?
qs.a: Lactated Ringer solution
qs.x: Isotonic crystalloids such as lactated Ringer and normal saline stay in the vascular space long enough to support perfusion. D5W is quickly distributed out of the vessels and dextrose concentrations are used for hypoglycemia, not volume.
w: Dextrose 5 percent in water
Dextrose 50 percent
Sterile water for injection

qs.q: A 30-year-old assault victim has a GCS of 8, shallow respirations at 8 per minute and an SpO2 of 88 percent. What is the most appropriate airway and breathing care?
qs.a: Assist ventilations with a BVM and oxygen at a normal rate
qs.x: Hypoxia sharply worsens secondary brain injury, so inadequate breathing is supported with BVM ventilation and oxygen at a normal rate. Routine hyperventilation constricts cerebral vessels and reduces brain blood flow.
w: Hyperventilate at 30 breaths per minute to lower intracranial pressure
Apply a nonrebreather mask and reassess in 10 minutes
Place a nasal cannula and position him on his side

qs.q: You are ventilating a 45-year-old with a severe head injury through a supraglottic airway. Her waveform ETCO2 is 26 mmHg and there are no signs of herniation. What should you do?
qs.a: Slow the ventilation rate
qs.x: An ETCO2 well below 35 mmHg means she is being hyperventilated, which narrows cerebral vessels and reduces brain perfusion. Slowing to about 10 breaths per minute aims for an ETCO2 of roughly 35 to 45 mmHg.
w: Ventilate faster
Increase the tidal volume of each breath
Remove the device and switch to a nonrebreather

qs.q: A 6-year-old struck by a car has a GCS of 9, a pulse of 140 and a BP of 72/40. How should you interpret the blood pressure?
qs.a: It is hypotensive for his age
qs.x: The lower limit of systolic BP for children 1 to 10 years old is about 70 plus twice the age in years, which is 82 mmHg here. Hypotension in a head-injured child sharply worsens outcome and calls for aggressive support of perfusion and oxygenation.
w: It is normal for age
It is expected because of rising intracranial pressure
It is too low to measure accurately in a child

qs.q: A 52-year-old was crushed against a steering wheel. A section of his right chest moves inward when he inhales, and he is breathing 30 times per minute with poor tidal volume and an SpO2 of 86 percent. What is the most appropriate care?
qs.a: Assist ventilations with a BVM and supplemental oxygen
qs.x: A flail segment with inadequate breathing needs positive-pressure ventilation, which splints the segment from the inside and improves oxygenation. Heavy objects and tight binding restrict chest expansion and worsen hypoventilation.
w: Tape a sandbag firmly over the moving segment
Wrap a cravat tightly around the chest to stop the movement
Have him take slow deep breaths through a nasal cannula

qs.q: A 26-year-old was stabbed just left of the sternum. He has distended neck veins, muffled heart tones, a BP of 76/60 and equal breath sounds bilaterally. What is the most likely injury?
qs.a: Pericardial tamponade
qs.x: Blood in the pericardial sac compresses the heart, producing JVD, muffled heart sounds and hypotension with a narrow pulse pressure. Equal breath sounds argue against a tension pneumothorax, and rapid transport for surgical decompression is needed.
w: Tension pneumothorax
Massive hemothorax
Isolated sternal fracture with chest wall bruising

qs.q: A 19-year-old has a gunshot wound to the right chest with bubbling at the wound on each breath. What should you do first?
qs.a: Cover the wound with a gloved hand
qs.x: An open chest wound is sealed immediately, first with a gloved hand and then with a vented or occlusive dressing. The patient is then watched closely for a developing tension pneumothorax.
w: Pack the wound tightly with gauze
Place him supine and assess the back
Apply a bulky dressing taped on all four sides with no occlusion

qs.q: After a fall from a roof, a 41-year-old has absent breath sounds on the left, flat neck veins, a pulse of 132 and a BP of 80/50. Which injury best explains these findings?
qs.a: Massive hemothorax
qs.x: Large blood loss into one side of the chest causes diminished breath sounds plus hypovolemic shock with flat neck veins. A tension pneumothorax or tamponade would more typically produce distended neck veins.
w: Tension pneumothorax
Pericardial tamponade
Diaphragmatic contusion

qs.q: A 14-year-old baseball catcher is struck in the center of the chest by a pitched ball and collapses. He is unresponsive, not breathing and pulseless. What should you do?
qs.a: Begin CPR and apply the AED as soon as possible
qs.x: A blow to the chest at a vulnerable point in the cardiac cycle can trigger ventricular fibrillation, called commotio cordis. Survival depends on immediate CPR and early defibrillation.
w: Apply a pelvic binder and treat for shock
Give fluid through an IO before starting compressions
Stabilize the spine and check for a pulse every 2 minutes

qs.q: You are applying a commercial pelvic binder to a patient with suspected pelvic fracture and shock. Where should the binder be centered?
qs.a: Over the greater trochanters
qs.x: Centering the binder over the greater trochanters compresses the pelvic ring where it is most effective at closing the pelvic volume and limiting venous bleeding. A binder at the iliac crests can actually widen the fracture.
w: Over the iliac crests at waist level
Over the lower ribs
Around the middle of both thighs

qs.q: A 35-year-old has partial- and full-thickness burns over about 30 percent of his body after a house fire. Ten minutes after the injury his BP is 78/50 and his pulse is 138. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Another source of shock, such as internal bleeding
qs.x: Burn shock develops gradually over hours as capillaries leak. Hypotension in the first minutes after a burn points to another cause, such as traumatic hemorrhage from a fall or explosion.
w: Normal early burn shock from fluid leaking into the tissues
An allergic reaction to the burn dressing
Carbon monoxide causing a falsely low blood pressure reading

qs.q: A 30-year-old with 40 percent TBSA burns is alert with a BP of 128/80. The burn center is 90 minutes away. Which fluid approach is most appropriate?
qs.a: A steady isotonic infusion at a guideline-directed hourly rate
qs.x: Large burns need ongoing isotonic fluid at a controlled hourly rate, not repeated boluses, because overresuscitation causes airway and tissue edema. Starting fluids during a long transport prevents burn shock from developing.
w: Repeated rapid 1-liter boluses until the burned skin stops weeping
Withhold all IV fluid until the patient becomes hypotensive
Dextrose 50 percent to replace energy lost through the skin

qs.q: A 48-year-old has partial-thickness burns over about half his body. The fire is out and the burning has been stopped. How should you manage the burned skin during transport?
qs.a: Cover him with dry sterile sheets and keep him warm
qs.x: Large burns destroy the skin barrier that holds in heat, so after brief cooling the patient is covered with dry clean dressings and kept warm. Ice and prolonged wet dressings over large areas cause hypothermia and further tissue injury.
w: Pack the burns in ice to stop deeper injury
Keep all the burns wet with cool saline throughout transport
Apply burn ointment before covering the wounds

qs.q: A 33-year-old lineman contacted a high-voltage wire. He is alert with a small burn on his hand and another on his foot. What is your greatest concern?
qs.a: Internal tissue damage and cardiac dysrhythmias
qs.x: Electrical current travels through deep tissue and the heart, so visible wounds badly understate the injury. These patients need cardiac monitoring and transport even when they appear well.
w: Infection developing in the small entry and exit wounds
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Allergic reaction to the electricity

qs.q: A 50-year-old has had both legs pinned under a collapsed wall for 4 hours. Rescuers are preparing to lift the wall. If possible, what should you do before the weight is removed?
qs.a: Establish IV access and begin isotonic fluid
qs.x: When prolonged compression is released, potassium, acids and muscle breakdown products rush into the circulation. Starting isotonic fluid before release dilutes these toxins and helps protect the heart and kidneys, and ALS should be requested early.
w: Apply tourniquets to both legs and leave them in place for transport
Give oral fluids containing potassium
Have rescuers lift the wall immediately before you assess him

qs.q: A 22-year-old has a splinted tibia fracture. An hour later he has severe pain that seems out of proportion to the injury and worsens when you gently move his toes, and the calf feels tense. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Compartment syndrome
qs.x: Rising pressure within a muscle compartment causes pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch, followed later by numbness and pulselessness. Loosen tight splints or dressings and transport promptly.
w: Fat embolism
Deep vein thrombosis
Normal fracture pain made worse by the splint position

qs.q: Which statement about long backboards reflects current guidance?
qs.a: They are mainly extrication tools, not transport devices
qs.x: Long backboards cause pain, pressure injury and restricted breathing. Spinal motion restriction can usually be achieved with a cervical collar and the patient secured flat on the stretcher once extricated.
w: Every patient with a significant mechanism must be secured to one
They protect the spine better than a padded stretcher for long transports
They make breathing easier for patients with chest injuries

qs.q: A 3-year-old needs spinal motion restriction after a fall. When you lay him flat, his neck flexes forward. What should you do?
qs.a: Place padding under his shoulders and torso
qs.x: Young children have a large occiput that pushes the head forward when lying flat. Padding beneath the shoulders and torso brings the spine into neutral alignment and keeps the airway open.
w: Place a folded towel under the back of his head
Tilt the board head-up to 30 degrees
Remove the cervical collar

qs.q: A 29-year-old motorcyclist is vomiting inside his full-face helmet and you cannot reach his airway. What should you do?
qs.a: Remove it using two rescuers with in-line stabilization
qs.x: A helmet that prevents airway management must be removed. Two rescuers work together, one holding the head and neck in line while the other spreads and slides the helmet off.
w: Leave the helmet on and suction through the face opening
Cut the chin strap and turn him prone to drain the vomit
Pull the helmet off quickly by yourself to save time

qs.q: A woman who is 30 weeks pregnant was in a low-speed collision. She has mild abdominal tenderness, normal vital signs and wants to refuse transport. What is the main reason to encourage evaluation?
qs.a: Placental abruption can occur even after minor trauma
qs.x: The placenta can shear away from the uterine wall after relatively minor forces, threatening the fetus before the mother shows signs of shock. Monitoring at the hospital is needed to detect fetal distress.
w: The fetus is unprotected by the uterine wall at this stage
Pregnancy makes her bones more likely to fracture
Seat belts cannot be worn safely during pregnancy

qs.q: A 4-year-old fell from a second-story window. He is anxious with a pulse of 164, a capillary refill of 4 seconds, cool hands and a BP of 98/62. How should you classify his condition?
qs.a: Compensated shock
qs.x: Children maintain their blood pressure until they lose a large share of their blood volume, so tachycardia, delayed refill and cool skin with a normal BP indicate compensated shock. A falling BP is a late, ominous sign.
w: Decompensated shock
Normal response to fear
Neurogenic shock

qs.q: A 3-year-old in hemorrhagic shock needs IO access. Which site is preferred?
qs.a: Anteromedial proximal tibia
qs.x: The anteromedial proximal tibia, about 1 to 2 cm below the tibial tuberosity, is a common pediatric IO site with thin overlying tissue. Growth plates and fractured bones must be avoided.
w: Directly into the growth plate just below the kneecap
The sternum
The upper arm on the side with a fractured humerus

qs.q: A restrained 31-year-old driver has a bruise across his lower abdomen from the lap belt and low back pain. What injuries should you suspect?
qs.a: Hollow organ and lumbar spine injury
qs.x: A seat belt sign across the lower abdomen is associated with injuries to the bowel and with flexion fractures of the lumbar spine. These injuries may show few early signs, so transport for evaluation is needed.
w: Isolated abdominal wall bruising only
Cervical spine injury only
Kidney stone

qs.q: A 79-year-old who takes a beta-blocker fell down several stairs. Her pulse is 72 and her BP is 104/70; her usual systolic is about 160. She is pale and slow to answer. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Shock masked by her medication
qs.x: Beta-blockers prevent the expected rise in heart rate, and a systolic below 110 is a warning sign in older adults. Compared with her baseline, she is relatively hypotensive and should be managed as possible shock.
w: A normal stress response
Stable condition because her pulse is not elevated
Neurogenic shock from a high spinal injury

qs.q: An 83-year-old woman is found on the floor with a shortened, externally rotated leg. She does not remember how she fell. Besides the hip injury, what is most important to investigate?
qs.a: A medical cause such as syncope
qs.x: Falls in older adults are often caused by syncope, dysrhythmias, stroke, infection or medication effects. Not remembering the fall raises concern for loss of consciousness, which needs its own assessment.
w: Whether her family can bring her walker to the hospital
Her shoe size
Whether her hip pain improves when she stands

qs.q: During START triage at a bus crash, an adult who cannot walk is breathing 34 times per minute, has a radial pulse and follows commands. How should you tag him?
qs.a: Immediate (red)
qs.x: In START, a respiratory rate above 30 places an adult in the immediate category regardless of the other findings.
w: Delayed (yellow)
Minor (green)
Expectant (black)

qs.q: During JumpSTART triage, a 5-year-old is not breathing after you position the airway but has a palpable pulse. What should you do?
qs.a: Give five rescue breaths
qs.x: Children often arrest from respiratory causes, so JumpSTART calls for five rescue breaths in an apneic child with a pulse. A child who resumes breathing is tagged immediate, and one who does not is tagged expectant.
w: Tag the child expectant and move on
Tag the child immediate and move on without intervening
Begin chest compressions

qs.q: During SALT triage at a mass casualty incident, which intervention may be performed before assigning a category?
qs.a: Applying a tourniquet for major hemorrhage
qs.x: SALT allows quick lifesaving interventions, such as controlling major hemorrhage, opening the airway and giving autoinjector antidotes, because they take little time and change survival. Time-consuming care is deferred until resources allow.
w: Starting an IV for fluid resuscitation
Splinting a closed forearm fracture
Starting an IV and running a fluid bolus for shock

qs.q: A 27-year-old has a knife wound to the abdomen with a loop of bowel protruding. What is the correct care?
qs.a: Moist sterile dressing covered by an occlusive layer
qs.x: An evisceration is covered with a sterile dressing moistened with saline and then an occlusive layer to keep it moist and warm. Replacing the organs can introduce contamination and cause further injury.
w: Gently push the bowel back into the abdomen
Cover it with a dry gauze pad that adheres to the bowel
Rinse the bowel with tap water and leave it uncovered

qs.q: A 20-year-old has a wooden object impaled through his cheek. Blood is pooling in his mouth faster than you can suction it, and he is struggling to breathe. What should you do?
qs.a: Remove the object and pack the inside of the cheek
qs.x: Impaled objects are normally stabilized, but one in the cheek that compromises the airway may be removed. Dressing material is placed between the cheek and teeth, and the airway is suctioned and protected.
w: Stabilize the object in place with bulky dressings
Cut the object flush with the skin
Insert a supraglottic airway alongside the object and ventilate

qs.q: A 34-year-old's thumb was amputated by a saw. Bleeding is controlled. How should you care for the amputated part?
qs.a: Wrap it in moist sterile gauze, seal it in a bag and keep it cool
qs.x: The part is wrapped in sterile gauze moistened with saline, sealed in a plastic bag and kept cool on a separate layer of ice or cold packs. Direct contact with ice or water damages the tissue.
w: Place it directly on ice to preserve the tissue
Submerge it in a cup of saline or tap water to keep it hydrated
Leave it on scene so it does not delay transport

qs.q: Why is preventing heat loss a priority in a patient with severe hemorrhage?
qs.a: Hypothermia impairs blood clotting
qs.x: Hypothermia, acidosis and impaired clotting reinforce one another in trauma patients. Covering the patient, warming the ambulance and using warmed fluids help prevent this cycle.
w: Warming the patient raises the BP to a normal level
Cold blood is more likely to clot excessively
Shivering stops bleeding

qs.q: A 23-year-old has a deep stab wound in the groin with heavy bleeding. A tourniquet cannot be placed above the wound. What should you do?
qs.a: Pack the wound tightly and hold firm direct pressure
qs.x: Junctional wounds such as the groin and axilla cannot be controlled with a limb tourniquet. Packing hemostatic or plain gauze deep into the wound and holding firm pressure for several minutes is the recommended technique.
w: Place a tourniquet below the wound on the thigh
Elevate the leg and apply a light dressing
Apply cold packs and elevate the leg until arrival at the hospital

qs.q: After a fall onto his left side, a 16-year-old has left upper abdominal pain and pain in his left shoulder, which was not injured. What does the shoulder pain suggest?
qs.a: Irritation of the diaphragm from splenic bleeding
qs.x: Blood under the diaphragm from a splenic injury can refer pain to the left shoulder, a finding known as Kehr sign. It should raise concern for internal bleeding and shock.
w: A separate shoulder dislocation
Referred pain from a fractured left femur or pelvis
Anxiety rather than injury

qs.q: Which factors worsen secondary brain injury in a patient with traumatic brain injury? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A single episode of hypotension; Hypoxia with an SpO2 below 90 percent; Routine hyperventilation
qs.x: Hypotension and hypoxia each markedly increase death and disability after TBI, and hyperventilation lowers brain blood flow. Neutral alignment and normothermia are part of good care.
opts: A single episode of hypotension
Hypoxia with an SpO2 below 90 percent
Routine hyperventilation
Keeping the head in line with the body
Maintaining a normal body temperature
ok: A single episode of hypotension
Hypoxia with an SpO2 below 90 percent
Routine hyperventilation

qs.q: Which actions are appropriate when managing a suspected unstable pelvic fracture? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Apply a pelvic binder when signs of shock are present; Pad the knees and ankles and bind the legs together
qs.x: A binder reduces pelvic volume and helps tamponade bleeding, and binding the legs adds stability. Repeated manipulation can disrupt clots, and the binder stays on until hospital staff remove it.
opts: Apply a pelvic binder when signs of shock are present
Pad the knees and ankles and bind the legs together
Rock the pelvis repeatedly to confirm instability
Remove the binder once the BP improves
Wait for hospital imaging before applying a binder
ok: Apply a pelvic binder when signs of shock are present
Pad the knees and ankles and bind the legs together

qs.q: Which findings suggest a developing tension pneumothorax? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Absent breath sounds on one side; Distended neck veins; Worsening hypotension
qs.x: Trapped air under pressure collapses the lung and impairs venous return, producing unilateral absent breath sounds, JVD and falling BP. A slow pulse with widening pulse pressure suggests increased intracranial pressure instead.
opts: Absent breath sounds on one side
Distended neck veins
Worsening hypotension
Equal breath sounds bilaterally
Slow pulse with a widening pulse pressure
ok: Absent breath sounds on one side
Distended neck veins
Worsening hypotension

qs.q: A 42-year-old was rescued from a burning apartment. Which findings suggest an inhalation injury? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Singed nasal hairs; Hoarse voice; Soot in the sputum
qs.x: Facial burns, singed hair, hoarseness and soot in the mouth or sputum indicate heat or smoke injury to the airway, which can swell quickly. These patients need close airway monitoring and early ALS involvement.
opts: Singed nasal hairs
Hoarse voice
Soot in the sputum
Blistering burn to the forearm only
Pain in the ankle
ok: Singed nasal hairs
Hoarse voice
Soot in the sputum

qs.q: Which findings indicate that a blunt trauma patient needs spinal motion restriction? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Intoxication or altered mental status; Midline neck or back tenderness; New numbness or weakness in the extremities
qs.x: Altered mentation, midline spinal tenderness and focal neurological deficits all suggest possible spinal injury. An alert, sober patient with no spinal pain, tenderness or deficit does not need SMR solely because of an extremity injury.
opts: Intoxication or altered mental status
Midline neck or back tenderness
New numbness or weakness in the extremities
Pain isolated to an ankle after a ground-level fall in an alert, sober patient
Anxiety about the crash
ok: Intoxication or altered mental status
Midline neck or back tenderness
New numbness or weakness in the extremities

qs.q: Which physiologic changes make older adults more vulnerable after trauma? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Medications may blunt the heart rate response to blood loss; Bones fracture with less force; A systolic BP below 110 may represent shock
qs.x: Older adults have less reserve, fragile bones and medications such as beta-blockers and anticoagulants that hide or worsen shock. National triage guidance treats a systolic below 110 in those over 65 as a concerning finding.
opts: Medications may blunt the heart rate response to blood loss
Bones fracture with less force
A systolic BP below 110 may represent shock
They lose blood volume more slowly than younger adults
Their pain response is always exaggerated
ok: Medications may blunt the heart rate response to blood loss
Bones fracture with less force
A systolic BP below 110 may represent shock

qs.q: Which statements about children involved in trauma are correct? Select all that apply.
qs.a: The head is large relative to the body, increasing head injury risk; Flexible ribs allow internal injury without rib fractures; Hypotension is a late sign of shock
qs.x: Children have proportionally large heads, pliable ribs and strong compensation that keeps BP normal until late. Their large surface area relative to mass makes them lose heat quickly.
opts: The head is large relative to the body, increasing head injury risk
Flexible ribs allow internal injury without rib fractures
Hypotension is a late sign of shock
They lose body heat more slowly than adults
Their BP drops early in blood loss
ok: The head is large relative to the body, increasing head injury risk
Flexible ribs allow internal injury without rib fractures
Hypotension is a late sign of shock

qs.q: Which are concerns specific to the injured pregnant patient in the third trimester? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Supine positioning can compress the vena cava and lower BP; Placental abruption may follow even minor trauma; Signs of shock may appear only after large blood loss
qs.x: Late pregnancy brings caval compression, abruption risk and an expanded blood volume that hides early shock. Heart rate normally rises in pregnancy, and the fetus may be in distress while the mother still appears stable.
opts: Supine positioning can compress the vena cava and lower BP
Placental abruption may follow even minor trauma
A resting heart rate slower than before pregnancy is expected
The fetus is safe as long as the mother is talking
Signs of shock may appear only after large blood loss
ok: Supine positioning can compress the vena cava and lower BP
Placental abruption may follow even minor trauma
Signs of shock may appear only after large blood loss

qs.q: A man has been trapped under machinery for 3 hours. Which complications are associated with crush syndrome? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hyperkalemia and dysrhythmias after release; Kidney failure from muscle breakdown products; Hypotension from fluid shifting into injured tissue
qs.x: Releasing a prolonged crush sends potassium, acids and myoglobin into the circulation, causing dysrhythmias, kidney injury and shock. Patients may deteriorate suddenly after appearing stable while trapped.
opts: Hyperkalemia and dysrhythmias after release
Kidney failure from muscle breakdown products
Hypoglycemia as the main life threat
Immediate improvement once the weight is removed
Hypotension from fluid shifting into injured tissue
ok: Hyperkalemia and dysrhythmias after release
Kidney failure from muscle breakdown products
Hypotension from fluid shifting into injured tissue

qs.q: A 62-year-old diabetic woman is confused and sweaty with a blood glucose of 48 mg/dL. She follows commands, swallows normally and protects her own airway. What is the most appropriate first treatment?
qs.a: Oral glucose, watching her airway closely
qs.x: A hypoglycemic patient who is awake enough to swallow safely can be treated quickly with oral glucose. IV dextrose or glucagon is reserved for patients who cannot swallow or protect the airway.
w: An isotonic fluid bolus to dilute the insulin in her blood
Withhold sugar until IV access is obtained for dextrose
High-flow oxygen and repeat glucose check in 15 minutes

qs.q: A 74-year-old who takes a long-acting oral diabetes medication was hypoglycemic. After IV dextrose his glucose is 118 mg/dL and he wants to refuse transport. What is the main concern?
qs.a: His glucose may fall again over the next several hours
qs.x: Some oral agents keep lowering glucose for many hours, so hypoglycemia can recur once a single dextrose dose is used up. He should be strongly encouraged to accept transport, and if he still refuses, he must eat and have someone stay with him.
w: The dextrose will push him into diabetic ketoacidosis within the hour
A glucose of 118 mg/dL is dangerously high for an older adult
He is likely to have a delayed allergic reaction to the dextrose

qs.q: A 68-year-old has new right-sided weakness and slurred speech that began 40 minutes ago. Which assessment should you perform early because its result could change your field impression?
qs.a: Blood glucose
qs.x: Hypoglycemia can produce focal weakness and speech changes that look exactly like a stroke. A glucose check is part of every stroke assessment and takes only seconds.
w: Oral temperature
Capillary refill in the fingers
Orthostatic vital signs before moving her

qs.q: A 30-year-old diabetic is pale, sweaty and confused. Her glucose reads 420 mg/dL from a fingertip that is sticky because she was just eating candy. What should you do next?
qs.a: Clean the skin, then recheck with a new sample
qs.x: Sugar on the skin can produce a falsely high reading, and her signs fit hypoglycemia. The site is cleaned and the test repeated before making treatment decisions.
w: Treat her for DKA with large fluid boluses
Accept the reading and withhold all sugar
Repeat the test immediately on the same fingertip

qs.q: An 80-year-old with type 2 diabetes has become more confused over several days. Her glucose reads HI and she is profoundly dehydrated, with no fruity odor and no rapid deep breathing. What is the most likely condition?
qs.a: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
qs.x: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state develops slowly in older type 2 diabetics, with extreme glucose levels and severe dehydration but little ketone production. It requires careful fluid replacement and hospital care.
w: Diabetic ketoacidosis from missed insulin
Hypoglycemia with a meter error
Insulin shock

qs.q: A 55-year-old malnourished alcoholic with a glucose of 34 mg/dL received IM glucagon 15 minutes ago and has not improved. What is the most likely reason?
qs.a: His liver has little stored glycogen
qs.x: Glucagon raises glucose by releasing glycogen stored in the liver, so it often fails in malnourished or alcoholic patients. IV or IO dextrose is needed when glucagon does not work.
w: Glucagon is effective only in children
Glucagon must be given by mouth to be absorbed
The meter always reads falsely low in alcoholics

qs.q: A 16-year-old with an insulin pump is unresponsive with a glucose of 38 mg/dL. Along with treating the hypoglycemia, what should be done with the pump?
qs.a: Suspend or disconnect it so insulin delivery stops
qs.x: An insulin pump keeps delivering insulin and will keep driving the glucose down. Suspending or disconnecting it stops further insulin while the hypoglycemia is treated, and the device goes to the hospital with the patient.
w: Leave it running because stopping it will cause immediate DKA
Increase its infusion rate to stabilize the glucose level
Pull out the infusion catheter and discard the entire device

qs.q: A 40-year-old is unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, respirations of 6 per minute and an SpO2 of 82 percent. What should you do first?
qs.a: Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen
qs.x: Inadequate breathing is corrected immediately with BVM ventilation and oxygen. Naloxone may follow, but ventilation is never delayed while waiting for a drug to work.
w: Give naloxone and wait for the breathing to improve
Apply a nonrebreather
Check a blood glucose level before any airway care

qs.q: A 58-year-old smells strongly of alcohol, is confused and was found at the bottom of a short staircase. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Check glucose and assess for head injury
qs.x: Alcohol odor does not explain an altered mental status. Intoxicated patients frequently have hypoglycemia, head injuries or other illness that must be looked for before attributing the confusion to alcohol.
w: Assume he is intoxicated and let him sleep it off in a quiet place
Request police custody
Give oral glucose without testing because alcoholics are often hypoglycemic

qs.q: A 35-year-old with a seizure disorder has been seizing continuously for 7 minutes. Which care is most appropriate within AEMT scope?
qs.a: Protect him, give oxygen, check glucose and request ALS
qs.x: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes is status epilepticus and needs anticonvulsant medications beyond AEMT scope. AEMT care is protecting the patient, supporting the airway and oxygenation, treating hypoglycemia and getting ALS or rapid transport.
w: Place a bite block between his teeth to protect his tongue
Hold his arms and legs firmly to stop the movements
Wait until the seizure stops before requesting any help

qs.q: A 27-year-old has just stopped seizing. She is breathing adequately with gurgling sounds and is not yet responsive. How should you position her?
qs.a: On her side with suction ready
qs.x: The recovery position lets secretions drain and keeps the tongue from blocking the airway during the postictal period. Suction and oxygen are provided as she recovers.
w: Supine with her legs elevated 12 inches
Sitting upright with her head supported
Prone, face turned aside

qs.q: A woman who is 33 weeks pregnant and has no seizure history has a generalized seizure. Her BP is 182/112 and her face and hands are swollen. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Eclampsia
qs.x: A seizure in a pregnant woman with hypertension and edema is eclampsia until proven otherwise. She needs ALS for anticonvulsant medication, a dim and quiet environment and rapid transport.
w: New-onset epilepsy
Hypoglycemia caused by the pregnancy
Supine hypotensive syndrome

qs.q: A 20-year-old fainted while standing in a long line, had a few seconds of jerking and was alert within a minute. Which finding would most suggest a seizure rather than syncope?
qs.a: Prolonged confusion afterward
qs.x: A prolonged postictal period of confusion favors a seizure. Brief jerking with a rapid return to alertness is common in ordinary fainting.
w: A brief feeling of lightheadedness before falling
Pale, sweaty skin just before the event
A few seconds of jerking movements during the faint

qs.q: A 72-year-old woman woke at 6 a.m. unable to speak clearly. She went to bed feeling normal at 10 p.m. When was she last known well?
qs.a: 10 p.m., when she was last seen normal
qs.x: Last known well is the last time the patient was seen at her baseline. For symptoms present on waking, that is when she went to sleep, which affects eligibility for time-sensitive stroke treatments.
w: 6 a.m., when she woke with the symptoms
The time EMS arrived and began the assessment
The time her husband called 911

qs.q: A 66-year-old with a suspected stroke has a BP of 188/104 and a normal glucose. What should you do about the BP?
qs.a: Monitor it without trying to lower it
qs.x: Elevated BP is common in acute stroke and helps perfuse the brain tissue around the injury. Lowering it in the field can enlarge the stroke, so BP management is left to the receiving hospital.
w: Give nitroglycerin to bring the systolic below 140
Run a fluid bolus to protect the brain from the high pressure
Coach slow breathing until the BP falls below 160

qs.q: A 70-year-old with a suspected stroke has a facial droop and slurred speech and asks for a drink of water. Why should you withhold anything by mouth?
qs.a: Her ability to swallow safely may be impaired
qs.x: Stroke often weakens the muscles of swallowing, so liquids and pills can be aspirated into the lungs. Patients are kept NPO until a formal swallow screen is done.
w: Water will raise the BP and extend the stroke
Fluids by mouth will dilute the blood glucose
Stroke patients cannot absorb water from the stomach

qs.q: A 24-year-old took a large amount of an over-the-counter antihistamine sleep aid. He is agitated and confused with hot, dry, flushed skin, dilated pupils and a pulse of 136. Which toxidrome does this fit?
qs.a: Anticholinergic
qs.x: Anticholinergic toxicity causes hot, dry, red skin, dilated pupils, tachycardia, delirium and urinary retention. Many antihistamines produce this pattern in overdose.
w: Cholinergic
Opioid
Sedative-hypnotic

qs.q: A 29-year-old is agitated after using a stimulant. He is tachycardic, hypertensive and hyperthermic with dilated pupils. Which finding best distinguishes this from an anticholinergic toxidrome?
qs.a: Sweaty skin
qs.x: Sympathomimetic toxicity causes heavy sweating, while anticholinergic toxicity produces dry skin. Both can cause dilated pupils, tachycardia and agitation.
w: Dilated pupils
Fast heart rate
Agitation

qs.q: A 19-year-old took about 40 acetaminophen tablets an hour ago. She feels fine and wants to refuse transport. What should you explain?
qs.a: Early symptoms can be mild even after a lethal dose
qs.x: Acetaminophen overdose often causes few early symptoms while liver damage develops over the next day or two. An antidote works best when started early, so prompt hospital evaluation is critical.
w: The overdose is harmless because she has no symptoms
Vomiting at home is enough to remove the tablets
She will have seizures within minutes if she stays home

qs.q: A family of four all have headaches and nausea that started after they began using a fuel-burning space heater. One adult has an SpO2 of 99 percent. How should you interpret this reading?
qs.a: It can read normal despite significant poisoning
qs.x: Standard pulse oximeters cannot tell carbon monoxide bound to hemoglobin from oxygen, so readings may look normal. Remove everyone from the source and give high-concentration oxygen.
w: It rules out carbon monoxide poisoning in that adult
It shows the headaches are most likely from a viral illness
It means none of the family needs supplemental oxygen

qs.q: A 32-year-old allergic to peanuts received epinephrine for wheezing, hives and hypotension and improved. Ten minutes later her wheezing and hypotension return. What should you do?
qs.a: Repeat the epinephrine and support breathing and BP
qs.x: Epinephrine acts briefly, and symptoms of anaphylaxis commonly return. A repeat dose is given for persistent or recurring signs, along with oxygen and IV fluid.
w: Give oral glucose for the stress response
Wait another 20 minutes for the first dose to take full effect
Give nitroglycerin to relieve the chest tightness

qs.q: A 28-year-old has a few itchy hives on one arm after eating shellfish. She has no breathing difficulty, no facial swelling, no GI symptoms and normal vital signs. What is the most appropriate care?
qs.a: Monitor closely during transport
qs.x: Localized hives without involvement of breathing, circulation or another body system are a mild allergic reaction. She is watched closely during transport for signs of progression to anaphylaxis.
w: Give epinephrine immediately to prevent progression
Start a fluid bolus
Place a supraglottic airway as a precaution against swelling

qs.q: A 50-year-old in anaphylaxis remains hypotensive at 78/48 after epinephrine. Breath sounds are clear. What should you add?
qs.a: An isotonic fluid bolus
qs.x: Anaphylaxis causes vasodilation and capillary leak, so persistent hypotension is treated with isotonic fluid boluses along with repeat epinephrine. Lung sounds and BP are reassessed during the infusion.
w: Dextrose 10 percent infusion
Sublingual nitroglycerin
Oral fluids to replace lost volume

qs.q: A 70-year-old has a productive cough, a temperature of 38.6 C (101.5 F), respirations of 28, a pulse of 112, a BP of 108/64 and new confusion. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Sepsis from pneumonia
qs.x: Infection with rapid breathing, tachycardia and new confusion indicates sepsis. Early recognition, oxygen, fluids when hypotensive and hospital notification improve survival.
w: Simple dehydration from poor oral intake
An asthma exacerbation
Acute stroke with aspiration

qs.q: You are giving fluid to a septic 65-year-old with a BP of 82/50. After 500 mL, which finding best shows the fluid is helping and being tolerated?
qs.a: Better mentation and BP with clear lungs
qs.x: Fluid in sepsis is given in boluses with reassessment between them. Improved mentation and BP with clear lung sounds show better perfusion without fluid overload.
w: New crackles in both bases with a rising BP
A rising heart rate and increasing confusion
A faster respiratory rate with a falling SpO2

qs.q: A 6-week-old has a temperature of 38.3 C (101 F) but is feeding normally and alert. What should you advise the parents?
qs.a: Transport for prompt evaluation of a possible serious infection
qs.x: Young infants can have serious bacterial infections with fever as the only sign. Any fever in an infant younger than about 2 to 3 months warrants prompt medical evaluation.
w: Treat it as a minor cold at home and call back if it worsens
Give a cool bath and have the pediatrician see her tomorrow
Wait until the fever is above 40 C (104 F) before seeking care

qs.q: A 19-year-old college student has a fever, stiff neck and a purple rash that does not blanch. Which infection control precaution is most important?
qs.a: Droplet precautions with masks for the patient and crew
qs.x: Fever, neck stiffness and a non-blanching rash suggest meningococcal infection, which spreads by respiratory droplets. A surgical mask on the patient and providers plus gloves and eye protection is appropriate.
w: Contact precautions with gloves and gown only
No precautions beyond standard handwashing
A respirator only after arrival at the hospital

qs.q: A 60-year-old has vomited coffee-ground material and has black, tarry stools. His BP is 88/56 and pulse is 124. Where is the bleeding most likely coming from?
qs.a: Upper GI tract
qs.x: Coffee-ground vomit and black, tarry stool indicate bleeding from the upper GI tract, such as an ulcer. With signs of shock he needs rapid transport and IV access.
w: Lower colon or rectum
Lungs, with swallowed blood
Urinary bladder

qs.q: A 52-year-old with liver disease is vomiting large amounts of bright red blood and is drowsy. What should you do first?
qs.a: Turn him on his side and suction the airway
qs.x: Massive upper GI bleeding in an altered patient creates a high aspiration risk. Side positioning and suction protect the airway before shock is addressed.
w: Give oral fluids to replace the lost volume
Lay him flat on his back with legs elevated
Apply a nasal cannula and start an IV

qs.q: A 72-year-old man has sudden tearing back pain, a pulsating abdominal mass and a BP of 84/50. What is the most appropriate care?
qs.a: Rapid transport with limited fluids
qs.x: A leaking or ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm needs immediate surgery. The abdomen is handled gently, and IV fluids are limited to maintaining minimal perfusion during rapid transport.
w: Deep palpation to estimate the size of the mass
Large fluid boluses until the systolic BP exceeds 120
Have him walk out

qs.q: A 64-year-old dialysis patient missed two treatments. He is weak with a pulse of 44, and the monitor shows tall, peaked T waves. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Hyperkalemia
qs.x: Missed dialysis lets potassium build up, causing weakness, bradycardia, peaked T waves and possible cardiac arrest. Rapid transport and ALS are needed.
w: Hypoglycemia
Hypothermia
Dehydration from fluid removal

qs.q: A 58-year-old dialysis patient missed treatments. She is breathing 30 times per minute with crackles throughout, an SpO2 of 88 percent and a BP of 178/98. What is the most appropriate care?
qs.a: Sit her up, give oxygen and avoid fluid boluses
qs.x: A dialysis patient who misses treatments accumulates fluid in the lungs. She needs upright positioning, oxygen or assisted ventilation and rapid transport, not more fluid.
w: Lay her flat and give a fluid bolus to support her kidneys
Give a fluid bolus first, then place her upright if she tolerates it
Insert a supraglottic airway

qs.q: In an 88-year-old, which finding is least reliable for judging dehydration?
qs.a: Skin turgor on the back of the hand
qs.x: Skin loses elasticity with age, so tenting does not reliably indicate dehydration in older adults. History, mucous membranes, mental status and vital signs are more useful.
w: Dry mucous membranes
Dizziness when standing
A rapid heart rate

qs.q: A 4-year-old is moderately dehydrated from vomiting and needs an IV fluid bolus. Which fluid is appropriate?
qs.a: Normal saline
qs.x: Isotonic fluids such as normal saline restore intravascular volume in pediatric dehydration. D5W and sterile water are hypotonic, and concentrated dextrose is for hypoglycemia, not volume.
w: 5 percent dextrose in water
Dextrose 50 percent
Sterile water for injection

qs.q: After placing an IO needle in a 2-year-old, which finding best confirms correct placement?
qs.a: Fluid flows freely without swelling
qs.x: A properly placed IO needle stands firmly in the bone and allows fluid to flow without swelling of the surrounding tissue. Swelling indicates infiltration, and the needle should be removed.
