qs.q: Which factors make a cardiac arrest patient a better candidate for ECPR? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Witnessed collapse with immediate bystander CPR; Refractory ventricular fibrillation; Younger age without major chronic illness
qs.x: ECPR works best with short no-flow times, shockable rhythms and patients without severe comorbidities; long no-flow periods and terminal illness predict poor outcomes.
opts: Witnessed collapse with immediate bystander CPR
Refractory ventricular fibrillation
Younger age without major chronic illness
Age 89 with metastatic cancer
Unwitnessed arrest found after at least 45 minutes
Asystole after a long period without CPR
ok: Witnessed collapse with immediate bystander CPR
Refractory ventricular fibrillation
Younger age without major chronic illness

qs.q: You are starting transcutaneous pacing on a conscious 79-year-old with complete heart block and BP 70/40. Which practices are correct? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Increase the output until each spike is followed by a wide QRS; Consider analgesia or sedation per protocol; Keep the monitoring leads attached for demand pacing
qs.x: Output is raised until capture, comfort measures are considered for the conscious patient, and demand mode needs the ECG leads; twitching is expected and carotid checks are unreliable.
opts: Increase the output until each spike is followed by a wide QRS
Consider analgesia or sedation per protocol
Keep the monitoring leads attached for demand pacing
Confirm capture by feeling the carotid pulse
Stop pacing when chest muscle twitching appears
ok: Increase the output until each spike is followed by a wide QRS
Consider analgesia or sedation per protocol
Keep the monitoring leads attached for demand pacing

qs.q: Which findings suggest cardiogenic shock in a patient with an acute MI? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Cool, clammy skin; Crackles in both lungs; Systolic BP below 90 mmHg with altered mental status
qs.x: Cardiogenic shock combines poor perfusion and hypotension with congestion; warm skin suggests distributive shock and flat veins with clear lungs suggest hypovolemia.
opts: Cool, clammy skin
Crackles in both lungs
Systolic BP below 90 mmHg with altered mental status
Warm, flushed skin with bounding pulses
Flat neck veins with clear lungs after vomiting
ok: Cool, clammy skin
Crackles in both lungs
Systolic BP below 90 mmHg with altered mental status

qs.q: A patient in PEA has a narrow QRS at a fast rate, suggesting a mechanical cause. Which conditions fit this pattern? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Cardiac tamponade; Tension pneumothorax; Massive pulmonary embolism
qs.x: Narrow, fast PEA usually means the heart is electrically intact but cannot fill or eject, as in tamponade, tension pneumothorax or PE; hyperkalemia and sodium channel toxins widen the QRS.
opts: Cardiac tamponade
Tension pneumothorax
Massive pulmonary embolism
Severe hyperkalemia
Overdose of a sodium channel blocking drug
ok: Cardiac tamponade
Tension pneumothorax
Massive pulmonary embolism

qs.q: You are transporting a suspected stroke patient. Which information is most important to give the receiving stroke team? Select all that apply.
qs.a: The last known well time; Whether the patient takes an anticoagulant; The blood glucose result
qs.x: Last known well, anticoagulant use and glucose directly affect treatment eligibility and mimic exclusion; the 911 call time is not the onset time.
opts: The last known well time
Whether the patient takes an anticoagulant
The blood glucose result
The exact time the 911 call was placed
Results of a cholesterol test from last year
ok: The last known well time
Whether the patient takes an anticoagulant
The blood glucose result

qs.q: A 45-year-old fainted while sitting at his desk. Which ECG findings make a dangerous cause of syncope more likely? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Second-degree AV block type II; A markedly prolonged QT interval; A delta wave with a short PR interval
qs.x: Conduction blocks, long QT and pre-excitation can cause sudden arrhythmic syncope; a normal ECG and respiratory sinus arrhythmia are reassuring.
opts: Second-degree AV block type II
A markedly prolonged QT interval
A delta wave with a short PR interval
Normal sinus rhythm at 72/min with normal intervals
Sinus arrhythmia that varies with breathing
ok: Second-degree AV block type II
A markedly prolonged QT interval
A delta wave with a short PR interval

qs.q: A woman who is 30 weeks pregnant is in cardiac arrest. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Manual left uterine displacement during CPR; Defibrillation at standard adult energy; Early notification for possible resuscitative delivery
qs.x: Displacing the uterus relieves aortocaval compression; standard defibrillation is safe in pregnancy, and early notification allows rapid delivery if ROSC is not achieved.
opts: Manual left uterine displacement during CPR
Defibrillation at standard adult energy
Early notification for possible resuscitative delivery
Compressions placed lower on the abdomen
Withholding defibrillation to protect the fetus
ok: Manual left uterine displacement during CPR
Defibrillation at standard adult energy
Early notification for possible resuscitative delivery

qs.q: A 2-year-old has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days. Which findings indicate compensated shock? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Tachycardia; Capillary refill of 4 seconds; Cool hands and feet
qs.x: Children maintain blood pressure until late, so tachycardia and poor peripheral perfusion signal compensated shock; hypotension and bradycardia are late signs of decompensation.
opts: Tachycardia
Capillary refill of 4 seconds
Cool hands and feet
Systolic hypotension
Bradycardia
ok: Tachycardia
Capillary refill of 4 seconds
Cool hands and feet

qs.q: A 29-year-old construction worker has a near-amputation of the left lower leg with massive bleeding. He has snoring respirations and a GCS of 10. Using the MARCH sequence, what do you address first?
qs.a: Apply a tourniquet high and tight on the leg
qs.x: MARCH puts massive hemorrhage before the airway because a person can bleed to death from a severed leg artery within minutes. The airway is managed right after the bleeding is controlled.
w: Insert a nasopharyngeal airway to relieve the snoring
Expose the chest and look for an open pneumothorax
Obtain a blood glucose and a full set of vital signs

qs.q: You have controlled bleeding, managed the airway, sealed a chest wound and started an IV on a 40-year-old gunshot victim lying on wet pavement on a cold night. Under MARCH, what should you do next?
qs.a: Remove wet clothing and cover him to prevent heat loss
qs.x: The H in MARCH covers hypothermia and head injury. Even mild hypothermia worsens bleeding by impairing clotting, so heat loss must be prevented early.
w: Start a second IV and give a large crystalloid bolus
Complete a detailed secondary exam before covering him
Splint his minor finger fractures

qs.q: A 25-year-old has a gunshot wound to the right groin with steady bright red bleeding. There is no room above the wound for a limb tourniquet. What should you do?
qs.a: Pack the wound tightly with hemostatic gauze and hold firm pressure
qs.x: Groin wounds are junctional and cannot be controlled with a limb tourniquet. Packing the wound cavity onto the bleeding vessel and holding direct pressure, or using a junctional device, is the correct approach.
w: Apply a limb tourniquet just below the wound
Elevate the leg and place a bulky dressing over the wound surface
Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters

qs.q: A 32-year-old with a tourniquet on his thigh for an arterial bleed asks you to loosen it because the pain is severe. Bleeding is controlled and transport time is 25 minutes. What should you do?
qs.a: Leave it in place and treat his pain
qs.x: A properly applied tourniquet is painful, and loosening it can restart life-threatening bleeding. It should stay in place, the time should be noted, and pain should be managed per protocol.
w: Loosen it briefly every 10 minutes to reduce pain
Remove it and replace it with a pressure dressing
Move it lower on the leg to a less painful spot

qs.q: A 70-kg man was crushed between two vehicles. He is confused and anxious, HR 128, BP 84/58, RR 32, with pale cool skin. Which class of hemorrhagic shock best fits these findings?
qs.a: Class III, about 30 to 40 percent blood loss
qs.x: Class III blood loss is the point where systolic pressure falls, with marked tachycardia and confusion. Class II usually keeps a normal systolic pressure, and class IV brings profound hypotension and lethargy.
w: Class I, under 15 percent blood loss
Class II, about 15 to 30 percent blood loss
Class IV, more than 40 percent with lethargy and no measurable pressure

qs.q: A 30-year-old fell from a ladder and is anxious, with HR 112, BP 124/100, RR 22 and capillary refill of 3 seconds. What does his blood pressure reading most likely reflect?
qs.a: Vasoconstriction narrowing the pulse pressure
qs.x: A rising diastolic pressure with a normal systolic gives a narrow pulse pressure, an early sign that the body is compensating for blood loss with vasoconstriction. A normal systolic pressure does not rule out shock.
w: Normal perfusion with no blood loss
Neurogenic shock from a spinal injury
A rising intracranial pressure

qs.q: A 34-year-old with a severe head injury has a GCS of 5, a fixed dilated right pupil and new extensor posturing. He is intubated and the BP is 142/80. What ETCO2 should you target while signs of herniation persist?
qs.a: 30 to 35 mmHg
qs.x: With active signs of herniation, brief controlled hyperventilation to an ETCO2 of about 30 to 35 mmHg is recommended. Driving it lower causes cerebral vasoconstriction severe enough to cause ischemia.
w: 20 to 25 mmHg
35 to 45 mmHg
45 to 50 mmHg

qs.q: You have been mildly hyperventilating an intubated head-injured adult with a blown pupil. After 10 minutes the pupil begins to react and his posturing stops. What should you do now?
qs.a: Return to a normal rate targeting an ETCO2 of 35 to 40
qs.x: Hyperventilation is a temporary bridge only while signs of herniation are present. Once they resolve, ventilation returns to normal to avoid the cerebral ischemia caused by prolonged low CO2.
w: Continue hyperventilating until arrival at the hospital
Increase the rate further to keep improving the pupil
Stop ventilating briefly to let the ETCO2 rise above 50

qs.q: In a patient with a severe traumatic brain injury, which pair of secondary insults most strongly worsens outcome and must be prevented in the field?
qs.a: Hypoxia and hypotension
qs.x: Even a single episode of hypoxia or hypotension is linked to markedly higher death rates after TBI. Field care focuses on keeping SpO2 at least 90 percent and avoiding low blood pressure.
w: Hyperthermia and hyperglycemia
Hypertension and tachycardia
Hypocarbia and hypernatremia

qs.q: A 19-year-old was hit in the temple with a baseball and was knocked out briefly. He then talked normally for 30 minutes but is now vomiting, with a GCS of 10 and a dilated right pupil. What is the most likely injury?
qs.a: Epidural hematoma
qs.x: A brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval and then rapid decline after a blow to the temple is the classic picture of an arterial epidural hematoma. This needs rapid transport for surgery.
w: Concussion
Chronic subdural hematoma
Diffuse axonal injury

qs.q: After a fall, a 50-year-old has bruising around both eyes and clear fluid draining from the nose. Which airway adjunct should you avoid?
qs.a: Nasopharyngeal airway
qs.x: Raccoon eyes and CSF rhinorrhea suggest a basilar skull fracture, and a nasal airway could pass through the fractured cribriform plate into the cranial vault. Oral routes are preferred.
w: Oropharyngeal airway
Bag-valve mask with oxygen
Nonrebreather mask

qs.q: A head-injured patient opens his eyes only to pain, says inappropriate words and withdraws from a painful stimulus. What is his GCS?
qs.x: Eye opening to pain scores 2, inappropriate words score 3, and withdrawal from pain scores 4, for a total of 9.

qs.q: A 22-year-old with a stab wound to the right chest had a vented chest seal placed. He is now more short of breath, SpO2 has dropped to 86 percent, HR is 132 and BP 84/52. What should you do first?
qs.a: Lift a corner of the seal to release trapped air
qs.x: A chest seal can clog or fail and allow a tension pneumothorax to build. Burping or briefly removing the dressing is the first step, followed by needle decompression if signs persist.
w: Add a second occlusive dressing over the first one
Increase oxygen and reassess in 5 minutes
Place him on his left side and start a fluid bolus

qs.q: You need to perform needle decompression on an adult with a tension pneumothorax but cannot use the second intercostal space at the midclavicular line. Which alternate site is accepted?
qs.a: Fourth or fifth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line
qs.x: The lateral site at the fourth or fifth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line often has a thinner chest wall. Sites next to the sternum risk the internal mammary vessels, and low anterior sites risk the heart, liver or spleen.
w: Second intercostal space right beside the sternum
Sixth intercostal space at the midclavicular line
Third intercostal space just medial to the nipple

qs.q: A 40-year-old crushed under a vehicle has absent breath sounds on the right, dullness to percussion on that side, flat neck veins and BP 78/50. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Massive hemothorax
qs.x: Dullness with absent breath sounds and flat neck veins point to a chest filling with blood. Tension pneumothorax gives hyperresonance and usually distended neck veins.
w: Tension pneumothorax
Pericardial tamponade
Simple pneumothorax

qs.q: A patient has a suspected massive hemothorax with hypotension, dullness on the left and flat neck veins. What is the best prehospital management?
qs.a: Oxygen, rapid transport and fluids to a radial pulse
qs.x: Needle decompression does not drain blood and will not help a hemothorax. Care is focused on oxygenation, hemorrhage-focused resuscitation that avoids overloading with fluids, and fast transport to surgery.
w: Needle decompression of the left chest
Supine position with legs raised and a 2-liter bolus
An occlusive dressing over the left chest wall

qs.q: A 28-year-old with a stab wound to the left chest is hypotensive. On the monitor the QRS amplitude alternates from tall to short with every beat. What does this suggest?
qs.a: Pericardial tamponade
qs.x: Electrical alternans comes from the heart swinging within a fluid-filled pericardial sac. In a penetrating chest injury with hypotension, it strongly suggests tamponade.
w: Tension pneumothorax
Blunt aortic injury
Ventricular tachycardia

qs.q: A 68-year-old driver struck the steering wheel. A segment of his right chest moves inward when he inhales. RR 30 and shallow, SpO2 88 percent. What is the most serious underlying problem?
qs.a: The bruised lung under the flail segment
qs.x: The paradoxical movement is dramatic, but the main cause of hypoxia is the pulmonary contusion beneath the flail segment. Pain also limits ventilation and adds to the problem.
w: The flail segment collapsing the lung completely
Rib ends lacerating the heart muscle
Loss of the cough reflex

qs.q: A patient with a flail chest has RR 36 with very shallow breaths and SpO2 84 percent on a nonrebreather. What should you do?
qs.a: Assist ventilations with a bag-valve mask
qs.x: Positive pressure ventilation supports gas exchange and splints the flail segment from the inside. Sandbags and tight wrapping restrict chest movement and worsen ventilation.
w: Splint the segment with a sandbag
Wrap the chest tightly with tape
Continue the nonrebreather and recheck in 10 minutes

qs.q: An unrestrained driver's chest struck the steering wheel. He has sternal bruising, HR 118 with frequent PVCs and BP 128/80. What injury should you suspect?
qs.a: Blunt cardiac injury
qs.x: Blunt cardiac injury commonly presents with unexplained tachycardia and dysrhythmias after a blow to the sternum. Cardiac monitoring and a 12-lead ECG are indicated.
w: Commotio cordis
Traumatic aortic rupture
Simple rib contusion

qs.q: After a high-speed frontal crash, a 45-year-old has pain between the shoulder blades and a BP of 150/90 in the right arm but 112/70 in the left. What injury is most likely?
qs.a: Traumatic aortic disruption
qs.x: Sudden deceleration can tear the aorta near the ligamentum arteriosum. Interscapular pain and a blood pressure difference between the arms are warning signs.
w: Blunt cardiac injury
Cervical spine fracture
Tension pneumothorax

qs.q: A 24-year-old snowboarder fell onto his left side. He now has left upper quadrant tenderness, left shoulder pain without shoulder injury, HR 118 and BP 104/70. Which organ is most likely injured?
qs.a: Spleen
qs.x: Pain referred to the left shoulder, called Kehr's sign, comes from blood irritating the diaphragm. With left upper quadrant tenderness it suggests a splenic injury.
w: Liver
Pancreas
Left kidney

qs.q: A 9-year-old restrained only by a lap belt has a band of bruising across the lower abdomen after a crash. Which injuries should you suspect?
qs.a: Bowel and lumbar spine injuries
qs.x: A seatbelt sign raises concern for hollow organ injury and a flexion-distraction fracture of the lumbar spine. Children riding in lap belts without proper boosters are at particular risk.
w: Splenic and left rib injuries
Femur and hip fractures
Cervical spine and facial injuries

qs.q: A 30-year-old with a knife wound to the abdomen has a loop of bowel protruding from the wound. What is the correct care?
qs.a: Cover it with a moist sterile dressing
qs.x: An evisceration is covered with a moist sterile dressing and then an occlusive or dry layer to keep it moist and warm. Replacing the organs risks contamination and further injury.
w: Gently push the bowel back inside
Tape a dry gauze pad tightly over it
Irrigate and leave it uncovered for inspection

qs.q: A motorcyclist has pelvic pain, leg length discrepancy and BP 86/50. How should you assess and handle his pelvis?
qs.a: Avoid rocking it and apply a binder
qs.x: Repeated pelvic compression or rocking can disrupt clots and worsen bleeding. When a fracture is suspected, a binder is applied and movement of the pelvis is kept to a minimum.
w: Rock the iliac crests firmly to confirm instability
Log roll him fully to inspect the back first
Flex his hips to relieve the pelvic pain

qs.q: Why is a pelvic binder applied to a hypotensive patient with a suspected open-book pelvic fracture?
qs.a: It reduces pelvic volume and stabilizes fragments
qs.x: Closing the widened pelvic ring decreases the space for blood to collect and limits fragment movement. This mostly slows venous and bone bleeding while the patient is moved to surgery.
w: It raises the blood pressure by compressing the aorta
It prevents spinal cord injury in the lumbar spine
It allows the legs to be elevated safely

qs.q: A 74-year-old fell forward and struck her chin. She has burning pain in her hands and much more weakness in her arms than in her legs. What spinal cord syndrome is most likely?
qs.a: Central cord syndrome
qs.x: Hyperextension of an arthritic neck in older adults damages the center of the cord, where the arm fibers lie. Weakness is greater in the arms than the legs.
w: Anterior cord syndrome
Brown-Sequard syndrome
Complete cord transection

qs.q: A 26-year-old was stabbed in the back. His right leg is weak with poor position sense, and he cannot feel pain or temperature in his left leg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Brown-Sequard syndrome
qs.x: Damage to one side of the cord causes loss of motor function and position sense on the same side, and loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side.
w: Central cord syndrome
Anterior cord syndrome
Neurogenic shock

qs.q: A 31-year-old ejected from a vehicle has a suspected cervical cord injury with no movement below the shoulders. He is pale, cool and clammy with HR 128 and BP 82/50. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Assume hemorrhage until proven otherwise
qs.x: Neurogenic shock typically causes warm dry skin and a normal or slow heart rate. Tachycardia with cool, clammy skin suggests blood loss, which must be found and treated.
w: Neurogenic shock alone fully explains these findings
This is spinal shock and no treatment is needed
These are signs of a normal stress response

qs.q: After a diving injury, a 20-year-old is quadriplegic with abdominal breathing, RR 28 and shallow, and a falling SpO2. Why is he at high risk for respiratory failure?
qs.a: Intercostal paralysis leaves only the diaphragm
qs.x: Cervical cord injuries paralyze the intercostal muscles, leaving the diaphragm, supplied by C3 to C5, to do all the work. Injuries at or above that level can stop breathing entirely.
w: The phrenic nerve is unaffected by neck injuries
Cord injuries cause bronchospasm
His airway is blocked by the tongue

qs.q: A 40-year-old was burned at 1400 hours and you reach the hospital at 1530. When does the first 8-hour period of the Parkland formula begin?
qs.a: At the time of the burn
qs.x: Half of the 24-hour Parkland volume is given in the first 8 hours counted from the time of injury. Delays in starting fluids mean the remaining volume must be given faster.
w: At hospital arrival
When the first IV is started
When the burn size is calculated

qs.q: An 80-kg man has partial- and full-thickness burns over 25 percent of his body. Using the Parkland formula of 4 mL x kg x percent TBSA, how much fluid is planned for the first 8 hours?
qs.x: The 24-hour total is 4 x 80 x 25, or 8,000 mL, and half of it, 4,000 mL, is planned for the first 8 hours from the burn. Many systems now start with a lower rate and adjust to urine output.

qs.q: A 30-year-old has superficial, red, unblistered burns on 20 percent of his body and partial-thickness blistered burns on 10 percent. What burn size is used for fluid calculations?
qs.a: 10 percent
qs.x: Superficial burns are not counted in the TBSA used for fluid resuscitation. Only partial- and full-thickness burns are included.
w: 20 percent
30 percent
15 percent

qs.q: A 2-year-old has partial-thickness burns to the entire head and both entire arms. Using the pediatric rule of nines, what is the burned surface area?
qs.a: 36 percent
qs.x: In young children the head is about 18 percent and each arm about 9 percent, giving 36 percent. The larger head proportion is the key difference from the adult chart.
w: 27 percent
18 percent
45 percent

qs.q: A 45-year-old has full-thickness circumferential burns around the chest. He is becoming harder to ventilate with a bag-valve mask despite a patent airway. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Stiff eschar restricting chest wall movement
qs.x: Leathery eschar does not stretch, so a circumferential chest burn can restrict ventilation. It may need surgical escharotomy at the hospital.
w: Bronchospasm from the oxygen
A misplaced oral airway
Fluid overload from the IV

qs.q: A lineman contacted a 10,000-volt line. He has a small burn on his hand and another on his foot and is alert with stable vital signs. What is the most important concern?
qs.a: Hidden deep tissue and cardiac injury
qs.x: High-voltage current travels through deep tissue, so small skin wounds hide extensive muscle damage and the risk of dysrhythmias. Cardiac monitoring and transport to a burn center are needed.
w: The burns are minor and need only dressings
He can be released if the ECG is normal on scene
Treat only the visible surface burns

qs.q: A 35-year-old has partial- and full-thickness burns over 45 percent of his body. The fire was put out 10 minutes ago. How should you dress the burns?
qs.a: Clean dry dressings or sheets, keeping him warm
qs.x: Large burns lose heat rapidly, and prolonged cooling causes hypothermia. After the burning process is stopped, cover with clean dry dressings and prevent heat loss.
w: Wet sheets for the whole transport
Ice packs on the deepest burns
Ointment over all burned areas

qs.q: A family of four has headaches, nausea and confusion after running a generator in the garage. The father's SpO2 reads 99 percent. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Standard pulse oximetry can't detect carbon monoxide
qs.x: Standard pulse oximeters read carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin, giving falsely normal values. High-flow oxygen is needed, and CO oximetry should be used if available.
w: His oxygenation is normal, so oxygen is not needed
The reading proves this is a viral illness
The reading rules out poisoning

qs.q: A man pulled from a house fire is unresponsive with seizures, BP 72/40 and a normal SpO2. Cyanide toxicity is suspected along with carbon monoxide. Which antidote approach is preferred?
qs.a: Hydroxocobalamin
qs.x: Nitrites work by creating methemoglobin, which further reduces oxygen delivery in a patient already poisoned with CO. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide without that harm.
w: Amyl and sodium nitrites
Naloxone and observation
Glucagon infusion

qs.q: A 38-year-old pulled from a burning building has singed nasal hair and soot in his mouth. Over 15 minutes his voice becomes hoarse and soft stridor develops. What is the priority?
qs.a: Secure the airway early
qs.x: Progressive hoarseness and stridor signal airway swelling that can close the airway within minutes. Early definitive airway management is safer than waiting.
w: Wait until stridor becomes severe before acting
Give oral fluids to soothe the throat
Place a nasal cannula at 2 L/min

qs.q: A 50-year-old's legs have been pinned under a concrete slab for 4 hours. Rescuers are ready to lift it. What should you do before the slab is lifted?
qs.a: Start IV fluids and apply the cardiac monitor
qs.x: Release of a prolonged crush sends potassium, acid and myoglobin into the circulation. Fluids before release and cardiac monitoring help prevent sudden dysrhythmias and kidney injury.
w: Apply tourniquets to both legs and leave them for transport
Lift the slab right away and assess afterward
Elevate his head and apply ice to his legs

qs.q: Minutes after a crushed leg is freed, the patient's ECG shows tall peaked T waves and a widening QRS. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Hyperkalemia
qs.x: Potassium released from damaged muscle causes peaked T waves and QRS widening and can lead to cardiac arrest. Treatment follows protocol for hyperkalemia.
w: Hypokalemia
Hypothermia
Hypocalcemia alone

qs.q: A 28-year-old with a splinted tibia fracture has worsening leg pain out of proportion to the injury and severe pain when you gently move his toes. Pedal pulses are present. What is the most likely problem?
qs.a: Compartment syndrome
qs.x: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are early signs of compartment syndrome. Pulses are often present until very late, so a pulse does not rule it out.
w: Arterial transection
Fat embolism
Deep vein thrombosis

qs.q: After a bomb blast, a woman has multiple penetrating wounds from flying glass. What category of blast injury is this?
qs.a: Secondary
qs.x: Secondary blast injuries come from debris and fragments driven by the explosion. Primary is the pressure wave, tertiary is the body being thrown, and quaternary includes burns and other effects.
w: Primary
Tertiary
Quaternary

qs.q: A woman 34 weeks pregnant was in a car crash. She is supine on a long board and complains of dizziness, BP 88/50, HR 110. What should you do first?
qs.a: Manually displace the uterus to the left
qs.x: In late pregnancy the uterus compresses the vena cava when the patient is supine. Moving the uterus to the left or tilting the board improves venous return.
w: Raise her legs and start a large fluid bolus
Place her in Trendelenburg
Sit her upright at 90 degrees

qs.q: A pregnant trauma patient seems stable, but her fetus may be in danger. What is the most effective way to protect the fetus in the field?
qs.a: Aggressively resuscitate the mother
qs.x: The body diverts blood away from the uterus to protect the mother, so the fetus may be in shock before maternal vital signs change. Supporting the mother's oxygenation and circulation is the best fetal care.
w: Focus on fetal heart tones before maternal care
Keep the mother supine for close monitoring
Withhold fluids to avoid placental swelling

qs.q: A woman 30 weeks pregnant had a car crash. She has steady abdominal pain, a rigid tender uterus and only slight vaginal bleeding. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Placental abruption
qs.x: A painful, rigid uterus after trauma suggests the placenta has separated. Bleeding may be concealed behind the placenta, so the amount seen does not reflect blood loss.
w: Placenta previa
Normal labor
Ectopic pregnancy

qs.q: An 8-year-old was run over by a car. You feel no rib fractures, but she has crackles, RR 34 and SpO2 89 percent. Why is lung injury likely despite intact ribs?
qs.a: Pliable ribs pass the force to the lungs
qs.x: A child's flexible chest wall bends without breaking and transfers energy to the lungs. Pulmonary contusion without rib fractures is common.
w: Children's lungs are larger than adults'
Rib fractures in children are always hidden
Hypoxia in children is normal after trauma

qs.q: You place a 3-year-old supine on a firm surface for spinal motion restriction. His neck flexes forward because of his large head. What should you do?
qs.a: Pad under the shoulders and torso
qs.x: A young child's large occiput flexes the neck when lying flat. Padding under the torso brings the spine into a neutral position.
w: Place a folded towel under the head
Tape the forehead down more tightly
Elevate the head of the board 30 degrees

qs.q: What systolic blood pressure indicates hypotension in a 5-year-old trauma patient?
qs.a: Below 80 mmHg
qs.x: Hypotension in children 1 to 10 years is a systolic pressure below 70 plus twice the age in years, so below 80 for a 5-year-old. Hypotension is a late sign in children.
w: Below 70 mmHg
Below 90 mmHg
Below 100 mmHg

qs.q: Under the 2021 National Guideline for Field Triage, which systolic pressure meets a red criterion in a trauma patient 65 or older?
qs.a: Below 110 mmHg
qs.x: The 2021 guideline uses a systolic pressure below 110 in patients 65 and older because older adults may be in shock at pressures that look normal. A heart rate greater than the systolic pressure is also a criterion.
w: Below 90 mmHg
Below 80 mmHg
Below 100 mmHg

qs.q: A 30-year-old fell 14 feet from scaffolding. He is alert with normal vital signs and only a sprained wrist. Under the 2021 field triage guideline, what is the right destination?
qs.a: A trauma center, not necessarily the highest level
qs.x: A fall from more than 10 feet is a yellow mechanism criterion that calls for a trauma center. Without red criteria, it need not be the highest level.
w: The highest-level trauma center only
The closest emergency department regardless of level
No transport is needed

qs.q: A 26-year-old shot in the left chest has just lost his pulse in front of you, with PEA on the monitor. Which intervention is most likely to help?
qs.a: Bilateral needle decompression
qs.x: In traumatic arrest, outcomes depend on correcting the cause, such as tension pneumothorax, bleeding or hypoxia. Decompressing the chest addresses a reversible cause quickly.
w: Repeated epinephrine with CPR on scene
Synchronized cardioversion
A prolonged search for medical causes

qs.q: A 36-year-old has a laceration on the side of the neck with dark blood flowing and sucking sounds from the wound. What should you apply?
qs.a: An occlusive dressing
qs.x: An open neck vein can draw in air and cause a fatal air embolism. An occlusive dressing with careful pressure seals the wound without obstructing the airway.
w: A tourniquet around the neck
A dry, loosely taped gauze pad
A circumferential pressure bandage

qs.q: A 79-year-old on metoprolol fell down stairs. He is pale with a firm, distended abdomen. HR 74, BP 112/70. How should you interpret his heart rate?
qs.a: Beta blockers may mask tachycardia from bleeding
qs.x: Beta blockers blunt the heart rate response to blood loss, and older adults may be in shock with pressures that look normal. Rely on other findings such as the abdomen and skin.
w: A normal heart rate rules out significant bleeding
He is in neurogenic shock
His blood pressure proves he is stable

qs.q: An 84-year-old on an anticoagulant fell yesterday and hit her head. Today she is more confused and has a headache. What injury is most likely?
qs.a: Subdural hematoma
qs.x: Brain atrophy stretches the bridging veins in older adults, and anticoagulants make them bleed more. Subdural bleeding often causes delayed decline hours to days later.
w: Epidural hematoma
Concussion with no bleeding
Basilar skull fracture

qs.q: Which components make up the lethal triad of trauma? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hypothermia; Acidosis; Coagulopathy
qs.x: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy feed one another and worsen bleeding. Field care aims to prevent heat loss and avoid diluting clotting factors with large fluid volumes.
opts: Hypothermia
Acidosis
Coagulopathy
Hyperglycemia
Hypertension
ok: Hypothermia
Acidosis
Coagulopathy

qs.q: Which findings make up Beck's triad? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Muffled heart sounds; Distended neck veins; Hypotension
qs.x: Beck's triad of muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distension and hypotension suggests pericardial tamponade. Tracheal deviation points to tension pneumothorax, and Cushing's response suggests raised ICP.
opts: Muffled heart sounds
Distended neck veins
Hypotension
Tracheal deviation
Bradycardia with hypertension
ok: Muffled heart sounds
Distended neck veins
Hypotension

qs.q: Which findings support a tension pneumothorax? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Absent breath sounds on one side; Distended neck veins; Hypotension with worsening respiratory distress
qs.x: Unilateral absent breath sounds, JVD and shock with increasing distress suggest tension pneumothorax. Dullness suggests blood, and bradycardia with warm skin suggests neurogenic shock.
opts: Absent breath sounds on one side
Distended neck veins
Hypotension with worsening respiratory distress
Dullness to percussion on the affected side
Bradycardia with warm, dry skin
ok: Absent breath sounds on one side
Distended neck veins
Hypotension with worsening respiratory distress

qs.q: Which findings are consistent with compartment syndrome? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Pain out of proportion to the injury; Pain on passive stretch of the muscles; A tense, firm compartment
qs.x: Severe pain, pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment are the important early findings. Pulses usually remain until late, so their presence does not rule it out.
opts: Pain out of proportion to the injury
Pain on passive stretch of the muscles
A tense, firm compartment
Absent distal pulses are required to make the diagnosis
Pain relieved completely by splinting
ok: Pain out of proportion to the injury
Pain on passive stretch of the muscles
A tense, firm compartment

qs.q: Which findings are typical of neurogenic shock? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hypotension; Bradycardia or a normal heart rate; Warm, dry skin below the injury
qs.x: Loss of sympathetic tone causes vasodilation and an unopposed vagal effect on the heart. Cool clammy skin and tachycardia suggest hemorrhagic shock instead.
opts: Hypotension
Bradycardia or a normal heart rate
Warm, dry skin below the injury
Pale, cool, clammy skin
Marked tachycardia
ok: Hypotension
Bradycardia or a normal heart rate
Warm, dry skin below the injury

qs.q: After a prolonged crush injury is released, which complications should you anticipate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hyperkalemia; Kidney injury from myoglobin; Hypovolemia from fluid shifting into tissues
qs.x: Damaged muscle releases potassium and myoglobin, and fluid moves into injured tissue. Calcium usually falls rather than rises.
opts: Hyperkalemia
Kidney injury from myoglobin
Hypovolemia from fluid shifting into tissues
Hypoglycemia
Hypercalcemia
ok: Hyperkalemia
Kidney injury from myoglobin
Hypovolemia from fluid shifting into tissues

qs.q: Which injuries result from the primary blast wave? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Ruptured eardrums; Blast lung; Bowel perforation
qs.x: The pressure wave injures air-filled organs. Shrapnel wounds are secondary, and injuries from being thrown are tertiary.
opts: Ruptured eardrums
Blast lung
Bowel perforation
Wounds from flying shrapnel
A fracture from being thrown into a wall
ok: Ruptured eardrums
Blast lung
Bowel perforation

qs.q: Which normal changes of late pregnancy affect trauma assessment? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Blood volume increases by up to about 50 percent; Resting heart rate is higher than usual; The uterus can compress the vena cava when supine
qs.x: Increased blood volume can hide early blood loss, and a higher heart rate is normal. Blood pressure tends to drop slightly, and reduced functional residual capacity makes pregnant patients desaturate quickly.
opts: Blood volume increases by up to about 50 percent
Resting heart rate is higher than usual
The uterus can compress the vena cava when supine
Blood pressure is usually higher than before pregnancy
Lung reserve volume is larger, so hypoxia develops slowly
ok: Blood volume increases by up to about 50 percent
Resting heart rate is higher than usual
The uterus can compress the vena cava when supine

qs.q: Which features make children more prone to certain injury patterns? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A proportionally larger and heavier head; Liver and spleen less protected by the ribs; A flexible chest wall
qs.x: A large head leads to more head injuries, the solid organs extend below a pliable rib cage, and force passes to the lungs. Children have thinner abdominal walls and relatively large tongues.
opts: A proportionally larger and heavier head
Liver and spleen less protected by the ribs
A flexible chest wall
Thicker abdominal wall muscles
A proportionally smaller tongue
ok: A proportionally larger and heavier head
Liver and spleen less protected by the ribs
A flexible chest wall

qs.q: Which factors increase the risk of serious injury in older trauma patients? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use; Beta blockers masking tachycardia; Brain atrophy that stretches bridging veins
qs.x: Anticoagulants increase bleeding, beta blockers hide signs of shock, and brain atrophy raises the risk of subdural bleeding. Bones become more brittle with age.
opts: Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use
Beta blockers masking tachycardia
Brain atrophy that stretches bridging veins
A stronger and more elastic rib cage
An exaggerated fever response to injury
ok: Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use
Beta blockers masking tachycardia
Brain atrophy that stretches bridging veins

qs.q: Under the 2021 field triage guideline, which findings are EMS judgment factors that should prompt consideration of a trauma center? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Anticoagulant use; Pregnancy beyond 20 weeks; A fall from standing with head impact in an older adult
qs.x: The guideline lists anticoagulant use, pregnancy over 20 weeks and low-level falls with head impact in older adults or young children as factors to weigh. Patient preference alone is not a triage criterion.
opts: Anticoagulant use
Pregnancy beyond 20 weeks
A fall from standing with head impact in an older adult
A minor finger laceration in a healthy adult
A patient request to go to a specific hospital
ok: Anticoagulant use
Pregnancy beyond 20 weeks
A fall from standing with head impact in an older adult

qs.q: Which wound locations are junctional areas where a limb tourniquet usually cannot control bleeding? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Groin; Axilla; Neck
qs.x: Junctional areas lie where the limbs or head join the torso. Wounds there need packing, direct pressure or junctional devices, while mid-limb wounds can take a tourniquet.
opts: Groin
Axilla
Neck
Mid-thigh
Mid-forearm
ok: Groin
Axilla
Neck

qs.q: Which findings suggest carbon monoxide poisoning? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Headache and nausea in several people from the same home; Symptoms that improve after leaving the building; Confusion with a normal standard SpO2 reading
qs.x: Grouped symptoms that improve away from the source and falsely normal pulse oximetry point to CO. Cherry red skin is a late and unreliable finding.
opts: Headache and nausea in several people from the same home
Symptoms that improve after leaving the building
Confusion with a normal standard SpO2 reading
A low SpO2 that improves with oxygen proves it is not CO
Cherry red skin is required for the diagnosis
ok: Headache and nausea in several people from the same home
Symptoms that improve after leaving the building
Confusion with a normal standard SpO2 reading

qs.q: Which findings suggest a basilar skull fracture? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Bruising behind the ear; Bruising around both eyes; Clear fluid draining from the ear
qs.x: Battle's sign, raccoon eyes and CSF leakage suggest a basilar skull fracture. Periumbilical and flank bruising suggest intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal bleeding.
opts: Bruising behind the ear
Bruising around both eyes
Clear fluid draining from the ear
Bruising around the umbilicus
Bruising along the flank
ok: Bruising behind the ear
Bruising around both eyes
Clear fluid draining from the ear

qs.q: You call a physician by radio for permission to give a treatment not covered by your standing orders. What type of medical direction is this?
qs.a: Online medical direction
qs.x: Online medical direction is real-time contact with a physician. Offline direction includes protocols, standing orders, training and quality review.
w: Offline medical direction
Retrospective medical direction
Prospective protocol direction

qs.q: Online medical direction orders a medication dose that you believe is ten times too high. What should you do?
qs.a: Repeat the order back and question it
qs.x: Repeating orders back is a safety step. If an order seems wrong, ask for clarification, and do not carry out an order you believe would harm the patient; document the exchange.
w: Give it as ordered because the physician is responsible
Give half the dose without telling anyone
Give the dose you think is correct

qs.q: A 45-year-old diabetic has a glucose of 38 mg/dL. He is confused and refuses care. What is true about his refusal?
qs.a: He lacks capacity, so treat under implied consent
qs.x: Hypoglycemia with confusion impairs the ability to understand and weigh choices. Without capacity, emergency treatment proceeds under implied consent per protocol.
w: His refusal must be honored because he is an adult
You must wait for police before giving any care
You must get written consent from his spouse first

qs.q: A married 17-year-old with a minor ankle injury declines transport. She is alert and understands the risks. How should you proceed?
qs.a: Treat her as an adult who may refuse
qs.x: Minors who are married or otherwise emancipated can usually consent to or refuse their own care. Local law defines emancipation, so follow protocol.
w: Transport her against her will because she is a minor
Call her parents to consent for her
Have police place her in custody

qs.q: A 70-year-old with a POLST marked do not resuscitate and selective treatment is in respiratory distress from pneumonia with a pulse. Which care fits his orders?
qs.a: CPAP, IV fluids and transport
qs.x: Selective treatment allows noninvasive care such as CPAP, IV fluids and hospital transport, but not intubation. A DNR applies to cardiac arrest, while the POLST guides care when a pulse is present.
w: Intubation and mechanical ventilation
No treatment because a DNR is in place
Comfort care only, with no transport

qs.q: A patient with a valid DNR order develops a narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 with chest pain and is still awake. How should you proceed?
qs.a: Treat the dysrhythmia per protocol
qs.x: A DNR applies to resuscitation after cardiac arrest. Conditions with a pulse are treated normally unless another order limits care.
w: Withhold all treatment because of the DNR
Wait until he becomes pulseless
Ask the family to decide

qs.q: An 88-year-old is found in cardiac arrest. The family says she has a DNR, but no one can find the document. What should you do?
qs.a: Begin resuscitation and contact medical direction
qs.x: Without valid documentation, most protocols require resuscitation. Medical direction can help while the family searches.
w: Withhold resuscitation based on the family's word
Wait until the document is found
Pronounce death without assessment

qs.q: Which statement is an example of a pertinent negative in a chest pain report?
qs.a: Denies shortness of breath
qs.x: A pertinent negative documents an important finding that is absent, such as no shortness of breath with chest pain. It shows the finding was checked.
w: Patient is a 54-year-old male
Patient was found sitting in a recliner

qs.q: You smell alcohol on a patient's breath. Which narrative entry is most appropriate?
qs.a: Odor of an alcoholic beverage on the breath
qs.x: Documentation should be objective and describe what you observed. Labels and opinions can be used against you and may be libelous.
w: Patient was drunk
Patient was intoxicated and belligerent
Typical drunk patient, uncooperative

qs.q: Your partner asks you to record a medication on the report that was never given, to match the narcotic count. What should you do?
qs.a: Refuse, document accurately and report it
qs.x: Falsifying a medical record is illegal and dishonest. Accurate records and reporting a narcotic discrepancy through proper channels are required.
w: Record it as given to keep things simple
Leave the medication off the report
Record it with a note that you are unsure

qs.q: An alert adult with capacity refuses care, but a paramedic threatens to restrain her if she does not comply. What has the paramedic committed?
qs.a: Assault
qs.x: Assault is causing a person to fear immediate bodily harm. Battery is unlawful touching without consent.
w: Battery
Libel
Abandonment

qs.q: You arrive at a hospital emergency department with a patient. The charge nurse asks you to take her to another hospital without being seen. What applies?
qs.a: EMTALA requires a medical screening exam
qs.x: Once a patient arrives on hospital property seeking emergency care, EMTALA requires a medical screening exam and stabilization. Hospitals cannot turn patients away for financial or capacity reasons alone.
w: The hospital may refuse any patient it chooses
You must leave right away for the other hospital
Only HIPAA applies to this situation

qs.q: An 85-year-old who depends on her son has pressure sores, soiled bedding and unexplained bruises. What must you do?
qs.a: Report suspected elder abuse per state law
qs.x: EMS providers are mandated reporters of suspected elder abuse and neglect in most states. Report as required and document objective findings.
w: Leave it to the family to manage
Confront the son on scene
Report it only if the patient asks you to

qs.q: You honor an alert, capable patient's decision to decline a treatment you recommend. Which ethical principle are you following?
qs.a: Autonomy
qs.x: Autonomy is the right of capable people to make their own decisions. Beneficence is doing good, nonmaleficence is avoiding harm, and justice is fairness.
w: Beneficence
Justice
Nonmaleficence

qs.q: You are asked to transfer a patient with an infusion outside your scope of practice. What should you do?
qs.a: Request a qualified provider to accompany the patient
qs.x: Paramedics cannot manage care beyond their scope. A qualified provider can accompany the patient, or the sending physician can change the treatment.
w: Transport and manage the infusion yourself
Stop the infusion yourself without asking
Refuse the transfer without discussion

qs.q: A large incident involves fire, police and EMS from several jurisdictions. What ICS structure should be used?
qs.a: Unified command
qs.x: Unified command lets agencies with responsibility share decisions and set common objectives. Separate commands lead to conflicts.
w: Single command
A separate command for each agency
Area command for each department

qs.q: What is the recommended span of control for a supervisor in ICS?
qs.a: Three to seven, ideally five
qs.x: A span of control of three to seven, with five ideal, keeps supervisors effective. Larger groups should be divided into more units.
w: One to two
Ten to fifteen
As many as the situation demands

qs.q: At a mass casualty incident, which officer manages arriving ambulances and assigns them when needed?
qs.a: Staging officer
qs.x: The staging officer tracks and releases resources as requested. This prevents vehicle congestion at the scene.
w: Treatment officer
Triage officer
Safety officer

qs.q: At a mass casualty incident, who coordinates patient destinations so the nearest hospital is not overwhelmed?
qs.a: Transport officer
qs.x: The transport officer works with hospitals to distribute patients. This prevents a single facility from being overloaded.
w: Staging officer
Public information officer
Liaison officer

qs.q: In SALT triage, which patients are assessed first after the global sort?
qs.a: Those who are still or have an obvious life threat
qs.x: SALT asks walking patients to move and others to wave. Patients who do neither are assessed first.
w: Those who walk to the designated area
Those who wave or move purposefully
Those who are crying loudly

qs.q: Under START triage, an adult who cannot walk has RR 22 and a radial pulse but cannot follow simple commands. What category is assigned?
qs.a: Immediate
qs.x: START checks respirations, perfusion and mental status. Failure to follow simple commands puts the patient in the immediate category.
w: Delayed
Minor
Expectant

qs.q: During JumpSTART triage, a 6-year-old who cannot walk has a respiratory rate of 48. What category is assigned?
qs.a: Immediate
qs.x: In JumpSTART, a respiratory rate below 15 or above 45 is immediate. The child's range differs from the adult threshold.
w: Delayed
Minor
Deceased

qs.q: At an MCI, a 7-month-old cannot walk because of her age. How is she triaged with JumpSTART?
qs.a: Continue through the full algorithm
qs.x: Infants who cannot walk because of development are evaluated with the rest of the algorithm. They are not automatically assigned minor.
w: Assign minor because she cannot walk
Assign immediate due to her age
Leave her for last

qs.q: You are approaching a tanker rollover with a placard on the tank. What is the safest approach?
qs.a: Approach from uphill and upwind, using binoculars
qs.x: Staying uphill and upwind keeps vapors and runoff away. Placards and the ERG can be read from a distance.
w: Approach downwind for a closer look
Approach from downhill to stay low
Approach directly to read the placard up close

qs.q: Patients from a chemical release are arriving at your location. Which single action removes the largest share of contamination?
qs.a: Removing their clothing
qs.x: Removing clothing removes much of the contaminant. Washing with water follows for liquid exposures.
w: Washing their hair first
Spraying them with bleach
Covering them in blankets

qs.q: After a subway vapor release, several commuters have runny noses and pinpoint pupils but no breathing problems. What exposure should you suspect?
qs.a: Mild nerve agent vapor exposure
qs.x: Miosis is the most consistent sign of nerve agent vapor exposure, often with rhinorrhea. More severe exposures add secretions, bronchospasm and seizures.
w: Cyanide poisoning
Opioid overdose
Chlorine gas exposure

qs.q: Several patients have a fever and a rash, with all lesions at the same stage and concentrated on the face and limbs. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Smallpox
qs.x: Smallpox lesions are at the same stage and concentrated on the face and limbs. Chickenpox lesions vary in stage and appear mostly on the trunk.
w: Chickenpox
Measles
Anthrax

qs.q: At an active shooter incident, you reach a victim with severe leg bleeding while the shooter is still active nearby. What should you do?
qs.a: Apply a tourniquet and move to cover
qs.x: In direct threat care, only massive bleeding is treated with a tourniquet before moving to cover. Other care waits for a safer zone.
w: Perform a full primary survey on the spot
Insert an airway and start an IV
Leave the victim because it is unsafe

qs.q: At an active shooter incident, where does a rescue task force operate?
qs.a: The warm zone, with police protection
qs.x: Rescue task forces work in areas that have been cleared but are not fully secured. Police provide protection while EMS treats and removes victims.
w: The hot zone, before police arrive
Only the cold zone
Inside the command post

qs.q: A helicopter has landed at your scene. How should you approach it?
qs.a: From the front, only when signaled by the crew
qs.x: Approach in view of the pilot and only after signaling. Tail rotors and uphill approaches risk serious injury.
w: From the tail to stay out of the pilot's sight
From uphill so you are close to the rotor
As soon as it lands to save time

qs.q: During air transport, what happens to an untreated pneumothorax as altitude increases?
qs.a: It expands
qs.x: Gas expands as pressure decreases, by Boyle's law. Air in the chest or a tube cuff expands with altitude.
w: It shrinks
It does not change
It resolves on its own

qs.q: You stick yourself with a used needle. What should you do first?
qs.a: Wash with soap and water and report right away
qs.x: Wash the area immediately and report so testing and prophylaxis can start quickly. Prophylaxis works best when started within hours.
w: Wait until the end of your shift to report
Squeeze the wound and apply bleach
Ignore it if the patient seems healthy

qs.q: After caring for a patient with C. difficile diarrhea, how should you clean your hands?
qs.a: Soap and water
qs.x: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores. Washing with soap and water removes them.
w: Alcohol gel only
A dry towel
Gloves alone without hand cleaning

qs.q: When removing PPE after caring for a patient on airborne precautions, which item is removed last?
qs.a: The respirator
qs.x: The respirator is removed last, after leaving the room, and then hands are cleaned.
w: The gloves
The gown
The eye protection

qs.q: Your partner says "give 1 mg of epinephrine," and you reply "giving 1 mg of epinephrine" before giving it, then confirm "1 mg given." What practice is this?
qs.a: Closed-loop communication
qs.x: Closed-loop communication confirms the order and its completion, reducing errors.
w: Situational awareness
Task fixation
Implied consent

qs.q: You are working on a highway crash. How should the fire apparatus be positioned?
qs.a: Upstream, to block traffic
qs.x: Positioning apparatus upstream protects workers from oncoming traffic. Responders should also wear high-visibility vests.
w: Downstream, beyond the scene
On the opposite side of the road
Parked as close to the patient as possible

qs.q: A colleague says he feels hopeless and has been thinking about not being here after a series of bad calls. What should you do?
qs.a: Ask directly about suicide and connect him to help
qs.x: Asking directly about suicide does not increase risk and allows you to connect the person with help.
w: Tell him to take a few days off and see
Avoid the topic so it does not upset him
Report him for disciplinary action

qs.q: Which type of study provides the strongest evidence for a treatment?
qs.a: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials
qs.x: Systematic reviews of well-designed randomized trials give the highest level of evidence.
w: Single case report
Expert opinion
Retrospective chart review

qs.q: What does high sensitivity in a diagnostic test mean?
qs.a: It correctly identifies most people with the condition
qs.x: Sensitivity is the ability to detect people who have the condition. Specificity is the ability to identify those who do not.
w: It correctly identifies most people without the condition
It never gives false positives
It works only in large populations

qs.q: Why are patients randomized in a clinical trial?
qs.a: To reduce bias between groups
qs.x: Randomization balances known and unknown factors so differences in outcome can be attributed to the treatment.
w: To make sure patients choose their treatment
To speed up enrollment
To avoid the need for consent

qs.q: Which elements show that a patient has decision-making capacity? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Understands information about his condition; Appreciates the consequences of his choice; Can communicate a clear choice
qs.x: Capacity means understanding, appreciating consequences, reasoning and communicating a choice. Disagreement or a mental health history alone does not remove capacity.
opts: Understands information about his condition
Appreciates the consequences of his choice
Can communicate a clear choice
Agrees with the paramedic's advice
Has no history of mental illness
ok: Understands information about his condition
Appreciates the consequences of his choice
Can communicate a clear choice

qs.q: Under EMTALA, which conditions should be met before an unstable patient is transferred? Select all that apply.
qs.a: The receiving facility has accepted the patient; Copies of medical records go with the patient; Transfer uses qualified staff and equipment
qs.x: EMTALA requires an accepting facility, records and appropriate transport. Payment cannot be a factor.
opts: The receiving facility has accepted the patient
Copies of medical records go with the patient
Transfer uses qualified staff and equipment
The patient has paid in advance
The sending hospital has run out of beds for any patient
ok: The receiving facility has accepted the patient
Copies of medical records go with the patient
Transfer uses qualified staff and equipment

qs.q: Which life-saving interventions are allowed during SALT triage? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Controlling major hemorrhage; Opening the airway; Needle chest decompression
qs.x: SALT permits fast interventions such as bleeding control, airway opening, chest decompression and antidote autoinjectors. Time-consuming care waits.
opts: Controlling major hemorrhage
Opening the airway
Needle chest decompression
Placing an endotracheal tube
Starting IV fluids
ok: Controlling major hemorrhage
Opening the airway
Needle chest decompression

qs.q: Which findings suggest severe nerve agent poisoning? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Pinpoint pupils; Copious secretions; Muscle twitching
qs.x: Nerve agents cause excess secretions, miosis and muscle twitching. Dry, flushed skin with dilated pupils suggests an anticholinergic syndrome.
opts: Pinpoint pupils
Copious secretions
Muscle twitching
Dilated pupils with dry skin
Warm, flushed skin
ok: Pinpoint pupils
Copious secretions
Muscle twitching

qs.q: Which actions are appropriate in the hot zone during an active threat? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Apply a tourniquet for severe bleeding; Move the patient to cover
qs.x: Care in the hot zone is limited to bleeding control and moving to cover. Other care waits for safer zones.
opts: Apply a tourniquet for severe bleeding
Move the patient to cover
Insert an advanced airway
Start an IV
Perform a full secondary assessment
ok: Apply a tourniquet for severe bleeding
Move the patient to cover

qs.q: Which practices are part of crew resource management? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Closed-loop communication; Encouraging any crew member to speak up about safety concerns; Using checklists for high-risk procedures
qs.x: CRM relies on clear communication, speaking up and checklists. Silent deference leads to errors.
opts: Closed-loop communication
Encouraging any crew member to speak up about safety concerns
Using checklists for high-risk procedures
Deferring to the most senior person without question
Keeping concerns to yourself to avoid conflict
ok: Closed-loop communication
Encouraging any crew member to speak up about safety concerns
Using checklists for high-risk procedures

qs.q: Which items should be included when documenting a refusal? Select all that apply.
qs.a: An assessment of the patient's capacity; The risks explained to the patient; The patient's signature or a witness
qs.x: Documentation should show capacity, the information given and the patient's decision. Opinions and false assurances are inappropriate.
opts: An assessment of the patient's capacity
The risks explained to the patient
The patient's signature or a witness
Your opinion that the patient is foolish
A promise that nothing bad will happen
ok: An assessment of the patient's capacity
The risks explained to the patient
The patient's signature or a witness

qs.q: Which practices help protect a restrained, combative patient? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Placing him supine or on his side; Monitoring breathing and SpO2 continuously; Using enough personnel to restrain safely
qs.x: Prone restraint and pressure on the back can cause positional asphyxia. Continuous monitoring and adequate staff improve safety.
opts: Placing him supine or on his side
Monitoring breathing and SpO2 continuously
Using enough personnel to restrain safely
Hog-tying him in the prone position
Placing a backboard on top of him
ok: Placing him supine or on his side
Monitoring breathing and SpO2 continuously
Using enough personnel to restrain safely

qs.q: Which practices make a helicopter landing zone safer? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Clearing loose debris; Identifying overhead wires; Keeping bystanders well away
qs.x: Debris, wires and bystanders are major hazards. Lights should not blind the pilot, and level ground is preferred.
opts: Clearing loose debris
Identifying overhead wires
Keeping bystanders well away
Shining lights into the pilot's eyes
Choosing a steep slope
ok: Clearing loose debris
Identifying overhead wires
Keeping bystanders well away

qs.q: Which ethical principles are shown in the following actions? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Avoiding unnecessary harm reflects nonmaleficence; Allocating scarce resources fairly reflects justice; Acting in the patient's best interest reflects beneficence
qs.x: Nonmaleficence, justice and beneficence are core principles. Hiding errors violates honesty, and overriding capable refusals violates autonomy.
opts: Avoiding unnecessary harm reflects nonmaleficence
Allocating scarce resources fairly reflects justice
Acting in the patient's best interest reflects beneficence
Hiding errors from patients reflects honesty
Overriding capable refusals reflects autonomy
ok: Avoiding unnecessary harm reflects nonmaleficence
Allocating scarce resources fairly reflects justice
Acting in the patient's best interest reflects beneficence

qs.q: A 29-year-old in status epilepticus stops seizing after a benzodiazepine. He remains unresponsive with snoring respirations at 6 per minute and SpO2 86 percent. What should you do next?
qs.a: Open the airway and assist ventilations
qs.x: Benzodiazepines and the postictal state can both depress breathing. A rate of 6 with snoring and hypoxia is inadequate, so the airway must be opened and ventilations assisted with a bag-valve mask.
w: Give a second benzodiazepine dose to prevent a recurrence
Place him in the recovery position and observe him
Give naloxone to reverse the respiratory depression

qs.q: A 52-year-old's generalized seizure stopped 20 minutes ago, but she is still unresponsive, with rhythmic twitching of the right eyelid and fingers and her eyes deviated to the right. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Ongoing subtle seizure activity
qs.x: Failure to wake combined with subtle rhythmic movements or gaze deviation suggests nonconvulsive status epilepticus, which needs treatment just like a visible convulsion.
w: A normal postictal recovery period
A psychogenic nonepileptic event
Expected sedation from the seizure

qs.q: A 67-year-old with diabetes is found with new right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Which assessment is most important to complete before activating a stroke alert?
qs.a: A blood glucose measurement
qs.x: Hypoglycemia is a common, quickly reversible stroke mimic that can produce focal deficits. A glucose check should precede stroke activation and destination decisions.
w: A 12-lead ECG to look for atrial fibrillation
Orthostatic blood pressure measurements
A check of the deep tendon reflexes

qs.q: A 74-year-old developed symptoms 40 minutes ago. She has dense left-sided weakness, her eyes are deviated to the right, and she ignores people standing on her left. What do these findings suggest?
qs.a: A large vessel occlusion stroke
qs.x: Cortical signs such as gaze deviation, neglect and aphasia with dense hemiparesis suggest a large vessel occlusion, which may benefit from transport to a thrombectomy-capable center under local destination protocols.
w: A small lacunar stroke deep in the brain
A transient ischemic attack that will resolve
Hypertensive encephalopathy

qs.q: A 62-year-old went to bed at 22:00 acting normally. His wife found him unable to speak when he woke at 06:30. What is his last known well time?
qs.a: 22:00 the previous night
qs.x: Last known well is the last time the patient was confirmed to be at baseline. For wake-up strokes that is the time he went to sleep, not the time the deficit was discovered.
w: 06:30, when his wife found him
The time the 911 call was placed
Midnight, at the start of the new day

qs.q: A 40-year-old has a new facial droop. Which finding most suggests Bell palsy rather than a stroke?
qs.a: Loss of forehead wrinkling on the affected side
qs.x: The forehead has nerve supply from both sides of the brain, so a central (stroke) lesion usually spares it. Inability to raise the brow on the affected side points to a peripheral facial nerve palsy.
w: Slurred speech with drift of the arm on the same side
Sudden onset of the droop within the last hour
Drooping at the corner of the mouth on smiling

qs.q: Which conditions are recognized mimics of an acute stroke? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hypoglycemia; Postictal weakness after a seizure; Complicated migraine
qs.x: Hypoglycemia, postictal (Todd) paralysis and complicated migraine can all cause focal neurologic deficits. Stroke still cannot be excluded in the field until a glucose check and full assessment are done.
opts: Hypoglycemia
Postictal weakness after a seizure
Complicated migraine
Renal colic
Acute otitis externa
Plantar fasciitis
ok: Hypoglycemia
Postictal weakness after a seizure
Complicated migraine

qs.q: A 19-year-old college student has fever, severe headache, a stiff neck and a purple rash on her legs that does not blanch. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Use droplet precautions with masks for the crew and the patient; Assess closely for signs of septic shock; Notify the receiving facility early
qs.x: Fever, meningismus and a non-blanching rash suggest meningococcal infection, which spreads by droplets and can progress rapidly to shock. Early notification speeds antibiotics and isolation.
opts: Use droplet precautions with masks for the crew and the patient
Assess closely for signs of septic shock
Notify the receiving facility early
Treat the rash as a drug reaction with an antihistamine alone
Skip masks because meningitis spreads only through blood
ok: Use droplet precautions with masks for the crew and the patient
Assess closely for signs of septic shock
Notify the receiving facility early

qs.q: A 2-month-old has a temperature of 38.6 C (101.5 F), poor feeding and irritability that worsens when his mother picks him up. His anterior fontanelle is bulging. What is the most concerning possibility?
qs.a: Meningitis
qs.x: Young infants with meningitis rarely show a stiff neck. Fever with paradoxical irritability, poor feeding and a bulging fontanelle should be treated as meningitis until proven otherwise.
w: Infant colic
Acute otitis media
Teething pain

qs.q: A 38-year-old has weakness that began in his feet two weeks after a diarrheal illness and has climbed to his hands. His reflexes are absent. Which findings suggest he is heading toward respiratory failure? Select all that apply.
qs.a: He cannot count to 20 in a single breath; His cough is weak and secretions are pooling; His ETCO2 is rising
qs.x: Ascending weakness with areflexia suggests Guillain-Barre syndrome, which can paralyze the respiratory muscles. A weak cough, short breath counts and rising CO2 signal failing ventilation, while a normal SpO2 can be falsely reassuring.
opts: He cannot count to 20 in a single breath
His cough is weak and secretions are pooling
His ETCO2 is rising
His SpO2 is 98 percent on room air
His voice is loud and strong
ok: He cannot count to 20 in a single breath
His cough is weak and secretions are pooling
His ETCO2 is rising

qs.q: A 58-year-old with myasthenia gravis has worsening ptosis, double vision, a nasal voice and trouble clearing secretions. RR 28 and shallow, SpO2 95 percent on room air, ETCO2 56 mmHg. How should you interpret these findings?
qs.a: Impending ventilatory failure
qs.x: Myasthenic crisis weakens the breathing muscles, so CO2 builds up while SpO2 may stay normal, especially early. Rising ETCO2 with shallow breathing and pooled secretions means she may soon need ventilatory support.
w: She is stable, because her oxygen saturation is normal
Hyperventilation from anxiety about her illness
Compensation for a metabolic acidosis

qs.q: A 30-year-old with a complete T4 spinal cord injury has a pounding headache, BP 210/118, HR 52, and flushing and sweating above the level of injury. What should you do first?
qs.a: Sit him up and look for a trigger such as a blocked catheter
qs.x: Autonomic dysreflexia is a dangerous hypertensive response to a stimulus below the injury, most often a full bladder or kinked catheter. Sitting upright lowers pressure, and removing the trigger usually resolves it.
w: Lay him flat, raise his legs and recheck the pressure in 15 minutes
Apply a cooling blanket to his trunk
Begin transcutaneous pacing for the bradycardia

qs.q: A 7-year-old with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt has had worsening headache, vomiting and sleepiness over the day. She has no fever. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Shunt malfunction
qs.x: Headache, vomiting and decreasing level of consciousness in a child with a shunt suggest obstruction and rising intracranial pressure, which needs prompt evaluation.
w: Viral gastroenteritis
Migraine headache
Dehydration from vomiting

qs.q: A 22-year-old in DKA has been breathing deeply at 34 per minute with an ETCO2 of 18 mmHg. He becomes obtunded and is intubated. How should he be ventilated?
qs.a: Keep a high rate that matches his own compensation
qs.x: His rapid deep breathing was blowing off CO2 to offset a severe metabolic acidosis. Slowing ventilation after intubation lets CO2 rise and can cause a dangerous fall in pH and cardiac arrest.
w: Ventilate at 10 per minute as for any adult patient
Ventilate to bring ETCO2 up to 35 to 45 mmHg as quickly as possible
Ventilate at 6 per minute to rest his respiratory muscles

qs.q: A 9-year-old in DKA is receiving IV fluids. During transport he develops a headache, becomes confused, and his HR falls from 130 to 64 while his BP rises. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Cerebral edema
qs.x: Cerebral edema is a leading cause of death in pediatric DKA. Headache, declining mental status, bradycardia and rising BP are warning signs of rising intracranial pressure.
w: Hypoglycemia from his insulin
Heart failure from fluid overload
Worsening dehydration

qs.q: Which features are more typical of DKA than of hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS)? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Deep, rapid Kussmaul respirations; A fruity odor on the breath; Onset over hours to a day or two
qs.x: DKA produces ketoacidosis, causing Kussmaul breathing and fruity breath, and it develops relatively quickly. HHS develops slowly in older type 2 patients and usually has higher glucose with little or no ketosis.
opts: Deep, rapid Kussmaul respirations
A fruity odor on the breath
Onset over hours to a day or two
Glucose often above 1,000 mg/dL
Most common in older adults with type 2 diabetes
Onset over many days to weeks
ok: Deep, rapid Kussmaul respirations
A fruity odor on the breath
Onset over hours to a day or two

qs.q: A 76-year-old taking glipizide was found with a glucose of 38 mg/dL. After IV dextrose he is alert with a glucose of 112 and wants to stay home. What should you advise?
qs.a: Transport, because hypoglycemia is likely to recur
qs.x: Sulfonylureas act for many hours, so hypoglycemia often recurs after dextrose wears off. These patients usually need observation and should be strongly encouraged to accept transport.
w: He can stay home since his glucose is now normal
Eat a meal and stay home with no further follow-up needed
Take a second dose of dextrose before you leave the scene

qs.q: A malnourished 50-year-old with chronic heavy alcohol use has a glucose of 32 mg/dL. No IV could be started, and IM glucagon 15 minutes ago has not helped. What is the most likely reason?
qs.a: Depleted glycogen stores in the liver
qs.x: Glucagon raises glucose by releasing liver glycogen. Malnourished and chronically alcoholic patients have little glycogen, so they need dextrose by IV or IO access.
w: IM absorption takes at least an hour
Alcohol binds and inactivates glucagon
Glucagon works only when given by the IV route

qs.q: A 45-year-old has taken prednisone daily for years but stopped 3 days ago because of vomiting. He is lethargic with BP 74/40 despite 2 liters of fluid and a glucose of 58 mg/dL. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Acute adrenal insufficiency
qs.x: Long-term steroid use suppresses the adrenal glands, and stopping suddenly can cause adrenal crisis with refractory hypotension and hypoglycemia. Treatment requires stress-dose steroids in addition to fluids.
w: Hypovolemic shock from vomiting alone
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Thyroid storm

qs.q: Which findings are typical of adrenal crisis? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hypotension that does not respond well to fluids; Hypoglycemia; Hyperkalemia
qs.x: Loss of cortisol and aldosterone causes refractory hypotension, low glucose, low sodium and high potassium.
opts: Hypotension that does not respond well to fluids
Hypoglycemia
Hyperkalemia
Hypernatremia
Marked hypertension
ok: Hypotension that does not respond well to fluids
Hypoglycemia
Hyperkalemia

qs.q: A 34-year-old with Graves disease stopped her medication a month ago. Which findings would suggest thyroid storm? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Temperature of 40.1 C (104.2 F); Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate; Agitation and delirium
qs.x: Thyroid storm causes high fever, tachydysrhythmias and altered mental status. Bradycardia, hypothermia and facial puffiness point the other way, toward severe hypothyroidism.
opts: Temperature of 40.1 C (104.2 F)
Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate
Agitation and delirium
Sinus bradycardia
Hypothermia with puffy facial swelling
ok: Temperature of 40.1 C (104.2 F)
Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate
Agitation and delirium

qs.q: An 81-year-old is found in a cold house in winter with a temperature of 33.8 C (92.8 F), HR 44, RR 8, a puffy face and coarse dry skin. She has not taken her levothyroxine in months. What is the most likely condition?
qs.a: Myxedema coma
qs.x: Myxedema coma is severe hypothyroidism with hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation and altered mental status, often triggered by cold or illness. Expect hypoglycemia and support ventilation.
w: Primary environmental hypothermia alone
Opioid overdose
Adrenal crisis

qs.q: A 38-year-old took an overdose of amitriptyline. QRS is 150 ms, HR 128, BP 82/50. Which intervention most directly treats the wide QRS?
qs.a: Sodium bicarbonate
qs.x: Tricyclics block cardiac sodium channels. Sodium bicarbonate supplies sodium and alkalinizes the blood, narrowing the QRS; class IA and IC antidysrhythmics worsen sodium channel blockade.
w: Amiodarone
Procainamide
Synchronized cardioversion

qs.q: A 60-year-old took an overdose of his blood pressure medicine. HR 38, BP 70/40, glucose 290 mg/dL. Which drug class is most likely?
qs.a: Calcium channel blocker
qs.x: Both beta blockers and calcium channel blockers cause bradycardia and hypotension. Calcium channel blockers also impair insulin release and cause hyperglycemia, while beta blocker overdose tends to cause hypoglycemia.
w: Beta blocker
Digoxin
Tricyclic antidepressant

qs.q: A 2-year-old may have swallowed one of his grandmother's extended-release verapamil tablets an hour ago. He is alert with normal vital signs. What is the best plan?
qs.a: Transport, since toxicity from extended-release tablets can be delayed
qs.x: A single tablet of some cardiac drugs can be dangerous to a toddler, and extended-release forms may not cause symptoms for many hours. The child needs transport and observation.
w: Leave him home with his parents, since one tablet cannot harm a toddler
Observe on scene for 30 minutes and release him if well
Induce vomiting before leaving the scene

qs.q: A farm worker was sprayed with an organophosphate pesticide and has heavy secretions and vomiting. What is the priority before you provide care?
qs.a: Proper PPE and decontamination
qs.x: Organophosphates are absorbed through skin, so responders must protect themselves and remove the patient's contaminated clothing and decontaminate before or alongside treatment.
w: Immediate intubation in the field
Starting an IV in the contaminated arm
Giving atropine through his wet clothing

qs.q: You are giving repeated doses of atropine to a patient with organophosphate poisoning. Which finding is the main endpoint for atropine?
qs.a: Drying of respiratory secretions
qs.x: Atropine is titrated to dry the bronchial secretions and ease breathing. Pupil size and heart rate are unreliable endpoints and may lag behind or mislead.
w: Dilation of the pupils to normal size or larger
A heart rate that rises above 120 per minute
Return to a normal level of consciousness

qs.q: A 41-year-old swallowed a large quantity of an over-the-counter pain reliever 6 hours ago. Which findings suggest salicylate toxicity? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Ringing in the ears; Rapid, deep breathing; Elevated temperature
qs.x: Salicylates cause tinnitus, stimulate breathing (respiratory alkalosis) and cause metabolic acidosis and hyperthermia. If intubation is needed, a high minute ventilation must be maintained.
opts: Ringing in the ears
Rapid, deep breathing
Elevated temperature
Pinpoint pupils
Marked bradycardia
ok: Ringing in the ears
Rapid, deep breathing
Elevated temperature

qs.q: A 17-year-old says she swallowed 30 acetaminophen tablets 2 hours ago. She feels fine and her vital signs are normal. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Liver injury may still develop, and the antidote works best early
qs.x: Acetaminophen toxicity often causes no symptoms for the first day, while liver injury silently develops. The antidote is most effective when started within about 8 hours, so early transport matters.
w: Normal vitals 2 hours after ingestion show the dose was not toxic
Liver damage occurs only if she vomits blood within 4 hours
She can be safely monitored at home by her parents

qs.q: A 48-year-old drank windshield washer fluid yesterday. He now has blurred vision he describes as like a snowstorm, and deep rapid respirations. Which substance most likely caused this?
qs.a: Methanol
