qs.x: Methanol is metabolized to formic acid, which damages the optic nerve and causes a severe metabolic acidosis. Visual changes after a delay are a hallmark.
w: Isopropyl alcohol
Ethanol
Propylene glycol

qs.q: A 55-year-old heavy daily drinker stopped drinking 3 days ago. He is confused and hallucinating, tremulous and sweating, with HR 138 and a temperature of 38.6 C (101.5 F). What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Delirium tremens
qs.x: Delirium tremens typically starts 2 to 4 days after the last drink, with autonomic hyperactivity, hallucinations and confusion. It is life-threatening and needs aggressive treatment.
w: Acute alcohol intoxication
Anticholinergic toxidrome
Wernicke encephalopathy alone

qs.q: A man pulled from an enclosed house fire is unresponsive with BP 78/40, SpO2 98 percent and SpCO 8 percent. Which treatment targets the most likely additional poison?
qs.a: Hydroxocobalamin
qs.x: Smoke from burning plastics contains cyanide. Coma and hypotension that are out of proportion to a modest carboxyhemoglobin level suggest cyanide toxicity, treated with hydroxocobalamin.
w: Naloxone
Atropine
Methylene blue

qs.q: A 32-year-old taking sertraline started tramadol 2 days ago. He is agitated and sweating, with a temperature of 39.0 C (102.2 F), HR 124, diarrhea, and sustained clonus and brisk reflexes in his legs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Serotonin syndrome
qs.x: Combining serotonergic drugs can cause serotonin syndrome, which comes on quickly and features clonus and hyperreflexia, most marked in the legs.
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Anticholinergic toxicity
Malignant hyperthermia

qs.q: A 44-year-old started haloperidol a week ago. He is confused, with a temperature of 40.2 C (104.4 F), rigid lead-pipe muscles, slow reflexes and a fluctuating blood pressure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
qs.x: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over days after starting antipsychotics, with hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, decreased reflexes and autonomic instability.
w: Serotonin syndrome
Bacterial meningitis
Exertional heat stroke

qs.q: Which features favor serotonin syndrome over neuroleptic malignant syndrome? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Onset within hours of a medication change; Clonus and hyperreflexia, worse in the legs; Diarrhea and hyperactive bowel sounds
qs.x: Serotonin syndrome is rapid and causes neuromuscular hyperactivity and GI hyperactivity. NMS is slower, with rigidity and sluggish reflexes.
opts: Onset within hours of a medication change
Clonus and hyperreflexia, worse in the legs
Diarrhea and hyperactive bowel sounds
Lead-pipe rigidity with slow reflexes
Gradual onset over days after starting an antipsychotic
ok: Onset within hours of a medication change
Clonus and hyperreflexia, worse in the legs
Diarrhea and hyperactive bowel sounds

qs.q: A 24-year-old used a stimulant at a party. He is agitated with HR 140, BP 176/100, temperature 38.8 C (101.8 F) and dilated pupils. Which finding best separates a sympathomimetic toxidrome from an anticholinergic one?
qs.a: Moist, sweaty skin
qs.x: Both toxidromes cause agitation, tachycardia, hyperthermia and mydriasis. Sympathomimetics cause diaphoresis, while anticholinergics cause hot, dry skin.
w: Dilated pupils
A fast heart rate
An elevated temperature

qs.q: You are ventilating a 40-year-old with an opioid overdose and a respiratory rate of 4. What is the goal of naloxone?
qs.a: Adequate spontaneous breathing
qs.x: Naloxone is titrated to restore adequate breathing. Pushing for full arousal can cause abrupt withdrawal, vomiting and agitation.
w: Full wakefulness so he can refuse care
Pupils that return to normal size
A heart rate above 100 per minute

qs.q: After naloxone, a 33-year-old who injected fentanyl now breathes 14 times a minute with SpO2 96 percent but remains deeply sedated, with HR 52 and chronic wounds on his forearms. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Supportive care, as a non-opioid sedative such as xylazine may be present
qs.x: Xylazine is a common adulterant that causes sedation, bradycardia and chronic wounds and does not respond to naloxone. Once breathing is adequate, support the airway and monitor rather than giving more naloxone.
w: Keep repeating naloxone doses until he is fully awake
Give flumazenil to reverse the remaining sedation
Begin transcutaneous pacing for the heart rate

qs.q: You find a person unresponsive in a closed car with a note on the window warning of toxic gas, and you notice a rotten egg odor. What should you do?
qs.a: Back away, isolate the area and request hazmat
qs.x: Chemical suicide with hydrogen sulfide can kill rescuers quickly. Scene safety comes first, and rescue requires proper respiratory protection.
w: Open the doors and rapidly remove the patient
Hold your breath and reach in to check a pulse
Break a window to air out the car, then enter

qs.q: A 70-year-old in septic shock has received 30 mL/kg of IV fluid. Her lungs remain clear, HR 118, MAP 56 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step under sepsis guidelines?
qs.a: Begin a vasopressor infusion
qs.x: When hypotension persists after initial fluid resuscitation, a vasopressor such as norepinephrine is started to reach a MAP of at least 65 mmHg.
w: Give a diuretic to mobilize the fluid
Accept the pressure, since a MAP above 50 is adequate
Give a steroid in place of a vasopressor

qs.q: A 66-year-old with pneumonia has HR 122, RR 30, BP 100/62 and an ETCO2 of 22 mmHg by nasal cannula. How should you interpret the low ETCO2?
qs.a: A sign of metabolic acidosis with likely high lactate
qs.x: In sepsis, a low ETCO2 reflects compensatory hyperventilation for metabolic acidosis and correlates with elevated lactate and poor perfusion.
w: Hypoventilation with CO2 retention that needs a bag-valve mask
A faulty sensor, since sick patients always have high CO2
A normal value for a patient with pneumonia

qs.q: A 57-year-old received chemotherapy 9 days ago. She has a temperature of 38.4 C (101.1 F), HR 112 and BP 104/66 but says she feels okay. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Treat it as possible sepsis and transport promptly
qs.x: Chemotherapy can lower the white cell count around 7 to 14 days after treatment. Fever in that window can signal sepsis that progresses quickly, and rectal procedures should be avoided.
w: Take a rectal temperature to confirm the fever
Advise acetaminophen and a call to her oncologist in the morning
Delay transport unless her fever rises above 39 C (102.2 F)

qs.q: An 88-year-old with dementia is more confused than usual. Temperature 35.6 C (96.1 F), HR 104, RR 24, BP 96/58, and her urine is cloudy. How should you interpret these findings?
qs.a: Sepsis is still likely despite the low temperature
qs.x: Older adults often have no fever with sepsis and may even become hypothermic. New confusion, tachycardia and tachypnea with a likely source should be treated as sepsis.
w: Infection is unlikely because she has no fever
She is simply having a bad day with her dementia
Her findings are explained by a cool room

qs.q: A 3-year-old has a fever and is lethargic. Which findings indicate compensated shock? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Capillary refill of 4 seconds; Heart rate of 168; Cool, mottled hands and feet
qs.x: Children maintain blood pressure until late, so tachycardia and poor peripheral perfusion signal shock before hypotension appears. Hypotension or bradycardia means decompensation.
opts: Capillary refill of 4 seconds
Heart rate of 168
Cool, mottled hands and feet
Systolic blood pressure of 60 mmHg
Heart rate of 58
ok: Capillary refill of 4 seconds
Heart rate of 168
Cool, mottled hands and feet

qs.q: A 74-year-old dialysis patient with suspected sepsis has BP 84/50 and clear lungs. How should IV fluid be given?
qs.a: Small boluses with frequent lung reassessment
qs.x: Patients with kidney failure or heart failure still need fluid for septic hypotension, but they are prone to pulmonary edema, so fluid is given in smaller amounts with frequent reassessment.
w: Withhold all fluid because he receives dialysis
Give 30 mL/kg as fast as possible without reassessing
Give oral fluids only and avoid IV access

qs.q: A dialysis patient with hyperkalemia has a wide QRS. What is the main purpose of giving IV calcium?
qs.a: Stabilize the heart muscle cell membranes
qs.x: Calcium protects the heart from dysrhythmias within minutes but does not lower potassium. Other treatments are needed to shift or remove potassium.
w: Move potassium out of the blood into the cells
Remove potassium through the kidneys
Bind potassium in the gut

qs.q: Which ECG changes are associated with worsening hyperkalemia? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Peaked T waves; Widening of the QRS complex; Flattened or absent P waves
qs.x: Hyperkalemia progresses from peaked T waves to loss of P waves and QRS widening, then to a sine wave and arrest. U waves suggest hypokalemia.
opts: Peaked T waves
Widening of the QRS complex
Flattened or absent P waves
Prominent U waves
Osborn J waves
Delta waves
ok: Peaked T waves
Widening of the QRS complex
Flattened or absent P waves

qs.q: A 34-year-old finished a marathon after drinking water at every station. She has nausea, headache and confusion, then has a seizure. Her glucose is normal and she has gained weight. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Exercise-associated hyponatremia
qs.x: Drinking more water than is lost can dilute the blood sodium, causing brain swelling with confusion and seizures. Giving more hypotonic fluid makes it worse.
w: Heat exhaustion
Hypoglycemia
Dehydration

qs.q: A 66-year-old is bleeding briskly from the puncture site of his dialysis fistula at home. What should you do first?
qs.a: Firm direct pressure over the bleeding site
qs.x: Fistula bleeding usually stops with steady direct pressure. A tourniquet is reserved for life-threatening bleeding that pressure cannot control.
w: Apply a tourniquet above the fistula before anything else
Elevate the arm and apply an ice pack without pressure
Clamp the fistula with a hemostat

qs.q: A 61-year-old missed two dialysis sessions. She is in severe respiratory distress with crackles throughout, BP 196/104 and SpO2 84 percent. Which intervention is most helpful prehospital?
qs.a: CPAP with the patient sitting upright
qs.x: Fluid overload from missed dialysis causes pulmonary edema. CPAP and upright positioning improve oxygenation and reduce the work of breathing while she is transported for dialysis.
w: A 1-liter fluid bolus
Lying her flat to rest
Nebulized albuterol alone

qs.q: A 46-year-old had thyroid surgery 2 days ago. She has tingling around her mouth and fingers, spasm of her hands and a prolonged QT interval. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Hypocalcemia
qs.x: The parathyroid glands can be injured during thyroid surgery, causing low calcium with paresthesias, carpopedal spasm and QT prolongation.
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypoglycemia
Hypermagnesemia

qs.q: An 81-year-old was found on the floor after about 2 days. His urine is dark brown. What is the most immediately dangerous complication?
qs.a: Hyperkalemia with dysrhythmias
qs.x: Prolonged immobility can cause rhabdomyolysis, releasing potassium from damaged muscle. Hyperkalemia can cause lethal dysrhythmias, and myoglobin can injure the kidneys.
w: Hypercalcemia with seizures
Hypernatremia from overhydration
Hypertension from fluid overload

qs.q: A 58-year-old with cirrhosis is vomiting large amounts of bright red blood. GCS 10, HR 132, BP 78/44. What is the first priority?
qs.a: Suction and position to protect the airway
qs.x: Massive hematemesis with a depressed level of consciousness puts the patient at high risk of aspiration. Airway protection comes first, then vascular access and resuscitation.
w: Start bilateral large-bore IVs before anything else
Insert an orogastric tube to empty the stomach
Obtain a 12-lead ECG

qs.q: Which findings suggest bleeding from the upper gastrointestinal tract? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Coffee-ground vomit; Black, tarry, sticky stools; Vomiting bright red blood
qs.x: Upper GI bleeding shows as hematemesis, coffee-ground vomit or melena from digested blood. Small amounts of bright red blood with stool usually come from the lower tract.
opts: Coffee-ground vomit
Black, tarry, sticky stools
Bright red blood on the toilet paper only
Painless blood after a hard stool
Vomiting bright red blood
ok: Coffee-ground vomit
Black, tarry, sticky stools
Vomiting bright red blood

qs.q: A 74-year-old taking metoprolol and an anticoagulant has had black stools for 2 days. He is pale and dizzy when standing. HR 76, BP 96/58. How should you interpret his heart rate?
qs.a: His medication may hide the tachycardia of blood loss
qs.x: Beta blockers blunt the heart rate response to hemorrhage, so a normal rate does not rule out significant blood loss in an anticoagulated patient with orthostatic symptoms.
w: A normal heart rate proves the blood loss is minor
His low pressure is from his BP medicine, not bleeding
His heart rate shows he is fully compensating

qs.q: A 70-year-old with several prior abdominal surgeries has crampy diffuse pain, a distended abdomen, foul brown vomit and no stool or gas for 2 days. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Small bowel obstruction
qs.x: Adhesions from earlier surgery are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction, which causes crampy pain, distension, vomiting and absent stool or flatus.
w: Appendicitis
Gastroenteritis
Diverticulitis

qs.q: A 42-year-old heavy drinker has severe constant upper abdominal pain boring through to his back, with vomiting. HR 118, BP 100/64. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Acute pancreatitis
qs.x: Pancreatitis causes severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and can cause large fluid shifts and shock. Alcohol and gallstones are the main causes.
w: Cholecystitis
Appendicitis
Kidney stone

qs.q: A 79-year-old with atrial fibrillation who is not anticoagulated has sudden severe abdominal pain, yet his abdomen is soft and barely tender. What should you be most concerned about?
qs.a: Mesenteric ischemia
qs.x: Pain out of proportion to the exam in an older patient with atrial fibrillation suggests an embolus to the mesenteric arteries, a time-critical emergency.
w: Constipation
Gastroenteritis
Anxiety

qs.q: A 30-year-old was stung by a bee 10 minutes ago. She is dizzy with BP 76/42 and HR 128. She has no hives. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Anaphylaxis, even without skin findings
qs.x: Hypotension soon after exposure to a known or likely allergen meets the criteria for anaphylaxis even without skin involvement. Give IM epinephrine promptly.
w: Not anaphylaxis, because hives are required
A vasovagal reaction to the pain of the sting
A local reaction that needs only ice

qs.q: A 22-year-old's food-related anaphylaxis resolved completely after one IM epinephrine dose. She wants to go home. What should you tell her?
qs.a: Symptoms can return hours later
qs.x: A biphasic reaction can recur hours later without re-exposure, and epinephrine wears off within minutes to hours. Patients should be observed after anaphylaxis.
w: Resolution after epinephrine means the reaction is over for good
An oral antihistamine taken now fully prevents any recurrence
A recurrence is only possible if she eats the food again

qs.q: A 64-year-old who has taken lisinopril for years has had swelling of the tongue and lips over 2 hours, without hives, itching or wheezing. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: ACE inhibitor angioedema
qs.x: ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin levels and can cause angioedema at any time, even after years of use. It often responds poorly to epinephrine and antihistamines.
w: Food anaphylaxis
Ludwig angina
Peritonsillar abscess

qs.q: The same patient now has drooling, stridor and cannot swallow. What is the most important airway consideration?
qs.a: Expect a difficult airway with a surgical backup ready
qs.x: Angioedema distorts the upper airway. Plan for a difficult intubation by the most experienced provider and prepare for a surgical airway. A supraglottic device does not bypass the swelling.
w: Insert a supraglottic airway as the first choice
Lay him flat to improve airway alignment
Wait for the swelling to respond to antihistamines

qs.q: Minutes after eating shrimp, which findings support anaphylaxis? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hives with wheezing; Hives with crampy abdominal pain and vomiting; Hypotension
qs.x: Anaphylaxis involves two or more body systems after exposure, or hypotension after a known allergen. Isolated mild local or eye and nose symptoms do not meet the criteria.
opts: Hives with wheezing
Hives with crampy abdominal pain and vomiting
Hypotension
Itchy eyes and sneezing only
Mild swelling limited to the lips without other signs
A single hive on the forearm
ok: Hives with wheezing
Hives with crampy abdominal pain and vomiting
Hypotension

qs.q: A 16-year-old with sickle cell disease has chest pain, a temperature of 38.7 C (101.7 F), cough, RR 30 and SpO2 89 percent. What is the most concerning diagnosis?
qs.a: Acute chest syndrome
qs.x: Acute chest syndrome is a leading cause of death in sickle cell disease, with chest pain, fever, respiratory symptoms and hypoxia. It needs oxygen and prompt transport.
w: A simple pain crisis
An asthma exacerbation
Anxiety

qs.q: A 2-year-old with sickle cell disease is pale and lethargic, with HR 180, capillary refill of 4 seconds and an enlarging mass in the left upper abdomen. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Splenic sequestration crisis
qs.x: In young children, sickled cells can pool in the spleen, enlarging it rapidly and causing anemia and hypovolemic shock.
w: Acute appendicitis
A simple pain crisis
Intussusception

qs.q: A 24-year-old is in a sickle cell pain crisis with severe leg and back pain. SpO2 97 percent and vital signs are stable. What is the most appropriate care?
qs.a: Prompt pain relief and transport
qs.x: Vaso-occlusive crisis needs early, adequate pain control and fluids if dehydrated. Oxygen is given for hypoxia, and cold can worsen sickling.
w: Withhold pain medication until the hospital confirms the crisis
High-flow oxygen for everyone with sickle cell, whatever the SpO2
Cold packs on the painful areas

qs.q: A 12-year-old with hemophilia A hit his head on a door 2 hours ago. He has a mild headache and GCS 15. What is the best plan?
qs.a: Transport, as bleeding inside the skull is a real risk
qs.x: Patients with clotting disorders can develop delayed intracranial bleeding after minor trauma and need evaluation and often factor replacement.
w: Release him because his neurologic exam is normal
Apply ice and have his parents watch him at home
Wait on scene for 1 hour to see if he gets worse

qs.q: A 52-year-old kidney transplant recipient on immunosuppressants has fatigue, a cough and a temperature of 37.9 C (100.2 F). How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Serious infection may be present despite mild signs
qs.x: Immunosuppression blunts fever and inflammation, so serious infections can look mild. These patients should be evaluated promptly.
w: A low-grade fever means only a minor infection
He should stop his immunosuppressants on scene
His new kidney protects him from infection

qs.q: An agitated 28-year-old with hyperactive delirium has been chemically sedated after physical restraint. What monitoring is required?
qs.a: Continuous ETCO2, SpO2 and ECG monitoring
qs.x: Sedated patients with hyperactive delirium are at risk of respiratory depression and sudden cardiac arrest. Continuous capnography and cardiac monitoring detect deterioration early.
w: A single set of vital signs before transport
Visual checks only, to avoid agitating him
Hourly vital signs as with any stable patient

qs.q: A restrained, combative, hyperthermic man suddenly becomes quiet and still during transport. What does this most likely mean?
qs.a: A possible arrest that needs immediate assessment
qs.x: Sudden calm after severe agitation can mean respiratory or cardiac arrest. Check breathing and pulse immediately.
w: He has calmed down and no longer needs monitoring
His sedation is working as expected
He is tired from the struggle and is sleeping

qs.q: A 42-year-old is tearful after a breakup and says she feels hopeless. How should you ask about suicide?
qs.a: Ask directly if she is thinking about killing herself
qs.x: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and is the only way to assess it accurately.
w: Avoid the topic, since asking may plant the idea
Ask her family privately instead, so as not to upset her
Wait for her to bring up the subject herself

qs.q: Which factors increase a patient's risk of suicide? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A previous suicide attempt; A specific plan with access to the means; Alcohol or drug use
qs.x: A prior attempt, a plan with access to lethal means and substance use raise risk. Social connection and future plans are protective, and asking does not increase risk.
opts: A previous suicide attempt
A specific plan with access to the means
Alcohol or drug use
Strong family ties and plans for the future
Being asked directly about suicidal thoughts
ok: A previous suicide attempt
A specific plan with access to the means
Alcohol or drug use

qs.q: A 30-year-old took a handful of pills to end his life and now refuses transport. He is alert and oriented. What is the correct approach?
qs.a: He cannot make a valid refusal
qs.x: A patient at immediate risk of self-harm lacks the capacity to refuse care. Follow local law and protocol, which may involve law enforcement.
w: He may refuse because he is alert and oriented
He may refuse if he signs in front of a witness
He may refuse if a family member stays with him

qs.q: Which practices are appropriate for a physically restrained, agitated patient? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Continuous monitoring of breathing and circulation; Frequent checks of circulation in the restrained limbs; Documenting the reason for restraint and each reassessment
qs.x: Restraint can cause positional asphyxia and sudden death. Patients should never be placed prone or hobbled, and they need ongoing monitoring and documentation.
opts: Continuous monitoring of breathing and circulation
Frequent checks of circulation in the restrained limbs
Prone positioning with weight on the back
Restraining the hands and feet together behind the back
Documenting the reason for restraint and each reassessment
ok: Continuous monitoring of breathing and circulation
Frequent checks of circulation in the restrained limbs
Documenting the reason for restraint and each reassessment

qs.q: You are cooling a patient with exertional heat stroke by cold water immersion. At about what core temperature should active cooling stop?
qs.a: About 39 C (102.2 F)
qs.x: Cooling is usually stopped at about 38.5 to 39 C (101.3-102.2 F) to avoid overshooting into hypothermia.
w: About 37 C (98.6 F)
About 36 C (96.8 F)

qs.q: Which cooling methods are effective for exertional heat stroke? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Cold water immersion; Rotating ice-water-soaked towels over the body; Misting with water and fanning
qs.x: Cold water immersion is the fastest method, and towels or evaporative cooling are used when immersion is not possible. Fever reducers do not work for heat stroke.
opts: Cold water immersion
Rotating ice-water-soaked towels over the body
Misting with water and fanning
Waiting until arrival at the hospital to start cooling
An oral fever reducer as the main treatment
ok: Cold water immersion
Rotating ice-water-soaked towels over the body
Misting with water and fanning

qs.q: A 35-year-old was pulled from an icy lake after 25 minutes. He is pulseless and in asystole with a core temperature of 26 C (78.8 F) and no lethal injuries. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Begin CPR and transport for active internal rewarming
qs.x: Hypothermia protects the brain, and people have survived long arrests after rewarming. Continue CPR and transport to a center capable of extracorporeal rewarming.
w: Pronounce death because asystole at 26 C (78.8 F) is unsurvivable
Delay CPR until he has been rewarmed above 30 C (86 F)
Give rescue breaths only, since compressions cause VF

qs.q: A hiker has frostbitten feet and must walk 3 hours to reach the trailhead. What should you do about rewarming?
qs.a: Do not thaw the feet if they could refreeze
qs.x: Thawing and refreezing causes more tissue damage than delaying rewarming. Walking on frozen feet is preferable to thawing them before a long walk out.
w: Rub the feet with snow to restore circulation
Thaw the feet with dry heat from a campfire
Thaw the feet in hot water before walking out

qs.q: For a drowning victim in cardiac arrest, what is emphasized compared with a typical adult cardiac arrest?
qs.a: Early effective ventilation
qs.x: Drowning causes a hypoxic arrest, so early ventilation is key. Spinal precautions are not routine unless there is a diving or trauma mechanism.
w: Hands-only CPR so compressions are not delayed
Defibrillation before any breaths are given
Full spinal motion restriction before CPR

qs.q: A climber at 4,200 meters has a headache, confusion and cannot walk heel to toe. What is the most important treatment?
qs.a: Descent to a lower altitude
qs.x: Ataxia and altered mental status at altitude suggest high-altitude cerebral edema, which can be fatal. Immediate descent is the definitive treatment.
w: Rest at the same altitude for 24 hours
Fluids and sleep, deciding in the morning
Continued ascent to finish the climb quickly

qs.q: After 2 days at 3,800 meters, a hiker has shortness of breath at rest, a cough with pink frothy sputum, crackles and SpO2 70 percent. What is the most likely condition?
qs.a: High-altitude pulmonary edema
qs.x: High-altitude pulmonary edema causes dyspnea at rest, cough and hypoxia. It is treated with oxygen and descent.
w: Bacterial pneumonia
Asthma exacerbation
Spontaneous pneumothorax

qs.q: A diver ran out of air and ascended rapidly. Within 3 minutes of surfacing, he became confused with weakness on one side. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Arterial gas embolism
qs.x: Rapid ascent can rupture alveoli and send gas bubbles into the arteries, causing stroke-like signs within minutes. Treat with 100 percent oxygen and arrange hyperbaric therapy.
w: Type I decompression sickness
Nitrogen narcosis
Hypoglycemia

qs.q: Six hours after a deep dive, a diver has deep aching pain in his shoulder and fatigue. He plans to fly home tonight. What is the best advice?
qs.a: 100 percent oxygen and evaluation for recompression
qs.x: Joint pain hours after diving suggests decompression sickness. Flying lowers ambient pressure and worsens bubbles, so he needs oxygen and evaluation for hyperbaric treatment.
w: Fly home and see a doctor afterward
Massage and heat for the sore shoulder
Return to depth to recompress in the water

qs.q: A 30-year-old was bitten on the ankle by a rattlesnake and swelling is spreading up his leg. Which treatment is appropriate?
qs.a: Keep the limb still and mark the edge of the swelling
qs.x: Pit viper bites are managed by immobilizing the limb, marking swelling progression and rapid transport for antivenom. Tourniquets, incisions and ice cause harm.
w: Apply a tight arterial tourniquet above the bite to stop the venom
Cut over the fang marks and suction out the venom
Pack the leg in ice to slow venom absorption

qs.q: A 22-year-old at 37 weeks has a generalized seizure. BP 172/110. What is the first-line medication to stop and prevent eclamptic seizures?
qs.a: Magnesium sulfate
qs.x: Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for eclampsia. A benzodiazepine may be used if magnesium is not available.
w: Phenytoin
Labetalol
Diphenhydramine

qs.q: A pregnant patient is receiving magnesium sulfate for severe preeclampsia. Which findings suggest magnesium toxicity? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Loss of the patellar reflexes; Respiratory rate of 8; Increasing drowsiness
qs.x: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is an early sign of magnesium toxicity, followed by respiratory depression and decreased consciousness. Stop the infusion, support breathing and consider calcium.
opts: Loss of the patellar reflexes
Respiratory rate of 8
Increasing drowsiness
Brisk reflexes with clonus
Respiratory rate of 26
ok: Loss of the patellar reflexes
Respiratory rate of 8
Increasing drowsiness

qs.q: A 29-year-old delivered a baby 10 days ago. She has a severe headache, BP 166/104 and is seeing spots. What is the most likely condition?
qs.a: Postpartum preeclampsia
qs.x: Preeclampsia can develop up to 6 weeks after delivery and carries the same risk of seizures and stroke.
w: Tension headache
Postpartum depression
Migraine

qs.q: A 32-year-old at 33 weeks has vaginal bleeding. Which findings favor placenta previa over placental abruption? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Painless bleeding; Bright red blood; A soft, nontender uterus
qs.x: Placenta previa causes painless bright red bleeding with a soft uterus. Abruption is painful with a tender, rigid uterus. Never perform a digital vaginal exam with third-trimester bleeding.
opts: Painless bleeding
Bright red blood
A soft, nontender uterus
A rigid, tender uterus
Dark blood with constant abdominal pain
ok: Painless bleeding
Bright red blood
A soft, nontender uterus

qs.q: A 30-year-old in active labor who had a prior cesarean section has sudden tearing abdominal pain, her contractions stop, and fetal parts are easily felt through the abdomen. HR 130, BP 84/50. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Uterine rupture
qs.x: A previous uterine scar increases the risk of rupture, which causes sudden pain, loss of contractions, palpable fetal parts and maternal shock.
w: Placenta previa
Braxton Hicks contractions
Normal transition stage of labor

qs.q: Which are recognized causes of postpartum hemorrhage? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Uterine atony; Retained placental tissue; Lacerations of the birth canal
qs.x: The main causes are tone (atony), tissue (retained placenta), trauma (lacerations) and thrombin (clotting disorders). Breastfeeding helps the uterus contract.
opts: Uterine atony
Retained placental tissue
Lacerations of the birth canal
Rh incompatibility
Breastfeeding the newborn
ok: Uterine atony
Retained placental tissue
Lacerations of the birth canal

qs.q: During a breech delivery the body and arms have delivered, but the head has not delivered after 3 minutes. What should you do?
qs.a: Make an airway with a gloved hand and transport
qs.x: If the head does not deliver, place gloved fingers to hold the vaginal wall away from the baby's face to create an airway, and transport rapidly.
w: Pull firmly on the baby's legs to deliver the head
Push the baby's body back into the vagina
Apply firm pressure to the top of the uterus

qs.q: You have placed the mother in the McRoberts position for a shoulder dystocia, but the shoulders still do not deliver. What should you do next?
qs.a: Firm suprapubic pressure
qs.x: Suprapubic pressure helps dislodge the anterior shoulder from behind the pubic bone. Fundal pressure worsens impaction.
w: Firm pressure on the top of the uterus
Strong downward traction on the head
Push the head back into the vagina

qs.q: The baby's head delivers with the cord wrapped tightly around the neck twice, and it cannot be slipped over the head. What should you do?
qs.a: Clamp the cord in two places and cut between the clamps
qs.x: A cord too tight to slip over the head must be clamped and cut to allow delivery.
w: Pull firmly on the head so the shoulders deliver more quickly
Push the head back and wait for the next contraction
Leave the cord in place and continue the delivery

qs.q: During labor, a 35-year-old suddenly becomes severely short of breath and hypoxic, then hypotensive, then has a seizure and arrests. After resuscitation she bleeds from her IV sites. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Amniotic fluid embolism
qs.x: Amniotic fluid embolism causes sudden hypoxia, shock and arrest during labor or just after delivery, often followed by a bleeding disorder.
w: Eclampsia
Pulmonary embolism
Anaphylaxis

qs.q: At what rate should positive-pressure ventilation be given to a newborn?
qs.a: 40 to 60 breaths per minute
qs.x: NRP recommends 40 to 60 breaths per minute during positive-pressure ventilation.
w: 12 to 20 breaths per minute
20 to 30 breaths per minute
80 to 100 breaths per minute

qs.q: You are giving PPV to a newborn, but the chest is not moving and the heart rate is not improving. Which corrective steps are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Readjust the mask to improve the seal; Reposition the head in the sniffing position; Gradually increase the ventilation pressure
qs.x: The MR SOPA steps correct ineffective ventilation: mask, reposition, suction, open mouth, pressure increase, alternative airway. Compressions begin only after 30 seconds of effective ventilation.
opts: Readjust the mask to improve the seal
Reposition the head in the sniffing position
Gradually increase the ventilation pressure
Start chest compressions right away
Lower the ventilation rate to 20 per minute
ok: Readjust the mask to improve the seal
Reposition the head in the sniffing position
Gradually increase the ventilation pressure

qs.q: You are starting chest compressions on a newborn. What oxygen concentration should be used?
qs.a: Increase to 100 percent
qs.x: NRP recommends increasing oxygen to 100 percent when compressions begin, then weaning it as soon as the heart rate recovers.
w: Keep at 21 percent
Stop oxygen during compressions
Decrease to 30 percent

qs.q: A newborn born at 30 weeks needs PPV. What oxygen concentration should you start with?
qs.a: 21 to 30 percent
qs.x: For newborns under 35 weeks, NRP recommends starting at 21 to 30 percent and adjusting to reach target saturations.
w: 100 percent
50 percent
60 to 70 percent

qs.q: A newborn delivered through thick meconium-stained fluid is limp and not breathing. What should you do?
qs.a: Initial steps, then PPV if still apneic
qs.x: Routine tracheal suctioning is no longer recommended for non-vigorous newborns with meconium. Start the initial steps and ventilation without delay.
w: Intubate and suction the trachea before any breaths
Suction the stomach before drying and warming
Wait for the 1-minute Apgar score

qs.q: A baby born at 28 weeks is delivered in the ambulance. How should you keep the baby warm?
qs.a: Place the body in plastic wrap without drying first
qs.x: Very premature newborns lose heat rapidly. Covering them up to the neck in plastic wrap without drying, along with a hat and a warm environment, reduces heat loss.
w: Dry vigorously and leave the skin uncovered for assessment
Bathe the baby with warm water to remove the vernix
Place the baby on a cool surface to prevent overheating

qs.q: During newborn resuscitation with chest compressions, which method gives the most accurate heart rate?
qs.a: A cardiac monitor with ECG leads
qs.x: NRP recommends an electronic cardiac monitor during compressions, since palpation and pulse oximetry can be inaccurate.
w: Palpating the umbilical cord
Palpating the brachial pulse
The pulse oximeter reading

qs.q: A newborn is apneic at birth. When should you calculate the 1-minute Apgar score before starting resuscitation?
qs.a: Do not wait for the Apgar score
qs.x: Apgar scores describe the newborn's condition but are not used to decide whether to resuscitate.
w: After the 1-minute score is done
After the 5-minute score is done
After both scores are averaged

qs.q: A 3-month-old has had a runny nose for 3 days and now has wheezing, retractions, poor feeding and SpO2 91 percent. What is the most helpful first step?
qs.a: Gentle nasal suctioning
qs.x: Infants breathe mainly through the nose, and secretions from bronchiolitis can block the airway. Suctioning improves breathing and feeding, while bronchodilators and steroids are not routinely helpful.
w: A routine albuterol nebulizer for the wheezing
An oral steroid dose for the inflammation
Chest physiotherapy with back percussion

qs.q: A 2-year-old has croup. Which finding indicates severe croup?
qs.a: Stridor at rest
qs.x: Stridor at rest, especially with retractions or agitation, means significant airway narrowing that needs treatment.
w: A loud barking cough that is worse at night
Low-grade fever with a runny nose
A hoarse voice while crying

qs.q: Which features favor croup rather than epiglottitis? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A barking, seal-like cough; Gradual onset after cold symptoms
qs.x: Croup is a viral illness with a gradual onset and a barking cough. Epiglottitis is sudden, with high fever, drooling and tripod positioning.
opts: A barking, seal-like cough
Gradual onset after cold symptoms
Drooling and difficulty swallowing
Sitting in a tripod position
Sudden high fever with a toxic appearance
ok: A barking, seal-like cough
Gradual onset after cold symptoms

qs.q: Which findings indicate significant dehydration in a 9-month-old? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A sunken anterior fontanelle; No wet diaper in 8 hours; Capillary refill of 4 seconds
qs.x: Sunken fontanelle, decreased urine and delayed capillary refill show significant volume loss. Tears and a normal fontanelle suggest adequate hydration.
opts: A sunken anterior fontanelle
No wet diaper in 8 hours
Capillary refill of 4 seconds
A bulging fontanelle
Tears when crying
ok: A sunken anterior fontanelle
No wet diaper in 8 hours
Capillary refill of 4 seconds

qs.q: Which feature makes a febrile seizure complex rather than simple?
qs.a: Lasting longer than 15 minutes
qs.x: Complex febrile seizures last longer than 15 minutes, are focal or recur within 24 hours. Simple seizures are brief and generalized.
w: Occurring in a 2-year-old
A generalized tonic-clonic seizure
A temperature of 39.5 C (103.1 F)

qs.q: A 20-month-old had a 2-minute generalized seizure with a temperature of 39.4 C (102.9 F). He is now drowsy but improving, with a patent airway. What is the best plan?
qs.a: Remove excess clothing, monitor and transport
qs.x: Simple febrile seizures are usually harmless, but children need evaluation. Cold baths, alcohol and objects in the mouth are dangerous.
w: Place the child in a cold bath to bring the fever down quickly
Sponge the child with rubbing alcohol
Place a bite block to protect the tongue

qs.q: Which findings should raise suspicion of child abuse? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A delay in seeking care for an injury; A history that changes between caregivers; An injury that does not fit the child's developmental stage
qs.x: Delays, inconsistent histories and injuries that do not fit the child's development are red flags. Crying and common toddler injuries are expected.
opts: A delay in seeking care for an injury
A history that changes between caregivers
An injury that does not fit the child's developmental stage
A child who cries when examined
A forehead bruise on a toddler learning to walk
ok: A delay in seeking care for an injury
A history that changes between caregivers
An injury that does not fit the child's developmental stage

qs.q: Which bruising pattern in a 2-year-old is most concerning for abuse?
qs.a: Bruising on the ears, neck or torso
qs.x: Bruises on protected areas such as the ears, neck and torso are rarely accidental in young children. Shins, forehead and knees are common sites for accidental injuries.
w: Bruises over the shins
A bump on the forehead
Scrapes on the knees and elbows

qs.q: A 4-month-old has irritability, vomiting, lethargy and an episode of apnea, without fever or visible injury. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Abusive head trauma
qs.x: Shaken infants may have no external injury. Unexplained lethargy, vomiting and apnea in an infant should raise concern for abusive head trauma.
w: Gastroenteritis
Infant colic
Reflux

qs.q: You suspect a child has been abused. What is your responsibility?
qs.a: Document objectively and report as required by law
qs.x: EMS providers are mandated reporters in most states. Reasonable suspicion is enough, and the report should be objective without accusations.
w: Confront the caregivers about your suspicion on scene
Report only if you are certain abuse occurred
Leave reporting to the hospital without telling staff

qs.q: A 10-month-old has bouts of inconsolable crying with his knees drawn up every 15 to 20 minutes, is lethargic between episodes and has passed red jelly-like stool. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Intussusception
qs.x: In intussusception the bowel telescopes into itself, causing intermittent severe pain, lethargy and currant jelly stool.
w: Colic
Gastroenteritis
Constipation

qs.q: A 6-week-old briefly turned pale and limp for 20 seconds, then recovered. She now looks normal. What is the best plan?
qs.a: Transport for evaluation despite the normal exam
qs.x: A brief resolved unexplained event can signal serious illness, such as infection, abuse or a cardiac problem, and needs medical evaluation.
w: Release her, since she now looks completely normal
Advise the parents to follow up within a week
Release her if her pulse oximetry is normal

qs.q: An 82-year-old has new confusion, dry mouth and urinary retention after starting an over-the-counter sleep aid containing diphenhydramine. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Anticholinergic side effects
qs.x: Older adults are very sensitive to anticholinergic drugs, which can cause delirium, urinary retention and constipation.
w: Normal progression of dementia
Alzheimer disease starting suddenly
Hyperthyroidism

qs.q: Which findings suggest elder abuse or neglect? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Bruises of different ages on protected areas; A caregiver who answers for the patient and will not leave; Severe pressure ulcers and soiled bedding
qs.x: Patterned or multiple bruises, controlling caregivers and signs of neglect are red flags. A single injury with a consistent history is not.
opts: Bruises of different ages on protected areas
A caregiver who answers for the patient and will not leave
Severe pressure ulcers and soiled bedding
A single bruised shin after a witnessed fall
A diagnosis of dementia
ok: Bruises of different ages on protected areas
A caregiver who answers for the patient and will not leave
Severe pressure ulcers and soiled bedding

qs.q: A 79-year-old hospice patient with a POLST for comfort measures only has new pauses in breathing and gurgling. She appears comfortable. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Follow the comfort-care plan and contact hospice
qs.x: These are normal changes near death. Follow the patient's wishes and support the family.
w: Begin aggressive suctioning and assist with a BVM
Start CPR if her breathing stops for 20 seconds
Transport emergently for intubation

qs.q: What is the best way to manage noisy upper airway secretions in a dying patient receiving comfort care?
qs.a: Turn the patient onto the side
qs.x: Repositioning helps secretions drain. Deep suction is uncomfortable and usually ineffective at this stage.
w: Deep nasotracheal suctioning every few minutes
A large IV fluid bolus to thin secretions
Intubation to clear the airway

qs.q: An 85-year-old with a valid do-not-resuscitate order has a pulse and acute respiratory distress. What should you do?
qs.a: Treat her distress within the limits of her orders
qs.x: A DNR order does not mean no treatment. Provide oxygen, positioning and other care allowed by her orders and local protocol.
w: Provide no treatment because she has a DNR
Intubate, since a DNR applies only to cardiac arrest
Call her family before any care is given

qs.q: A 24-year-old has a partial leg amputation with bright red spurting blood, snoring respirations and a GCS of 9. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
qs.a: 1. Control the massive bleeding with a tourniquet  2. Open the airway with a jaw thrust  3. Assess breathing and assist ventilations if inadequate  4. Assess circulation and treat for shock  5. Check disability: GCS and pupils
qs.x: Massive external bleeding can cause death within minutes, so it comes first in modern trauma care (often taught as X-ABCDE or MARCH). The airway follows, then breathing, then circulation and shock care, and finally a quick neurologic check.
opts: Control the massive bleeding with a tourniquet
Open the airway with a jaw thrust
Assess breathing and assist ventilations if inadequate
Assess circulation and treat for shock
Check disability: GCS and pupils
ok: Control the massive bleeding with a tourniquet
Open the airway with a jaw thrust
Assess breathing and assist ventilations if inadequate
Assess circulation and treat for shock
Check disability: GCS and pupils

qs.q: A 58-year-old collapses in front of you and is pulseless and apneic. Your monitor is at the patient's side. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
qs.a: 1. Start high-quality chest compressions  2. Apply defibrillation pads while compressions continue  3. Deliver one shock for ventricular fibrillation  4. Resume compressions immediately for 2 minutes  5. Give epinephrine after the second shock
qs.x: For a witnessed arrest, compressions begin right away and continue while the pads go on. A shockable rhythm gets one shock, followed immediately by 2 minutes of CPR. In AHA adult guidance for VF or pulseless VT, epinephrine is given after the second shock.
opts: Start high-quality chest compressions
Apply defibrillation pads while compressions continue
Deliver one shock for ventricular fibrillation
Resume compressions immediately for 2 minutes
Give epinephrine after the second shock
ok: Start high-quality chest compressions
Apply defibrillation pads while compressions continue

Resume compressions immediately for 2 minutes
Give epinephrine after the second shock

qs.q: A 31-year-old stung by a bee has hives, stridor and a blood pressure of 78/40. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
qs.a: 1. Give intramuscular epinephrine  2. Apply high-flow oxygen  3. Start an IV fluid bolus for the hypotension  4. Give an antihistamine as an add-on treatment  5. Reassess and repeat epinephrine per protocol if no improvement
qs.x: Epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis and treats both the airway swelling and the low blood pressure. Oxygen and IV fluids support it. Antihistamines ease hives and itching but do not treat the airway or shock, so they are add-on care. Epinephrine can be repeated per protocol if there is no response.
opts: Give intramuscular epinephrine
Apply high-flow oxygen
Start an IV fluid bolus for the hypotension
Give an antihistamine as an add-on treatment
Reassess and repeat epinephrine per protocol if no improvement
ok: Give intramuscular epinephrine
Apply high-flow oxygen
Start an IV fluid bolus for the hypotension
Give an antihistamine as an add-on treatment
Reassess and repeat epinephrine per protocol if no improvement

qs.q: An unresponsive 60-year-old with no trauma has gurgling respirations at 6 per minute. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
qs.a: 1. Open the airway with a head tilt-chin lift  2. Suction the airway  3. Insert an oropharyngeal airway  4. Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen  5. Consider an advanced airway
qs.x: An airway cannot be cleared or ventilated until it is opened. Gurgling means fluid, so suction comes before the oral airway. Bag-valve-mask ventilation with oxygen treats the slow breathing, and an advanced airway is considered once basic ventilation is under way.
opts: Open the airway with a head tilt-chin lift
Suction the airway
Insert an oropharyngeal airway
Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
Consider an advanced airway
ok: Open the airway with a head tilt-chin lift

qs.q: A term newborn is limp and not breathing after delivery. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
qs.a: 1. Warm, dry and stimulate the newborn  2. Position the airway and clear secretions if needed  3. Start positive-pressure ventilation if apneic or heart rate below 100  4. Start chest compressions if heart rate stays below 60 despite effective ventilation  5. Give epinephrine if heart rate stays below 60 with compressions and ventilation
qs.x: NRP begins with warming, drying and stimulating, then positioning and clearing the airway. Ventilation is the single most important step in newborn resuscitation. Compressions start only if the heart rate stays below 60 after effective ventilation, and epinephrine follows if it still stays below 60.

Position the airway and clear secretions if needed
Start positive-pressure ventilation if apneic or heart rate below 100

Give epinephrine if heart rate stays below 60 with compressions and ventilation

Give epinephrine if heart rate stays below 60 with compressions and ventilation

qs.q: A 71-year-old has a heart rate of 34, confusion and a blood pressure of 72/40. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
qs.a: 1. Support the airway and breathing, with oxygen if hypoxic  2. Attach the monitor and obtain IV access  3. Give atropine  4. Start transcutaneous pacing or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion if atropine is not effective
qs.x: Unstable bradycardia care in the AHA algorithm starts with the airway, breathing and oxygen if hypoxic, along with the monitor and IV access. Atropine is the first drug. If atropine does not work, transcutaneous pacing or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion is the next step.
opts: Support the airway and breathing, with oxygen if hypoxic
Attach the monitor and obtain IV access
Give atropine
Start transcutaneous pacing or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion if atropine is not effective
ok: Support the airway and breathing, with oxygen if hypoxic

qs.q: A worker's clothing caught fire. The flames are out but the fabric is still smoldering, and his voice is hoarse. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
qs.a: 1. Stop the burning process  2. Assess the airway for signs of inhalation injury  3. Remove jewelry and constricting clothing  4. Cover the burns with dry sterile dressings and keep him warm  5. Estimate the burned body surface area
qs.x: Smoldering clothing keeps burning tissue, so stopping the burning process is first. The airway is next, because soot or hoarseness can mean swelling that closes the airway. Jewelry comes off before swelling traps it, the burns are covered dry and the patient kept warm, and the size of the burn is estimated for fluid and destination decisions.

Assess the airway for signs of inhalation injury
Remove jewelry and constricting clothing
Cover the burns with dry sterile dressings and keep him warm
Estimate the burned body surface area

qs.q: A 27-year-old with a suspected opioid overdose is apneic with a carotid pulse. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
qs.a: 1. Open the airway  2. Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen  3. Give naloxone  4. Reassess breathing and responsiveness
qs.x: For an apneic patient with a pulse, AHA guidance puts ventilation first: opening the airway and breathing for the patient fixes the low oxygen right away. Naloxone treats the cause but takes time to work, and the patient is reassessed afterward.

Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
Give naloxone
Reassess breathing and responsiveness

qs.q: A 52-year-old with diabetes is unresponsive with snoring respirations at 14 per minute. Her family says she took insulin and skipped lunch. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
qs.a: 1. Open the airway  2. Check the blood glucose  3. Give IV dextrose for a low reading  4. Reassess mental status and recheck the glucose
qs.x: The snoring airway is the immediate threat, so it is opened first. A glucose check confirms the cause before treatment. IV dextrose corrects the low sugar, and the patient is reassessed with a repeat glucose because long-acting insulin can cause the level to fall again.
opts: Open the airway
Check the blood glucose
Give IV dextrose for a low reading
Reassess mental status and recheck the glucose

Check the blood glucose

qs.q: A 19-year-old runner collapses at the finish line. He is confused, his skin is hot, and his core temperature is 41 C (105.8 F). What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
qs.a: 1. Move him out of the heat  2. Start rapid cooling, such as cold-water immersion or ice and wet sheets  3. Check the blood glucose  4. Monitor his temperature and mental status during transport
qs.x: Exertional heat stroke damages organs the longer the temperature stays high, so the patient is removed from the heat and cooled as fast as possible; cold-water immersion is the fastest method. qs.q: An AEMT is giving D50 IV to a hypoglycemic adult. Which findings mean the AEMT should stop giving it and notify medical direction? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Swelling around the IV site; Pain and burning at the IV site; The site is pale and cool and the fluid stops flowing freely
qs.x: Swelling, burning, coolness and poor flow suggest infiltration, and extravasated dextrose can cause tissue necrosis. Hunger, less shakiness and a slowing heart rate reflect improvement, not a complication.

qs.q: An AEMT gives D10 IV per protocol to an adult with a blood glucose of 40 mg/dL and altered mental status. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Give it in 50 to 100 mL (5 to 10 g) aliquots; Recheck mental status and blood glucose between aliquots; Confirm the IV is patent before and during the infusion
qs.x: D10 is titrated in 5-10 g aliquots with reassessment, and IV patency is checked because extravasation causes tissue injury. A confused patient may not protect the airway for oral glucose, and treatment does not wait for a lower reading.

qs.x: Stable reentrant SVT is treated with vagal maneuvers, then 6 mg adenosine as a rapid push with flush while recording the rhythm. A slow push is ineffective because of the drug's very short half-life, 12 mg is the second dose, and irregular wide-complex rhythms are a contraindication.

Intubate him to protect the airway
ok: Hold droperidol and notify the provider

qs.q: An intubated patient is paralyzed with a vecuronium infusion for a 2-hour flight. Which findings suggest inadequate sedation or analgesia? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Unexplained tachycardia; Rising blood pressure; Tearing
qs.x: Vecuronium paralyzes without sedating, so awareness under paralysis must be watched for through sympathetic signs such as tachycardia, hypertension and tearing. Lack of movement is expected from the paralytic and does not show adequate sedation.
opts: Unexplained tachycardia
No patient movement
Rising blood pressure
SpO2 of 98%
Tearing
Equal, reactive pupils
ok: Unexplained tachycardia
Rising blood pressure
Tearing

qs.q: A non-intubated 80-kg burn patient with an SBP of 92 mm Hg has severe pain despite fentanyl, and low-dose ketamine is ordered for the flight. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Give 8-24 mg IV (0.1-0.3 mg/kg); Watch for dysphoria and reassess pain
qs.x: Analgesic ketamine is 0.1-0.3 mg/kg IV, and dysphoria or emergence reactions can occur, so pain and mental status are reassessed. It tends to raise BP rather than lower it, 4-5 mg/kg is an IM agitation dose, and continuous SpO2 monitoring continues.
opts: Give 8-24 mg IV (0.1-0.3 mg/kg)
Give 320-400 mg IV (4-5 mg/kg)
Watch for dysphoria and reassess pain
Withhold it because of the borderline BP
Remove the SpO2 probe once pain eases
ok: Give 8-24 mg IV (0.1-0.3 mg/kg)
Watch for dysphoria and reassess pain

qs.q: Right after a large, rapid fentanyl bolus in an intubated patient, the crew cannot ventilate and the chest feels rigid. Tube position is confirmed. Which drug-related complications explain these findings? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Opioid-induced chest wall rigidity
qs.x: Chest wall rigidity is a serious effect of fentanyl that makes ventilation difficult. The other conditions do not cause sudden rigidity with inability to ventilate.
opts: Opioid-induced chest wall rigidity
Opioid-induced adrenal suppression
Drug-induced methemoglobinemia
Opioid-induced hypoglycemia
Opioid-induced hyponatremia
ok: Opioid-induced chest wall rigidity

qs.q: After intubation, a trauma patient in hemorrhagic shock has a BP of 84/50 mm Hg and needs ongoing sedation and analgesia for transport. Which choices are reasonable? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Ketamine for sedation; Small, titrated doses of fentanyl
qs.x: Ketamine maintains BP and small titrated fentanyl doses limit hypotension. Full-dose propofol, large midazolam boluses and a dexmedetomidine load all commonly cause hypotension, which is dangerous in hemorrhagic shock.
opts: Ketamine for sedation
Propofol 2.5 mg/kg IV bolus
Small, titrated doses of fentanyl
Repeated large midazolam boluses
Dexmedetomidine with a 1 mcg/kg load
ok: Ketamine for sedation
Small, titrated doses of fentanyl

qs.q: A septic patient with a BP of 78/44 mm Hg and an SpO2 of 86% on a nonrebreather needs RSI before the flight. Which measures reduce the risk of peri-intubation cardiac arrest? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Resuscitate with fluids or pressors first; Have push-dose epinephrine ready; Use a reduced induction dose; Maximize preoxygenation before induction
qs.x: Hypotension and hypoxia before RSI raise arrest risk, so resuscitation, a ready push-dose pressor, a reduced induction dose and thorough preoxygenation are used. Propofol in unstable patients is reduced to 0.5-1 mg/kg, and skipping preoxygenation worsens hypoxia.
opts: Resuscitate with fluids or pressors first
Give propofol 2.5 mg/kg for induction
Have push-dose epinephrine ready
Use a reduced induction dose
Skip preoxygenation to save time
Maximize preoxygenation before induction
ok: Resuscitate with fluids or pressors first
Have push-dose epinephrine ready
Use a reduced induction dose
Maximize preoxygenation before induction

qs.q: Right after intubation, a septic patient's BP falls to 68/40 mm Hg while a norepinephrine infusion is being prepared, and push-dose epinephrine is ordered. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Give 10-20 mcg IV every 2-5 minutes
qs.x: Push-dose epinephrine is 10-20 mcg IV every 2-5 minutes as a bridge to an infusion. 1 mg is the arrest dose, 0.3 mg IM is the anaphylaxis dose, higher PEEP lowers venous return and BP, and profound post-intubation hypotension should not go untreated.
opts: Give 1 mg IV push every 3-5 minutes
Give 10-20 mcg IV every 2-5 minutes
Give 0.3 mg IM in the thigh
Increase PEEP to raise the BP
Hold all pressors until the drip is ready
ok: Give 10-20 mcg IV every 2-5 minutes

qs.q: A 66-year-old with low-output heart failure (BP 94/60 mm Hg, cool extremities, rising creatinine) is transferred on a milrinone infusion. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Stop and notify for new runs of VT; Trend BP and urine output
qs.x: Milrinone commonly causes hypotension and ventricular ectopy, and new ventricular arrhythmias, hypotension or declining urine output require stopping or notifying. A large bolus worsens congestion, a higher rate deepens hypotension, the label load runs over 10 minutes, and continuous monitoring is required.
opts: Stop and notify for new runs of VT
Trend BP and urine output
Bolus 1 L of saline for the SBP of 94
Double the rate if BP falls
Give the 50 mcg/kg load over 1 minute
Stop cardiac monitoring once stable
ok: Stop and notify for new runs of VT
Trend BP and urine output

qs.q: A patient with stable monomorphic VT received amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes, converted to sinus rhythm, and is transferred on the maintenance infusion with a BP of 108/70 mm Hg. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Run the infusion at 1 mg/min for 6 hours; Keep defibrillation pads applied; Stop and notify for new AV block
qs.x: After the load, amiodarone runs at 1 mg/min for 6 hours, then 0.5 mg/min, and AV block, hypotension or QT prolongation are reasons to stop and notify. Pads stay on in case VT recurs; recurrent stable VT receives 150 mg over 10 minutes, while 300 mg push is the arrest dose.
opts: Run the infusion at 1 mg/min for 6 hours
Run the infusion at 1 mg/kg/min
Keep defibrillation pads applied
Stop and notify for new AV block
Give 300 mg IV push for recurrent stable VT
Stop monitoring once in sinus rhythm
ok: Run the infusion at 1 mg/min for 6 hours
Keep defibrillation pads applied
Stop and notify for new AV block

qs.q: A 70-year-old in AF with RVR at 150/min has a BP of 82/50 mm Hg, diaphoresis and new confusion before transfer. IV diltiazem was suggested by the sending clinic. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Withhold diltiazem because SBP is under 90; Apply pads and prepare to cardiovert; Sedate before cardioversion if time allows; Use synchronized, not unsynchronized, shocks
qs.x: This patient is unstable from the tachycardia, so synchronized cardioversion with sedation when feasible is indicated, and SBP under 90 is a contraindication to diltiazem. Adenosine does not convert AF and is not used for an irregular rhythm.
opts: Withhold diltiazem because SBP is under 90
Apply pads and prepare to cardiovert
Sedate before cardioversion if time allows
Use synchronized, not unsynchronized, shocks
Give diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg over 2 minutes
Give adenosine 6 mg rapid IV
ok: Withhold diltiazem because SBP is under 90
Apply pads and prepare to cardiovert
Sedate before cardioversion if time allows
Use synchronized, not unsynchronized, shocks

qs.q: A patient on a heparin infusion for PE has a platelet count that has fallen 60% from baseline, and a new leg clot is suspected. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Stop the heparin infusion; Notify the provider of possible HIT
qs.x: A platelet drop of 50% or more with new thrombosis suggests HIT, so heparin is stopped and the provider notified. Increasing heparin worsens HIT, and four-factor PCC contains heparin and is contraindicated in HIT.
opts: Stop the heparin infusion
Increase the rate to treat the clot
Notify the provider of possible HIT
Give four-factor PCC to reverse heparin
Continue if the aPTT is in range
ok: Stop the heparin infusion
Notify the provider of possible HIT

qs.q: A 75-kg patient with an acute ischemic stroke 2 hours from last known well has a BP of 172/96 mm Hg and a glucose of 124 mg/dL, and is a lytic candidate before the flight to a thrombectomy center. Which orders are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Tenecteplase 20 mg IV bolus over 5 seconds
qs.x: Stroke tenecteplase for 70-79 kg is a single 20 mg bolus over 5 seconds, and a BP under 185/110 is acceptable. 40 mg is the STEMI dose for that weight, 0.9 mg/kg with a 10% bolus is alteplase, BP is not normalized, and antiplatelets are withheld for 24 hours after a lytic.
opts: Tenecteplase 20 mg IV bolus over 5 seconds
Tenecteplase 40 mg IV bolus over 5 seconds
0.9 mg/kg with 10% given as a bolus
Lower BP below 120/80 mm Hg first
Aspirin 324 mg with the bolus
ok: Tenecteplase 20 mg IV bolus over 5 seconds

qs.q: A crew prepares to move a patient on norepinephrine, propofol and heparin infusions from the ICU bed to the aircraft. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Trace each line from bag to patient; Label each line and pump channel; Confirm each concentration with the sending nurse; Verify each rate against the current order
qs.x: Tracing, labeling and verifying concentration and rate for every infusion prevents wrong-line and wrong-dose errors during handoff. Interrupting a vasopressor or pushing drugs through its line can cause abrupt swings in BP.
opts: Trace each line from bag to patient
Label each line and pump channel
Pause norepinephrine during the move
Confirm each concentration with the sending nurse
Push IV meds through the norepinephrine line
Verify each rate against the current order
ok: Trace each line from bag to patient
Label each line and pump channel
Confirm each concentration with the sending nurse
Verify each rate against the current order

qs.q: A 130-kg patient with an open tibia fracture is being transferred, and cefazolin is ordered before departure. He reports a childhood rash with amoxicillin. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Give cefazolin 3 g IV; Cover the wound with a sterile dressing
qs.x: Cefazolin is 2 g IV, or 3 g for patients 120 kg or more, and the open wound is covered with a sterile dressing. Only penicillin anaphylaxis is a relative contraindication, and the routes are IV and IM.
opts: Give cefazolin 3 g IV
Give 1 g IV, the standard adult dose
Withhold it because of the rash history
Cover the wound with a sterile dressing
Give it by mouth to avoid reactions
ok: Give cefazolin 3 g IV
Cover the wound with a sterile dressing

qs.q: A patient with an acute ischemic stroke is a candidate for alteplase, but the BP is 204/118 mm Hg. Which statements about BP management are accurate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: BP must be under 185/110 before alteplase
qs.x: Uncontrolled BP over 185/110 is a contraindication to alteplase for stroke, so BP is lowered below that level first, with agents such as labetalol or nicardipine. Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated, and normalizing BP is not the goal.
opts: BP must be under 185/110 before alteplase
Alteplase may be given if BP is under 220/120
A sublingual nifedipine capsule is preferred
BP must be lowered under 120/80 first
BP is treated only after the bolus
ok: BP must be under 185/110 before alteplase

qs.q: A 4-kg infant becomes bradycardic at 50/min with poor perfusion during transport despite effective oxygenation and ventilation, and atropine is ordered for suspected increased vagal tone. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Begin chest compressions; Give atropine 0.1 mg IV
qs.x: An infant with HR under 60 and poor perfusion despite effective ventilation needs CPR. PALS atropine is 0.02 mg/kg with a 0.1 mg minimum, so a 4-kg infant receives 0.1 mg; 0.5 mg is the maximum single pediatric dose, and ventilation should not be interrupted.
opts: Begin chest compressions
Give atropine 0.1 mg IV
Give atropine 0.08 mg IV (0.02 mg/kg)
Give atropine 0.5 mg IV
Withhold atropine because of age
Pause ventilation to recheck the rhythm
ok: Begin chest compressions
Give atropine 0.1 mg IV

qs.q: In cardiac arrest, which effect of epinephrine is mainly responsible for improving coronary perfusion pressure during CPR?
qs.a: Alpha-adrenergic peripheral vasoconstriction
w: Beta-2 mediated bronchodilation
Direct electrical conversion of fibrillation
Reduction of myocardial oxygen demand
qs.x: Epinephrine's alpha effect constricts peripheral vessels, raising aortic diastolic pressure and coronary perfusion during compressions. It does not convert ventricular fibrillation; defibrillation does that.

qs.q: A patient in cardiac arrest has no peripheral IV, and attempts at access have failed. Which route is an accepted alternative for giving epinephrine during resuscitation?
qs.a: Intraosseous
w: Subcutaneous
Sublingual
Oral
qs.x: The intraosseous route reaches the central circulation about as reliably as IV access and is the preferred alternative in arrest. Subcutaneous absorption is unreliable when there is no spontaneous circulation.

qs.q: For which cardiac arrest rhythm is epinephrine recommended as early as possible, because no shock is indicated?
qs.a: Asystole
w: Ventricular fibrillation
Pulseless ventricular tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia
qs.x: In nonshockable rhythms such as asystole and PEA, epinephrine is given as soon as feasible. In VF and pulseless VT, defibrillation comes first and epinephrine follows after initial shocks.

qs.q: Epinephrine belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: Sympathomimetic catecholamine
w: Parasympatholytic anticholinergic
Cardiac glycoside
Beta-adrenergic blocker
qs.x: Epinephrine is an endogenous catecholamine that stimulates alpha and beta adrenergic receptors. Atropine, not epinephrine, is the anticholinergic used in emergency care.

qs.q: After return of spontaneous circulation in a patient who received several doses of epinephrine, which finding is an expected drug effect to monitor for?
qs.a: Tachycardia and ventricular ectopy
w: Bradycardia and heart block
Pinpoint pupils and miosis
Bronchospasm and wheezing
qs.x: Epinephrine's beta-1 stimulation raises heart rate and myocardial irritability, so tachycardia and ectopy are common after ROSC. It causes bronchodilation, not bronchospasm.

qs.q: How does aspirin benefit a patient with a suspected acute coronary syndrome?
qs.a: It irreversibly inhibits platelet aggregation
w: It dissolves the existing fibrin clot
It dilates the coronary arteries directly
It lowers myocardial oxygen demand directly
qs.x: Aspirin blocks cyclooxygenase and thromboxane A2 production, keeping platelets from clumping onto the clot. It is not a fibrinolytic and does not break down existing fibrin.

qs.q: When aspirin is given for suspected acute coronary syndrome, how should the patient take the tablets?
qs.a: Chew them before swallowing
w: Swallow them whole with water
Let them dissolve under the tongue
Hold them between cheek and gum
qs.x: Chewing speeds absorption through the oral and gastric mucosa so platelet inhibition begins sooner. Sublingual placement is the route for nitroglycerin, not aspirin.

qs.q: A patient with chest pain suggestive of acute coronary syndrome reports which history that is a contraindication to aspirin?
qs.a: Known aspirin allergy with prior hives and wheezing
w: Daily use of a cholesterol-lowering medication
Taking a baby aspirin earlier in the week
History of controlled high blood pressure
qs.x: A true aspirin hypersensitivity is a contraindication because it can trigger urticaria, bronchospasm or anaphylaxis. Prior aspirin use earlier in the week does not prevent its use now.

qs.q: A patient with chest pain has ST elevation in the inferior leads and is hypotensive. Why is nitroglycerin used with great caution in this patient?
qs.a: Possible right ventricular infarction makes the patient preload dependent
w: Inferior infarction makes the patient resistant to vasodilators
Nitroglycerin increases the risk of ventricular fibrillation here
Nitroglycerin worsens platelet clumping in inferior infarction
qs.x: Inferior MI often involves the right ventricle, which depends on preload to fill the left heart; venodilation can cause profound hypotension. The concern is preload, not resistance to the drug.

qs.q: Before each dose of sublingual nitroglycerin for ischemic chest pain, which assessment is most essential?
qs.a: Blood pressure
w: Blood glucose level
Pupil size and reactivity
Capillary refill in the toes
qs.x: Nitroglycerin's vasodilation can drop blood pressure sharply, so blood pressure is checked before every dose and reassessed after. Glucose is useful in many patients but does not determine whether nitroglycerin is safe.

qs.q: A hypertensive patient presents with acute pulmonary edema. What is the main way nitroglycerin relieves the respiratory distress?
qs.a: Venodilation reduces preload and pulmonary congestion
w: Bronchodilation opens constricted small airways
Diuresis removes excess fluid through the kidneys
Increased contractility strengthens the left ventricle
qs.x: Nitroglycerin dilates veins, pooling blood peripherally and lowering the volume returning to the congested lungs. It is not a diuretic; fluid is redistributed, not excreted.

qs.q: A patient with very high blood pressure and chest pain says he took a medication for erectile dysfunction yesterday. Why is this important before nitroglycerin?
qs.a: Combined use can cause severe, prolonged hypotension
w: Combined use can cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure
The combination blocks nitroglycerin from being absorbed
The combination causes rapid bleeding from the gums
qs.x: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil and tadalafil potentiate nitrate vasodilation and can cause life-threatening hypotension. The interaction lowers, not raises, blood pressure.

qs.q: Which side effect is most commonly reported after a patient takes nitroglycerin?
qs.a: Throbbing headache
w: Severe constipation
Slowed respirations
Blurred yellow vision
qs.x: Dilation of cerebral blood vessels commonly produces a pounding headache. Yellow-tinted vision is associated with digoxin toxicity, not nitrates.

qs.q: Which teaching point helps a patient keep prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin tablets effective?
qs.a: Keep them in the original tightly closed container
w: Store them in a moist bathroom cabinet
Transfer them to a plastic weekly pill box
Keep them open in a sunny window sill
qs.x: Nitroglycerin tablets lose potency with exposure to light, heat, air and moisture, so they belong in the original closed glass container. Plastic pill organizers and humid bathrooms speed degradation.

qs.q: A patient becomes lightheaded and hypotensive a few minutes after nitroglycerin. What is the most appropriate interpretation and action?
qs.a: Recognize an expected vasodilator effect, place supine, and reassess
w: Recognize an allergic reaction and give glucagon
Recognize hypoglycemia and give oral glucose
Recognize opioid toxicity and give naloxone
qs.x: Nitroglycerin-induced venodilation can cause hypotension; laying the patient flat and reassessing vital signs is appropriate, along with reporting the change. This is a predictable effect, not anaphylaxis or hypoglycemia.

qs.q: In anaphylactic shock, which epinephrine effect most directly counters the drop in blood pressure?
qs.a: Alpha-1 vasoconstriction
w: Beta-2 bronchodilation
Muscarinic receptor blockade
Histamine-1 receptor blockade
qs.x: Alpha-1 stimulation tightens dilated, leaky vessels and raises systemic vascular resistance. Beta-2 effects open the airways but do not restore blood pressure.

qs.q: What is the preferred initial route for epinephrine in a patient with anaphylactic shock in the field?
qs.a: Intramuscular injection in the lateral thigh
w: Subcutaneous injection in the upper arm
Inhaled by small-volume nebulizer
Sublingual tablet under the tongue
qs.x: Intramuscular injection into the vastus lateralis gives faster, more reliable absorption than subcutaneous injection. Nebulized epinephrine does not treat systemic shock.

qs.q: A patient in hemorrhagic shock remains hypotensive. Why is epinephrine not the primary treatment?
qs.a: The problem is lost volume, which needs bleeding control and fluids
w: Epinephrine is absorbed too slowly in trauma patients
Epinephrine causes too much bronchodilation in trauma
The problem is vasodilation, which needs antihistamines
qs.x: Hemorrhagic shock is a volume problem; controlling bleeding and restoring circulating volume address the cause. Vasoconstrictors cannot fill an empty vascular space.

qs.q: A patient in anaphylaxis takes a beta-blocker daily. How might this affect the response to epinephrine?
qs.a: The response may be blunted, causing refractory hypotension
w: The response is usually exaggerated, causing hypertension
The beta-blocker fully prevents any alpha effects
The beta-blocker has no effect on epinephrine response
qs.x: Beta-blockade can blunt epinephrine's cardiac and bronchial effects, leading to persistent hypotension; glucagon is sometimes used in this situation. Alpha effects are not blocked by beta-blockers.

qs.q: After epinephrine is given for shock, which combination of reassessments is most appropriate?
qs.a: Blood pressure, heart rate and rhythm, and mental status
w: Pupil size, temperature, and capillary glucose only
Skin turgor, bowel sounds, and urine color
Grip strength, pupil size, and pain score
qs.x: Epinephrine changes blood pressure, heart rate and rhythm, and the response should show in perfusion and mental status. The other choices do not track its hemodynamic effect.

qs.q: Albuterol belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: Short-acting beta-2 agonist
w: Long-acting anticholinergic
Inhaled corticosteroid
Leukotriene receptor antagonist
qs.x: Albuterol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist used as rescue therapy for bronchospasm. Inhaled corticosteroids control inflammation but do not provide rapid relief.

qs.q: A patient receiving nebulized albuterol becomes shaky and reports a racing heart. How should these findings be interpreted?
qs.a: Common expected side effects of beta stimulation
w: Signs of a severe allergic reaction
Signs of opioid withdrawal
Signs of acute hypoglycemia
qs.x: Tremor and tachycardia are common albuterol effects from beta-receptor stimulation; they should be monitored and reported if significant. They do not indicate an allergy.

qs.q: After a nebulized albuterol treatment for wheezing, which finding best shows the treatment is working?
qs.a: Improved air movement and decreased work of breathing
w: Wheezing disappears and breath sounds become absent
Heart rate rises well above baseline
Patient becomes drowsy and difficult to arouse
qs.x: Better air movement with less accessory muscle use shows reversal of bronchospasm. Wheezing that fades into silent breath sounds signals worsening obstruction, not improvement.

qs.q: How does ipratropium produce bronchodilation?
qs.a: It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the airways
w: It stimulates beta-2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle
It blocks histamine release from mast cells
It reduces airway inflammation like a corticosteroid
qs.x: Ipratropium is an anticholinergic that blocks vagally mediated bronchoconstriction. Beta-2 stimulation is how albuterol works, which is why the two are often combined.

qs.q: In the emergency treatment of moderate to severe bronchospasm, ipratropium is most often given in which way?
qs.a: Nebulized together with albuterol
w: Injected intramuscularly in the thigh
Chewed and swallowed as a tablet
Injected by slow intravenous push
qs.x: Ipratropium is an inhaled drug and is commonly nebulized with albuterol because the two act on different pathways. It is not given by injection.

qs.q: Which side effect is most commonly reported with inhaled ipratropium?
qs.a: Dry mouth
w: Hypoglycemia
Excess salivation
Slowed heart rate
qs.x: As an anticholinergic, ipratropium reduces secretions and commonly causes dry mouth. Excess salivation would be the opposite, cholinergic effect.

qs.q: How is levalbuterol related to albuterol?
qs.a: It is the active isomer of albuterol, also a beta-2 agonist
w: It is a long-acting form used only for prevention
It is an anticholinergic combined with albuterol
It is an inhaled steroid derived from albuterol
qs.x: Levalbuterol is the R-isomer of albuterol and works the same way, relaxing bronchial smooth muscle by stimulating beta-2 receptors. It is used for acute bronchospasm, not as a steroid or anticholinergic.

qs.q: A patient with asthma receives nebulized levalbuterol. Which adverse effects should be monitored for?
qs.a: Tachycardia, tremor, and nervousness
w: Bradycardia, miosis, and drooling
Hypertension, hives, and fever
Constipation, sedation, and slowed breathing
