qs.x: Like albuterol, levalbuterol is a beta agonist and can cause tachycardia, tremor and nervousness. Bradycardia and drooling are cholinergic effects not expected with this drug.

qs.q: A patient in severe asthma exacerbation is too fatigued to use a nebulizer effectively. Why may intramuscular epinephrine be considered under protocol?
qs.a: It causes bronchodilation without depending on inhalation
w: It sedates the patient to reduce air hunger
It reduces airway inflammation over several hours
It thins mucus so it can be coughed up
qs.x: Systemic epinephrine reaches bronchial smooth muscle through the blood, so it works even when air movement is too poor to deliver inhaled drugs. It is not a sedative or anti-inflammatory.

qs.q: A child with croup improves after nebulized epinephrine. Why is continued observation important?
qs.a: Stridor can return as the drug's effect wears off
w: The drug commonly causes delayed hypoglycemia
The drug commonly causes delayed hives
Stridor typically worsens permanently after epinephrine
qs.x: Nebulized epinephrine shrinks swollen airway tissue only temporarily, so symptoms can return once it wears off. Delayed hypoglycemia and hives are not the expected concern.

qs.q: What is the first-line medication for a patient with anaphylaxis?
qs.a: Epinephrine
w: Diphenhydramine
Albuterol
Methylprednisolone
qs.x: Epinephrine reverses vasodilation, airway swelling and bronchospasm and is the only first-line drug for anaphylaxis. Antihistamines relieve itching and hives but do not reverse shock or airway compromise.

qs.q: Where is an epinephrine auto-injector given?
qs.a: Anterolateral thigh
w: Deltoid muscle of the arm
Abdominal wall near the navel
Dorsal gluteal muscle
qs.x: Auto-injectors are labeled for the anterolateral thigh, which provides rapid intramuscular absorption and can be reached through clothing. The abdomen is a common site for other injected drugs, not auto-injectors.

qs.q: A patient's hives and wheezing resolve after self-administered epinephrine. Why does the patient still need emergency department evaluation?
qs.a: Symptoms can return as epinephrine wears off or in a biphasic reaction
w: Epinephrine routinely causes delayed liver injury
Epinephrine must be reversed with an antidote
Hives always progress to shock within one hour
qs.x: Epinephrine is short-acting and symptoms may recur, including in a biphasic reaction hours later, so observation is needed. There is no antidote that must be given after epinephrine.

qs.q: Which epinephrine effect relieves the upper airway swelling of anaphylaxis?
qs.a: Vasoconstriction that reduces mucosal edema
w: Blocking histamine at H1 receptors
Increased mucus production in the airway
Relaxation of the skeletal muscles of the neck
qs.x: Alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction decreases capillary leak and swelling in airway tissues. Blocking H1 receptors is how antihistamines work.

qs.q: A patient with anaphylaxis has received epinephrine but still has wheezing. What role does albuterol play?
qs.a: An adjunct for persistent bronchospasm
w: A replacement for epinephrine in anaphylaxis
The primary treatment for hypotension
A treatment for laryngeal swelling
qs.x: Albuterol can relieve lower-airway bronchospasm that persists after epinephrine. It does not raise blood pressure or reduce upper-airway edema, so it never replaces epinephrine.

qs.q: Why is albuterol alone inadequate treatment for anaphylaxis?
qs.a: It does not reverse vasodilation or airway edema
w: It worsens hives by releasing histamine
It acts too slowly to relieve wheezing
It is only effective in children
qs.x: Albuterol is a selective beta-2 agonist that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle but lacks the alpha effects needed for hypotension and swelling. It acts quickly on wheezing.

qs.q: During nebulized albuterol for an allergic reaction, which finding should the AEMT recognize as a common drug effect rather than worsening allergy?
qs.a: Mild tremor of the hands
w: New swelling of the tongue
Spreading hives on the chest
Dropping blood pressure
qs.x: Fine tremor is a common beta-agonist effect. Tongue swelling, spreading hives and hypotension suggest progression of the allergic reaction.

qs.q: A patient in anaphylaxis who takes a beta-blocker remains hypotensive after repeated epinephrine. Which medication may be used for this situation?
qs.a: Glucagon
w: Naloxone
Ondansetron
Aspirin
qs.x: Glucagon raises heart rate and contractility through a pathway that does not use beta receptors, so it may help when beta-blockade blunts epinephrine. The other drugs do not address this problem.

qs.q: Why can glucagon work when beta-blockers blunt the response to epinephrine?
qs.a: It increases cardiac cAMP without using beta receptors
w: It directly blocks the beta-blocker in the blood
It stimulates alpha receptors more strongly
It speeds the liver's removal of the beta-blocker
qs.x: Glucagon binds its own receptors on heart cells and raises cAMP, bypassing the blocked beta receptors. It does not bind or clear the beta-blocker.

qs.q: Which common side effect of glucagon requires the AEMT to be prepared to protect the airway?
qs.a: Vomiting
w: Bronchospasm
Seizures
Jaw rigidity
qs.x: Nausea and vomiting are frequent after glucagon, so suction and positioning should be ready, especially in a patient with altered mental status. Bronchospasm is not a typical effect.

qs.q: Acetaminophen is best described by which set of properties?
qs.a: Analgesic and antipyretic with little anti-inflammatory effect
w: Opioid analgesic with strong sedating effects
Anti-inflammatory that strongly inhibits platelets
Local anesthetic that blocks nerve conduction
qs.x: Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever but has minimal anti-inflammatory action and does not affect platelets. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are the anti-inflammatory choice.

qs.q: What is the most serious toxic effect of an acetaminophen overdose?
qs.a: Liver injury
w: Respiratory depression
Gastric ulcer bleeding
Bone marrow failure
qs.x: Excess acetaminophen overwhelms normal metabolism and produces a metabolite that damages the liver. Respiratory depression is typical of opioid overdose, not acetaminophen.

qs.q: Before giving acetaminophen, which question is most important to ask the patient?
qs.a: Whether they recently took any product containing acetaminophen
w: Whether they have ever had a tetanus shot
Whether they are allergic to shellfish or iodine
Whether they have had recent dental work
qs.x: Many cold, sleep and prescription pain combinations contain acetaminophen, so asking prevents unintentional excess intake. Shellfish allergy has no bearing on acetaminophen.

qs.q: For a patient with a history of stomach ulcers who needs a mild pain reliever, why might acetaminophen be preferred over an NSAID?
qs.a: It does not irritate the stomach lining or impair platelets
w: It is a stronger anti-inflammatory than NSAIDs
It works by coating and protecting the stomach
It is safer than NSAIDs in severe liver disease
qs.x: Acetaminophen lacks the GI irritation and antiplatelet effects of NSAIDs, which can cause ulcer bleeding. It is not safer in severe liver disease, where acetaminophen requires caution.

qs.q: Which patient history calls for the most caution with acetaminophen?
qs.a: Chronic heavy alcohol use with liver disease
w: Seasonal allergies treated with nasal spray
Recent ankle sprain with swelling
Well-controlled hypothyroidism
qs.x: Chronic alcohol use and liver disease increase the risk of acetaminophen liver toxicity. The other conditions do not meaningfully raise that risk.

qs.q: Why are dextrose-in-water solutions a poor choice for volume replacement in hemorrhagic shock?
qs.a: Once the sugar is metabolized, the free water leaves the vessels
w: The sugar binds red cells and blocks oxygen delivery
The solution raises blood pressure too quickly
The solution causes immediate allergic reactions
qs.x: After the dextrose is used by cells, the remaining free water distributes into all body compartments and little stays in the vascular space. Isotonic crystalloids such as normal saline are used for volume.

qs.q: Before giving concentrated IV dextrose, why must the AEMT confirm that the IV line is patent and well secured?
qs.a: Extravasation can cause severe tissue damage
w: Dextrose clots quickly inside the IV catheter
Dextrose cannot be pushed through a saline lock
A patent line prevents low blood sugar from recurring
qs.x: Hypertonic dextrose is irritating, and if it leaks into tissue it can cause necrosis. Checking flow and flushing before and during administration reduces that risk.

qs.q: During IV dextrose administration, the site becomes swollen, cool, and painful. What should the AEMT recognize?
qs.a: Infiltration of the IV
w: An expected drug effect
Hyperglycemic crisis
Fluid volume overload
qs.x: Swelling, coolness and pain at the site indicate the solution is entering tissue rather than the vein, which must be recognized and managed per protocol. These are local signs, not systemic overload.

qs.q: Why is a large, proximal vein preferred when giving concentrated dextrose?
qs.a: Hypertonic solution irritates small veins
w: Dextrose is absorbed only by large veins
Small veins remove dextrose too quickly
Large veins prevent rebound hyperglycemia
qs.x: Concentrated dextrose is hypertonic and can cause phlebitis; larger veins with more blood flow dilute it faster. Vein size does not change how the body absorbs glucose.

qs.q: After IV dextrose is given for hypoglycemia, which assessment confirms the treatment effect?
qs.a: Repeat blood glucose with mental status check
w: Repeat pupil check with grip strength
Repeat lung sounds with oxygen saturation
Repeat skin turgor with urine output
qs.x: Rechecking the glucose level and the patient's mental status shows whether hypoglycemia has been corrected. Lung sounds and urine output do not reflect the response to dextrose.

qs.q: How does albuterol lower serum potassium in hyperkalemia?
qs.a: It shifts potassium from the blood into cells
w: It increases potassium excretion in urine
It binds potassium in the intestines
It removes potassium through the lungs
qs.x: Beta-2 stimulation drives potassium into cells, temporarily lowering serum levels. It does not remove potassium from the body, which requires the kidneys, binders or dialysis.

qs.q: Why is albuterol considered only a temporary measure for hyperkalemia?
qs.a: Total body potassium is unchanged and levels can rebound
w: Its effect lasts only seconds after inhalation
It causes the kidneys to retain more potassium
It is quickly neutralized by stomach acid
qs.x: Albuterol moves potassium into cells but does not eliminate it, so serum levels can rise again as the effect fades. Definitive removal is needed afterward.

qs.q: Which patient is at highest risk for hyperkalemia, a condition sometimes treated with albuterol?
qs.a: A dialysis patient who missed treatments
w: A runner with prolonged vomiting
A patient taking a loop diuretic
A patient with ongoing diarrhea
qs.x: Kidney failure with missed dialysis prevents potassium excretion, causing hyperkalemia. Vomiting, diarrhea and loop diuretics tend to cause low potassium.

qs.q: Repeated high-dose albuterol can cause which electrolyte disturbance?
qs.a: Hypokalemia
w: Hypernatremia
Hypercalcemia
Hypermagnesemia
qs.x: Because albuterol shifts potassium into cells, heavy use can lower serum potassium. It does not raise sodium, calcium or magnesium.

qs.q: While albuterol is given to a patient with suspected hyperkalemia, which monitoring is most important?
qs.a: Continuous cardiac rhythm and heart rate
w: Hourly temperature measurements
Pupil size and reactivity
Peak flow every few minutes
qs.x: Potassium abnormalities cause dysrhythmias, and albuterol itself raises heart rate, so cardiac monitoring is essential. Peak flow measures airflow, not the potassium effect.

qs.q: How does naloxone reverse opioid toxicity?
qs.a: It competitively blocks opioid receptors
w: It speeds liver breakdown of the opioid
It binds the opioid in the stomach
It directly stimulates the breathing center
qs.x: Naloxone displaces opioids from mu receptors and blocks them, reversing respiratory and CNS depression. It does not change how quickly the opioid is metabolized.

qs.q: When giving naloxone to an unresponsive patient with suspected opioid overdose, what is the primary goal?
qs.a: Restore adequate spontaneous breathing
w: Restore full alertness and orientation
Induce vomiting of any pills swallowed
Lower the heart rate to normal
qs.x: The aim is adequate ventilation; full awakening is unnecessary and risks abrupt withdrawal and agitation. Naloxone does not cause vomiting of pills.

qs.q: After naloxone reverses an opioid overdose, why must the patient be monitored closely?
qs.a: Naloxone may wear off before the opioid, causing re-sedation
w: Naloxone often causes delayed liver failure
Naloxone often causes delayed anaphylaxis
Naloxone causes a late drop in blood glucose
qs.x: Many opioids, especially long-acting or high-potency ones, outlast naloxone, so respiratory depression can return. Liver failure and hypoglycemia are not expected naloxone effects.

qs.q: A patient who uses opioids daily becomes agitated, vomits, and has goosebumps right after naloxone. What should the AEMT recognize?
qs.a: Acute opioid withdrawal
w: Allergic reaction to naloxone
Serotonin syndrome
Hypoglycemic reaction
qs.x: Naloxone abruptly reverses opioid effects in a dependent patient, producing withdrawal with agitation, vomiting and piloerection. These signs are not an allergic reaction.

qs.q: How does activated charcoal reduce the absorption of an ingested poison?
qs.a: It adsorbs the toxin on its surface in the gut
w: It neutralizes acids by chemical reaction
It induces vomiting of stomach contents
It blocks the toxin at its receptor site
qs.x: Activated charcoal's large surface area binds many drugs in the GI tract so less is absorbed. It is not an emetic or a receptor antagonist.

qs.q: Which patient should NOT receive activated charcoal?
qs.a: A drowsy patient who cannot protect the airway
w: An alert adult who swallowed pills recently
An alert patient who took an acetaminophen overdose
An alert patient with nausea but no vomiting
qs.x: Charcoal given to a patient with decreased consciousness or an unprotected airway risks aspiration. An alert patient with a recent ingestion is the typical candidate if ordered.

qs.q: Activated charcoal binds poorly to which ingested substance?
qs.a: Iron
w: Aspirin
Acetaminophen
Tricyclic antidepressants
qs.x: Metals such as iron and lithium, alcohols and caustics are poorly adsorbed by charcoal. Aspirin, acetaminophen and tricyclics bind well.

qs.q: Glucagon may be used as an antidote for an overdose of which medication class?
qs.a: Beta-blockers
w: Benzodiazepines
Opioids
Anticholinergics
qs.x: Glucagon raises heart rate and contractility through its own receptors, bypassing blocked beta receptors in beta-blocker overdose. Opioid overdose is reversed with naloxone.

qs.q: A patient with beta-blocker overdose has bradycardia and hypotension. Which effect of glucagon makes it useful?
qs.a: Increases heart rate and contractility
w: Lowers heart rate and contractility
Causes peripheral vasodilation
Blocks calcium entry into cardiac cells
qs.x: Glucagon has positive chronotropic and inotropic effects independent of beta receptors, countering beta-blocker toxicity. Blocking calcium entry would worsen the problem.

qs.q: When glucagon is given for beta-blocker toxicity, which side effect should the AEMT be prepared to manage?
qs.a: Vomiting with aspiration risk
w: Severe bronchospasm
Muscle rigidity
Pinpoint pupils
qs.x: Vomiting is a common glucagon effect, so suction and airway positioning should be ready. Bronchospasm and pinpoint pupils are not expected glucagon effects.

qs.q: Before IV dextrose is given to a patient with altered mental status, which finding should be confirmed?
qs.a: A low blood glucose reading
w: A high blood glucose reading
A normal blood pressure
A slow pulse rate
qs.x: Dextrose is indicated for documented hypoglycemia, so a glucose check guides its use. Blood pressure and pulse do not determine the need for dextrose.

qs.q: Why is IV dextrose preferred over oral glucose for a hypoglycemic patient who is unresponsive?
qs.a: The patient cannot safely swallow, risking aspiration
w: Oral glucose raises blood sugar too much
Oral glucose is only for children
IV dextrose lasts longer than any food
qs.x: Oral glucose requires an intact gag reflex and ability to swallow; an unresponsive patient could aspirate. IV dextrose bypasses the airway.

qs.q: A known diabetic is confused, pale, and sweaty. Which finding most strongly supports hypoglycemia as the cause?
qs.a: Rapid onset after skipping a meal following insulin
w: Gradual onset over days with heavy thirst
Fruity breath with deep, rapid breathing
Frequent urination with dry mucous membranes
qs.x: Taking insulin without eating commonly causes rapid hypoglycemia with diaphoresis and confusion, which dextrose treats. Fruity breath and Kussmaul breathing suggest DKA.

qs.q: A hypoglycemic patient is unresponsive and no IV access can be obtained. How can glucagon be given?
qs.a: Intramuscularly or by the intranasal form
w: Orally as a chewable tablet
Sublingually as a dissolving film
Rectally as a suppository
qs.x: Glucagon is available for IM injection and as an intranasal powder, so it can be given without IV access. It is not effective by mouth.

qs.q: Why may glucagon be less effective in a malnourished patient with chronic alcohol use?
qs.a: Liver glycogen stores may be depleted
w: Alcohol blocks glucagon receptors directly
Alcohol speeds glucagon excretion by kidneys
Alcohol inactivates glucagon in the blood
qs.x: Glucagon raises blood sugar by releasing glucose from liver glycogen; if those stores are low, the response is weak. IV dextrose supplies glucose directly.

qs.q: Ondansetron belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: Serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist
w: Dopamine D2 receptor agonist
Histamine H2 receptor blocker
Proton pump inhibitor
qs.x: Ondansetron blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors in the gut and brainstem vomiting center. H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors reduce acid but do not treat nausea directly.

qs.q: Which cardiac effect of ondansetron is listed as a warning in its labeling?
qs.a: QT interval prolongation
w: Sudden heart block
Marked hypertension
ST segment elevation
qs.x: Ondansetron can prolong the QT interval and, rarely, cause torsades de pointes, so caution is needed in patients with long QT or electrolyte problems. ST elevation is not an expected effect.

qs.q: How should an orally disintegrating ondansetron tablet be given?
qs.a: Placed on the tongue to dissolve, then swallowed
w: Crushed and inhaled through a nebulizer
Swallowed whole with a large glass of water
Chewed thoroughly with a meal
qs.x: The orally disintegrating tablet dissolves on the tongue in seconds and is swallowed with saliva, useful for nauseated patients. It does not need to be swallowed whole with water.

qs.q: Which side effect is commonly reported after ondansetron?
qs.a: Headache
w: Hallucinations
Hypoglycemia
Excess tearing
qs.x: Headache is among the most common ondansetron side effects; constipation is another. Hallucinations are not a typical effect.

qs.q: Which patient history calls for the most caution before ondansetron?
qs.a: Congenital long QT syndrome
w: Seasonal pollen allergies
Recent knee replacement surgery
Well-controlled asthma
qs.x: Ondansetron's labeling advises avoiding it in congenital long QT syndrome because of the risk of dangerous rhythms. The other histories do not raise this risk.

qs.q: A child stung by a bee develops hives, wheezing, and lethargy. What is the priority medication?
qs.a: Intramuscular epinephrine
w: Oral diphenhydramine
Nebulized ipratropium
Oral acetaminophen
qs.x: Hives with respiratory involvement and altered mental status indicate anaphylaxis, for which IM epinephrine is first-line. Antihistamines do not reverse airway or circulatory compromise.

qs.q: When helping a parent use a child's epinephrine auto-injector, which teaching point is correct?
qs.a: Press firmly into the outer thigh for the labeled time
w: Inject into the buttock for faster absorption
Remove clothing completely before injecting
Inject into the upper arm muscle
qs.x: Auto-injectors go into the anterolateral thigh and are held in place for the labeled time so the full amount is delivered; they can be given through clothing. Labeling warns against injecting into the buttocks.

qs.q: An infant is jittery, poorly feeding, and has a weak cry. Which assessment should guide whether dextrose is given?
qs.a: Blood glucose measurement
w: Temperature measurement
Head circumference
Pupil response
qs.x: Signs of hypoglycemia in infants are vague, so a glucose check confirms the need for dextrose. Temperature and head size do not establish hypoglycemia.

qs.q: A school-age child with asthma is wheezing. Which device helps the child get more albuterol into the lungs from a metered-dose inhaler?
qs.a: A spacer attached to the inhaler
w: A nasal cannula
A bag-valve mask with reservoir
A peak flow meter
qs.x: A spacer keeps the medication in a chamber so the child can inhale it with less need for coordination, improving delivery to the lungs. A peak flow meter measures airflow but delivers no medication.

qs.q: A toddler is found drowsy with slow, shallow breathing and pinpoint pupils near a grandparent's pill bottle. Which medication addresses the likely cause?
qs.a: Naloxone
w: Glucagon
Ondansetron
Albuterol
qs.x: Pinpoint pupils with respiratory depression suggest opioid toxicity, which naloxone reverses; ventilation support comes first. Glucagon is for hypoglycemia or beta-blocker toxicity.

qs.q: A child with type 1 diabetes is unresponsive with a low glucose reading and no IV access. Which medication can be given?
qs.a: Glucagon
w: Oral glucose gel
Ondansetron
Activated charcoal
qs.x: Glucagon by IM injection or intranasally raises blood sugar without IV access. Oral glucose is unsafe because an unresponsive child cannot protect the airway.

qs.q: Why is ondansetron given to some children with vomiting from gastroenteritis?
qs.a: To reduce vomiting so oral rehydration can succeed
w: To cure the underlying viral infection
To slow diarrhea by firming the stool
To treat dehydration directly by adding fluid
qs.x: Controlling vomiting allows the child to keep down oral fluids and may avoid IV therapy. Ondansetron does not treat the infection or replace fluid itself.

qs.q: Why is acetaminophen preferred over aspirin for fever in a child with a viral illness?
qs.a: Aspirin is linked to Reye syndrome in children
w: Aspirin does not reduce fever in children
Acetaminophen also treats the viral infection
Acetaminophen has stronger anti-inflammatory effects
qs.x: Aspirin use in children with viral illnesses such as influenza or chickenpox is associated with Reye syndrome, a dangerous liver and brain disorder. Acetaminophen does not treat the infection.

qs.q: Which teaching point helps a parent avoid giving too much liquid acetaminophen to a child?
qs.a: Use the measuring device that comes with the product
w: Use a household kitchen spoon
Mix it into a full bottle of formula
Give an adult tablet cut into pieces
qs.x: The dosing device packaged with the product matches its labeled concentration and reduces measuring errors. Kitchen spoons vary in size and commonly lead to dosing mistakes.

qs.q: A child has had several days of vomiting and diarrhea with very little urine output. Why is ibuprofen a concern?
qs.a: Dehydration increases its risk of kidney injury
w: Dehydration makes it cause liver failure
It worsens diarrhea by speeding the gut
It causes dangerous drops in blood sugar
qs.x: NSAIDs reduce blood flow to the kidneys, and in a dehydrated child this can contribute to acute kidney injury. Liver failure is the major concern with acetaminophen overdose, not ibuprofen.

qs.q: A resident takes amlodipine for high blood pressure. Which change is a common side effect a nursing assistant should report to the nurse?
qs.a: Swelling in the ankles and feet
w: Bright orange-colored urine
Increased hunger at night
White patches inside the mouth
qs.x: Amlodipine often causes swelling (edema) in the ankles and feet, which should be reported. It does not change urine color or cause mouth patches.

qs.q: A resident who takes atorvastatin to lower cholesterol complains of new, unexplained muscle pain and weakness. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Report the muscle pain to the nurse
w: Give the resident a warm bath and recheck tomorrow
Tell the resident this is normal for everyone
Encourage extra exercise to work out the soreness
qs.x: Statins like atorvastatin can rarely cause serious muscle damage, so new muscle pain or weakness must be reported. It should not be brushed off as normal soreness.

qs.q: A resident on digoxin says food has lost its appeal, feels sick to the stomach, and sees yellow-green halos around lights. What do these changes suggest?
qs.a: Possible signs of too much digoxin
w: Expected signs the medicine is working
Normal changes from aging eyes
Signs of a mild seasonal allergy
qs.x: Nausea, loss of appetite, and vision changes such as yellow-green halos can mean digoxin levels are too high. These must be reported to the nurse right away, not treated as normal aging.

qs.q: Why is furosemide usually given in the morning rather than at bedtime?
qs.a: It causes frequent urination for several hours
w: It works better on an empty stomach at night
It causes sleepiness during the day
It must be taken with the evening meal
qs.x: Furosemide is a strong water pill that makes the person urinate a lot for several hours. Morning timing helps avoid nighttime trips to the bathroom and falls.

qs.q: A resident who takes hydrochlorothiazide feels lightheaded when getting out of bed. What is the safest action for the nursing assistant?
qs.a: Have the resident sit on the edge of the bed before standing
w: Help the resident stand up quickly to get it over with
Have the resident walk to the bathroom alone
Lay the resident flat and leave the room
qs.x: Water pills can lower blood pressure, especially when standing up. Sitting first and rising slowly lowers fall risk; standing quickly makes dizziness worse.

qs.q: A resident who recently started lisinopril has a dry, tickly cough that will not go away. What should the nursing assistant know?
qs.a: A dry cough is a known side effect to report
w: A dry cough means the dose is working well
A dry cough is caused only by a cold
A dry cough means the resident needs more fluids
qs.x: Lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) commonly causes a dry, nagging cough, which should be reported to the nurse. It is not a sign the medicine is working.

qs.q: A resident taking lisinopril suddenly has swelling of the lips, tongue, and face. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Call for the nurse right away and stay with the resident
w: Offer cold water and check back in an hour
Apply lotion to the lips and face
Write it down to report at the end of the shift
qs.x: Swelling of the face, lips, or tongue (angioedema) is a rare but dangerous reaction to lisinopril that can block the airway. It is an emergency, not something to report later.

qs.q: When taking vital signs on a resident who takes metoprolol, which finding is most important to report to the nurse?
qs.a: A pulse that is much slower than usual
w: A pulse that is the same as yesterday
A temperature that is normal
A blood pressure that is unchanged
qs.x: Metoprolol slows the heart rate, so an unusually slow pulse can mean too strong an effect. Readings that match the resident's normal values are not a concern.

qs.q: Metoprolol belongs to which group of heart medicines?
qs.a: Beta blockers
w: Water pills (diuretics)
Blood thinners
Cholesterol-lowering statins
qs.x: Metoprolol is a beta blocker that slows the heart and lowers blood pressure. It is not a water pill; furosemide and hydrochlorothiazide are diuretics.

qs.q: A resident with chest pain is given nitroglycerin by the nurse. Which side effect is common and should be expected?
qs.a: Headache and feeling lightheaded
w: Increased appetite and thirst
Itchy rash on the arms
Dark brown urine
qs.x: Nitroglycerin widens blood vessels, which commonly causes headache and dizziness from lower blood pressure. The resident should stay seated or lying down to prevent falls.

qs.q: What is digoxin commonly used to treat?
qs.a: Heart failure and certain irregular heartbeats
w: High cholesterol and fatty blood
Asthma and other breathing problems
Low thyroid hormone levels
qs.x: Digoxin helps the heart pump more strongly and can slow some irregular heart rhythms like atrial fibrillation. It is not a cholesterol or breathing medicine.

qs.q: Before a resident's morning digoxin, the nursing assistant counts an apical pulse that is much lower than the resident's usual rate. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Report the pulse to the nurse before the medication pass
w: Have the resident walk to raise the pulse
Recheck the pulse tomorrow morning
Record it without telling anyone
qs.x: Digoxin slows the heart rate, and a low pulse can be a sign of too much medicine. The nurse needs this information right away to decide what to do.

qs.q: What is apixaban given for?
qs.a: To help prevent blood clots and stroke
w: To raise a low red blood cell count
To lower high blood sugar
To relieve joint pain and swelling
qs.x: Apixaban is a blood thinner (anticoagulant) used to prevent clots, such as strokes in atrial fibrillation or clots in the legs and lungs. It does not treat anemia or pain.

qs.q: A resident who takes apixaban slips and falls but says they feel fine and has no visible cuts. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Report the fall to the nurse right away
w: Help the resident up and not mention it
Report it only if a bruise appears tomorrow
Give the resident an ice pack and leave
qs.x: People on blood thinners can bleed inside the body, even in the head, without visible injury. Every fall must be reported right away so the nurse can assess.

qs.q: A resident takes daily low-dose aspirin. Which stool change should be reported to the nurse?
qs.a: Black, tarry stools
w: Soft, formed brown stools
One bowel movement a day
Stool that is light brown
qs.x: Aspirin can irritate the stomach and cause bleeding, which may show up as black, tarry stools. Normal soft brown stools are not a concern.

qs.q: Why do many people with heart disease take a daily low-dose aspirin?
qs.a: To help keep platelets from forming clots
w: To lower cholesterol in the blood
To make the heart beat slower
To help the body get rid of fluid
qs.x: Aspirin makes platelets less sticky, which helps prevent clots that cause heart attacks and strokes. It does not lower cholesterol or remove fluid.

qs.q: Clopidogrel belongs to which group of medicines?
qs.a: Antiplatelet medicines (blood thinners)
w: Antibiotics that fight infection
Water pills (diuretics)
Medicines that raise blood pressure
qs.x: Clopidogrel keeps platelets from sticking together, so it is an antiplatelet blood thinner. It is often given after a stent or stroke.

qs.q: A resident on clopidogrel needs to be shaved. Which is the safest choice?
qs.a: Use an electric razor
w: Use a straight-edge razor
Use a new disposable blade razor
Shave against the hair growth quickly
qs.x: People taking blood thinners bleed more easily from small cuts. An electric razor lowers the chance of nicks compared with blade razors.

qs.q: A resident recently started ferrous sulfate (iron). Which change in stool is a common, expected effect of iron pills?
qs.a: Dark green or black color
w: Bright red streaks of blood
Pale clay color
Very loose watery stool
qs.x: Iron pills commonly turn stool dark green or black. Bright red blood is not caused by iron and should always be reported.

qs.q: Iron pills often cause which bowel problem that the nursing assistant should watch for and report?
qs.a: Constipation
w: Bowel incontinence
Bright yellow stools
Rectal itching
qs.x: Constipation is a very common side effect of iron pills. Tracking bowel movements and encouraging fluids and fiber as allowed by the care plan helps.

qs.q: A resident who takes warfarin has pink urine, bleeding gums, and new large bruises. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Report these signs of bleeding to the nurse
w: Give the resident extra fluids and recheck later
Treat the bruises with a heating pad
Record it as a normal effect of warfarin
qs.x: Pink or red urine, bleeding gums, and unusual bruising can be signs warfarin is causing bleeding. These need to be reported, not treated as normal.

qs.q: A resident who takes warfarin suddenly starts eating much larger amounts of green leafy vegetables like spinach and kale. Why should this be shared with the nurse?
qs.a: Vitamin K in these foods can change how warfarin works
w: These foods make warfarin cause more headaches
These foods turn warfarin into a laxative
These foods make warfarin taste bitter
qs.x: Green leafy vegetables are high in vitamin K, which works against warfarin. People on warfarin should keep the amount of these foods steady, so big changes matter.

qs.q: What does an albuterol inhaler do?
qs.a: Quickly relaxes and opens the airways
w: Slowly reduces swelling over weeks
Loosens and thins thick mucus
Kills bacteria in the lungs
qs.x: Albuterol is a quick-relief (rescue) inhaler that opens tight airways within minutes. It is not a long-term anti-swelling medicine or an antibiotic.

qs.q: After using an albuterol inhaler, a resident says they feel shaky and their heart is beating fast. What should the nursing assistant know?
qs.a: These are common side effects to report to the nurse
w: These mean the resident is allergic to air
These mean the inhaler is empty
These are signs of low blood sugar only
qs.x: Albuterol commonly causes shakiness and a fast heartbeat. These should be reported so the nurse can check the resident, especially if they are strong or do not go away.

qs.q: After a resident uses a fluticasone inhaler, why is rinsing the mouth with water and spitting encouraged?
qs.a: To help prevent a fungal mouth infection (thrush)
w: To make the medicine work faster
To prevent the teeth from staining
To keep the throat from getting too cold
qs.x: Fluticasone is an inhaled steroid that can leave medicine in the mouth and lead to thrush. Rinsing and spitting lowers that risk.

qs.q: A resident with asthma has a fluticasone inhaler and an albuterol inhaler. Which is true about the fluticasone inhaler?
qs.a: It is used every day to control swelling, not for sudden attacks
w: It is the rescue inhaler for sudden attacks
It is only used when the resident has a cold
It works within seconds to open the airways
qs.x: Fluticasone is a controller medicine that reduces airway swelling over time. Albuterol, not fluticasone, is the quick-relief rescue inhaler.

qs.q: What is guaifenesin used for?
qs.a: To loosen mucus so it is easier to cough up
w: To stop all coughing completely
To open the airways during an asthma attack
To treat a bacterial lung infection
qs.x: Guaifenesin is an expectorant that thins mucus so coughs bring it up more easily. It does not treat infection or open the airways.

qs.q: A resident is taking guaifenesin for chest congestion. Which daily care action helps this medicine work best, if allowed by the care plan?
qs.a: Encouraging the resident to drink fluids
w: Keeping the resident lying flat all day
Limiting fluids to keep mucus thick
Keeping the room very dry and warm
qs.x: Drinking enough fluids helps thin mucus, which supports what guaifenesin does. Limiting fluids or lying flat makes mucus harder to clear.

qs.q: What is levocetirizine mainly used to treat?
qs.a: Allergy symptoms like sneezing and a runny nose
w: Chest pain from heart disease
Constipation and bloating
Pain and swelling in the joints
qs.x: Levocetirizine is an antihistamine that relieves allergy symptoms such as sneezing, runny nose, and itchy eyes. It is not a heart, bowel, or pain medicine.

qs.q: A resident who started levocetirizine seems more sleepy than usual. How might this affect daily care?
qs.a: The resident may need extra help to prevent falls
w: The resident needs less help with walking
The resident should skip meals until alert
The resident will need extra salt in meals
qs.x: Levocetirizine can cause drowsiness, which raises fall risk. Sleepiness should be reported and the resident may need closer help with walking and transfers.

qs.q: A resident with diabetes is taking prednisone for a lung flare-up. Which change is most likely to happen?
qs.a: Blood sugar levels may go up
w: Blood sugar levels will drop very low
The resident will lose their appetite
The resident's skin will become oily
qs.x: Steroids like prednisone raise blood sugar, which is especially important in people with diabetes. Prednisone usually increases, rather than decreases, appetite.

qs.q: Prednisone belongs to which group of medicines?
qs.a: Steroids (corticosteroids)
w: Antibiotics
Antihistamines
Opioid pain relievers
qs.x: Prednisone is a corticosteroid that reduces swelling and calms the immune system. It is not an antibiotic, so it does not kill bacteria.

qs.q: What is carbidopa/levodopa used to treat?
qs.a: Parkinson's disease symptoms like tremor and stiffness
w: Memory loss from Alzheimer's disease
Seizures from epilepsy
Dizziness from inner ear problems
qs.x: Carbidopa/levodopa replaces dopamine in the brain to ease Parkinson's symptoms such as shaking, stiffness, and slow movement. It does not treat memory loss or seizures.

qs.q: A resident who takes carbidopa/levodopa has new jerky, twisting movements of the arms and face that they cannot control. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Report the new movements to the nurse
w: Restrain the arms to keep them still
Ignore it because it is part of aging
Encourage the resident to sleep it off
qs.x: Uncontrolled jerky or twisting movements (dyskinesias) are a known side effect of carbidopa/levodopa and need to be reported. Restraining the resident is unsafe.

qs.q: What is donepezil used for?
qs.a: To help with memory and thinking in Alzheimer's dementia
w: To cure Alzheimer's disease completely
To treat seizures in older adults
To help people fall asleep at night
qs.x: Donepezil may help memory and thinking symptoms of Alzheimer's dementia, but it does not cure the disease. It is not a seizure or sleep medicine.

qs.q: Which side effects of donepezil should a nursing assistant watch for and report?
qs.a: Nausea, diarrhea, and a slow pulse or fainting
w: Increased hair growth and acne
Bright red urine and nosebleeds
Very fast pulse and sweating
qs.x: Donepezil commonly causes stomach upset such as nausea and diarrhea, and can slow the heart rate, leading to fainting. These should be reported.

qs.q: Gabapentin is used for which conditions?
qs.a: Certain seizures and nerve pain
w: High blood pressure and heart failure
Bacterial infections of the skin
Low thyroid and weight gain
qs.x: Gabapentin is used to help control certain seizures and to treat nerve pain, such as pain after shingles. It is not a blood pressure medicine or antibiotic.

qs.q: An older resident who takes gabapentin is dizzy and sleepy. Which safety step is most important?
qs.a: Help with walking and keep the call light within reach
w: Have the resident walk alone to stay strong
Raise the bed to its highest position
Remove the resident's walker from the room
qs.x: Gabapentin commonly causes dizziness and sleepiness, raising fall risk. Assistance with walking and a call light within reach help prevent falls.

qs.q: Lorazepam belongs to which group of medicines?
qs.a: Benzodiazepines
w: Antibiotics
Antidepressants
Blood thinners
qs.x: Lorazepam is a benzodiazepine that calms the brain and can be used for anxiety or to stop seizures. It is not an antidepressant.

qs.q: An older resident received lorazepam and is now confused and unsteady on their feet. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Report the changes and help keep the resident safe from falls
w: Encourage the resident to walk the hallway alone
Assume it is normal and keep the usual routine
Give the resident coffee to wake them up
qs.x: Lorazepam can cause confusion, sleepiness, and poor balance, especially in older adults. These changes should be reported and fall precautions used.

qs.q: A resident takes meclizine for dizziness from an inner ear problem. Which side effect makes extra fall precautions important?
qs.a: Drowsiness
w: Increased energy
Faster reaction time
Better balance right away
qs.x: Meclizine is an antihistamine that commonly causes drowsiness, which can raise fall risk. It does not improve alertness.

qs.q: A resident with Alzheimer's disease takes memantine. Which side effects should be reported to the nurse?
qs.a: Dizziness, headache, or new confusion
w: Shiny skin and hair loss
Heavy sweating and shaking
Bright orange urine
qs.x: Memantine can cause dizziness, headache, and confusion. New or worse confusion should be reported, and dizziness increases fall risk.

qs.q: Acetaminophen is used to relieve which problems?
qs.a: Pain and fever
w: Pain and blood clots
Fever and constipation
Swelling and high blood pressure
qs.x: Acetaminophen treats mild to moderate pain and lowers fever. It does not thin the blood like aspirin, and does little for swelling.

qs.q: Which organ can be harmed if a person takes too much acetaminophen, including from combination products?
qs.a: Liver
w: Lungs
Eyes
Bladder
qs.x: Too much acetaminophen can cause serious liver damage. Many combination pain and cold products also contain acetaminophen, so the total amount matters.

qs.q: A resident with burning, tingling pain in the feet from diabetes is given gabapentin. What kind of pain is gabapentin used for?
qs.a: Nerve pain
w: Headache from high blood pressure
Muscle pain from a strain
Chest pain from the heart
qs.x: Gabapentin is used for nerve pain, such as burning or tingling from diabetic nerve damage or after shingles. It does not treat heart-related chest pain.

qs.q: A resident received hydrocodone for pain and now wants to walk to the bathroom. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Stay with the resident and help them walk
w: Let the resident walk alone to stay independent
Tell the resident to wait until the next shift
Have the resident walk quickly before getting sleepy
qs.x: Hydrocodone is an opioid that can cause dizziness and sleepiness, which raise fall risk. Staying with the resident and assisting keeps them safe.

qs.q: Ibuprofen belongs to which group of medicines?
qs.a: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
w: Opioid pain relievers
Steroids (corticosteroids)
Antihistamines
qs.x: Ibuprofen is an NSAID that reduces pain, fever, and swelling. It is not an opioid or a steroid.

qs.q: A resident taking ibuprofen regularly complains of stomach pain and has dark, tarry stools. Why is this important?
qs.a: It may be a sign of stomach bleeding
w: It means the ibuprofen is working
It is caused by drinking too much water
It means the resident needs more fiber
qs.x: Ibuprofen can irritate the stomach lining and cause ulcers and bleeding, which may show as black, tarry stools. This must be reported to the nurse.

qs.q: A resident taking oxycodone has not had a bowel movement in several days. What does this likely relate to?
qs.a: Opioids commonly cause constipation
w: Oxycodone always causes diarrhea
The resident is eating too much fiber
Oxycodone makes the bladder overactive
qs.x: Constipation is one of the most common side effects of opioids like oxycodone. Tracking bowel movements and reporting constipation helps the nurse manage it.

qs.q: After a dose of oxycodone, a resident is very hard to wake up and is breathing slowly and shallowly. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Call for the nurse immediately
w: Let the resident sleep and check later
Offer a glass of water and leave
Turn off the lights so they can rest
qs.x: Extreme sleepiness with slow, shallow breathing can be a sign of opioid overdose and is an emergency. The nurse must be called right away.

qs.q: Tramadol belongs to which group of medicines?
qs.a: Opioid pain relievers
w: Antibiotics
Water pills (diuretics)
Antacids
qs.x: Tramadol is an opioid pain reliever, so it can cause sleepiness, dizziness, constipation, and slowed breathing like other opioids.

qs.q: A resident took zolpidem at bedtime and gets up in the middle of the night. Which concern is most important?
qs.a: Unsteadiness and falls from the sleep medicine
w: Higher blood sugar from the sleep medicine
Sunburn from the sleep medicine
Hearing loss from the sleep medicine
qs.x: Zolpidem is a sleep medicine that can cause dizziness, confusion, and unusual sleep behaviors, raising the risk of falls at night. The resident should be helped and the call light kept close.

qs.q: Lorazepam is commonly used in behavioral health to treat what?
qs.a: Anxiety
w: Depression that lasts for months
Schizophrenia hallucinations
Attention problems
qs.x: Lorazepam is a benzodiazepine used for short-term relief of anxiety. It is not a treatment for long-term depression or psychosis.

qs.q: A resident takes both lorazepam and an opioid pain medicine. Which change is most important to report right away?
qs.a: Very slow breathing and being hard to wake
w: A mild increase in appetite
Asking for an extra blanket
Wanting to watch television
qs.x: Taking a benzodiazepine like lorazepam together with an opioid can dangerously slow breathing and cause deep sedation. These signs need immediate reporting.

qs.q: Quetiapine belongs to which group of medicines?
qs.a: Antipsychotics
w: Antibiotics
Blood thinners
Stool softeners
qs.x: Quetiapine is an antipsychotic used for conditions such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. It is not an antibiotic or a blood thinner.

qs.q: A resident who takes quetiapine gets dizzy when standing up. Which care step helps keep the resident safe?
qs.a: Have the resident rise slowly and assist with standing
w: Have the resident stand up quickly
Have the resident skip meals to avoid dizziness
Have the resident walk without a walker
qs.x: Quetiapine can lower blood pressure when standing and cause sleepiness, which raises fall risk. Rising slowly with help lowers that risk.

qs.q: A resident started sertraline for depression last week and says it is not helping yet. What should the nursing assistant know?
qs.a: It often takes several weeks to feel the full effect
w: It should work within a few hours
It only works if taken with alcohol
It works only when the resident is sleeping
qs.x: Antidepressants like sertraline usually take several weeks to reach full effect. Concerns should still be shared with the nurse.

qs.q: A resident on sertraline says, "Everyone would be better off without me." What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Stay with the resident and report it to the nurse right away
w: Change the subject to something more cheerful
Keep it private because the resident trusted you
Tell the resident to talk about it tomorrow
qs.x: Antidepressants carry a warning about worsening depression and suicidal thoughts. Any talk of self-harm must be reported immediately, and the resident should not be left alone.

qs.q: Trazodone is an antidepressant that is also often used to help with what?
qs.a: Sleep
w: Constipation
High blood pressure
Seasonal allergies
qs.x: Trazodone is an antidepressant that causes sleepiness, so it is often given at bedtime to help with sleep. It is not a laxative or allergy medicine.

qs.q: A resident who takes trazodone at bedtime needs to use the bathroom during the night. Which action is safest?
qs.a: Keep the bed low, the call light close, and assist with walking
w: Have the resident walk in the dark alone
Raise the bed rails and leave the bed high
Tell the resident to hurry to the bathroom
qs.x: Trazodone can cause drowsiness and dizziness on standing, so night trips to the bathroom can lead to falls. A low bed, call light, and help with walking improve safety.

qs.q: Some behavioral health medicines cause constipation, so senna may be ordered. How does senna work?
qs.a: It stimulates the bowel muscles to move stool
w: It adds bulk by soaking up fat
It coats the stomach to stop acid
It slows the bowel to firm up stool
qs.x: Senna is a stimulant laxative that makes the bowel muscles push stool along. It does not coat the stomach or slow the bowel.

qs.q: A resident received bisacodyl for constipation. Which side effect is common and may be reported if it is strong?
qs.a: Belly cramping
w: Hair loss
Blurred vision
Fast weight gain
qs.x: Bisacodyl is a stimulant laxative that commonly causes belly cramping. Severe cramping, pain, or many watery stools should be reported.

qs.q: A resident takes furosemide and is weighed every day. Which practice gives the most accurate daily weights?
qs.a: Same scale, same time of day, and similar clothing
w: Different scale each day to compare
Weigh only after the resident eats
Weigh at a different time each day
qs.x: Daily weights show fluid gain or loss, so they must be taken the same way every day. Using a different scale or time makes changes hard to trust.

qs.q: A resident on furosemide has a dry mouth, is very dizzy, and is urinating much less than usual. What might these signs mean?
qs.a: The resident may be losing too much fluid
w: The medicine is not strong enough
The resident is getting too much potassium
These are normal signs the medicine works
qs.x: Furosemide removes fluid, and too much fluid loss can cause dry mouth, dizziness, and low urine output. These signs of dehydration should be reported.

qs.q: A resident starts hydrochlorothiazide, a water pill. How might this affect daily care?
qs.a: The resident may need help getting to the bathroom more often
w: The resident will need fewer bathroom trips
The resident should have fluids taken away
The resident will need to stay in bed all day
qs.x: Water pills increase urination, so the resident may need more frequent toileting help. Keeping the call light within reach and the path clear lowers fall risk.

qs.q: Why is potassium chloride often given to people who take water pills like furosemide?
qs.a: To replace potassium lost in the urine
w: To make the water pill work faster
To lower blood sugar after meals
To keep the urine from smelling
qs.x: Some water pills cause the body to lose potassium in the urine. Potassium chloride replaces it to keep levels in a safe range.

qs.q: A resident takes potassium chloride. Which side effect should the nursing assistant report to the nurse?
qs.a: Stomach pain, vomiting, or trouble swallowing
w: Increased hunger at mealtime
Feeling cold in a cool room
Mild dry skin on the hands
qs.x: Potassium pills can irritate the stomach and throat, causing pain, nausea, vomiting, or trouble swallowing. These should be reported.

qs.q: A resident taking nitrofurantoin has urine that looks darker yellow or brownish. What should the nursing assistant know?
qs.a: This color change is a known effect of the medicine
w: This means the resident has kidney stones
This means the resident needs less water
This color means the medicine has expired
qs.x: Nitrofurantoin can turn urine dark yellow or brown, which is a known, usually harmless effect. The nursing assistant can still mention it to the nurse.

qs.q: What is oxybutynin used to treat?
qs.a: Overactive bladder with sudden urges and leaking
w: Urinary tract infections
Kidney stones
High blood pressure
qs.x: Oxybutynin relaxes the bladder muscle to reduce sudden urges, frequent urination, and leaking. It is not an antibiotic for infection.

qs.q: An older resident started oxybutynin and now has a dry mouth, constipation, and new confusion. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Report these side effects to the nurse
w: Offer salty snacks to fix the dry mouth
Assume the confusion is unrelated
Limit fluids to reduce bathroom trips
qs.x: Oxybutynin can cause dry mouth, constipation, and confusion, especially in older adults. These changes should be reported, and limiting fluids is not appropriate.

qs.q: What is tamsulosin used for?
qs.a: Making urination easier in men with an enlarged prostate
w: Treating a bladder infection
Lowering blood sugar
Increasing the amount of urine made
qs.x: Tamsulosin relaxes muscles in the prostate and bladder opening so urine flows more easily. It is not an antibiotic or a water pill.

qs.q: A resident who takes tamsulosin gets lightheaded when standing up. What is the main safety concern?
qs.a: Falling from low blood pressure when standing
w: Choking during meals
Getting a skin rash
Losing hearing
qs.x: Tamsulosin can lower blood pressure when a person stands, causing dizziness and fainting. Standing slowly with help lowers fall risk.

qs.q: A resident takes alendronate in the morning. Why must the resident stay sitting up or standing for at least 30 minutes afterward?
qs.a: To help keep the pill from irritating the esophagus
w: To help the pill lower blood sugar
To prevent the pill from causing sleepiness
To make the pill work as a laxative
qs.x: Alendronate can irritate and injure the esophagus if it stays there or backs up. Staying upright after taking it lowers this risk.

qs.q: A resident who takes alendronate for osteoporosis complains of new heartburn, chest pain, and pain when swallowing. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Report these symptoms to the nurse
w: Lay the resident flat to rest
Offer a large meal to settle the stomach
Wait until the next week to see if it improves
qs.x: Heartburn, chest pain, or painful swallowing can be signs alendronate has irritated the esophagus. These must be reported, and lying flat can make it worse.

qs.q: Cephalexin belongs to which group of medicines?
qs.a: Antibiotics
w: Antifungals
Antihistamines
Antacids
qs.x: Cephalexin is an antibiotic (a cephalosporin) used for bacterial infections such as skin infections. It does not treat fungal infections.

qs.q: A resident taking cephalexin develops frequent, watery diarrhea. Why is this important to report?
qs.a: Antibiotics can lead to a serious bowel infection
w: It means the infection is fully cured
It means the resident drank too much water
It shows the antibiotic is too weak
qs.x: Antibiotics can upset normal gut bacteria and allow C. difficile, a serious bowel infection, to grow. Frequent watery diarrhea must be reported.

qs.q: Nitrofurantoin is most often used to treat which type of infection?
qs.a: Bladder (urinary tract) infection
w: Pneumonia in the lungs
Fungal infection of the mouth
Ear infection
qs.x: Nitrofurantoin concentrates in the urine, so it is used for bladder infections. It does not work well for lung or ear infections.

qs.q: An older resident taking nitrofurantoin develops a new cough, fever, and shortness of breath. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Report the breathing changes to the nurse right away
w: Encourage the resident to lie flat and rest
Assume it is a normal cold and wait
Offer cough drops and recheck tomorrow
qs.x: Nitrofurantoin can rarely cause a serious lung reaction, with cough, fever, and shortness of breath. Breathing changes must be reported promptly.

qs.q: A resident has creamy white patches in the mouth that do not wipe off easily, and nystatin is ordered. What is nystatin used to treat?
qs.a: Fungal (yeast) infections
w: Bacterial infections
Viral infections
Allergic reactions
qs.x: Nystatin is an antifungal used for yeast infections such as oral thrush. Antibiotics do not treat yeast and can actually make thrush more likely.

qs.q: Nystatin powder is ordered for a red, moist rash in a resident's skin folds. Which care step supports the treatment?
qs.a: Keep the skin folds clean and dry
w: Cover the area with thick wet towels
Wash the area with hot water often
Apply heavy lotion to keep it damp
qs.x: Yeast grows in warm, moist skin folds. Keeping the area clean and dry helps the antifungal powder work and prevents the rash from coming back.

qs.q: A resident with diabetes who takes glipizide becomes shaky, sweaty, and confused before lunch. What do these signs most likely mean?
qs.a: Low blood sugar
w: High blood sugar
Low thyroid level
A urinary infection
qs.x: Glipizide makes the pancreas release more insulin and can cause low blood sugar. Shakiness, sweating, and confusion are classic signs and need to be reported right away.

qs.q: A resident who takes glipizide refuses most of breakfast. Why should the nursing assistant tell the nurse?
qs.a: Not eating raises the risk of low blood sugar
w: Not eating makes glipizide cause diarrhea
Not eating makes blood pressure very high
Not eating has no effect with this medicine
qs.x: Glipizide lowers blood sugar even when a person does not eat, so a skipped meal increases the risk of low blood sugar. The nurse needs to know about poor intake.

qs.q: Insulin glargine is which type of insulin?
qs.a: Long-acting insulin
w: Rapid-acting mealtime insulin
Short-acting insulin given only by IV
Oral insulin pill
qs.x: Insulin glargine is a long-acting basal insulin that works steadily over about a day. Rapid-acting insulins like lispro are the mealtime insulins.

qs.q: A resident receives insulin lispro right before meals. Why is it important for the meal tray to be delivered on time?
qs.a: Lispro works quickly and can cause low blood sugar without food
w: Lispro needs food to dissolve in the stomach
Lispro works only after a full night's sleep
Lispro makes the resident too full to eat
qs.x: Insulin lispro is rapid-acting and starts lowering blood sugar within minutes. If the meal is late, the resident may develop low blood sugar.

qs.q: A resident received mealtime insulin lispro but ate only a few bites of lunch. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Report the poor intake to the nurse
w: Remove the tray and say nothing
Offer coffee instead of food
Record the meal as fully eaten
qs.x: After rapid-acting insulin, eating very little can lead to low blood sugar. The nurse needs to know so the resident can be watched and treated if needed.

qs.q: Insulin NPH is which type of insulin?
qs.a: Intermediate-acting insulin
w: Rapid-acting insulin
Long-acting insulin with no peak
Insulin taken by mouth
qs.x: NPH is an intermediate-acting insulin that has a peak several hours after it is given. It usually looks cloudy, unlike clear rapid- and long-acting insulins.

qs.q: What is levothyroxine used to treat?
qs.a: Low thyroid hormone (hypothyroidism)
w: High blood sugar (diabetes)
Overactive bladder
Allergic sneezing
qs.x: Levothyroxine replaces thyroid hormone in people whose thyroid does not make enough. It is not a diabetes or bladder medicine.

qs.q: A resident who takes levothyroxine has a fast heartbeat, feels nervous, and cannot sleep. What might these signs mean?
qs.a: Possible signs of too much thyroid medicine
w: Expected signs of low blood sugar only
Normal signs the dose is too low
Signs of a urinary tract infection
qs.x: Too much levothyroxine can cause symptoms like a fast heartbeat, nervousness, and trouble sleeping. These should be reported to the nurse.

qs.q: Metformin is most commonly used to treat which condition?
qs.a: Type 2 diabetes
w: Low thyroid
High cholesterol
Seizures
qs.x: Metformin lowers blood sugar in type 2 diabetes, mainly by reducing sugar made by the liver. It does not treat thyroid or cholesterol problems.

qs.q: Why is metformin usually given with meals?
qs.a: To lessen stomach upset and diarrhea
w: To make it work as a laxative
To make the resident sleepy after eating
To prevent a fast heartbeat
qs.x: Metformin commonly causes nausea, stomach upset, and diarrhea. Taking it with meals helps reduce these side effects.

qs.q: How does docusate help with constipation?
qs.a: It softens stool by letting water mix into it
w: It strongly squeezes the bowel muscles
It neutralizes stomach acid
It slows the bowel to reduce diarrhea
qs.x: Docusate is a stool softener that lets water and fat mix into stool so it is easier to pass. Stimulant laxatives like senna are the ones that push the bowel muscles.

qs.q: A resident takes docusate. Which daily care action helps it work best, if allowed by the care plan?
qs.a: Offering fluids throughout the day
w: Limiting fluids at meals
Keeping the resident in bed all day
Serving only low-fiber foods
qs.x: Stool softeners work better when the person drinks enough fluids. Activity and fiber, as allowed, also help prevent constipation.

qs.q: Omeprazole belongs to which group of medicines?
qs.a: Proton pump inhibitors that lower stomach acid
w: Stimulant laxatives
Antihistamines for allergies
Antibiotics for infection
qs.x: Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) that reduces stomach acid for heartburn and ulcers. It is not a laxative or antibiotic.

qs.q: When is omeprazole usually taken for best effect?
qs.a: Before a meal, often before breakfast
w: Right after a large dinner
Only when lying down at night
Only during a heartburn attack
qs.x: Omeprazole works best when taken before a meal, commonly before breakfast. It is not a quick-acting antacid for sudden heartburn.

qs.q: How is polyethylene glycol powder usually taken?
qs.a: Mixed and dissolved in a glass of liquid
w: Sprinkled dry on the tongue
Rubbed onto the skin
Inhaled with a mouthpiece
qs.x: Polyethylene glycol powder is dissolved in a beverage such as water or juice before drinking. It is not taken dry or inhaled.

qs.q: How does polyethylene glycol relieve constipation?
qs.a: It keeps water in the bowel to soften stool
w: It irritates the bowel lining to cause cramping
It coats the stool with oil
It adds bulk by soaking up fat
qs.x: Polyethylene glycol is an osmotic laxative that keeps water in the bowel, making stool softer and easier to pass. It does not work by irritating the bowel.

qs.q: A resident received magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia) and now has many loose, watery stools. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Report the diarrhea to the nurse
w: Offer another laxative
Limit the resident's fluids
Ignore it because it is expected
qs.x: Magnesium hydroxide is a laxative, and too strong an effect can cause frequent watery stools and fluid loss. This should be reported.

qs.q: Magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia) is used for which purposes?
qs.a: Constipation and upset stomach from acid
w: Nausea from motion sickness and vertigo
Allergies and itchy eyes
Pain and fever
qs.x: Milk of magnesia works as a laxative for constipation and as an antacid for acid indigestion. It does not treat motion sickness or allergies.

qs.q: Meclizine is used to prevent or treat which problem?
qs.a: Nausea and dizziness from motion sickness
w: Heartburn from stomach acid
Constipation from pain pills
Diarrhea from antibiotics
qs.x: Meclizine is an antihistamine that helps prevent nausea, vomiting, and dizziness from motion sickness. It is not an antacid or laxative.

qs.q: A resident takes calcium carbonate often for heartburn. Which side effect should the nursing assistant watch for?
qs.a: Constipation
w: Diarrhea
Increased urination
Hair loss
qs.x: Calcium carbonate antacids commonly cause constipation. Magnesium-containing antacids are more likely to cause diarrhea.

qs.q: A pregnant woman has heartburn. Calcium carbonate is often used for this. How does it work?
qs.a: It neutralizes stomach acid
w: It speeds up the bowels
It numbs the throat
It reduces allergic swelling
qs.x: Calcium carbonate is an antacid that neutralizes stomach acid to relieve heartburn, which is common in pregnancy. It also provides calcium.

qs.q: Besides relieving heartburn, calcium carbonate is a source of a mineral that is important for which body part?
qs.a: Bones and teeth
w: Hair and nails only
Eyes and ears
Lungs and airways
qs.x: Calcium carbonate supplies calcium, which helps build and keep strong bones and teeth. During pregnancy, calcium supports the mother's and baby's bones.

qs.q: Why is ferrous sulfate (iron) often given during pregnancy?
qs.a: To treat or prevent iron-deficiency anemia
w: To prevent morning sickness
To lower blood pressure
To prevent urinary infections
qs.x: Pregnancy increases the body's need for iron, and low iron can cause anemia. Ferrous sulfate supplies iron to build healthy red blood cells.

qs.q: Which drink taken with iron pills can help the body absorb the iron better?
qs.a: Orange juice
w: Milk
Coffee
Tea
qs.x: Vitamin C in orange juice helps the body absorb iron. Milk, coffee, and tea can reduce how much iron is absorbed.

qs.q: A woman is taking nitrofurantoin for a bladder infection. Which symptom shows the infection may not be improving and should be reported?
qs.a: Continued burning and urgency when urinating
w: Urine that is pale yellow and clear
Normal number of bathroom trips
Feeling more energetic each day
qs.x: Burning, urgency, and frequent urination are signs of bladder infection. If they continue or get worse, the nurse needs to know.

qs.q: Besides seasonal allergies, levocetirizine may also be used to relieve which skin problem?
qs.a: Itchy hives
w: Pressure ulcers
Fungal skin rash
Sunburn blisters
qs.x: Levocetirizine is an antihistamine labeled for chronic hives (urticaria) as well as allergies. It does not heal pressure ulcers or fungal rashes.

qs.q: Why is levocetirizine usually taken in the evening?
qs.a: It can cause drowsiness
w: It must be taken with dinner
It keeps people awake
It works only in the dark
qs.x: Levocetirizine can make people sleepy, so it is labeled for evening use. Being drowsy at night is safer than during daytime activities.

qs.q: Loratadine belongs to which group of medicines?
qs.a: Antihistamines
w: Antibiotics
Steroids (corticosteroids)
Blood thinners
qs.x: Loratadine is an antihistamine that blocks histamine to relieve allergy symptoms. It is less likely to cause sleepiness than older antihistamines.

qs.q: A resident who takes loratadine for allergies suddenly has swelling of the lips and trouble breathing. What should the nursing assistant do?
qs.a: Call for the nurse immediately and stay with the resident
w: Give the resident another allergy pill
Wait to see if the swelling goes away
Have the resident lie down and rest alone
qs.x: Lip swelling and trouble breathing can be a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), which is an emergency. Antihistamines like loratadine are not enough to treat it.

qs.q: Meclizine belongs to which group of medicines?
qs.a: Antihistamines
w: Antibiotics
Opioid pain relievers
Water pills (diuretics)
qs.x: Meclizine is an antihistamine used for motion sickness and dizziness. Like other antihistamines, it can cause drowsiness and dry mouth.

qs.q: During cardiac arrest, ALS providers give epinephrine. What is its main intended benefit during CPR?
qs.a: Constricting blood vessels to improve blood flow to the heart and brain
w: Dissolving the clot that caused the arrest
Converting the rhythm back to normal by itself
Opening the airway by relaxing the throat muscles
qs.x: Epinephrine's alpha effects constrict blood vessels, raising the pressure that drives blood to the heart and brain during compressions. It does not dissolve clots or reliably convert a rhythm on its own.

qs.q: An EMT crew arrives first at a witnessed cardiac arrest. ALS with epinephrine is several minutes away. What should the crew focus on?
qs.a: High-quality CPR and early use of the AED
w: Waiting for ALS before starting compressions
Giving the patient's epinephrine auto-injector first
Placing the patient in the recovery position
qs.x: Survival from cardiac arrest depends most on early high-quality CPR and defibrillation; epinephrine supports these but never replaces them. An epinephrine auto-injector is not an EMT treatment for cardiac arrest.

qs.q: Epinephrine belongs to which group of medications?
qs.a: Sympathomimetics (adrenergic agonists)
w: Beta-blockers
Opioid antagonists
Anticholinergics
qs.x: Epinephrine is a catecholamine that stimulates alpha and beta adrenergic receptors, mimicking the sympathetic nervous system. Beta-blockers have the opposite effect on beta receptors.

qs.q: Which effect of epinephrine on the heart comes from stimulating beta-1 receptors?
qs.a: Faster heart rate and stronger contractions
w: Slower heart rate and weaker contractions
Relaxation of the coronary smooth muscle only
No change in rate but lower blood pressure
qs.x: Beta-1 stimulation increases heart rate and the force of contraction. This raises the heart's oxygen demand, which is why chest pain or palpitations can follow a dose.

qs.q: A patient with anaphylaxis improves after an epinephrine auto-injector but then reports new chest pain and a racing heart. What is the best interpretation and action?
qs.a: Recognize a possible cardiac side effect, reassess, and report it to ALS
w: Expect this as proof the dose was too small and repeat it now
Treat this as anxiety and reassure the patient only
Assume a new allergic reaction and ignore the vital signs
qs.x: Epinephrine increases heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand and can cause chest pain or dysrhythmias, especially in older adults or those with heart disease. New chest pain needs reassessment and prompt reporting, not simple reassurance.

qs.q: How does aspirin help a patient with a suspected heart attack?
qs.a: It reduces platelet clumping so the clot is less likely to grow
w: It dissolves the existing clot in the coronary artery
It dilates the coronary arteries to relieve chest pain
It slows the heart rate to lower oxygen demand
qs.x: Aspirin is an antiplatelet drug that blocks thromboxane production, limiting further clot growth. It does not dissolve an existing clot; that is the role of fibrinolytics or catheter procedures.

qs.q: Why are patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome told to chew aspirin rather than swallow it whole?
qs.a: Chewing allows faster absorption and quicker antiplatelet effect
w: Chewing prevents the tablet from irritating the stomach
Chewing is needed to activate the medication
Chewing reduces the risk of an allergic reaction
qs.x: Chewing breaks the tablet up so it is absorbed more quickly, speeding the antiplatelet effect. It does not activate the drug or prevent allergic reactions.

qs.q: Which finding in a patient with chest pain is a contraindication to giving aspirin?
qs.a: A known allergy to aspirin
w: A history of high blood pressure
Chest pain that began while resting
A history of type 2 diabetes
qs.x: A known aspirin allergy (or active GI bleeding) is a contraindication. Hypertension, diabetes and chest pain at rest are common in heart attack patients and are not reasons to avoid aspirin.

qs.q: Which finding is a contraindication to assisting a chest pain patient with nitroglycerin?
qs.a: Recent use of an erectile dysfunction medication such as sildenafil
w: A blood pressure higher than the patient's usual
Chest pain that radiates to the left arm
A history of a previous heart attack
qs.x: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil or tadalafil combined with nitroglycerin can cause severe, prolonged hypotension. High blood pressure and typical cardiac pain are not contraindications.

qs.q: Before an EMT assists a patient with nitroglycerin, which condition must generally be met?
qs.a: It is prescribed to the patient and medical direction approves
w: The patient has taken aspirin within the past day
The patient's pain has lasted longer than usual
A family member has a prescription for it
qs.x: At the EMT level, nitroglycerin is an assisted medication: it must be the patient's own prescription and given with online or protocol-based medical direction. Another person's prescription does not qualify.

qs.q: Nitroglycerin lowers blood pressure and cardiac workload mainly by which action?
qs.a: Dilating veins so less blood returns to the heart
w: Blocking beta receptors to slow the heart
Causing the kidneys to remove extra fluid
Constricting arteries to redirect blood flow
qs.x: Nitroglycerin is a vasodilator that mainly dilates veins, reducing preload and the heart's oxygen demand. It is not a beta-blocker or a diuretic.

qs.q: Shortly after taking nitroglycerin, a patient reports a pounding headache. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: An expected side effect from dilation of blood vessels
w: A sign of an allergic reaction to the tablet
Proof that the tablets have lost their potency
A sign that the patient is having a stroke
qs.x: Headache is a common, expected side effect caused by vasodilation of blood vessels in the head. It is not a sign of allergy, and a headache actually suggests the tablet is active.

qs.q: Which vital sign is most important for an EMT to reassess after each nitroglycerin dose?
qs.a: Blood pressure
w: Body temperature
Pupil size
Blood glucose
qs.x: The main danger of nitroglycerin is hypotension from vasodilation, so blood pressure is checked before and after each dose. Temperature and glucose are not directly affected.

qs.q: A patient has a very high blood pressure and a headache but no chest pain. Why is nitroglycerin not an EMT treatment here?
qs.a: At the EMT level it is used for suspected cardiac chest pain, not high blood pressure alone
w: Nitroglycerin raises blood pressure and would make this worse
Nitroglycerin only works when blood pressure is low
Nitroglycerin is only given by injection in hypertension
qs.x: EMTs assist with nitroglycerin for chest pain of suspected cardiac origin under medical direction. Treating severe hypertension is an ALS and hospital decision; nitroglycerin lowers, not raises, blood pressure.

qs.q: How is a nitroglycerin tablet given?
qs.a: Placed under the tongue and allowed to dissolve
w: Swallowed whole with a full glass of water
Chewed and swallowed like aspirin
Placed between the cheek and gum and chewed
qs.x: Nitroglycerin tablets and spray are given sublingually for rapid absorption through the mucosa. Swallowing exposes the drug to first-pass liver breakdown, which greatly reduces its effect.

qs.q: Anaphylactic shock is classified as which type of shock?
qs.a: Distributive shock
w: Hypovolemic shock
Cardiogenic shock
Obstructive shock
qs.x: In anaphylaxis, widespread vasodilation and leaky capillaries cause distributive shock. Hypovolemic shock comes from fluid or blood loss, and cardiogenic shock from pump failure.

qs.q: Which action of epinephrine most directly raises blood pressure in anaphylactic shock?
qs.a: Alpha-1 stimulation that constricts blood vessels
w: Beta-2 stimulation that relaxes the airways
Blocking histamine at its receptors
Increasing urine output by the kidneys
qs.x: Alpha-1 vasoconstriction reverses the vasodilation of anaphylaxis and raises blood pressure. Beta-2 bronchodilation helps breathing but does not raise blood pressure; epinephrine is not an antihistamine.

qs.q: A patient in anaphylactic shock takes a beta-blocker daily. What should the EMT anticipate after giving epinephrine?
qs.a: The response may be weaker, so call for ALS early
w: The patient will be unusually sensitive to epinephrine
Epinephrine will have no effect at all on breathing
The beta-blocker will fully reverse the reaction
qs.x: Beta-blockers can blunt the response to epinephrine and make anaphylaxis harder to treat, so early ALS backup is important. The effect is reduced, not absent, and the beta-blocker does not treat the reaction.

qs.q: A patient's blood pressure and breathing improve after an epinephrine auto-injector. Why is continued transport and monitoring still needed?
qs.a: Epinephrine's effects are short-lived and symptoms can return
w: Epinephrine causes lasting low blood pressure later
The improvement shows the reaction was not anaphylaxis
A second injection is required by law after any use
qs.x: Epinephrine wears off quickly and symptoms may recur, including biphasic reactions hours later. Improvement after epinephrine supports, rather than rules out, anaphylaxis.

qs.q: After giving epinephrine to a patient in shock, how should the EMT reassess?
qs.a: Repeat vital signs, mental status and skin findings frequently, as for an unstable patient
w: Recheck vital signs once on arrival at the hospital
Reassess only if the patient reports new symptoms
Check blood glucose first, then vital signs at the hospital
qs.x: A patient in shock is unstable and needs frequent reassessment of vital signs, mental status, breathing and skin to detect improvement or deterioration. Waiting for new complaints can miss a decline.

qs.q: How does albuterol relieve wheezing in an asthma attack?
qs.a: It stimulates beta-2 receptors to relax bronchial smooth muscle
w: It blocks histamine to reduce airway swelling
It thins mucus so it can be coughed up
It reduces airway inflammation like a steroid
qs.x: Albuterol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and opens the airways. It does not reduce inflammation like a corticosteroid or block histamine.

qs.q: Which step is part of correct metered-dose inhaler technique?
qs.a: Breathe out fully, then press the inhaler while inhaling slowly and deeply
w: Press the inhaler while breathing out forcefully
Take quick, shallow breaths while spraying
Spray into the air first and then breathe it in
qs.x: The patient should exhale, seal the lips on the mouthpiece or spacer, activate the inhaler during a slow deep breath, and hold the breath. Spraying during exhalation or shallow breaths delivers little drug to the lungs.

qs.q: An asthma patient who was wheezing loudly now has very quiet breath sounds, is drowsy, and is still working hard to breathe. What does this most likely mean?
qs.a: Airflow is worsening; prepare to assist ventilations and call ALS
w: The inhaler has worked and the attack is ending
The patient is relaxing and can be reassured
The wheezing was caused by anxiety alone
qs.x: A quiet or silent chest with fatigue and altered mental status signals severe obstruction and impending respiratory failure. Improvement would show easier breathing and better alertness, not drowsiness.

qs.q: Which finding in a patient having an allergic reaction shows airway involvement that calls for epinephrine?
qs.a: Hoarse voice, stridor, or a feeling of throat tightness
w: Itchy hives limited to the arms
Watery eyes and a runny nose
Mild redness around an insect sting
qs.x: Hoarseness, stridor and throat tightness suggest upper airway swelling, a sign of anaphylaxis that needs epinephrine. Localized hives or mild local reactions alone do not meet anaphylaxis criteria.

qs.q: A patient in anaphylaxis is wheezing and has throat swelling. Why is epinephrine preferred over an albuterol inhaler as the first medication?
qs.a: Epinephrine treats airway swelling, bronchospasm and low blood pressure together
w: Albuterol is not safe in any allergic reaction
Epinephrine works only on the lungs and acts faster
Albuterol would make the throat swelling worse
qs.x: Epinephrine counters the whole systemic reaction: airway edema, bronchospasm and vasodilation. Albuterol only relaxes bronchial muscle and does not treat swelling or shock, though it can be used as an add-on.

qs.q: Where is an epinephrine auto-injector given?
qs.a: Into the outer (anterolateral) thigh
w: Into the upper arm deltoid muscle
Into the abdominal wall near the navel
Into the buttock's upper outer area
qs.x: Auto-injectors are designed for the anterolateral thigh, where absorption is reliable, and can be given through clothing. Injection into the buttock or other sites is not recommended.

qs.q: After an epinephrine auto-injector, which set of effects should the EMT expect as common side effects?
