qs.a: Fast heart rate, shakiness, anxiety and pale skin
w: Slow heart rate, drowsiness and flushed skin
Pinpoint pupils and slowed breathing
Low blood sugar and sweating
qs.x: Epinephrine stimulates the sympathetic system, causing tachycardia, tremor, anxiety and pallor. Slowing of the heart or breathing is not expected.

qs.q: Which patient best meets the criteria for anaphylaxis requiring epinephrine?
qs.a: Hives after a bee sting with difficulty breathing and low blood pressure
w: Swelling and pain only at the bee sting site
Itchy rash on one arm after touching a plant
Sneezing and watery eyes during pollen season
qs.x: Anaphylaxis involves more than one body system, such as skin signs plus respiratory compromise or hypotension. Local swelling, contact rashes and seasonal allergy symptoms are not anaphylaxis.

qs.q: After epinephrine, a patient with anaphylaxis still has some wheezing. What is the role of an albuterol inhaler here?
qs.a: An add-on for remaining bronchospasm, not a replacement for epinephrine
w: The main treatment that makes epinephrine unnecessary
A treatment for the low blood pressure of anaphylaxis
A way to reverse the side effects of epinephrine
qs.x: Albuterol may help persistent bronchospasm, but it does not treat airway swelling or shock. Epinephrine remains the first-line drug for anaphylaxis.

qs.q: After assisting an allergic patient with an albuterol inhaler, what should the EMT reassess first?
qs.a: Work of breathing, breath sounds and oxygen saturation
w: Pupil size and reaction to light
Blood glucose and skin temperature
Bowel sounds and abdominal tenderness
qs.x: Albuterol targets bronchospasm, so its effect is judged by breathing effort, wheezing and oxygenation. Pupils and glucose are not the main markers of response.

qs.q: Acetaminophen is best described as which type of medication?
qs.a: A pain reliever and fever reducer with little anti-inflammatory effect
w: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that thins the blood
An opioid pain reliever that can slow breathing
A sedative that reduces anxiety and causes sleep
qs.x: Acetaminophen is an analgesic and antipyretic but has minimal anti-inflammatory action and does not affect platelets. It is not an NSAID or an opioid.

qs.q: Which organ is most at risk from acetaminophen overdose?
qs.a: Liver
w: Kidneys
Lungs
Stomach lining
qs.x: Excess acetaminophen produces a toxic metabolite that damages the liver. Stomach irritation and bleeding are more typical of NSAIDs such as aspirin or ibuprofen.

qs.q: A patient took a large amount of acetaminophen a few hours ago and feels only mildly nauseated. What is important to understand?
qs.a: Serious liver damage can develop later even if the patient looks well now
w: Mild symptoms mean the amount taken was not harmful
Acetaminophen overdose mainly causes immediate breathing problems
The patient can be observed at home if symptoms stay mild
qs.x: Early acetaminophen poisoning often causes few or mild symptoms, while liver injury appears a day or more later. Transport for evaluation is needed regardless of how well the patient appears.

qs.q: Why should an EMT ask about all cold remedies and prescription pain pills when a patient reports taking acetaminophen?
qs.a: Many combination products also contain acetaminophen, adding to the total amount
w: Cold remedies block acetaminophen so it stops working
Prescription pain pills cancel out acetaminophen's effects
Acetaminophen cannot be taken with any other medication
qs.x: Acetaminophen is in many cold and flu products and some opioid combination pills, so accidental overdose is common. These products add to the total exposure rather than block it.

qs.q: Which medication is used in the hospital as the antidote for acetaminophen poisoning?
qs.a: Acetylcysteine
w: Naloxone
Flumazenil
Atropine
qs.x: Acetylcysteine replenishes the liver's protective glutathione and prevents liver injury. Naloxone reverses opioids, not acetaminophen, even in combination products.

qs.q: ALS arrives for an unresponsive patient with a very low blood sugar. Which form of dextrose is appropriate for this patient?
qs.a: Intravenous dextrose
w: Oral glucose gel between cheek and gum
Intramuscular dextrose into the thigh
Dextrose tablets dissolved under the tongue
qs.x: An unresponsive patient cannot protect the airway, so oral glucose risks aspiration; ALS gives dextrose intravenously. Dextrose is not given intramuscularly.

qs.q: Why is it important to watch the IV site closely when concentrated dextrose is given?
qs.a: Leakage into surrounding tissue can cause serious tissue damage
w: Dextrose often causes a severe allergic rash at the site
Dextrose makes the vein clot and stops all flow
Dextrose leaking out causes the blood sugar to drop
qs.x: Concentrated dextrose is irritating, and extravasation can injure or kill surrounding tissue. Allergy to dextrose is not a typical concern.

qs.q: Before giving glucose to a diabetic patient with altered mental status, which assessment should be done if local protocol allows?
qs.a: Check the blood glucose level with a glucometer
w: Check the core body temperature
Measure the patient's urine output
Listen for bowel sounds in each quadrant
qs.x: A glucometer reading confirms hypoglycemia and gives a baseline to judge the response to treatment. Temperature and bowel sounds do not guide glucose administration.

qs.q: A diabetic patient takes a long-acting oral diabetes medication such as glipizide. After oral glucose, the patient is alert and wants to refuse transport. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Blood sugar may fall again hours later as the medication keeps working
w: The glucose will cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure
The medication will make the glucose ineffective right away
Glipizide causes an allergy to glucose after treatment
qs.x: Sulfonylureas such as glipizide can cause prolonged or recurrent hypoglycemia that outlasts a single glucose dose. This is why medical direction and hospital observation are strongly encouraged.

qs.q: A known diabetic is confused but can swallow, and blood sugar cannot be measured. Why is giving oral glucose still considered reasonable?
qs.a: A small amount of sugar will not harm a high-sugar patient but may help a low-sugar one
w: Oral glucose lowers blood sugar if it is already too high
Confusion in diabetics is always caused by high blood sugar
Oral glucose has no effect unless blood sugar is low
qs.x: The brief rise from oral glucose is unlikely to harm a hyperglycemic patient, while untreated hypoglycemia can quickly cause brain injury. Glucose does not lower blood sugar.

qs.q: What effect does albuterol have on blood potassium levels?
qs.a: It lowers blood potassium by shifting potassium into the cells
w: It raises blood potassium by releasing it from cells
It removes potassium from the body through the urine
It has no effect on potassium at any amount
qs.x: Beta-2 stimulation drives potassium into cells, temporarily lowering the blood level. It does not remove potassium from the body.

qs.q: Hospitals sometimes give nebulized albuterol for high potassium. What is a limitation of this treatment?
qs.a: The effect is temporary because potassium is moved, not removed
w: It permanently removes potassium from the body
It only works if the patient is wheezing
It raises potassium briefly before lowering it for good
qs.x: Albuterol shifts potassium into cells for a short time, so other treatments such as dialysis are needed to remove it from the body. It does not need wheezing to work.

qs.q: ALS may give albuterol for suspected high potassium. Which patient history most suggests this problem?
qs.a: A dialysis patient who missed treatments and now has weakness and a slow pulse
w: A young athlete with leg cramps after a long run
A patient with vomiting and diarrhea for several days
A patient taking a water pill who feels thirsty
qs.x: Missed dialysis allows potassium to build up, which can cause weakness and dangerous slow rhythms. Vomiting, diarrhea and diuretics more often cause low potassium.

qs.q: A patient with severe asthma has used albuterol repeatedly for hours. Which electrolyte problem might cause muscle weakness and irregular heartbeats?
qs.a: Low potassium
w: High potassium
High calcium
Low sodium
qs.x: Repeated albuterol doses shift potassium into cells and can cause hypokalemia, leading to weakness and dysrhythmias. Albuterol does not raise potassium.

qs.q: Which medication taken together with frequent albuterol most increases the risk of low potassium?
qs.a: Furosemide, a loop diuretic
w: Spironolactone, a potassium-sparing diuretic
Lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor
Acetaminophen, a pain reliever
qs.x: Loop diuretics like furosemide cause potassium loss in the urine, adding to albuterol's potassium-lowering effect. Spironolactone and ACE inhibitors tend to raise potassium.

qs.q: How does naloxone reverse an opioid overdose?
qs.a: It blocks opioid receptors and displaces the opioid from them
w: It speeds up the liver's breakdown of opioids
It stimulates the breathing center directly like caffeine
It binds the opioid in the stomach so it is not absorbed
qs.x: Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist that pushes opioids off their receptors. Binding drugs in the gut describes activated charcoal, not naloxone.

qs.q: A patient wakes and breathes normally after naloxone, then refuses care. Why is continued monitoring important?
qs.a: Naloxone can wear off before the opioid, so breathing may slow again
w: Naloxone causes delayed breathing problems of its own
The patient will now be immune to further opioid effects
Naloxone permanently removes the opioid from the body
qs.x: Many opioids, especially long-acting or potent ones, last longer than naloxone, so re-sedation and respiratory depression can return. Naloxone does not remove the opioid.

qs.q: A patient with a suspected opioid overdose is breathing a few shallow breaths per minute and is cyanotic. What should the EMT do first?
qs.a: Open the airway and ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
w: Give naloxone and wait for the patient to wake up
Place the patient in the recovery position and observe
Give activated charcoal to absorb the opioid
qs.x: Inadequate breathing is immediately treated with airway management and ventilation; naloxone follows but takes time to work. Charcoal is unsafe in a patient who cannot protect the airway.

qs.q: How does activated charcoal work in some oral poisonings?
qs.a: It adsorbs the poison in the gut so less is absorbed
w: It neutralizes poisons already in the bloodstream
It causes vomiting to empty the stomach
It coats the stomach to stop pain and burning
qs.x: Activated charcoal binds many substances in the gastrointestinal tract, reducing absorption. It does not act on poison already absorbed and is not an emetic.

qs.q: Which patient is NOT a candidate for activated charcoal?
qs.a: A drowsy patient who cannot protect the airway
w: An alert adult who swallowed pills recently
An alert patient who agrees to drink it
An alert patient with a known ingestion and stable vitals
qs.x: Charcoal given to a patient with altered mental status risks vomiting and aspiration into the lungs. It is considered only for alert patients who can swallow and protect the airway, per medical direction.

qs.q: Which patient meets the usual criteria for oral glucose?
qs.a: A known diabetic with altered mental status who can swallow
w: An unresponsive diabetic with no gag reflex
A diabetic who is alert with no complaints
A confused patient who is actively seizing
qs.x: Oral glucose is for a patient with a history of diabetes and altered mental status who can swallow and protect the airway. Unresponsive or seizing patients risk aspiration.

qs.q: Why is oral glucose contraindicated in a patient who cannot swallow?
qs.a: The patient could aspirate the gel into the airway
w: The gel will not absorb unless it is swallowed whole
It will raise blood sugar dangerously fast
It causes vomiting in unresponsive patients
qs.x: A patient who cannot swallow or protect the airway may aspirate the gel. The danger is airway compromise, not a rapid rise in blood sugar.

qs.q: How is oral glucose gel given?
qs.a: Placed between the cheek and gum or on the tongue in small portions
w: Injected into the muscle of the outer thigh
Sprayed into the nostrils with an atomizer
Swallowed all at once as a single large mouthful
qs.x: Oral glucose is placed between the cheek and gum (or on a tongue depressor) a little at a time so it can be absorbed and swallowed safely. Giving it all at once raises the risk of choking.

qs.q: Several minutes after oral glucose, a diabetic patient's mental status has not improved. What should the EMT consider?
qs.a: Other causes of altered mental status and the need for ALS
w: That the glucose was absorbed and no change is expected
That the patient must have high blood sugar instead
That transport is unnecessary since glucose was given
qs.x: Lack of improvement suggests the hypoglycemia is severe or something else, such as stroke, head injury or overdose, is causing the altered mental status. ALS and further assessment are needed.

qs.q: Which presentation in a diabetic patient most suggests low blood sugar rather than high blood sugar?
qs.a: Sudden confusion with cool, pale, sweaty skin
w: Gradual onset with warm, dry skin and fruity breath
Deep rapid breathing and several days of thirst
Frequent urination and slowly worsening fatigue
qs.x: Hypoglycemia comes on quickly with sympathetic signs such as cool, clammy skin. Gradual onset, fruity breath and deep rapid breathing suggest diabetic ketoacidosis.

qs.q: A child with a peanut allergy has hives, wheezing and vomiting after a snack. The child has a prescribed auto-injector. What is the best interpretation?
qs.a: Anaphylaxis; epinephrine is indicated per protocol
w: A mild reaction that only needs an antihistamine
Food poisoning that needs no medication
An asthma attack that needs only an inhaler
qs.x: Skin signs plus respiratory and GI symptoms after a known allergen meet anaphylaxis criteria, and epinephrine is first-line. Antihistamines and inhalers do not treat the systemic reaction.

qs.q: While using a parent's epinephrine auto-injector, a child accidentally injects it into his own thumb. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Reduced blood flow to the thumb from vasoconstriction; report it
w: A severe allergic reaction to the epinephrine itself
Immediate cardiac arrest from the injection
Low blood sugar caused by the epinephrine
qs.x: Epinephrine constricts blood vessels and can reduce circulation to a finger or thumb, so the injury should be reported and evaluated. Allergy to epinephrine is not the concern.

qs.q: A young child with diabetes is suddenly irritable, sweaty and sleepy. What should the EMT suspect first?
qs.a: Low blood sugar
w: High blood sugar
Simple tiredness
Dehydration from heat
qs.x: Sudden behavior change, sweating and lethargy in a diabetic child are classic signs of hypoglycemia. High blood sugar usually develops more gradually with thirst and frequent urination.

qs.q: Why should blood glucose be checked in a sick infant or child with altered mental status, even without diabetes?
qs.a: Children have small glucose stores and can become hypoglycemic during illness
w: Children cannot develop low blood sugar unless diabetic
Glucose checks are required before any pediatric transport
Altered mental status in children is always from fever
qs.x: Young children have limited glycogen reserves, so poor feeding or illness can cause hypoglycemia. Checking glucose helps identify a treatable cause.

qs.q: Which finding in a child with asthma suggests significant respiratory distress?
qs.a: Retractions between the ribs and nasal flaring
w: Clear breath sounds and normal skin color
A dry cough only at night
Talking in full sentences while playing
qs.x: Retractions, nasal flaring and use of accessory muscles show increased work of breathing. Talking in full sentences and clear lungs suggest mild or no distress.

qs.q: A young child cannot coordinate breathing with a metered-dose inhaler. What device helps deliver the medication?
qs.a: A spacer with a face mask
w: A nasal cannula
A bag-valve mask alone
A nonrebreather mask
qs.x: A spacer holds the medication so the child can inhale it over several breaths, and a mask helps with young children. Oxygen masks and cannulas do not deliver inhaler medication.

qs.q: A toddler found near a grandparent's pain pills is very sleepy with slow, shallow breathing. Which additional finding suggests opioid poisoning?
qs.a: Pinpoint pupils
w: Widely dilated pupils
Hot, flushed, dry skin
Rapid heart rate and agitation
qs.x: Constricted pupils with respiratory depression and decreased responsiveness form the classic opioid toxidrome. Dilated pupils and agitation suggest stimulant or anticholinergic poisoning.

qs.q: What is an advantage of giving naloxone by the intranasal route?
qs.a: It is absorbed through the nasal lining without needing a needle
w: It works only after it is swallowed
It lasts much longer than injected naloxone
It does not need the airway to be managed
qs.x: Intranasal naloxone is absorbed through the nasal mucosa and avoids needlestick risk. It still wears off, and airway and ventilation remain the first priorities.

qs.q: A caregiver says a feverish child was given acetaminophen. What information is most important for the EMT to obtain?
qs.a: When it was given and whether other medicines with acetaminophen were used
w: Which brand name and flavor of the product was used
Whether the child liked the taste of the medicine
Whether the bottle was bought at a pharmacy or a store
qs.x: Timing and use of multiple products help identify possible accidental overdose, which is common with children's fever and cold medicines. Brand and flavor do not change the risk.

qs.q: Compared with acetaminophen, ibuprofen also has which effect?
qs.a: It reduces inflammation as well as pain and fever
w: It reverses opioid effects as well as pain
It raises blood sugar as well as fever
It causes sleep as well as reducing pain
qs.x: Ibuprofen is an NSAID that relieves pain, fever and inflammation. Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever but has little anti-inflammatory effect.

qs.q: During an amiodarone infusion for stable wide-complex tachycardia, which adverse effects are most important to watch for?
qs.a: Hypotension and bradycardia
w: Hypertension and tachycardia
Hypoglycemia and seizures
Hyperkalemia and peaked T waves
qs.x: IV amiodarone commonly causes hypotension and bradycardia through vasodilation and its beta-blocking and calcium-channel effects. It does not typically cause hypertension or tachycardia.

qs.q: Amiodarone is primarily classified as which type of antiarrhythmic?
qs.a: Class III agent that prolongs repolarization by blocking potassium channels
w: Class IB agent that shortens repolarization by blocking sodium channels
Class II agent that works only by blocking beta-1 receptors
Class IV agent that works only by blocking L-type calcium channels
qs.x: Amiodarone is a Class III antiarrhythmic that prolongs repolarization and the refractory period, though it also has Class I, II and IV effects. Lidocaine, not amiodarone, is the Class IB agent.

qs.q: How is adenosine administered for stable narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia?
qs.a: Rapid IV push followed immediately by a saline flush
w: Slow IV push over several minutes
Intramuscular injection into the deltoid
Diluted continuous infusion titrated to rate
qs.x: Adenosine has a half-life of seconds, so it must be pushed rapidly through a proximal IV and flushed right away to reach the heart. A slow push lets it be metabolized before it reaches the AV node.

qs.q: Which patient factor may blunt the effect of adenosine, so the expected response may not occur?
qs.a: Recent theophylline use or heavy caffeine intake
w: Current dipyridamole therapy
History of heart transplant
Current carbamazepine therapy
qs.x: Methylxanthines such as theophylline and caffeine block adenosine receptors and can reduce its effect. Dipyridamole and a transplanted heart do the opposite and increase sensitivity to adenosine.

qs.q: In which patient with rapid atrial fibrillation is IV diltiazem contraindicated?
qs.a: Atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White pre-excitation
w: Atrial fibrillation in a patient with COPD
Atrial fibrillation in a patient with diabetes
New atrial fibrillation with narrow QRS and normal blood pressure
qs.x: Blocking the AV node in pre-excited atrial fibrillation can speed conduction down the accessory pathway and trigger ventricular fibrillation. COPD is not a contraindication; diltiazem is often chosen over beta blockers in these patients.

qs.q: Which ECG change is most important to monitor during a procainamide infusion?
qs.a: Widening of the QRS complex and prolongation of the QT interval
w: Shortening of the PR interval
New ST elevation in the inferior leads
Peaked T waves with a shortened QT interval
qs.x: Procainamide is a sodium-channel blocker with Class III effects, so it widens the QRS and lengthens the QT, raising the risk of torsades. Peaked T waves with a short QT point to hyperkalemia, not procainamide toxicity.

qs.q: Why is a central line or large, secure IV preferred when giving calcium chloride?
qs.a: Extravasation can cause severe tissue necrosis
w: It precipitates when exposed to light
It is only effective when given into a central vein
It causes anaphylaxis when given peripherally
qs.x: Calcium chloride is very irritating to tissue, and extravasation can cause necrosis and sloughing. It works when given peripherally in an emergency; a secure line is chosen for safety, not effectiveness.

qs.q: In cardiac arrest, sodium bicarbonate is reasonable in which situation rather than as routine therapy?
qs.a: Known pre-existing hyperkalemia
w: Any arrest that lasts longer than ten minutes
Asystole of unknown cause
Pulseless electrical activity from hypovolemia
qs.x: Current guidelines advise against routine bicarbonate in arrest, but it is reasonable in special cases such as hyperkalemia or sodium-channel blocker overdose. Arrest length alone is not an indication.

qs.q: The main benefit of epinephrine during cardiac arrest comes from which effect?
qs.a: Alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction that raises coronary perfusion pressure
w: Beta-2 bronchodilation that improves oxygenation
Direct conversion of ventricular fibrillation to sinus rhythm
Beta-1 slowing of conduction through the AV node
qs.x: Epinephrine's alpha-1 vasoconstriction raises aortic diastolic pressure and improves coronary and cerebral perfusion during CPR. It does not convert VF by itself, and its beta-1 effect speeds rather than slows conduction.

qs.q: Atropine is least likely to increase heart rate in which patient with symptomatic bradycardia?
qs.a: A heart transplant recipient with a denervated heart
w: Sinus bradycardia during vomiting
Bradycardia from increased vagal tone
Sinus bradycardia during endotracheal suctioning
qs.x: Atropine works by blocking vagal input, and a transplanted heart has no vagal innervation, so atropine has little effect. Vagally mediated bradycardia, such as during vomiting or suctioning, usually responds well.

qs.q: How does aspirin reduce clot formation in acute coronary syndrome?
qs.a: Irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase, reducing thromboxane A2
w: Reversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor
Directly inhibits thrombin in the clot
Converts plasminogen to plasmin to dissolve the clot
qs.x: Aspirin permanently inactivates platelet cyclooxygenase, lowering thromboxane A2 and platelet aggregation for the life of the platelet. P2Y12 blockade describes drugs like clopidogrel and ticagrelor.

qs.q: Why is aspirin chewed rather than swallowed whole in suspected acute coronary syndrome?
qs.a: Chewing speeds absorption and the onset of platelet inhibition
w: Chewing prevents gastrointestinal bleeding
Swallowed tablets are inactivated by stomach acid
Chewing lowers the risk of an allergic reaction
qs.x: Chewing a non-enteric-coated tablet allows faster absorption through the oral and gastric mucosa, so platelet inhibition starts sooner. It does not prevent GI bleeding.

qs.q: Which recent medication use is a contraindication to nitroglycerin in a patient with chest pain?
qs.a: Sildenafil taken for erectile dysfunction
w: Atorvastatin taken for high cholesterol
Metformin taken for diabetes
Lisinopril taken for hypertension
qs.x: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil combined with nitrates can cause severe, refractory hypotension. Statins, metformin and ACE inhibitors are not contraindications.

qs.q: A patient has ST elevation in II, III and aVF plus ST elevation in V4R. Why is nitroglycerin used with great caution?
qs.a: Right ventricular infarction makes the patient preload dependent
w: Nitroglycerin causes coronary artery vasospasm
Nitroglycerin increases left ventricular afterload
Nitroglycerin is ineffective in inferior wall ischemia
qs.x: ST elevation in V4R suggests right ventricular involvement, and these patients rely on preload to maintain output, so venodilation from nitroglycerin can cause profound hypotension. Nitroglycerin relieves, rather than causes, vasospasm.

qs.q: During transfer, a patient on a heparin infusion has a platelet count that has fallen by more than half from baseline and a new leg clot. What should be recognized?
qs.a: Possible heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
w: Dilutional thrombocytopenia from IV fluids
Expected heparin effect needing no action
Immune reaction to aspirin given earlier
qs.x: A platelet drop of more than half with new thrombosis is classic for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which should be reported to the provider right away. It is a paradoxically prothrombotic immune reaction, not an expected effect.

qs.q: What is a concern with giving morphine for chest pain in acute coronary syndrome?
qs.a: It may delay absorption and onset of oral P2Y12 inhibitors
w: It directly increases myocardial oxygen demand
It causes coronary artery vasospasm
It inactivates heparin in the IV line
qs.x: Opioids slow gastric emptying, which can delay absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors such as ticagrelor and clopidogrel. Morphine tends to lower, not raise, myocardial oxygen demand.

qs.q: Why might fentanyl be preferred over morphine for ischemic chest pain in a patient with borderline blood pressure?
qs.a: It causes less histamine release and less hypotension
w: It has a longer duration so fewer doses are needed
It has added antiplatelet effects
It does not cause respiratory depression
qs.x: Fentanyl releases little histamine, so it is less likely than morphine to cause vasodilation and hypotension. It is shorter acting than morphine and still causes respiratory depression.

qs.q: Which finding makes early IV metoprolol inappropriate in a patient with STEMI?
qs.a: Signs of heart failure or a low-output state
w: Sinus tachycardia with hypertension
Ongoing ischemic chest pain
History of hyperlipidemia
qs.x: Early IV beta blockade increases the risk of cardiogenic shock in patients with heart failure, low output or other shock risk factors. Hypertension with ongoing ischemia is a setting where it may be reasonable.

qs.q: How is tenecteplase given for STEMI?
qs.a: As a single weight-based IV bolus
w: As a bolus followed by a 90-minute infusion
As a continuous infusion over a full day
As an intracoronary injection only during PCI
qs.x: Tenecteplase is given as one weight-based IV bolus, which is convenient in transport. The bolus-plus-infusion regimen describes alteplase.

qs.q: Which is an absolute contraindication to alteplase for STEMI?
qs.a: Any prior intracranial hemorrhage
w: Hypertension controlled on medication
Age older than 75 years
Current daily aspirin use
qs.x: Any history of intracranial hemorrhage is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis. Advanced age and chronic hypertension are factors to weigh, not absolute contraindications.

qs.q: Nicardipine belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
w: Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
Organic nitrate vasodilator
Selective beta-1 blocker
qs.x: Nicardipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that mainly dilates arterioles with little effect on the AV node. Nondihydropyridines such as diltiazem slow AV conduction.

qs.q: Which adverse effects should be monitored during a nicardipine infusion?
qs.a: Reflex tachycardia and headache
w: Bradycardia and heart block
Bronchospasm and wheezing
Hyperkalemia and peaked T waves
qs.x: Arterial vasodilation from nicardipine can cause headache and reflex tachycardia. It has little effect on the AV node, so heart block is unlikely.

qs.q: How does labetalol lower blood pressure?
qs.a: Blocks alpha-1 receptors and beta receptors
w: Blocks only beta-1 receptors
Stimulates central alpha-2 receptors
Directly relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle
qs.x: Labetalol combines alpha-1 blockade, which lowers vascular resistance, with nonselective beta blockade, which limits reflex tachycardia. A pure beta-1 blocker would be something like metoprolol.

qs.q: Which history makes labetalol a poor choice for a hypertensive emergency?
qs.a: Severe asthma with active bronchospasm
w: Pregnancy with severe preeclampsia
Acute aortic dissection
Acute ischemic stroke before thrombolysis
qs.x: Labetalol's nonselective beta blockade can worsen bronchospasm in asthma. It is a first-line choice in severe preeclampsia, aortic dissection and stroke blood pressure control.

qs.q: In which hypertensive emergency is IV nitroglycerin especially useful?
qs.a: Hypertensive acute pulmonary edema
w: Eclampsia
Hypertensive intracranial hemorrhage
Aortic dissection as the only agent
qs.x: Nitroglycerin quickly reduces preload, and afterload at higher doses, which helps in hypertensive pulmonary edema. In aortic dissection it should not be used alone because it can cause reflex tachycardia that raises shear stress.

qs.q: How does hydralazine lower blood pressure?
qs.a: Directly relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle
w: Blocks beta-1 receptors in the heart
Blocks calcium channels in the AV node
Inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme
qs.x: Hydralazine is a direct arteriolar vasodilator, which is why reflex tachycardia is common. It does not block beta receptors or ACE.

qs.q: Which allergy is a contraindication to clevidipine?
qs.a: Allergy to soy or egg products
w: Allergy to sulfonamide antibiotics
Allergy to penicillin
Allergy to iodinated contrast
qs.x: Clevidipine comes in a lipid emulsion that contains soy and egg components, so these allergies are contraindications. Sulfa and penicillin allergies are unrelated.

qs.q: What property makes clevidipine easy to titrate?
qs.a: Ultra-short half-life from breakdown by blood and tissue esterases
w: Long half-life that keeps levels steady
Elimination unchanged by the kidneys
Liver metabolism into long-acting active metabolites
qs.x: Clevidipine is broken down by esterases within minutes, so blood pressure responds quickly to rate changes. A long half-life would make it harder, not easier, to titrate.

qs.q: In acute aortic dissection, why is esmolol started before a vasodilator?
qs.a: To prevent reflex tachycardia and reduce shear stress on the aorta
w: To increase cardiac contractility
To raise preload before vasodilation
To reverse vasodilator toxicity
qs.x: Lowering heart rate and contractility first reduces the force on the aortic wall and prevents the reflex tachycardia a vasodilator would cause. Esmolol decreases, not increases, contractility.

qs.q: After a prolonged nitroprusside infusion, a patient develops worsening metabolic acidosis and confusion. What should be suspected?
qs.a: Cyanide toxicity
w: Serotonin syndrome
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Thyroid storm
qs.x: Nitroprusside releases cyanide as it is metabolized, and accumulation causes metabolic acidosis and altered mental status. Report these findings to the provider promptly.

qs.q: Per Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines, which vasopressor is first-line for septic shock in adults?
qs.a: Norepinephrine
w: Dopamine
Phenylephrine
Vasopressin
qs.x: Norepinephrine is the recommended first-line vasopressor in septic shock. Vasopressin is usually added to norepinephrine rather than used first.

qs.q: Norepinephrine is infusing through a peripheral IV and the site becomes blanched and cool. Which agent is infiltrated into the area?
qs.a: Phentolamine
w: Hyaluronidase
Dexrazoxane
Sodium thiosulfate
qs.x: Phentolamine is an alpha blocker that reverses local vasoconstriction from norepinephrine extravasation. Hyaluronidase is used for some non-vasopressor extravasations.

qs.q: Which lab change is an expected effect of an epinephrine infusion and can complicate lactate interpretation?
qs.a: Rising lactate from beta-2 stimulated glycolysis
w: Falling lactate from improved perfusion alone
Hypoglycemia from increased insulin release
Hyperkalemia from potassium leaving cells
qs.x: Epinephrine stimulates beta-2 receptors on muscle, increasing glycolysis and lactate even when perfusion is adequate. It tends to raise glucose and lower potassium.

qs.q: Compared with norepinephrine in shock, dopamine is associated with which outcome?
qs.a: More tachyarrhythmias
w: Fewer tachyarrhythmias
Better protection of kidney function
Lower mortality in cardiogenic shock
qs.x: Trials comparing the two found more arrhythmias with dopamine, and a subgroup of cardiogenic shock patients did worse. Low-dose dopamine does not protect the kidneys.

qs.q: How does vasopressin raise blood pressure?
qs.a: Stimulates V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
w: Stimulates alpha-1 adrenergic receptors
Stimulates beta-1 receptors to increase contractility
Inhibits phosphodiesterase-3 in cardiac muscle
qs.x: Vasopressin acts on V1 receptors to cause vasoconstriction independently of adrenergic receptors. This is why it still works when catecholamine receptors respond poorly.

qs.q: In septic shock, how is vasopressin typically used?
qs.a: Added to norepinephrine to raise MAP or reduce norepinephrine need
w: As the first-line single vasopressor
As an inotrope for low cardiac output
As a treatment for symptomatic bradycardia
qs.x: Guidelines suggest adding vasopressin to norepinephrine rather than using it as first-line therapy. It has no inotropic effect.

qs.q: A patient in cardiogenic shock is started on dobutamine. Which effect may cause blood pressure to fall?
qs.a: Beta-2 mediated peripheral vasodilation
w: Alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction
Activation of vasopressin receptors
Negative inotropy on the myocardium
qs.x: Dobutamine is mainly a beta-1 inotrope but also has beta-2 effects that dilate vessels and can lower blood pressure. It increases, not decreases, contractility.

qs.q: Which effect is expected after phenylephrine is given for hypotension?
qs.a: Reflex bradycardia as blood pressure rises
w: Marked tachycardia from beta-1 stimulation
Bronchodilation from beta-2 stimulation
Increased myocardial contractility
qs.x: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist, so rising blood pressure triggers a baroreceptor reflex that slows the heart. It has essentially no beta activity.

qs.q: Which patient factor increases the risk of milrinone accumulation and hypotension?
qs.a: Renal impairment
w: Hepatic impairment
Current beta-blocker therapy
Obesity
qs.x: Milrinone is cleared mainly by the kidneys, so it accumulates in renal impairment and can cause hypotension and arrhythmias. Because it works beyond the beta receptor, beta blockers do not raise its levels.

qs.q: Before methylene blue is given for refractory vasoplegic shock, which medication history raises concern?
qs.a: Use of an SSRI or other serotonergic drug
w: Use of a statin
Use of a proton pump inhibitor
Use of a loop diuretic
qs.x: Methylene blue inhibits monoamine oxidase and carries a boxed warning for serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs. Statins and PPIs do not share this risk.

qs.q: During continuous albuterol for severe bronchospasm, which electrolyte change should be monitored?
qs.a: Hypokalemia
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypercalcemia
Hypernatremia
qs.x: Beta-2 stimulation shifts potassium into cells, so repeated or continuous albuterol can lower serum potassium. Albuterol is actually used to treat hyperkalemia.

qs.q: How can albuterol be delivered to an intubated patient during transport?
qs.a: In-line nebulizer or inhaler with spacer in the ventilator circuit
w: Direct liquid instillation down the endotracheal tube
Continuous IV infusion through a central line
Subcutaneous injection into the abdomen
qs.x: Albuterol is delivered as an aerosol placed in the ventilator circuit, by nebulizer or an inhaler with an adapter. IV albuterol is not available in the US.

qs.q: How does ipratropium produce bronchodilation?
qs.a: Blocks muscarinic receptors in airway smooth muscle
w: Stimulates beta-2 receptors in airway smooth muscle
Blocks leukotriene receptors
Stabilizes mast cells to prevent histamine release
qs.x: Ipratropium is an anticholinergic that blocks vagally mediated bronchoconstriction. Beta-2 stimulation describes albuterol.

qs.q: Why is a corticosteroid such as methylprednisolone given early in a severe asthma exacerbation?
qs.a: It reduces airway inflammation, with benefit developing over hours
w: It causes bronchodilation within minutes
It thins and clears mucus plugs
It suppresses the cough reflex
qs.x: Steroids treat the inflammation behind the exacerbation, but the effect takes hours, so they are given early alongside bronchodilators. They are not rapid bronchodilators.

qs.q: During an IV magnesium infusion for severe asthma, which adverse effects should be watched for?
qs.a: Hypotension and flushing
w: Tremor and tachycardia
Hyperkalemia and peaked T waves
Hypertension and seizures
qs.x: Magnesium relaxes smooth muscle, including blood vessels, so hypotension and flushing are common. Tremor and tachycardia are typical of beta agonists.

qs.q: After nebulized racemic epinephrine for croup, why must the child be observed for a period of time?
qs.a: Symptoms can return as the effect wears off
w: It can cause delayed hypoglycemia
It can trigger a delayed allergic reaction
It causes late-onset bronchospasm
qs.x: Racemic epinephrine reduces airway swelling for a limited time, so stridor can come back once it wears off. That is why observation after treatment is standard.

qs.q: Levalbuterol is best described as which of the following?
qs.a: The active R-enantiomer of albuterol
w: A long-acting beta-2 agonist for maintenance
An inhaled anticholinergic bronchodilator
A methylxanthine bronchodilator
qs.x: Levalbuterol is the R-isomer of albuterol and is a short-acting beta-2 agonist used for acute bronchospasm. It is not a long-acting maintenance agent.

qs.q: In severe asthma when inhaled therapy is not reaching the airways, by which route is terbutaline given?
qs.a: Subcutaneous injection
w: Rectal suppository
Intranasal spray
Inhaled dry powder
qs.x: Injectable terbutaline is given subcutaneously, reaching the airways through the bloodstream when bronchospasm limits inhaled delivery. It is not available as an inhaler in the US.

qs.q: Why is dexamethasone used for a child with croup?
qs.a: It is a long-acting steroid that reduces airway swelling
w: It causes immediate vasoconstriction of the airway
It has direct antiviral activity
It causes bronchodilation through beta-2 receptors
qs.x: Dexamethasone reduces subglottic inflammation for a prolonged period and decreases return visits and severity. Immediate vasoconstriction describes racemic epinephrine.

qs.q: In anaphylaxis with wheezing, how does epinephrine relieve bronchospasm?
qs.a: Stimulates beta-2 receptors to relax bronchial smooth muscle
w: Stimulates alpha-1 receptors to relax bronchial smooth muscle
Blocks muscarinic receptors in the airway
Blocks histamine-1 receptors in the airway
qs.x: Epinephrine's beta-2 effect relaxes airway smooth muscle, while its alpha-1 effect reduces mucosal swelling and raises blood pressure. Alpha-1 stimulation does not relax bronchial smooth muscle.

qs.q: Which adverse effect is associated with etomidate?
qs.a: Transient adrenal suppression
w: Profound hypotension on induction
Triggering of malignant hyperthermia
Bronchospasm from histamine release
qs.x: Etomidate inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase, briefly reducing cortisol production. It is chosen for induction precisely because it rarely causes hypotension.

qs.q: Why is etomidate often selected for induction in a hypotensive trauma patient?
qs.a: It has minimal effect on blood pressure and heart rate
w: It provides strong analgesia
It has a long duration of sedation
It causes significant bronchodilation
qs.x: Etomidate is hemodynamically neutral, making it useful in unstable patients. It provides no analgesia and is short acting, so analgesia and sedation must follow.

qs.q: Why is ketamine a good induction agent for a patient intubated for severe asthma?
qs.a: It has bronchodilating properties
w: It reduces airway secretions
It lowers heart rate
It never causes emergence reactions
qs.x: Ketamine's sympathomimetic effects relax bronchial smooth muscle, which helps in severe bronchospasm. It increases, rather than reduces, secretions.

qs.q: Which agent rapidly reverses rocuronium neuromuscular blockade?
qs.a: Sugammadex
w: Flumazenil
Dantrolene
Naloxone
qs.x: Sugammadex encapsulates aminosteroid blockers such as rocuronium and vecuronium, reversing them quickly. Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia, not paralysis.

qs.q: After RSI with rocuronium, why is early post-intubation sedation and analgesia critical?
qs.a: Paralysis outlasts the induction agent, risking awareness
w: Rocuronium itself lowers the seizure threshold
Rocuronium has sedative effects that wear off quickly
Sedation speeds the metabolism of rocuronium
qs.x: Rocuronium has no sedative or analgesic effect and lasts much longer than etomidate or ketamine induction doses, so a paralyzed patient may be awake. Paralysis also hides signs of distress, so sedation must be given proactively.

qs.q: Which patient should not receive succinylcholine?
qs.a: A patient with a spinal cord injury from two weeks ago
w: A patient with a femur fracture from one hour ago
A patient with a history of asthma
A patient intubated for an ongoing seizure
qs.x: After denervation injuries, burns or crush injuries older than a few days, extra acetylcholine receptors develop and succinylcholine can cause dangerous hyperkalemia. An acute fracture does not carry this risk.

qs.q: After succinylcholine, a patient develops jaw rigidity, a rapidly rising end-tidal CO2, tachycardia and then fever. What should be recognized?
qs.a: Malignant hyperthermia
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
Anaphylaxis
qs.x: Succinylcholine can trigger malignant hyperthermia in susceptible patients, and a rapid rise in end-tidal CO2 is often the earliest sign. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows antipsychotics and develops over days.

qs.q: Which hemodynamic effect is most common after propofol induction?
qs.a: Hypotension from vasodilation and myocardial depression
w: Hypertension and tachycardia
Bradycardia with a rise in blood pressure
No significant change in blood pressure
qs.x: Propofol dilates vessels and depresses the heart, so hypotension is common, especially in volume-depleted patients. Hypertension and tachycardia are more typical of ketamine.

qs.q: Vecuronium belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker
w: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker
Benzodiazepine sedative
Dissociative anesthetic
qs.x: Vecuronium is a nondepolarizing aminosteroid paralytic that competes with acetylcholine at the motor end plate. Succinylcholine is the only depolarizing blocker in common use.

qs.q: Why might atropine be given around RSI in a young infant receiving succinylcholine?
qs.a: To prevent or treat bradycardia from vagal stimulation
w: To prolong the neuromuscular blockade
To prevent succinylcholine-induced hyperkalemia
To lower intracranial pressure
qs.x: Infants have high vagal tone, and laryngoscopy and succinylcholine can cause bradycardia, which atropine blocks. It has no effect on paralysis or potassium.

qs.q: What is the preferred first route for epinephrine in anaphylaxis?
qs.a: Intramuscular injection into the anterolateral thigh
w: Subcutaneous injection into the upper arm
Oral solution swallowed
Rapid IV push of the cardiac arrest formulation
qs.x: IM injection into the thigh gives faster, more reliable absorption than subcutaneous injection. IV push of the arrest concentration in a patient with a pulse risks severe hypertension and arrhythmias.

qs.q: Hypotension persists despite repeated IM epinephrine and IV fluids in anaphylaxis. What epinephrine approach is next?
qs.a: A titrated IV epinephrine infusion
w: Switching to an oral antihistamine
Repeating a corticosteroid instead
Changing to subcutaneous epinephrine
qs.x: Refractory anaphylaxis is treated with a closely monitored IV epinephrine infusion. Antihistamines and steroids do not reverse shock.

qs.q: Why is diphenhydramine not a substitute for epinephrine in anaphylaxis?
qs.a: It relieves itching and hives but does not reverse airway swelling or shock
w: It severely worsens hypotension
It is only available as an oral tablet
It blocks the effect of epinephrine
qs.x: H1 antihistamines treat skin symptoms but do not reverse airway obstruction, bronchospasm or shock. Epinephrine is the only first-line treatment.

qs.q: Which adverse effects of diphenhydramine are most likely in an older adult?
qs.a: Sedation, confusion and urinary retention
w: Bradycardia and bronchospasm
Hypoglycemia and sweating
Diarrhea and excess salivation
qs.x: Diphenhydramine is sedating and strongly anticholinergic, causing confusion and urinary retention in older adults. Salivation and diarrhea are cholinergic, the opposite effect.

qs.q: Which statement about corticosteroids such as methylprednisolone in anaphylaxis is correct?
qs.a: They have a delayed onset and are adjuncts, not first-line therapy
w: They act within minutes to reverse hypotension
They can replace epinephrine in mild cases
They should be given before epinephrine
qs.x: Steroids take hours to work and do not treat the immediate life threats of anaphylaxis. Epinephrine always comes first.

qs.q: Which lab change is common after IV methylprednisolone, especially in patients with diabetes?
qs.a: Hyperglycemia
w: Hypoglycemia
Hyperkalemia
Hypercalcemia
qs.x: Glucocorticoids increase glucose production and insulin resistance, raising blood glucose. They tend to lower, not raise, potassium.

qs.q: How does dexamethasone compare with methylprednisolone?
qs.a: Longer acting with minimal mineralocorticoid activity
w: Shorter acting with strong mineralocorticoid activity
It is an antihistamine rather than a steroid
It is a mast cell stabilizer rather than a steroid
qs.x: Dexamethasone is a long-acting glucocorticoid with almost no salt-retaining effect. Both drugs are corticosteroids.

qs.q: A patient in anaphylaxis treated with IM epinephrine is still wheezing. Why is albuterol added?
qs.a: To treat persistent bronchospasm despite epinephrine
w: To treat persistent hypotension
To treat laryngeal edema and stridor
To treat widespread hives
qs.x: Inhaled albuterol is an adjunct for lower-airway bronchospasm that persists after epinephrine. It does not treat shock or upper-airway swelling.

qs.q: A patient taking metoprolol has anaphylaxis that does not respond to repeated epinephrine. Which medication may help?
qs.a: Glucagon
w: Additional diphenhydramine
Ondansetron
Calcium chloride
qs.x: Beta blockers can blunt the response to epinephrine, and glucagon raises heart rate and contractility through a non-beta pathway. More antihistamine will not reverse the shock.

qs.q: Why does glucagon work in a beta-blocked patient?
qs.a: It raises intracellular cAMP without using beta receptors
w: It blocks histamine receptors
It is a potent alpha-1 agonist
It stabilizes mast cells
qs.x: Glucagon activates its own receptor, which increases cAMP and improves cardiac output even when beta receptors are blocked. Nausea and vomiting are common, so protect the airway.

qs.q: After IV lorazepam for status epilepticus, what is most important to monitor?
qs.a: Respiratory effort and airway patency
w: Blood glucose for hyperglycemia
Blood pressure for hypertension
Heart rate for tachycardia
qs.x: Benzodiazepines can cause respiratory depression and airway loss, especially with repeated doses. Hypotension, not hypertension, is the hemodynamic concern.

qs.q: A patient is actively seizing with no IV access. Which route of midazolam has been shown to be effective?
qs.a: Intramuscular
w: Oral
Subcutaneous
Transdermal
qs.x: IM midazolam stops seizures as well as IV lorazepam and is faster to give when there is no IV. Oral and transdermal routes are too slow and impractical.

qs.q: Seizures continue after an adequate benzodiazepine dose. What is the role of levetiracetam?
qs.a: Second-line IV antiseizure medicine after benzodiazepines
w: First-line agent given before benzodiazepines
Agent used only for alcohol withdrawal
Sedative used for intubation
qs.x: Levetiracetam is one of the second-line agents for benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus. Benzodiazepines remain first line.

qs.q: How does hypertonic saline lower intracranial pressure?
qs.a: It creates an osmotic gradient that draws water out of brain tissue
w: It constricts the cerebral arteries
It reduces CSF production by inhibiting carbonic anhydrase
It causes diuresis of free water by the kidneys
qs.x: Raising serum sodium pulls water from brain tissue into the blood, reducing edema and ICP. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition describes acetazolamide.

qs.q: During hypertonic saline therapy for raised ICP, which lab is most important to monitor?
qs.a: Serum sodium
w: Serum potassium
Serum magnesium
Serum phosphate
qs.x: Hypertonic saline works by raising serum sodium, so levels are monitored to keep them in target and avoid overcorrection. Potassium is not the main concern.

qs.q: How does diazepam compare with lorazepam?
qs.a: It has a longer half-life with active metabolites
w: It has no active metabolites
It is much shorter acting
It is not a benzodiazepine
qs.x: Diazepam is highly lipid soluble with active metabolites that prolong its effect. Lorazepam has no active metabolites.

qs.q: In a hypotensive patient with traumatic brain injury, why might hypertonic saline be favored over mannitol?
qs.a: Mannitol causes osmotic diuresis that can worsen hypotension
w: Mannitol raises intracranial pressure
Mannitol cannot cross into the bloodstream
Mannitol causes severe hyperkalemia
qs.x: Mannitol lowers ICP but also causes diuresis and volume loss, which can worsen hypotension and lower cerebral perfusion. Hypertonic saline tends to support blood pressure.

qs.q: Before alteplase for acute ischemic stroke, blood pressure must be lowered below which level?
w: 160/90 mmHg
140/80 mmHg
qs.x: Guidelines require blood pressure below 185/110 before thrombolysis and below 180/105 afterward to limit bleeding risk. The 220/120 threshold applies to patients not receiving thrombolytics.

qs.q: During an alteplase infusion for stroke, the patient develops a sudden severe headache, vomiting and a falling level of consciousness. What should be recognized?
qs.a: Possible symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage
w: Expected reperfusion headache
Recurrent stroke in a new vascular territory
Orolingual angioedema
qs.x: New headache, vomiting or neurologic decline during thrombolysis suggests intracranial hemorrhage and must be reported immediately. Angioedema causes tongue and lip swelling, not these signs.

qs.q: What practical advantage does tenecteplase have over alteplase for stroke transport?
qs.a: It is a single IV bolus with no infusion running during transport
w: It carries no risk of bleeding
It can be given regardless of blood pressure
It does not require brain imaging first
qs.x: Tenecteplase is given as one bolus, avoiding an hour-long infusion. It still carries bleeding risk and requires imaging and blood pressure control.

qs.q: After a rapid IV fentanyl push, the patient becomes very hard to ventilate with a rigid chest. What should be recognized?
qs.a: Opioid-induced chest wall rigidity
w: Bronchospasm from histamine release
Anaphylaxis to fentanyl
Malignant hyperthermia
qs.x: Rapid, large fentanyl doses can cause chest wall and glottic rigidity that makes ventilation difficult. Fentanyl releases little histamine, so bronchospasm is unlikely.

qs.q: Why is morphine used cautiously in renal failure?
qs.a: Active metabolites accumulate, prolonging sedation and respiratory depression
w: It is directly toxic to the kidneys
It causes severe hyperkalemia
It is eliminated unchanged only by the liver
qs.x: Morphine's active metabolites are cleared by the kidneys and build up in renal failure. Morphine itself is not nephrotoxic.

qs.q: Why is flumazenil used cautiously to reverse midazolam?
qs.a: It can trigger seizures in patients on long-term benzodiazepines
w: It causes respiratory depression
It worsens hypotension
It increases the effect of midazolam
qs.x: Flumazenil can provoke withdrawal seizures in benzodiazepine-dependent patients or those with seizure-prone ingestions. It reverses, rather than increases, benzodiazepine effects.

qs.q: Which adverse effect is characteristic of ketamine?
qs.a: Emergence reactions such as vivid dreams or agitation
w: Profound bradycardia and hypotension
Apnea at analgesic doses
Adrenal suppression
qs.x: Ketamine can cause hallucinations, vivid dreams and agitation on emergence. It usually supports, rather than lowers, heart rate and blood pressure.

qs.q: An intubated trauma patient on propofol grimaces and becomes tachycardic when moved. Which concept applies?
qs.a: Propofol provides no analgesia, so pain needs separate treatment
w: Propofol is a strong analgesic so more is needed
Tachycardia is a common propofol side effect
Propofol causes pain only on injection
qs.x: Propofol is a sedative-hypnotic without pain relief, so signs of pain call for an analgesic. Propofol more often causes bradycardia and hypotension than tachycardia.

qs.q: What is a key safety point when a patient is switched from morphine to hydromorphone?
qs.a: Hydromorphone is several times more potent, so mix-ups can cause overdose
w: Hydromorphone is much weaker, so pain may increase
Hydromorphone has no risk of respiratory depression
Hydromorphone must be given only by mouth
qs.x: Hydromorphone is much more potent than morphine, and confusing the two is a known cause of fatal overdoses. It still causes respiratory depression.

qs.q: A patient on a prolonged high-rate lorazepam infusion develops rising anion gap and osmolar gap. What should be suspected?
qs.a: Propylene glycol toxicity from the drug's diluent
w: Methanol poisoning
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Lactic acidosis from sepsis
qs.x: IV lorazepam contains propylene glycol, which can accumulate and cause metabolic acidosis and a high osmolar gap. Report this to the provider.

qs.q: Which feature distinguishes dexmedetomidine from most other sedatives?
qs.a: Sedation with little respiratory depression
w: Strong amnesia through GABA receptors
Analgesia through mu-opioid receptors
Dissociation through NMDA blockade
qs.x: Dexmedetomidine is a central alpha-2 agonist that sedates while largely preserving respiratory drive. GABA-mediated amnesia describes benzodiazepines and propofol.

qs.q: In which patient is ketorolac inappropriate?
qs.a: A trauma patient with suspected active hemorrhage
w: A patient with renal colic and normal kidney function
A patient with musculoskeletal back pain
A patient with a migraine headache
qs.x: Ketorolac inhibits platelet function and raises bleeding risk, so it is avoided with active or suspected bleeding. Renal colic with normal kidneys is a common indication.

qs.q: What is the main toxicity risk with IV acetaminophen?
qs.a: Liver injury, especially when combined with other sources
w: Respiratory depression
Gastrointestinal bleeding
Platelet dysfunction
qs.x: Acetaminophen overdose, often from stacking IV and oral products, can cause liver failure. Unlike NSAIDs, it does not impair platelets or cause GI bleeding.

qs.q: What does droperidol's boxed warning concern?
qs.a: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes
w: Severe liver toxicity
Agranulocytosis
Serotonin syndrome
qs.x: Droperidol carries a boxed warning for QT prolongation and torsades, so ECG monitoring is important. Agranulocytosis is associated with clozapine.

qs.q: What makes droperidol useful for severe agitation in emergency settings?
qs.a: Rapid onset of sedation when given IM or IV
w: It has no cardiac effects
It is a long-acting benzodiazepine
It reverses alcohol intoxication
qs.x: Droperidol, a butyrophenone, sedates quickly by IM or IV route. It does have cardiac effects, including QT prolongation.

qs.q: Hours after haloperidol, a patient has a twisted neck and eyes fixed upward. What should be recognized?
qs.a: Acute dystonic reaction
w: Generalized seizure
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
qs.x: Sustained muscle spasms of the neck, eyes or jaw are an acute dystonic reaction from dopamine blockade. The patient stays awake, unlike in a seizure.

qs.q: Days after starting haloperidol, a patient has high fever, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion and unstable blood pressure. What should be recognized?
qs.a: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
w: Serotonin syndrome
Malignant hyperthermia
Acute dystonic reaction
qs.x: Fever, rigidity, altered mental status and autonomic instability after an antipsychotic suggest neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Serotonin syndrome more often shows clonus and hyperreflexia.

qs.q: What is an advantage of IM midazolam for an agitated patient without IV access?
qs.a: Rapid absorption and onset compared with other IM benzodiazepines
w: It causes no respiratory depression
It has a very long duration of action
It requires no monitoring afterward
qs.x: Midazolam is water soluble and absorbed quickly after IM injection, while IM lorazepam is slower. It can still depress breathing, so monitoring is needed.

qs.q: An agitated patient who is heavily intoxicated with alcohol is given midazolam. What is the main risk?
qs.a: Additive respiratory depression
w: Hypertensive crisis
QT prolongation
Severe hyperthermia
qs.x: Alcohol and benzodiazepines both act on GABA receptors, so together they can cause marked respiratory depression. Close airway monitoring is needed.

qs.q: After IM ketamine for severe agitation, which complications should the crew be ready to manage?
qs.a: Laryngospasm and hypersalivation
w: Bradycardia and hypotension
QT prolongation and torsades
Hypoglycemia and seizures
qs.x: Ketamine increases secretions and can rarely cause laryngospasm, so suction and airway equipment should be ready. It usually raises heart rate and blood pressure.

qs.q: For an agitated patient with tremor and sweating from alcohol withdrawal, why is a benzodiazepine such as lorazepam preferred?
qs.a: It treats the withdrawal itself and lowers seizure risk
w: It has no effect on breathing
It is an antipsychotic
It lowers the seizure threshold
qs.x: Benzodiazepines replace alcohol's GABA effect, treating withdrawal and preventing seizures. Antipsychotics can lower the seizure threshold.

qs.q: Which medication treats an acute dystonic reaction to haloperidol?
qs.a: Diphenhydramine
w: Flumazenil
Naloxone
Dantrolene
qs.x: Diphenhydramine's anticholinergic effect restores the dopamine-acetylcholine balance and relieves dystonia, often within minutes. Dantrolene is used for malignant hyperthermia.

qs.q: Why can diphenhydramine make agitation worse in an older adult?
qs.a: Its anticholinergic effects can cause delirium
w: It is a stimulant
It causes hypoglycemia
It causes serotonin syndrome
qs.x: Older adults are sensitive to anticholinergic drugs, which can cause confusion and delirium. It is sedating, not stimulating, in most adults.

qs.q: How does tranexamic acid reduce bleeding?
qs.a: Blocks plasminogen from breaking down fibrin clots
w: Activates platelets at the injury site
Replaces depleted clotting factors
Directly inhibits thrombin
qs.x: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic that blocks lysine binding sites on plasminogen, so clots are not broken down. It does not replace clotting factors.

qs.q: In trauma with significant hemorrhage, when is tranexamic acid beneficial?
qs.a: When given within 3 hours of injury
w: Only when started more than 3 hours after injury
Only after surgical control of bleeding
Only on the day after injury
qs.x: Trial data show benefit when TXA is started within 3 hours of injury, with possible harm when started later. Earlier is better.

qs.q: Why is calcium given during massive transfusion?
qs.a: Citrate in stored blood binds ionized calcium
w: Blood products contain excess calcium
Calcium reverses tranexamic acid
Calcium prevents hemolytic transfusion reactions
qs.x: Citrate used to preserve blood binds calcium, and hypocalcemia worsens coagulopathy and cardiac function. Stored blood does not contain extra calcium.

qs.q: How does calcium chloride compare with calcium gluconate?
qs.a: It delivers more elemental calcium per volume and is more irritating to veins
w: It delivers less calcium and is safer peripherally
It is identical in calcium content and irritation
It can only be given intramuscularly
qs.x: Calcium chloride contains about three times the elemental calcium of the same volume of gluconate but is more caustic. Gluconate is gentler on peripheral veins.

qs.q: Why should calcium gluconate not be infused through the same line as a blood product?
qs.a: Calcium can overcome the citrate anticoagulant and cause clotting in the line
w: Calcium destroys red blood cells
Calcium inactivates tranexamic acid
Calcium causes potassium release from platelets
qs.x: Calcium reverses citrate's anticoagulant effect, so clots can form in the tubing. Only normal saline should be run with blood products.

qs.q: Which route of fentanyl can provide rapid analgesia when IV access is not yet established?
qs.a: Intranasal by atomizer
w: Swallowed oral tablet
Rectal suppository
Transdermal patch
qs.x: Intranasal fentanyl is absorbed quickly across the nasal mucosa. A transdermal patch takes many hours to work and is not for acute pain.

qs.q: What is an advantage of ketamine for analgesia in a trauma patient at risk of hypotension?
qs.a: It tends to preserve blood pressure and respiratory drive
w: It lowers heart rate
It causes marked vasodilation
It has an antiplatelet effect
qs.x: Ketamine's sympathomimetic effect helps maintain blood pressure, and breathing is usually preserved. It does not cause marked vasodilation like propofol.

qs.q: How does ketamine produce analgesia and dissociation?
qs.a: Blocks NMDA receptors
w: Stimulates mu-opioid receptors
Enhances GABA-A receptor activity
Stimulates alpha-2 receptors
qs.x: Ketamine is an NMDA receptor antagonist. Opioids act on mu receptors and dexmedetomidine on alpha-2 receptors.

qs.q: Why is cefazolin given early for an open fracture?
qs.a: To lower the risk of deep infection from skin organisms
w: To cover anaerobic bowel bacteria
To treat tetanus
To cover MRSA
qs.x: Early cefazolin targets the staphylococci and streptococci that commonly infect open fractures. It does not cover MRSA or replace tetanus prophylaxis.

qs.q: Cefazolin belongs to which antibiotic class?
qs.a: First-generation cephalosporin
w: Third-generation cephalosporin
Carbapenem
Fluoroquinolone
qs.x: Cefazolin is a first-generation cephalosporin with strong gram-positive coverage. Ceftriaxone is a third-generation agent.

qs.q: Why should concentrated dextrose be given through a large, patent vein?
qs.a: It is hypertonic and can cause tissue necrosis if it extravasates
w: It precipitates when mixed with saline
It causes immediate anaphylaxis in small veins
It is inactive unless given centrally
qs.x: Concentrated dextrose is very hypertonic and irritating, so extravasation can cause tissue injury. Confirm a patent line before and during administration.

qs.q: After dextrose for hypoglycemia from a sulfonylurea overdose, why are frequent glucose rechecks needed?
qs.a: Hypoglycemia often recurs as the long-acting drug persists
w: Dextrose causes delayed hyperkalemia
Dextrose is metabolized into insulin
Sulfonylureas block dextrose absorption
qs.x: Sulfonylureas keep stimulating insulin release for many hours, so glucose may fall again after a bolus. Frequent checks catch recurrence early.

qs.q: Why is D5W a poor choice for volume resuscitation in hemorrhagic shock?
qs.a: The glucose is metabolized, leaving free water that moves mostly into cells
w: It is a colloid that stays in the bloodstream
It is hypertonic and pulls fluid from cells
It contains potassium that causes arrhythmias
qs.x: Once dextrose is metabolized, D5W acts like free water and distributes into cells, with little staying in the vessels. Blood products are the preferred replacement in hemorrhage.

qs.q: Why is a dextrose-containing solution not run in the same line as packed red blood cells?
qs.a: It can cause red cell clumping and hemolysis
w: It inactivates the citrate anticoagulant
It causes the blood to clot immediately
It raises potassium in the stored blood
qs.x: Dextrose solutions can cause red cells to clump and swell, leading to hemolysis. Normal saline is the only solution routinely run with blood.

qs.q: Before giving dextrose to a patient with altered mental status, what should be confirmed?
qs.a: Low blood glucose on point-of-care testing
w: Serum potassium level
Arterial blood gas results
Serum ketone level
qs.x: A quick glucose check confirms hypoglycemia and gives a baseline to judge the response. Waiting for lab tests would delay treatment.

qs.q: In hyperkalemia with ECG changes, how does calcium help?
qs.a: It stabilizes the cardiac membrane without lowering potassium
w: It shifts potassium into cells
It increases kidney excretion of potassium
It binds potassium in the gut
qs.x: Calcium protects the heart against potassium's effects but does not change the potassium level. Other therapies such as insulin and albuterol shift potassium into cells.

qs.q: Which ECG finding suggests hypocalcemia that calcium gluconate would treat?
qs.a: Prolonged QT interval
w: Peaked T waves
Prominent U waves
Shortened QT interval
qs.x: Low calcium lengthens the ST segment and QT interval. Peaked T waves suggest hyperkalemia and U waves suggest hypokalemia.

qs.q: In hyperkalemia with a widening QRS, how long does calcium's protective effect last?
qs.a: It begins within minutes but is temporary
w: It takes several hours to begin
It is permanent once given
It begins only after dialysis
qs.x: Calcium works within minutes but wears off, so it may need repeating while potassium is lowered by other means. It does not remove potassium.

qs.q: A patient with a prolonged QT develops polymorphic VT with a twisting pattern. Which medication is first-line?
qs.a: Magnesium sulfate
w: Calcium chloride
Sodium bicarbonate
Adenosine
qs.x: Magnesium is the treatment of choice for torsades de pointes, even with a normal magnesium level. Adenosine has no role in polymorphic VT.

qs.q: During a magnesium infusion, the patient's patellar reflexes disappear. What does this indicate?
qs.a: Rising magnesium levels approaching toxicity
w: The expected therapeutic effect
Improving hypocalcemia
Developing hypokalemia
qs.x: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is an early sign of magnesium toxicity and can be followed by respiratory depression. Report it to the provider promptly.

qs.q: Why should calcium and sodium bicarbonate not be given together in the same IV line without flushing?
qs.a: They form a calcium carbonate precipitate
w: They cancel each other's cardiac effects
They cause hemolysis in the line
They form a toxic gas
qs.x: Calcium and bicarbonate combine to form an insoluble precipitate that can block the line. Flush well between them.

qs.q: How does furosemide cause diuresis?
qs.a: Inhibits the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter in the loop of Henle
w: Inhibits sodium reabsorption in the distal tubule
Blocks aldosterone in the collecting duct
Inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
qs.x: Furosemide is a loop diuretic acting on the thick ascending limb. Distal tubule action describes thiazides.

qs.q: Which adverse effect is associated with rapid high-dose IV furosemide?
qs.a: Hearing loss or tinnitus
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypoglycemia
Bradycardia
qs.x: Rapid IV injection of large furosemide doses can cause ototoxicity. Furosemide causes potassium loss, not hyperkalemia.

qs.q: How does nebulized albuterol lower serum potassium?
qs.a: Stimulates the sodium-potassium pump to shift potassium into cells
w: Increases kidney excretion of potassium
Binds potassium in the gut
Stabilizes the cardiac membrane
qs.x: Beta-2 stimulation activates Na-K-ATPase, moving potassium into cells temporarily. Total body potassium is unchanged.

qs.q: After IV regular insulin with dextrose for hyperkalemia, what is most important to monitor?
qs.a: Blood glucose for delayed hypoglycemia
w: Serum calcium
Serum magnesium
Urine output for diuresis
qs.x: Hypoglycemia is a common complication, sometimes hours after the insulin dose, especially with kidney disease. Glucose should be checked repeatedly.

qs.q: Why is a patient observed after naloxone reverses an opioid overdose?
qs.a: Naloxone may wear off before the opioid, causing recurrent respiratory depression
w: Naloxone causes a delayed allergic reaction
Naloxone causes delayed hypotension
Withdrawal always starts hours later
qs.x: Many opioids last longer than naloxone, so sedation and hypoventilation can return. Withdrawal, if it occurs, starts quickly rather than hours later.

qs.q: In tricyclic antidepressant overdose with a widening QRS and hypotension, how does sodium bicarbonate help?
qs.a: The sodium load and alkalinization overcome sodium-channel blockade
w: It binds the drug in the gut
It speeds kidney elimination of the drug
It blocks muscarinic receptors
qs.x: Tricyclics block cardiac sodium channels, and bicarbonate counters this with extra sodium and a higher pH. It does not meaningfully increase elimination.

qs.q: Activated charcoal is ineffective for which ingestion?
qs.a: Lithium
w: Aspirin
Acetaminophen
Carbamazepine
qs.x: Charcoal does not bind metals such as lithium and iron or alcohols. Aspirin, acetaminophen and carbamazepine are well adsorbed.

qs.q: Which effect is expected after hydroxocobalamin for suspected cyanide poisoning?
qs.a: Red discoloration of skin and urine
w: Blue discoloration of skin
Green discoloration of urine
Yellow discoloration of skin
qs.x: Hydroxocobalamin is deep red and colors skin and urine, and it can interfere with some lab tests. This is expected and not a sign of harm.

qs.q: What is the endpoint for atropine in organophosphate poisoning?
qs.a: Drying of bronchial secretions and improved oxygenation
w: Full dilation of the pupils
Resolution of muscle fasciculations
Return of normal muscle strength
qs.x: Atropine is titrated to clear airway secretions and reverse bronchorrhea. It does not treat nicotinic effects such as fasciculations or weakness.

qs.q: What is the role of pralidoxime in organophosphate poisoning?
qs.a: It reactivates acetylcholinesterase, improving muscle weakness
w: It blocks muscarinic receptors to dry secretions
It binds the organophosphate in the gut
It stops seizures through GABA receptors
qs.x: Pralidoxime restores acetylcholinesterase before the bond ages, helping nicotinic effects such as weakness. Drying secretions is atropine's job.

qs.q: How does fomepizole treat ethylene glycol or methanol poisoning?
qs.a: It inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing toxic metabolites
w: It speeds kidney elimination of the toxic alcohol
It binds the toxic alcohol in the blood
It directly corrects metabolic acidosis
qs.x: Blocking alcohol dehydrogenase stops conversion of the parent alcohol into its toxic acids. Dialysis may still be needed to remove the alcohol itself.

qs.q: When should physostigmine be avoided in suspected anticholinergic toxicity?
qs.a: When the ECG shows QRS widening suggesting a tricyclic ingestion
w: When the patient is agitated
When the skin is dry and flushed
When there is urinary retention
qs.x: Physostigmine can cause bradycardia, asystole and seizures in tricyclic overdose. Agitation and dry flushed skin are typical anticholinergic findings it may treat.

qs.q: Which finding in acute digoxin overdose supports giving digoxin immune fab?
qs.a: A life-threatening dysrhythmia or marked hyperkalemia
w: Mild nausea only
Yellow-tinted vision alone
Low potassium with a normal rhythm
qs.x: Digoxin immune fab is indicated for dangerous dysrhythmias or significant hyperkalemia, which signals severe acute toxicity. Mild symptoms alone do not require it.

qs.q: How does N-acetylcysteine protect the liver in acetaminophen overdose?
qs.a: It replenishes glutathione to detoxify the toxic metabolite NAPQI
w: It binds acetaminophen in the blood
It blocks acetaminophen absorption
It speeds kidney excretion of acetaminophen
qs.x: NAC restores glutathione, which neutralizes the toxic metabolite NAPQI. It works best when started early after ingestion.

qs.q: How does cefazolin kill bacteria?
qs.a: It inhibits cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins
w: It inhibits protein synthesis at the 30S ribosome
It inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase
It blocks bacterial folate synthesis
qs.x: Cefazolin is a beta-lactam that disrupts cell wall formation. Ribosome inhibition describes drugs such as aminoglycosides.

qs.q: Which organism is not reliably covered by cefazolin?
qs.a: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
w: Methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus
Streptococcus pyogenes
Streptococcus agalactiae
qs.x: Cefazolin covers MSSA and streptococci well but not MRSA. Suspected MRSA needs an agent such as vancomycin.

qs.q: Several days after a course of cefazolin, a patient has frequent watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps. What should be recognized?
qs.a: Possible Clostridioides difficile infection
w: Expected mild stomach upset
A new food allergy
An unrelated thyroid problem
qs.x: Antibiotics disrupt normal gut flora and can allow C. difficile to overgrow. Frequent watery diarrhea after antibiotics should be reported.

qs.q: Cefazolin is mainly eliminated by which route, which matters in kidney disease?
qs.a: Excretion by the kidneys
w: Metabolism by the liver
Excretion in bile
Exhalation by the lungs
qs.x: Cefazolin is cleared unchanged by the kidneys, so dosing is adjusted in kidney impairment. It undergoes little liver metabolism.

qs.q: When cefazolin is ordered for suspected infection, what is best practice regarding blood cultures?
qs.a: Obtain cultures before the first dose if this does not delay it
w: Obtain cultures only after the first day of therapy
Skip cultures because they do not change care
Wait for culture results before giving the antibiotic
qs.x: Cultures drawn before antibiotics are more likely to identify the organism, but antibiotics should not be meaningfully delayed. Waiting for results would delay treatment.

qs.q: Before an insulin infusion is started for diabetic ketoacidosis, which lab must be confirmed?
qs.a: That serum potassium is not low
w: That blood glucose has normalized
That ketones have cleared
That serum calcium is normal
qs.x: Insulin shifts potassium into cells, so starting it with low potassium can cause dangerous hypokalemia and arrhythmias. Potassium is replaced first if low.

qs.q: During DKA treatment, glucose falls toward the target range but the anion gap is still open. What is the usual approach?
qs.a: Add dextrose to IV fluids while the insulin infusion continues
w: Switch to subcutaneous insulin right away
Give a bolus of sodium bicarbonate
Give a large bolus of IV insulin
qs.x: Insulin is needed to clear ketoacidosis, so dextrose is added to prevent hypoglycemia while insulin keeps closing the gap. Bicarbonate is not routine in DKA.

qs.q: During transport of a patient on an insulin infusion for DKA, how often is glucose usually checked?
qs.a: About every hour by point-of-care testing
w: Only once on arrival
About every six hours
Only if the patient has symptoms
qs.x: Insulin infusions can lower glucose quickly, so hourly checks are standard. Waiting for symptoms would miss hypoglycemia in a sedated or altered patient.

qs.q: A hypoglycemic patient wakes up after IV dextrose. What is the next step?
qs.a: Recheck glucose and give a longer-acting carbohydrate when able to eat
w: Assume the problem is resolved
Give insulin to prevent rebound
Give a second bolus without rechecking
qs.x: IV dextrose works quickly but briefly, so glucose is rechecked and complex carbohydrates are given when safe. Insulin would worsen hypoglycemia.

qs.q: Why is unnecessary hyperglycemia from dextrose-containing fluids avoided in acute stroke or brain injury?
qs.a: Hyperglycemia is linked to worse neurologic outcomes
w: Hyperglycemia lowers intracranial pressure
Hyperglycemia improves outcomes
Glucose level has no effect on the brain
qs.x: High glucose is associated with larger infarcts and worse outcomes after stroke and brain injury. Treat confirmed hypoglycemia but avoid unneeded dextrose.

qs.q: A hypoglycemic patient is unconscious and has no IV access. Which routes can be used for glucagon?
qs.a: Intramuscular, subcutaneous or intranasal
w: Oral, sublingual or buccal
Rectal or transdermal only
Inhaled by nebulizer only
qs.x: Glucagon is approved for IM, SC and, as a nasal powder, intranasal use. An unconscious patient should never receive anything by mouth.

qs.q: In which patient is glucagon less likely to raise blood glucose?
qs.a: A patient with chronic alcohol use and poor nutrition
w: A patient with type 1 diabetes on insulin
A patient who ate a meal recently
A school-age child
qs.x: Glucagon works by releasing stored liver glycogen, which is depleted in starvation and chronic alcohol use. IV dextrose is preferred in these patients.

qs.q: Which adverse effect is common after glucagon, and how should the crew prepare?
qs.a: Nausea and vomiting, so protect the airway
w: Bradycardia, so prepare atropine
Hypokalemia, so prepare potassium
Bronchospasm, so prepare albuterol
qs.x: Vomiting is common after glucagon, especially as the patient wakes up. Positioning and suction reduce aspiration risk.

qs.q: A malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder has confusion, unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements. Which deficiency should be suspected?
qs.a: Thiamine deficiency causing Wernicke encephalopathy
w: Vitamin B12 deficiency causing anemia
Folate deficiency causing neural tube defects
Vitamin K deficiency causing bleeding
qs.x: Confusion, ataxia and eye movement abnormalities are the classic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency. It is treated with IV thiamine.

qs.q: A hypoglycemic patient with chronic alcohol use needs dextrose. How should thiamine fit in?
qs.a: Give thiamine as well, without delaying dextrose
w: Delay dextrose until thiamine levels return
Give dextrose only, since thiamine has no role
Give thiamine only, since dextrose is harmful
qs.x: Glucose metabolism uses thiamine, so at-risk patients should receive thiamine too, but hypoglycemia is treated right away. Delaying dextrose is more dangerous.

qs.q: How does ondansetron prevent nausea and vomiting?
qs.a: Blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors
w: Blocks dopamine D2 receptors
