Blocks histamine H1 receptors
Blocks neurokinin-1 receptors
qs.x: Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 receptors in the gut and brainstem. Dopamine blockade describes metoclopramide and droperidol.

qs.q: Which adverse effect warrants caution with ondansetron in a patient with long QT syndrome?
qs.a: QT prolongation
w: Extrapyramidal symptoms
Tissue necrosis at the IV site
Hypoglycemia
qs.x: Ondansetron can prolong the QT interval, and its labeling advises avoiding it in congenital long QT syndrome. Extrapyramidal effects are more typical of dopamine blockers.

qs.q: Which adverse effects of ondansetron are most common?
qs.a: Headache and constipation
w: Diarrhea and excess salivation
Drowsiness and dry mouth
Restlessness and muscle spasms
qs.x: Headache and constipation are the most frequent side effects. Restlessness and spasms are typical of metoclopramide.

qs.q: How does metoclopramide relieve nausea?
qs.a: Blocks dopamine D2 receptors and increases gut motility
w: Blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors only
Blocks histamine H1 receptors
Blocks muscarinic receptors
qs.x: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and speeds gastric emptying. 5-HT3 blockade describes ondansetron.

qs.q: After rapid IV metoclopramide, a patient feels intense restlessness and cannot sit still. What should be recognized?
qs.a: Akathisia
w: Panic attack
Serotonin syndrome
Hypoglycemia
qs.x: Akathisia is an extrapyramidal effect of dopamine blockade and is more common with rapid IV push. Report it so it can be treated.

qs.q: In which patient is metoclopramide contraindicated?
qs.a: A patient with a suspected mechanical bowel obstruction
w: A patient with diabetic gastroparesis
A patient with a migraine headache
A patient with nausea after surgery
qs.x: Metoclopramide increases gut motility, which can be harmful with obstruction, perforation or GI bleeding. Gastroparesis is an approved indication.

qs.q: What does the boxed warning for injectable promethazine describe?
qs.a: Severe tissue injury, including gangrene, from extravasation or arterial injection
w: Severe liver failure
Torsades de pointes
Serotonin syndrome
qs.x: Injectable promethazine is very irritating and can cause severe tissue injury and gangrene. Deep IM injection is the preferred route.

qs.q: Promethazine is contraindicated in which population?
qs.a: Children younger than 2 years
w: Adults older than 65 years
Pregnant patients
Patients with motion sickness
qs.x: Promethazine has a boxed warning for fatal respiratory depression in children under 2. Motion sickness is one of its indications.

qs.q: Which adverse effects can droperidol share with metoclopramide?
qs.a: Akathisia and other extrapyramidal symptoms
w: Constipation and headache
Red skin and urine
Bradycardia and bronchospasm
qs.x: Both drugs block dopamine receptors and can cause akathisia and dystonia. Constipation and headache are typical of ondansetron.

qs.q: Where does droperidol act to relieve nausea?
qs.a: Dopamine receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone
w: Serotonin receptors in the gut wall
Histamine receptors in the inner ear
Neurokinin receptors in the vomiting center
qs.x: Droperidol is a butyrophenone that blocks dopamine in the chemoreceptor trigger zone. Serotonin blockade in the gut describes ondansetron.

qs.q: How does oxytocin control postpartum hemorrhage?
qs.a: It stimulates uterine contraction, compressing bleeding vessels
w: It promotes clotting factor production
It relaxes the uterus to reduce bleeding
It causes widespread systemic vasoconstriction
qs.x: Most postpartum hemorrhage is from uterine atony, and oxytocin makes the uterus contract and clamp down on vessels. It does not affect clotting factors.

qs.q: After a prolonged oxytocin infusion, a patient develops headache, confusion and low sodium. What should be suspected?
qs.a: Water intoxication from oxytocin's antidiuretic effect
w: Preeclampsia with severe features
Amniotic fluid embolism
Magnesium toxicity
qs.x: Oxytocin resembles vasopressin and in prolonged infusions can cause water retention and hyponatremia. Report these findings promptly.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of magnesium sulfate in severe preeclampsia?
qs.a: To prevent eclamptic seizures
w: To lower blood pressure as the main agent
To strengthen uterine contractions
To prevent postpartum hemorrhage
qs.x: Magnesium is the drug of choice for preventing and treating eclamptic seizures. Separate antihypertensives are used for blood pressure.

qs.q: A patient on a magnesium infusion has a respiratory rate of 8 and absent reflexes. Which medication reverses magnesium toxicity?
qs.a: Calcium gluconate
w: Naloxone
Flumazenil
Sodium bicarbonate
qs.x: Calcium antagonizes magnesium at the neuromuscular junction and heart. Naloxone reverses opioids, not magnesium.

qs.q: Which maternal adverse effects are most important to monitor after terbutaline?
qs.a: Tachycardia, chest pain and arrhythmias
w: Bradycardia and hypotension
Hypoglycemia and sweating
Respiratory depression
qs.x: Terbutaline is a beta agonist, and its boxed warning cites serious maternal heart problems with prolonged tocolysis. It raises, not lowers, glucose.

qs.q: What is the role of tranexamic acid in postpartum hemorrhage?
qs.a: An adjunct to uterotonics that slows clot breakdown
w: A replacement for oxytocin
A drug that contracts the uterus
A reversal agent for anticoagulants
qs.x: TXA reduces fibrinolysis and is given alongside uterotonics, not instead of them. It has no effect on uterine tone.

qs.q: Which condition is a contraindication to methylergonovine?
qs.a: Preeclampsia or chronic hypertension
w: Asthma
Type 2 diabetes
Prior cesarean delivery
qs.x: Methylergonovine causes vasoconstriction and can raise blood pressure sharply. Asthma is the main contraindication for carboprost.

qs.q: Which condition is a contraindication to carboprost?
qs.a: Asthma
w: Chronic hypertension
Type 2 diabetes
Prior cesarean delivery
qs.x: Carboprost is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analog that can cause bronchospasm. Hypertension is the main concern with methylergonovine.

qs.q: Misoprostol belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: Prostaglandin E1 analog
w: Prostaglandin F2-alpha analog
Ergot alkaloid
Synthetic oxytocin
qs.x: Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analog. Carboprost is the F2-alpha analog and methylergonovine is the ergot alkaloid.

qs.q: A patient at 34 weeks gestation has severe-range blood pressure. Which IV agent is first-line?
qs.a: Labetalol
w: Nitroprusside
Enalaprilat
Furosemide
qs.x: Labetalol, hydralazine and nifedipine are first-line for severe hypertension in pregnancy. ACE inhibitors such as enalaprilat are contraindicated because of fetal harm.

qs.q: An infant has a heart rate below 60 with poor perfusion despite effective oxygenation and ventilation. Along with CPR, which medication is given first?
qs.a: Epinephrine
w: Atropine
Adenosine
Amiodarone
qs.x: Pediatric bradycardia is usually caused by hypoxia, and epinephrine is the first drug when it persists despite good ventilation. Atropine is reserved for vagal causes or primary AV block.

qs.q: In which child is atropine preferred over epinephrine for bradycardia?
qs.a: A child whose bradycardia is from increased vagal tone during intubation
w: A child whose bradycardia is from hypoxia
A child in pulseless electrical activity
A child in ventricular fibrillation
qs.x: Atropine treats bradycardia from vagal stimulation or primary AV block. Hypoxic bradycardia is treated with ventilation and epinephrine.

qs.q: Why is glucose checked often in a sick neonate during transport?
qs.a: Neonates have small glycogen stores and become hypoglycemic quickly
w: Neonates cannot metabolize glucose
Dextrose is contraindicated in neonates
Neonates are prone to severe hyperkalemia
qs.x: Newborns, especially when sick or stressed, use up limited glycogen stores fast. Frequent checks catch hypoglycemia before it causes harm.

qs.q: A child with asthma has less wheezing after albuterol but now has poor air movement and is tired. What does this suggest?
qs.a: Worsening obstruction with impending respiratory failure
w: Improvement from the albuterol
Expected albuterol side effect
Anxiety now resolving
qs.x: A quiet chest with poor air movement and fatigue means too little air is moving to wheeze. This is an ominous sign that needs immediate reporting.

qs.q: A child becomes agitated and combative after receiving midazolam. What should be recognized?
qs.a: A paradoxical reaction to the benzodiazepine
w: Expected effect of correct sedation
A sign of opioid withdrawal
An allergic reaction to midazolam
qs.x: Benzodiazepines can cause paradoxical agitation, especially in children. It is not an allergy and should be reported.

qs.q: Why is naloxone avoided in a newborn whose mother uses opioids long term?
qs.a: It can precipitate acute withdrawal, including seizures
w: It causes severe neonatal hypoglycemia
It is ineffective in newborns
It worsens respiratory depression
qs.x: Infants exposed to opioids in the womb can have abrupt, severe withdrawal and seizures after naloxone. Ventilatory support is the priority.

qs.q: An infant has a regular, narrow-complex heart rate too fast to count with no visible P waves. Why is adenosine given?
qs.a: To briefly block the AV node and end the SVT
w: To slow sinus tachycardia from fever
To convert ventricular fibrillation
To increase cardiac contractility
qs.x: These findings suggest SVT, and adenosine briefly blocks AV conduction to break the reentry circuit. Sinus tachycardia is treated by addressing the cause.

qs.q: What is the benefit of ondansetron for a child with vomiting from gastroenteritis?
qs.a: It reduces vomiting so oral rehydration is more likely to succeed
w: It cures the viral infection
It replaces lost electrolytes
It stops diarrhea completely
qs.x: Ondansetron decreases vomiting and the need for IV fluids or admission. It does not treat the infection or diarrhea.

qs.q: Which antipyretic is appropriate for an infant younger than 6 months?
qs.a: Acetaminophen
w: Ibuprofen
Aspirin
Naproxen
qs.x: Acetaminophen can be used in young infants, while ibuprofen is generally not used under 6 months. Aspirin is avoided in children because of Reye syndrome.

qs.q: In which child should ibuprofen be used with caution?
qs.a: A child who is significantly dehydrated with poor urine output
w: A child with a mild ear infection
A child with a sprained ankle
A child with a sore throat
qs.x: NSAIDs reduce kidney blood flow and can cause kidney injury in dehydrated children. The other children are typical candidates.

qs.q: A patient on a prolonged high-rate propofol infusion develops metabolic acidosis, rising CK, hyperkalemia and new arrhythmias. What should be suspected?
qs.a: Propofol infusion syndrome
w: Malignant hyperthermia
Serotonin syndrome
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
qs.x: Propofol infusion syndrome causes acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia and cardiac failure and can be fatal. Report these findings immediately.

qs.q: Because propofol comes in a lipid emulsion, which lab is monitored during prolonged infusion?
qs.a: Triglyceride level
w: Serum ammonia
Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Serum lithium
qs.x: Propofol's lipid vehicle can raise triglycerides and lead to pancreatitis. The emulsion also supports bacterial growth, so strict aseptic handling is required.

qs.q: Which adverse effects are most common with a dexmedetomidine infusion?
qs.a: Bradycardia and hypotension
w: Apnea and respiratory arrest
Hyperkalemia and peaked T waves
Seizures and myoclonus
qs.x: Alpha-2 stimulation lowers sympathetic tone, causing bradycardia and hypotension. Respiratory drive is relatively preserved.

qs.q: Why is esmolol useful for rate control in an unstable transport patient?
qs.a: Its very short duration allows rapid offset if hypotension develops
w: Its long duration means fewer adjustments
It increases contractility while slowing rate
It has no effect on blood pressure
qs.x: Esmolol is broken down quickly by red cell esterases, so its effects fade within minutes when the rate is changed. It does reduce contractility and can lower blood pressure.

qs.q: How does milrinone increase contractility and cause vasodilation?
qs.a: Inhibits phosphodiesterase-3, raising cAMP
w: Stimulates beta-1 receptors
Stimulates alpha-1 receptors
Inhibits the sodium-potassium pump
qs.x: Milrinone blocks the breakdown of cAMP in heart and vascular muscle, making it an inodilator. Sodium-potassium pump inhibition describes digoxin.

qs.q: Why is a nitroprusside infusion protected from light?
qs.a: It breaks down when exposed to light
w: Light makes it more potent
Light turns it into an opioid
Light causes it to crystallize
qs.x: Nitroprusside is light sensitive, so the bag is wrapped in an opaque cover. Degraded solution may be discolored.

qs.q: During interfacility transport on norepinephrine, what is the best way to monitor its effect?
qs.a: Continuous arterial line MAP with perfusion assessment
w: Urine output alone
Pulse oximetry alone
Hourly cuff blood pressure
qs.x: An arterial line gives beat-to-beat pressure for titration, and perfusion signs show whether organs are benefiting. Cuff readings every hour are too infrequent for a titrated vasopressor.

qs.q: Which agent reverses unfractionated heparin in major bleeding?
qs.a: Protamine sulfate
w: Vitamin K
Idarucizumab
Andexanet alfa
qs.x: Protamine binds and neutralizes heparin. Vitamin K reverses warfarin and idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.

qs.q: When nicardipine is given through a peripheral IV, which complication should be monitored at the site?
qs.a: Phlebitis at the infusion site
w: Hyperkalemia
Bronchospasm
Bleeding at the site
qs.x: Peripheral nicardipine infusions often irritate veins, and the labeling advises rotating peripheral sites regularly. It does not affect potassium or clotting.

qs.q: Which adverse effect should be monitored during a vasopressin infusion?
qs.a: Ischemia of the fingers, gut or heart
w: Hypokalemia
Bronchospasm
Severe hyperglycemia
qs.x: Vasopressin's strong vasoconstriction can reduce blood flow to the digits, bowel and heart. Check distal perfusion and report changes.

qs.q: A stable patient in narrow-complex SVT is to receive IV adenosine during transport. How should it be given?
qs.a: Rapid IV push through a proximal site, followed immediately by a saline flush
w: Slow IV push over several minutes to limit flushing and chest discomfort
Intramuscular injection into the deltoid, repeated if the rhythm persists
Diluted continuous infusion that is titrated to the patient's heart rate
qs.x: Adenosine has a half-life of only seconds, so it must reach the heart as a rapid bolus chased by a flush. A slow push lets it be metabolized before it can act on the AV node.

qs.q: A patient with SVT takes theophylline daily. What effect should the flight nurse anticipate when adenosine is given?
qs.a: A reduced response, because methylxanthines block adenosine receptors
w: An exaggerated response with prolonged asystole after the first push
Severe hyperkalemia, because both drugs shift potassium out of cells
No change in response, because the two drugs share no common pathway
qs.x: Theophylline and caffeine are adenosine receptor antagonists, so adenosine may be less effective. Prolonged asystole is a concern with dipyridamole or carbamazepine and in heart transplant patients, not with methylxanthines.

qs.q: During an IV amiodarone infusion after conversion of ventricular tachycardia, which finding most needs prompt reporting?
qs.a: Hypotension and new bradycardia
w: Mild headache and fatigue
Transient metallic taste
Increased urine output
qs.x: IV amiodarone commonly causes hypotension and can cause bradycardia and AV block, which can compromise perfusion. The other findings are minor or unrelated and do not threaten hemodynamic stability.

qs.q: In suspected acute aortic dissection, why is esmolol commonly started before a vasodilator such as nitroprusside?
qs.a: It lowers heart rate and shear force, preventing reflex tachycardia from vasodilation
w: It directly dilates the aorta to reduce wall tension at the site of the tear
It increases myocardial contractility to keep distal organs well perfused
It reverses any anticoagulant effect that could worsen bleeding into the wall
qs.x: Beta blockade first reduces heart rate and the force of ejection (dP/dt), which limits propagation of the tear; a vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia. Esmolol is titratable and short acting, but it does not dilate the aorta itself.

qs.q: Which patient with a rapid irregular tachycardia should NOT receive IV diltiazem?
qs.a: A patient with a wide, irregular rhythm and known Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
w: A patient with a long history of well-controlled essential hypertension
A patient with chronic stable COPD who uses an albuterol inhaler
A patient who takes a daily statin for high cholesterol levels
qs.x: AV nodal blockers such as diltiazem can speed conduction down an accessory pathway in pre-excited atrial fibrillation and trigger ventricular fibrillation. Hypertension, COPD and statin use are not contraindications to diltiazem.

qs.q: Before starting a clevidipine infusion for severe hypertension, which allergy history is most important to ask about?
qs.a: Allergy to soybeans or egg products
w: Allergy to shellfish or iodine contrast
Allergy to sulfonamide antibiotics
Allergy to latex gloves or tubing
qs.x: Clevidipine is formulated in a lipid emulsion containing soybean oil and egg yolk phospholipids, so these allergies are contraindications. Shellfish and iodine allergies are a common but unrelated distractor.

qs.q: A patient with inferior STEMI has ST elevation in V4R and borderline blood pressure. Why is nitroglycerin a particular concern?
qs.a: Right ventricular infarction is preload dependent, so venodilation can cause profound hypotension
w: Right ventricular infarction causes severe bronchospasm when nitrates are given
Nitroglycerin is ineffective in inferior infarction because the vessel is too small
Nitroglycerin raises heart rate so much that it extends the right-sided infarct
qs.x: The infarcted right ventricle depends on venous return to fill, and nitrates reduce preload, which can drop blood pressure sharply. Nitrates do not cause bronchospasm, and the main issue is preload, not reflex tachycardia.

qs.q: During a procainamide infusion for stable monomorphic VT, which finding should be reported to the provider right away?
qs.a: QRS widening by half or more from baseline
w: Narrowing of the QRS toward a normal width
A shorter PR interval than on arrival
Return of upright P waves before each QRS
qs.x: Procainamide slows conduction, and marked QRS widening, hypotension or QT prolongation signal toxicity and are standard endpoints to report. A narrowing QRS or visible P waves suggest the rhythm is converting, not that the drug is toxic.

qs.q: After digoxin immune fab is given, the total serum digoxin level rises sharply. How should the nurse interpret this?
qs.a: It is expected, because most measured digoxin is now bound to the fab and inactive
w: It shows worsening toxicity, so a repeat dose of the antidote is clearly required
It reflects a lab error from hemolysis, so the sample should simply be redrawn
It means the fab caused acute kidney injury that is blocking digoxin clearance
qs.x: Standard assays measure both free and fab-bound digoxin, so total levels rise after treatment and no longer reflect toxicity. Clinical response and potassium, not the total level, guide further care.

qs.q: A patient on a prolonged nitroprusside infusion develops rising lactate and worsening metabolic acidosis. Which problem should the nurse suspect?
qs.a: Cyanide toxicity
w: Thiamine deficiency
Serotonin syndrome
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
qs.x: Nitroprusside releases cyanide as it is metabolized, and cyanide blocks cellular oxygen use, causing lactic acidosis. Thiocyanate toxicity, more common in renal failure, presents mainly with neurologic signs rather than acidosis.

qs.q: After adequate fluid resuscitation, which vasopressor do Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines recommend first for septic shock?
qs.a: Norepinephrine
w: Dopamine
Phenylephrine
Dobutamine
qs.x: Norepinephrine is recommended as the first-line vasopressor in septic shock. Dopamine causes more arrhythmias and is no longer preferred.

qs.q: A peripheral IV running norepinephrine has infiltrated, and the surrounding skin is pale and cool. Which agent is used to infiltrate the area?
qs.a: Phentolamine
w: Hyaluronidase
Atropine
Naloxone
qs.x: Phentolamine is an alpha blocker that reverses the local vasoconstriction caused by norepinephrine extravasation. Hyaluronidase is used for some non-vasopressor extravasations but does not counter alpha-mediated ischemia.

qs.q: Vasopressin is added to norepinephrine for a patient in septic shock. How does vasopressin raise blood pressure?
qs.a: It stimulates V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
w: It stimulates alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in vessels
It inhibits phosphodiesterase-3 in vascular tissue
It stimulates beta-1 receptors to raise cardiac output
qs.x: Vasopressin causes vasoconstriction through V1 receptors, independent of adrenergic receptors, which is why it helps when catecholamine response is blunted. Alpha-1 stimulation is how norepinephrine and phenylephrine work.

qs.q: Which adverse effect should the transport nurse watch for in a patient receiving a vasopressin infusion for shock?
qs.a: Digital and mesenteric ischemia
w: Bronchospasm and wheezing
Severe hyperglycemia
Serotonin syndrome
qs.x: Strong V1-mediated vasoconstriction can reduce blood flow to the fingers, skin and gut. Vasopressin does not cause bronchospasm or serotonin toxicity.

qs.q: A patient on an epinephrine infusion has rising lactate and glucose, yet skin perfusion and urine output are improving. What is the best interpretation?
qs.a: Beta-2 stimulation can raise lactate and glucose even without worsening tissue hypoperfusion
w: The rising lactate proves shock is worsening and more fluid is the only correct response
The rising glucose indicates new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis triggered by the infusion
The lab values reflect contamination from drawing blood above the infusion site only
qs.x: Epinephrine increases aerobic glycolysis and glycogenolysis through beta-2 receptors, so lactate and glucose can rise even when perfusion is better. Lactate must be interpreted with other perfusion markers, not alone.

qs.q: A patient in cardiogenic shock is started on dobutamine, and the blood pressure falls. What is the most likely reason?
qs.a: Beta-2 mediated vasodilation lowers systemic vascular resistance
w: Alpha-1 stimulation causes intense constriction of coronary vessels
Dobutamine directly depresses contractility of the left ventricle
Dobutamine blocks vasopressin receptors and causes fluid loss
qs.x: Dobutamine is mainly a beta-1 inotrope but also has beta-2 vasodilating effects, which can lower blood pressure, so a vasopressor may be needed. It increases, not decreases, contractility.

qs.q: Why might milrinone be preferred over dobutamine for a low-output patient who takes a beta blocker long term?
qs.a: It increases contractility through PDE-3 inhibition, bypassing beta receptors
w: It is a pure vasoconstrictor that does not depend on any receptor at all
It is a beta-1 agonist that competes better against the beta blocker
It slows heart rate further and improves filling time in the ventricle
qs.x: Milrinone raises intracellular cAMP by blocking its breakdown, so its effect does not depend on beta receptors that are occupied by a beta blocker. It is an inodilator, not a vasoconstrictor.

qs.q: Which lab value is most important to review when a patient is receiving milrinone during a long transport?
qs.a: Renal function, because milrinone is cleared by the kidneys and can accumulate
w: Liver enzymes, because milrinone is cleared almost entirely by the liver
Platelet count, because milrinone commonly causes immune thrombocytopenia
Serum amylase, because milrinone is a frequent cause of acute pancreatitis
qs.x: Milrinone is eliminated mainly by the kidneys, so renal impairment leads to accumulation, hypotension and arrhythmias. It is not primarily hepatically cleared.

qs.q: When a phenylephrine infusion raises a patient's blood pressure, which heart rate change is expected?
qs.a: Reflex bradycardia
w: Reflex tachycardia
Sudden heart block
No change in rate
qs.x: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist with no beta activity, so the rise in pressure triggers a baroreceptor reflex that slows the heart. Reflex tachycardia is typical of vasodilators, not vasoconstrictors.

qs.q: Compared with norepinephrine in patients with shock, dopamine is associated with which outcome?
qs.a: More tachyarrhythmias
w: Fewer tachyarrhythmias
Better kidney protection
Lower blood glucose levels
qs.x: Trials comparing the two agents found more arrhythmias with dopamine. So-called renal-dose dopamine does not protect the kidneys, which is a common misconception.

qs.q: A patient on IV heparin for several days has a platelet count that has dropped by more than half and a new arm vein thrombosis. What should the nurse recognize?
qs.a: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with high risk of new clotting
w: Expected dilutional thrombocytopenia from IV fluids
Heparin resistance caused by low antithrombin levels
Normal response showing heparin is working as intended
qs.x: HIT is an immune reaction that typically appears 5 to 10 days into therapy with a large platelet drop and paradoxical thrombosis. It requires notifying the provider for a non-heparin anticoagulant; it is not a sign of effective therapy.

qs.q: Which patient history increases the risk of a serious reaction when protamine is given to reverse heparin?
qs.a: Previous use of NPH or other protamine-containing insulin
w: Previous use of regular insulin by IV infusion
Previous allergic reaction to penicillin antibiotics
Previous hypersensitivity to iodine contrast media
qs.x: Prior exposure to protamine in NPH insulin, fish allergy, vasectomy and prior protamine use raise the risk of hypotension, anaphylaxis and pulmonary hypertension. Regular insulin contains no protamine.

qs.q: When 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate is given to reverse warfarin in an intracranial bleed, why is IV vitamin K also given?
qs.a: PCC's effect is temporary, while vitamin K restores the liver's own production of clotting factors
w: Vitamin K is needed to activate the factors in PCC before they can begin to work
Vitamin K prevents the allergic reactions that commonly occur during PCC infusion
Vitamin K blocks the clotting risk of PCC so that thrombosis cannot occur at all
qs.x: Replaced factors are consumed and cleared over hours, but warfarin's effect persists, so vitamin K is needed for sustained reversal. PCC factors do not require vitamin K to function once infused.

qs.q: How does idarucizumab reverse the anticoagulant effect of dabigatran?
qs.a: It is an antibody fragment that binds dabigatran and neutralizes it
w: It replaces vitamin K-dependent clotting factors in the bloodstream
It binds heparin and low-molecular-weight heparin through charge
It blocks plasminogen activation to slow breakdown of formed clots
qs.x: Idarucizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with high affinity. It has no effect on factor Xa inhibitors or heparin, which protamine partly reverses.

qs.q: Why is early timing emphasized when tranexamic acid is given to a bleeding trauma patient?
qs.a: Its benefit is greatest when given soon after injury, and late doses lose that benefit
w: It must be given late so it does not interfere with early platelet plug formation
It only works after a full massive transfusion protocol has been completed
It has no timing effect, and any dose at any point gives the same benefit
qs.x: Trauma trials showed reduced bleeding death when tranexamic acid was started early, ideally within 3 hours of injury, with no benefit or possible harm afterward. It is an antifibrinolytic that protects clots already forming.

qs.q: Why is tenecteplase practical for fibrinolysis in a STEMI patient when transport time to a PCI center is long?
qs.a: It is given as a single weight-based IV bolus
w: It is given orally and absorbed within minutes
It is given as a long infusion over a full day
It is given subcutaneously in several doses
qs.x: Tenecteplase is a fibrin-specific lytic administered as one IV bolus, which simplifies use in the field. Alteplase, by contrast, requires a bolus plus infusion.

qs.q: Which clotting factors are reduced by warfarin?
qs.a: Factors II, VII, IX and X
w: Factors V, VIII, XI and XII
Factors I, V, VIII and XIII
Factors III, IV, X and XII
qs.x: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, lowering production of the vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S). Factors V and VIII are not vitamin K dependent.

qs.q: Which statement about reversing enoxaparin in a bleeding patient is accurate?
qs.a: Protamine only partially neutralizes its anti-Xa activity
w: Protamine completely reverses all of its anticoagulant effect
Vitamin K is the preferred antidote for this anticoagulant
Idarucizumab is the specific reversal agent for this drug
qs.x: Protamine fully reverses unfractionated heparin's anti-IIa effect but neutralizes only part of enoxaparin's anti-Xa activity. Vitamin K reverses warfarin, and idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.

qs.q: Desmopressin is given to a uremic patient with bleeding. Which effect explains its benefit, and which electrolyte should be monitored?
qs.a: It releases von Willebrand factor and factor VIII; monitor sodium for hyponatremia
w: It activates platelets directly in bone marrow; monitor potassium for hyperkalemia
It replaces fibrinogen in the plasma; monitor calcium for transfusion hypocalcemia
It inhibits fibrinolysis in the clot; monitor magnesium for hypermagnesemia
qs.x: Desmopressin releases von Willebrand factor and factor VIII from endothelial stores, improving platelet adhesion. Its antidiuretic effect causes water retention and hyponatremia, so sodium must be watched.

qs.q: During a tirofiban infusion for acute coronary syndrome, which lab change should be reported promptly?
qs.a: A sudden drop in platelet count
w: A small rise in hemoglobin level
A mild fall in serum glucose
A slight increase in sodium level
qs.x: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors can cause acute, profound thrombocytopenia, which sharply raises bleeding risk. The other changes are not typical effects of tirofiban.

qs.q: For which patient is succinylcholine contraindicated during rapid sequence intubation?
qs.a: A patient with a spinal cord injury and paralysis that occurred one week ago
w: A patient with a large burn injury that occurred within the past hour
A patient with an isolated closed femur fracture from a fall today
A patient with a suspected opioid overdose and poor respiratory effort
qs.x: After denervation, major burns or crush injury, extra junctional receptors develop over days, and succinylcholine can cause life-threatening hyperkalemia. In the first hours after a burn, this receptor upregulation has not yet occurred.

qs.q: Shortly after succinylcholine is given, which finding is an early sign of malignant hyperthermia?
qs.a: An unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2 with tachycardia
w: A sudden fall in end-tidal CO2 with bradycardia
Brief fasciculations followed by flaccid paralysis
Mild hypotension that responds to a fluid bolus
qs.x: Rising end-tidal CO2, tachycardia and muscle rigidity (including masseter spasm) are early signs; high temperature often comes later. Fasciculations followed by paralysis are the normal expected effect of succinylcholine.

qs.q: For an RSI patient with known hyperkalemia, what is the main advantage of rocuronium over succinylcholine?
qs.a: It does not raise serum potassium
w: It has a much shorter duration
It provides deep sedation as well
It lowers intracranial pressure
qs.x: Rocuronium is a nondepolarizing agent and does not cause the potassium release seen with succinylcholine. It lasts longer than succinylcholine and has no sedative effect.

qs.q: A woman of childbearing age received sugammadex to reverse rocuronium. What teaching point is important?
qs.a: Use a backup nonhormonal birth control method for a period, as hormonal contraception may be less effective
w: Expect permanent loss of effect from any hormonal contraceptive and plan surgical sterilization
Double the next birth control pill dose, since sugammadex speeds hormone metabolism in the liver
No contraceptive precautions are needed, because sugammadex binds only neuromuscular blockers
qs.x: Sugammadex can bind progestogen, reducing hormonal contraceptive effect, so labeling advises a backup method for 7 days. It does not permanently alter contraception and it does bind steroids besides rocuronium.

qs.q: A septic patient receives etomidate for intubation. Which adverse effect is a known concern with this drug?
qs.a: Transient adrenal suppression from inhibition of cortisol synthesis
w: Severe hypotension from strong histamine release after injection
Marked bronchospasm in patients with reactive airway disease
Prolonged paralysis in patients with pseudocholinesterase deficiency
qs.x: Etomidate inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase and can briefly suppress cortisol production, which is debated in sepsis. It is valued for hemodynamic stability, not for causing hypotension.

qs.q: Why is ketamine often chosen as the induction agent for a patient in status asthmaticus?
qs.a: It has bronchodilating effects and tends to support blood pressure
w: It is a strong anticholinergic that fully reverses bronchospasm
It causes no increase in airway secretions or salivation at all
It is a long-acting paralytic that improves chest wall compliance
qs.x: Ketamine releases catecholamines, which relax bronchial smooth muscle and help maintain blood pressure. It can increase secretions and is not a paralytic.

qs.q: In which patient is propofol for RSI induction most likely to cause a dangerous complication?
qs.a: A hypotensive trauma patient with ongoing hemorrhage
w: A normotensive patient with an isolated seizure
A hypertensive patient with an intracranial bleed
A stable patient with an uncomplicated overdose
qs.x: Propofol causes vasodilation and myocardial depression, which can lead to profound hypotension in hypovolemic patients. In hypertensive patients, a drop in blood pressure is less likely to cause harm.

qs.q: Why might atropine be given to an infant before laryngoscopy for intubation?
qs.a: To prevent bradycardia caused by vagal stimulation
w: To provide sedation and amnesia for the procedure
To relax skeletal muscle and improve the view
To raise blood glucose before a period of apnea
qs.x: Infants are especially prone to vagally mediated bradycardia during laryngoscopy, and atropine blocks this muscarinic response. It is not a sedative or a muscle relaxant.

qs.q: Why is cisatracurium often selected for ongoing paralysis in a patient with both kidney and liver failure?
qs.a: It is broken down by Hofmann elimination in plasma, independent of organ function
w: It is filtered unchanged by the kidneys at a rate that does not change in failure
It is cleared by the liver through a pathway that is preserved in liver failure
It is reversed instantly by sugammadex if any accumulation begins to occur
qs.x: Cisatracurium degrades spontaneously at normal pH and temperature (Hofmann elimination), so it does not accumulate in organ failure. Sugammadex reverses aminosteroids such as rocuronium, not benzylisoquinolines like cisatracurium.

qs.q: After a rapid IV push of fentanyl, a patient becomes very difficult to ventilate with a bag-valve mask, and the chest feels stiff. What should the nurse recognize?
qs.a: Opioid-induced chest wall rigidity
w: Acute tension pneumothorax
Severe anaphylactic bronchospasm
Malignant hyperthermia onset
qs.x: Rapid, large doses of potent opioids such as fentanyl can cause skeletal muscle rigidity of the chest wall and glottis. It is treated with a neuromuscular blocker or naloxone, whereas malignant hyperthermia is triggered by succinylcholine and volatile agents.

qs.q: A patient with severe asthma is on continuous nebulized albuterol. Which lab value should be monitored for a drug-related change?
qs.a: Serum potassium, because albuterol shifts potassium into cells
w: Serum sodium, because albuterol causes water retention
Serum calcium, because albuterol binds calcium in plasma
Platelet count, because albuterol suppresses bone marrow
qs.x: Beta-2 agonists drive potassium into cells and can cause hypokalemia, along with tachycardia and hyperglycemia. Albuterol does not meaningfully affect sodium, calcium or platelets.

qs.q: How does ipratropium produce bronchodilation when added to albuterol for an acute exacerbation?
qs.a: It blocks muscarinic receptors, reducing vagal bronchoconstriction
w: It stimulates beta-2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle cells
It inhibits leukotriene receptors that drive airway inflammation
It stabilizes mast cells so they cannot release their histamine
qs.x: Ipratropium is an inhaled anticholinergic that blocks acetylcholine-mediated bronchoconstriction, which complements the beta-2 agonist effect of albuterol. It is not a beta agonist or leukotriene blocker.

qs.q: IV magnesium sulfate is given for a severe asthma exacerbation. Which findings should the nurse monitor for?
qs.a: Hypotension and diminished deep tendon reflexes
w: Hypertension and brisk deep tendon reflexes
Hyperglycemia and a new tremor of the hands
Tachycardia and severe agitation or anxiety
qs.x: Magnesium relaxes smooth muscle and can cause flushing and hypotension; high levels depress reflexes and breathing. Brisk reflexes and tremor are not signs of magnesium excess.

qs.q: A patient with severe asthma is too dyspneic to use nebulized therapy effectively. By which route can terbutaline be given in this situation?
qs.a: Subcutaneous injection
w: Intrathecal injection
Transdermal patch
Rectal suppository
qs.x: Terbutaline is a beta-2 agonist that can be given subcutaneously when inhaled delivery is inadequate. It is not given by the other routes listed.

qs.q: After nebulized racemic epinephrine improves stridor in a child with croup, why is a period of observation needed?
qs.a: Symptoms can return as the drug's effect wears off
w: The drug often causes delayed severe hypoglycemia
It routinely triggers seizures within a few hours
It suppresses the child's ability to swallow fluids
qs.x: Racemic epinephrine reduces airway edema through vasoconstriction, but its effect lasts only a few hours, so stridor may recur. Corticosteroids are given to provide longer-lasting relief.

qs.q: Why is dexamethasone given to a child with moderate croup who has also received nebulized epinephrine?
qs.a: It reduces airway inflammation and provides longer-lasting relief
w: It works within seconds to open the airway before epinephrine
It is a bronchodilator that relaxes the smooth muscle in bronchi
It treats the viral cause and shortens the infection itself
qs.x: Dexamethasone decreases subglottic inflammation over hours and reduces return visits and need for further care. It does not act within seconds and has no antiviral effect.

qs.q: Why must a backup delivery system be ready when transporting a patient on inhaled nitric oxide?
qs.a: Sudden interruption can cause rebound pulmonary hypertension and hypoxemia
w: Sudden interruption causes immediate severe systemic hypertension
Interruption causes nitric oxide to convert into carbon monoxide gas
Interruption triggers dangerous methemoglobin levels within seconds
qs.x: Abrupt loss of inhaled nitric oxide can lead to rebound pulmonary vasoconstriction, worsening oxygenation and hemodynamic collapse. Methemoglobinemia is a risk of ongoing exposure, not of interruption.

qs.q: After a preterm infant receives intratracheal surfactant, what change should the transport team anticipate?
qs.a: Rapid improvement in lung compliance that may require ventilator adjustments
w: Rapid worsening of lung compliance that requires higher ventilator pressures
Gradual improvement that takes several weeks before any change is visible
No change in compliance, since surfactant acts only on the pulmonary vessels
qs.x: Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension and can improve compliance and oxygenation quickly, so pressures and oxygen may need to be reduced to avoid overdistension and pneumothorax. Its effect is on the alveoli, not the vessels.

qs.q: A patient with pulmonary arterial hypertension arrives on a home continuous IV epoprostenol infusion. Which line management principle is correct?
qs.a: Keep it on a dedicated line and never flush or bolus that line
w: Flush the line with saline each hour to keep the catheter patent
Piggyback other IV medications into the line to save IV access
Draw routine blood samples from the line to avoid extra needle sticks
qs.x: Epoprostenol has a half-life of minutes, so interruption can cause rebound pulmonary hypertension, and flushing delivers an unintended bolus that can cause severe hypotension. A dedicated line protects delivery.

qs.q: IV methylprednisolone is given for a severe COPD exacerbation. Which adverse effect should the nurse monitor for during care?
qs.a: Hyperglycemia
w: Hypoglycemia
Bradycardia
Hyperkalemia
qs.x: Systemic corticosteroids increase gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance, often raising blood glucose. They tend to lower, not raise, potassium.

qs.q: An adult with IV access has been seizing continuously for 5 minutes. Which medication is a first-line choice?
qs.a: IV lorazepam
w: IV levetiracetam
IV phenobarbital
IV lacosamide
qs.x: Benzodiazepines are the first-line treatment for status epilepticus, and IV lorazepam is preferred when access is available. Levetiracetam and other agents are second-line after benzodiazepines.

qs.q: A patient is actively seizing and IV access cannot be obtained. Which option is an effective first-line treatment?
qs.a: Intramuscular midazolam
w: Oral levetiracetam
Intramuscular phenytoin
Oral valproic acid
qs.x: IM midazolam is rapidly absorbed and was at least as effective as IV lorazepam in prehospital status epilepticus. Oral agents are unsafe during a seizure, and phenytoin is not given IM.

qs.q: During an IV fosphenytoin infusion for status epilepticus, which monitoring is required?
qs.a: Continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring for hypotension and dysrhythmias
w: Hourly serum glucose checks for severe hypoglycemia from the infusion
Peak flow measurements for bronchospasm caused by the drug vehicle
Serial urine output measurements for acute crystal nephropathy
qs.x: Rapid infusion of fosphenytoin can cause hypotension and serious arrhythmias, so labeling requires cardiac and blood pressure monitoring. Hypoglycemia and bronchospasm are not typical effects.

qs.q: Why is levetiracetam often chosen as a second-line agent for status epilepticus in critically ill patients?
qs.a: It has few drug interactions and little effect on blood pressure or heart rhythm
w: It is the only agent that can be given safely as an intramuscular injection
It strongly induces liver enzymes, which helps clear other sedating drugs
It is a benzodiazepine with a longer duration than lorazepam or midazolam
qs.x: Levetiracetam is not metabolized by liver enzymes and is generally hemodynamically well tolerated. It is not a benzodiazepine, and enzyme induction is a drawback of drugs like phenytoin.

qs.q: Before giving IV mannitol for raised intracranial pressure, the nurse inspects the solution and uses an in-line filter. Why?
qs.a: Mannitol can crystallize, and the filter keeps crystals from being infused
w: Mannitol is light sensitive, and the filter blocks breakdown products
Mannitol foams when shaken, and the filter removes trapped air bubbles
Mannitol binds to IV tubing, and the filter improves drug delivery
qs.x: Concentrated mannitol can form crystals, especially at low temperatures, so solutions are inspected and filtered. Light sensitivity is a feature of drugs like nitroprusside, not mannitol.

qs.q: A hypotensive patient with traumatic brain injury shows signs of herniation. Why might hypertonic saline be chosen over mannitol?
qs.a: It lowers intracranial pressure without causing an osmotic diuresis
w: It lowers intracranial pressure by causing a strong osmotic diuresis
It lowers intracranial pressure by sedating the injured brain tissue
It lowers intracranial pressure by directly constricting cerebral veins
qs.x: Hypertonic saline draws water from brain tissue while expanding intravascular volume, which supports blood pressure. Mannitol's diuresis can worsen hypovolemia and hypotension, which worsens outcomes in brain injury.

qs.q: A patient with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage is ordered nimodipine. By which route must it be given?
qs.a: Orally or through a nasogastric tube
w: Intravenous push through a central line
Intravenous infusion through a peripheral line
Intramuscular injection into a large muscle
qs.x: Nimodipine has a boxed warning against IV administration; capsule contents given IV have caused cardiac arrest and death. If the patient cannot swallow, the contents are given by enteral tube using an oral syringe.

qs.q: During or after alteplase for acute ischemic stroke, which finding most strongly suggests intracranial hemorrhage?
qs.a: Sudden severe headache, worsening neurologic exam and vomiting
w: Mild oozing at the IV site that stops with gentle pressure
A small area of bruising on the arm from the BP cuff
Mild improvement in arm strength with residual facial droop
qs.x: New headache, nausea and vomiting, acute hypertension or neurologic decline after lysis must be treated as a possible hemorrhage and reported immediately. Minor IV site oozing is common and usually managed locally.

qs.q: A patient with intracerebral hemorrhage is started on a nicardipine infusion for blood pressure control. Which side effects are common?
qs.a: Reflex tachycardia and headache
w: Marked bradycardia and heart block
Bronchospasm and severe wheezing
Hyperkalemia and peaked T waves
qs.x: Nicardipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that dilates arterioles, which commonly causes reflex tachycardia, flushing and headache. Bradycardia and AV block are more typical of nondihydropyridines such as diltiazem.

qs.q: A patient on valproic acid becomes increasingly confused, though liver enzymes are normal. Which lab abnormality should the nurse suspect?
qs.a: Elevated serum ammonia
w: Low serum ammonia
Elevated serum calcium
Low serum magnesium
qs.x: Valproate can cause hyperammonemic encephalopathy even when liver function tests are normal. Checking ammonia helps identify this cause of altered mental status.

qs.q: Why is fentanyl often preferred over morphine for analgesia in a hemodynamically unstable patient?
qs.a: It causes little histamine release and less hypotension
w: It has a much longer duration and needs fewer doses
It has no risk of respiratory depression at any dose
It has strong anti-inflammatory effects on tissue
qs.x: Morphine can release histamine, causing vasodilation and hypotension, while fentanyl has minimal histamine effect. Fentanyl still causes respiratory depression and is shorter acting.

qs.q: A patient with acute kidney injury becomes increasingly sedated after several doses of morphine. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: Active morphine metabolites accumulate when renal function is impaired
w: Morphine is converted into naloxone, which builds up in the kidney
Kidney injury makes the brain resistant to all opioid effects
Morphine causes acute liver failure in patients with kidney injury
qs.x: Morphine's active metabolites, especially morphine-6-glucuronide, are renally cleared and accumulate in kidney failure, causing prolonged sedation and respiratory depression. This is why other opioids are often preferred in renal impairment.

qs.q: A ventilated patient on a prolonged high-rate propofol infusion develops metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia and new arrhythmias. What should the nurse suspect?
qs.a: Propofol infusion syndrome
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
Diabetic ketoacidosis
qs.x: Propofol infusion syndrome is a rare, often fatal complication of high-dose prolonged infusion marked by acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, lipemia and cardiac failure. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows antipsychotic use and features rigidity and fever.

qs.q: Why does propofol require strict aseptic handling and timely changes of the vial and tubing?
qs.a: Its lipid emulsion supports rapid growth of microorganisms
w: It breaks down into cyanide when exposed to room air
It loses all sedative potency within minutes of opening
It reacts with plastic tubing to form toxic byproducts
qs.x: Propofol is formulated in a lipid emulsion that can support bacterial growth, so labeling requires aseptic technique and limits on hang time. Cyanide release is a feature of nitroprusside.

qs.q: Which property makes dexmedetomidine useful for sedating a patient who is not intubated?
qs.a: It provides sedation with minimal respiratory depression
w: It provides deep general anesthesia and complete amnesia
It provides strong analgesia equal to high-dose opioids
It provides paralysis that prevents patient-ventilator dyssynchrony
qs.x: Dexmedetomidine, a central alpha-2 agonist, produces arousable sedation with little effect on respiratory drive. It does not reliably provide amnesia or deep anesthesia.

qs.q: Which adverse effects should be monitored most closely in a patient receiving a dexmedetomidine infusion?
qs.a: Bradycardia and hypotension
w: Tachycardia and hypertension
Hyperthermia and rigidity
Bronchospasm and wheezing
qs.x: By reducing central sympathetic outflow, dexmedetomidine commonly causes bradycardia and hypotension. A transient rise in blood pressure can occur with a loading dose, but sustained hypertension is not typical.

qs.q: How does ketamine produce analgesia and dissociative sedation?
qs.a: It blocks NMDA receptors in the central nervous system
w: It stimulates mu opioid receptors in the spinal cord
It enhances GABA-A receptor activity in the brain
It stimulates alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem
qs.x: Ketamine is an NMDA receptor antagonist, which explains its analgesic and dissociative effects. Enhancing GABA-A is the mechanism of propofol and benzodiazepines.

qs.q: A patient wakes after IV naloxone for a suspected long-acting opioid overdose. Why is continued monitoring essential?
qs.a: Naloxone may wear off before the opioid, and respiratory depression can return
w: Naloxone causes delayed severe hypoglycemia that appears hours after a dose
Naloxone frequently triggers a delayed allergic reaction after waking
Naloxone permanently blocks opioid receptors, so pain cannot be treated
qs.x: Naloxone's duration is often shorter than that of methadone, extended-release opioids or potent synthetic opioids, so sedation and apnea can recur. Repeat doses or an infusion may be needed.

qs.q: In which patient is flumazenil most likely to cause a dangerous complication?
qs.a: A long-term benzodiazepine user with a mixed overdose that includes a tricyclic antidepressant
w: A healthy adult who is slow to awaken after procedural midazolam for a brief procedure
A child who accidentally swallowed one of a grandparent's benzodiazepine tablets
A patient who received lorazepam before a short procedure and has no other ingestions
qs.x: Flumazenil can precipitate seizures in benzodiazepine-dependent patients and in overdoses involving seizure-provoking drugs such as tricyclics. Its safest use is reversing procedural sedation in patients without dependence.

qs.q: Which patient should NOT receive ketorolac for pain control?
qs.a: A trauma patient with active bleeding and acute kidney injury
w: An adult with renal colic and normal kidney function
An adult with a musculoskeletal back strain and no history
An adult with a migraine and no bleeding or kidney risks
qs.x: Ketorolac is an NSAID that impairs platelet function and reduces renal blood flow, so active bleeding and kidney injury are contraindications. Renal colic with normal kidney function is a common appropriate use.

qs.q: Shortly after IM haloperidol for agitation, a young patient develops sustained neck twisting and upward eye deviation. What should the nurse recognize?
qs.a: An acute dystonic reaction
w: A generalized tonic-clonic seizure
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Tardive dyskinesia
qs.x: Acute dystonia is an early extrapyramidal effect of high-potency antipsychotics and responds to diphenhydramine or benztropine. Tardive dyskinesia develops after long-term use, not within hours.

qs.q: A patient on haloperidol develops high fever, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion and unstable blood pressure. Which condition should be suspected?
qs.a: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
w: Serotonin syndrome
Anticholinergic toxicity
Alcohol withdrawal
qs.x: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows dopamine blockade and features hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental status and autonomic instability, often with high CK. Serotonin syndrome develops faster and typically shows clonus and hyperreflexia.

qs.q: Droperidol is ordered for severe agitation. Which assessment is especially important because of its boxed warning?
qs.a: Cardiac monitoring for QT prolongation and torsades de pointes
w: Serial liver enzymes for drug-induced hepatitis
Blood glucose checks for severe hypoglycemia
Platelet counts for immune thrombocytopenia
qs.x: Droperidol carries a boxed warning for QT prolongation and torsades, so ECG monitoring and attention to other QT-prolonging drugs and electrolytes are needed. Liver injury and hypoglycemia are not its main concerns.

qs.q: Which combination raises particular concern for cardiorespiratory depression in an agitated patient?
qs.a: IM olanzapine given close in time to a parenteral benzodiazepine
w: IM olanzapine given along with an oral acetaminophen dose
IM olanzapine given after a dose of ondansetron for nausea
IM olanzapine given with a normal saline fluid bolus
qs.x: Labeling warns against using IM olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepines because of reports of hypotension, bradycardia and respiratory depression. Acetaminophen and saline do not share this risk.

qs.q: When ketamine is used to sedate a patient with severe agitation, which airway complication must the team be prepared to manage?
qs.a: Laryngospasm and increased salivation
w: Bronchospasm and wheezing
Complete loss of muscle tone
Angioedema of the tongue
qs.x: Ketamine generally preserves airway reflexes but can cause hypersalivation and, uncommonly, laryngospasm, so suction and airway equipment should be ready. Ketamine is a bronchodilator, so bronchospasm is unlikely.

qs.q: Which factor is most likely to raise lithium levels and lead to toxicity?
qs.a: Dehydration with regular NSAID use
w: Drinking extra fluids during illness
Adding a daily vitamin D supplement
Taking acetaminophen for a headache
qs.x: Lithium is cleared by the kidneys, and dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides reduce its clearance. Acetaminophen does not affect lithium elimination.

qs.q: A patient who overdosed on amitriptyline has a widening QRS and hypotension. Which treatment is indicated?
qs.a: IV sodium bicarbonate
w: IV physostigmine
IV flumazenil
IV procainamide
qs.x: Sodium bicarbonate counteracts tricyclic sodium channel blockade by raising serum sodium and pH. Physostigmine and flumazenil can provoke seizures or arrhythmias, and procainamide worsens sodium channel blockade.

qs.q: What is the major toxicity concern after an overdose of extended-release bupropion?
qs.a: Seizures, which may be delayed
w: Isolated severe hypoglycemia
Massive internal bleeding
Acute pulmonary fibrosis
qs.x: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold, and seizures are common in overdose; with extended-release forms they can appear many hours later. QRS widening and cardiac toxicity can also occur in large ingestions.

qs.q: How does benztropine relieve acute dystonia caused by an antipsychotic?
qs.a: It blocks central muscarinic receptors, restoring dopamine-acetylcholine balance
w: It stimulates dopamine receptors directly, reversing the antipsychotic effect
It enhances GABA activity in the spinal cord, causing muscle relaxation
It blocks serotonin receptors, reducing excess muscle contraction
qs.x: Antipsychotic dopamine blockade leaves relative cholinergic excess in the basal ganglia, and benztropine's anticholinergic action corrects this. It is not a dopamine agonist.

qs.q: Why is lorazepam often preferred over diazepam for alcohol withdrawal in a patient with severe liver disease?
qs.a: It is metabolized by glucuronidation and has no active metabolites
w: It is excreted unchanged in the urine without any metabolism
It is the only benzodiazepine that does not cause sedation
It is a much longer-acting drug that needs fewer doses
qs.x: Lorazepam's metabolism by glucuronidation is relatively preserved in liver disease, so it accumulates less. Diazepam relies on oxidative liver metabolism and has long-acting active metabolites.

qs.q: Which practice is correct when giving IV potassium chloride to a patient with hypokalemia?
qs.a: Give it diluted as an infusion on a pump, never as an IV push
w: Give it as a rapid IV push followed by a large saline flush
Give it as an intramuscular injection into a large muscle
Give it as an undiluted bolus through the central line port
qs.x: IV potassium given by push can cause fatal arrhythmias and cardiac arrest, so it must be diluted and infused by pump with cardiac monitoring. Even through a central line, it is never pushed.

qs.q: A patient with hyperkalemia has peaked T waves and a widening QRS. Why is IV calcium given first?
qs.a: It stabilizes the cardiac cell membrane but does not lower potassium
w: It shifts potassium into the cells and lowers the serum level
It binds potassium in the gut and removes it from the body
It increases potassium excretion by the kidneys within minutes
qs.x: Calcium raises the threshold potential and protects against arrhythmias within minutes, but the potassium level is unchanged. Insulin, beta agonists and bicarbonate shift potassium, and binders or dialysis remove it.

qs.q: IV regular insulin and dextrose are given for hyperkalemia. What is the most important follow-up assessment?
qs.a: Frequent blood glucose checks for several hours
w: Hourly serum calcium levels for a full day
Repeat chest radiograph for pulmonary edema
Repeat liver enzymes for insulin hepatotoxicity
qs.x: Insulin shifts potassium into cells but can cause hypoglycemia, which may be delayed, especially in kidney failure. Dextrose reduces but does not remove this risk.

qs.q: Why should sodium bicarbonate and calcium not be given together in the same IV line without flushing between them?
qs.a: They form a calcium carbonate precipitate in the line
w: They cancel each other's effects on the heart
They produce carbon monoxide gas in the tubing
They cause the IV catheter to dissolve quickly
qs.x: Bicarbonate and calcium salts precipitate as calcium carbonate, which can block the line or cause embolization. Lines must be flushed between them.

qs.q: Chronic severe hyponatremia is being corrected with 3% saline. Which complication can result from overly rapid correction?
qs.a: Osmotic demyelination syndrome
w: Acute cerebral edema
Malignant hyperthermia
Acute adrenal crisis
qs.x: Brain cells adapt to chronic hyponatremia, and raising sodium too fast can damage myelin, especially in the pons, causing quadriparesis and dysphagia. Cerebral edema is a risk of the hyponatremia itself or of correcting hypernatremia too fast.

qs.q: Which electrolyte disturbances should be monitored in a patient receiving repeated IV furosemide?
qs.a: Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia
w: Hyperkalemia and hypermagnesemia
Hypercalcemia and hyperkalemia
Hypernatremia and hyperkalemia
qs.x: Loop diuretics increase urinary loss of potassium, magnesium and calcium. Hyperkalemia is more typical of potassium-sparing diuretics.

qs.q: A trauma patient received large volumes of 0.9% sodium chloride. Which acid-base disturbance is most likely to develop?
qs.a: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis
w: Hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis
Primary respiratory alkalosis
Anion gap metabolic acidosis
qs.x: Normal saline contains more chloride than plasma, and large volumes lower bicarbonate and cause a non-anion gap acidosis. Hypochloremic alkalosis is typical of vomiting or diuretic use.

qs.q: 23.4% sodium chloride is ordered for a patient with refractory intracranial hypertension. How must it be given?
qs.a: Through a central venous line
w: Through a small peripheral IV
By intramuscular injection
By the subcutaneous route
qs.x: Highly concentrated saline is extremely hyperosmolar and can cause severe vein damage and tissue necrosis, so it is given only through a central line. It is also a high-alert medication that must be clearly distinguished from standard saline.

qs.q: How does IV albumin help expand intravascular volume?
qs.a: It increases plasma oncotic pressure and draws fluid into the vessels
w: It increases plasma osmolality by adding sodium to the bloodstream
It constricts blood vessels by stimulating alpha-1 receptors
It stimulates the kidneys to retain free water and concentrate urine
qs.x: Albumin is the main contributor to plasma oncotic pressure, so infusing it pulls fluid from the interstitium into the vascular space. It is not a vasoconstrictor.

qs.q: Which statement about sodium zirconium cyclosilicate in hyperkalemia is accurate?
qs.a: It is an oral binder that removes potassium through the GI tract and acts more slowly than IV shifting agents
w: It is an IV agent that stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes of being given to the patient
It is an IV agent that shifts potassium into cells and is given along with dextrose to the patient
It is an inhaled agent that shifts potassium into cells by stimulating the beta-2 receptors
qs.x: Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate exchanges sodium and hydrogen for potassium in the gut, lowering levels over hours. It is not suitable as the only treatment for life-threatening hyperkalemia, where calcium and shifting agents are given first.

qs.q: In severe hypercalcemia of malignancy, why is calcitonin often given along with a bisphosphonate?
qs.a: It lowers calcium within hours while the bisphosphonate takes days to work
w: It permanently cures hypercalcemia so the bisphosphonate is only a backup
It prevents the kidney damage that bisphosphonates always cause
It is more effective over weeks, while the bisphosphonate acts in minutes
qs.x: Calcitonin acts quickly but loses effect within a couple of days due to tachyphylaxis, bridging the gap until the bisphosphonate takes effect. Bisphosphonates have a slower onset.

qs.q: Before giving zoledronic acid for hypercalcemia of malignancy, which lab value is most important to review?
qs.a: Serum creatinine
w: Serum amylase
Serum ammonia
Serum troponin
qs.x: Zoledronic acid can cause kidney injury, so renal function is checked before each dose and dosing is adjusted. Amylase, ammonia and troponin are not routinely affected.

qs.q: How does pamidronate lower serum calcium in hypercalcemia of malignancy?
qs.a: It inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption
w: It increases calcium excretion in the urine
It binds calcium in the gut and blocks absorption
It increases parathyroid hormone release
qs.x: Bisphosphonates such as pamidronate bind bone and inhibit osteoclasts, reducing calcium release into the blood. Increasing urinary calcium loss is the role of saline hydration.

qs.q: Before rasburicase is given for tumor lysis syndrome, which condition must be ruled out?
qs.a: G6PD deficiency
w: Sulfa allergy
Celiac disease
Iron deficiency
qs.x: Rasburicase produces hydrogen peroxide when breaking down uric acid, which can cause severe hemolysis and methemoglobinemia in G6PD deficiency. Testing is recommended for patients at higher risk.

qs.q: Why must blood samples for uric acid be placed on ice after a patient receives rasburicase?
qs.a: The drug keeps breaking down uric acid in the tube, falsely lowering results
w: The drug makes blood clot rapidly, so cooling keeps the sample liquid
The drug raises uric acid in warm samples, falsely elevating results
The drug causes hemolysis at room temperature, which ruins the sample
qs.x: Rasburicase continues to act in the sample at room temperature, so uric acid levels appear falsely low unless the sample is chilled and analyzed promptly. It does not cause clotting in the tube.

qs.q: How does allopurinol differ from rasburicase in managing tumor lysis syndrome?
qs.a: It prevents new uric acid formation but does not break down existing uric acid
w: It breaks down existing uric acid into a more soluble compound very rapidly
It binds uric acid in the intestine and removes it in the stool over days
It increases urinary uric acid excretion by blocking renal reabsorption
qs.x: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, lowering production, while rasburicase converts existing uric acid into allantoin. Increasing renal excretion is how probenecid works.

qs.q: A patient taking colchicine for gout is started on another drug. Which addition most increases the risk of colchicine toxicity?
qs.a: Clarithromycin
w: Acetaminophen
Amoxicillin
Famotidine
qs.x: Clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, raising colchicine levels and causing potentially fatal toxicity. Acetaminophen, amoxicillin and famotidine do not significantly interact.

qs.q: Which complication is a particular concern after denosumab in a patient with advanced kidney disease?
qs.a: Severe hypocalcemia
w: Severe hypercalcemia
Severe hyperkalemia
Severe hypoglycemia
qs.x: Denosumab strongly inhibits bone resorption, and patients with advanced CKD are at high risk of severe, sometimes fatal hypocalcemia. Calcium and vitamin D status should be checked and monitored.

qs.q: Phenobarbital is given for refractory seizures. Which adverse effects should be monitored most closely?
qs.a: Respiratory depression and hypotension
w: Hypertension and tachycardia
Hyperthermia and muscle rigidity
Hyperglycemia and polyuria
qs.x: Phenobarbital is a barbiturate that causes sedation, respiratory depression and hypotension, especially after benzodiazepines. Airway and hemodynamic support should be ready.

qs.q: A dialysis patient taking cinacalcet reports tingling around the mouth and muscle cramps. What does this most likely indicate?
qs.a: Hypocalcemia
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypernatremia
Hypercalcemia
qs.x: Cinacalcet increases the sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor and lowers PTH and serum calcium. Perioral paresthesias and cramps are classic signs of low calcium and should be reported.

qs.q: After hydroxocobalamin is given to a smoke inhalation patient, the skin and urine turn red. What else should the nurse expect?
qs.a: Interference with some colorimetric lab tests and oximetry readings
w: A sudden drop in blood pressure from vasodilation
Severe hemolysis that requires urgent transfusion
Rapid development of methemoglobinemia
qs.x: Hydroxocobalamin's red color is expected and can interfere with lab assays and co-oximetry. It often raises, rather than lowers, blood pressure.

qs.q: How does fomepizole treat ethylene glycol poisoning?
qs.a: It inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, blocking formation of toxic metabolites
w: It binds ethylene glycol in the gut and prevents its absorption
It speeds kidney elimination of ethylene glycol by alkalinizing urine
It converts ethylene glycol directly into harmless carbon dioxide
qs.x: Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing the conversion of ethylene glycol and methanol into toxic acids. Activated charcoal does not meaningfully bind toxic alcohols.

qs.q: How does N-acetylcysteine protect the liver in acetaminophen overdose?
qs.a: It replenishes glutathione, which detoxifies the toxic acetaminophen metabolite
w: It blocks absorption of acetaminophen from the stomach and small intestine
It binds acetaminophen in the blood and carries it to the kidneys for excretion
It inhibits the liver enzyme that would otherwise clear acetaminophen safely
qs.x: N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione, which neutralizes NAPQI, the toxic metabolite. It works best when started early, ideally within 8 hours of ingestion.

qs.q: In organophosphate poisoning, which clinical endpoint best guides further atropine dosing?
qs.a: Drying of bronchial secretions and easier breathing
w: Return of normal pupil size in both eyes
Heart rate falling to a normal range
Resolution of muscle weakness and twitching
qs.x: Atropine is titrated to clear bronchorrhea and improve oxygenation; tachycardia is not a reason to limit it. Atropine does not reverse nicotinic effects such as weakness, which require pralidoxime.

qs.q: In organophosphate poisoning, what does pralidoxime add to treatment with atropine?
qs.a: It reactivates acetylcholinesterase and improves nicotinic muscle weakness
w: It blocks muscarinic receptors and dries respiratory secretions
It binds the organophosphate in the gut and prevents absorption
It sedates the patient and controls organophosphate seizures
qs.x: Pralidoxime regenerates acetylcholinesterase before the enzyme bond ages, helping reverse weakness and paralysis. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects, and benzodiazepines treat seizures.

qs.q: Methylene blue is ordered for methemoglobinemia. Which medication history raises the most concern?
qs.a: Current use of an SSRI antidepressant
w: Current use of a statin for cholesterol
Current use of a daily proton pump inhibitor
Current use of a thiazide for blood pressure
qs.x: Methylene blue inhibits monoamine oxidase and has a boxed warning for serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs. G6PD deficiency is also an important concern.

qs.q: During a nerve block with bupivacaine, a patient has a seizure and then cardiovascular collapse. Which antidote is indicated?
qs.a: IV lipid emulsion
w: IV flumazenil
IV naloxone
IV fomepizole
qs.x: Lipid emulsion is the specific therapy for local anesthetic systemic toxicity and is given alongside airway support and seizure control. Flumazenil and naloxone do not reverse local anesthetic toxicity.

qs.q: Why is glucagon used for symptomatic beta-blocker overdose?
qs.a: It raises intracellular cAMP through its own receptor, bypassing beta receptors
w: It competitively displaces the beta blocker from beta receptors in the heart
It enhances hepatic metabolism of the beta blocker into inactive products
It blocks calcium channels to reduce the beta blocker's toxic effects
qs.x: Glucagon stimulates its own receptor to increase cAMP, improving heart rate and contractility. Nausea and vomiting are common, so airway protection matters.

qs.q: Before giving physostigmine for suspected anticholinergic toxicity, which ECG finding is a major concern?
qs.a: A wide QRS suggesting tricyclic ingestion
w: A narrow-complex sinus tachycardia
Peaked T waves from mild hyperkalemia
A normal sinus rhythm with no changes
qs.x: Physostigmine can cause bradyasystole and seizures in tricyclic overdose, which commonly shows QRS widening. Sinus tachycardia is an expected finding in anticholinergic toxicity.

qs.q: After antivenom for rattlesnake envenomation, why are follow-up coagulation labs needed after discharge?
qs.a: Venom effects can recur as antivenom is cleared
w: Antivenom itself causes delayed liver failure
Antivenom destroys platelets for several weeks
Antivenom triggers heparin-like anticoagulation
qs.x: Fab fragments clear faster than some venom components, so coagulopathy and low platelets can recur days later. Delayed serum sickness can also occur.

qs.q: During a rapid vancomycin infusion, the patient develops flushing and itching of the face, neck and upper chest. What should the nurse recognize?
qs.a: An infusion-related reaction linked to rapid infusion
w: A true IgE-mediated penicillin cross allergy
Early signs of Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Red man rash caused by acute kidney injury
qs.x: Vancomycin infusion reaction (formerly red man syndrome) is caused by histamine release with rapid infusion and is typically managed by slowing the rate and giving an antihistamine. It is not an IgE allergy or a sign of kidney injury.

qs.q: Which monitoring is most important during prolonged IV vancomycin therapy for sepsis?
qs.a: Serum creatinine and drug levels for nephrotoxicity
w: Serum glucose for drug-induced hypoglycemia
Serum amylase for drug-induced pancreatitis
Pulmonary function tests for lung fibrosis
qs.x: Vancomycin can cause kidney injury, especially at high exposures or with other nephrotoxins such as piperacillin-tazobactam, so creatinine and levels guide dosing. Pancreatitis and lung fibrosis are not typical effects.

qs.q: A patient with acute kidney injury on cefepime becomes confused, with myoclonus. What should the nurse suspect?
qs.a: Cefepime-induced neurotoxicity
w: Expected sepsis-related delirium only
Vancomycin infusion reaction
Hypoglycemia from the antibiotic
qs.x: Cefepime can accumulate in renal impairment and cause encephalopathy, myoclonus and nonconvulsive seizures. Recognizing it matters because it can be mistaken for septic delirium.

qs.q: Why is IV ceftriaxone used with special caution in neonates?
qs.a: It can precipitate with IV calcium and displace bilirubin
w: It causes severe hyperkalemia in newborn kidneys
It is inactivated by breast milk in the infant's gut
It produces gray baby syndrome in premature infants
qs.x: Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in hyperbilirubinemic neonates and in neonates receiving IV calcium because of fatal precipitates. Gray baby syndrome is caused by chloramphenicol.

qs.q: A patient with a seizure disorder controlled on valproic acid is started on meropenem. What interaction should the nurse anticipate?
qs.a: Valproate levels drop sharply, raising seizure risk
w: Valproate levels rise sharply, causing toxicity
Meropenem levels rise, causing kidney damage
No interaction is expected between the two drugs
qs.x: Carbapenems rapidly and markedly lower valproic acid levels, which can lead to breakthrough seizures, and increasing the valproate dose does not overcome it. An alternative antibiotic or anticonvulsant is generally needed.

qs.q: Which adverse effects should be monitored during gentamicin therapy?
qs.a: Kidney injury and hearing or balance loss
w: Liver failure and jaundice
Bone marrow suppression
Severe hypertension
qs.x: Aminoglycosides are nephrotoxic and ototoxic, and the hearing damage can be permanent. Levels and renal function guide dosing.

qs.q: IV acyclovir is started for suspected HSV encephalitis. Which nursing measure helps prevent a known adverse effect?
qs.a: Ensure adequate hydration to prevent crystal nephropathy
w: Limit fluids to prevent drug-induced cerebral edema
Give with calcium to prevent drug-induced hypocalcemia
Keep the patient supine to prevent orthostatic hypotension
qs.x: Acyclovir can crystallize in the renal tubules, especially with dehydration or rapid infusion, so adequate hydration is important. Fluid restriction would increase this risk.

qs.q: A patient taking sertraline is started on linezolid. Which complication should the nurse watch for?
qs.a: Serotonin syndrome
w: Red man syndrome
Disulfiram reaction
Gray baby syndrome
qs.x: Linezolid is a weak monoamine oxidase inhibitor and can cause serotonin syndrome with SSRIs and other serotonergic drugs. Red man syndrome is a vancomycin infusion reaction.

qs.q: Why is clindamycin often added to beta-lactam therapy for necrotizing fasciitis or toxic shock syndrome?
qs.a: It suppresses bacterial toxin production
w: It provides coverage for Pseudomonas
It prevents C. difficile infection
It reduces nephrotoxicity of other drugs
qs.x: Clindamycin inhibits protein synthesis and reduces toxin production by streptococci and staphylococci. It does not cover Pseudomonas and actually raises the risk of C. difficile.

qs.q: Which best describes piperacillin-tazobactam as an empiric sepsis antibiotic?
qs.a: An antipseudomonal penicillin combined with a beta-lactamase inhibitor
w: A carbapenem combined with a renal enzyme inhibitor
A glycopeptide that targets resistant gram-positive cocci
A third-generation cephalosporin without antipseudomonal activity
qs.x: Piperacillin is an extended-spectrum penicillin with Pseudomonas activity, and tazobactam protects it from many beta-lactamases. It does not cover MRSA, which is why vancomycin is often added.

qs.q: Before starting an IV insulin infusion for diabetic ketoacidosis, which lab result must be reviewed?
qs.a: Serum potassium
w: Serum calcium
Serum amylase
Serum albumin
qs.x: Insulin drives potassium into cells, and starting it when potassium is low can cause life-threatening hypokalemia. Guidelines call for potassium replacement first if the level is low.

qs.q: When a DKA patient is ready to transition off the insulin infusion, why is subcutaneous basal insulin such as glargine given before the drip ends?
qs.a: It prevents a gap in insulin coverage that could cause rebound ketoacidosis
w: It is needed to counter hypoglycemia caused by the IV insulin infusion
It speeds clearance of the remaining IV insulin from the bloodstream
It lowers serum potassium more quickly than IV insulin alone
qs.x: IV regular insulin has a very short half-life, so subcutaneous basal insulin is overlapped for a period to keep insulin levels steady. Without this overlap, hyperglycemia and ketosis can return quickly.

qs.q: Why is hydrocortisone the preferred steroid for adrenal crisis?
qs.a: It provides both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity
w: It has no glucocorticoid activity and only replaces aldosterone
It is the only steroid that can be given by the IV route
It has the longest half-life of all available corticosteroids
qs.x: High-dose hydrocortisone replaces cortisol and has enough mineralocorticoid effect to support sodium and volume. Dexamethasone has no meaningful mineralocorticoid activity.

qs.q: In septic shock, which situation is the usual indication for adding IV hydrocortisone?
qs.a: Shock that requires ongoing vasopressor therapy despite fluids
w: Any fever above normal with a positive blood culture
Sepsis without hypotension in a patient with mild confusion
Shock that resolves completely after the first fluid bolus
qs.x: Guidelines suggest IV hydrocortisone for adults with septic shock and an ongoing vasopressor requirement. It is not used for sepsis without shock.

qs.q: Concentrated dextrose is given for hypoglycemia through a small peripheral vein. Which complication should the nurse watch for?
qs.a: Phlebitis and tissue injury if it extravasates
w: Rebound hypercalcemia within several minutes
Immediate severe bronchospasm from the solution
Hemolysis from the low osmolality of the fluid
qs.x: Concentrated dextrose is hypertonic and irritating to veins, and extravasation can cause tissue damage, so a patent, large vein is preferred. Diluted concentrations are used in children for the same reason.

qs.q: Why might IM glucagon be less effective for hypoglycemia in a patient with chronic alcohol use and poor nutrition?
qs.a: Liver glycogen stores may be depleted
w: Alcohol blocks glucagon receptors directly
Glucagon is inactivated by alcohol in muscle
Malnutrition prevents absorption from muscle
