qs.q: Why is diphenhydramine a poor choice as a hospital sleep aid for an older adult?
qs.a: Its anticholinergic effects contribute to delirium and urinary retention
w: It causes severe hypertension in older adults
It is ineffective at causing drowsiness
It causes hyperkalemia in older adults
qs.x: Diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic and is on the Beers list because it causes confusion, constipation, and urinary retention in older adults. It does cause drowsiness, which is why it is often misused for sleep.

qs.q: A patient on pembrolizumab develops several days of watery diarrhea and abdominal pain. What should be recognized?
qs.a: Immune-mediated colitis
w: Expected tumor response
Lactose intolerance unrelated to therapy
Neutropenic fever
qs.x: Checkpoint inhibitors can cause immune-related adverse events, and colitis is a common one that may need corticosteroids. It should be reported promptly rather than treated as routine diarrhea.

qs.q: Which monitoring is recommended for a patient on long-term hydroxychloroquine?
qs.a: Baseline and periodic eye exams for retinal toxicity
w: Monthly liver biopsies
Periodic bone marrow biopsies
Annual pulmonary function tests only
qs.x: Hydroxychloroquine can cause irreversible retinopathy, so screening exams are done at baseline and periodically. It can also prolong the QT interval.

qs.q: Which toxicity is most important to prevent and monitor with cisplatin?
qs.a: Nephrotoxicity with magnesium wasting
w: Hemorrhagic cystitis
Cardiomyopathy
Pulmonary fibrosis
qs.x: Cisplatin damages renal tubules, so aggressive hydration and monitoring of creatinine and magnesium are standard. Hemorrhagic cystitis is linked to cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide.

qs.q: Before doxorubicin is started, which baseline study is most important?
qs.a: Assessment of left ventricular ejection fraction
w: Pulmonary function testing
Audiometry
Bone density scan
qs.x: Doxorubicin causes cumulative, dose-related cardiomyopathy, so ejection fraction is checked at baseline and during treatment. Pulmonary function testing is used for bleomycin.

qs.q: Which toxicity of high-dose cyclophosphamide is reduced by giving mesna and hydration?
qs.a: Hemorrhagic cystitis
w: Peripheral neuropathy
Cardiomyopathy
Ototoxicity
qs.x: The metabolite acrolein irritates the bladder lining; mesna binds it in the urine. Neuropathy and ototoxicity are not prevented by mesna.

qs.q: How must vincristine be given?
qs.a: Intravenously only, because intrathecal use is fatal
w: Intrathecally only, to reach the CSF
Intramuscularly into a large muscle
Subcutaneously into the abdomen
qs.x: Vincristine given intrathecally causes fatal ascending neurotoxicity, so it carries strict labeling and is often prepared in minibags. Its common dose-limiting toxicity is peripheral neuropathy.

qs.q: Which toxicity is most characteristic of bleomycin?
qs.a: Pulmonary toxicity that can progress to fibrosis
w: Hemorrhagic cystitis
Cumulative cardiomyopathy
Severe myelosuppression
qs.x: Bleomycin causes pneumonitis and fibrosis, so pulmonary function and new cough or dyspnea are watched closely. Unlike most chemotherapies, it causes little myelosuppression.

qs.q: Shortly after starting capecitabine, a patient develops severe mucositis, diarrhea, and neutropenia. Which enzyme deficiency should be suspected?
qs.a: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase
w: Thiopurine methyltransferase
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Pseudocholinesterase
qs.x: DPD breaks down fluorouracil, the active form of capecitabine, so deficiency causes severe, sometimes fatal toxicity. TPMT deficiency affects thiopurines, not fluoropyrimidines.

qs.q: A patient taking tamoxifen is admitted with leg swelling. Which serious adverse effect should be considered?
qs.a: Venous thromboembolism
w: Hemorrhagic cystitis
Pulmonary fibrosis
Peripheral neuropathy
qs.x: Tamoxifen has estrogen-like effects on clotting and raises the risk of DVT and PE, along with endometrial cancer. Leg swelling in this setting warrants evaluation for DVT.

qs.q: What is the purpose of leucovorin after high-dose methotrexate?
qs.a: It bypasses dihydrofolate reductase to rescue normal cells
w: It speeds renal excretion of methotrexate
It neutralizes methotrexate in the blood
It prevents methotrexate-induced nausea
qs.x: Leucovorin is a reduced folate that does not need DHFR, so it restores folate-dependent processes in healthy cells. It does not remove methotrexate; glucarpidase breaks down methotrexate in delayed clearance.

qs.q: Which factor most increases the risk of toxicity from high-dose methotrexate?
qs.a: Reduced kidney function
w: Mildly elevated blood glucose
A history of hypothyroidism
Well-controlled hypertension
qs.x: Methotrexate is cleared mainly by the kidneys, so impaired renal function causes delayed clearance and severe marrow, mucosal, and kidney toxicity. Alkalinization, hydration, and level monitoring are used to protect clearance.

qs.q: During an irinotecan infusion, a patient develops cramping, diarrhea, sweating, and salivation. Which treatment is appropriate?
qs.a: Atropine for the acute cholinergic syndrome
w: Loperamide for delayed diarrhea
Ondansetron for nausea
Diphenhydramine for allergy
qs.x: Irinotecan inhibits acetylcholinesterase and can cause early cholinergic symptoms that respond to atropine. Loperamide is used for the separate delayed diarrhea that starts later.

qs.q: An older patient is admitted with symptomatic bradycardia. Which home eye drop could be contributing?
qs.a: Timolol ophthalmic solution
w: Latanoprost ophthalmic solution
Artificial tear drops
Ketotifen ophthalmic solution
qs.x: Ophthalmic timolol is absorbed systemically and can cause bradycardia, heart block, and bronchospasm. Prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost do not cause beta-blocker effects.

qs.q: A patient on acetazolamide for glaucoma has an abnormal chemistry panel. Which acid-base change is expected?
qs.a: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
w: Metabolic alkalosis
High anion gap metabolic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis
qs.x: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, causing bicarbonate loss and a hyperchloremic acidosis, along with hypokalemia. It does not add unmeasured anions.

qs.q: A burn patient treated with silver sulfadiazine cream has a low white blood cell count a few days later. What should be recognized?
qs.a: Transient leukopenia associated with silver sulfadiazine
w: Expected sign of burn wound sepsis only
Allergic reaction requiring epinephrine
Lab error caused by the cream
qs.x: Silver sulfadiazine is associated with a transient drop in white cells that often recovers. It should be recognized and monitored rather than assumed to be lab error.

qs.q: Before certain surgeries, nasal mupirocin may be applied. What is its purpose?
qs.a: Decolonize the nose of Staphylococcus aureus to reduce infection
w: Treat bacterial sinusitis
Relieve nasal congestion
Prevent viral upper respiratory infections
qs.x: Intranasal mupirocin reduces S. aureus carriage, including MRSA, which lowers surgical site and other infection risk. It is not a treatment for sinusitis.

qs.q: Scabies is diagnosed in a hospitalized adult. Which teaching about permethrin cream is correct?
qs.a: Apply to the whole body from the neck down and treat close contacts
w: Apply only to itchy areas and wash off after a minute
Apply to the face and scalp only
Take it by mouth with food
qs.x: Permethrin is applied to all skin from the neck down, left on for the recommended time, and close contacts are treated at the same time. Treating only itchy spots misses mites elsewhere.

qs.q: Why is a topical lidocaine patch useful for localized pain in an older inpatient?
qs.a: It gives local pain relief with minimal systemic absorption
w: It provides strong systemic opioid-like effects
It reduces inflammation like an oral NSAID
It is safe to apply to broken or open skin
qs.x: Lidocaine patches act locally on peripheral nerves with little systemic absorption, avoiding sedation and kidney effects. They should be applied to intact skin, not open wounds.

qs.q: Which areas should generally be avoided when applying clobetasol, a superpotent topical steroid?
qs.a: The face, groin, and armpits
w: The palms and soles
The elbows and knees
The scalp
qs.x: Thin skin absorbs more steroid and is prone to atrophy and striae, so superpotent steroids are generally avoided on the face and skin folds. Thick-skinned areas like palms and soles often need stronger steroids.

qs.q: What is the most important safety requirement for a patient of reproductive potential prescribed isotretinoin?
qs.a: Pregnancy prevention under a restricted program
w: Annual chest radiography
Weekly kidney function testing
Avoiding all dairy products
qs.x: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen and is available only through the iPLEDGE program with pregnancy testing and contraception. The other measures are not required.

qs.q: Why is proparacaine eye drop not given to patients for home use?
qs.a: Repeated use damages the corneal epithelium and masks injury
w: It causes systemic hypertension
It is ineffective after a single dose
It permanently dilates the pupil
qs.x: Topical ocular anesthetics delay healing and can cause corneal ulceration with repeated use, while removing pain that signals worsening injury. They are used only for brief exams and procedures.

qs.q: Which skin finding in an obese inpatient is best treated with topical nystatin?
qs.a: Beefy red intertrigo with satellite pustules in skin folds
w: Honey-crusted lesions on the face
Silvery plaques on the elbows
Painful vesicles in a band on one side
qs.x: Bright red rash in skin folds with satellite lesions suggests Candida, which nystatin treats. Honey-crusted lesions suggest impetigo, which needs an antibacterial.

qs.q: A resident taking lisinopril reports a persistent dry, hacking cough. How should the LVN interpret this?
qs.a: A common ACE inhibitor side effect to report to the provider
w: An expected sign of the drug working that needs no follow-up
An early sign of digoxin toxicity to report to the provider
A symptom of low potassium that needs a dietary change
qs.x: ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril commonly cause a dry cough from bradykinin buildup, and it should be reported so the provider can decide on therapy. It is not a sign of the drug working or of low potassium.

qs.q: Before giving oral metoprolol to a resident, which assessment is most important?
qs.a: Apical pulse and blood pressure
w: Blood glucose and temperature
Serum potassium and urine output
Pain level and bowel sounds
qs.x: Metoprolol is a beta blocker that slows heart rate and lowers blood pressure, so both are checked before each dose. Potassium and urine output matter more for diuretics.

qs.q: Which lab value does the LVN check to monitor the effect of warfarin?
qs.a: International normalized ratio (INR)
w: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
Platelet count
Serum potassium
qs.x: Warfarin is monitored with the PT/INR. The aPTT is the test used for unfractionated heparin, which makes it the most tempting wrong choice.

qs.q: Which electrolyte imbalance is the most common concern with furosemide?
qs.a: Hypokalemia
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypernatremia
Hypercalcemia
qs.x: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that causes loss of potassium in the urine, so low potassium is the classic concern. High potassium is a concern with potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone, not loop diuretics.

qs.q: A patient taking atorvastatin reports new, unexplained muscle pain and weakness. What is the best action by the LVN?
qs.a: Report the symptoms promptly to the RN or provider
w: Reassure the patient that this is expected and harmless
Apply a heating pad and recheck the next week
Suggest taking an extra dose at bedtime instead
qs.x: Statins can cause myopathy and, rarely, rhabdomyolysis, so unexplained muscle pain or weakness must be reported. It should not be dismissed as harmless.

qs.q: A patient with angina uses sublingual nitroglycerin. Which other medicine can cause a dangerous drop in blood pressure if taken with it?
qs.a: Sildenafil
w: Atorvastatin
Acetaminophen
Metformin
qs.x: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil greatly increase the blood-pressure-lowering effect of nitrates and the combination is contraindicated. Atorvastatin is often taken by the same patients but does not cause this interaction.

qs.q: Which teaching is most important for a patient taking spironolactone?
qs.a: Avoid salt substitutes that contain potassium
w: Eat extra bananas and oranges every day
Take a potassium supplement with each dose
Limit fluids to prevent low sodium
qs.x: Spironolactone is potassium-sparing and can cause hyperkalemia, so potassium-based salt substitutes and extra potassium should be avoided. Encouraging high-potassium foods is teaching for loop or thiazide diuretics.

qs.q: Apixaban belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: Direct factor Xa inhibitor
w: Vitamin K antagonist
Direct thrombin inhibitor
P2Y12 platelet inhibitor
qs.x: Apixaban directly blocks factor Xa. Dabigatran is the oral direct thrombin inhibitor, and warfarin is the vitamin K antagonist.

qs.q: A resident taking digoxin reports loss of appetite, nausea, and seeing yellow-green halos around lights. How should the LVN interpret this?
qs.a: Possible digoxin toxicity that needs prompt reporting
w: Expected mild side effects that will pass
Signs of an allergic reaction to digoxin
Signs that the digoxin level is too low
qs.x: Anorexia, nausea, and visual changes such as yellow-green halos are classic early signs of digoxin toxicity. They are not normal side effects to ignore or signs of a low level.

qs.q: Which side effect is common with amlodipine and should be assessed at each visit?
qs.a: Swelling of the ankles and feet
w: Persistent dry cough
High blood sugar
Low serum potassium
qs.x: Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that commonly causes peripheral edema. A dry cough is linked to ACE inhibitors, not calcium channel blockers.

qs.q: How long should the LVN count the apical pulse before giving digoxin?
qs.a: A full minute
w: Fifteen seconds, then multiply by four
Thirty seconds, then multiply by two
Ten seconds, then multiply by six
qs.x: The apical pulse is counted for a full minute before digoxin because the drug slows heart rate and can cause irregular rhythms. Shorter counts can miss irregular beats.

qs.q: Which lab finding increases a patient's risk of digoxin toxicity?
qs.a: Low serum potassium
w: High serum sodium
Low hemoglobin
High blood glucose
qs.x: Hypokalemia makes the heart more sensitive to digoxin and raises the risk of toxicity, which is why patients on diuretics need potassium monitoring. Sodium, hemoglobin, and glucose do not have this effect.

qs.q: Droxidopa is given to treat which condition?
qs.a: Symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
w: Resistant essential hypertension
Atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate
Heart failure with fluid overload
qs.x: Droxidopa is converted to norepinephrine and raises blood pressure in patients who become dizzy on standing from neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. It would worsen hypertension, not treat it.

qs.q: Which teaching helps reduce the risk named in droxidopa's boxed warning?
qs.a: Rest and sleep with the head of the bed elevated
w: Lie flat for an hour after each dose
Take the last daily dose at bedtime
Take each dose with a salty snack
qs.x: Droxidopa carries a boxed warning for supine hypertension, so patients should rest and sleep with the head raised and take the last dose well before bedtime. Lying flat after a dose would raise the risk.

qs.q: In anaphylaxis, epinephrine improves the patient's condition mainly by doing what?
qs.a: Constricting blood vessels and opening the airways
w: Blocking histamine at H1 receptors
Reducing airway swelling over several hours
Slowing the heart to improve filling
qs.x: Epinephrine's alpha effects raise blood pressure and its beta-2 effects relax airway muscle, which is why it is first-line for anaphylaxis. Blocking histamine is how antihistamines work, and they act too slowly to treat shock.

qs.q: After an epinephrine auto-injector relieves an allergic reaction, why does the patient still need emergency care?
qs.a: Symptoms can return as the drug wears off
w: The injection usually causes low blood sugar
A second dose is always needed for the vaccine record
The injection site must be stitched closed
qs.x: Epinephrine is short-acting, and anaphylaxis symptoms can return, so the patient needs further monitoring and care. It does not typically cause low blood sugar; it tends to raise it.

qs.q: Milrinone belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor
w: Beta-1 adrenergic agonist
Cardiac glycoside
Alpha-1 adrenergic agonist
qs.x: Milrinone inhibits phosphodiesterase-3, which strengthens heart contraction and dilates blood vessels. Dobutamine, not milrinone, is the beta-1 agonist inotrope.

qs.q: For a patient receiving IV milrinone, which adverse effects should the nurse watch for?
qs.a: Low blood pressure and ventricular arrhythmias
w: High blood pressure and slow heart rate
Low blood sugar and seizures
Wheezing and hives
qs.x: Because milrinone dilates blood vessels and increases heart contractility, hypotension and ventricular arrhythmias are its main risks. It does not usually cause high blood pressure with a slow rate, which is more typical of phenylephrine.

qs.q: How does phenylephrine raise blood pressure?
qs.a: It stimulates alpha-1 receptors to constrict vessels
w: It stimulates beta-1 receptors to speed the heart
It inhibits phosphodiesterase in heart muscle
It increases blood volume by holding sodium
qs.x: Phenylephrine is a nearly pure alpha-1 agonist that raises blood pressure by vasoconstriction. It has little beta-1 effect, so it does not directly speed up the heart.

qs.q: A patient on IV phenylephrine has a rising blood pressure and a slowing heart rate. What does this most likely represent?
qs.a: Reflex bradycardia from the blood pressure rise
w: A severe allergic reaction to the drug
The drug's direct effect on beta-1 receptors
Early signs of digoxin toxicity
qs.x: When phenylephrine raises blood pressure, the body's baroreceptor reflex slows the heart. It does not stimulate beta-1 receptors, so a direct cardiac effect would not explain this.

qs.q: Which dietary teaching is correct for a patient taking warfarin?
qs.a: Keep intake of leafy green vegetables consistent
w: Eat as many leafy green vegetables as possible
Avoid every food that contains vitamin K
Double the next dose if one is missed
qs.x: Vitamin K reduces warfarin's effect, so a steady day-to-day intake keeps the INR stable. Avoiding all vitamin K is unnecessary and can make the INR swing when intake changes.

qs.q: Which agent is used to reverse the effect of warfarin?
qs.a: Phytonadione (vitamin K)
w: Protamine sulfate
Idarucizumab
Andexanet alfa
qs.x: Vitamin K restores the clotting factors that warfarin blocks. Protamine reverses heparin, idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, and andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors.

qs.q: Which agent is the antidote for an unfractionated heparin overdose?
qs.a: Protamine sulfate
w: Phytonadione (vitamin K)
Idarucizumab
Naloxone
qs.x: Protamine binds heparin and neutralizes it. Vitamin K is the reversal agent for warfarin, not heparin.

qs.q: When giving subcutaneous enoxaparin from a prefilled syringe, what should the nurse do?
qs.a: Leave the air bubble in the syringe before injecting
w: Massage the site well after injecting
Inject into the deltoid muscle
Aspirate for blood before injecting
qs.x: The labeling says not to expel the air bubble from the prefilled syringe, and the injection is given subcutaneously, usually in the abdomen. Massaging or aspirating increases bruising.

qs.q: Which teaching is most important for a patient taking clopidogrel?
qs.a: Report black, tarry stools or unusual bruising
w: Expect bright orange urine during treatment
Take it with antacids to protect the stomach
Report any increase in appetite
qs.x: Clopidogrel blocks platelet activation, so bleeding is the key risk and signs like black stools or easy bruising must be reported. Orange urine is linked to drugs like phenazopyridine, not clopidogrel.

qs.q: Which statement about oral ferrous sulfate is accurate teaching?
qs.a: Stools may turn dark green or black
w: Take it with an antacid to prevent upset stomach
Take it with milk to improve absorption
Urine may turn bright orange
qs.x: Iron commonly darkens the stool, and patients should know this is expected. Antacids and milk reduce iron absorption, so taking iron with them is incorrect.

qs.q: Before giving epoetin alfa, which assessment is the priority?
qs.a: Blood pressure and the most recent hemoglobin
w: Apical pulse and serum digoxin level
Blood glucose and hemoglobin A1C
Respiratory rate and oxygen saturation
qs.x: Epoetin alfa can raise blood pressure, and a hemoglobin that is too high increases the risk of heart attack, stroke, and clots. Glucose monitoring is not specifically needed for this drug.

qs.q: Which teaching about dabigatran capsules is correct?
qs.a: Swallow the capsules whole without opening them
w: Open the capsules and sprinkle on applesauce
Crush the capsules if swallowing is hard
Chew the capsules for faster absorption
qs.x: Opening or chewing dabigatran capsules greatly increases absorption and the risk of bleeding, so they must be swallowed whole. Sprinkling on applesauce is acceptable for some other drugs but not this one.

qs.q: Which side effect is common with filgrastim?
qs.a: Bone pain
w: Hair loss
Slow heart rate
Low blood sugar
qs.x: Filgrastim stimulates the bone marrow to make neutrophils, which commonly causes bone pain. Hair loss is associated with chemotherapy, not filgrastim.

qs.q: Which history should be reported before a patient starts tranexamic acid for heavy menstrual bleeding?
qs.a: A history of blood clots, such as a DVT
w: Iron-deficiency anemia
Seasonal allergies
Recent mild sinus infection
qs.x: Tranexamic acid prevents clot breakdown, so it is contraindicated with active or prior thromboembolic disease. Iron-deficiency anemia is common in these patients and is not a reason to avoid it.

qs.q: After onabotulinumtoxinA injections, which symptom should the patient report right away?
qs.a: New trouble swallowing or breathing
w: Mild tenderness at the injection sites
A small bruise at an injection site
Slight tiredness on the day of treatment
qs.x: Botulinum toxins carry a boxed warning that the effect can spread beyond the injection site and weaken swallowing and breathing muscles. Mild tenderness or bruising at the site is expected.

qs.q: OnabotulinumtoxinA relaxes muscles by doing what?
qs.a: Blocking acetylcholine release at nerve endings
w: Blocking dopamine receptors in the brain
Increasing calcium release in muscle cells
Stimulating GABA receptors in the spinal cord
qs.x: Botulinum toxin prevents acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, which weakens the injected muscle. GABA stimulation in the spinal cord is how baclofen works, not botulinum toxin.

qs.q: By which route is abobotulinumtoxinA given for cervical dystonia?
qs.a: Intramuscular injection
w: Oral tablet
Intravenous infusion
Inhaled powder
qs.x: AbobotulinumtoxinA is injected directly into the affected muscles. It is not given orally, intravenously, or by inhalation.

qs.q: Which group of symptoms after abobotulinumtoxinA suggests the toxin effect has spread?
qs.a: Hoarseness, double vision, and trouble swallowing
w: Redness and itching at the injection sites
Mild headache and a stuffy nose
Brief soreness in the treated muscle
qs.x: Distant toxin spread can cause generalized weakness, double vision, drooping eyelids, hoarseness, and swallowing or breathing problems, which must be reported promptly. Local redness or soreness is expected.

qs.q: DaxibotulinumtoxinA works by doing what?
qs.a: Blocking acetylcholine release at nerve endings
w: Blocking histamine release from mast cells
Stimulating collagen growth in the skin
Blocking pain signals in sensory nerves
qs.x: Like other botulinum toxins, daxibotulinumtoxinA prevents acetylcholine release so the injected muscle relaxes, smoothing lines or easing dystonia. It does not work by building collagen.

qs.q: Which finding is a contraindication to daxibotulinumtoxinA injection?
qs.a: Infection at the planned injection site
w: Mild seasonal allergies
Well-controlled high blood pressure
A history of migraine headaches
qs.x: The labeling lists infection at the injection site and hypersensitivity as contraindications. Controlled hypertension and seasonal allergies do not prevent treatment.

qs.q: During and after IV fentanyl, which assessment is the priority?
qs.a: Respiratory rate and oxygen saturation
w: Blood glucose and temperature
Bowel sounds and urine output
Pupil size and reflexes only
qs.x: Fentanyl is a potent opioid whose most dangerous effect is respiratory depression, so breathing and oxygen levels are watched closely. Constipation and urinary retention matter but are not the priority.

qs.q: Which drug reverses respiratory depression caused by fentanyl?
qs.a: Naloxone
w: Flumazenil
Atropine
Protamine sulfate
qs.x: Naloxone is an opioid antagonist that reverses fentanyl's effects. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids.

qs.q: Over-the-counter pyrantel pamoate is used to treat which condition?
qs.a: Pinworm infection
w: Head lice
Scabies
Vaginal yeast infection
qs.x: Pyrantel is an anthelmintic that paralyzes intestinal worms such as pinworms so they pass in the stool. Lice and scabies are treated with topical products such as permethrin.

qs.q: When one family member is treated with pyrantel for pinworms, what does the product labeling advise?
qs.a: Treat the entire household unless told otherwise
w: Treat only the person with symptoms
Treat only the children in the home
Treat household pets instead of people
qs.x: Pinworms spread easily within households, so the OTC labeling advises treating everyone in the home unless a provider says otherwise. Pets do not carry human pinworms.

qs.q: Which side effects are expected after using an albuterol inhaler?
qs.a: Shakiness and a faster heart rate
w: Drowsiness and a slower heart rate
Oral thrush and hoarseness
Dry cough and swollen lips
qs.x: Albuterol is a beta-2 agonist that can also stimulate the heart and skeletal muscle, causing tremor and tachycardia. Thrush and hoarseness are linked to inhaled corticosteroids.

qs.q: Albuterol belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: Short-acting beta-2 agonist
w: Long-acting beta-2 agonist
Inhaled corticosteroid
Long-acting muscarinic antagonist
qs.x: Albuterol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist used as a rescue inhaler. Salmeterol and formoterol are long-acting beta-2 agonists.

qs.q: Which teaching helps prevent oral thrush with an inhaled fluticasone inhaler?
qs.a: Rinse the mouth with water and spit after each use
w: Use it only during an asthma attack
Swallow a glass of milk after each use
Hold the breath as briefly as possible
qs.x: Rinsing and spitting removes steroid left in the mouth and lowers the risk of candidiasis. Inhaled steroids are maintenance medicines, not rescue inhalers.

qs.q: Which teaching about tiotropium capsules used with a dry powder inhaler device is correct?
qs.a: Place the capsule in the device; never swallow it
w: Swallow the capsule with a full glass of water
Open the capsule and mix it with water
Dissolve the capsule under the tongue
qs.x: Tiotropium capsules for the dry powder device are pierced inside the device and inhaled. They are not meant to be swallowed or dissolved.

qs.q: Montelukast carries a boxed warning about which type of adverse effect?
qs.a: Neuropsychiatric events such as mood changes
w: Severe liver failure
Life-threatening bleeding
Tendon rupture
qs.x: Montelukast has a boxed warning for serious neuropsychiatric events, including agitation, depression, sleep disturbance, and suicidal thoughts. Tendon rupture is a fluoroquinolone warning.

qs.q: A patient asks whether salmeterol can be used during a sudden asthma attack. What is the correct response?
qs.a: No; it is long-acting and not for quick relief
w: Yes; it is the preferred rescue inhaler
Yes; but only if albuterol is unavailable
No; it is used only for allergies
qs.x: Salmeterol is a long-acting beta-2 agonist with a slow onset, so it is not used for acute symptoms. A short-acting agent such as albuterol is the rescue inhaler.

qs.q: Which teaching about benzonatate capsules is correct?
qs.a: Swallow them whole without chewing or sucking
w: Chew them to coat the throat faster
Dissolve them in the mouth like a lozenge
Open them and mix with warm tea
qs.x: Chewing or sucking benzonatate can numb the mouth and throat and cause choking or serious reactions. The capsules must be swallowed whole.

qs.q: When is oseltamivir most effective for treating influenza?
qs.a: When started within 48 hours of symptom onset
w: Only after a positive culture returns
After the fever has lasted a full week
Only once pneumonia has developed
qs.x: Oseltamivir is labeled to start within 48 hours of flu symptoms, when viral replication is highest. Waiting for complications reduces its benefit.

qs.q: Which patient should talk with the provider before using pseudoephedrine?
qs.a: A patient with uncontrolled high blood pressure
w: A patient with seasonal allergies
A patient with a mild sinus headache
A patient with a recent common cold
qs.x: Pseudoephedrine is a sympathomimetic decongestant that can raise blood pressure and heart rate. Allergies and colds are common reasons it is used, not reasons for caution.

qs.q: A resident with diabetes starts a course of prednisone. Which assessment should the LVN expect to increase?
qs.a: Blood glucose checks
w: Apical pulse checks
Serum digoxin levels
Peak flow readings only
qs.x: Corticosteroids such as prednisone raise blood glucose, so closer glucose monitoring is needed in diabetes. Apical pulse checks are linked to drugs like digoxin and beta blockers.

qs.q: Which teaching is important for a patient on long-term phenytoin?
qs.a: Brush, floss, and get regular dental care
w: Expect the urine to turn bright orange
Eat extra protein at every meal
Avoid all dairy products
qs.x: Phenytoin commonly causes gingival hyperplasia, and good oral hygiene helps limit it. Orange urine is linked to drugs like rifampin and phenazopyridine.

qs.q: Which effect should a patient taking levetiracetam report?
qs.a: New irritability, aggression, or depression
w: Mild drowsiness during the first days
A small increase in appetite
Slightly darker yellow urine
qs.x: Levetiracetam can cause behavioral and mood changes, including suicidal thoughts, which should be reported. Mild drowsiness early in therapy is common and expected.

qs.q: Which symptoms in a patient taking carbamazepine should be reported promptly?
qs.a: Sore throat, fever, or easy bruising
w: Mild dizziness when first starting
Slight nausea that improves with food
Mild drowsiness in the evening
qs.x: Carbamazepine can cause serious blood disorders such as agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia, which show up as infection or bleeding signs. Mild dizziness and nausea are common early effects.

qs.q: Which finding should a patient taking lamotrigine report right away?
qs.a: Any new skin rash
w: Mild headache
Occasional dizziness
Slight weight change
qs.x: Lamotrigine has a boxed warning for serious rashes, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, so any rash needs prompt evaluation. Headache and dizziness are common, less urgent side effects.

qs.q: Which lab values are monitored in a patient taking valproic acid?
qs.a: Liver function tests and platelet count
w: Serum potassium and magnesium
Thyroid levels and hemoglobin A1C
Serum amylase only
qs.x: Valproic acid can cause liver injury and low platelets, so liver tests and platelet counts are monitored. Pancreatitis is also a risk, but monitoring amylase alone would miss the liver and bleeding risks.

qs.q: Which teaching about carbidopa-levodopa is correct?
qs.a: Large high-protein meals can reduce its effect
w: It must be taken with a high-protein shake
It works best when taken with iron pills
It cures Parkinson disease over time
qs.x: Dietary protein competes with levodopa for absorption, so large protein meals can weaken its effect. Iron supplements also reduce absorption, and the drug treats symptoms but does not cure Parkinson disease.

qs.q: Which finding in a resident taking donepezil should the LVN report?
qs.a: Fainting spells with a slow pulse
w: Mild forgetfulness about recent events
Improved interest in daily activities
Occasional mild nausea after meals
qs.x: Donepezil is a cholinesterase inhibitor that can slow the heart and cause fainting, which should be reported. Mild nausea is a common, less urgent side effect.

qs.q: Which history should be reported before a patient takes rizatriptan for migraine?
qs.a: Coronary artery disease or prior heart attack
w: Seasonal allergic rhinitis
Mild osteoarthritis of the knees
A history of motion sickness
qs.x: Triptans constrict blood vessels and are contraindicated in ischemic heart disease. Allergies and arthritis are not reasons to avoid them.

qs.q: Baclofen is used to treat which problem?
qs.a: Muscle spasticity from multiple sclerosis or spinal cord injury
w: Partial seizures in adults and children
Tremor from Parkinson disease
Nerve pain from shingles
qs.x: Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist muscle relaxant used for spasticity from MS and spinal cord conditions. It is not used to treat seizures or Parkinson tremor.

qs.q: Which teaching helps reduce the risk of kidney stones with topiramate?
qs.a: Drink plenty of fluids throughout the day
w: Limit fluids in the evening
Take it with calcium supplements
Eat a high-protein diet
qs.x: Topiramate can cause kidney stones, and good hydration lowers that risk. Limiting fluids would increase the risk.

qs.q: Taking too much acetaminophen mainly damages which organ?
qs.a: Liver
w: Kidneys
Stomach lining
Heart
qs.x: Acetaminophen overdose causes liver injury, which can be fatal. Stomach bleeding is more typical of NSAIDs such as ibuprofen.

qs.q: Which teaching helps reduce stomach upset from ibuprofen?
qs.a: Take it with food or milk
w: Take it on an empty stomach
Take it with an alcoholic drink
Take it lying down
qs.x: Taking ibuprofen with food or milk reduces GI irritation. Alcohol increases the risk of stomach bleeding with NSAIDs.

qs.q: Before giving oral morphine to a resident, which assessment is the priority?
qs.a: Respiratory rate and level of sedation
w: Blood glucose and temperature
Apical pulse and potassium level
Bowel sounds only
qs.x: Respiratory depression is morphine's most dangerous effect, and increasing sedation often comes first. Constipation is common but is not the priority before a dose.

qs.q: Which teaching is most important for a patient taking hydrocodone-acetaminophen?
qs.a: Avoid other products that contain acetaminophen
w: Take extra doses if the pain is severe
Take it with alcohol to improve sleep
Expect the urine to turn green
qs.x: Many OTC cold and pain products contain acetaminophen, and adding them can cause liver damage. Alcohol adds to opioid sedation and liver risk.

qs.q: Which teaching is important for a patient using a fentanyl transdermal patch?
qs.a: Avoid heating pads, hot tubs, and electric blankets
w: Cut the patch to adjust the effect
Apply a heating pad to speed relief
Rub the patch to warm it before use
qs.x: Heat increases fentanyl absorption from the patch and can cause a fatal overdose. Patches must not be cut.

qs.q: After naloxone reverses an opioid overdose, why must the patient be monitored closely?
qs.a: The opioid may outlast naloxone and sedation may return
w: Naloxone often causes very low blood pressure
Naloxone commonly causes low blood sugar
Naloxone often causes bleeding
qs.x: Many opioids last longer than naloxone, so breathing problems can return after it wears off. Low blood sugar and bleeding are not typical naloxone effects.

qs.q: Taking tramadol with which drug raises the risk of serotonin syndrome?
qs.a: Sertraline
w: Acetaminophen
Docusate
Loratadine
qs.x: Tramadol has serotonergic activity, and combining it with an SSRI such as sertraline can cause serotonin syndrome. Acetaminophen is often combined with tramadol and does not cause this.

qs.q: Which effect of zolpidem should be reported right away?
qs.a: Sleepwalking or driving while not fully awake
w: Feeling sleepy shortly after taking it
Falling asleep faster than before
Mild dry mouth in the morning
qs.x: Zolpidem has a boxed warning for complex sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking and sleep-driving, which can cause serious injury. Sleepiness after the dose is the intended effect.

qs.q: For an older adult taking lorazepam, which safety concern is the priority?
qs.a: Falls from sedation and unsteady gait
w: High blood pressure
Low blood sugar
Bleeding gums
qs.x: Benzodiazepines cause drowsiness, confusion, and poor balance in older adults, increasing fall risk. They do not typically cause high blood pressure or low blood sugar.

qs.q: Which teaching about the lidocaine patch is correct?
qs.a: Apply it only to intact skin, not open wounds
w: Cover it with a heating pad to work faster
Apply it over broken skin for best relief
Cut it into pieces and swallow if needed
qs.x: Lidocaine patches go on intact skin; broken skin increases absorption and toxicity. Heat also increases absorption, so heating pads should not be used over the patch.

qs.q: Which symptoms suggest early lithium toxicity?
qs.a: Vomiting, diarrhea, and a coarse hand tremor
w: A fine hand tremor and increased thirst
Constipation and urinary retention
High fever and rigid muscles
qs.x: GI upset with a coarse tremor and drowsiness are early signs of lithium toxicity. A fine tremor and thirst are common expected side effects at therapeutic levels.

qs.q: Which over-the-counter drug can raise lithium levels?
qs.a: Ibuprofen
w: Acetaminophen
Loratadine
Docusate
qs.x: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen reduce lithium clearance by the kidneys and can cause toxicity. Acetaminophen is generally the safer OTC pain reliever for patients on lithium.

qs.q: Which teaching is most important for a young adult starting sertraline?
qs.a: Report new or worsening suicidal thoughts right away
w: Expect full benefit within the first day
Take it with grapefruit juice for best effect
Expect the urine to turn dark brown
qs.x: Antidepressants carry a boxed warning for increased suicidal thinking in children and young adults, especially early in therapy. Full benefit usually takes several weeks.

qs.q: Which lab value must be monitored regularly in a patient taking clozapine?
qs.a: Absolute neutrophil count
w: Serum lithium level
Serum potassium
Thyroid-stimulating hormone
qs.x: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia, so the absolute neutrophil count is monitored. Lithium levels are not related to clozapine.

qs.q: A resident on long-term haloperidol has repetitive lip smacking and tongue movements. What is this most likely?
qs.a: Tardive dyskinesia
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
Acute dystonic reaction
qs.x: Tardive dyskinesia is a late effect of antipsychotics marked by involuntary face, lip, and tongue movements and should be reported. Acute dystonia is a sudden muscle spasm that usually occurs early in therapy.

qs.q: Which assessments are important for a patient taking olanzapine long term?
qs.a: Weight, blood glucose, and lipid levels
w: Serum lithium and sodium levels
INR and platelet count
Peak flow and oxygen saturation
qs.x: Olanzapine commonly causes weight gain, high blood sugar, and high lipids, so metabolic monitoring is needed. INR monitoring is for warfarin.

qs.q: Which foods should a patient taking tranylcypromine avoid?
qs.a: Aged cheeses and cured or fermented meats
w: Fresh fruits and vegetables
Plain rice and pasta
Fresh chicken and fish
qs.x: Tranylcypromine is an MAO inhibitor, and tyramine-rich foods such as aged cheese and cured meats can cause a hypertensive crisis. Fresh foods are low in tyramine.

qs.q: Which history is a contraindication to bupropion?
qs.a: A seizure disorder
w: Seasonal allergies
Mild osteoarthritis
Smoking cigarettes
qs.x: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in seizure disorders and in bulimia or anorexia. It is actually used to help people stop smoking.

qs.q: Which adverse effect of trazodone requires immediate reporting in a male patient?
qs.a: A prolonged, painful erection
w: Mild morning drowsiness
Dry mouth
A mild headache
qs.x: Trazodone can cause priapism, a medical emergency. Drowsiness and dry mouth are common and expected.

qs.q: Which teaching helps reduce insomnia from methylphenidate?
qs.a: Give doses early in the day
w: Give the dose at bedtime
Give it with a caffeinated drink
Give it only after a large evening meal
qs.x: Methylphenidate is a stimulant, so late doses can interfere with sleep. Caffeine adds to stimulant effects.

qs.q: Which teaching about extended-release potassium chloride tablets is correct?
qs.a: Swallow them whole with food and a full glass of water
w: Crush them and mix with a small sip of water
Chew them on an empty stomach
Dissolve them under the tongue
qs.x: Extended-release potassium tablets are swallowed whole with meals and plenty of water to reduce GI irritation and injury. Crushing destroys the extended-release design.

qs.q: When is the best time to give once-daily oral furosemide?
qs.a: In the morning
w: At bedtime
In the middle of the night
Right before an afternoon nap
qs.x: Giving a diuretic in the morning keeps the peak urine output during waking hours and prevents nighttime urination and falls. A bedtime dose would disrupt sleep.

qs.q: Which teaching is appropriate for a patient taking hydrochlorothiazide?
qs.a: Use sunscreen and protective clothing outdoors
w: Avoid all foods that contain potassium
Take it at bedtime for best effect
Drink grapefruit juice with each dose
qs.x: Hydrochlorothiazide can increase sun sensitivity and is linked to a higher risk of some skin cancers. Because it lowers potassium, avoiding potassium-rich foods would be wrong.

qs.q: Which teaching is important when a patient starts tamsulosin?
qs.a: Rise slowly from lying or sitting to prevent dizziness
w: Expect the urine to turn bright red
Limit fluids to reduce urine output
Expect improved vision at night
qs.x: Tamsulosin is an alpha-1 blocker that can cause orthostatic hypotension, especially early in therapy. Red urine is not an expected effect.

qs.q: Which safety teaching is correct for finasteride?
qs.a: Women who are or may become pregnant should not handle broken tablets
w: The tablets should be crushed before giving
Women should take it to prevent hair loss in pregnancy
It is safe for anyone to handle in any form
qs.x: Finasteride can be absorbed through the skin and may harm a male fetus, so pregnant women should avoid crushed or broken tablets. It is not used in pregnancy.

qs.q: Which side effects are expected with oxybutynin?
qs.a: Dry mouth and constipation
w: Diarrhea and excess saliva
Urinary frequency and urgency
Slow heart rate and wheezing
qs.x: Oxybutynin is anticholinergic, so dry mouth and constipation are common. Diarrhea and excess saliva are cholinergic effects, the opposite of what oxybutynin does.

qs.q: Which teaching about nitrofurantoin is correct?
qs.a: Take it with food; urine may turn brown
w: Take it on an empty stomach; urine may turn blue
Take it with antacids; urine may turn green
Take it at bedtime only; urine will be clear
qs.x: Food improves nitrofurantoin absorption and reduces stomach upset, and the drug may harmlessly darken urine to yellow or brown. Magnesium-containing antacids reduce its absorption.

qs.q: Which statement shows understanding of phenazopyridine teaching?
qs.a: This relieves burning but does not cure the infection
w: This will cure the infection in a single day
This should turn my urine light green
This replaces the need for an antibiotic
qs.x: Phenazopyridine is a urinary analgesic that eases burning and urgency but has no antibacterial effect. It turns urine reddish-orange, not green.

qs.q: When should sevelamer be given to a patient with chronic kidney disease?
qs.a: With meals, to bind dietary phosphate
w: At bedtime on an empty stomach
Only when serum calcium is low
One hour after the evening meal
qs.x: Sevelamer is a phosphate binder that must be in the gut with food to bind phosphate. Giving it apart from meals greatly reduces its effect.

qs.q: Which lab finding is the main concern in a patient taking triamterene?
qs.a: A high serum potassium level
w: A low serum potassium level
A high serum calcium level
A low blood glucose level
qs.x: Triamterene is potassium-sparing and carries a boxed warning for hyperkalemia. Low potassium is a concern with loop and thiazide diuretics instead.

qs.q: How should oral alendronate be taken?
qs.a: First thing in the morning with plain water, staying upright
w: With breakfast and a glass of orange juice
At bedtime with a glass of milk
With a calcium supplement and coffee
qs.x: Alendronate must be taken on an empty stomach with plain water, and staying upright reduces the risk of esophageal irritation. Food, juice, coffee, milk, and calcium all reduce absorption.

qs.q: Which symptom should a patient taking alendronate report?
qs.a: Jaw pain or a tooth socket that does not heal
w: Mild constipation
A slight headache
Mild muscle soreness after exercise
qs.x: Bisphosphonates have been linked to osteonecrosis of the jaw, which can show up as jaw pain or poor healing after dental work. Mild constipation and headache are less concerning.

qs.q: How does allopurinol lower uric acid?
qs.a: It blocks xanthine oxidase to reduce uric acid production
w: It increases uric acid excretion by the kidneys
It blocks neutrophil movement into the joint
It breaks down uric acid with an enzyme
qs.x: Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that reduces how much uric acid the body makes. Increasing kidney excretion is how probenecid works.

qs.q: Which finding in a patient taking allopurinol should be reported right away?
qs.a: Any new skin rash
w: Mild stomach upset
Slightly darker yellow urine
Mild drowsiness
qs.x: Allopurinol can cause severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, which often begin as a rash. Mild stomach upset is a less urgent side effect.

qs.q: Which symptoms are often the first signs of colchicine toxicity?
qs.a: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea
w: Dry mouth and constipation
Rash and itching
Headache and blurred vision
qs.x: GI symptoms are the most common early signs of colchicine toxicity and should be reported. Constipation is not a typical colchicine effect.

qs.q: Which drug can greatly raise colchicine levels and cause toxicity?
qs.a: Clarithromycin
w: Acetaminophen
Docusate
Loratadine
qs.x: Clarithromycin strongly inhibits the enzymes and transporters that clear colchicine, and fatal toxicity has occurred. Acetaminophen does not have this interaction.

qs.q: Febuxostat carries a boxed warning for which risk?
qs.a: Cardiovascular death
w: Tendon rupture
Lactic acidosis
Severe hypoglycemia
qs.x: Febuxostat's boxed warning is for a higher rate of cardiovascular death than allopurinol in gout patients with heart disease. Tendon rupture is a fluoroquinolone warning.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for calcitonin-salmon nasal spray?
qs.a: Alternate nostrils daily and report nasal sores or nosebleeds
w: Use the same nostril every day for consistency
Swallow the spray after it reaches the throat
Spray it into the mouth if the nose is congested
qs.x: Alternating nostrils reduces nasal irritation, and rhinitis, sores, and nosebleeds are known side effects that should be reported. The spray is meant to be absorbed through the nasal lining.

qs.q: How does cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) support bone health?
qs.a: It increases calcium absorption from the gut
w: It blocks cells that break down bone
It directly builds new bone protein
It increases calcium loss in the urine
qs.x: Vitamin D increases intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate, supporting bone mineralization. Blocking bone breakdown is how bisphosphonates work.

qs.q: Which symptoms suggest low calcium in a patient taking cinacalcet?
qs.a: Tingling around the mouth and muscle cramps
w: Increased thirst and constipation
Dry mouth and blurred vision
Flushing and a fast heart rate
qs.x: Cinacalcet lowers parathyroid hormone and calcium, and hypocalcemia causes tingling, cramps, and spasms. Thirst and constipation suggest high calcium instead.

qs.q: Naloxone reverses an overdose of which type of drug?
qs.a: Opioids such as fentanyl or oxycodone
w: Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam
Acetaminophen
Beta blockers such as metoprolol
qs.x: Naloxone is an opioid receptor antagonist. Benzodiazepine overdose is reversed by flumazenil, not naloxone.

qs.q: After naloxone is given to a patient who takes opioids daily, which response should the nurse anticipate?
qs.a: Acute withdrawal with agitation, sweating, and vomiting
w: Deep sleep with very slow breathing
A severe allergic rash and hives
Very low blood sugar and confusion
qs.x: In opioid-dependent patients, naloxone can bring on sudden withdrawal symptoms. Slow breathing is what naloxone is given to reverse.

qs.q: Acetylcysteine is the antidote for an overdose of which drug?
qs.a: Acetaminophen
w: Aspirin
Iron
Digoxin
qs.x: Acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and protects the liver after acetaminophen overdose. Aspirin overdose is managed differently, without a specific antidote like this.

qs.q: When is acetylcysteine most effective after an acetaminophen overdose?
qs.a: When started within the first 8 hours after ingestion
w: Only after liver enzymes begin to rise
Only after jaundice appears
After waiting a full day for the drug to clear
qs.x: Acetylcysteine works best when started early, ideally within 8 hours, before liver damage develops. Waiting for liver tests to rise or jaundice to appear loses much of its benefit.

qs.q: In which situation is glucagon used?
qs.a: Severe low blood sugar in a person who cannot swallow
w: Mild low blood sugar in an alert person
High blood sugar with ketones in the urine
Routine daily control of type 2 diabetes
qs.x: Glucagon raises blood glucose by releasing liver glycogen and is used when a person is unconscious or cannot safely take sugar by mouth. An alert person with mild low blood sugar should take fast-acting oral carbohydrates.

qs.q: After glucagon is given for severe low blood sugar and the person wakes up, what should happen next?
qs.a: Give oral carbohydrates once the person can swallow
w: Give a dose of rapid-acting insulin
Have the person lie flat and fast for several hours
Give nothing by mouth for the rest of the day
qs.x: Glucagon's effect is brief, so the person should eat carbohydrates once able to swallow safely to prevent another low. Insulin would lower the blood sugar again.

qs.q: Why is IV phytonadione given slowly with close monitoring?
qs.a: It can cause severe, sometimes fatal hypersensitivity reactions
w: It commonly causes dangerous low blood sugar
It often causes sudden seizures
It frequently causes kidney failure
qs.x: Phytonadione has a boxed warning for severe hypersensitivity and anaphylactic reactions with IV and IM use, so other routes are preferred when possible. Low blood sugar and seizures are not its known risks.

qs.q: Nalmefene belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: Opioid receptor antagonist
w: Opioid receptor agonist
Benzodiazepine receptor antagonist
Partial opioid agonist
qs.x: Nalmefene, like naloxone, blocks opioid receptors and reverses opioid overdose. Flumazenil is the benzodiazepine receptor antagonist.

qs.q: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is used as an antidote for seizures caused by an overdose of which drug?
qs.a: Isoniazid
w: Lithium
Digoxin
Acetaminophen
qs.x: Isoniazid overdose depletes vitamin B6 and causes seizures that respond to pyridoxine. Acetaminophen overdose is treated with acetylcysteine.

qs.q: Which symptoms should a patient taking deferiprone report right away?
qs.a: Fever, sore throat, or other signs of infection
w: Reddish-brown urine
Mild nausea after doses
A mild increase in appetite
qs.x: Deferiprone has a boxed warning for agranulocytosis, so signs of infection must be reported and the neutrophil count checked. Reddish-brown urine is an expected, harmless effect of the iron complex.

qs.q: Before giving the first dose of amoxicillin, what should the LVN ask about?
qs.a: Any prior allergic reaction to penicillin
w: Any prior reaction to iodine or shellfish
Any history of kidney stones
Any recent use of acetaminophen
qs.x: Amoxicillin is a penicillin, so a penicillin allergy can cause a serious reaction. Shellfish or iodine reactions are not related to penicillins.

qs.q: Which symptom should a patient taking ciprofloxacin report right away?
qs.a: Pain or swelling in the back of the heel
w: Mild loose stools for a day
A slight metallic taste
Mild drowsiness
qs.x: Fluoroquinolones carry a boxed warning for tendinitis and tendon rupture, often of the Achilles tendon. Mild GI upset is a less urgent side effect.

qs.q: Which teaching is most important for a patient taking metronidazole?
qs.a: Avoid alcohol during treatment and for several days after
w: Take it with grapefruit juice
Avoid dairy products for a week
Expect the urine to turn bright orange
qs.x: Metronidazole with alcohol can cause a disulfiram-like reaction with flushing, nausea, and vomiting. It may darken urine, but bright orange urine is typical of other drugs.

qs.q: Which teaching about oral doxycycline is correct?
qs.a: Separate it from antacids and iron supplements
w: Take it lying down with a small sip of water
Take it together with an antacid
Take it with an iron pill to prevent upset
qs.x: Antacids and iron bind doxycycline and reduce absorption, and the drug should be taken with plenty of water while upright to prevent esophageal injury. Taking it lying down increases that risk.

qs.q: Which teaching is important for a patient taking trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole?
qs.a: Drink plenty of fluids during treatment
w: Limit fluids to concentrate the drug
Take it with an antacid
Avoid all fruits and vegetables
qs.x: Good fluid intake helps prevent crystals from forming in the urine with sulfonamides. Limiting fluids increases that risk.

qs.q: Which symptom in a patient taking oral clindamycin should be reported?
qs.a: Frequent watery diarrhea
w: A mild metallic taste
Mild stomach discomfort
Slightly darker yellow urine
qs.x: Clindamycin has a boxed warning for C. difficile-associated diarrhea, which can be severe. Mild stomach discomfort is common and less urgent.

qs.q: During IV vancomycin, a patient develops flushing and a red rash on the face, neck, and upper body. What does this most likely represent?
qs.a: An infusion reaction often related to a fast infusion rate
w: An expected sign that the infection is clearing
A sign of vancomycin-induced kidney stones
Early signs of hearing loss
qs.x: Vancomycin infusion reaction causes flushing and rash of the upper body, often with rapid infusion, and should be reported. It is not a sign of the infection improving.

qs.q: A patient on warfarin is prescribed fluconazole. What interaction is the concern?
qs.a: Increased bleeding risk from a higher INR
w: Lower INR and higher clot risk
Higher blood sugar from both drugs
Lower potassium from both drugs
qs.x: Fluconazole inhibits the enzymes that clear warfarin, raising the INR and bleeding risk. It does not lower the INR.

qs.q: Which statement about the recombinant zoster (shingles) vaccine is accurate?
qs.a: It is non-live and given as a two-dose intramuscular series
w: It is live and given once subcutaneously
It is non-live and given once intradermally
It is live and given as a two-dose oral series
qs.x: The recombinant zoster vaccine is a non-live, adjuvanted vaccine given intramuscularly in two doses. The older live zoster vaccine was a single subcutaneous dose and is no longer used in the US.

qs.q: When should a patient start valacyclovir for a cold sore outbreak?
qs.a: At the first sign of tingling or burning
w: After the blisters have crusted over
Only after the sore has lasted a week
Once the sore becomes infected
qs.x: Antivirals for cold sores work best when started at the earliest symptoms, before blisters fully form. Starting after crusting gives little benefit.

qs.q: Which side effects are common when a patient starts metformin?
qs.a: Diarrhea, nausea, and stomach upset
w: Weight gain and fluid retention
Frequent low blood sugar when used alone
Genital yeast infections
qs.x: GI upset is the most common side effect of metformin and is reduced by taking it with meals. Metformin alone rarely causes low blood sugar; weight gain and fluid retention are linked to pioglitazone.

qs.q: Which statement about insulin glargine is correct?
qs.a: It should not be mixed with other insulins in the same syringe
w: It is cloudy and must be rolled before use
It is given only right before each meal
It can be mixed with regular insulin in one syringe
qs.x: Insulin glargine is a clear, long-acting insulin that must not be mixed or diluted with other insulins. NPH is the cloudy insulin that is rolled to mix.

qs.q: When is insulin lispro given in relation to meals?
qs.a: Within about 15 minutes before a meal or right after eating
w: Once a day at the same time without regard to meals
At bedtime regardless of food intake
About an hour after finishing a meal
qs.x: Insulin lispro is rapid-acting and is timed to meals to cover the rise in blood glucose. Once-daily dosing without regard to meals describes basal insulin such as glargine.

qs.q: How should NPH insulin be prepared before drawing up or injecting?
qs.a: Gently roll the vial or pen to evenly mix the cloudy suspension
w: Shake it hard until it foams
Use only if the liquid is completely clear
Warm it in a microwave before use
qs.x: NPH is a cloudy suspension that must be gently mixed for a consistent dose. Shaking hard causes foaming, and heating can damage the insulin.

qs.q: What is the main adverse effect to watch for with glipizide?
qs.a: Low blood sugar, especially if a meal is skipped
w: High blood sugar after meals
Genital yeast infections
Lactic acidosis
qs.x: Glipizide is a sulfonylurea that stimulates insulin release and can cause hypoglycemia, especially in older adults or with missed meals. Lactic acidosis is a rare concern with metformin.

qs.q: How should levothyroxine be taken?
qs.a: On an empty stomach with water, before breakfast
w: With breakfast and a calcium supplement
At bedtime with a glass of milk
With an iron pill to improve absorption
qs.x: Levothyroxine is best absorbed on an empty stomach, usually 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast. Calcium, iron, and food reduce absorption.

qs.q: How does methimazole treat hyperthyroidism?
qs.a: It blocks the thyroid gland from making new thyroid hormone
w: It replaces missing thyroid hormone
It destroys thyroid tissue with radiation
It blocks the effects of thyroid hormone on the heart
qs.x: Methimazole is an antithyroid drug that inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis. Replacing hormone is what levothyroxine does, and blocking cardiac effects describes beta blockers.

qs.q: Which history is a contraindication to semaglutide?
qs.a: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer
w: Seasonal allergies
Mild osteoarthritis
A history of migraine
qs.x: GLP-1 agonists such as semaglutide carry a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors and are contraindicated with a history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2. Allergies and arthritis are not contraindications.

qs.q: Which side effect is common with empagliflozin?
qs.a: Genital yeast infections
w: Weight gain
Frequent low blood sugar when used alone
Dry cough
qs.x: SGLT2 inhibitors increase glucose in the urine, which raises the risk of genital yeast infections and urinary tract infections. They usually cause slight weight loss, not gain.

qs.q: Which symptoms in a patient taking pioglitazone should be reported?
qs.a: Rapid weight gain, swelling, and shortness of breath
w: Mild headache in the morning
Mild nasal congestion
A slight increase in appetite
qs.x: Pioglitazone causes fluid retention and has a boxed warning for heart failure, so these symptoms must be reported. Mild congestion is a less urgent side effect.

qs.q: Ondansetron belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: Serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist
w: Dopamine receptor antagonist
Histamine H2 receptor antagonist
Proton pump inhibitor
qs.x: Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 serotonin receptors to prevent nausea and vomiting. Metoclopramide and prochlorperazine are the dopamine antagonist antiemetics.

qs.q: Which symptom in a patient taking metoclopramide should be reported?
qs.a: Involuntary movements of the face or tongue
w: Mild loose stools
Mild fatigue
Slight increase in appetite
qs.x: Metoclopramide has a boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia, which may be irreversible. Mild fatigue is a common, less urgent side effect.

qs.q: When is oral omeprazole usually given for best effect?
qs.a: Before a meal, typically before breakfast
w: After the largest meal of the day
At bedtime on a full stomach
With an antacid to speed action
qs.x: Proton pump inhibitors work best when taken before a meal, when acid pumps are being activated. Taking it after eating reduces its effect.

qs.q: Which teaching about sucralfate is correct?
qs.a: Take it on an empty stomach, apart from other oral medicines
w: Take it with every meal and with other pills
Take it with an antacid at the same time
Chew it with milk for faster action
qs.x: Sucralfate forms a protective coating and works best on an empty stomach; it can bind other drugs and reduce their absorption. Taking it together with antacids reduces its effect.

qs.q: How does lactulose help a patient with hepatic encephalopathy?
qs.a: It traps ammonia in the colon so it passes in the stool
w: It helps the liver make more albumin
It kills all bacteria in the bowel
It increases protein absorption from food
qs.x: Lactulose acidifies the colon, converting ammonia to a form that is trapped and excreted, which lowers blood ammonia. It does not improve albumin production.

qs.q: Which finding should be reported before a patient uses loperamide for diarrhea?
qs.a: Bloody stools with a fever
w: Two loose stools in one day
Mild stomach cramping
A recent change in diet
qs.x: Bloody diarrhea with fever can signal an invasive infection, and slowing the bowel may make it worse. Mild cramping with loose stools is a common reason for using loperamide.

qs.q: Which teaching about bisacodyl enteric-coated tablets is correct?
qs.a: Do not take within an hour of antacids or milk
w: Chew the tablets for faster relief
Take them with milk to protect the stomach
Crush them and mix into applesauce
qs.x: Antacids and milk can dissolve the enteric coating early, causing stomach irritation and cramping. The tablets must be swallowed whole.

qs.q: A patient receiving IV promethazine reports burning pain at the IV site. How should the LVN interpret this?
qs.a: Possible severe tissue injury that must be reported right away
w: An expected sensation that needs no follow-up
A sign the drug is working on nausea
A mild allergy best treated with ice
qs.x: Promethazine has a boxed warning for severe tissue injury, including gangrene, from IV use or extravasation. Burning or pain at the site must be reported promptly.

qs.q: Which teaching about pancrelipase capsules is correct?
qs.a: Take with every meal and snack, swallowing capsules whole
w: Take once a day at bedtime on an empty stomach
Crush and chew the capsule contents
Take only when stools become loose
qs.x: Pancrelipase replaces digestive enzymes, so it must be taken with food. Crushing or chewing the beads can irritate the mouth and reduce effectiveness.

qs.q: Before a patient starts misoprostol to prevent NSAID-related ulcers, what is most important to confirm?
qs.a: That the patient is not pregnant
w: That the patient has no seasonal allergies
That the patient avoids dairy products
That the patient has normal vision
qs.x: Misoprostol can cause miscarriage and birth defects and has a boxed warning against use in pregnancy for ulcer prevention. Allergies and dairy are not relevant.

qs.q: Why is folic acid recommended before and during early pregnancy?
qs.a: To reduce the risk of neural tube defects
w: To prevent morning sickness
To reduce the risk of preterm labor
To prevent gestational diabetes
qs.x: Adequate folic acid before conception and early in pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida. It does not treat nausea or prevent gestational diabetes.

qs.q: Which teaching is important for a patient taking doxylamine-pyridoxine for nausea in pregnancy?
qs.a: It can cause drowsiness, so avoid driving until effects are known
w: It commonly causes insomnia, so take it in the morning
It must be chewed for best absorption
It causes the urine to turn blue
qs.x: Doxylamine is a sedating antihistamine, so drowsiness is common. The tablets are delayed-release and should be swallowed whole, not chewed.

qs.q: When is levonorgestrel emergency contraception most effective?
qs.a: When taken as soon as possible after unprotected sex
w: When taken a week after unprotected sex
When taken only after a missed period
When taken daily for a full month
qs.x: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception works mainly by delaying ovulation, so it is most effective when taken as soon as possible. It is not effective once pregnancy is established.

qs.q: Labetalol belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: Combined alpha-1 and nonselective beta blocker
w: Calcium channel blocker
ACE inhibitor
Direct arterial vasodilator
qs.x: Labetalol blocks both alpha-1 and beta receptors and is commonly used for hypertension in pregnancy. Hydralazine is the direct vasodilator, and ACE inhibitors are avoided in pregnancy.

qs.q: Terbutaline carries a boxed warning about which use?
qs.a: Prolonged use to prevent preterm labor
w: Short-term use for an asthma attack
Use for chronic bronchitis
Use in patients with seasonal allergies
qs.x: Terbutaline should not be used for prolonged tocolysis, and oral terbutaline should not be used for preterm labor, because of serious maternal heart problems and death. It is approved for bronchospasm.

qs.q: Which factor increases the risk of serious cardiovascular events with drospirenone-ethinyl estradiol?
qs.a: Cigarette smoking, especially over age 35
w: Taking it at the same time each day
A history of seasonal allergies
Drinking caffeinated coffee
qs.x: Combined hormonal contraceptives carry a boxed warning that smoking increases the risk of heart attack, stroke, and clots, especially in women over 35. Taking the pill at the same time daily is correct use.

qs.q: Which symptom in a patient taking an ethinyl estradiol-norgestimate pill should be reported right away?
qs.a: Sudden pain and swelling in one calf
w: Mild breast tenderness in the first month
Light spotting between periods early on
Mild nausea that improves with food
qs.x: Calf pain and swelling may signal a deep vein thrombosis, a serious risk with estrogen-containing contraceptives. Breast tenderness, spotting, and mild nausea are common early side effects.

qs.q: Why is erythromycin ophthalmic ointment given to newborns?
qs.a: To prevent gonococcal eye infection
w: To prevent newborn jaundice
To treat blocked tear ducts
To prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding
qs.x: Erythromycin eye ointment is given shortly after birth to prevent ophthalmia neonatorum from gonorrhea. Vitamin K deficiency bleeding is prevented with an injection of vitamin K.

qs.q: Which lab tests are checked before and during treatment with fezolinetant?
qs.a: Liver function tests
w: Thyroid function tests
Serum potassium
Hemoglobin A1C
qs.x: Fezolinetant has a boxed warning for liver injury, so liver tests are checked before starting and periodically during treatment. Thyroid and potassium tests are not specifically required.

qs.q: Which teaching improves absorption of ferrous sulfate in a pregnant patient?
qs.a: Take it with a source of vitamin C, such as orange juice
w: Take it with milk or yogurt
Take it with a calcium-based antacid
Take it with a cup of tea
qs.x: Vitamin C helps the body absorb iron. Milk, calcium antacids, and tea reduce iron absorption.

qs.q: Where is an epinephrine auto-injector given?
qs.a: The outer thigh, through clothing if needed
w: The upper arm deltoid muscle only
The abdomen, at least two inches from the navel
Into a vein in the forearm
qs.x: Epinephrine auto-injectors are injected into the anterolateral thigh, and can be given through clothing. Abdominal injection describes subcutaneous drugs such as enoxaparin.

qs.q: Which adverse effects make diphenhydramine risky for older adults?
qs.a: Confusion and urinary retention
w: Diarrhea and excess saliva
High blood sugar and weight loss
Muscle pain and dark urine
qs.x: Diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic and sedating, causing confusion, urinary retention, and falls in older adults. Diarrhea and excess saliva are cholinergic effects, the opposite.

qs.q: How does loratadine compare with diphenhydramine?
qs.a: It is a second-generation antihistamine that causes less drowsiness
w: It is more sedating and used mainly for sleep
It works by blocking leukotriene receptors
It is a nasal steroid that reduces swelling
qs.x: Loratadine is a second-generation H1 antihistamine that crosses into the brain less and causes little drowsiness. Blocking leukotrienes is how montelukast works.

qs.q: Which item should a patient taking oral cyclosporine avoid?
qs.a: Grapefruit and grapefruit juice
w: Fresh green vegetables
Plain yogurt
Whole-grain bread
qs.x: Grapefruit inhibits the enzymes that break down cyclosporine and can raise levels to toxic amounts. The other foods do not have this effect.

qs.q: Which monitoring is routine for a patient taking oral tacrolimus after a transplant?
qs.a: Trough blood levels and kidney function
w: Peak flow and oxygen saturation
INR and platelet count only
Thyroid levels and vitamin D
qs.x: Tacrolimus has a narrow therapeutic range and can harm the kidneys, so trough levels and kidney function are checked regularly. INR monitoring is for warfarin.

qs.q: Mycophenolate carries a boxed warning for which risk?
qs.a: Pregnancy loss and birth defects
w: Tendon rupture
Severe hypoglycemia
Hearing loss
qs.x: Mycophenolate has boxed warnings for embryo-fetal toxicity, serious infections, and malignancy, so pregnancy prevention is required. Tendon rupture is a fluoroquinolone warning.

qs.q: Which lab test is monitored regularly in a patient taking azathioprine?
qs.a: Complete blood count
w: Serum lithium level
Hemoglobin A1C
Serum amylase
qs.x: Azathioprine can suppress the bone marrow, so the CBC is checked for low white cells, red cells, and platelets. Lithium levels are not related.

qs.q: Which screening is done before a patient starts golimumab?
qs.a: Testing for latent tuberculosis
w: A bone density scan
An eye pressure check
A hearing test
qs.x: TNF blockers such as golimumab carry a boxed warning for serious infections, including reactivation of tuberculosis, so TB testing is done first. Bone density is not routinely required.

qs.q: Which side effect is common with dupilumab?
qs.a: Eye redness, itching, or irritation
w: Severe low blood sugar
Hair loss
Slow heart rate
qs.x: Conjunctivitis and other eye problems are among the most common side effects of dupilumab and should be reported if new or worsening. Low blood sugar and slow heart rate are not typical.

qs.q: Which lab tests are monitored in a patient taking leflunomide?
qs.a: Liver function tests
w: Serum digoxin level
Thyroid function tests
Serum lithium level
qs.x: Leflunomide has a boxed warning for liver injury, so liver tests are monitored. It also requires pregnancy prevention because of fetal harm.

qs.q: Which symptom in a patient taking capecitabine should be reported?
qs.a: Redness, swelling, or pain of the palms and soles
w: Mild darkening of the urine
A mild increase in appetite
Slight dryness of the lips
qs.x: Capecitabine commonly causes hand-foot syndrome, which can worsen without dose changes by the provider. The other findings are not typical concerns.

qs.q: Letrozole belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: Aromatase inhibitor
w: Selective estrogen receptor modulator
Antiandrogen
Tyrosine kinase inhibitor
qs.x: Letrozole blocks aromatase, lowering estrogen production in postmenopausal women. Tamoxifen is the selective estrogen receptor modulator.

qs.q: Which assessments are monitored in a patient taking abiraterone with prednisone?
qs.a: Blood pressure, serum potassium, and swelling
w: Peak flow and oxygen saturation
Vision and hearing
Blood glucose and ketones only
qs.x: Abiraterone can cause mineralocorticoid excess with high blood pressure, low potassium, and fluid retention, which is why prednisone is given with it. Liver tests are also monitored.

qs.q: Which symptom in a patient taking megestrol should be reported?
qs.a: Swelling and pain in one leg
w: A mild increase in appetite
Slight weight gain
Mild hot flashes
qs.x: Megestrol can cause blood clots, and leg pain with swelling may signal a DVT. Increased appetite and weight gain are the intended effects when used for cachexia.

qs.q: Which symptoms in a patient taking temozolomide should be reported?
qs.a: Fever, unusual bruising, or bleeding
w: Mild tiredness after doses
Slight decrease in appetite
Mild headache
qs.x: Temozolomide suppresses the bone marrow, causing low white cells and platelets, so infection and bleeding signs need prompt reporting. Mild fatigue is common.

qs.q: Why is lenalidomide available only through a restricted program?
qs.a: It can cause severe birth defects
w: It is highly addictive
It must be given only by IV in hospitals
It causes allergic reactions in most patients
qs.x: Lenalidomide is a thalidomide analog with a boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity, so a REMS program requires pregnancy testing and contraception. It is an oral drug and not addictive.

qs.q: Which findings in a patient taking ibrutinib should be reported?
qs.a: Unusual bleeding or an irregular heartbeat
w: Mild constipation
Mild dry skin
Slight increase in appetite
qs.x: Ibrutinib increases bleeding risk and can cause atrial fibrillation, so these findings need prompt reporting. Mild dry skin is not a priority concern.

qs.q: Which side effect is very common with everolimus?
qs.a: Mouth sores and ulcers
w: Excess salivation
Hearing loss
Blue-tinted vision
qs.x: Stomatitis is one of the most common everolimus side effects, and alcohol-free mouth care is encouraged. Hearing loss and blue-tinted vision are not typical.

qs.q: Which side effect is common with erlotinib?
qs.a: An acne-like rash on the face and chest
w: Hair darkening
Weight gain from fluid retention
Very slow heart rate
qs.x: EGFR inhibitors such as erlotinib commonly cause an acneiform rash, along with diarrhea. The other effects are not typical of this drug.

qs.q: Which history should be reported before a patient starts enzalutamide?
qs.a: A history of seizures
w: Seasonal allergies
Mild osteoarthritis
Lactose intolerance
qs.x: Enzalutamide can lower the seizure threshold, so a seizure history or seizure risk factors must be reported. Allergies and arthritis do not affect its use.

qs.q: Which effect should a patient be taught to expect with latanoprost eye drops?
qs.a: Gradual, possibly permanent darkening of the iris
w: Constricted pupils and dim vision at night
Bright orange discoloration of tears
Rapid loss of eyelashes
qs.x: Prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost can increase brown pigment in the iris and lengthen and darken eyelashes. Constricted pupils with poor night vision are typical of pilocarpine.

qs.q: Which history should be reported before a patient starts timolol eye drops?
qs.a: Asthma or severe COPD
w: Seasonal allergic rhinitis
Mild osteoarthritis
Recent sunburn
qs.x: Timolol is a nonselective beta blocker that can be absorbed into the bloodstream and trigger bronchospasm or slow the heart. It is contraindicated in asthma and severe COPD.

qs.q: How is permethrin cream applied to an adult for scabies?
qs.a: Over the whole body from the neck to the soles of the feet
w: Only on the visible bumps and burrows
On the scalp only, then rinsed off quickly
Only on the hands and wrists
qs.x: For scabies, permethrin is massaged into all skin from the neck down and washed off after the labeled time. Short scalp application with rinsing is how it is used for head lice.

qs.q: Which history is a contraindication to silver sulfadiazine cream?
qs.a: A known allergy to sulfa drugs
w: A known allergy to penicillin
A history of type 2 diabetes
A history of seasonal allergies
qs.x: Silver sulfadiazine is a sulfonamide, so sulfa allergy is a concern. Penicillin allergy is not a cross-reaction with sulfonamides.

qs.q: Which effect of isotretinoin should be reported promptly?
qs.a: Depressed mood or thoughts of self-harm
w: Dry, chapped lips
Mild dry skin
Mild nosebleeds in dry weather
qs.x: Isotretinoin has been linked to depression and suicidal thoughts, which require prompt reporting. Dry lips and skin are very common and expected.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for a patient using topical tretinoin?
qs.a: Use sunscreen daily since the skin burns more easily
w: Apply it to wet skin right after washing
Use it with a tanning bed for faster results
Apply a thick layer several times a day
qs.x: Topical tretinoin increases sun sensitivity, so sunscreen and sun protection are important. Applying it to wet skin or using thick layers increases irritation.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for clobetasol cream?
qs.a: Avoid applying it to the face, groin, or underarms
w: Apply it thickly under a tight bandage daily
Use it long term as an everyday moisturizer
Apply it to the eyelids for eczema
qs.x: Clobetasol is a super-high-potency steroid that can thin skin, so it is avoided on the face, groin, and underarms and used for limited periods. It is not used as a moisturizer.

qs.q: Which effect should a patient using pilocarpine eye drops expect?
qs.a: Trouble seeing in dim light, such as night driving
w: Darkening of the iris color
Dilated pupils and sensitivity to light
Yellow discoloration of the skin
qs.x: Pilocarpine constricts the pupil, which reduces vision in dim light. Dilated pupils are the opposite of its effect.

qs.q: How is lidocaine-prilocaine cream applied before a needle procedure?
qs.a: As a thick layer under an occlusive dressing, ahead of time
w: Rubbed in thoroughly right before the needle stick
Applied only after the procedure for pain
Swabbed on and rinsed off right away
qs.x: The cream needs time under an occlusive dressing to numb the skin. Rubbing it in just before the needle stick does not allow enough time for it to work.

qs.q: Mupirocin ointment is used to treat which condition?
qs.a: Impetigo caused by staph or strep bacteria
w: Ringworm and other fungal skin infections
Cold sores caused by herpes virus
Scabies infestation
qs.x: Mupirocin is a topical antibacterial used for impetigo. Fungal infections such as ringworm need an antifungal.

qs.q: What is the primary mechanism by which digoxin increases myocardial contractility?
qs.a: Inhibition of the Na+/K+ ATPase, raising intracellular calcium
w: Blockade of L-type calcium channels in myocytes
Stimulation of cardiac beta-1 adrenergic receptors
