qs.x: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen, so the iPLEDGE program requires pregnancy testing and contraception for patients who can become pregnant. Hepatotoxicity is not the reason for the restricted program.

qs.q: Which adverse effect is characteristic of latanoprost eye drops?
qs.a: Increased brown pigmentation of the iris
w: Systemic bronchospasm
Metabolic acidosis
Dry mouth
qs.x: Latanoprost, a prostaglandin F2-alpha analog that increases uveoscleral outflow, can permanently darken the iris and lengthen eyelashes. Systemic bronchospasm is a risk with timolol eye drops.

qs.q: Why should timolol eye drops be used with caution in a patient with asthma?
qs.a: Systemic absorption can block bronchial beta-2 receptors and cause bronchospasm
w: Local absorption can stimulate muscarinic receptors in the airways
It increases aqueous humor production and pulmonary secretions
It causes histamine release from conjunctival mast cells
qs.x: Timolol is a nonselective beta blocker; drops absorbed through the nasolacrimal duct can reach systemic circulation and cause bronchospasm or bradycardia. It lowers intraocular pressure by reducing aqueous production, not increasing it.

qs.q: How does pilocarpine lower intraocular pressure?
qs.a: Muscarinic agonism contracts the ciliary muscle, opening the trabecular meshwork
w: Muscarinic antagonism relaxes the ciliary muscle, increasing outflow
Beta blockade reduces aqueous humor production
Carbonic anhydrase inhibition reduces aqueous humor production
qs.x: Pilocarpine stimulates muscarinic receptors, causing miosis and ciliary muscle contraction that increases trabecular outflow. Muscarinic antagonists dilate the pupil and can worsen angle-closure glaucoma.

qs.q: What is the mechanism of dorzolamide in glaucoma?
qs.a: Inhibits carbonic anhydrase, reducing aqueous humor production
w: Activates prostaglandin receptors, increasing uveoscleral outflow
Stimulates muscarinic receptors, increasing trabecular outflow
Inhibits Rho kinase, increasing trabecular outflow
qs.x: Dorzolamide is a topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that decreases bicarbonate and aqueous humor formation by the ciliary body. Increasing uveoscleral outflow describes prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost.

qs.q: Brimonidine eye drops belong to which drug class?
qs.a: Alpha-2 adrenergic agonist
w: Beta-adrenergic antagonist
Prostaglandin analog
Muscarinic antagonist
qs.x: Brimonidine is a selective alpha-2 agonist that reduces aqueous humor production and increases uveoscleral outflow. Beta-adrenergic antagonists, such as timolol, are a separate class of glaucoma drops.

qs.q: Tropicamide is used before eye exams for which effect, and what risk should be recognized?
qs.a: Pupil dilation; it can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma
w: Pupil constriction; it can cause retinal detachment
Corneal anesthesia; it can cause corneal ulceration
Reduced eye pressure; it can cause bronchospasm
qs.x: Tropicamide is a short-acting muscarinic antagonist that causes mydriasis and cycloplegia; in narrow angles, dilation can block outflow and trigger angle closure. Pupil constriction is caused by muscarinic agonists such as pilocarpine.

qs.q: How does permethrin kill scabies mites and lice?
qs.a: Prolongs sodium channel opening in arthropod nerve cells, causing paralysis
w: Inhibits arthropod chitin synthesis, preventing molting
Binds glutamate-gated chloride channels, causing hyperpolarization
Inhibits acetylcholinesterase irreversibly in arthropod nerves
qs.x: Permethrin is a pyrethroid that delays sodium channel inactivation in parasite nerve membranes, leading to paralysis and death. Glutamate-gated chloride channels are the target of ivermectin.

qs.q: What is the mechanism of action of terbinafine?
qs.a: Inhibits squalene epoxidase, blocking ergosterol synthesis
w: Inhibits lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, blocking ergosterol synthesis
Binds ergosterol to form pores in the fungal membrane
Inhibits beta-glucan synthase in the fungal cell wall
qs.x: Terbinafine blocks squalene epoxidase, so ergosterol falls and toxic squalene builds up in fungal cells. Lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase inhibition describes azole antifungals.

qs.q: Why is topical tacrolimus useful for atopic dermatitis on the face and eyelids?
qs.a: It inhibits calcineurin in T cells without causing skin atrophy
w: It is a potent corticosteroid that penetrates thin skin well
It blocks histamine H1 receptors on skin mast cells
It inhibits squalene epoxidase in skin fungi
qs.x: Topical calcineurin inhibitors reduce T-cell cytokine production and, unlike corticosteroids, do not thin the skin, making them useful on sensitive areas. It is not a corticosteroid.

qs.q: A patient with hypertension develops a persistent dry, nonproductive cough several weeks after starting lisinopril. Which mechanism best explains this adverse effect?
qs.a: Accumulation of bradykinin from reduced breakdown
w: Direct blockade of airway beta-2 receptors
Increased aldosterone-driven airway edema
Histamine release from airway mast cells
qs.x: ACE also degrades bradykinin, so ACE inhibition lets bradykinin and substance P accumulate and trigger cough. Beta-2 blockade causes bronchospasm with beta-blockers, not ACE inhibitors.

qs.q: A patient with type 2 diabetes and albuminuric chronic kidney disease develops an intolerable dry cough on enalapril. Which medication is the best replacement that preserves renal protection?
qs.a: Losartan
w: Amlodipine
Hydrochlorothiazide
Metoprolol
qs.x: An ARB such as losartan blocks the angiotensin II receptor, reduces albuminuria, and does not raise bradykinin, so cough is uncommon. Amlodipine lowers blood pressure but lacks the antiproteinuric benefit of RAAS blockade.

qs.q: A patient with atrial fibrillation is starting long-term amiodarone. Which baseline evaluation is most appropriate?
qs.a: Thyroid function, liver enzymes, chest imaging, and pulmonary function tests
w: Serum uric acid, lipid panel, urinalysis, and bone density scan
Serum ferritin, vitamin B12 level, and peripheral smear
Fasting glucose, hemoglobin A1c, and urine albumin level
qs.x: Amiodarone can cause thyroid dysfunction, hepatotoxicity, and pulmonary toxicity, so baseline and periodic thyroid, liver, and lung assessments (plus an eye exam and ECG) are recommended. The other panels do not target amiodarone's major toxicities.

qs.q: A patient with heart failure taking digoxin and a loop diuretic presents with nausea, confusion, and yellow-tinted vision. Which electrolyte abnormality most increases the risk of this toxicity?
qs.a: Hypokalemia
w: Hypernatremia
Hypophosphatemia
Hypermagnesemia
qs.x: Digoxin competes with potassium at the Na+/K+-ATPase, so diuretic-induced hypokalemia increases digoxin binding and toxicity. Hypercalcemia can also potentiate toxicity, but hypokalemia is the classic and most common precipitant in diuretic-treated patients.

qs.q: A man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction develops painful gynecomastia on spironolactone. Which medication is the most appropriate substitute?
qs.a: Eplerenone
w: Hydralazine
Triamterene
Chlorthalidone
qs.x: Eplerenone is a selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist with minimal anti-androgen activity and has mortality benefit in HFrEF. Triamterene is potassium sparing but does not block the mineralocorticoid receptor or improve HFrEF outcomes.

qs.q: A patient with HFrEF is being transitioned to sacubitril-valsartan. Concomitant use with which drug class is contraindicated because of angioedema risk?
qs.a: ACE inhibitors
w: Loop diuretics
Beta-blockers
SGLT2 inhibitors
qs.x: Neprilysin inhibition plus ACE inhibition markedly raises bradykinin and angioedema risk, so an ACE inhibitor must be stopped with a washout before starting sacubitril-valsartan. Beta-blockers and SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended alongside it in HFrEF.

qs.q: A patient with a stable INR on warfarin is diagnosed with a urinary tract infection. Which antibiotic is most likely to cause a marked rise in INR?
qs.a: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
w: Fosfomycin
Cephalexin
Nitrofurantoin
qs.x: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits CYP2C9, the main enzyme that clears the more potent S-warfarin, so INR can rise sharply. Fosfomycin and nitrofurantoin have little effect on warfarin metabolism.

qs.q: In which patient with atrial fibrillation is apixaban NOT an appropriate choice for stroke prevention?
qs.a: A patient with a mechanical mitral valve
w: A patient older than eighty with mild anemia
A patient with well-controlled type 2 diabetes
A patient with a prior ischemic stroke
qs.x: Direct oral anticoagulants are not recommended with mechanical heart valves; warfarin is the anticoagulant of choice. Advanced age, diabetes, and prior stroke raise stroke risk and favor anticoagulation with a DOAC.

qs.q: A patient is discharged after an acute myocardial infarction. Which lipid-lowering regimen is most appropriate to start?
qs.a: High-intensity atorvastatin
w: Moderate-intensity pravastatin
Ezetimibe monotherapy
Fenofibrate monotherapy
qs.x: Patients with clinical ASCVD should receive high-intensity statin therapy, such as atorvastatin or rosuvastatin, to maximize LDL lowering and event reduction. Ezetimibe is an add-on when LDL remains above goal on a maximally tolerated statin.

qs.q: A patient presents with acute chest pain. Which history item is a contraindication to sublingual nitroglycerin?
qs.a: Use of sildenafil the previous evening
w: Daily low-dose aspirin use
Chronic metoprolol therapy
Current atorvastatin therapy
qs.x: Nitrates combined with PDE-5 inhibitors cause synergistic vasodilation and severe, potentially fatal hypotension. Aspirin, beta-blockers, and statins are all part of standard coronary disease therapy and do not contraindicate nitroglycerin.

qs.q: A patient with septic shock remains hypotensive after adequate fluid resuscitation. Which vasopressor is recommended first-line?
qs.a: Norepinephrine
w: Dopamine
Phenylephrine
Dobutamine
qs.x: Surviving Sepsis guidelines recommend norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor for septic shock. Dopamine causes more tachyarrhythmias and is no longer preferred.

qs.q: A patient receiving norepinephrine through a peripheral IV develops a cool, pale, blanched area around the insertion site. Which agent is used to treat this extravasation?
qs.a: Phentolamine infiltrated into the affected area
w: Hyaluronidase infiltrated into the affected area
Topical nitroglycerin applied to the hand only
Subcutaneous epinephrine near the site
qs.x: Phentolamine is an alpha-adrenergic antagonist that reverses local vasoconstriction from norepinephrine extravasation and limits tissue necrosis. Hyaluronidase is used for some non-vasopressor extravasations, not alpha-agonist injury.

qs.q: Vasopressin is added to norepinephrine in a patient with refractory septic shock. What is its mechanism of raising blood pressure?
qs.a: Activation of V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
w: Stimulation of beta-1 receptors on the myocardium
Inhibition of phosphodiesterase-3 in vascular tissue
Direct activation of alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem
qs.x: Vasopressin causes vasoconstriction through V1 receptors, independent of adrenergic receptors, which helps lower catecholamine requirements. Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibition describes milrinone, which tends to lower blood pressure.

qs.q: A patient develops hives, wheezing, and hypotension minutes after a bee sting. What is the preferred route for the first dose of epinephrine?
qs.a: Intramuscular injection into the anterolateral thigh
w: Subcutaneous injection into the upper arm
Slow intravenous push through a peripheral line
Nebulized inhalation through a face mask
qs.x: Intramuscular injection into the vastus lateralis gives faster, more reliable absorption than subcutaneous dosing and is first-line for anaphylaxis. IV bolus epinephrine is reserved for cardiac arrest or carefully titrated infusions because of arrhythmia risk.

qs.q: A patient with an acute anterior MI has cool extremities, low urine output, and low cardiac output with borderline blood pressure. Which agent primarily increases myocardial contractility through beta-1 stimulation?
qs.a: Dobutamine
w: Phenylephrine
Vasopressin
Midodrine
qs.x: Dobutamine is a predominantly beta-1 agonist inotrope used in low-output cardiogenic shock. Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist that raises afterload without improving contractility.

qs.q: A patient on chronic beta-blocker therapy develops low-output decompensated heart failure. Why might milrinone be chosen over dobutamine?
qs.a: It inhibits phosphodiesterase-3 and bypasses beta receptors
w: It stimulates alpha-1 receptors to raise vascular tone
It blocks the sodium-potassium ATPase in myocytes
It activates dopamine receptors to improve renal flow
qs.x: Milrinone raises cAMP by inhibiting PDE-3, so its inotropic effect does not depend on beta receptors occupied by a beta-blocker. Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition is digoxin's mechanism.

qs.q: Shortly after a phenylephrine infusion is started for hypotension, the patient's heart rate falls. What best explains this finding?
qs.a: Reflex bradycardia from increased vascular resistance
w: Direct beta-1 receptor blockade at the sinus node
Drug-induced complete heart block from conduction toxicity
Muscarinic receptor stimulation at the AV node
qs.x: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist; the rise in blood pressure triggers a baroreceptor-mediated reflex slowing of heart rate. It has no beta-blocking or direct muscarinic activity.

qs.q: A patient with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is started on midodrine. Which adverse effect is most important to monitor for?
qs.a: Supine hypertension
w: Severe hypokalemia
Bronchospasm
Profound bradycardia at rest
qs.x: Midodrine is an alpha-1 agonist prodrug that can cause marked supine hypertension, so patients are taught to take it during daytime upright hours and avoid lying flat afterward. Bronchospasm is a beta-blocker concern.

qs.q: Compared with norepinephrine in septic shock, dopamine is associated with which disadvantage?
qs.a: Higher rate of tachyarrhythmias
w: Greater risk of digital ischemia
Inability to raise mean arterial pressure
Need for administration through an arterial line
qs.x: Trials comparing the two agents found more arrhythmic events with dopamine, which is why norepinephrine is first-line. Dopamine does raise blood pressure, and both agents can cause peripheral ischemia.

qs.q: Synthetic angiotensin II is added for a patient with refractory vasodilatory shock. Which adverse effect requires concurrent prophylaxis?
qs.a: Venous and arterial thromboembolism
w: Severe hypoglycemia
Acute pancreatitis
Drug-induced lupus
qs.x: Angiotensin II was associated with more thromboembolic events in its pivotal trial, so the label recommends concurrent VTE prophylaxis. Hypoglycemia and pancreatitis are not characteristic effects.

qs.q: On day seven of IV heparin, a patient's platelet count has fallen by more than half and a new DVT is found. Heparin has been discontinued. Which anticoagulant is most appropriate now?
qs.a: Argatroban
w: Enoxaparin
Warfarin
Dalteparin
qs.x: Suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia requires a non-heparin anticoagulant such as the direct thrombin inhibitor argatroban. Low-molecular-weight heparins cross-react with HIT antibodies, and starting warfarin alone in acute HIT can cause venous limb gangrene.

qs.q: A patient on a continuous unfractionated heparin infusion develops major bleeding. Which agent reverses the anticoagulant effect?
qs.a: Protamine sulfate
w: Vitamin K
Idarucizumab
Desmopressin
qs.x: Protamine is a positively charged protein that binds and neutralizes heparin rapidly. Vitamin K reverses warfarin, and idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.

qs.q: Enoxaparin is being considered for VTE treatment. Which patient factor most warrants adjustment or an alternative anticoagulant?
qs.a: Severe renal impairment
w: Mild hepatic steatosis
History of penicillin allergy
Well-controlled hypothyroidism
qs.x: Enoxaparin is renally cleared, so it accumulates in severe renal impairment and raises bleeding risk; dose adjustment or unfractionated heparin is used. Mild liver disease and the other conditions do not significantly alter its clearance.

qs.q: A patient taking warfarin presents with an intracranial hemorrhage and a markedly elevated INR. Which is the most appropriate reversal strategy?
qs.a: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K
w: Protamine sulfate plus fresh frozen plasma
Oral vitamin K alone with repeat INR
Idarucizumab plus IV tranexamic acid
qs.x: 4F-PCC rapidly replaces factors II, VII, IX, and X, and IV vitamin K sustains reversal as the liver makes new factors. Oral vitamin K alone is far too slow for life-threatening bleeding.

qs.q: A patient taking dabigatran needs emergency surgery for a perforated bowel. Which agent specifically reverses dabigatran?
qs.a: Idarucizumab
w: Andexanet alfa
Protamine sulfate
Phytonadione
qs.x: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with high affinity. Andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban and rivaroxaban.

qs.q: A patient with a DVT has triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome. Why is rivaroxaban not recommended for long-term anticoagulation?
qs.a: It was linked to more thrombotic events than warfarin
w: It cannot be given to patients with lupus anticoagulant tests
It requires frequent INR monitoring in this population
It causes heparin-induced thrombocytopenia in these patients
qs.x: In triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome, rivaroxaban was associated with higher rates of recurrent thrombosis than warfarin, so warfarin is preferred. Rivaroxaban does not require INR monitoring.

qs.q: A patient after coronary stenting has a CYP2C19 poor-metabolizer genotype. Why is clopidogrel likely to be less effective?
qs.a: Reduced conversion of the prodrug to its active metabolite
w: Faster renal elimination of the active drug
Increased binding of the drug to plasma albumin
Upregulation of platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors
qs.x: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated mainly by CYP2C19, so poor metabolizers generate less active metabolite and get weaker P2Y12 inhibition. An alternative such as ticagrelor or prasugrel is often chosen.

qs.q: A patient with acute coronary syndrome is undergoing PCI. Which history is a contraindication to prasugrel?
qs.a: Prior transient ischemic attack
w: Prior hip replacement
Well-controlled asthma
History of gout
qs.x: Prasugrel carries a boxed warning and is contraindicated in patients with prior stroke or TIA because of increased intracranial bleeding. Asthma is a caution with ticagrelor because of dyspnea, not prasugrel.

qs.q: A patient with iron deficiency anemia is starting oral ferrous sulfate. Which counseling point is accurate?
qs.a: Dark stools and constipation are expected effects
w: Take it together with calcium carbonate for absorption
Take it with milk to improve absorption
Bright red blood in stool is an expected effect
qs.x: Oral iron commonly darkens stools and causes constipation or GI upset. Calcium, antacids, and dairy decrease iron absorption, and bright red blood suggests bleeding that needs evaluation.

qs.q: A patient with CKD-related anemia is being evaluated for epoetin alfa. What should be assessed before starting therapy?
qs.a: Iron stores, including ferritin and transferrin saturation
w: Serum uric acid and lactate dehydrogenase
Hemoglobin A2 by electrophoresis
Serum haptoglobin and direct antiglobulin test
qs.x: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents need adequate iron to work, so iron deficiency is assessed and corrected first. Hemolysis tests and hemoglobin electrophoresis are not routine prerequisites.

qs.q: Rapid sequence intubation is planned. In which patient is succinylcholine contraindicated?
qs.a: A patient with a spinal cord injury two weeks ago
w: A patient with a full stomach after a meal
A patient with well-controlled asthma
A patient with a history of migraine
qs.x: After denervation injury, upregulated extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors can release large amounts of potassium with succinylcholine and cause fatal hyperkalemia. A full stomach is an indication for rapid sequence intubation, not a contraindication to succinylcholine.

qs.q: After succinylcholine for intubation, a patient develops masseter rigidity, rising end-tidal carbon dioxide, tachycardia, and fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Malignant hyperthermia
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
Thyroid storm
qs.x: Succinylcholine and volatile anesthetics can trigger malignant hyperthermia in susceptible patients through uncontrolled RyR1 calcium release; dantrolene is the treatment. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows antipsychotics and develops over days.

qs.q: How does sugammadex reverse rocuronium-induced neuromuscular blockade?
qs.a: It encapsulates rocuronium in plasma
w: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the junction
It competitively blocks nicotinic receptors
It enhances renal excretion of rocuronium
qs.x: Sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin that binds rocuronium and vecuronium, pulling them away from the neuromuscular junction. Neostigmine reverses blockade by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase.

qs.q: A woman using an oral hormonal contraceptive receives sugammadex after surgery. Which counseling point is most important?
qs.a: Use a backup nonhormonal contraceptive method for a week
w: Expect permanent loss of contraceptive effect
Double the next contraceptive pill to compensate
No interaction with hormonal contraception occurs
qs.x: Sugammadex can bind progestogen, so the label advises treating its use like a missed pill and using backup nonhormonal contraception for the following seven days. The effect is temporary, not permanent.

qs.q: Etomidate is chosen as an induction agent for a hemodynamically unstable patient. Which adverse effect is characteristic of this drug?
qs.a: Transient adrenal suppression
w: Malignant hyperthermia
Marked hypotension
Bronchospasm from histamine release
qs.x: Etomidate inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase, which transiently suppresses cortisol synthesis. It is chosen precisely because it causes little hypotension.

qs.q: A hypotensive trauma patient with a history of severe asthma needs rapid sequence intubation. Which induction agent is most appropriate?
qs.a: Ketamine
w: Propofol
Methohexital
Thiopental
qs.x: Ketamine, an NMDA antagonist, tends to preserve blood pressure through sympathetic stimulation and causes bronchodilation. Propofol often causes significant hypotension in hemodynamically unstable patients.

qs.q: A ventilated patient has been sedated with a propofol infusion for several days. Which laboratory value should be monitored because of the drug's formulation?
qs.a: Serum triglycerides
w: Serum ammonia
Serum lithium level
Serum uric acid
qs.x: Propofol is delivered in a lipid emulsion, so prolonged infusions can cause hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis. Ammonia monitoring relates to valproate or liver disease, not propofol.

qs.q: Midazolam is given for procedural sedation. Which effect is most characteristic of this drug?
qs.a: Anterograde amnesia
w: Dissociative anesthesia with nystagmus
Prolonged neuromuscular paralysis
Significant analgesia without sedation
qs.x: Benzodiazepines such as midazolam produce sedation, anxiolysis, and anterograde amnesia but no meaningful analgesia. Dissociative anesthesia with nystagmus describes ketamine.

qs.q: A rapid IV bolus of fentanyl is given during induction, and bag-mask ventilation suddenly becomes very difficult. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Opioid-induced chest wall rigidity
w: Histamine-mediated anaphylaxis
Tension pneumothorax from positive pressure
Malignant hyperthermia crisis
qs.x: Rapid administration of potent opioids such as fentanyl can cause chest wall and glottic rigidity that impairs ventilation; it responds to neuromuscular blockade or naloxone. Fentanyl causes little histamine release compared with morphine.

qs.q: A patient has symptomatic sinus bradycardia with hypotension and dizziness. Which medication is first-line?
qs.a: Atropine
w: Adenosine
Metoprolol
Diltiazem
qs.x: Atropine blocks vagal muscarinic tone at the sinus and AV nodes and is the first-line drug in ACLS bradycardia algorithms. Adenosine, metoprolol, and diltiazem all slow the heart rate further.

qs.q: A patient receives repeated albuterol nebulizer treatments for an asthma exacerbation. Which laboratory change is expected?
qs.a: Decreased serum potassium
w: Increased serum sodium
Decreased serum glucose
Increased serum calcium
qs.x: Beta-2 stimulation activates Na+/K+-ATPase and shifts potassium into cells, which lowers serum potassium. Beta-agonists tend to raise, not lower, serum glucose.

qs.q: Budesonide-formoterol can be used as both daily maintenance and as-needed reliever therapy in asthma. Which property of formoterol makes this possible?
qs.a: Rapid onset of bronchodilation
w: Antimuscarinic action on airway smooth muscle
Absence of any systemic absorption
Inhibition of leukotriene synthesis
qs.x: Formoterol is a long-acting beta-2 agonist with a fast onset, so it relieves symptoms quickly while the paired corticosteroid treats inflammation. Salmeterol has a slower onset and is not used as a reliever.

qs.q: A patient with persistent asthma starts inhaled fluticasone. Which counseling point best prevents its most common local adverse effect?
qs.a: Rinse the mouth and spit after each use
w: Use it only during acute wheezing episodes
Take it with food to reduce stomach upset
Inhale it immediately before exercise
qs.x: Inhaled corticosteroids can cause oropharyngeal candidiasis and dysphonia; rinsing and spitting, plus using a spacer, reduces this. ICS are controllers and are not used as rescue therapy.

qs.q: Why must salmeterol be combined with an inhaled corticosteroid in a patient with asthma?
qs.a: LABA monotherapy in asthma increases asthma-related deaths
w: Salmeterol is inactive without a corticosteroid present
Corticosteroids are needed to prevent salmeterol tolerance
Salmeterol monotherapy causes severe oral candidiasis
qs.x: Long-acting beta-agonist monotherapy in asthma was associated with increased severe exacerbations and asthma-related death, so it is used only with an ICS. Oral candidiasis is a corticosteroid effect, not a salmeterol effect.

qs.q: A patient with COPD is being started on tiotropium. Which coexisting condition warrants the most caution?
qs.a: Urinary retention from prostatic hyperplasia
w: Hypothyroidism on replacement therapy
Mild chronic kidney disease
Osteoarthritis of the knees
qs.x: Tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist and can worsen urinary retention and narrow-angle glaucoma. Hypothyroidism and osteoarthritis are not affected by anticholinergic bronchodilators.

qs.q: A teenager with asthma and allergic rhinitis is taking montelukast. Which adverse effect carries an FDA boxed warning?
qs.a: Neuropsychiatric events, including suicidal thoughts
w: Severe hepatotoxicity requiring liver transplant
Cardiac arrhythmias with QT prolongation
Agranulocytosis with severe infection
qs.x: The FDA added a boxed warning for serious neuropsychiatric events such as agitation, sleep disturbance, depression, and suicidality with montelukast. Hepatotoxicity is associated with zileuton, another leukotriene modifier.

qs.q: A patient with COPD on long-term theophylline develops nausea, tachycardia, and a seizure after starting a new antibiotic. Which antibiotic most likely caused this?
qs.a: Ciprofloxacin
w: Amoxicillin
Cephalexin
Doxycycline
qs.x: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, the main enzyme that metabolizes theophylline, so levels rise into the toxic range. Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index and toxicity causes arrhythmias and seizures.

qs.q: Roflumilast is added for a patient with severe COPD, chronic bronchitis, and frequent exacerbations. What is its mechanism of action?
qs.a: Selective inhibition of phosphodiesterase-4
w: Blockade of muscarinic M3 receptors
Antagonism of cysteinyl leukotriene receptors
Binding and neutralizing circulating IgE
qs.x: Roflumilast inhibits PDE-4, increasing cAMP in inflammatory cells and reducing exacerbations. It is not a bronchodilator; M3 blockade describes tiotropium.

qs.q: A patient with severe allergic asthma and an elevated serum IgE is started on omalizumab. What should be done after each injection?
qs.a: Observe the patient for anaphylaxis
w: Check a serum theophylline level
Obtain an ECG to check the QT interval
Measure blood glucose over several hours
qs.x: Omalizumab, an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody, carries a boxed warning for anaphylaxis, so patients are observed after administration and taught to recognize symptoms. It does not affect theophylline levels or the QT interval.

qs.q: A patient with cystic fibrosis is starting elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor. Which laboratory test requires routine monitoring?
qs.a: Liver function tests
w: Serum lithium levels
Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Serum uric acid
qs.x: CFTR modulators can raise transaminases and bilirubin, and serious liver injury has been reported, so liver tests are checked at baseline and periodically. Thyroid and uric acid monitoring are not required.

qs.q: A patient on phenytoin for epilepsy presents with horizontal nystagmus, ataxia, and slurred speech after a recent dose increase. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: Phenytoin toxicity from saturable metabolism
w: New posterior circulation stroke
Expected effect of subtherapeutic dosing
Vitamin B12 deficiency from phenytoin
qs.x: Phenytoin follows zero-order kinetics at therapeutic levels, so small dose increases can cause large rises in serum level and cerebellar signs such as nystagmus and ataxia. Stroke is possible but less likely given the timing with a dose change.

qs.q: Fosphenytoin is chosen instead of IV phenytoin in a patient with status epilepticus. What is a key advantage of fosphenytoin?
qs.a: Less risk of local tissue injury at the infusion site
w: No need for cardiac monitoring during infusion
No effect on hepatic enzyme metabolism
No risk of hypotension during infusion
qs.x: Fosphenytoin is a water-soluble prodrug with less infusion-site injury, including purple glove syndrome, and it can be given IM. Cardiac monitoring is still needed because hypotension and arrhythmias can occur.

qs.q: A patient has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting several minutes and has IV access. Which medication is the first-line treatment?
qs.a: Intravenous lorazepam
w: Intravenous levetiracetam
Intravenous phenobarbital
Intravenous propofol
qs.x: Benzodiazepines such as IV lorazepam are first-line for status epilepticus. Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate are second-line agents if seizures continue, and propofol is reserved for refractory status.

qs.q: A woman of reproductive age with generalized epilepsy is considering valproic acid. Which risk is most important to discuss?
qs.a: Neural tube defects and other major birth defects
w: Gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism
Kidney stones and metabolic acidosis
Stevens-Johnson syndrome in carriers of HLA-B*1502
qs.x: Valproate carries a boxed warning for major congenital malformations, especially neural tube defects, and reduced IQ after in utero exposure. Gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism are typical of phenytoin.

qs.q: A patient on valproic acid has lamotrigine added. Why does this combination require especially slow lamotrigine titration?
qs.a: Valproate raises lamotrigine levels and serious rash risk
w: Valproate lowers lamotrigine levels and causes seizures
Lamotrigine induces valproate metabolism and causes hepatotoxicity
The combination causes severe QT prolongation
qs.x: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation, roughly doubling its levels and raising the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome. A slower, lower titration schedule is used.

qs.q: Before starting carbamazepine in a patient of Han Chinese ancestry, which test is recommended?
qs.a: HLA-B*1502 genotyping
w: TPMT enzyme activity
G6PD enzyme activity
CYP2C19 genotyping
qs.x: Patients with HLA-B*1502, common in many Asian populations, have a much higher risk of carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. TPMT testing applies to thiopurines.

qs.q: Which patient with migraine has a contraindication to sumatriptan?
qs.a: A patient with known coronary artery disease
w: A patient with well-controlled asthma
A patient with mild chronic kidney disease
A patient with seasonal allergic rhinitis
qs.x: Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists that can cause coronary vasoconstriction, so they are contraindicated in ischemic heart disease, prior stroke, and uncontrolled hypertension. Asthma does not limit triptan use.

qs.q: Why is carbidopa combined with levodopa in Parkinson disease?
qs.a: It blocks peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine
w: It directly stimulates central dopamine receptors
It inhibits monoamine oxidase B in the brain
It blocks central muscarinic receptors
qs.x: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral dopa decarboxylase and does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so more levodopa reaches the brain and peripheral nausea is reduced. MAO-B inhibition describes selegiline and rasagiline.

qs.q: A patient presents with acute ischemic stroke symptoms within the treatment window. Which finding is an absolute contraindication to alteplase?
qs.a: Intracranial hemorrhage on noncontrast head CT
w: Age older than eighty years
Mild facial droop on the affected side
History of well-controlled hypertension
qs.x: Any intracranial hemorrhage on CT rules out thrombolysis. Advanced age and controlled hypertension are not absolute contraindications, and blood pressure must simply be controlled before treatment.

qs.q: A patient with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage is started on nimodipine. What is the purpose of this therapy?
qs.a: To improve outcomes from delayed cerebral ischemia
w: To lower blood pressure to normal levels quickly
To prevent rebleeding from the aneurysm
To prevent early post-hemorrhage seizures
qs.x: Nimodipine improves neurologic outcome after subarachnoid hemorrhage by reducing delayed ischemic deficits. It is given orally or by feeding tube only; IV administration of the capsule contents can cause cardiac arrest.

qs.q: A patient with an overdose of extended-release morphine awakens after IV naloxone. Why does this patient still need prolonged observation?
qs.a: Naloxone's effect may wear off before the opioid's
w: Naloxone causes delayed respiratory depression itself
Naloxone enhances later absorption of the opioid
Naloxone blocks the liver's metabolism of morphine
qs.x: Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than many opioids, especially extended-release or long-acting agents, so sedation and respiratory depression can recur. Repeat doses or an infusion may be needed.

qs.q: Which patient factor most increases the risk of hepatotoxicity from acetaminophen within the usual dosing range?
qs.a: Chronic heavy alcohol use
w: Concurrent use of omeprazole
Mild chronic kidney disease
History of peptic ulcer disease
qs.x: Chronic alcohol use induces CYP2E1 and depletes glutathione, increasing toxic NAPQI and liver injury. Peptic ulcer disease is a concern with NSAIDs, not acetaminophen.

qs.q: In which postoperative patient should ketorolac be avoided?
qs.a: A patient with acute kidney injury after surgery
w: A patient with well-controlled hypothyroidism
A patient with mild seasonal allergies
A patient with controlled hyperlipidemia
qs.x: Ketorolac is a potent NSAID that reduces renal prostaglandins and can worsen kidney injury; it is also avoided in active GI bleeding and for perioperative pain in CABG. The other conditions do not limit its use.

qs.q: A patient taking sertraline is prescribed tramadol for back pain. Which adverse effect is of greatest concern?
qs.a: Serotonin syndrome
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Severe hypertensive crisis
Agranulocytosis
qs.x: Tramadol inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake in addition to its opioid effect, so combining it with an SSRI raises serotonin syndrome risk. Tramadol also lowers the seizure threshold.

qs.q: A patient is starting methadone for opioid use disorder. Which test is most important to monitor for its cardiac risk?
qs.a: Electrocardiogram for QT interval
w: Echocardiogram for ejection fraction
Serum troponin for myocardial injury
Exercise stress test for ischemia
qs.x: Methadone prolongs the QT interval and can cause torsades de pointes, particularly at higher doses or with other QT-prolonging drugs. It does not reduce ejection fraction or cause ischemia.

qs.q: A patient with opioid use disorder who used heroin a few hours ago requests buprenorphine induction. What is the main risk of giving it now?
qs.a: Precipitated opioid withdrawal
w: Severe respiratory depression
Serotonin syndrome
Malignant hyperthermia
qs.x: Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial mu agonist that displaces full agonists and can precipitate withdrawal, so induction usually waits until mild-to-moderate withdrawal is present. Its ceiling effect makes respiratory depression less likely than with full agonists.

qs.q: A patient with end-stage renal disease received repeated meperidine and now has tremor and myoclonus followed by a seizure. What is the cause?
qs.a: Accumulation of the metabolite normeperidine
w: Accumulation of morphine-6-glucuronide
Opioid-induced hypoglycemia
Direct histamine release in the brain
qs.x: Normeperidine is a renally cleared metabolite that causes CNS excitation and seizures, which is why meperidine is avoided in renal impairment and older adults. Morphine-6-glucuronide is morphine's metabolite.

qs.q: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease needs an opioid for severe pain. Why is morphine a poor choice?
qs.a: Its active metabolites accumulate and cause toxicity
w: It is only available by the intravenous route
It is eliminated mainly by the liver unchanged
It has no effect on visceral pain
qs.x: Morphine's glucuronide metabolites are renally cleared and accumulate in kidney failure, causing sedation, respiratory depression, and neurotoxicity. Fentanyl or hydromorphone with caution are often preferred.

qs.q: Compared with nonselective NSAIDs such as naproxen, celecoxib is associated with which characteristic?
qs.a: Lower GI ulcer risk with similar cardiovascular warnings
w: Higher GI ulcer risk with no cardiovascular warnings
No renal effects and no cardiovascular warnings
Strong antiplatelet effect similar to aspirin
qs.x: Selective COX-2 inhibition spares gastric protective prostaglandins, but celecoxib carries the same boxed warnings for cardiovascular thrombotic events and GI bleeding as other NSAIDs. It has no meaningful antiplatelet effect.

qs.q: A mechanically ventilated patient is sedated with dexmedetomidine. Which adverse effect is most common?
qs.a: Bradycardia and hypotension
w: Severe respiratory depression
Hypertriglyceridemia
Malignant hyperthermia
qs.x: Dexmedetomidine is a central alpha-2 agonist that reduces sympathetic outflow, causing bradycardia and hypotension with relatively little respiratory depression. Hypertriglyceridemia is a propofol effect.

qs.q: A patient stable on lithium for bipolar disorder develops coarse tremor, confusion, and ataxia after starting a new medication for hypertension. Which medication most likely caused this?
qs.a: Hydrochlorothiazide
w: Amlodipine
Hydralazine
Doxazosin
qs.x: Thiazides increase proximal sodium and lithium reabsorption, raising lithium levels into the toxic range. ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs have a similar effect, while amlodipine does not meaningfully change lithium clearance.

qs.q: Which laboratory tests should be monitored periodically in a patient on long-term lithium?
qs.a: Renal function and thyroid function
w: Liver enzymes and serum lipase
Complete blood count and haptoglobin
Serum prolactin and fasting lipids
qs.x: Lithium can cause hypothyroidism and chronic kidney effects, including nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, so TSH and renal function are checked along with drug levels. Lithium tends to cause leukocytosis rather than cytopenias.

qs.q: A patient with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is starting clozapine. Which monitoring is required?
qs.a: Absolute neutrophil count
w: Serum lithium level
Serum ammonia level
Thyroid antibodies
qs.x: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia, so the absolute neutrophil count is monitored on a set schedule. Myocarditis, seizures, and metabolic effects are other important clozapine risks.

qs.q: A patient has generalized anxiety disorder without other psychiatric conditions. Which medication is an appropriate first-line long-term treatment?
qs.a: Sertraline
w: Alprazolam
Hydroxyzine
Propranolol
qs.x: SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line maintenance therapy for generalized anxiety disorder. Benzodiazepines such as alprazolam carry dependence and misuse risks and are not first-line long-term therapy.

qs.q: A patient with major depression asks about bupropion. Which history is a contraindication?
qs.a: Current bulimia nervosa
w: Prior SSRI-related sexual dysfunction
Current tobacco use
History of hypothyroidism
qs.x: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in seizure disorders and in bulimia or anorexia nervosa. SSRI-related sexual dysfunction and smoking are reasons bupropion may be preferred.

qs.q: A few hours after receiving IM haloperidol, a patient develops sustained neck twisting and upward eye deviation. Which treatment is most appropriate?
qs.a: Benztropine
w: Bromocriptine
Dantrolene
Propranolol
qs.x: This is acute dystonia from dopamine blockade, treated with an anticholinergic such as benztropine or with diphenhydramine. Bromocriptine and dantrolene are used for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and propranolol for akathisia.

qs.q: A patient with schizophrenia is starting olanzapine. Which monitoring is most important for its major long-term adverse effects?
qs.a: Weight, fasting glucose, and lipid panel
w: Absolute neutrophil count each week
Serum lithium and creatinine levels
Liver biopsy before therapy
qs.x: Olanzapine has high risk of weight gain, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia, so metabolic monitoring is essential. Weekly neutrophil monitoring is specific to clozapine.

qs.q: A patient taking phenelzine eats aged cheese and develops a severe occipital headache and very high blood pressure. What is the mechanism?
qs.a: Tyramine is not broken down and releases norepinephrine
w: Serotonin reuptake is blocked in the brainstem
Dopamine receptors are blocked in the hypothalamus
Histamine is released from intestinal mast cells
qs.x: MAO inhibitors prevent breakdown of dietary tyramine in the gut and liver, and tyramine then releases norepinephrine, causing a hypertensive crisis. Patients are counseled to avoid aged, fermented, and cured foods.

qs.q: A patient with alcohol use disorder and cirrhosis also takes daily oxycodone for chronic pain. Which medication for alcohol use disorder is most appropriate?
qs.a: Acamprosate
w: Naltrexone
Disulfiram
Chlordiazepoxide
qs.x: Acamprosate is renally cleared and does not interact with opioids, making it suitable in liver disease. Naltrexone would precipitate opioid withdrawal, and disulfiram is risky in cirrhosis.

qs.q: How does varenicline help with smoking cessation?
qs.a: Partial agonism at alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic receptors
w: Inhibition of dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake
Full agonism at nicotinic receptors in muscle
Antagonism of mu opioid receptors in the brain
qs.x: Varenicline partially stimulates nicotinic receptors to reduce cravings and withdrawal while blocking the rewarding effect of nicotine from smoking. Dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition describes bupropion.

qs.q: A patient with severe hyperkalemia has peaked T waves and a widened QRS complex. Which medication should be given first to stabilize the cardiac membrane?
qs.a: IV calcium gluconate
w: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate
IV furosemide
Oral patiromer
qs.x: IV calcium antagonizes the membrane effects of potassium and acts within minutes but does not lower potassium. Binders and diuretics remove potassium too slowly to be the first step.

qs.q: IV regular insulin is given with dextrose to treat hyperkalemia. Which monitoring is most important afterward?
qs.a: Frequent blood glucose checks for hypoglycemia
w: Serum magnesium checks for hypermagnesemia
Urine output for osmotic diuresis
Serum calcium checks for hypercalcemia
qs.x: Insulin shifts potassium into cells but can cause delayed hypoglycemia, especially in kidney disease, so glucose is checked frequently. The other effects are not expected from this treatment.

qs.q: A patient with CKD on an ACE inhibitor is started on patiromer for chronic hyperkalemia. Which electrolyte abnormality should be monitored?
qs.a: Hypomagnesemia
w: Hypernatremia
Hypercalcemia
Hyperphosphatemia
qs.x: Patiromer exchanges calcium for potassium and also binds magnesium, so hypomagnesemia is a recognized adverse effect. Other oral drugs should be separated in time from patiromer to avoid binding.

qs.q: A patient with heart failure on high-intensity furosemide therapy is most likely to show which laboratory pattern?
qs.a: Hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis
w: Hyperkalemia with metabolic acidosis
Hypercalcemia with metabolic acidosis
Hypernatremia with respiratory acidosis
qs.x: Loop diuretics increase distal sodium delivery and potassium and hydrogen ion loss, causing hypokalemic contraction alkalosis. They also increase calcium excretion, unlike thiazides.

qs.q: A patient develops an acute gout flare a few weeks after starting hydrochlorothiazide. What explains this?
qs.a: Decreased renal excretion of uric acid
w: Increased purine production in the liver
Direct crystal deposition of the drug
Increased intestinal absorption of purines
qs.x: Thiazides compete with uric acid for proximal tubular secretion and cause volume contraction, both raising serum urate. Thiazides can also cause hypercalcemia, hyponatremia, and hyperglycemia.

qs.q: A patient with cirrhosis has new moderate ascites. Which diuretic regimen is first-line?
qs.a: Spironolactone with or without furosemide
w: Hydrochlorothiazide alone
Acetazolamide alone
Mannitol with furosemide
qs.x: Secondary hyperaldosteronism drives sodium retention in cirrhosis, so the aldosterone antagonist spironolactone is the foundation, often paired with furosemide. Thiazides add hyponatremia risk without targeting the mechanism.

qs.q: A patient taking acetazolamide for prevention of acute mountain sickness has which expected acid-base change?
qs.a: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
w: High anion gap metabolic acidosis
Hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis
Primary respiratory acidosis
qs.x: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition causes bicarbonate loss in the urine, producing a hyperchloremic, normal anion gap acidosis that stimulates ventilation. Hypochloremic alkalosis is seen with loop and thiazide diuretics.

qs.q: A man taking tamsulosin for benign prostatic hyperplasia is scheduled for cataract surgery. What is the most important counseling point?
qs.a: Inform the eye surgeon about tamsulosin before surgery
w: Expect the drug to lower intraocular pressure
Tamsulosin has no relevance to eye surgery
Expect improved pupil dilation during surgery
qs.x: Alpha-1A blockade affects the iris dilator muscle and can cause intraoperative floppy iris syndrome, so the surgeon needs to know in advance. Pupil dilation tends to be poorer, not better.

qs.q: A man has taken finasteride for benign prostatic hyperplasia for a year. How does it affect prostate cancer screening?
qs.a: It lowers PSA, so measured values should be doubled
w: It raises PSA, so measured values should be halved
It has no effect on PSA results
It makes PSA undetectable and unusable
qs.x: Finasteride, a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor, lowers PSA by about half after several months, so values are doubled for interpretation. Any confirmed PSA rise on finasteride warrants evaluation.

qs.q: An older adult with mild dementia has overactive bladder. Which medication is preferred to avoid anticholinergic cognitive effects?
qs.a: Mirabegron
w: Oxybutynin
Tolterodine
Trospium
qs.x: Mirabegron is a beta-3 agonist that relaxes the detrusor without anticholinergic effects; blood pressure should be monitored. Oxybutynin is strongly anticholinergic and can worsen confusion in older adults.

qs.q: A patient is starting oral alendronate for osteoporosis. Which counseling point is correct?
qs.a: Take with plain water on an empty stomach and stay upright
w: Take with milk at bedtime to reduce nausea
Take with breakfast and a calcium supplement
Lie down after taking to improve absorption
qs.x: Alendronate is poorly absorbed and can cause pill esophagitis, so it is taken first thing in the morning with plain water, fasting, and the patient stays upright before eating. Calcium and food greatly reduce absorption.

qs.q: A woman on alendronate for several years reports new dull pain in the anterior thigh. Which complication should be considered?
qs.a: Atypical femoral fracture
w: Osteosarcoma of the femur
Septic arthritis of the hip
Rhabdomyolysis of the quadriceps
qs.x: Long-term bisphosphonate use is linked to atypical subtrochanteric or femoral shaft fractures, often preceded by thigh or groin pain, so imaging is warranted. Osteosarcoma was a historic concern with teriparatide, not bisphosphonates.

qs.q: A patient taking azathioprine for autoimmune hepatitis is started on allopurinol for gout. Which complication is most likely if this combination is not adjusted?
qs.a: Severe bone marrow suppression
w: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
Severe hypercalcemia
Rapid loss of azathioprine effect
qs.x: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which normally breaks down azathioprine and mercaptopurine, so levels rise and can cause life-threatening myelosuppression. The thiopurine dose must be substantially reduced or the combination avoided.

qs.q: A patient taking colchicine for gout is prescribed clarithromycin. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Colchicine toxicity from inhibited CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein
w: Reduced antibacterial effect of clarithromycin
Accelerated colchicine clearance and gout flare
Severe hyperuricemia from the antibiotic
qs.x: Clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4 and P-gp, which raises colchicine levels and can cause fatal toxicity with GI symptoms, myopathy, and cytopenias. The interaction does not weaken the antibiotic.

qs.q: Febuxostat is considered for a patient with gout and established coronary artery disease. Which FDA boxed warning applies?
qs.a: Higher risk of cardiovascular death than allopurinol
w: Fatal hepatic failure in most patients
Severe hypercalcemia with kidney stones
Serious neuropsychiatric events and suicide
qs.x: In a large trial, febuxostat was associated with higher cardiovascular and all-cause mortality than allopurinol in patients with cardiovascular disease, so it is reserved for those who cannot take allopurinol. Neuropsychiatric warnings apply to montelukast, not febuxostat.

qs.q: Which patient is the poorest candidate for probenecid to lower uric acid?
qs.a: A patient with a history of uric acid kidney stones
w: A patient with normal renal function and low urate excretion
A patient who cannot tolerate xanthine oxidase inhibitors
A patient with no history of kidney stones
qs.x: Probenecid is a uricosuric that increases urinary uric acid, raising the risk of stone formation, so it is avoided with uric acid stones and urate overproduction. It works best in underexcreters with normal kidney function.

qs.q: Before each dose of denosumab for osteoporosis, what should be assessed?
qs.a: Serum calcium and vitamin D status
w: Serum potassium and magnesium only
Thyroid-stimulating hormone and free T4
Fasting glucose and lipid panel
qs.x: Denosumab inhibits RANKL and osteoclast activity and can cause significant hypocalcemia, especially in kidney disease, so calcium and vitamin D must be adequate. Patients also need to know that delaying doses can cause rebound vertebral fractures.

qs.q: How does teriparatide improve bone density in severe osteoporosis?
qs.a: Intermittent PTH receptor stimulation increases bone formation
w: Inhibition of RANK ligand blocks osteoclast formation
Binding to hydroxyapatite inhibits osteoclast activity
Estrogen receptor agonism in bone reduces turnover
qs.x: Teriparatide is a recombinant PTH analog; given intermittently, it favors osteoblast activity and new bone formation, making it an anabolic agent. RANKL inhibition is denosumab's mechanism, and hydroxyapatite binding describes bisphosphonates.

qs.q: Which history is a contraindication to raloxifene for postmenopausal osteoporosis?
qs.a: A prior deep vein thrombosis
w: A family history of breast cancer
A history of vertebral fracture
Mild hot flashes after menopause
qs.x: Raloxifene is a SERM with a boxed warning for venous thromboembolism and fatal stroke. It lowers invasive breast cancer risk, so a family history of breast cancer may actually favor it.

qs.q: A patient at high risk for tumor lysis syndrome is being considered for rasburicase. Which test should be done before treatment?
qs.a: G6PD deficiency screening
w: HLA-B*5801 genotyping
TPMT enzyme activity
Serum methylmalonic acid
qs.x: Rasburicase converts uric acid to allantoin and produces hydrogen peroxide, which can cause severe hemolysis and methemoglobinemia in G6PD deficiency. HLA-B*5801 testing relates to allopurinol hypersensitivity.

qs.q: A patient presents several hours after an intentional acetaminophen overdose. How does N-acetylcysteine prevent liver injury?
qs.a: It replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI
w: It blocks acetaminophen absorption from the gut
It enhances renal excretion of acetaminophen
It inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase in the liver
qs.x: NAC restores glutathione stores and serves as a substitute that conjugates the toxic metabolite NAPQI. Alcohol dehydrogenase inhibition is fomepizole's mechanism.

qs.q: A patient presents with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, an elevated osmolal gap, and calcium oxalate crystals in the urine. Which antidote acts by inhibiting alcohol dehydrogenase?
qs.a: Fomepizole
w: Pralidoxime
Deferoxamine
Flumazenil
qs.x: These findings suggest ethylene glycol poisoning; fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase and prevents formation of toxic metabolites. Hemodialysis may also be needed.

qs.q: Physostigmine is considered for a patient with suspected anticholinergic toxicity. Which ECG finding is a contraindication?
qs.a: A widened QRS suggesting tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
w: Sinus tachycardia with a narrow QRS
Mild nonspecific T-wave flattening
Normal sinus rhythm with a narrow QRS
qs.x: Physostigmine can precipitate bradyasystole and seizures in tricyclic overdose, which is suggested by QRS widening. Sinus tachycardia is an expected anticholinergic finding and does not preclude its use.

qs.q: A patient with an amitriptyline overdose has hypotension and a widened QRS complex. Which treatment is indicated?
qs.a: IV sodium bicarbonate
w: IV physostigmine
IV flumazenil
IV procainamide
qs.x: Sodium bicarbonate counteracts tricyclic sodium channel blockade through sodium loading and alkalinization, narrowing the QRS. Procainamide is a sodium channel blocker and would worsen toxicity.

qs.q: A farmworker with organophosphate poisoning is receiving repeated IV atropine. Which clinical endpoint guides further atropine doses?
qs.a: Drying of bronchial secretions
w: Return of normal pupil size
Resolution of muscle fasciculations
Normalization of heart rate below normal
qs.x: Atropine is titrated to clear bronchorrhea and improve oxygenation, since airway secretions are the main cause of death. Atropine does not reverse nicotinic effects such as fasciculations or weakness; pralidoxime addresses those.

qs.q: Why should pralidoxime be given early in organophosphate poisoning?
qs.a: It must reactivate acetylcholinesterase before aging occurs
w: It is only absorbed well during the first hour
It must block muscarinic receptors before they upregulate
It is converted to an inactive form by the liver
qs.x: Pralidoxime regenerates acetylcholinesterase by removing the phosphate group, but once the enzyme-organophosphate bond ages it can no longer be reactivated. Muscarinic blockade is the role of atropine.

qs.q: A patient with digoxin toxicity receives digoxin immune Fab. How should the serum digoxin level be interpreted afterward?
qs.a: Total digoxin rises and no longer reflects active drug
w: Total digoxin falls to zero within minutes
Total digoxin accurately guides redosing
Total digoxin is unaffected by the antibody
qs.x: Most assays measure both free and Fab-bound digoxin, so total levels rise after treatment even though active drug is neutralized. Clinical response, not total level, guides further management.

qs.q: A patient rescued from a house fire has altered mental status, hypotension, and severe lactic acidosis. Which antidote is recommended?
qs.a: Hydroxocobalamin
w: Methylene blue
Fomepizole
Deferoxamine
qs.x: Smoke inhalation can cause cyanide poisoning, and hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, which is excreted in the urine. It commonly causes red skin and urine; methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia.

qs.q: A patient develops cyanosis and chocolate-brown blood after topical benzocaine. Before giving methylene blue, which condition should be considered?
qs.a: G6PD deficiency
w: Iron deficiency anemia
Hereditary hemochromatosis
Vitamin K deficiency
qs.x: Methylene blue requires NADPH from the G6PD pathway to reduce methemoglobin, and it can cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. It also carries serotonin syndrome risk with serotonergic drugs.

qs.q: A child with severe iron poisoning receives IV deferoxamine. Which finding is expected as iron is chelated and excreted?
qs.a: Reddish-brown urine
w: Bright green urine
Black, tarry urine
Blue-tinged skin
qs.x: Deferoxamine binds free iron to form ferrioxamine, which is excreted in urine and gives it a reddish-brown color. Prolonged infusion is linked to ARDS.

qs.q: During an IV vancomycin infusion, a patient develops flushing and pruritus of the face, neck, and upper chest without wheezing or hypotension. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Infusion rate-related histamine release
w: IgE-mediated anaphylaxis
Drug-induced lupus
Stevens-Johnson syndrome
qs.x: Vancomycin infusion reaction is a non-immune histamine release linked to rapid infusion and is managed by slowing the rate and giving antihistamines. It is not a true allergy, unlike anaphylaxis.

qs.q: An adult has uncomplicated urethral gonorrhea. Which treatment is recommended by current CDC guidelines?
qs.a: Intramuscular ceftriaxone
w: Oral ciprofloxacin
Oral azithromycin alone
Oral amoxicillin
qs.x: CDC recommends a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone for uncomplicated gonorrhea, with doxycycline added if chlamydia has not been excluded. Fluoroquinolone and azithromycin monotherapy are limited by resistance.

qs.q: An older adult on lisinopril is treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely?
qs.a: Hyperkalemia
w: Hypokalemia
Hypercalcemia
Hypernatremia
qs.x: Trimethoprim blocks the epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct like amiloride, reducing potassium excretion, and risk is greater with ACE inhibitors. It can also raise serum creatinine by blocking tubular secretion.

qs.q: An older adult taking chronic prednisone is prescribed ciprofloxacin. Which adverse effect is of particular concern?
qs.a: Achilles tendon rupture
w: Red man syndrome
Gray baby syndrome
Ototoxicity with vestibular loss
qs.x: Fluoroquinolones carry a boxed warning for tendinitis and tendon rupture, with higher risk in older adults and those taking corticosteroids. Ototoxicity is typical of aminoglycosides.

qs.q: A patient is prescribed metronidazole for bacterial vaginosis. Which counseling point is most important?
qs.a: Avoid alcohol during treatment and shortly after
w: Take with dairy products to improve absorption
Avoid sunlight exposure for several weeks
Expect orange discoloration of urine and tears
qs.x: Metronidazole can cause a disulfiram-like reaction with flushing, nausea, and vomiting when combined with alcohol. Orange secretions are seen with rifampin.

qs.q: A patient taking escitalopram develops agitation, hyperthermia, and clonus after starting an antibiotic for MRSA pneumonia. Which antibiotic is most likely responsible?
qs.a: Linezolid
w: Vancomycin
Clindamycin
Doxycycline
qs.x: Linezolid is a weak monoamine oxidase inhibitor and can cause serotonin syndrome with SSRIs. It also causes thrombocytopenia with prolonged use.

qs.q: A patient starts isoniazid for latent tuberculosis. Which supplement is given to prevent a common adverse effect?
qs.a: Pyridoxine to prevent peripheral neuropathy
w: Folic acid to prevent megaloblastic anemia
Vitamin K to prevent bleeding
Thiamine to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
qs.x: Isoniazid increases pyridoxine excretion and can cause peripheral neuropathy, so vitamin B6 is given to at-risk patients. Liver enzymes are also monitored because isoniazid causes hepatitis.

qs.q: A woman taking a combined oral contraceptive is starting rifampin. Which counseling point is most important?
qs.a: Use a nonhormonal backup method of contraception
w: Increase fluid intake to prevent kidney stones
Expect blue-green discoloration of the urine
No interaction with hormonal contraception occurs
qs.x: Rifampin is a strong CYP3A4 inducer that lowers estrogen and progestin levels and can cause contraceptive failure. It also turns urine, sweat, and tears orange-red, not blue-green.

qs.q: An adult has a first episode of non-severe Clostridioides difficile infection. Which antibiotic is preferred by current IDSA guidelines?
qs.a: Oral fidaxomicin
w: Intravenous vancomycin
Oral clindamycin
Oral ciprofloxacin
qs.x: Fidaxomicin is preferred for initial C. difficile infection because of lower recurrence, with oral vancomycin as an alternative. IV vancomycin does not reach the colon, and clindamycin is a major cause of C. difficile.

qs.q: Why is nitrofurantoin not appropriate for acute pyelonephritis?
qs.a: It does not reach adequate concentrations in kidney tissue
w: It is inactive against Escherichia coli
It is only available as an intravenous form
It causes severe hyperkalemia in kidney infection
qs.x: Nitrofurantoin concentrates in the urine but achieves poor serum and renal tissue levels, so it is used only for cystitis. It is active against most E. coli.

qs.q: A patient on metformin for many years develops numbness in the feet and a macrocytic anemia. Which deficiency should be evaluated?
qs.a: Vitamin B12 deficiency
w: Iron deficiency
Vitamin D deficiency
Zinc deficiency
qs.x: Long-term metformin reduces vitamin B12 absorption, which can cause neuropathy and macrocytic anemia; periodic B12 checks are recommended. Iron deficiency causes a microcytic anemia.

qs.q: A patient with type 2 diabetes and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction needs an additional glucose-lowering agent. Which drug has proven heart failure benefit?
qs.a: Empagliflozin
w: Pioglitazone
Saxagliptin
Glipizide
qs.x: SGLT2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin reduce heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular death in HFrEF. Pioglitazone causes fluid retention and can worsen heart failure, and saxagliptin was associated with increased heart failure hospitalization.

qs.q: Which history is a contraindication to semaglutide?
qs.a: Family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma
w: History of hypothyroidism on levothyroxine
History of type 2 diabetes with obesity
History of well-controlled hypertension
qs.x: GLP-1 receptor agonists carry a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors and are contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2. Hypothyroidism is not a contraindication.

qs.q: An older adult with chronic kidney disease has type 2 diabetes. Why is glyburide a poor choice?
qs.a: It has active metabolites that cause prolonged hypoglycemia
w: It causes lactic acidosis in kidney disease
It causes fluid retention and heart failure
It causes genital yeast infections
qs.x: Glyburide is long acting with renally cleared active metabolites, so hypoglycemia can be severe and prolonged in older adults and in CKD. Lactic acidosis is a metformin concern, and fluid retention is a thiazolidinedione effect.

qs.q: In which patient with type 2 diabetes is pioglitazone contraindicated?
qs.a: A patient with NYHA class III heart failure
w: A patient with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
A patient with mild osteoarthritis
A patient with insulin resistance and obesity
qs.x: Thiazolidinediones cause fluid retention and carry a boxed warning against use in symptomatic heart failure. Pioglitazone may actually benefit fatty liver disease.

qs.q: A patient is starting insulin glargine as basal insulin. Which counseling point is correct?
qs.a: Do not mix it in the same syringe with other insulins
w: Inject it immediately before each meal
Expect a sharp peak in action after injection
Shake the vial vigorously before each injection
qs.x: Insulin glargine is a long-acting, relatively peakless basal insulin with an acidic formulation, so it should not be mixed with other insulins. Mealtime coverage is provided by rapid-acting insulin.

qs.q: A patient on a stable levothyroxine dose has a rising TSH after starting a new supplement. Which supplement most likely caused this?
qs.a: Calcium carbonate taken at the same time
w: Vitamin C taken with breakfast
A daily probiotic capsule
A melatonin tablet at bedtime
qs.x: Calcium, iron, and antacids bind levothyroxine in the gut and reduce absorption, so doses should be separated by several hours. Vitamin C does not decrease absorption.

qs.q: A woman in the first trimester of pregnancy has Graves disease requiring antithyroid medication. Which drug is generally preferred during this period?
qs.a: Propylthiouracil
w: Methimazole
Radioactive iodine
Liothyronine
qs.x: Methimazole is linked to embryopathy in the first trimester, so propylthiouracil is preferred then, with switching to methimazole often considered afterward because of PTU hepatotoxicity. Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy.

qs.q: A patient taking methimazole for hyperthyroidism should be taught to report which symptoms promptly?
qs.a: Fever and sore throat
w: Weight gain and constipation
Increased appetite and warmth
Dry skin and hair thinning
qs.x: Methimazole can cause agranulocytosis, which presents with fever and sore throat and requires a prompt CBC. Weight gain and dry skin suggest hypothyroidism from overtreatment, which is less urgent.

qs.q: A patient with known primary adrenal insufficiency presents with vomiting, hypotension, and hyponatremia after a viral illness. Which medication is most appropriate immediately?
qs.a: IV hydrocortisone
w: Oral fludrocortisone
IV levothyroxine
Subcutaneous octreotide
qs.x: Adrenal crisis requires parenteral hydrocortisone with IV fluids; at stress doses hydrocortisone also provides mineralocorticoid activity. Oral fludrocortisone acts too slowly and does not replace cortisol.

qs.q: A patient with a prolonged baseline QTc needs an antiemetic. Why should ondansetron be used with caution?
qs.a: It can prolong the QT interval
w: It causes tardive dyskinesia
It causes severe hypertension
It causes anticholinergic delirium
qs.x: Ondansetron, a 5-HT3 antagonist, can prolong the QT interval, especially with electrolyte abnormalities or other QT-prolonging drugs. Tardive dyskinesia is linked to metoclopramide.

qs.q: A patient with diabetic gastroparesis has taken metoclopramide for many months and develops involuntary lip smacking and tongue movements. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Tardive dyskinesia
w: Serotonin syndrome
Acute dystonia
Hepatic encephalopathy
qs.x: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine D2 receptors and carries a boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia, with risk rising with duration and cumulative exposure. Acute dystonia occurs within hours to days of starting therapy.

qs.q: A patient on long-term omeprazole develops muscle cramps and arrhythmia. Which electrolyte abnormality is a recognized cause?
qs.a: Hypomagnesemia
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypernatremia
Hyperphosphatemia
qs.x: Prolonged PPI use can reduce intestinal magnesium absorption and cause hypomagnesemia, sometimes with secondary hypocalcemia or hypokalemia. Other long-term risks include C. difficile infection and B12 deficiency.

qs.q: How does lactulose improve hepatic encephalopathy?
qs.a: It acidifies the colon, trapping ammonia as ammonium
w: It inhibits ammonia production in the liver
It increases ammonia excretion in the kidneys
It blocks ammonia from crossing the blood-brain barrier
qs.x: Colonic bacteria break down lactulose into acids, converting ammonia to non-absorbable ammonium that is excreted in stool; it is titrated to a few soft bowel movements daily. Rifaximin is added to reduce ammonia-producing bacteria.

qs.q: In which patient is loperamide inappropriate?
qs.a: A patient with fever and bloody diarrhea
w: A patient with mild traveler's diarrhea without fever
A patient with chronic diarrhea from irritable bowel syndrome
A patient with watery diarrhea after a viral illness
qs.x: Antimotility agents can worsen invasive bacterial infections such as Shigella or Shiga toxin-producing E. coli and can precipitate toxic megacolon. Loperamide is reasonable for nonbloody, afebrile diarrhea.

qs.q: A patient with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis is started on mesalamine. Which monitoring is recommended?
qs.a: Periodic renal function tests
w: Monthly pulmonary function tests
Weekly absolute neutrophil counts
Periodic serum drug levels
qs.x: Mesalamine can rarely cause interstitial nephritis, so renal function is checked before and periodically during therapy. Weekly neutrophil monitoring is specific to clozapine.

qs.q: A man with ulcerative colitis on sulfasalazine is concerned about fertility. Which adverse effect explains this concern?
qs.a: Reversible oligospermia
w: Permanent testicular atrophy
Retrograde ejaculation
Hyperprolactinemia
qs.x: The sulfapyridine component of sulfasalazine can cause reversible oligospermia. It can also cause folate deficiency and orange-yellow discoloration of urine and skin.

qs.q: Misoprostol is considered to prevent NSAID-induced gastric ulcers. Which patient should not receive it for this purpose?
qs.a: A patient who is pregnant
w: A patient with osteoarthritis
A patient older than sixty-five
A patient with a prior gastric ulcer
qs.x: Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analog that stimulates uterine contractions and carries a boxed warning against use in pregnancy for ulcer prevention. Older age and prior ulcer are indications for gastroprotection.

qs.q: How does sucralfate protect against peptic ulcer injury?
qs.a: It forms a protective barrier over the ulcer in acid
w: It blocks the proton pump in parietal cells
It blocks histamine-2 receptors on parietal cells
It neutralizes gastric acid as a strong base
qs.x: Sucralfate polymerizes in an acidic environment and binds to exposed ulcer protein, forming a barrier against acid and pepsin. Because it binds other drugs, they should be taken at separate times.

qs.q: A middle-aged woman has fatigue, pruritus, an elevated alkaline phosphatase, and positive antimitochondrial antibodies. Which medication is first-line?
qs.a: Ursodiol
w: Cholestyramine
Prednisone
Azathioprine
qs.x: Primary biliary cholangitis is treated first-line with ursodiol, which slows disease progression. Cholestyramine may relieve pruritus but does not modify disease.

qs.q: A patient receiving magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia with severe features is being monitored for toxicity. Which finding is typically the earliest sign?
qs.a: Loss of deep tendon reflexes
w: Respiratory arrest
Cardiac arrest
Seizure activity
qs.x: Loss of patellar reflexes appears at lower magnesium levels than respiratory depression or cardiac arrest, so reflexes are checked regularly. Seizures are what magnesium prevents.

qs.q: A patient on magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia has absent reflexes and a slowing respiratory rate. Which medication is the antidote?
qs.a: Calcium gluconate
w: Naloxone
Flumazenil
Protamine
qs.x: IV calcium gluconate antagonizes magnesium's effects at the neuromuscular junction and myocardium. Naloxone reverses opioids, not magnesium.

qs.q: A patient has heavy bleeding after vaginal delivery and a boggy uterus. Which uterotonic is first-line?
qs.a: Oxytocin
w: Methylergonovine
Carboprost
Terbutaline
qs.x: Oxytocin is the first-line uterotonic for postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony, alongside uterine massage. Terbutaline is a tocolytic that relaxes the uterus and would worsen bleeding.

qs.q: A patient with postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony has preeclampsia. Which uterotonic is contraindicated?
qs.a: Methylergonovine
w: Oxytocin
Carboprost
Misoprostol
qs.x: Methylergonovine is an ergot alkaloid that causes vasoconstriction and can provoke severe hypertension, so it is avoided in hypertension and preeclampsia. Carboprost is avoided in asthma instead.

qs.q: Carboprost is considered for refractory postpartum hemorrhage. Which history is a contraindication?
qs.a: Asthma
w: Chronic hypertension
Gestational diabetes
Hypothyroidism
qs.x: Carboprost is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analog that can cause bronchospasm, so it is avoided in asthma. Hypertension is the contraindication for methylergonovine.

qs.q: A pregnant patient at term has a severe-range blood pressure on repeat measurement. Which medication is an appropriate first-line treatment?
qs.a: IV labetalol
w: Oral lisinopril
IV nitroprusside
Oral losartan
qs.x: IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, and oral immediate-release nifedipine are first-line for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are fetotoxic, and nitroprusside is reserved for refractory cases.

qs.q: A pregnant patient has severe-range hypertension, and IV access cannot be obtained. Which medication is an appropriate first-line option?
qs.a: Oral immediate-release nifedipine
w: Oral methyldopa
Oral hydrochlorothiazide
Oral enalapril
qs.x: ACOG lists oral immediate-release nifedipine as a first-line agent for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy, which is useful without IV access. Methyldopa is used for chronic hypertension but acts too slowly for urgent control.

qs.q: In which situation is Rh(D) immune globulin indicated?
qs.a: Rh-negative, unsensitized mother after delivering an Rh-positive newborn
w: Rh-positive mother after delivering an Rh-negative newborn
Rh-negative mother already sensitized with anti-D antibodies
Rh-positive mother with a positive antibody screen
qs.x: Rh(D) immune globulin prevents alloimmunization in Rh-negative women who are not already sensitized after exposure to Rh-positive fetal blood. It does not help once anti-D antibodies have formed.

qs.q: A patient in preterm labor is given IM betamethasone. What is the main purpose?
qs.a: To accelerate fetal lung maturity
w: To stop uterine contractions
To prevent maternal seizures
To prevent neonatal group B strep infection
qs.x: Antenatal corticosteroids speed fetal lung maturation and reduce respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular hemorrhage, and neonatal death. Tocolytics stop contractions, and magnesium provides neuroprotection or seizure prophylaxis.

qs.q: A woman planning pregnancy asks about folic acid. Which statement is most accurate?
qs.a: It should begin before conception to reduce neural tube defects
w: It should begin in the third trimester to prevent anemia
It is only needed after a positive pregnancy test
It mainly prevents congenital heart defects
qs.x: Neural tube closure occurs early, often before pregnancy is recognized, so folic acid supplementation should begin before conception. Starting late misses the critical window.

qs.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is starting weekly methotrexate. Which supplement is given to reduce adverse effects?
qs.a: Folic acid
w: Vitamin D
Vitamin B12
Iron
qs.x: Folic acid reduces methotrexate adverse effects such as mouth sores, GI upset, and liver enzyme elevation without reducing efficacy in RA. Liver tests and blood counts are also monitored.

qs.q: Before starting adalimumab for rheumatoid arthritis, which test is most important?
qs.a: Screening for latent tuberculosis
w: Serum uric acid level
Thyroid ultrasound
Bone density scan
qs.x: TNF-alpha inhibitors raise the risk of reactivating latent tuberculosis, so screening with an IGRA or TST is required before therapy. Hepatitis B screening is also recommended.

qs.q: A patient with Crohn disease is being considered for infliximab. Which comorbidity is a reason for caution?
qs.a: Moderate-to-severe heart failure
w: Well-controlled hypothyroidism
Mild osteoarthritis
Iron deficiency anemia
qs.x: TNF inhibitors such as infliximab can worsen moderate-to-severe heart failure, and the label warns against higher doses in this setting. The other conditions do not limit its use.

qs.q: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus is starting long-term hydroxychloroquine. Which monitoring is recommended?
qs.a: Baseline and periodic retinal eye examinations
w: Monthly pulmonary function tests
Weekly absolute neutrophil counts
Periodic bone marrow biopsy
qs.x: Hydroxychloroquine can cause irreversible retinopathy, so a baseline exam and annual screening after the early years of therapy are recommended. Weekly neutrophil counts apply to clozapine.

qs.q: Before starting azathioprine, which test helps identify patients at high risk for severe myelosuppression?
qs.a: TPMT enzyme activity or genotype
w: HLA-B*1502 genotype
G6PD enzyme activity
CYP2C19 genotype
qs.x: Thiopurine methyltransferase metabolizes azathioprine, and low or absent activity leads to toxic metabolite buildup and severe bone marrow suppression. HLA-B*1502 testing relates to carbamazepine.

qs.q: A kidney transplant recipient on tacrolimus has a rising creatinine and a fine hand tremor. Which adverse effect profile best explains this?
qs.a: Calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity
w: Antimetabolite bone marrow suppression
mTOR inhibitor impaired wound healing
Corticosteroid-induced myopathy
qs.x: Tacrolimus inhibits calcineurin and commonly causes nephrotoxicity, tremor, hyperkalemia, and hyperglycemia, so levels are monitored. Bone marrow suppression is typical of azathioprine and mycophenolate.

qs.q: Which adverse effects help distinguish cyclosporine from tacrolimus?
qs.a: Gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism
w: Nephrotoxicity and hyperkalemia
Tremor and headache
Hypertension and hyperglycemia
qs.x: Both calcineurin inhibitors cause nephrotoxicity, hypertension, and tremor, but gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism are characteristic of cyclosporine. Tacrolimus is more likely to cause hyperglycemia and neurotoxicity.

qs.q: A woman of reproductive age with lupus nephritis is starting mycophenolate. Which counseling point is most important?
qs.a: It causes birth defects and requires effective contraception
w: It causes hearing loss and needs audiometry
It causes kidney stones and needs extra fluids
It causes red-orange urine that is harmless
qs.x: Mycophenolate carries a boxed warning for embryofetal toxicity, including miscarriage and congenital malformations, and requires reliable contraception under a REMS program. The other effects are not characteristic.
