qs.q: A patient receiving magnesium sulfate develops slow, shallow breathing and absent reflexes. Why is calcium gluconate given?
qs.a: It antagonizes magnesium's effects on nerves and muscle
w: It increases kidney excretion of magnesium
It binds magnesium and inactivates it
It sedates the patient to reduce oxygen need
qs.x: Calcium counteracts magnesium at the neuromuscular junction and heart, temporarily reversing toxicity while ventilation is supported. It does not remove magnesium from the body.

qs.q: An infant's heart rate remains below normal with poor perfusion despite effective oxygenation and ventilation. Which drug is first-line?
qs.a: Epinephrine
w: Atropine
Adenosine
Amiodarone
qs.x: Pediatric bradycardia is usually caused by hypoxia, and when it persists with poor perfusion despite good ventilation, epinephrine is the first drug. Atropine is for vagal causes or primary AV block.

qs.q: During intubation, a child's heart rate suddenly drops. Which cause of bradycardia is atropine most appropriate for?
qs.a: Increased vagal tone from airway manipulation
w: Hypoxia from a failed airway attempt
Hypothermia after cold-water drowning
Hyperkalemia from kidney failure
qs.x: Atropine blocks vagal effects, so it is appropriate for vagally mediated bradycardia or primary AV block. Hypoxic bradycardia is treated first with oxygenation and ventilation.

qs.q: Why are lower concentrations of dextrose used for infants and young children than the concentrated form used in adults?
qs.a: Concentrated solutions are hypertonic and can damage small veins
w: Children cannot metabolize concentrated glucose
Concentrated dextrose causes seizures in children
Lower concentrations raise glucose faster
qs.x: Highly concentrated dextrose is very hypertonic and can injure small veins and tissues, so diluted forms are used in children. Lower concentrations do not work faster.

qs.q: A child is having a prolonged seizure and no IV can be started. Which route of midazolam is commonly used?
qs.a: Intranasal via a mucosal atomizer
w: Oral liquid
Transdermal patch
Inhaled nebulizer
qs.x: Intranasal midazolam is absorbed quickly through the nasal mucosa and is effective for pediatric seizures without IV access. Oral and transdermal routes are not practical during a seizure.

qs.q: Why is caution needed with naloxone in a newborn whose mother has used opioids regularly during pregnancy?
qs.a: It can cause abrupt, life-threatening withdrawal including seizures
w: It has no effect in newborns
It causes severe hypoglycemia
It blocks the newborn's breathing reflex
qs.x: Abrupt reversal in an opioid-dependent newborn can trigger severe withdrawal and seizures, so ventilation support is the priority. Naloxone does work in newborns.

qs.q: An infant has a very fast, narrow-complex rhythm. Which feature suggests SVT that may respond to adenosine rather than sinus tachycardia?
qs.a: Abrupt onset with a fixed rate and absent P waves
w: Gradual rise in rate with fever and dehydration
Rate that varies with crying and activity
Visible P waves before every QRS complex
qs.x: SVT starts and stops abruptly, has little rate variability and usually lacks visible P waves. Sinus tachycardia varies with activity, has P waves and usually has a cause such as fever.

qs.q: How does ondansetron help a child with vomiting from gastroenteritis?
qs.a: It reduces vomiting so oral rehydration can succeed
w: It cures the underlying viral infection
It stops diarrhea by slowing the gut
It replaces lost electrolytes
qs.x: By reducing vomiting, ondansetron helps children tolerate oral fluids and may avoid an IV. It does not treat the infection or replace fluids.

qs.q: What should caregivers be taught when giving liquid acetaminophen to a child?
qs.a: Use the measuring device supplied and dose by weight
w: Use a kitchen spoon for convenience
Combine it with adult cold medicines
Give extra doses if the fever persists
qs.x: Kitchen spoons are inaccurate and many combination products also contain acetaminophen, so mixing them risks overdose and liver injury. The supplied device and weight-based dosing reduce errors.

qs.q: Which child should not receive ibuprofen without provider guidance?
qs.a: A child with severe vomiting and signs of dehydration
w: A child with a fever and earache
A child with a sprained ankle
A child with teething discomfort
qs.x: NSAIDs reduce blood flow to the kidneys and can cause kidney injury in dehydrated children. The other children are common, appropriate uses.

qs.q: A child in severe asthma has diminished breath sounds and no audible wheezing after albuterol. How should this be interpreted?
qs.a: Worsening obstruction with very little air movement
w: Full recovery from the asthma attack
An expected side effect of albuterol
A sign the child is ready for discharge
qs.x: A quiet or silent chest in severe asthma means too little air is moving to produce wheezing, which is ominous. Improvement would include better air movement and less work of breathing.

qs.q: During transport of a patient with norepinephrine running through a peripheral IV, what is essential?
qs.a: Frequent checks of the IV site for infiltration
w: Flushing the line hourly to keep it open
Hanging it on the same line as the antibiotic
Checking the site only at arrival
qs.x: Peripheral norepinephrine is acceptable short term in a large, proximal vein, but extravasation can cause tissue necrosis, so the site must be checked often. Sharing or flushing the line risks boluses.

qs.q: Which finding suggests excessive vasoconstriction from a norepinephrine infusion?
qs.a: Cold, mottled fingers and toes with poor perfusion
w: Warm, flushed skin and bounding pulses
Low blood pressure with a slow heart rate
Increased urine output and thirst
qs.x: Intense alpha-1 vasoconstriction can reduce blood flow to the extremities and organs, causing cool, mottled skin. Warm, flushed skin suggests vasodilation.

qs.q: Why should a norepinephrine infusion run through a dedicated line that is not flushed?
qs.a: Flushing would deliver an unintended bolus and spike the blood pressure
w: Flushing would dilute it and make it inactive
Flushing would cause the drug to crystallize
Flushing would cause a drop in heart rate
qs.x: Norepinephrine is potent and short acting, so pushing the drug remaining in the line can cause a sudden rise in blood pressure. A dedicated line prevents unplanned boluses.

qs.q: Why may a fentanyl infusion have a longer effect than expected after several days?
qs.a: It is fat soluble and accumulates in tissues during prolonged infusion
w: It is converted into a long-acting toxic metabolite
It is excreted unchanged only by the lungs
It loses potency the longer it is infused
qs.x: Fentanyl is highly lipophilic, so it builds up in fat and muscle and is slowly released, prolonging its effect. Its short duration applies to single doses.

qs.q: An intubated patient is fighting the ventilator. Why does an analgesia-first approach often start with fentanyl?
qs.a: Pain often drives agitation, and treating it may reduce sedative needs
w: Fentanyl paralyzes the patient so they cannot fight
Fentanyl has no effect on breathing in ventilated patients
Fentanyl prevents delirium completely
qs.x: Many ventilated patients are agitated from pain, so treating pain first can reduce the need for deeper sedation. Fentanyl does not cause paralysis.

qs.q: Why may a patient with kidney failure remain sedated long after a midazolam infusion ends?
qs.a: An active metabolite builds up when kidney function is poor
w: Midazolam is not removed by the liver at all
Kidney failure makes midazolam more water soluble
Midazolam converts into an opioid in kidney failure
qs.x: Midazolam's active metabolite is cleared by the kidneys and accumulates in renal failure, prolonging sedation. Prolonged infusion also causes accumulation in fat.

qs.q: What concern is linked to prolonged benzodiazepine sedation such as a midazolam infusion in critically ill patients?
qs.a: Increased risk of delirium and longer time on the ventilator
w: Increased risk of high blood pressure
Increased risk of hypoglycemia
Increased risk of excessive alertness
qs.x: Critical care guidelines prefer non-benzodiazepine sedation where possible because benzodiazepines are associated with delirium and longer ventilation. They do not cause hypertension.

qs.q: How should the depth of sedation be assessed during a midazolam infusion?
qs.a: Use a validated sedation scale such as the RASS
w: Rely on the heart rate alone
Check pupil size only
Assume sedation if the patient is quiet
qs.x: Validated scales such as the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale give an objective measure to avoid under- or over-sedation. Heart rate and pupils are unreliable sedation markers.

qs.q: In which patient should ketamine be used with caution due to its cardiovascular effects?
qs.a: A patient with severe, uncontrolled hypertension or active ischemia
w: A patient with septic shock and low blood pressure
A patient with asthma who needs sedation
A patient with a long bone fracture
qs.x: Ketamine's sympathomimetic effects raise heart rate and blood pressure, which can worsen severe hypertension or myocardial ischemia. In hypotension or asthma these effects can be helpful.

qs.q: Which effect of ketamine may require more frequent suctioning?
qs.a: Increased salivation and airway secretions
w: Dry mouth and thick mucus
Decreased gag reflex
Bronchospasm
qs.x: Ketamine increases salivary and airway secretions, which may need suctioning. It tends to relax, not tighten, bronchial smooth muscle.

qs.q: Before giving a scheduled dose of digoxin, which assessment is most important for the nurse to perform?
qs.a: Count the apical pulse for one full minute
w: Check the radial pulse for fifteen seconds
Measure blood pressure in both arms
Auscultate bowel sounds in all four quadrants
qs.x: Digoxin slows conduction through the AV node, so a full apical count is needed to detect bradycardia before giving it. A brief radial check can miss irregular beats and undercount the rate.

qs.q: A patient taking digoxin and furosemide reports nausea, poor appetite, and yellow-green halos around lights. What does the nurse recognize?
qs.a: Possible digoxin toxicity, which low potassium can worsen
w: Expected adjustment effects of digoxin therapy
An allergic reaction to furosemide
Dehydration from drinking too much water
qs.x: GI upset and visual changes are classic signs of digoxin toxicity, and loop diuretics can lower potassium, which makes toxicity more likely. These are not expected effects and should be reported along with a digoxin level and potassium.

qs.q: A patient is on long-term amiodarone. Which set of tests does the nurse expect to be monitored periodically?
qs.a: Thyroid, liver, and lung function tests
w: Amylase, lipase, and uric acid levels
Hemoglobin A1c, lipase, and bone density
Creatine kinase, ammonia, and lactate levels
qs.x: Amiodarone can cause thyroid dysfunction, liver injury, and pulmonary toxicity, so these organs are monitored over time. The other panels do not target its known organ toxicities.

qs.q: Before a scheduled dose of oral metoprolol, the nurse finds a heart rate well below the patient's usual rate and the patient reports dizziness. What is the priority action?
qs.a: Notify the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose and recheck vital signs later
Give the dose with a full glass of water
Have the patient walk to assess tolerance
qs.x: Beta blockers slow the heart rate, and symptomatic bradycardia needs provider review before more drug is given. Giving the dose and rechecking later could worsen the bradycardia.

qs.q: A patient taking lisinopril develops sudden swelling of the lips and tongue. What does the nurse recognize?
qs.a: Angioedema, a possible airway emergency
w: Expected first-dose low blood pressure
A mild contact allergy to a food
Fluid overload from heart failure
qs.x: ACE inhibitors can cause angioedema at any time during therapy, and tongue or throat swelling can block the airway. It is not a first-dose blood pressure effect and needs urgent airway assessment and provider notification.

qs.q: Which laboratory value is the nurse's priority to monitor in a patient receiving furosemide?
qs.a: Serum potassium, for hypokalemia
w: Serum calcium, for hypercalcemia
Serum sodium, for hypernatremia
Blood glucose, for hypoglycemia
qs.x: Loop diuretics cause loss of potassium, and low potassium can trigger dangerous dysrhythmias. Furosemide tends to lower, not raise, sodium and calcium.

qs.q: A patient prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin for angina asks about other medicines. Which medicine should the nurse teach the patient to avoid combining with it?
qs.a: Sildenafil or other PDE-5 inhibitors
w: Acetaminophen for headaches
Aspirin for heart protection
Atorvastatin for cholesterol
qs.x: Nitrates combined with PDE-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil can cause severe, life-threatening hypotension. Aspirin is commonly used together with nitroglycerin in coronary disease.

qs.q: A patient takes spironolactone and lisinopril. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider?
qs.a: High serum potassium with muscle weakness
w: Low serum potassium with leg cramps
A mild increase in daytime urination
Mild breast tenderness that is unchanged
qs.x: Spironolactone is potassium-sparing, and ACE inhibitors also raise potassium, so hyperkalemia is the key risk. Low potassium is the concern with loop and thiazide diuretics, not this combination.

qs.q: A patient with atrial fibrillation and a rapid ventricular rate is receiving IV diltiazem. Which monitoring is the priority?
qs.a: Continuous heart rhythm and frequent blood pressure
w: Hourly bedside blood glucose checks
Daily serum digoxin level
Strict intake and output only
qs.x: IV diltiazem slows AV conduction and dilates vessels, so bradycardia, heart block, and hypotension can develop quickly. Intake and output alone would miss these changes.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing a patient for IV adenosine to treat SVT. Which expected effect should the nurse explain?
qs.a: A few seconds of very slow heartbeat with flushing or chest pressure
w: Drowsiness that lasts for several hours
A sustained rise in blood pressure
Gradual slowing of the heart over a day
qs.x: Adenosine is given by rapid IV push with a saline flush and briefly blocks the AV node, often causing a few seconds of very slow or absent heartbeat, flushing, or chest discomfort. Its effects last seconds, not hours.

qs.q: During a peripheral norepinephrine infusion, the nurse notes blanching, coolness, and swelling at the IV site. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?
qs.a: Phentolamine infiltrated into the affected area
w: Protamine given by IV push
Naloxone given intramuscularly
Vitamin K given subcutaneously
qs.x: Norepinephrine extravasation causes intense local vasoconstriction, and phentolamine, an alpha blocker, is infiltrated into the area to limit tissue damage. Protamine reverses heparin and has no role here.

qs.q: Which route is preferred for a continuous norepinephrine infusion whenever possible?
qs.a: A central venous catheter
w: A small vein in the back of the hand
An intramuscular injection site
A subcutaneous infusion site
qs.x: A central line lowers the risk of tissue injury from extravasation of this potent vasoconstrictor. Small hand veins carry the highest risk of infiltration.

qs.q: A patient in anaphylactic shock needs epinephrine right away and has no IV access. Which route is recommended?
qs.a: Intramuscular injection into the outer thigh
w: Subcutaneous injection into the upper arm
Undiluted IV push through a new line
A dissolving tablet under the tongue
qs.x: Intramuscular injection into the anterolateral thigh gives faster, more reliable absorption than subcutaneous injection. Undiluted IV push epinephrine can cause dangerous dysrhythmias.

qs.q: A patient receiving a dopamine infusion develops a new rapid, irregular heart rhythm. How does the nurse interpret this finding?
qs.a: A known adverse effect that needs prompt reporting
w: An expected sign that the drug is working
A sign of low blood volume only
An allergic reaction to the IV diluent
qs.x: Dopamine stimulates beta-1 receptors and can cause tachydysrhythmias, which should be reported promptly. A new dysrhythmia is not a marker of therapeutic effect.

qs.q: Which statement best describes how dobutamine helps a patient in cardiogenic shock?
qs.a: It increases heart contractility through beta-1 stimulation
w: It constricts arteries through alpha-1 stimulation
It blocks calcium channels in vascular muscle
It inhibits phosphodiesterase-3 in heart muscle
qs.x: Dobutamine is mainly a beta-1 agonist that strengthens contraction and raises cardiac output. Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibition describes milrinone, another inotrope.

qs.q: A patient receives IV phenylephrine for hypotension. Which change in vital signs should the nurse watch for as blood pressure rises?
qs.a: Reflex bradycardia
w: Marked tachycardia
Rising respiratory rate
Falling body temperature
qs.x: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist, and the rise in blood pressure can trigger a reflex slowing of the heart. It lacks the beta effects that would cause tachycardia.

qs.q: How does vasopressin raise blood pressure in septic shock?
qs.a: It constricts blood vessels through V1 receptors
w: It speeds the heart through beta-1 receptors
It dilates renal arteries through dopamine receptors
It boosts contractility by inhibiting PDE-3
qs.x: Vasopressin acts on V1 receptors in vascular smooth muscle, causing vasoconstriction without beta-adrenergic effects. It does not directly increase heart rate.

qs.q: A patient with decompensated heart failure is started on milrinone. Which assessment is the nurse's priority?
qs.a: Blood pressure and heart rhythm
w: Blood glucose for hyperglycemia
Respiratory rate for depression
Temperature for malignant hyperthermia
qs.x: Milrinone is an inotrope and vasodilator, so hypotension and ventricular dysrhythmias are the main risks. It does not cause respiratory depression.

qs.q: Which teaching is appropriate for a patient taking midodrine for orthostatic hypotension?
qs.a: Take doses during daytime hours, not close to bedtime
w: Take the last dose at bedtime for overnight effect
Lie flat for an hour after each dose
Take each dose only while lying down
qs.x: Midodrine can cause supine hypertension, so doses are taken while upright during the day and not near bedtime. Lying flat after a dose increases that risk.

qs.q: Which adverse effect is the main safety concern with droxidopa, and what does the nurse teach?
qs.a: Supine hypertension; rest with the head of the bed raised
w: Hypoglycemia; carry a fast-acting sugar source
Bradycardia; check the pulse before standing
Hyperkalemia; avoid salt substitutes
qs.x: Droxidopa carries a boxed warning for supine hypertension, so patients sleep with the head of the bed elevated and supine blood pressure is monitored. Hypoglycemia is not a known effect.

qs.q: Which laboratory test does the nurse use to evaluate the therapeutic effect of warfarin?
qs.a: International normalized ratio (INR)
w: Activated partial thromboplastin time
Anti-factor Xa level
Platelet count
qs.x: Warfarin is monitored with the INR, which reflects its effect on vitamin K-dependent clotting factors. The aPTT is used for unfractionated heparin.

qs.q: Which dietary teaching is appropriate for a patient starting warfarin?
qs.a: Keep intake of leafy green vegetables consistent
w: Avoid all green vegetables completely
Eat extra leafy greens when bruising occurs
Take a vitamin K supplement every morning
qs.x: Vitamin K in leafy greens counters warfarin, so a steady intake keeps the INR stable. Cutting out greens entirely is unnecessary and can make the INR swing when intake changes.

qs.q: Several days after starting heparin, a patient's platelet count has dropped by more than half and a new clot is suspected. What does the nurse recognize?
qs.a: Possible heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
w: Expected dilution from IV fluids
Vitamin K deficiency bleeding
Warfarin-induced skin necrosis
qs.x: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is an immune reaction that lowers platelets and paradoxically causes clotting, and it must be reported right away. Dilution would not explain a large drop with new thrombosis.

qs.q: Which laboratory test is commonly used to monitor a continuous IV infusion of unfractionated heparin?
qs.a: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
w: International normalized ratio (INR)
Serum fibrinogen level
Bleeding time
qs.x: Unfractionated heparin is monitored with the aPTT (or an anti-Xa level by facility protocol) to keep it in the therapeutic range. The INR is used for warfarin.

qs.q: Which technique is correct when giving enoxaparin from a prefilled syringe?
qs.a: Inject subcutaneously in the abdomen without expelling the air bubble
w: Inject intramuscularly into the deltoid muscle
Rub the site firmly afterward to reduce bruising
Expel the air bubble, then inject into the thigh muscle
qs.x: Enoxaparin is given by deep subcutaneous injection, usually in the abdomen, and the air bubble in the prefilled syringe is not expelled. Rubbing the site increases bruising.

qs.q: Which statement by a patient taking apixaban shows correct understanding?
qs.a: "I will report black stools or unusual bruising."
w: "I need weekly INR checks to adjust my dose."
"I will double my next dose if I miss one."
"I can take ibuprofen freely for pain."
qs.x: Bleeding is the main risk with apixaban, so signs like black stools or easy bruising should be reported. Apixaban does not need routine INR monitoring, unlike warfarin.

qs.q: A patient with acute ischemic stroke symptoms is being considered for alteplase. Which finding must be confirmed before it is given?
qs.a: A head CT showing no bleeding in the brain
w: A normal lipid panel
A recent urine culture result
That the patient has been fasting
qs.x: Alteplase dissolves clots and is contraindicated in intracranial hemorrhage, so imaging must rule out bleeding first. A lipid panel has no bearing on eligibility.

qs.q: While giving protamine to reverse heparin, which adverse effects should the nurse watch for?
qs.a: Low blood pressure, slow heart rate, and allergic reaction
w: High blood pressure and seizures
High potassium and peaked T waves
Low blood glucose and sweating
qs.x: Protamine can cause hypotension, bradycardia, and anaphylaxis-like reactions, especially if given too fast. It does not cause hypertension or seizures.

qs.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease receives epoetin alfa. Which finding should the nurse report?
qs.a: A rapid rise in hemoglobin or new high blood pressure
w: A gradual rise in reticulocyte count
Mild tenderness at the injection site
Improved energy over several weeks
qs.x: Epoetin raises the risk of hypertension, clots, and stroke, especially when hemoglobin rises quickly or too high. A rising reticulocyte count is an expected sign it is working.

qs.q: Which medicine can reduce the antiplatelet effect of clopidogrel and is generally avoided with it?
qs.a: Omeprazole
w: Acetaminophen
Levothyroxine
Metformin
qs.x: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, the enzyme that activates clopidogrel, which can reduce its effect. Acetaminophen has no meaningful interaction with clopidogrel.

qs.q: Which patient is at the highest risk for dangerous hyperkalemia if given succinylcholine?
qs.a: A patient with a severe burn injury several days ago
w: A patient with mild dehydration
A patient with well-controlled asthma
A patient who takes a daily multivitamin
qs.x: After major burns, crush injuries, or denervation, extra receptors on muscle allow succinylcholine to release large amounts of potassium. Mild dehydration does not create this risk.

qs.q: Shortly after succinylcholine is given, the patient develops jaw rigidity, rising end-tidal carbon dioxide, and a fast heart rate. What does the nurse recognize?
qs.a: Malignant hyperthermia
w: Expected fasciculations
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Latex anaphylaxis
qs.x: Masseter rigidity with rising end-tidal CO2 and tachycardia are early signs of malignant hyperthermia, which is treated with dantrolene. Fasciculations are brief twitches, not sustained rigidity.

qs.q: After intubation, a patient is receiving rocuronium. Which nursing priority applies?
qs.a: Ensure adequate sedation and pain control, since it provides neither
w: Reduce sedation, since rocuronium causes deep sleep
Expect the patient to breathe well without support
Ask the patient to rate pain on a numeric scale
qs.x: Neuromuscular blockers paralyze muscles but do not affect awareness or pain, so sedation and analgesia must be given. A paralyzed patient cannot breathe or report pain.

qs.q: How does sugammadex reverse neuromuscular blockade?
qs.a: It binds and encapsulates rocuronium or vecuronium
w: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the synapse
It blocks nicotinic receptors on muscle
It stimulates muscarinic receptors in the heart
qs.x: Sugammadex forms a tight complex with rocuronium or vecuronium, removing it from the junction. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is how neostigmine works.

qs.q: A patient who takes oral hormonal contraceptives received sugammadex during surgery. Which teaching is appropriate?
qs.a: Use a backup nonhormonal method for the next week
w: No change is needed; contraceptives are unaffected
Take two contraceptive pills the next day
Skip the next week of contraceptive pills
qs.x: Sugammadex can bind progestogen and lower contraceptive effect, so labeling advises a backup method for seven days. It is not true that contraceptives are unaffected.

qs.q: Which adverse effect is associated with etomidate used for rapid sequence intubation?
qs.a: Temporary adrenal suppression
w: Severe hypertension
Histamine-related bronchospasm
Malignant hyperthermia
qs.x: Etomidate briefly inhibits cortisol production, a concern in critically ill or septic patients. It is not a trigger for malignant hyperthermia.

qs.q: Why may ketamine be chosen for induction in a patient with low blood pressure?
qs.a: It tends to maintain blood pressure and breathing drive
w: It lowers heart rate and blood pressure
It reliably abolishes all airway reflexes
It has a specific reversal agent
qs.x: Ketamine's sympathetic stimulation usually supports blood pressure and heart rate while preserving respiratory drive. It has no specific reversal agent.

qs.q: Which handling practice is important when giving propofol?
qs.a: Use strict aseptic technique, since the lipid supports bacterial growth
w: Shake the vial and give it intramuscularly
Mix it with other drugs in the same syringe
Save an opened vial in the refrigerator for tomorrow
qs.x: Propofol is a lipid emulsion that can grow bacteria, so aseptic technique and timely disposal of opened product are required. It is given IV, not intramuscularly.

qs.q: A patient becomes oversedated after midazolam. Which reversal agent should the nurse anticipate?
qs.a: Flumazenil
w: Naloxone
Sugammadex
Neostigmine
qs.x: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines such as midazolam. Naloxone reverses opioids, not benzodiazepines.

qs.q: After a rapid IV push of fentanyl, ventilation becomes difficult because the chest feels stiff. What does the nurse recognize?
qs.a: Opioid-induced chest wall rigidity
w: A severe hypertensive reaction
Malignant hyperthermia
Hyperkalemia from muscle injury
qs.x: Rapid, large IV doses of potent opioids like fentanyl can cause chest wall rigidity that impairs ventilation. Fentanyl is not a malignant hyperthermia trigger.

qs.q: Which side effects should the nurse teach a patient to expect after using albuterol?
qs.a: Tremor, nervousness, and a fast heart rate
w: Drowsiness and a slow heart rate
Oral thrush and hoarseness
Constipation and dry eyes
qs.x: Albuterol is a beta-2 agonist, and some beta stimulation causes tremor and tachycardia. Thrush and hoarseness are linked to inhaled corticosteroids.

qs.q: Which teaching is appropriate for a patient using an inhaled fluticasone inhaler?
qs.a: Rinse the mouth and spit after each use
w: Use it first for sudden wheezing
Swallow the rinse water after each use
Use it only on days with symptoms
qs.x: Rinsing and spitting lowers the risk of oral thrush from inhaled corticosteroids. Fluticasone is a daily controller and does not relieve sudden wheezing.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct about salmeterol?
qs.a: It is not used to relieve a sudden asthma attack
w: It works within seconds for acute wheezing
It can be used alone without a controller in asthma
It may be used several times every hour as needed
qs.x: Salmeterol is a long-acting beta agonist with slow onset for maintenance, not rescue. In asthma it should be paired with an inhaled corticosteroid, never used alone.

qs.q: Which history should the nurse report before a patient starts tiotropium?
qs.a: Narrow-angle glaucoma or urinary retention
w: Seasonal allergic rhinitis
Osteoarthritis of the knees
Treated hypothyroidism
qs.x: Tiotropium is an anticholinergic that can worsen narrow-angle glaucoma and urinary retention. Seasonal allergies are not a concern.

qs.q: Which effect should the nurse teach patients and families to report while taking montelukast?
qs.a: Mood changes, agitation, or suicidal thoughts
w: Black, tarry stools
Yellow-green halos around lights
Gum overgrowth
qs.x: Montelukast has a boxed warning for serious neuropsychiatric events. Yellow-green halos are a sign of digoxin toxicity.

qs.q: A patient on theophylline starts ciprofloxacin and then reports nausea, restlessness, and a racing heart. What does the nurse recognize?
qs.a: Possible theophylline toxicity from a drug interaction
w: Expected adjustment to the antibiotic
An allergic reaction to ciprofloxacin
Worsening asthma control
qs.x: Ciprofloxacin slows theophylline clearance, and theophylline has a narrow therapeutic range, so toxicity can follow. A theophylline level should be checked and the provider notified.

qs.q: A patient with diabetes is started on a short course of prednisone for an asthma flare. Which change should the nurse anticipate?
qs.a: Higher blood glucose levels
w: Lower blood glucose levels
Higher serum potassium
Lower white blood cell count
qs.x: Corticosteroids raise blood glucose, so closer monitoring is needed in diabetes. Prednisone tends to lower potassium and raise the white cell count.

qs.q: When is oseltamivir treatment most effective for influenza?
qs.a: When started within two days of symptom onset
w: Only after a fever has lasted a full week
After a culture confirms flu several days later
Only if pneumonia has already developed
qs.x: Oseltamivir works best when started within 48 hours of symptoms, though it may still be used later for hospitalized or high-risk patients. Waiting for culture results delays benefit.

qs.q: Which teaching is essential for a patient prescribed benzonatate capsules?
qs.a: Swallow capsules whole without chewing or sucking
w: Chew the capsules for faster relief
Open the capsule and mix it in applesauce
Let the capsule dissolve under the tongue
qs.x: Releasing benzonatate in the mouth numbs the throat and can cause choking or severe reactions. It should also be stored away from children, for whom accidental ingestion can be fatal.

qs.q: Which history should the nurse report before a patient takes pseudoephedrine for congestion?
qs.a: Uncontrolled high blood pressure
w: Seasonal allergies
Mild osteoarthritis
Iron deficiency
qs.x: Pseudoephedrine is a sympathomimetic decongestant that can raise blood pressure and heart rate. Seasonal allergies are a common reason it is used.

qs.q: Which IV fluid is compatible for flushing before and after IV phenytoin?
qs.a: Normal saline
w: Dextrose in water
Lactated Ringer's with dextrose
Any fluid already running in the line
qs.x: Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose solutions, so the line is flushed with normal saline. It should not be mixed with other fluids or drugs.

qs.q: Which teaching helps a patient manage a common long-term effect of phenytoin?
qs.a: Brush and floss carefully and see a dentist regularly
w: Expect hair thinning and use a mild shampoo
Avoid all dairy products to protect the liver
Take it with grapefruit juice to improve absorption
qs.x: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia, and good oral hygiene reduces it. Phenytoin levels are also monitored by name since it has a narrow therapeutic range.

qs.q: Which new symptom in a patient taking carbamazepine should be reported right away?
qs.a: Skin rash with blisters, fever, or mouth sores
w: Mild drowsiness during the first days
Mild nausea relieved by taking with food
Slight dizziness that improves with time
qs.x: Carbamazepine can cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, which need urgent attention. Mild early drowsiness is common and usually fades.

qs.q: Which effect should the nurse teach a patient and family to watch for with levetiracetam?
qs.a: Irritability, mood changes, or thoughts of self-harm
w: Overgrowth of the gums
Excess facial and body hair
Yellowing of the skin and eyes
qs.x: Levetiracetam is linked to behavioral changes, and antiepileptics carry a warning for suicidal thoughts. Gum overgrowth is linked to phenytoin.

qs.q: Which instruction is most important for a patient starting lamotrigine?
qs.a: Report any new rash, since it may signal a serious skin reaction
w: Expect weight gain during the first month
Have gum checks for overgrowth
Expect a fine hand tremor as it starts working
qs.x: Lamotrigine has a boxed warning for serious rashes, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, especially early in therapy. Gum overgrowth is a phenytoin effect.

qs.q: Which laboratory tests does the nurse expect to be monitored for a patient taking valproic acid?
qs.a: Liver function tests and platelet count
w: Thyroid panel and lipid panel
Serum lithium and sodium
Serum magnesium and phosphate
qs.x: Valproic acid can cause hepatotoxicity and thrombocytopenia, so liver tests and platelets are checked, along with valproic acid levels. A lithium level is unrelated.

qs.q: After IV lorazepam is given for status epilepticus, which assessment is the nurse's priority?
qs.a: Respiratory rate and oxygen saturation
w: Blood pressure for hypertension
Hourly bedside blood glucose
Bladder for urinary retention
qs.x: Benzodiazepines can depress breathing, especially after repeated doses, so airway and breathing are monitored closely. Hypertension is not a typical effect.

qs.q: Which teaching is appropriate for a patient taking carbidopa-levodopa?
qs.a: Large high-protein meals may reduce how well it works
w: High-protein shakes boost its effect
Its full effect is felt minutes after the first dose
It works best when taken with iron supplements
qs.x: Dietary protein competes with levodopa for absorption and transport into the brain, so large protein loads near doses can blunt its effect. Iron also reduces levodopa absorption.

qs.q: Which history is a contraindication to sumatriptan?
qs.a: Coronary artery disease
w: Seasonal allergies
Iron deficiency anemia
Osteoarthritis
qs.x: Triptans cause vasoconstriction and are contraindicated in coronary artery disease and uncontrolled hypertension. Seasonal allergies do not affect triptan use.

qs.q: Which finding should the nurse report in a patient taking donepezil?
qs.a: Slow heart rate or fainting
w: Dry mouth and constipation
Increased appetite
Thinning hair
qs.x: As a cholinesterase inhibitor, donepezil increases vagal tone and can cause bradycardia and syncope. Dry mouth and constipation are anticholinergic effects, the opposite of its action.

qs.q: Before giving IV morphine, which assessment is most important?
qs.a: Respiratory rate and level of sedation
w: Presence of bowel sounds
Pupil response to light only
Oral temperature
qs.x: Respiratory depression is the most dangerous opioid effect, and increasing sedation usually comes before it. Bowel sounds matter for constipation but are not the priority.

qs.q: After naloxone reverses an opioid overdose, what must the nurse continue to monitor for?
qs.a: Return of respiratory depression as naloxone wears off
w: Persistent hypertensive crisis
Severe hypoglycemia
Prolonged muscle paralysis
qs.x: Naloxone often wears off before longer-acting opioids, so sedation and slow breathing can return. Repeat doses may be needed.

qs.q: Which teaching helps prevent accidental acetaminophen overdose?
qs.a: Check cold and sleep products for hidden acetaminophen
w: Take it with alcohol to improve its effect
Any amount is safe because it is sold over the counter
Combine it freely with other pain relievers
qs.x: Many combination products contain acetaminophen, and taking several at once can cause liver injury. Over-the-counter status does not make any amount safe.

qs.q: Which finding should the nurse report in a patient receiving ketorolac?
qs.a: Decreased urine output or black stools
w: Mild drowsiness after a dose
Improved pain scores
Slight warmth at the injection site
qs.x: Ketorolac is a potent NSAID with boxed warnings for kidney injury and GI bleeding, and its total course is limited. Improved pain is the intended effect.

qs.q: Which teaching is essential for a patient using a fentanyl transdermal patch?
qs.a: Avoid heating pads, hot tubs, and direct heat over the patch
w: Cut the patch in half for a smaller effect
Apply each new patch to the same spot
Cover the patch with a heating pad at night
qs.x: Heat increases fentanyl absorption from the patch and can cause a fatal overdose. Cutting the patch damages the release system.

qs.q: Why is hydromorphone considered a high-alert medicine?
qs.a: It is far more potent than morphine, so mix-ups can cause overdose
w: It has no reversal agent
It causes severe hypertension
It is given only by the intrathecal route
qs.x: Hydromorphone is several times more potent than morphine, and look-alike names and products have led to fatal errors. Naloxone does reverse it.

qs.q: Which adverse effect requires ECG monitoring in a patient taking methadone?
qs.a: QT prolongation and dysrhythmias
w: Hyperkalemia
Gum overgrowth
Malignant hyperthermia
qs.x: Methadone can prolong the QT interval and cause torsades de pointes. It does not cause hyperkalemia.

qs.q: A patient taking warfarin asks about using ibuprofen for back pain. Which response is accurate?
qs.a: It increases bleeding risk when combined with warfarin
w: It lowers the INR and makes warfarin weaker
It has no interaction with warfarin
It speeds up clotting and raises clot risk
qs.x: NSAIDs impair platelet function and irritate the GI tract, adding to warfarin's bleeding risk. They do not make warfarin weaker.

qs.q: Which adverse effects should the nurse monitor for during a dexmedetomidine infusion?
qs.a: Bradycardia and hypotension
w: Hyperthermia and muscle rigidity
Hyperkalemia and peaked T waves
Severe hypertension and fast heart rate
qs.x: Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist that lowers sympathetic tone, so bradycardia and hypotension are its most common effects. It usually causes little respiratory depression.

qs.q: Which interaction is a concern when tramadol is given to a patient taking an SSRI?
qs.a: Serotonin syndrome
w: Hypoglycemia
Hyperkalemia
Neutropenia
qs.x: Tramadol has serotonergic activity, and combining it with SSRIs raises the risk of serotonin syndrome and seizures. Hyperkalemia is not linked to this combination.

qs.q: A patient taking lithium has vomiting, diarrhea, coarse hand tremor, and confusion. What does the nurse recognize?
qs.a: Possible lithium toxicity needing a lithium level
w: Expected side effects that will pass
Anxiety that needs a benzodiazepine
Food poisoning unrelated to lithium
qs.x: GI symptoms, coarse tremor, and confusion are signs of lithium toxicity, which has a narrow therapeutic range. A fine tremor can be expected, but a coarse tremor with confusion is not.

qs.q: Which teaching helps keep lithium levels stable?
qs.a: Keep salt and fluid intake consistent day to day
w: Follow a very low-salt diet
Limit fluids to reduce urination
Use ibuprofen freely for headaches
qs.x: Low sodium or dehydration causes the kidneys to retain lithium and raises levels. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen also raise lithium levels.

qs.q: Which symptom should a patient taking clozapine report right away?
qs.a: Fever, sore throat, or flu-like symptoms
w: Mild weight gain over months
Drowsiness after evening doses
Increased saliva at night
qs.x: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia, so signs of infection need urgent evaluation with an ANC. Weight gain and drooling are common but not emergencies.

qs.q: A patient on haloperidol develops high fever, rigid muscles, confusion, and unstable blood pressure. What does the nurse recognize?
qs.a: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Acute dystonia
Akathisia
qs.x: Fever, lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability define neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a medical emergency. Tardive dyskinesia causes involuntary movements without fever.

qs.q: A young adult is starting sertraline for depression. Which monitoring is most important early in treatment?
qs.a: Watch for worsening depression or suicidal thoughts
w: Check blood glucose before each dose
Monitor for gum overgrowth
Check a sertraline level weekly
qs.x: Antidepressants carry a boxed warning for increased suicidal thinking in children and young adults, especially early or after dose changes. Routine sertraline levels are not used.

qs.q: Which foods should a patient taking tranylcypromine avoid?
qs.a: Aged cheeses, cured meats, and tap beer
w: Fresh chicken, rice, and apples
Plain yogurt, oatmeal, and bananas
Fresh fish, pasta, and green beans
qs.x: MAOIs block the breakdown of tyramine, and high-tyramine foods can trigger a hypertensive crisis. Fresh meats and fish are low in tyramine.

qs.q: Which monitoring is most important for a patient taking olanzapine long term?
qs.a: Weight, blood glucose, and lipid levels
w: Thyroid function and calcium
Lithium level and sodium
Uric acid and creatine kinase
qs.x: Olanzapine commonly causes weight gain, hyperglycemia, and high lipids, so metabolic monitoring is routine. Lithium levels are unrelated.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for a buprenorphine-naloxone sublingual film?
qs.a: Let the film dissolve fully under the tongue
w: Swallow the film whole with water
Chew the film for a faster effect
Dissolve the film in juice and drink it
qs.x: The film is designed to be absorbed under the tongue, and swallowing or chewing it lowers absorption. Naloxone is included to discourage injection misuse.

qs.q: Which teaching is essential for a patient taking disulfiram?
qs.a: Avoid hidden alcohol in mouthwash, cough syrup, and sauces
w: Small amounts of beer are safe
Alcohol is fine once a week
Only hard liquor causes a reaction
qs.x: Even small amounts of alcohol, including in mouthwash or cooking, can cause flushing, vomiting, and a racing heart. Any form of alcohol can trigger the reaction.

qs.q: Which history is a concern before a patient starts bupropion?
qs.a: An eating disorder such as bulimia
w: Current cigarette smoking
Controlled high blood pressure
Seasonal allergic rhinitis
qs.x: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in seizure disorders and in bulimia or anorexia nervosa. Smoking cessation is one of its uses.

qs.q: Which practice is essential when giving IV potassium chloride?
qs.a: Give it only as a diluted infusion on a pump, never IV push
w: Give it by slow IV push over a few seconds
Give it undiluted to save fluid volume
Hang it by gravity without a pump
qs.x: IV push or concentrated potassium can cause fatal cardiac arrest, so it is a high-alert medicine given diluted by infusion pump. Slow push is still unsafe.

qs.q: Before starting IV potassium replacement, which assessment is most important?
qs.a: Adequate urine output and kidney function
w: Pupil size and reaction
Bedside blood glucose
Skin turgor on the forearm
qs.x: The kidneys excrete potassium, so poor urine output raises the risk of dangerous hyperkalemia. Pupil checks do not guide potassium safety.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for a patient taking patiromer?
qs.a: Separate it from other oral medicines by a few hours
w: Take it together with all other morning pills
Take it only when potassium is very low
Mix it with hot liquids before drinking
qs.x: Patiromer can bind other oral drugs, so labeling advises spacing other medicines by about three hours. It lowers, not raises, potassium.

qs.q: Why is IV calcium gluconate given to a patient with severe hyperkalemia and ECG changes?
qs.a: It stabilizes the heart muscle membrane against dysrhythmias
w: It shifts potassium into the cells
It removes potassium from the body
It increases potassium loss in the urine
qs.x: Calcium protects the heart quickly but does not lower serum potassium. Insulin with dextrose shifts potassium into cells.

qs.q: After IV regular insulin with dextrose is given for hyperkalemia, which assessment is the nurse's priority?
qs.a: Blood glucose, since hypoglycemia can follow
w: Deep tendon reflexes for depression
Urine color for hematuria
Pupil size for constriction
qs.x: Insulin shifts potassium into cells, and hypoglycemia is a common complication even with dextrose. Frequent glucose checks are needed.

qs.q: Which practice is important when preparing an IV mannitol infusion?
qs.a: Inspect for crystals and use an in-line filter
w: Mix it with blood products in the same line
Shake vigorously to dissolve any crystals
Give it as a rapid intramuscular injection
qs.x: Mannitol can form crystals, so it is inspected and given through a filter. It is not given intramuscularly.

qs.q: A patient with a history of gout is starting hydrochlorothiazide. Which effect should the nurse watch for?
qs.a: Raised uric acid that may trigger a gout flare
w: Lowered blood glucose
Raised serum potassium
Lowered serum calcium
qs.x: Thiazides reduce uric acid excretion and can provoke gout. They tend to raise glucose and calcium and lower potassium.

qs.q: Which finding should the nurse report in a patient receiving desmopressin?
qs.a: Low serum sodium with headache or confusion
w: High serum sodium with thirst
Low blood glucose with sweating
High potassium with weakness
qs.x: Desmopressin causes water retention, which can lead to hyponatremia and seizures. Fluid intake is monitored and sodium checked.

qs.q: A patient with heart failure is receiving a normal saline bolus. Which finding should the nurse report?
qs.a: New lung crackles and shortness of breath
w: Improved urine output
A rise in blood pressure toward baseline
Moist mucous membranes
qs.x: Crackles and dyspnea suggest fluid overload, a risk with isotonic fluids in heart failure. Improved urine output is an expected response.

qs.q: Which effects should the nurse watch for in an older adult taking oxybutynin?
qs.a: Confusion, constipation, and dry mouth
w: Diarrhea and excess saliva
Slow heart rate and wheezing
Low blood glucose and sweating
qs.x: Oxybutynin is anticholinergic, and older adults are especially prone to confusion and falls. Diarrhea and salivation are cholinergic effects, the opposite.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for a patient taking oral alendronate?
qs.a: Take it with plain water on an empty stomach and stay upright
w: Take it with breakfast and coffee
Lie down afterward to prevent dizziness
Take it together with a calcium supplement
qs.x: Alendronate is poorly absorbed with food or minerals and can irritate the esophagus, so it is taken with plain water and the patient remains upright. Calcium blocks its absorption.

qs.q: Which symptom should a patient taking alendronate report?
qs.a: New heartburn or pain when swallowing
w: Mild muscle aches after the first dose
Improved posture over time
Slight increase in appetite
qs.x: Alendronate can cause esophagitis and esophageal ulcers. Heartburn or painful swallowing should be reported promptly.

qs.q: Which teaching is appropriate for a patient starting allopurinol?
qs.a: Drink plenty of fluids and report any skin rash
w: Limit fluids to reduce urination
Take it only during a gout attack
Expect a rash as a normal effect
qs.x: Fluids reduce kidney stone risk, and a rash can signal a severe hypersensitivity reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Allopurinol prevents attacks rather than treating an acute flare.

qs.q: Which early symptoms may signal colchicine toxicity?
qs.a: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea
w: Constipation and bloating
High blood glucose
Excess hair growth
qs.x: GI symptoms are often the first signs of colchicine toxicity, which is more likely with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as clarithromycin. Constipation is not typical.

qs.q: Which symptoms should the nurse teach a patient taking febuxostat to report right away?
qs.a: Chest pain, shortness of breath, or stroke symptoms
w: Mild joint pain early in therapy
Mild nausea after doses
Slight headache that resolves
qs.x: Febuxostat has a boxed warning for increased cardiovascular death. Gout flares can occur early in therapy and are expected.

qs.q: Which lab values should be checked before an IV zoledronic acid infusion?
qs.a: Serum creatinine and calcium
w: Serum lipase and amylase
Hemoglobin A1c and lipids
INR and aPTT
qs.x: Zoledronic acid can harm the kidneys and lower calcium, so kidney function and calcium are checked and the patient is well hydrated. Clotting tests are unrelated.

qs.q: Which adverse effect is a particular concern with denosumab, especially in patients with kidney disease?
qs.a: Low serum calcium
w: High serum potassium
Low blood glucose
High serum sodium
qs.x: Denosumab can cause significant hypocalcemia, so calcium is checked and calcium with vitamin D is often given. Potassium is not affected.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for a patient using calcitonin salmon nasal spray?
qs.a: Alternate nostrils each day
w: Use the same nostril every day
Tilt the head back and sniff hard
Use it only when bone pain occurs
qs.x: Alternating nostrils reduces nasal irritation, a common side effect. Nasal dryness, crusting, or nosebleeds should be reported.

qs.q: Which teaching is important for a patient taking raloxifene?
qs.a: Report leg pain or swelling and avoid long periods sitting still
w: Expect leg swelling as a normal effect
Use it to relieve hot flashes
Take it with a high-fat meal for absorption
qs.x: Raloxifene raises the risk of blood clots, so signs of DVT should be reported and prolonged immobility avoided. It can cause, not relieve, hot flashes.

qs.q: Which screening test is needed before the first pegloticase infusion?
qs.a: G6PD deficiency testing
w: HLA-B*5801 genotype
Tuberculosis skin test
Hepatitis C antibody
qs.x: Pegloticase can cause hemolysis and methemoglobinemia in G6PD deficiency, so patients at risk are screened. HLA-B*5801 testing relates to allopurinol.

qs.q: Acetylcysteine is the antidote for overdose of which medicine?
qs.a: Acetaminophen
w: Aspirin
Ibuprofen
Diphenhydramine
qs.x: Acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione, protecting the liver from acetaminophen's toxic metabolite. Aspirin overdose is treated with supportive care and bicarbonate.

qs.q: Which risk is greatest when flumazenil is given to a patient who uses benzodiazepines long term?
qs.a: Seizures
w: Respiratory depression
Hypoglycemia
Bradycardia
qs.x: Flumazenil can trigger withdrawal seizures in patients with benzodiazepine dependence or mixed overdoses. It reverses rather than causes respiratory depression.

qs.q: After digoxin immune fab is given for toxicity, which lab change should the nurse watch for?
qs.a: Serum potassium may fall quickly
w: Serum sodium may rise sharply
Blood glucose may rise sharply
Platelet count may fall sharply
qs.x: As digoxin is bound, potassium shifts back into cells and can drop, so potassium is monitored closely. Total digoxin levels also become unreliable afterward.

qs.q: Which adverse reaction is a concern when phytonadione is given intravenously?
qs.a: A severe hypersensitivity reaction
w: Severe hyperglycemia
Acute kidney stones
Rapid hair loss
qs.x: IV vitamin K carries a boxed warning for severe, sometimes fatal hypersensitivity reactions, so it is infused slowly with monitoring. Other routes are preferred when practical.

qs.q: Which substance is not well bound by activated charcoal?
qs.a: Lithium
w: Aspirin
Acetaminophen
Carbamazepine
qs.x: Charcoal binds poorly to metals and ions such as lithium and iron, and to alcohols. Aspirin and acetaminophen are well adsorbed.

qs.q: Fomepizole is used as an antidote for ingestion of which substance?
qs.a: Ethylene glycol in antifreeze
w: Iron tablets
Organophosphate insecticide
Tricyclic antidepressants
qs.x: Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing formation of toxic metabolites of ethylene glycol and methanol. Organophosphates are treated with atropine and pralidoxime.

qs.q: After hydroxocobalamin is given for cyanide poisoning, the patient's skin and urine turn red. What does the nurse recognize?
qs.a: An expected effect of the antidote's red color
w: A sign of acute kidney failure
A transfusion reaction
Worsening cyanide poisoning
qs.x: Hydroxocobalamin is deep red and commonly discolors skin and urine; it can also interfere with some lab tests. It does not indicate kidney failure.

qs.q: In organophosphate poisoning, which finding shows atropine is having the desired effect?
qs.a: Drying of airway secretions and easier breathing
w: Pinpoint pupils
Increased salivation
Slower heart rate
qs.x: The goal of atropine in organophosphate poisoning is drying of bronchial secretions. Pupil size is not a reliable endpoint.

qs.q: Before methylene blue is given for methemoglobinemia, which medication history is a concern?
qs.a: Use of an SSRI or other serotonergic drug
w: Use of a daily multivitamin
Use of an inhaled corticosteroid
Use of a topical antifungal
qs.x: Methylene blue inhibits MAO-A and can cause serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs. G6PD deficiency is another important concern.

qs.q: Glucagon may be used as an antidote for which overdose?
qs.a: Beta blocker overdose
w: Opioid overdose
Benzodiazepine overdose
Iron overdose
qs.x: Glucagon raises cAMP in heart cells independently of beta receptors, improving heart rate and contractility. Vomiting is common, so airway protection is monitored.

qs.q: During an IV vancomycin infusion, the patient develops flushing and itching of the face, neck, and upper body. What does the nurse recognize?
qs.a: An infusion reaction linked to fast infusion
w: Expected effect of a working antibiotic
Ototoxicity from high drug levels
Clostridioides difficile infection
qs.x: Vancomycin infusion reaction is a histamine release related to infusion speed, managed by slowing the infusion and notifying the provider. It is not true anaphylaxis or ototoxicity.

qs.q: Which monitoring is routine for a patient on IV vancomycin?
qs.a: Vancomycin levels and kidney function
w: Liver enzymes and ammonia
INR and aPTT
Blood glucose and A1c
qs.x: Vancomycin is nephrotoxic and dosed using vancomycin levels or AUC, so kidney function is followed closely. Liver toxicity is not its main concern.

qs.q: Which symptom should a patient on gentamicin report?
qs.a: Ringing in the ears, hearing loss, or dizziness
w: Orange-colored urine
Metallic taste
Darkening of the tongue
qs.x: Aminoglycosides can cause ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity, so hearing changes and gentamicin levels are monitored. Orange urine is linked to rifampin.

qs.q: Before the first dose of IV cefazolin, which assessment is most important?
qs.a: Ask about drug allergies, including penicillin reactions
w: Check a fasting blood glucose
Measure abdominal girth
Test deep tendon reflexes
qs.x: Cephalosporins can cause allergic reactions, and a history of severe penicillin reaction raises concern. Allergy assessment comes before any first antibiotic dose.

qs.q: Which teaching is essential for a patient taking metronidazole?
qs.a: Avoid alcohol during therapy and for a few days after
w: Take it with milk to improve absorption
Expect orange urine as a harmless effect
Use extra sun exposure to speed healing
qs.x: Alcohol with metronidazole can cause a disulfiram-like reaction with flushing, nausea, and vomiting. Orange urine is caused by rifampin, not metronidazole.

qs.q: Which symptom should a patient taking ciprofloxacin report right away?
qs.a: Sudden pain or swelling at the heel or a tendon
w: Mild nausea after meals
Slight change in taste
Mild headache that resolves
qs.x: Fluoroquinolones carry a boxed warning for tendinitis and tendon rupture, especially in older adults and those on corticosteroids. Mild nausea is common.

qs.q: Which vitamin is often given with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy?
qs.a: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6)
w: Cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12)
Ascorbic acid (vitamin C)
Phytonadione (vitamin K)
qs.x: Isoniazid depletes pyridoxine, which can cause numbness and tingling. Liver function is also monitored because of hepatotoxicity.

qs.q: Which teaching is appropriate for a patient starting rifampin?
qs.a: Body fluids may turn orange, and soft contact lenses can stain
w: Urine may turn blue-green and is a sign of toxicity
It strengthens birth control pills
It must be taken with antacids
qs.x: Rifampin harmlessly colors urine, sweat, and tears orange-red. It reduces, not strengthens, hormonal contraceptive effectiveness.

qs.q: Which symptom should a patient taking clindamycin report, even weeks after finishing?
qs.a: Frequent watery diarrhea
w: Mild metallic taste
Darkened urine for a day
Mild injection-site soreness
qs.x: Clindamycin carries a boxed warning for Clostridioides difficile infection, which can appear weeks after therapy. Frequent watery diarrhea needs evaluation.

qs.q: Which route is correct for penicillin G benzathine?
qs.a: Deep intramuscular injection only
w: Intravenous infusion
Subcutaneous injection
Intravenous push
qs.x: Penicillin G benzathine has a boxed warning that IV use can cause cardiac arrest and death. It is given only by deep IM injection.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for insulin glargine?
qs.a: Do not mix it in the same syringe with other insulins
w: Draw it up together with regular insulin
Shake it until it looks cloudy
Give it only with high blood glucose
qs.x: Insulin glargine is a clear, long-acting basal insulin that must not be mixed with other insulins. It is given on schedule, not only for high readings.

qs.q: When is rapid-acting insulin lispro given relative to meals?
qs.a: Shortly before a meal, so food follows soon after
w: At bedtime regardless of food
An hour after finishing a meal
Only for high readings without food
qs.x: Lispro starts working quickly, so it is given shortly before or right after eating to avoid hypoglycemia. Giving it without food raises the risk of low blood glucose.

qs.q: When drawing up regular insulin and NPH insulin in one syringe, which order is correct?
qs.a: Draw up the clear regular insulin before the cloudy NPH
w: Draw up the cloudy NPH before the clear regular
Mix both in the vial before drawing up
Draw them in either order without difference
qs.x: Drawing clear before cloudy keeps NPH from contaminating the regular insulin vial. NPH is gently rolled, not shaken, before use.

qs.q: Which upcoming event should the nurse report to the provider for a patient taking metformin?
qs.a: A procedure using iodinated contrast dye
w: A routine dental cleaning
An annual flu vaccine
A scheduled eye exam
qs.x: Iodinated contrast can impair kidney function and increase the risk of metformin-associated lactic acidosis, so the provider decides on timing of doses. Routine dental care does not affect metformin.

qs.q: Which adverse effect is most important to teach a patient taking glipizide?
qs.a: Low blood glucose, especially if meals are skipped
w: High blood potassium
Genital yeast infections
Swelling of the lips
qs.x: Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin release and can cause hypoglycemia, especially in older adults or with missed meals. Genital yeast infections are linked to SGLT2 inhibitors.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for a patient taking levothyroxine?
qs.a: Take it on an empty stomach, apart from calcium or iron
w: Take it with a calcium supplement at breakfast
Take it with a large meal for absorption
Take it whenever convenient during the day
qs.x: Levothyroxine absorbs best on an empty stomach, and calcium and iron bind it. Taking it with calcium reduces its effect.

qs.q: Which findings may indicate that a patient's levothyroxine effect is too strong?
qs.a: Palpitations, heat intolerance, and weight loss
w: Fatigue, cold intolerance, and weight gain
Dry skin, constipation, and slow pulse
Puffy face, hoarseness, and drowsiness
qs.x: Excess thyroid hormone mimics hyperthyroidism. Fatigue, cold intolerance, and weight gain suggest the effect is too weak.

qs.q: Which symptom should a patient taking methimazole report right away?
qs.a: Fever or sore throat
w: Mild itching
Mild weight gain
Slight change in taste
qs.x: Methimazole can cause agranulocytosis, and fever or sore throat may be the first sign. A CBC is checked when these occur.

qs.q: Which history is a contraindication to semaglutide?
qs.a: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer
w: Personal history of iron deficiency
Family history of type 2 diabetes
Personal history of seasonal allergies
qs.x: GLP-1 receptor agonists carry a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors and are contraindicated with medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2. Family history of diabetes is common in those who use it.

qs.q: After glucagon is given for severe hypoglycemia, the patient wakes and can swallow. What is the next step?
qs.a: Give oral carbohydrate to prevent glucose dropping again
w: Give a second glucagon injection right away
Have the patient sleep without eating
Give rapid-acting insulin
qs.x: Glucagon's effect is short-lived, so oral carbohydrate is given once the person can swallow safely. The patient is placed on their side beforehand because vomiting is common.

qs.q: Which ECG change is a concern with ondansetron, especially at higher doses or with other risk factors?
qs.a: QT interval prolongation
w: ST segment elevation
Peaked T waves
Shortened PR interval
qs.x: Ondansetron can prolong the QT interval, increasing the risk of torsades de pointes. Electrolytes such as potassium and magnesium are corrected before use in at-risk patients.

qs.q: Which finding should a patient taking metoclopramide report?
qs.a: Involuntary movements of the face, tongue, or limbs
w: Mild loose stools
Mild drowsiness
Improved appetite
qs.x: Metoclopramide has a boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia, which can be irreversible. Mild drowsiness is common and less concerning.

qs.q: During IV promethazine administration, which patient complaint is the nurse's priority?
qs.a: Burning or pain at the IV site
w: Mild drowsiness
Dry mouth
Mild dizziness
qs.x: Promethazine has a boxed warning for severe tissue injury, including gangrene, from extravasation or inadvertent arterial injection. Drowsiness is expected.

qs.q: Which outcome shows lactulose is effective for hepatic encephalopathy?
qs.a: Improved mental status with soft stools
w: Firm stools once every few days
Rising serum ammonia level
More drowsiness and confusion
qs.x: Lactulose traps ammonia in the colon and removes it in stool, which improves mental status. A rising ammonia level shows it is not working.

qs.q: Which risks are associated with long-term pantoprazole use?
qs.a: Low magnesium, bone fractures, and C. difficile diarrhea
w: High potassium, gout, and kidney stones
Weight loss, tremor, and insomnia
Hair loss, gum overgrowth, and rash
qs.x: Long-term proton pump inhibitor use is linked to hypomagnesemia, fractures, and Clostridioides difficile infection. Gum overgrowth is a phenytoin effect.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for a patient taking sucralfate?
qs.a: Take it on an empty stomach, apart from other medicines
w: Take it with antacids at the same time
Take it immediately after large meals
Chew it together with other pills
qs.x: Sucralfate forms a protective barrier over ulcers and can bind other drugs, reducing their absorption. Antacids taken at the same time interfere with it.

qs.q: For which patient is misoprostol for NSAID ulcer prevention contraindicated?
qs.a: A patient who is pregnant
w: A patient with osteoarthritis
A patient with controlled hypertension
A patient who takes daily aspirin
qs.x: Misoprostol can cause uterine contractions and pregnancy loss, so it is contraindicated in pregnancy for ulcer prevention. Arthritis patients on NSAIDs are its main users.

qs.q: Which situation should be reported to the provider rather than self-treated with loperamide?
qs.a: Diarrhea with fever or blood in the stool
w: Mild diarrhea after a new food
Loose stools for half a day
Diarrhea with mild cramping only
qs.x: Bloody diarrhea or fever can signal an invasive infection, where slowing the gut may cause harm. Mild, short-lived diarrhea is a common use for loperamide.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for bisacodyl enteric-coated tablets?
qs.a: Swallow whole, and not with milk or antacids
w: Crush them for a faster effect
Take them with a glass of milk
Chew them with an antacid
qs.x: Milk, antacids, or crushing can dissolve the coating early, causing stomach irritation and cramping. The tablets work in the colon.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for a patient taking pancrelipase capsules?
qs.a: Take with every meal and snack, swallowing capsules whole
w: Take once daily at bedtime
Crush the beads and mix with milk
Take only when stools become oily
qs.x: Pancrelipase replaces pancreatic enzymes for digestion, so it must be taken with food. Crushing or chewing the beads destroys the protective coating.

qs.q: Which findings suggest magnesium toxicity in a patient receiving IV magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia?
qs.a: Absent deep tendon reflexes and slow breathing
w: Brisk reflexes and ankle clonus
Rising urine output and thirst
Fast heart rate and tremor
qs.x: Loss of reflexes, respiratory depression, and low urine output are signs of magnesium toxicity, along with a high magnesium level. Brisk reflexes and clonus suggest worsening preeclampsia instead.

qs.q: Which medicine should be readily available as the antidote for magnesium sulfate toxicity?
qs.a: Calcium gluconate
w: Naloxone
Protamine
Flumazenil
qs.x: IV calcium gluconate counters the effects of magnesium on the heart and neuromuscular junction. Naloxone reverses opioids.

qs.q: During an oxytocin infusion for labor, which finding requires immediate action?
qs.a: Contractions too frequent with a nonreassuring fetal heart rate
w: Contractions every few minutes with moderate variability
Mild maternal nausea
Gradual cervical change
qs.x: Uterine tachysystole with fetal heart rate changes signals reduced placental blood flow and needs immediate intervention per protocol and provider notification. Regular contractions with moderate variability are reassuring.

qs.q: With prolonged oxytocin use, which complication should the nurse monitor for?
qs.a: Water intoxication with low serum sodium
w: High serum potassium
High blood glucose
Low serum calcium
qs.x: Oxytocin has an antidiuretic effect, and prolonged infusion with large amounts of fluid can cause water intoxication and hyponatremia. Headache, confusion, or seizures are warning signs.

qs.q: Which condition is a contraindication to methylergonovine for postpartum hemorrhage?
qs.a: Hypertension or preeclampsia
w: Asthma
Anemia
Gestational diabetes
qs.x: Methylergonovine causes vasoconstriction that can sharply raise blood pressure. Asthma is the key contraindication for carboprost, not methylergonovine.

qs.q: Which history is a concern before carboprost is given for postpartum hemorrhage?
qs.a: Asthma
w: Hypertension
Migraine headaches
Hypothyroidism
qs.x: Carboprost, a prostaglandin, can cause bronchospasm and is avoided in asthma. Hypertension is the key concern with methylergonovine.

qs.q: Which patient is a candidate for Rho(D) immune globulin after birth?
qs.a: An Rh-negative mother with an Rh-positive newborn
w: An Rh-positive mother with an Rh-negative newborn
An Rh-positive mother with an Rh-positive newborn
An Rh-negative mother with an Rh-negative newborn
qs.x: Rho(D) immune globulin prevents an Rh-negative mother from forming antibodies after exposure to Rh-positive fetal blood. It is given within 72 hours of birth.

qs.q: Which maternal assessment is the priority when terbutaline is given?
qs.a: Heart rate, since tachycardia is common
w: Deep tendon reflexes
Blood glucose for hypoglycemia
Urine for protein
qs.x: Terbutaline is a beta agonist that causes maternal tachycardia and can cause serious cardiac effects; it carries a boxed warning against prolonged use for preterm labor. It tends to raise, not lower, glucose.

qs.q: Why is betamethasone given to a patient in preterm labor?
qs.a: To speed fetal lung maturity before birth
w: To stop uterine contractions
To prevent maternal seizures
To prevent newborn eye infection
qs.x: Antenatal corticosteroids speed fetal lung maturation and reduce neonatal respiratory distress. They do not relax the uterus.

qs.q: Why is erythromycin ophthalmic ointment applied to the newborn's eyes after birth?
qs.a: To prevent gonococcal eye infection
w: To prevent neonatal jaundice
To treat newborn conjunctival hemorrhage
To promote tear production
qs.x: Erythromycin eye ointment prevents gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum. It does not affect jaundice.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for using an epinephrine auto-injector?
qs.a: Inject into the outer thigh, then seek emergency care
w: Inject into the upper arm muscle, then rest
Inject into a vein for faster action
Inject only after an antihistamine fails
qs.x: The auto-injector is given into the anterolateral thigh, even through clothing, and emergency care is needed because symptoms can return. Waiting for an antihistamine delays life-saving treatment.

qs.q: Which effects should the nurse watch for when an older adult takes diphenhydramine?
qs.a: Confusion, urinary retention, and falls
w: Diarrhea and excess saliva
Insomnia and agitation only
Low blood pressure and wheezing
qs.x: Diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic and sedating, which raises the risk of confusion and falls in older adults. Diarrhea and salivation are the opposite effects.

qs.q: Which teaching is most important for a patient taking oral methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis?
qs.a: It is usually taken once a week, not daily
w: It is taken every day with breakfast
Extra doses help during a flare
Alcohol is safe in any amount
qs.x: Daily dosing errors with weekly methotrexate have caused fatal toxicity. Alcohol increases liver toxicity, and blood counts and liver tests are monitored.

qs.q: Which screening is required before a patient starts adalimumab?
qs.a: Tuberculosis screening
w: Bone density scan
Hearing test
Thyroid ultrasound
qs.x: TNF inhibitors carry a boxed warning for serious infections, including reactivation of latent tuberculosis. Hepatitis B screening is also done.

qs.q: During an infliximab infusion, which findings should the nurse report?
qs.a: Fever, chills, hives, or shortness of breath
w: Mild fatigue after the infusion
Improved joint stiffness
Slight warmth at the IV site
qs.x: Infliximab can cause infusion reactions ranging from mild to anaphylaxis. Improved stiffness is the desired effect.

qs.q: Which monitoring is routine for a transplant patient taking cyclosporine?
qs.a: Kidney function, blood pressure, and cyclosporine levels
w: Hearing tests and visual fields
Bone density and vitamin D
Uric acid and lipase
qs.x: Cyclosporine is nephrotoxic, raises blood pressure, and has a narrow therapeutic range, so cyclosporine levels guide therapy. Grapefruit juice can raise levels.

qs.q: Which adverse effects are common with tacrolimus?
qs.a: Tremor, high blood glucose, and kidney injury
w: Low blood pressure and weight loss
Gum overgrowth and hair growth
Bradycardia and wheezing
qs.x: Tacrolimus can cause neurotoxicity such as tremor, new-onset diabetes, and nephrotoxicity, and tacrolimus levels are monitored. Gum overgrowth and excess hair are more typical of cyclosporine.

qs.q: Which monitoring is recommended for a patient taking hydroxychloroquine long term?
qs.a: Regular eye exams for retinal damage
w: Monthly hearing tests
Weekly INR checks
Yearly bone density scans
qs.x: Hydroxychloroquine can cause irreversible retinal toxicity, so baseline and periodic eye exams are recommended. Hearing loss is not a typical concern.

qs.q: Which teaching is essential for a patient of childbearing potential taking mycophenolate?
qs.a: It can cause pregnancy loss and birth defects, so reliable contraception is needed
w: It is safe during pregnancy
It improves fertility
It only matters for male patients
qs.x: Mycophenolate has a boxed warning for embryofetal toxicity and a REMS program requiring pregnancy testing and contraception. It is not safe in pregnancy.

qs.q: Which adverse effect requires monitoring of blood counts in a patient taking azathioprine?
qs.a: Bone marrow suppression
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypoglycemia
Hypercalcemia
qs.x: Azathioprine can suppress the bone marrow, especially in patients with low TPMT or NUDT15 activity. CBCs are monitored regularly.

qs.q: Which route is correct for vinblastine?
qs.a: Intravenous only; it is fatal if given intrathecally
w: Intrathecal injection into the spinal fluid
Intramuscular injection into the thigh
Subcutaneous injection into the abdomen
qs.x: Vinca alkaloids carry a boxed warning that intrathecal administration is fatal and must be labeled for IV use only. It is also a vesicant, so extravasation is watched for.

qs.q: Why is a corticosteroid premedication given before docetaxel?
qs.a: To reduce fluid retention and hypersensitivity reactions
w: To prevent hair loss
To raise the white blood cell count
To prevent hemorrhagic cystitis
qs.x: Corticosteroid premedication lowers the risk and severity of fluid retention and hypersensitivity reactions with docetaxel. It does not prevent hair loss.

qs.q: Which symptom should a patient taking tamoxifen report?
qs.a: Abnormal vaginal bleeding or one-sided leg swelling
w: Mild hot flashes
Mild joint stiffness
Mild nausea
qs.x: Tamoxifen increases the risk of uterine cancer and blood clots. Hot flashes are common and expected.

qs.q: Which adverse effect should a patient taking capecitabine report?
qs.a: Redness, swelling, or pain on the palms and soles
w: Mild fatigue
Slight loss of appetite
Darker fingernails
qs.x: Capecitabine commonly causes hand-foot syndrome, which can limit therapy if not addressed early. Diarrhea is another important effect to report.

qs.q: Which finding is a key concern with ifosfamide?
qs.a: Blood in the urine
w: Orange urine
Ringing in the ears
Gum overgrowth
qs.x: Ifosfamide can cause hemorrhagic cystitis, which mesna and hydration help prevent. Neurotoxicity such as confusion is another concern.

qs.q: Which symptoms should a patient receiving nivolumab report promptly?
qs.a: New diarrhea, cough, or rash
w: Mild fatigue after infusions
Slight decrease in appetite
Mild joint aches
qs.x: Immune checkpoint inhibitors can cause immune-related inflammation of the colon, lungs, skin, and other organs. These effects can become serious if not treated early.

qs.q: Which adverse effect of irinotecan needs prompt reporting?
qs.a: Diarrhea, which can become severe
w: Hiccups
Taste changes
Mild hair thinning
qs.x: Irinotecan causes early and late diarrhea that can lead to dehydration and electrolyte loss. Early cholinergic diarrhea may be treated with atropine.

qs.q: Which teaching is appropriate for a patient receiving oxaliplatin?
qs.a: Avoid cold drinks and cold objects for several days after
w: Use ice chips during the infusion
Drink only cold fluids that day
Apply ice packs to the hands
qs.x: Oxaliplatin causes cold-triggered peripheral neuropathy and throat discomfort. Ice chips, used with some other drugs, can worsen these symptoms.

qs.q: Which symptoms should a patient receiving trastuzumab deruxtecan report right away?
qs.a: New cough, shortness of breath, or fever
w: Mild hair thinning
Mild nausea after infusions
Mild fatigue
qs.x: Trastuzumab deruxtecan has a boxed warning for interstitial lung disease, which can be fatal. New respiratory symptoms need prompt evaluation.

qs.q: Which teaching is appropriate after intravesical BCG treatment?
qs.a: Sit to urinate and add bleach to the toilet before flushing
w: Stand to urinate and flush right away
Avoid drinking any fluids that day
Hold urine for a full day
qs.x: BCG is a live organism, so urine is disinfected with bleach for several hours after treatment to protect others. Sitting reduces splashing.

qs.q: Which requirement applies to a patient who can become pregnant and is starting isotretinoin?
qs.a: Use two forms of birth control and complete pregnancy tests
w: Use one form of birth control as needed
Take a pregnancy test only once at the end
Avoid contraception to monitor cycles
qs.x: Isotretinoin causes severe birth defects, and the iPLEDGE program requires two forms of contraception and regular pregnancy testing. A single test at the end is not enough.

qs.q: Which technique reduces systemic effects of timolol eye drops?
qs.a: Press on the inner corner of the eye after instilling
w: Blink rapidly after instilling the drops
Tilt the head forward after instilling
Rub the eye gently after instilling
qs.x: Punctal occlusion limits drainage into the nose and bloodstream, reducing beta-blocker effects such as bradycardia and bronchospasm. Rubbing the eye does not help.

qs.q: Which effect should a patient using latanoprost be taught about?
qs.a: Permanent darkening of iris color
w: Temporary loss of eyelashes
Constricted pupils at night
Yellow-tinted vision
qs.x: Prostaglandin analogs can increase brown pigment in the iris, which may be permanent, and can lengthen eyelashes. They do not cause eyelash loss.

qs.q: Which allergy is a concern before applying silver sulfadiazine to a burn?
qs.a: Sulfonamide drug allergy
w: Latex allergy
Iodine allergy
Egg allergy
qs.x: Silver sulfadiazine is a sulfonamide and can cause reactions in sulfa-allergic patients. It can also cause transient leukopenia.

qs.q: Which teaching is appropriate when permethrin cream is prescribed for scabies?
qs.a: Treat close contacts and wash bedding in hot water
w: Treat only the itchy areas
Reapply every day for a month
No cleaning of bedding is needed
qs.x: Scabies spreads by close contact, so household members are treated and bedding and clothing are washed hot. Itching may persist for weeks even after successful treatment.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for clobetasol topical cream?
qs.a: Avoid the face, groin, and tight coverings
w: Apply it thickly under plastic wrap
Use it on the face for best results
Use it continuously for many months
qs.x: Clobetasol is a very high-potency corticosteroid that can cause skin thinning and systemic absorption. Occlusion and thin-skin areas increase these risks.

qs.q: Which teaching is appropriate for a patient using topical tretinoin?
qs.a: Use sunscreen and limit sun exposure
w: Apply it right before sunbathing
Use it with harsh scrubs for faster results
Expect no skin irritation
qs.x: Tretinoin increases sensitivity to sunlight and commonly causes irritation at first. Harsh scrubs worsen irritation.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for a lidocaine patch?
qs.a: Avoid heat over the patch and fold used patches before disposal
w: Cover the patch with a heating pad
Apply it to broken or irritated skin
