Leave used patches where pets can reach
qs.x: Heat increases absorption, and used patches still contain drug that can harm children and pets. Patches are applied only to intact skin.

qs.q: Which teaching is appropriate for a patient using pilocarpine eye drops?
qs.a: Use caution driving at night because vision may be dim
w: Expect wider pupils and light sensitivity
Expect improved night vision
Use the drops only when eyes are dry
qs.x: Pilocarpine constricts the pupils, which reduces light entry and can make night vision dim or blurred. Pupil dilation is caused by anticholinergic drops.

qs.q: Which teaching is correct for prednisolone acetate eye drops?
qs.a: Shake the bottle well before each use
w: Store the bottle in the freezer
Rinse the eye right after instilling
Share the bottle with family members
qs.x: Prednisolone acetate is a suspension, so shaking ensures an even dose. Long-term use can raise eye pressure, so follow-up eye exams are needed.

qs.q: A client has used omeprazole daily for six years. Which nutrient deficiency is most associated with long-term proton pump inhibitor use?
qs.a: Vitamin B12
w: Vitamin C
Vitamin A
Riboflavin
qs.x: Gastric acid and pepsin release protein-bound B12 from food. Long-term acid suppression lowers B12 absorption.

qs.q: A client on a proton pump inhibitor needs a calcium supplement. Which form is absorbed well without stomach acid?
qs.a: Calcium citrate
w: Calcium carbonate
Oyster shell calcium
Dolomite calcium
qs.x: Calcium carbonate needs acid to dissolve. Calcium citrate is absorbed well with or without food and acid.

qs.q: Which electrolyte problem carries an FDA warning for long-term proton pump inhibitor use?
qs.a: Hypomagnesemia
w: Hypernatremia
Hyperkalemia
Hypercalcemia
qs.x: Prolonged PPI use can cause low magnesium, which can lead to cramps, arrhythmias and secondary low calcium or potassium.

qs.q: Why can long-term acid suppression worsen iron status?
qs.a: Acid helps convert ferric iron to the more absorbable ferrous form
w: Acid suppression increases urinary iron losses
Acid-suppressing drugs bind iron in the small intestine
Acid suppression blocks transferrin production in the liver
qs.x: Nonheme iron absorption depends on an acidic stomach. Heme iron is less affected.

qs.q: A client taking cholestyramine for high LDL cholesterol is at greatest risk of deficiency of which nutrients?
qs.a: Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K
w: Water-soluble B vitamins
Sodium and chloride
Essential amino acids
qs.x: Bile acid sequestrants bind bile acids, impairing fat and fat-soluble vitamin absorption. Folate can also be affected.

qs.q: Which counseling point applies to bile acid sequestrants such as colestipol?
qs.a: Other medicines are spaced apart in time because the resin can bind them
w: The resin works best mixed with grapefruit juice
The resin increases absorption of fat-soluble vitamins
The resin must be taken with a high-fat meal to work
qs.x: Resins bind many drugs and nutrients in the gut. Other medicines are usually timed well before or after the resin.

qs.q: A client starting orlistat asks about vitamins. Which statement is accurate?
qs.a: Fat-soluble vitamin absorption falls, so a multivitamin is advised at a separate time
w: Orlistat blocks starch digestion, so B vitamins are lost
Orlistat raises vitamin K absorption, which lowers INR
Orlistat increases vitamin D absorption from fatty foods
qs.x: Orlistat inhibits lipase, so dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins pass unabsorbed. A multivitamin is typically separated by at least 2 hours, often at bedtime.

qs.q: A client on furosemide for heart failure is at risk for loss of which electrolytes?
qs.a: Potassium, magnesium and calcium
w: Potassium only, with calcium retention
Sodium only, with potassium retention
Phosphorus and bicarbonate only
qs.x: Loop diuretics block sodium reabsorption in the loop of Henle, increasing urinary loss of potassium, magnesium and calcium.

qs.q: How do thiazide diuretics differ from loop diuretics in calcium handling?
qs.a: Thiazides lower urinary calcium loss, while loop diuretics raise it
w: Thiazides raise urinary calcium loss more than loop diuretics
Both classes retain calcium to the same degree
Neither class has any effect on urinary calcium
qs.x: Thiazides increase calcium reabsorption and can cause mild hypercalcemia; loop diuretics increase calcium excretion.

qs.q: Which timing best supports levothyroxine absorption?
qs.a: On an empty stomach with water, 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast
w: With breakfast and a glass of milk to ease stomach upset
With a high-fiber cereal to keep absorption steady
At any time, since food does not change absorption
qs.x: Food, coffee, fiber, soy, calcium and iron reduce levothyroxine absorption. Consistent empty-stomach timing keeps levels stable.

qs.q: A client on levothyroxine is prescribed ferrous sulfate. What is the best counseling?
qs.a: Separate the two by about 4 hours, since iron lowers levothyroxine absorption
w: Combine them in one dose to improve absorption of both
Iron raises levothyroxine levels, so watch for tremor
No interaction exists between these two products
qs.x: Iron and calcium bind levothyroxine in the gut. Separating the doses by about 4 hours limits the interaction.

qs.q: Which description matches how alendronate is taken?
qs.a: First thing in the morning with plain water, staying upright at least 30 minutes before eating
w: With breakfast and coffee to reduce esophageal irritation
At bedtime with milk to increase calcium uptake
With orange juice to improve its absorption
qs.x: Food, beverages other than water and minerals block alendronate absorption. Staying upright reduces esophageal injury.

qs.q: A client taking phenelzine asks which cheese is the greatest concern. Which is correct?
qs.a: Aged cheddar
w: Fresh mozzarella
Cottage cheese
Cream cheese
qs.x: Aged cheeses are high in tyramine. Fresh, unaged cheeses are low in tyramine.

qs.q: Eating aged salami while taking tranylcypromine can cause which reaction?
qs.a: Hypertensive crisis from tyramine-driven norepinephrine release
w: Severe hypoglycemia from increased insulin release
Serotonin syndrome from excess dietary tryptophan
Hyperkalemia from reduced renal potassium excretion
qs.x: MAOIs block tyramine breakdown. Tyramine then releases norepinephrine, causing severe headache and dangerous blood pressure elevation.

qs.q: How long are tyramine restrictions usually continued after an MAOI such as phenelzine is discontinued?
qs.a: About 2 weeks
w: About 24 hours
About 3 days
About 6 months
qs.x: MAO enzyme activity takes about 2 weeks to recover after an irreversible MAOI ends.

qs.q: Which antipsychotic pair carries the highest risk of weight gain and metabolic syndrome?
qs.a: Olanzapine and clozapine
w: Aripiprazole and ziprasidone
Haloperidol and lurasidone
Ziprasidone and lurasidone
qs.x: Olanzapine and clozapine cause the most weight gain, hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia among antipsychotics.

qs.q: A client recently started olanzapine. Which labs should the RD expect to be monitored?
qs.a: Fasting glucose or A1C and a lipid panel
w: Serum ammonia and lipase
Serum zinc and copper
Prealbumin and transferrin
qs.x: Second-generation antipsychotics require metabolic monitoring: weight, waist, blood pressure, glucose and lipids.

qs.q: Besides weight gain, which GI effect of clozapine matters most for diet planning?
qs.a: Severe constipation from slowed gut motility
w: Profuse watery diarrhea
Fat malabsorption with steatorrhea
New-onset lactose intolerance
qs.x: Clozapine slows GI motility and can cause serious constipation and ileus. Fiber, fluids and bowel habits are monitored.

qs.q: A client takes prednisone each morning. When is hyperglycemia most often seen?
qs.a: Afternoon and evening
w: Early morning fasting
Overnight around 3 a.m.
Only after the drug is tapered
qs.x: Morning prednisone raises glucose mostly later in the day, so fasting glucose may look normal while afternoon values are high.

qs.q: Which diet pattern is often advised with long-term prednisone therapy?
qs.a: Moderate sodium restriction with adequate calcium and vitamin D
w: High sodium intake to prevent low blood pressure
Low-protein diet to protect the kidneys
Low-calcium diet to prevent kidney stones
qs.x: Corticosteroids cause sodium and fluid retention and bone loss. Protein needs are maintained to limit muscle wasting.

qs.q: Long-term corticosteroids raise the risk of which nutrition-related problems?
qs.a: Bone loss, muscle wasting and increased appetite
w: Iron overload and liver injury
Hypoglycemia and appetite loss
Hyperkalemia and weight loss
qs.x: Glucocorticoids increase appetite, break down muscle protein, reduce calcium absorption and cause hypokalemia rather than hyperkalemia.

qs.q: A client new to metformin reports nausea and diarrhea. Which counseling is appropriate?
qs.a: GI effects often ease when it is taken with meals and over the first weeks
w: Taking it on an empty stomach reduces these effects
A high-fat meal with each dose prevents these effects
These effects mean the drug is not being absorbed
qs.x: Metformin GI upset is common at the start and is reduced by taking it with food. Extended-release forms may also help.

qs.q: A client on chemotherapy reports a metallic taste when eating meat. Which suggestion is appropriate?
qs.a: Plastic utensils and other proteins such as eggs, beans or dairy
w: Metal utensils and more red meat for iron
Avoiding all seasonings and marinades
Eating only very hot foods to mask taste
qs.x: Dysgeusia is common with chemotherapy. Plastic utensils, marinades, tart flavors and alternative proteins can improve intake.

qs.q: Which food choice is best for chemotherapy-related oral mucositis?
qs.a: Soft, moist, bland foods served cool or at room temperature
w: Citrus fruits and tomato-based sauces
Crunchy toast and dry crackers
Spicy foods to stimulate saliva
qs.x: Acidic, spicy, rough and hot foods irritate inflamed mucosa. Soft, moist, bland foods are easier to eat.

qs.q: A hospitalized client develops frequent watery diarrhea after a course of clindamycin. Which complication should be suspected and reported?
qs.a: Clostridioides difficile infection
w: Lactose intolerance from the formula
Celiac disease triggered by antibiotics
Pancreatic insufficiency from the drug
qs.x: Antibiotics such as clindamycin, fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins disrupt gut flora and allow C. difficile overgrowth.

qs.q: Why is Saccharomyces boulardii used with caution in critically ill or immunocompromised clients with central lines?
qs.a: Risk of fungemia from the live yeast
w: It raises serum potassium
It contains a large amount of lactose
It blocks vitamin K absorption
qs.x: Live probiotic yeast can enter the bloodstream, especially via central catheters, in vulnerable patients.

qs.q: A child on methylphenidate for ADHD is losing weight. Which strategy is appropriate?
qs.a: A nutrient-dense breakfast before the morning dose and an evening snack
w: The largest meal at midday when the drug effect peaks
Limiting snacks so appetite returns at dinner
Replacing meals with low-calorie beverages
qs.x: Stimulants suppress appetite during the day. Meals before the dose and after it wears off support growth.

qs.q: When megestrol is used for cachexia, which outcome is most typical?
qs.a: Increased appetite, with weight gain mostly as fat and fluid
w: Lean muscle gain through anabolic effects
Faster gastric emptying and less bloating
A higher basal metabolic rate
qs.x: Megestrol improves appetite and weight, but gains are mainly fat and fluid rather than lean mass.

qs.q: A client on megestrol reports one swollen, painful calf. What does this suggest?
qs.a: A possible blood clot that needs prompt reporting
w: An expected effect of increased appetite
Normal fluid gain from better intake
A sign the drug is working well
qs.x: Megestrol increases thromboembolism risk. Leg swelling or pain should be reported promptly.

qs.q: Dronabinol is FDA-approved for which nutrition-related use?
qs.a: Anorexia with weight loss in AIDS
w: Obesity in adolescents
Hypercalcemia of cancer
Diabetic gastroparesis
qs.x: Dronabinol is approved for AIDS-related anorexia with weight loss and for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.

qs.q: Insulin lispro begins to lower blood glucose within about how long?
qs.a: About 15 minutes
w: About 1 to 2 hours
About 4 hours
About 6 hours
qs.x: Rapid-acting insulins start in about 15 minutes, peak in 1 to 2 hours and last 3 to 5 hours.

qs.q: Because of its rapid onset, insulin aspart is usually given at what time relative to a meal?
qs.a: About 5 to 10 minutes before the meal
w: About 1 hour after the meal
Only at bedtime
About 2 hours before the meal
qs.x: Rapid-acting insulin is matched closely to meals. A delayed meal after a dose raises hypoglycemia risk.

qs.q: Regular insulin peaks about how long after a subcutaneous injection?
qs.a: About 2 to 4 hours
w: About 15 to 30 minutes
About 10 to 14 hours
It has no peak
qs.x: Regular insulin starts in 30 to 60 minutes, peaks in 2 to 4 hours and lasts 5 to 8 hours, so it is given about 30 minutes before meals.

qs.q: A client injects NPH insulin at breakfast. When is hypoglycemia risk highest?
qs.a: Afternoon, during its peak about 4 to 12 hours later
w: Within 15 minutes of the injection
Right before breakfast the next day
Late night, about 18 to 24 hours later
qs.x: NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours after injection. Missing lunch or an afternoon snack is a classic cause of lows.

qs.q: Which describes the action of insulin glargine?
qs.a: Relatively peakless basal action lasting about 24 hours
w: Rapid onset with a peak at about 1 hour
A sharp peak at 6 hours, lasting 12 hours
Onset in 15 minutes, lasting 4 hours
qs.x: Glargine provides a steady basal level with no pronounced peak, so hypoglycemia risk is lower than with NPH.

qs.q: Insulin detemir is classified as which type?
qs.a: Long-acting basal insulin
w: Rapid-acting mealtime insulin
Short-acting regular insulin
Intermediate premixed insulin
qs.x: Detemir is a long-acting basal analog with a relatively flat profile lasting up to 24 hours. The US brand was discontinued in 2024.

qs.q: What is the primary action of metformin?
qs.a: Lowers liver glucose production and improves insulin sensitivity
w: Stimulates insulin release from the pancreas
Blocks glucose reabsorption in the kidney
Slows starch digestion in the small intestine
qs.x: Metformin is a biguanide. It does not stimulate insulin release, so it rarely causes hypoglycemia alone.

qs.q: Long-term metformin use is linked to deficiency of which vitamin?
qs.a: Vitamin B12
w: Vitamin K
Vitamin C
Thiamine
qs.x: Metformin reduces B12 absorption in the ileum. Periodic B12 checks are recommended, especially with neuropathy or anemia.

qs.q: How does empagliflozin lower blood glucose?
qs.a: Blocks kidney glucose reabsorption so glucose is lost in urine
w: Increases insulin release from beta cells
Slows gastric emptying after meals
Inhibits starch digestion in the gut
qs.x: SGLT2 inhibitors cause glucosuria, which also produces a modest calorie loss and weight loss.

qs.q: Which counseling point is important for a client on empagliflozin?
qs.a: Adequate fluids, and watching for dehydration and genital yeast infections
w: Extra sodium to prevent high potassium
Expecting weight gain from fluid retention
Fluid restriction to reduce urination
qs.x: Glucosuria causes osmotic diuresis and a sugary urinary environment, raising dehydration, genital infection and UTI risk.

qs.q: A client on empagliflozin wants to start a very-low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet. Which risk should be discussed with the provider?
qs.a: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis
w: Severe hyperkalemia
Lactic acidosis
Hypercalcemia
qs.x: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause ketoacidosis with only mildly elevated glucose, especially with carbohydrate restriction, fasting or illness.

qs.q: Which best describes how semaglutide works?
qs.a: Boosts glucose-dependent insulin release, lowers glucagon and slows gastric emptying
w: Blocks glucose reabsorption in the kidney tubule
Lowers liver glucose output without other effects
Inhibits intestinal fat absorption by blocking lipase
qs.x: GLP-1 agonists also increase satiety, which drives weight loss.

qs.q: A client on semaglutide reports nausea after meals. Which diet strategy helps?
qs.a: Smaller meals eaten slowly, ending at first fullness and limiting high-fat foods
w: Larger meals less often to reduce total eating time
High-fat meals to settle the stomach
Lying down right after each meal
qs.x: Slowed gastric emptying causes early fullness and nausea. Small, low-fat meals and eating slowly reduce GI symptoms.

qs.q: Why is hydration emphasized for clients on semaglutide?
qs.a: Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration and acute kidney injury
w: It causes glucose loss in urine and osmotic diuresis
It causes sodium retention and edema
It permanently blunts the thirst response
qs.x: GI fluid losses plus reduced intake can lead to dehydration and kidney injury. Osmotic diuresis is an SGLT2 effect.

qs.q: During GLP-1 agonist weight loss, which focus best helps preserve lean mass?
qs.a: Adequate protein with resistance exercise
w: Very-low-protein meals to limit calories
Carbohydrate loading before each meal
Extended fasting on alternate days
qs.x: Rapid weight loss includes lean tissue. Meeting protein needs and strength training help preserve muscle.

qs.q: A client on glipizide skips lunch. Which risk increases?
qs.a: Hypoglycemia
w: Hyperkalemia
Euglycemic ketoacidosis
Lactic acidosis
qs.x: Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin release regardless of food intake, so missed meals raise hypoglycemia risk.

qs.q: Propofol provides about 1.1 kcal/mL. How should the RD account for it?
qs.a: Count it as fat calories and adjust the nutrition regimen
w: Ignore it, since sedatives provide no usable energy
Count it as protein calories
Count it as carbohydrate calories
qs.x: Propofol is a 10% lipid emulsion. Its calories can be substantial and are counted toward lipid and total energy.

qs.q: The calories in propofol come mainly from which source?
qs.a: Its soybean oil lipid emulsion vehicle
w: Dextrose in the diluent
Amino acids added for stability
The propofol molecule itself
qs.x: Propofol is delivered in a 10% soybean oil emulsion with egg lecithin, providing about 1.1 kcal/mL.

qs.q: Which lab should be monitored during prolonged propofol infusion?
qs.a: Serum triglycerides
w: Serum ammonia
Serum ferritin
Serum prealbumin
qs.x: The lipid load can cause hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis, especially at high rates or long durations.

qs.q: A ventilated patient on propofol and full-goal enteral feeding has rising triglycerides and CO2. What is the likely cause?
qs.a: Overfeeding from uncounted propofol lipid calories
w: Inadequate protein provision
Refeeding syndrome from low dextrose
Vitamin K deficiency from antibiotics
qs.x: Propofol calories added to a full feeding goal can cause overfeeding, raising CO2 production and triglycerides.

qs.q: Propofol contains egg lecithin and soybean oil. Which history should be relayed to the team?
qs.a: Egg or soy allergy
w: Shellfish allergy
Lactose intolerance
Gluten intolerance
qs.x: US labeling lists allergy to eggs, egg products, soybeans or soy products as a contraindication.

qs.q: Which other ICU infusion is a lipid emulsion that adds fat calories?
qs.a: Clevidipine
w: Norepinephrine
Regular insulin
Heparin
qs.x: Clevidipine is a 20% lipid emulsion providing about 2 kcal/mL, so it is counted like propofol.

qs.q: A patient receives phenytoin suspension via feeding tube during continuous feeds. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Reduced phenytoin absorption and low drug levels
w: Phenytoin toxicity from increased absorption
Formula curdling and diarrhea
Hyperkalemia from the formula
qs.x: Phenytoin binds formula components and tubing, lowering absorption. Seizure control can be lost.

qs.q: Which practice is commonly used to manage the phenytoin and tube feeding interaction?
qs.a: Separating the feeding and the dose by about 2 hours on each side and monitoring levels
w: Mixing the dose directly into the formula bag
Giving the dose with a bolus of formula
Increasing the formula rate around the dose
qs.x: Many protocols separate feeds around each phenytoin dose, flush the tube and check drug levels, with feeding rates adjusted to meet goals.

qs.q: In a malnourished patient with low albumin, why can a total phenytoin level be misleading?
qs.a: More of the drug is unbound and active
w: Less of the drug reaches the brain
Low albumin speeds phenytoin metabolism
Formula protein binds phenytoin in the blood
qs.x: Phenytoin is highly protein bound. Low albumin raises the free fraction, so toxicity can occur with a normal total level.

qs.q: Which practice best prevents feeding tube occlusion from medications?
qs.a: Flushing with water before and after each medication
w: Mixing all medications into the formula
Routine flushing with cola or cranberry juice
Crushing enteric-coated tablets very finely
qs.x: Water flushes clear the tube. Mixing drugs with formula and acidic flushes promote clumping.

qs.q: Which dosage form should not be crushed for tube administration?
qs.a: Extended-release tablets
w: Plain immediate-release tablets
Oral liquid solutions
Powder from immediate-release capsules
qs.x: Crushing extended-release or enteric-coated products can cause dose dumping or clogging. A liquid or alternative form is requested.

qs.q: Why is ciprofloxacin absorption reduced when given with enteral formula?
qs.a: Divalent cations in the formula chelate the drug
w: Formula protein breaks down the drug
Formula fiber raises gastric pH and destroys it
Formula fat traps the drug in micelles
qs.x: Calcium, magnesium, iron and zinc in formula bind fluoroquinolones, lowering absorption. Separating timing reduces the effect.

qs.q: Which medication is known to form bezoars or clog tubes when mixed with enteral formula?
qs.a: Sucralfate
w: Ondansetron
Famotidine
Metoclopramide
qs.x: Sucralfate binds proteins in formula, forming a sticky mass that can obstruct tubes.

qs.q: A patient on warfarin who starts continuous enteral feeding develops a low INR. What may contribute?
qs.a: Formula vitamin K and binding of warfarin to formula protein
w: Formula sodium speeding warfarin metabolism
Enteral feeds raising platelet counts
Formula blocking vitamin K absorption
qs.x: Enteral feeding can lower warfarin effect. INR is monitored closely when feeds start, stop or change.

qs.q: A tube-fed patient develops diarrhea soon after several liquid medications are started. What common cause should be considered?
qs.a: Sorbitol in liquid medication formulations
w: Formula osmolality being too low
Water flushes being too frequent
Use of a fiber-free formula
qs.x: Many liquid medicines contain sorbitol, which causes osmotic diarrhea. The medication list is reviewed before changing the formula.

qs.q: When is sevelamer taken for best effect?
qs.a: With meals
w: At bedtime on an empty stomach
About 2 hours after meals
Only on dialysis days
qs.x: Phosphate binders must be in the gut with food to bind dietary phosphorus.

qs.q: A client asks why calcium acetate is taken with the first bite of a meal. What is the best answer?
qs.a: It binds dietary phosphorus in the gut so less is absorbed
w: It is absorbed better when taken with dietary fat
It prevents nausea related to dialysis
It lowers serum potassium after meals
qs.x: Calcium acetate binds phosphate from food. Taken apart from meals, it mainly adds calcium.

qs.q: Which lab abnormality is a key concern with calcium acetate?
qs.a: Hypercalcemia
w: Hypokalemia
Hyponatremia
Hypermagnesemia
qs.x: Calcium-based binders add calcium load, which can cause hypercalcemia and vascular calcification.

qs.q: Which is an advantage of sevelamer over calcium-based binders?
qs.a: It adds no calcium and may lower LDL cholesterol
w: It also lowers serum potassium
It provides calcium for bone health
It raises urinary phosphorus excretion
qs.x: Sevelamer is a non-calcium polymer. It also binds bile acids, which can lower LDL.

qs.q: How are lanthanum carbonate tablets taken?
qs.a: Chewed completely with or right after meals
w: Swallowed whole on an empty stomach
Dissolved in juice at bedtime
Taken once weekly with water
qs.x: Lanthanum chewable tablets must be chewed fully and taken with meals to bind phosphorus.

qs.q: A dialysis client routinely misses phosphate binders when eating out. What lab change is expected?
qs.a: Rising serum phosphorus
w: Rising serum calcium
Falling serum potassium
Falling serum phosphorus
qs.x: Without a binder present at meals, dietary phosphorus is absorbed, raising serum phosphorus.

qs.q: Which vitamin K counseling is correct for a client on warfarin?
qs.a: Keep vitamin K intake consistent from day to day
w: Avoid all green leafy vegetables
Eat as many greens as possible
Vitamin K has no effect on warfarin
qs.x: Warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling. Consistent intake keeps the INR stable; sudden changes shift it.

qs.q: A client on warfarin starts eating a large spinach salad every day. What INR change is expected?
qs.a: Decreased INR
w: Increased INR
No change in INR
Increased INR only at night
qs.x: More vitamin K counteracts warfarin, lowering the INR and the anticoagulant effect.

qs.q: Which supplement may increase bleeding risk with warfarin?
qs.a: Fish oil
w: Coenzyme Q10
St. John's wort
Vitamin K
qs.x: Fish oil has antiplatelet effects. CoQ10, St. John's wort and vitamin K tend to reduce warfarin effect.

qs.q: Which food is notably high in vitamin K2 and can affect warfarin?
qs.a: Natto
w: White rice
Bananas
Plain pasta
qs.x: Natto, fermented soybeans, is very high in menaquinone-7 and can lower the INR.

qs.q: Lisinopril increases the risk of which electrolyte disturbance?
qs.a: Hyperkalemia
w: Hypokalemia
Hypercalcemia
Hypernatremia
qs.x: ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone, so the kidney excretes less potassium.

qs.q: Why do ACE inhibitors and ARBs raise serum potassium?
qs.a: Less aldosterone means less potassium excreted by the kidney
w: They increase intestinal potassium absorption
They release potassium stored in bone
They block insulin-driven potassium shifts
qs.x: Lower aldosterone activity reduces renal potassium secretion, especially in CKD.

qs.q: A client with CKD on lisinopril wants to use a salt substitute. What is the concern?
qs.a: Many salt substitutes contain potassium chloride, raising hyperkalemia risk
w: Salt substitutes are high in sodium chloride
Salt substitutes contain phosphate additives
Salt substitutes block lisinopril absorption
qs.x: Potassium-based salt substitutes can cause dangerous hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors, ARBs or CKD.

qs.q: A client on losartan with hyperkalemia needs a potassium-restricted diet. Which fruit is the lowest potassium choice?
qs.a: Apple
w: Banana
Orange
Cantaloupe
qs.x: Apples, berries and grapes are lower in potassium; bananas, oranges and melons are higher.

qs.q: Which drug adds to hyperkalemia risk when combined with an ACE inhibitor?
qs.a: Spironolactone, a potassium-sparing diuretic
w: Furosemide, a loop diuretic
Hydrochlorothiazide, a thiazide diuretic
Colestipol, a bile acid sequestrant
qs.x: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone, adding to the potassium retention caused by ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

qs.q: Which preparation lowers the potassium content of potatoes for a potassium-restricted diet?
qs.a: Peeling, dicing and boiling in a large amount of water
w: Baking with the skin on
Microwaving whole
Roasting in oil
qs.x: Leaching by boiling small pieces in plenty of water removes some potassium; draining the water matters.

qs.q: After a continuous albuterol nebulizer, a patient's heart rate rises from 96 to 122 and a fine hand tremor appears. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: Expected beta-agonist effects of albuterol
w: Anticholinergic blockade from albuterol
An allergic reaction to the albuterol
Worsening hypoxemia from the treatment
qs.x: Albuterol stimulates beta-2 receptors in skeletal muscle (tremor) and has some beta-1 crossover plus reflex effects (tachycardia). These are common, expected side effects to monitor and report.

qs.q: A patient with recent myocardial infarction and frequent tachycardia needs a short-acting bronchodilator. Why might levalbuterol be ordered instead of albuterol?
qs.a: It is the pure R-isomer and may cause less tachycardia
w: It works through muscarinic receptor blockade instead
It lasts twelve hours so fewer treatments are needed
It has no effect on beta-2 receptors in the heart
qs.x: Levalbuterol is the active R-enantiomer of albuterol. It is often selected for patients sensitive to tachycardia, although heart rate still needs monitoring.

qs.q: A patient says she uses her salmeterol inhaler whenever she feels an asthma attack starting. What is the key teaching point?
qs.a: Salmeterol has a slow onset and is for maintenance, not rescue
w: Salmeterol works best only when taken during attacks
Salmeterol is an anticholinergic and must be paired with albuterol
Salmeterol is a steroid and works only after weeks
qs.x: Salmeterol is a LABA with an onset of roughly 10-20 minutes and a long duration. A SABA such as albuterol is the rescue medication.

qs.q: Per FDA labeling, how should a long-acting beta agonist such as salmeterol be used in a patient with asthma?
qs.a: Only in combination with an inhaled corticosteroid
w: As a stand-alone controller without an inhaled steroid
Only as a rescue inhaler during acute symptoms
Only by continuous nebulization in the emergency room
qs.x: LABA monotherapy in asthma is associated with severe exacerbations and asthma deaths. LABAs are used with an ICS, usually in a single combination inhaler.

qs.q: What is the mechanism of action of ipratropium bromide?
qs.a: Blocks muscarinic receptors, reducing vagally mediated bronchoconstriction
w: Stimulates beta-2 receptors to relax airway smooth muscle
Inhibits leukotriene receptors on airway inflammatory cells
Breaks disulfide bonds in airway mucus glycoproteins
qs.x: Ipratropium is a short-acting muscarinic antagonist (SAMA). It reduces cholinergic bronchoconstriction and can dry secretions.

qs.q: Why is albuterol combined with ipratropium (DuoNeb) for a COPD exacerbation?
qs.a: Two different mechanisms produce greater bronchodilation than either alone
w: Ipratropium speeds the onset of albuterol to a few seconds
Albuterol prevents the dry mouth caused by ipratropium
The combination replaces the need for systemic steroids
qs.x: Beta-2 stimulation and muscarinic blockade relax airway smooth muscle by separate pathways. The combination gives additive bronchodilation in COPD and severe asthma exacerbations.

qs.q: During an ipratropium nebulizer given by face mask, a patient reports blurred vision and eye pain. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Aerosol reaching the eyes causing pupil dilation
w: Beta-2 stimulation of the ciliary muscle
Systemic absorption causing low potassium
Bronchospasm causing reduced oxygen to the eye
qs.x: Anticholinergic aerosol leaking around a mask can dilate the pupil and may precipitate acute narrow-angle glaucoma. A mouthpiece reduces eye exposure; eye symptoms should be reported.

qs.q: Which medication is a once-daily long-acting muscarinic antagonist used for COPD maintenance?
qs.a: Tiotropium
w: Ipratropium
Levalbuterol
Cromolyn
qs.x: Tiotropium is a LAMA dosed once daily for COPD maintenance. Ipratropium is short-acting, levalbuterol is a SABA and cromolyn is a mast cell stabilizer.

qs.q: An older man with an enlarged prostate starts tiotropium. Which adverse effect should he be taught to report?
qs.a: Difficulty urinating
w: Fine hand tremor
Oral thrush
Low blood sugar
qs.x: Anticholinergic effects can cause urinary retention, especially with benign prostatic hyperplasia. Dry mouth and constipation are also common.

qs.q: A patient using a fluticasone inhaler has white patches on the tongue. What teaching helps prevent this problem?
qs.a: Rinse the mouth with water and spit after each use
w: Use the inhaler right before eating a meal
Take an extra puff of albuterol after each dose
Exhale into the inhaler before every puff
qs.x: Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) is a local effect of inhaled corticosteroids. Rinsing and spitting, and using a spacer with MDIs, reduce oral deposition.

qs.q: Which inhaled corticosteroid is available in the US as a nebulizer suspension for young children?
qs.a: Budesonide
w: Fluticasone propionate
Mometasone
Ciclesonide
qs.x: Budesonide inhalation suspension can be given by nebulizer to young children who cannot use an MDI or DPI. The others are MDI or DPI products.

qs.q: A parent asks why her child's inhaled fluticasone did not stop his wheezing during an attack. Which explanation is correct?
qs.a: It controls airway inflammation over days to weeks, not acute bronchospasm
w: It is a rescue bronchodilator that needs a higher dose
It only works when given through a nebulizer
It blocks muscarinic receptors and acts slowly
qs.x: Inhaled corticosteroids are controllers that reduce inflammation over time. A SABA relieves acute bronchospasm.

qs.q: A patient is ordered nebulized acetylcysteine for thick secretions. Why is a bronchodilator given with or before it?
qs.a: Acetylcysteine can irritate the airway and cause bronchospasm
w: The bronchodilator inactivates the unpleasant odor of the drug
Acetylcysteine is only active in an alkaline solution
The bronchodilator prevents acetylcysteine from thinning mucus too much
qs.x: Acetylcysteine breaks disulfide bonds in mucus but is irritating and can trigger bronchospasm, particularly in asthma. A bronchodilator is paired with it and breath sounds are reassessed.

qs.q: How does inhaled hypertonic saline improve secretion clearance in cystic fibrosis?
qs.a: It draws water into the airway surface liquid by osmosis
w: It digests extracellular DNA in purulent sputum
It kills Pseudomonas by disrupting cell walls
It corrects the defective CFTR chloride channel
qs.x: Hypertonic saline osmotically hydrates the airway surface, improving mucociliary clearance. It can cause cough and bronchospasm, so bronchodilator pretreatment is common.

qs.q: What is the mechanism of dornase alfa in cystic fibrosis?
qs.a: It cleaves extracellular DNA released by neutrophils in sputum
w: It breaks disulfide bonds in mucus glycoproteins
It hydrates the airway by osmotic water movement
It potentiates the CFTR channel to move chloride
qs.x: Dornase alfa is recombinant human DNase. It reduces sputum viscosity by breaking down neutrophil DNA and should not be mixed with other drugs in the nebulizer.

qs.q: A child with cystic fibrosis receives several inhaled therapies each morning. Which sequence is most appropriate?
qs.a: Bronchodilator, hypertonic saline, airway clearance, then inhaled antibiotic
w: Inhaled antibiotic, airway clearance, bronchodilator, then hypertonic saline
Airway clearance, inhaled antibiotic, hypertonic saline, then bronchodilator
Hypertonic saline, inhaled antibiotic, bronchodilator, then airway clearance
qs.x: Opening the airways first, then thinning and clearing secretions, lets the inhaled antibiotic deposit in cleaner airways. An inhaled corticosteroid, if used, usually comes last.

qs.q: Right after succinylcholine is pushed during RSI, which finding is expected?
qs.a: Brief muscle fasciculations followed by flaccid paralysis
w: Gradual paralysis without any muscle twitching
Sustained muscle rigidity lasting several hours
Immediate bronchodilation with rising tidal volumes
qs.x: Succinylcholine is a depolarizing blocker. It first depolarizes the motor end plate (fasciculations) and then keeps it refractory, producing paralysis.

qs.q: How does rocuronium produce paralysis?
qs.a: It competitively blocks nicotinic receptors without depolarizing them
w: It depolarizes the motor end plate, causing fasciculations
It inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
It blocks calcium release inside skeletal muscle cells
qs.x: Rocuronium is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker. It competes with acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors, so there are no fasciculations.

qs.q: A patient with 40% total body surface area burns from 4 days ago needs emergent intubation. Why is succinylcholine a concern?
qs.a: It can cause life-threatening hyperkalemia from upregulated receptors
w: It causes severe bronchospasm in burned airways
It is ineffective in patients with large burns
It causes adrenal suppression that worsens burn shock
qs.x: After the first day following major burns, crush injury or major trauma, acetylcholine receptors proliferate. Succinylcholine then releases large amounts of potassium, risking cardiac arrest; rocuronium is the usual alternative.

qs.q: Which patient has the greatest risk of dangerous hyperkalemia if given succinylcholine?
qs.a: A patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome bedbound for two weeks
w: A healthy adult with a closed ankle fracture today
A patient with an acute asthma exacerbation
A patient intubated within an hour of a minor burn
qs.x: Denervation, neuromuscular disease and prolonged immobilization upregulate extrajunctional receptors. Hyperkalemia risk is low in the first hours after an injury.

qs.q: Minutes after succinylcholine, the ETCO2 climbs rapidly despite increased ventilation, the jaw is rigid, and temperature is rising. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Malignant hyperthermia
w: Pseudocholinesterase deficiency
Right mainstem intubation
Propofol infusion syndrome
qs.x: Succinylcholine and volatile anesthetics can trigger malignant hyperthermia, a hypermetabolic crisis. Rising ETCO2 is often the earliest sign; dantrolene is the antidote.

qs.q: A patient remains completely paralyzed several hours after a single RSI dose of succinylcholine. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: Plasma pseudocholinesterase deficiency
w: Hyperkalemia from receptor upregulation
Etomidate-induced adrenal suppression
Malignant hyperthermia crisis
qs.x: Succinylcholine is normally broken down by plasma pseudocholinesterase within minutes. Inherited or acquired deficiency prolongs paralysis; the patient needs full ventilation and sedation until it wears off.

qs.q: Which adverse effect of succinylcholine is a particular concern in infants and young children?
qs.a: Bradycardia
w: Hypertensive crisis
Bronchodilation
Hyperglycemia
qs.x: Succinylcholine stimulates muscarinic receptors and can cause bradycardia, especially in children and with repeated doses.

qs.q: Which agent reverses rocuronium by encapsulating the drug molecule?
qs.a: Sugammadex
w: Neostigmine
Dantrolene
Flumazenil
qs.x: Sugammadex binds rocuronium and vecuronium directly. Neostigmine works indirectly by increasing acetylcholine, dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia, and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.

qs.q: Why is rocuronium usually preferred over vecuronium for rapid sequence intubation?
qs.a: Rocuronium has a faster onset of paralysis
w: Vecuronium causes fasciculations and hyperkalemia
Rocuronium has no effect on respiratory muscles
Vecuronium cannot be reversed by any agent
qs.x: At RSI doses rocuronium reaches intubating conditions in about a minute, approaching succinylcholine. Vecuronium is slower and must be reconstituted.

qs.q: After RSI, a patient is paralyzed with rocuronium. Which statement about this patient is correct?
qs.a: Without ongoing sedation, the patient may be fully aware
w: Rocuronium also provides deep sedation and amnesia
Rocuronium provides strong analgesia for the procedure
The patient will continue to breathe spontaneously
qs.x: Neuromuscular blockers have no sedative, amnestic or analgesic effect. Awareness under paralysis is a serious harm, so sedation must be adequate and ongoing.

qs.q: Shortly after propofol induction, the patient's blood pressure falls sharply. What explains this?
qs.a: Vasodilation and myocardial depression from propofol
w: Histamine release causing bronchospasm
Adrenal suppression from propofol
Hyperkalemia from propofol
qs.x: Propofol lowers systemic vascular resistance and depresses contractility. Hypotension is most marked in hypovolemic, septic or elderly patients.

qs.q: Why is etomidate often chosen to induce a hypotensive trauma patient for intubation?
qs.a: It causes minimal change in blood pressure and heart rate
w: It raises blood pressure through catecholamine release
It produces long-lasting analgesia after intubation
It reverses hypovolemia by expanding plasma volume
qs.x: Etomidate has a favorable hemodynamic profile, making it common in unstable patients. It provides no analgesia.

qs.q: Which adverse effect is associated with even a single induction dose of etomidate?
qs.a: Transient adrenal suppression from inhibited cortisol synthesis
w: Malignant hyperthermia triggered in susceptible patients
Severe hyperkalemia in patients with recent burns
Prolonged bronchospasm from histamine release
qs.x: Etomidate inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase, temporarily reducing cortisol production. Myoclonus and nausea are other known effects.

qs.q: A patient in status asthmaticus needs intubation. Why is ketamine a preferred induction agent?
qs.a: It produces bronchodilation and helps maintain blood pressure
w: It is the only agent with no effect on secretions
It reliably lowers heart rate and blood pressure
It provides neuromuscular blockade without a paralytic
qs.x: Ketamine releases catecholamines, relaxing bronchial smooth muscle and supporting hemodynamics. It also preserves respiratory drive and airway reflexes.

qs.q: When ketamine is used for sedation or induction, which airway effect should the respiratory therapist anticipate?
qs.a: Increased oral and airway secretions
w: Marked bronchospasm
Loss of all airway reflexes
Severe chest wall rigidity
qs.x: Ketamine increases salivation and bronchial secretions; suction should be ready. Emergence reactions and raised heart rate and blood pressure also occur.

qs.q: Which feature makes dexmedetomidine useful for sedation around the time of extubation?
qs.a: It sedates with little respiratory depression
w: It provides deep amnesia and paralysis
It reliably raises heart rate and blood pressure
It reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression
qs.x: Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist that produces arousable sedation while largely preserving respiratory drive, so it can continue through extubation.

qs.q: A ventilated patient on a dexmedetomidine infusion has a heart rate of 44 and falling blood pressure. What should the respiratory therapist recognize?
qs.a: Bradycardia and hypotension are known effects to report
w: This is a sign of dexmedetomidine withdrawal
This indicates the patient is too lightly sedated
This is expected malignant hyperthermia
qs.x: Alpha-2 agonism reduces sympathetic outflow, so bradycardia and hypotension are the main adverse effects of dexmedetomidine.

qs.q: A patient on pressure support ventilation is started on a fentanyl infusion. Which change is most likely?
qs.a: Falling spontaneous rate with possible apnea and rising PaCO2
w: Rising respiratory rate with respiratory alkalosis
Increased tidal volumes from bronchodilation
Increased secretions requiring frequent suction
qs.x: Opioids depress the brainstem response to CO2. On spontaneous modes, watch for low rate, apnea alarms and rising PaCO2; backup ventilation settings matter.

qs.q: After a rapid IV push of a large fentanyl bolus, the patient becomes very difficult to ventilate with high airway pressures. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Opioid-induced chest wall rigidity
w: Fentanyl-induced histamine bronchospasm
Pseudocholinesterase deficiency
Tension pneumothorax from fentanyl
qs.x: Rapid high-dose fentanyl can cause skeletal muscle rigidity of the chest wall ('wooden chest'), which is treated with a neuromuscular blocker and ventilation.

qs.q: Why do current ICU guidelines favor propofol or dexmedetomidine over continuous midazolam for ventilated adults?
qs.a: Midazolam accumulates and is linked to delirium and longer ventilation
w: Midazolam has no sedative effect in critically ill patients
Midazolam causes malignant hyperthermia during infusions
Midazolam cannot be given by continuous infusion
qs.x: Benzodiazepine infusions accumulate, especially in older adults and organ failure, delaying awakening and extubation and increasing delirium.

qs.q: What is the main benefit of pairing a daily spontaneous awakening trial with a spontaneous breathing trial?
qs.a: Fewer ventilator days and shorter ICU stays
w: Elimination of the need for any analgesia
Higher sedative requirements but fewer alarms
Guaranteed extubation on the same day
qs.x: Coordinated 'wake up and breathe' protocols reduce sedative exposure and have shortened time on the ventilator and in the ICU.

qs.q: Which patient is ready to begin a spontaneous breathing trial?
qs.a: Awake, following commands, on low FiO2 and PEEP, hemodynamically stable
w: Deeply sedated on a continuous neuromuscular blocker infusion
Requiring rising vasopressor doses and high PEEP
Agitated with an SpO2 of 84% on high FiO2
qs.x: SBT readiness includes improving underlying illness, adequate oxygenation on modest settings, hemodynamic stability and the ability to initiate breaths.

qs.q: During a spontaneous awakening trial after a midazolam infusion, which finding indicates the trial has failed?
qs.a: Sustained agitation with a respiratory rate over 35 and falling SpO2
w: Opening eyes to voice and following simple commands
Mild anxiety that settles with reassurance
A spontaneous rate of 18 with stable SpO2
qs.x: SAT failure criteria include sustained anxiety or agitation, tachypnea, desaturation, arrhythmia and acute distress; failure is reported to the team.

qs.q: During a spontaneous breathing trial, which rapid shallow breathing index (RSBI) value best predicts successful extubation?
qs.a: Below about 105
w: Between 130 and 150
Above 200
Exactly zero
qs.x: RSBI is respiratory frequency divided by tidal volume in liters. Values under about 105 favor successful weaning; higher values suggest rapid, shallow breathing.

qs.q: Why is cisatracurium often chosen for neuromuscular blockade in a patient with liver and kidney failure?
qs.a: It undergoes Hofmann elimination independent of organ function
w: It is cleared unchanged by the kidneys
It has no effect on the diaphragm
It is reversed by sugammadex
qs.x: Cisatracurium breaks down spontaneously in plasma by pH- and temperature-dependent Hofmann elimination, so its effect is predictable in organ failure.

qs.q: A patient with early severe ARDS and marked dyssynchrony is started on cisatracurium. What must be ensured before and during paralysis?
qs.a: Deep sedation and analgesia so the patient is not aware
w: A spontaneous breathing trial to confirm readiness
A pressure support mode to allow triggering
Light sedation so neurologic checks are easy
qs.x: Paralytics give no sedation. Patients must be deeply sedated before paralysis begins and throughout the infusion to prevent awareness.

qs.q: How is the depth of a cisatracurium infusion commonly monitored in the ICU?
qs.a: Train-of-four testing with a peripheral nerve stimulator
w: Measuring peak expiratory flow each shift
Pulse oximetry trend analysis alone
Serial serum potassium levels
qs.x: Train-of-four counts guide the degree of blockade, along with clinical assessment of ventilator synchrony.

qs.q: A patient receives a prolonged cisatracurium infusion along with high-dose corticosteroids. Which complication is more likely?
qs.a: ICU-acquired weakness and prolonged myopathy
w: Malignant hyperthermia with rising ETCO2
Acute hyperkalemia during the infusion
Bronchospasm from histamine release
qs.x: Neuromuscular blockers combined with corticosteroids increase the risk of critical illness myopathy and polyneuropathy, prolonging ventilation.

qs.q: A patient is receiving a continuous vecuronium infusion. Which ventilator mode is appropriate?
qs.a: A full-support mode with a set rate, such as volume or pressure A/C
w: CPAP with pressure support alone
A T-piece spontaneous breathing trial
Pressure support with no backup rate
qs.x: A paralyzed patient cannot trigger breaths. Full support with a mandatory rate, tight alarms and a manual resuscitator at the bedside are required.

qs.q: A patient on a prolonged propofol infusion develops unexplained metabolic acidosis, rising CK and new arrhythmias. What should be suspected and reported?
qs.a: Propofol infusion syndrome
w: Dexmedetomidine withdrawal
Etomidate adrenal crisis
Serotonin syndrome
qs.x: Propofol infusion syndrome is rare but often fatal, featuring metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, arrhythmias and lipemia. Triglycerides are also monitored because propofol is a lipid emulsion.

qs.q: How does inhaled nitric oxide improve oxygenation?
qs.a: It dilates vessels next to ventilated alveoli, improving V/Q matching
w: It increases surfactant production in collapsed alveoli
It raises hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen
It stimulates the respiratory center to raise minute ventilation
qs.x: iNO activates guanylate cyclase and raises cGMP in vascular smooth muscle of ventilated lung units, redirecting blood flow to them.

qs.q: Why does inhaled nitric oxide cause little systemic hypotension?
qs.a: It is rapidly inactivated by binding to hemoglobin
w: It cannot cross the alveolar-capillary membrane
It constricts systemic arteries while dilating pulmonary ones
It is exhaled completely before reaching the blood
qs.x: Nitric oxide that enters the blood binds hemoglobin almost immediately, forming methemoglobin and nitrate, so its vasodilating effect stays in the lungs.

qs.q: What is the FDA-approved indication for inhaled nitric oxide?
qs.a: Term and near-term neonates with hypoxic respiratory failure and PPHN
w: Adults with ARDS to reduce mortality
Outpatient treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension
Premature infants to prevent bronchopulmonary dysplasia
qs.x: iNO is approved for neonates born at more than 34 weeks with hypoxic respiratory failure and evidence of pulmonary hypertension, to improve oxygenation and reduce the need for ECMO.

qs.q: Inhaled nitric oxide is used as rescue therapy in an adult with severe ARDS. Which statement is accurate?
qs.a: It may improve oxygenation but has not been shown to reduce mortality
w: It is FDA-approved first-line therapy for adult ARDS
It reliably reduces mortality in moderate ARDS
It worsens oxygenation in nearly all adult patients
qs.x: Trials in ARDS show transient oxygenation improvement without survival benefit, so adult use is off-label rescue therapy.

qs.q: Why is nitrogen dioxide (NO2) monitored continuously during iNO therapy?
qs.a: NO reacts with oxygen to form NO2, which injures the lungs
w: NO2 is the active vasodilator and must stay high
NO2 measures the patient's methemoglobin level
NO2 indicates how much NO the patient has absorbed
qs.x: Nitric oxide combines with oxygen to form toxic NO2, more so with high FiO2 and long contact time. Delivery systems analyze NO and NO2 in the inspired gas.

qs.q: A neonate on iNO has SpO2 stuck in the mid-80s despite high FiO2, and a blood sample appears chocolate brown. What should be suspected?
qs.a: Methemoglobinemia
w: Carbon monoxide poisoning
Sulfhemoglobinemia from NO2
Polycythemia
qs.x: NO oxidizes hemoglobin to methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen. Methemoglobin levels are measured by co-oximetry during iNO therapy and rising levels are reported.

qs.q: Why is inhaled nitric oxide weaned gradually rather than turned off all at once?
qs.a: Abrupt withdrawal can cause rebound pulmonary hypertension and hypoxemia
w: Rapid weaning causes dangerous NO2 accumulation
Gradual weaning prevents methemoglobinemia
Abrupt withdrawal causes systemic hypertension
qs.x: Exogenous NO suppresses endogenous NO production. Sudden withdrawal can cause severe rebound pulmonary vasoconstriction, so weaning is stepwise with close monitoring.

qs.q: A neonate on iNO must be manually ventilated during a circuit change. What should the respiratory therapist ensure?
qs.a: Backup iNO delivery continues through the manual resuscitator
w: The bag is used without iNO to avoid NO2 buildup
The FiO2 is lowered to minimize NO2 formation
Methemoglobin is measured before bagging begins
qs.x: Even brief interruption of iNO can cause rebound hypoxemia. Delivery systems include a backup mode to supply NO to a manual resuscitation bag.

qs.q: Which patient is at risk of worsening if inhaled nitric oxide is started?
qs.a: A patient with severe left ventricular dysfunction
w: A neonate with PPHN and normal heart structure
An adult with ARDS and right heart strain
A patient after mitral valve repair with good LV function
qs.x: iNO increases pulmonary blood flow and can raise left atrial pressure, causing pulmonary edema when the left ventricle is failing. Duct-dependent heart lesions are another concern.

qs.q: Where in the ventilator circuit is gas sampled to analyze NO and NO2 during iNO therapy?
qs.a: Inspiratory limb near the patient wye
w: Expiratory limb near the ventilator
At the humidifier water chamber
At the exhalation valve outlet
qs.x: NO is injected into the inspiratory limb and sampled close to the patient so readings reflect what the patient actually inhales.

qs.q: Why is inhaled epoprostenol delivered by continuous nebulization in the ICU?
qs.a: Its half-life is only a few minutes
w: It must be heated to become active
It works only when mixed with heliox
Intermittent doses cause methemoglobinemia
qs.x: Epoprostenol is a prostacyclin with a very short half-life. Continuous delivery keeps a steady pulmonary vasodilating effect.

qs.q: A patient on continuously nebulized epoprostenol suddenly becomes hypoxemic and hypotensive. The nebulizer syringe pump is alarming empty. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Rebound pulmonary hypertension from interrupted delivery
w: Epoprostenol overdose from a pump malfunction
Methemoglobinemia from epoprostenol
Bronchospasm from the drug diluent
qs.x: Interrupting epoprostenol, even briefly, can cause rebound pulmonary vasoconstriction. Delivery should be restored promptly and the change reported.

qs.q: A ventilated patient on continuously nebulized epoprostenol develops rising peak pressures and auto-PEEP over several hours. What is a likely cause?
qs.a: Drug deposits clogging the expiratory filter
w: Methemoglobin buildup in the circuit
Increased surfactant from prostacyclin
Overhydration of airway secretions
qs.x: Epoprostenol's sticky diluent collects on the expiratory filter, raising resistance. Scheduled filter changes and pressure monitoring are part of the protocol.

qs.q: Because epoprostenol inhibits platelet aggregation, which finding should be reported?
qs.a: New bleeding from the airway or line sites
w: A rise in methemoglobin level
Increased NO2 in the circuit
A new fine hand tremor
qs.x: Prostacyclins inhibit platelet aggregation and can increase bleeding risk, particularly with anticoagulants. Flushing and hypotension are other effects.

qs.q: A child cannot be weaned off inhaled nitric oxide without rebound hypoxemia. Which oral agent may be used to blunt rebound during the wean?
qs.a: Sildenafil
w: Montelukast
Theophylline
Guaifenesin
qs.x: Sildenafil inhibits PDE-5, preserving cGMP and supporting pulmonary vasodilation as exogenous NO is withdrawn.

qs.q: What is the main reason epinephrine is given during cardiac arrest?
qs.a: Alpha-mediated vasoconstriction raises coronary perfusion pressure
w: Beta-2 stimulation dilates the airways during CPR
It directly converts ventricular fibrillation
It reverses metabolic acidosis from low flow
qs.x: Epinephrine's alpha-1 effect increases aortic diastolic pressure, improving coronary and cerebral perfusion during compressions.

qs.q: During adult cardiac arrest, how often is epinephrine repeated under current ACLS guidelines?
qs.a: Every 3-5 minutes
w: Every 30 seconds
Every 15-20 minutes
Only once per arrest
qs.x: AHA guidelines recommend epinephrine every 3-5 minutes during cardiac arrest.

qs.q: A patient in asystole has CPR in progress and IV access established. When should epinephrine be given?
qs.a: As soon as feasible
w: After three defibrillation attempts
Only after an advanced airway is placed
Only if ETCO2 falls below 10
qs.x: For non-shockable rhythms, early epinephrine is associated with better outcomes. Asystole is not shocked.

qs.q: An adult in ventricular fibrillation remains in VF after defibrillation and epinephrine. Which antiarrhythmic is recommended?
qs.a: Amiodarone
w: Adenosine
Atropine
Diltiazem
qs.x: Amiodarone (or lidocaine) is recommended for shock-refractory VF or pulseless VT. Adenosine and diltiazem are for certain tachycardias with a pulse; atropine is for bradycardia.

qs.q: Which drug is an accepted alternative to amiodarone for shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation?
qs.a: Lidocaine
w: Magnesium sulfate
Sodium bicarbonate
Calcium chloride
qs.x: Lidocaine is an acceptable alternative antiarrhythmic in refractory VF/pVT. Magnesium is reserved for torsades de pointes.

qs.q: A patient on long-term amiodarone reports increasing dyspnea and dry cough, and DLCO has fallen. What should be suspected?
qs.a: Amiodarone pulmonary toxicity
w: Beta-agonist tolerance
Acute asthma exacerbation
Ventilator-associated pneumonia
qs.x: Chronic amiodarone can cause interstitial pneumonitis and fibrosis. New dyspnea, cough, infiltrates or falling DLCO should be reported.

qs.q: During an arrest, neither IV nor IO access can be obtained, but the patient is intubated. Which drug can be given through the endotracheal tube?
qs.a: Epinephrine
w: Amiodarone
Sodium bicarbonate
Calcium chloride
qs.x: Naloxone, atropine, epinephrine and lidocaine can be given by ETT, though absorption is unpredictable and IV or IO is preferred.

qs.q: After sodium bicarbonate is given during resuscitation, what change should the respiratory therapist anticipate?
qs.a: A transient rise in ETCO2 and PaCO2
w: A sharp fall in ETCO2
Immediate bronchospasm
A drop in serum sodium
qs.x: Bicarbonate buffers acid and generates CO2, which must be ventilated off. It is not routine in arrest but is used for hyperkalemia or tricyclic overdose.

qs.q: A patient with opioid overdose has a respiratory rate of 4. After IV naloxone, when is improvement in rate and depth typically seen?
qs.a: Within about 1-2 minutes
w: After about 20-30 minutes
After about 1-2 hours
Only after a second dose
qs.x: IV naloxone acts within a couple of minutes; intranasal and IM routes take a few minutes longer. Breathing rate, depth, SpO2 and ETCO2 are reassessed.

qs.q: An overdose patient breathes normally after naloxone, then an hour later becomes drowsy with shallow respirations. What best explains this?
qs.a: Naloxone wore off before the opioid did
w: Naloxone itself causes delayed sedation
The patient developed naloxone tolerance
Naloxone triggered benzodiazepine release
qs.x: Naloxone's effect typically lasts about 30-90 minutes, shorter than many opioids, including long-acting and some synthetic opioids. Continued monitoring is essential.

qs.q: Shortly after naloxone, a patient with heroin overdose develops frothy sputum, crackles and worsening hypoxemia. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Pulmonary edema associated with abrupt opioid reversal
w: Aspiration of naloxone into the airway
Bronchospasm from naloxone allergy
Methemoglobinemia from naloxone
qs.x: Rapid opioid reversal produces a catecholamine surge that can cause noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. Oxygen and ventilatory support may be needed.

qs.q: An apneic patient with suspected opioid overdose has a pulse. What is the first priority?
qs.a: Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
w: Wait for naloxone to restore breathing
Begin chest compressions immediately
Obtain an arterial blood gas
qs.x: Oxygenation and ventilation come first. Naloxone restores drive but should not delay rescue breathing.

qs.q: Why is flumazenil used cautiously in a patient who takes benzodiazepines daily?
qs.a: It can precipitate withdrawal seizures
w: It causes severe opioid withdrawal
It produces prolonged neuromuscular blockade
It causes rebound pulmonary hypertension
qs.x: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines but can trigger seizures in chronic users and in mixed overdoses involving tricyclic antidepressants.

qs.q: After procedural sedation with midazolam, flumazenil restores alertness, but 45 minutes later the patient is drowsy with slow, shallow breathing. What explains this?
qs.a: Flumazenil's effect ended before midazolam's
w: Flumazenil causes delayed respiratory depression
Midazolam was converted into an opioid
Flumazenil raises the effect of midazolam
qs.x: Flumazenil acts within 1-2 minutes but lasts roughly an hour or less, so re-sedation can occur. Respiratory rate, depth and SpO2 are monitored afterward.

qs.q: A patient sedated with midazolam and fentanyl receives flumazenil. He wakes slightly, but his respiratory rate stays at 6. Why?
qs.a: Flumazenil does not reverse opioid respiratory depression
w: Flumazenil needs an hour to reach full effect
Flumazenil worsens respiratory depression
The midazolam blocks flumazenil's receptor site
qs.x: Flumazenil antagonizes only benzodiazepine receptors. Opioid-induced respiratory depression is reversed with naloxone, after ventilation is supported.

qs.q: A client started sertraline 8 days ago and says, "This isn't working, I still feel down." Which response is most accurate?
qs.a: Full benefit usually takes about 4 to 6 weeks of regular use.
w: Sertraline should work within the first 2 to 3 days if effective.
No improvement after one week means the medicine has failed.
Mood usually improves only after side effects fully go away.
qs.x: SSRIs often cause side effects before benefit. Full antidepressant effect commonly takes 4-6 weeks, so early teaching supports adherence.

qs.q: The boxed warning on fluoxetine and other antidepressants concerns which risk?
qs.a: Increased suicidal thoughts in children, teens and young adults
w: Life-threatening liver failure in adults over age 65
Sudden cardiac death in people with heart disease
Severe low white blood cell counts in all age groups
qs.x: All antidepressants carry a boxed warning for increased suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents and young adults, especially early in treatment.

qs.q: A 19-year-old begins escitalopram for depression. When is close monitoring for suicidal thoughts most important?
qs.a: During the first few months and after any dose change
w: Only after the medicine reaches full effect at 6 weeks
Mainly after a year of stable, continuous treatment
Only if the client has a prior suicide attempt
qs.x: Risk is highest early in treatment and around dose changes. Energy may return before mood improves, giving a window of increased risk.

qs.q: Duloxetine belongs to which class, which also explains its use for chronic nerve pain?
qs.a: Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI)
w: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)
Monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI)
Norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor
qs.x: Duloxetine is an SNRI. The norepinephrine effect helps with diabetic neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia and chronic musculoskeletal pain.

qs.q: A client on an SSRI asks about side effects that may affect a relationship. Which effect is common and worth discussing openly?
qs.a: Sexual side effects such as low desire or delayed orgasm
w: Permanent hair loss within the first month
Loss of taste for sweet and salty foods
Gradual darkening of the skin and nails
qs.x: Sexual dysfunction is one of the most common reasons people quietly quit SSRIs. Asking about it supports adherence and lets the prescriber adjust the plan.

qs.q: Which finding in a client taking lithium most strongly suggests toxicity?
qs.a: Coarse hand tremor with slurred speech and confusion
w: Fine hand tremor and mild thirst in the first week
Gradual weight gain over several months
Increased urination at night with normal thinking
qs.x: Fine tremor, thirst and frequent urination are expected. Coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhea, slurred speech, unsteady gait and confusion signal toxicity and need prompt reporting.

qs.q: A client on lithium mentions taking over-the-counter ibuprofen daily for back pain. Why is this important to report?
qs.a: NSAIDs can raise lithium levels toward toxicity.
w: Ibuprofen makes lithium work much more slowly.
NSAIDs lower lithium levels and cause relapse.
Ibuprofen and lithium together cause severe rash.
qs.x: NSAIDs, thiazide diuretics and ACE inhibitors reduce lithium clearance by the kidneys and can raise levels into the toxic range.

qs.q: Which teaching about fluids and diet is most appropriate for a client taking lithium?
qs.a: Keep fluid and salt intake steady from day to day.
w: Cut back sharply on salt to protect the heart.
Limit fluids so the medicine stays concentrated.
Eat a high-salt diet on days with low mood.
qs.x: Lithium is handled like sodium. Low salt intake, dehydration or heavy sweating raise lithium levels, so steady intake helps keep levels stable.

qs.q: Besides lithium levels, which labs are monitored periodically during long-term lithium therapy?
qs.a: Kidney function and thyroid function
w: Liver enzymes and blood ammonia
Platelet count and clotting times
Creatine kinase and serum potassium
qs.x: Lithium can cause hypothyroidism and affect kidney function, so thyroid and kidney tests are checked at baseline and periodically.

qs.q: When is a blood sample for a routine lithium level usually drawn?
qs.a: About 12 hours after the last dose, before the next one
w: Within 1 hour after swallowing the last dose
Any time of day, since timing does not matter
Right after a meal to reflect peak absorption
qs.x: Lithium levels are trough levels, typically drawn about 12 hours after the last dose, so results can be compared reliably over time.

qs.q: A client on lithium has had vomiting and diarrhea for two days from a stomach virus. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Fluid and sodium loss may push lithium to toxic levels.
w: The virus will make lithium completely ineffective.
Lithium will cause the virus to last much longer.
Diarrhea means the client is allergic to lithium.
qs.x: Dehydration and sodium loss reduce lithium excretion and raise levels. Illness with vomiting or diarrhea should be reported to the prescriber.

qs.q: A client taking valproate for bipolar disorder reports severe abdominal pain radiating to the back with vomiting. What should be suspected?
qs.a: Pancreatitis, a boxed warning for valproate
w: Expected stomach upset that fades in days
A sign that the dose is too low to work
Lithium-like toxicity from dehydration
qs.x: Valproate carries boxed warnings for pancreatitis, liver injury and birth defects. Severe abdominal pain with vomiting needs prompt reporting.

qs.q: Why is valproate use in people who could become pregnant a major counseling topic?
qs.a: It carries a high risk of birth defects such as neural tube defects.
w: It reliably causes birth control pills to fail.
It causes infertility that is usually permanent.
It is safe in pregnancy but not while breastfeeding.
qs.x: Valproate is strongly teratogenic, with risk of neural tube defects and lower IQ in exposed children. Pregnancy plans should be discussed with the prescriber.

qs.q: A client taking phenelzine is planning lunch. Which choice is of greatest concern?
qs.a: Aged cheddar cheese and salami on crackers
w: Grilled chicken breast with steamed rice
Fresh cottage cheese with sliced peaches
Scrambled eggs with toast and fresh milk
qs.x: Aged cheeses and cured or fermented meats are high in tyramine, which can trigger a hypertensive crisis with an MAOI. Fresh dairy and fresh meats are low in tyramine.

qs.q: A client on phenelzine suddenly develops a severe headache at the back of the head, stiff neck and pounding heartbeat. What does this suggest?
qs.a: Hypertensive crisis from a tyramine or drug interaction
w: Expected tension headache from depression
Lithium toxicity from poor fluid intake
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome from dopamine block
qs.x: Occipital headache, stiff neck, palpitations and sweating are classic signs of MAOI hypertensive crisis, an emergency to report immediately.

qs.q: Combining phenelzine with which medicine poses the highest risk of serotonin syndrome?
qs.a: Sertraline
w: Acetaminophen
Docusate
Loratadine
qs.x: MAOIs combined with SSRIs, SNRIs, meperidine, tramadol or dextromethorphan can cause serotonin syndrome. A washout period is required between them.

qs.q: A client recently had an antidepressant added to another serotonergic drug and now has agitation, sweating, fever, diarrhea and jerking reflexes in the legs. Which condition fits best?
qs.a: Serotonin syndrome
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Lithium toxicity
Acute dystonic reaction
qs.x: Rapid onset of agitation, hyperthermia, diaphoresis, diarrhea, hyperreflexia and clonus after combining serotonergic drugs is typical of serotonin syndrome.

qs.q: A young adult received haloperidol for the first time 6 hours ago. The neck is twisted to one side and the eyes are rolled upward. What is this?
qs.a: Acute dystonic reaction
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Akathisia
qs.x: Acute dystonia appears within hours to days of starting a high-potency antipsychotic, often in young males, with torticollis or oculogyric crisis.

qs.q: Which medicine is commonly used to treat acute dystonia caused by an antipsychotic?
qs.a: Benztropine
w: Buspirone
Lithium
Trazodone
qs.x: Anticholinergics such as benztropine (or diphenhydramine) rapidly relieve acute dystonia and help drug-induced parkinsonism.

qs.q: A client started on fluphenazine paces the hall and says, "I can't sit still, I feel jittery inside." Which effect is most likely?
qs.a: Akathisia
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Serotonin syndrome
Catatonia
qs.x: Akathisia is a subjective inner restlessness with an urge to move. It is often mistaken for worsening anxiety or agitation and is linked to nonadherence.

qs.q: After years of fluphenazine, a client has repeated lip smacking, tongue thrusting and grimacing. What is the most likely condition?
qs.a: Tardive dyskinesia
w: Acute dystonia
Drug-induced parkinsonism
Akathisia
qs.x: Tardive dyskinesia is a late effect of long-term dopamine blockade, with involuntary orofacial movements that may be permanent.

qs.q: Which tool is used to screen clients on antipsychotics for tardive dyskinesia?
qs.a: Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS)
w: Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9)
Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA-Ar)
Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale
qs.x: The AIMS is a structured exam for involuntary movements, done at baseline and periodically during antipsychotic treatment.

qs.q: A client on haloperidol for several weeks now has a shuffling gait, masklike face, stiff arms and a pill-rolling tremor. What is this?
qs.a: Drug-induced parkinsonism
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
qs.x: Dopamine blockade can mimic Parkinson disease, usually appearing after weeks. It is a form of EPS and often responds to anticholinergic treatment.

qs.q: Which antipsychotic carries the highest risk of extrapyramidal symptoms?
qs.a: Haloperidol
w: Quetiapine
Clozapine
Olanzapine
qs.x: High-potency first-generation agents like haloperidol and fluphenazine cause the most EPS. Quetiapine and clozapine have very low EPS risk.

qs.q: Which monitoring set is most important for a client starting olanzapine?
qs.a: Weight, waist size, fasting glucose or A1c, and lipids
w: Thyroid function, kidney function, and sodium
Liver enzymes, ammonia, and platelet count
Absolute neutrophil count every week
qs.x: Olanzapine has high risk of weight gain, diabetes and high lipids. Metabolic monitoring is recommended at baseline and regularly afterward.

qs.q: A client recently started on quetiapine reports feeling very sleepy and dizzy when standing up. These effects are best explained by:
qs.a: Sedation and orthostatic hypotension, common with quetiapine
w: Early neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Acute dystonia affecting the inner ear
An allergic reaction needing epinephrine
qs.x: Quetiapine is strongly sedating and blocks alpha receptors, causing orthostatic hypotension. Teach rising slowly and report fainting or falls.

qs.q: A client taking risperidone reports breast enlargement and milky nipple discharge. What is the likely cause?
qs.a: Elevated prolactin from dopamine blockade
w: Low thyroid hormone from the medicine
High blood sugar from metabolic effects
Low sodium from fluid retention
qs.x: Risperidone raises prolactin more than most antipsychotics, causing gynecomastia, galactorrhea, missed periods and sexual dysfunction.

qs.q: A client on haloperidol has a temperature of 104 F, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion and a fluctuating blood pressure. What is the priority?
qs.a: Report immediately as possible neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
w: Document it as expected antipsychotic sedation.
Recheck vital signs at the next routine round.
Offer fluids and reassess in a few hours.
qs.x: Fever, lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental status and autonomic instability suggest NMS, a life-threatening emergency needing immediate medical care.

qs.q: Which lab result is typically markedly elevated in neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
qs.a: Creatine kinase (CK)
w: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
Serum lithium level
Hemoglobin A1c
qs.x: Muscle rigidity and breakdown raise CK, sometimes dramatically. White blood cell count is often elevated as well.

qs.q: Which finding favors neuroleptic malignant syndrome over serotonin syndrome?
qs.a: Lead-pipe rigidity developing over several days
w: Clonus and hyperreflexia within a few hours
Diarrhea with shivering soon after a new SSRI
Dilated pupils and agitation after tramadol
qs.x: NMS develops over days with lead-pipe rigidity and slowed movement. Serotonin syndrome starts within hours with clonus, hyperreflexia and GI symptoms.

qs.q: What is a main advantage of haloperidol decanoate over daily oral tablets?
qs.a: It supports adherence because one injection lasts for weeks.
w: It has no risk of extrapyramidal side effects at all.
It works within minutes for acute agitation.
It cannot cause neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
qs.x: Long-acting injectable antipsychotics release medicine over weeks, helping people who struggle with daily pills. Side effect risks remain.

qs.q: A client taking clozapine reports a sore throat and fever. Why is this important to report promptly?
qs.a: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia and serious infection.
w: Clozapine commonly causes seasonal allergies.
Fever means the clozapine level is too low.
Sore throat is an early sign of tardive dyskinesia.
qs.x: Clozapine carries a boxed warning for severe neutropenia. ANC is monitored, and signs of infection need prompt evaluation.

qs.q: What is the boxed warning shared by all antipsychotics?
qs.a: Increased death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis
w: Increased suicidal thoughts in children and teenagers
Fatal liver failure in the first months of therapy
Life-threatening rash in people of Asian ancestry
qs.x: Antipsychotics are not approved for dementia-related psychosis because they raise mortality in older adults with dementia, largely from cardiovascular and infectious causes.

qs.q: A client prescribed lorazepam says they still drink a few beers every evening. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Additive sedation and dangerously slowed breathing
w: Alcohol will make lorazepam stop working entirely
The combination causes a sudden spike in blood pressure
Alcohol triggers a disulfiram-like flushing reaction
qs.x: Benzodiazepines and alcohol are both CNS depressants. Together they can cause deep sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death.

qs.q: The boxed warning for alprazolam highlights danger when it is combined with which drugs?
qs.a: Opioids
w: SSRIs
Antacids
Stimulants
qs.x: Benzodiazepines plus opioids can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death. The label also warns about misuse and dependence.

qs.q: A client who has taken alprazolam daily for years wants to quit abruptly on their own. What is the most serious risk?
qs.a: Withdrawal seizures
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Serotonin syndrome
Hypertensive crisis
qs.x: Abrupt cessation after long-term benzodiazepine use can cause severe withdrawal, including seizures. Changes should be planned with the prescriber as a gradual taper.

qs.q: Why does alprazolam carry a higher risk of rebound anxiety and dependence than longer-acting benzodiazepines?
qs.a: It has a fast onset and short duration of action.
w: It is converted into an opioid in the liver.
It stays in the body for several weeks.
It blocks serotonin reuptake like an SSRI.
qs.x: Short-acting, fast-onset benzodiazepines produce stronger reinforcement and more interdose rebound symptoms, increasing misuse and dependence risk.

qs.q: An 82-year-old has been taking diazepam for sleep. Which concern is greatest?
qs.a: Falls and confusion from long-acting active metabolites
w: Rapid weight gain and new-onset diabetes
Hypertensive crisis with aged cheese
Uncontrollable lip smacking and grimacing
qs.x: Diazepam and its metabolites last a long time and accumulate in older adults, raising risk of falls, confusion and oversedation. It is on the Beers list.

qs.q: Which agent reverses benzodiazepine sedation but may trigger seizures in someone physically dependent?
qs.a: Flumazenil
w: Naloxone
Naltrexone
Benztropine
qs.x: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist. In dependent patients it can provoke acute withdrawal and seizures, so it is used cautiously.

qs.q: A client wants to use buspirone only when a panic attack starts. Which teaching is accurate?
qs.a: It works only with regular daily use and takes weeks to help.
w: It works within minutes, just like lorazepam.
It is most effective when taken only at bedtime.
It should be chewed for faster relief of panic.
qs.x: Buspirone has a delayed onset of about 2-4 weeks and must be taken regularly. It is not useful as an as-needed medicine.

qs.q: Why might buspirone be chosen for anxiety in a client with a history of substance use disorder?
qs.a: It is not habit forming and has low misuse potential.
w: It also reverses opioid overdose in an emergency.
It blocks the high from alcohol and opioids.
It works faster than any benzodiazepine.
qs.x: Buspirone does not cause dependence, euphoria or significant withdrawal and is not a controlled substance.

qs.q: Which monitoring is especially important for a client on methadone maintenance?
qs.a: ECG for QT interval prolongation
w: Lithium levels for toxicity
Weekly absolute neutrophil counts
AIMS exams for involuntary movements
qs.x: Methadone can prolong the QT interval and cause torsades de pointes, especially with other QT-prolonging drugs. ECG monitoring is recommended.

qs.q: Where is methadone dispensed for treatment of opioid use disorder?
qs.a: Through federally certified opioid treatment programs
w: At any retail pharmacy with a routine prescription
Only in hospital emergency departments
Through online pharmacies by mail order
qs.x: For opioid use disorder, methadone is dispensed through certified opioid treatment programs, often with supervised daily dosing at first.

qs.q: A client used heroin 4 hours ago and has no withdrawal signs. Why is starting buprenorphine now a concern?
qs.a: It can cause precipitated withdrawal by displacing the opioid.
w: It will cause a dangerous overdose with heroin.
It will be ineffective for at least two weeks.
