It causes severe rebound high blood pressure.
qs.x: Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial agonist. Given while a full agonist is still active, it displaces it and triggers sudden withdrawal; induction usually waits for mild to moderate withdrawal.

qs.q: Why is naloxone included in buprenorphine-naloxone films and tablets?
qs.a: To discourage injecting the product to get high
w: To make buprenorphine absorb faster under the tongue
To treat constipation caused by the buprenorphine
To lower the risk of liver injury from buprenorphine
qs.x: Naloxone is poorly absorbed under the tongue, but if the product is injected it blocks opioid effects and can trigger withdrawal, deterring misuse.

qs.q: A client being considered for naltrexone used opioids two days ago. What is the concern?
qs.a: Naltrexone can cause sudden, severe opioid withdrawal.
w: Naltrexone will intensify the opioid high.
Naltrexone causes a disulfiram-like reaction.
Naltrexone will be absorbed too slowly to help.
qs.x: Naltrexone is a full opioid antagonist. People need to be opioid-free for about 7-10 days first to avoid precipitated withdrawal.

qs.q: Which safety teaching applies to people who have been taking naltrexone and later return to opioid use?
qs.a: Lower tolerance raises the risk of fatal overdose.
w: Opioids will have no effect for several months.
Naltrexone will protect against any overdose.
Tolerance stays high, so overdose is unlikely.
qs.x: After a period of opioid blockade, tolerance falls. Using previous amounts of opioids can cause fatal overdose; naloxone access is important.

qs.q: A client on disulfiram drinks a glass of wine. Which reaction is expected?
qs.a: Flushing, throbbing headache, vomiting and a fast heartbeat
w: Sudden calm, drowsiness and slow breathing
Lead-pipe rigidity with very high fever
Lip smacking and tongue thrusting movements
qs.x: Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde builds up with any alcohol, causing flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia and hypotension.

qs.q: Which product should a client on disulfiram be taught to check labels on because it may contain alcohol?
qs.a: Mouthwash
w: Toothpaste
Bar soap
Sunscreen
qs.x: Hidden alcohol in mouthwash, cough syrups, some sauces and vinegars, and some skin products can trigger a disulfiram reaction.

qs.q: Which two side effects are most common when a child starts methylphenidate?
qs.a: Trouble sleeping and decreased appetite
w: Weight gain and daytime sleepiness
Hair loss and dry cough
Increased thirst and frequent urination
qs.x: Stimulants commonly cause insomnia and appetite suppression, along with headache and stomach ache.

qs.q: Why are stimulant doses for ADHD usually scheduled in the morning?
qs.a: Late-day doses are more likely to cause insomnia.
w: Stimulants are absorbed only on an empty stomach.
Morning doses prevent tardive dyskinesia.
Evening doses can trigger a hypertensive crisis.
qs.x: Stimulants increase alertness for hours. Doses taken later in the day commonly interfere with falling asleep.

qs.q: Which routine monitoring is especially important for a school-age child on amphetamine salts?
qs.a: Height and weight plotted on growth charts
w: Weekly white blood cell counts
Lithium levels every three months
Thyroid function before each refill
qs.x: Stimulants can slow growth through appetite suppression. Height and weight are tracked, and slowed growth is reported to the prescriber.

qs.q: Methylphenidate and amphetamine products are in which controlled substance schedule?
qs.a: Schedule II
w: Schedule IV
Schedule V
Not controlled
qs.x: Stimulants for ADHD are Schedule II because of their high potential for misuse and dependence, which limits refills.

qs.q: The boxed warning for amphetamine products focuses on which risk?
qs.a: Abuse, misuse and addiction
w: Increased suicidal thoughts in teens
Severe low white blood cell counts
Fatal liver failure in young children
qs.x: Stimulant labeling carries a boxed warning about abuse, misuse and addiction, including risk of overdose and death; risk should be assessed before and during treatment.

qs.q: Before starting a stimulant, which history is most important to ask about?
qs.a: Heart disease, fainting, or sudden death in the family
w: Seasonal allergies or hay fever
Prior childhood ear infections
Lactose intolerance or food allergy
qs.x: Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure. Structural heart disease, arrhythmias and family history of sudden cardiac death need evaluation.

qs.q: A teen on methylphenidate notices fingers turning white and painful in the cold. What should be done with this information?
qs.a: Report it as possible stimulant-related circulation problems.
w: Ignore it, since it is a normal part of puberty.
Treat it as an allergy to the medicine's dye.
Assume it is a sign of low blood sugar.
qs.x: Stimulants carry a warning for peripheral vasculopathy, including Raynaud's phenomenon. New color changes, pain or sores in fingers or toes should be reported.

qs.q: A college student on a stimulant says friends keep asking for pills during exams. Which response is most appropriate?
qs.a: Sharing is illegal and risky; keep the medicine stored securely.
w: Sharing is fine if friends take a smaller amount.
Giving pills to friends is legal if no money changes hands.
It is safe to share since stimulants are not addictive.
qs.x: Diversion of Schedule II stimulants is common on campuses, illegal and dangerous. Secure storage and open discussion reduce misuse.

qs.q: Which group of findings suggests stimulant misuse or overdose?
qs.a: Agitation, fast heart rate, high blood pressure and fever
w: Pinpoint pupils, slow breathing and sleepiness
Low blood pressure, slow pulse and drowsiness
Lip smacking, tongue thrusting and grimacing
qs.x: Stimulant toxicity causes sympathetic overdrive: agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, and sometimes psychosis or seizures.

qs.q: A child on methylphenidate begins hearing voices and becomes very suspicious. What is the best interpretation?
qs.a: New psychotic symptoms can be a stimulant effect and need reporting.
w: Hallucinations are expected for the first week.
This shows ADHD symptoms are being undertreated.
These are normal side effects of growth spurts.
qs.x: Stimulants can cause new psychotic or manic symptoms even at usual doses. These should be reported to the prescriber promptly.

qs.q: How does atomoxetine differ from methylphenidate?
qs.a: It is a non-stimulant that takes several weeks for full effect.
w: It is a stimulant that works within one hour.
It is a Schedule II drug with high misuse risk.
It is an injectable used only in hospitals.
qs.x: Atomoxetine is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. It is not controlled and builds benefit over weeks, unlike stimulants.

qs.q: For an adolescent with ADHD and a history of substance misuse, which medicine is often preferred?
qs.a: Atomoxetine
w: Methylphenidate
Dextroamphetamine
Lisdexamfetamine
qs.x: Atomoxetine has negligible misuse potential and is not a controlled substance, making it a common choice when misuse is a concern.

qs.q: Atomoxetine carries a boxed warning for which risk?
qs.a: Suicidal thoughts in children and adolescents
w: Abuse, misuse and addiction
Sudden cardiac death in adults
Severe neutropenia and infection
qs.x: Like antidepressants, atomoxetine has a boxed warning for increased suicidal ideation in children and adolescents. Mood changes should be monitored.

qs.q: A teen on atomoxetine reports dark urine, itching and yellowing of the eyes. What is the concern?
qs.a: Possible liver injury, which should be reported promptly
w: Expected dehydration from reduced appetite
A harmless color change from the capsule dye
Normal effect of the medicine reaching full strength
qs.x: Rare severe liver injury has been reported with atomoxetine. Jaundice, dark urine or right upper abdominal pain need prompt evaluation.

qs.q: What makes lisdexamfetamine different from immediate-release amphetamine?
qs.a: It is a prodrug activated in the blood after absorption.
w: It is not a controlled substance in the US.
It is a non-stimulant that acts on serotonin.
It works only when applied as a skin patch.
qs.x: Lisdexamfetamine is converted to dextroamphetamine in the blood, giving smooth, long action and less appeal for snorting or injecting. It remains Schedule II.

qs.q: Extended-release clonidine for ADHD has which important safety issue?
qs.a: Rebound high blood pressure if it is ended abruptly
w: Severe insomnia and appetite loss
High misuse risk as a Schedule II drug
Tardive dyskinesia after long-term use
qs.x: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist that causes drowsiness and low blood pressure; abrupt cessation can cause rebound hypertension, so changes are tapered by the prescriber.

qs.q: A patient with a spinal cord injury has an intrathecal baclofen pump. During therapy he has high fever, itching, rebound spasticity and confusion. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Baclofen withdrawal from pump failure or an empty reservoir
w: Autonomic dysreflexia from a full bladder
Malignant hyperthermia from exercise
Expected response to increased activity
qs.x: Abrupt loss of intrathecal baclofen causes fever, rebound spasticity, pruritus, altered mental status and can progress to seizures and death. It is a medical emergency.

qs.q: Baclofen reduces spasticity mainly by acting at which site?
qs.a: GABA-B receptors in the spinal cord
w: Calcium release in skeletal muscle
Acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
Alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem only
qs.x: Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist that inhibits reflexes at the spinal level.

qs.q: A patient with hemiplegia uses extensor tone in the affected leg to stand. After oral baclofen is started, what change should the therapist anticipate?
qs.a: Reduced ability to bear weight through the affected leg during transfers
w: Improved standing because of increased leg strength
Greater extensor tone during gait
No change in function, only in reflexes
qs.x: Spasticity reduction can unmask weakness, and some patients rely on extensor tone for standing and transfers.

qs.q: Which statement about suddenly running out of oral baclofen is correct?
qs.a: It can cause hallucinations, seizures and rebound spasticity
w: It is harmless because baclofen has a short half-life
It only causes mild muscle soreness
It improves strength within a day
qs.x: Abrupt withdrawal of oral baclofen can cause hallucinations, seizures and severe rebound spasticity, so missed supplies should be reported.

qs.q: A patient on tizanidine reports dizziness when standing at the start of each session. Which effect of the drug best explains this?
qs.a: Hypotension from central alpha-2 agonist action
w: Hypoglycemia from increased insulin release
Bradykinesia from dopamine blockade
Vestibular damage from ototoxicity
qs.x: Tizanidine is a central alpha-2 agonist like clonidine and commonly causes hypotension and sedation.

qs.q: Which laboratory value is monitored in patients taking tizanidine long term?
qs.a: Liver function tests
w: Serum creatine kinase only
Thyroid stimulating hormone
Hemoglobin A1c
qs.x: Tizanidine can cause liver injury, so liver tests are monitored.

qs.q: Which antispasticity drug works directly on skeletal muscle rather than in the central nervous system?
qs.a: Dantrolene
w: Baclofen
Tizanidine
Diazepam
qs.x: Dantrolene reduces calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so it causes generalized muscle weakness with less sedation.

qs.q: Besides spasticity, dantrolene is used to treat which emergency condition?
qs.a: Malignant hyperthermia
w: Autonomic dysreflexia
Neuroleptic-induced tardive dyskinesia
Status asthmaticus
qs.x: IV dantrolene is the treatment for malignant hyperthermia triggered by certain anesthetics.

qs.q: Which adverse effect of dantrolene is most important to report?
qs.a: Yellowing of the skin or dark urine
w: Mild dry mouth
Brief tingling in the feet
Slight increase in appetite
qs.x: Dantrolene carries a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity; jaundice and dark urine suggest liver injury.

qs.q: After botulinum toxin injection into the elbow flexors for spasticity, when is the peak effect usually seen?
qs.a: About 2 to 6 weeks after injection
w: Within the first hour
On the first day only
About 6 months after injection
qs.x: Effect begins in several days, peaks in a few weeks and wears off over about 3 months, so stretching and splinting are timed to the peak.

qs.q: Botulinum toxin reduces focal spasticity by which mechanism?
qs.a: Blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
w: Blocking calcium release inside muscle fibers
Stimulating GABA-B receptors in the cord
Destroying the motor nerve permanently
qs.x: The toxin cleaves proteins needed for acetylcholine release; nerve sprouting restores function over months.

qs.q: Which intervention best complements botulinum toxin injection for a spastic plantarflexor?
qs.a: Serial casting or stretching to gain dorsiflexion range
w: Vigorous strengthening of the injected calf
Heat over the injection site for the first day
Complete rest of the limb for a month
qs.x: The window of reduced tone is used to lengthen tissue with stretching, casting or splinting and to train the antagonist.

qs.q: Cyclobenzaprine is structurally similar to which drug class, explaining its sedation and dry mouth?
qs.a: Tricyclic antidepressants
w: Benzodiazepines
Opioid agonists
Beta-blockers
qs.x: Cyclobenzaprine resembles tricyclics and has anticholinergic effects, making it a Beers Criteria drug for older adults.

qs.q: For which condition is cyclobenzaprine most appropriate?
qs.a: Acute muscle spasm from a back strain
w: Spasticity after spinal cord injury
Spasticity in multiple sclerosis
Rigidity in Parkinson disease
qs.x: Cyclobenzaprine is labeled for acute musculoskeletal spasm, not for spasticity from upper motor neuron lesions.

qs.q: An older adult takes diazepam for muscle spasm. Which therapy concern is greatest?
qs.a: Sedation and impaired balance increasing fall risk
w: Rapid heart rate during exercise
Excess muscle tone after sessions
Low risk of interaction with opioids
qs.x: Benzodiazepines cause sedation, slowed reaction time and falls, especially in older adults, and add to opioid sedation.

qs.q: Which skeletal muscle relaxant carries the greatest concern for misuse and dependence?
qs.a: Carisoprodol
w: Metaxalone
Methocarbamol
Chlorzoxazone
qs.x: Carisoprodol is metabolized to meprobamate and is a controlled substance with misuse potential.

qs.q: A patient takes immediate-release oral oxycodone for post-op knee pain. When is a therapy session most likely to coincide with peak pain relief?
qs.a: About 1 hour after the dose
w: About 5 minutes after the dose
About 8 hours after the dose
Right before the next dose is due
qs.x: Oral immediate-release opioids peak in roughly 30 to 60 minutes, so coordinating with nursing for timing improves participation.

qs.q: A patient on opioids says pain is zero during aggressive range of motion after a tendon repair. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Pain relief may mask warning pain and allow tissue overstress
w: Opioids speed tendon healing
The patient cannot be on an opioid
Pain-free motion confirms the repair is strong
qs.x: Analgesics blunt protective pain; the therapist should follow protocol limits rather than pain alone.

qs.q: Which opioid side effect most directly increases fall risk when moving from supine to standing?
qs.a: Orthostatic hypotension and sedation
w: Constipation
Pruritus
Urinary retention
qs.x: Opioids cause vasodilation and sedation, so check vitals with position changes and guard during early mobility.

qs.q: Which side effect of opioids does NOT usually lessen with ongoing use and should be asked about often?
qs.a: Constipation
w: Sedation
Nausea
Respiratory depression
qs.x: Tolerance develops to most opioid effects but not to constipation; mobility and fluids help, and changes should be reported.

qs.q: A patient wears a fentanyl transdermal patch on the low back. What is the main concern with using a hot pack over that area?
qs.a: Heat increases drug absorption and can cause overdose
w: Heat makes the patch stop working
Heat causes the patch to lose adhesion only
There is no interaction between heat and the patch
qs.x: FDA labeling warns that external heat raises fentanyl absorption and can cause fatal respiratory depression.

qs.q: Which finding during a session in a patient on opioids should be reported right away?
qs.a: Difficult to arouse with slow, shallow breathing
w: Mild itching of the forearms
Report of a dry mouth
Pain rated lower than yesterday
qs.x: Excess sedation and slowed breathing signal opioid-induced respiratory depression.

qs.q: A patient takes tramadol and an SSRI. Which symptom pattern should be reported as a possible drug interaction?
qs.a: Agitation, tremor, sweating and fast heart rate
w: Slow heart rate and dry skin
Gradual weight gain and fatigue
Improved mood and energy
qs.x: Tramadol adds serotonin effects and can lead to serotonin syndrome; it also lowers the seizure threshold.

qs.q: A patient with osteoarthritis takes ibuprofen daily. Which adverse effect is most important to ask about?
qs.a: Black, tarry stools or stomach pain
w: Increased muscle tone
Excessive thirst and hunger
Sudden hair loss
qs.x: NSAIDs can cause GI ulcers and bleeding; black stools suggest upper GI bleeding.

qs.q: Long-term NSAID use can affect cardiovascular status in therapy because NSAIDs can:
qs.a: Raise blood pressure and cause fluid retention
w: Lower blood pressure dramatically
Slow heart rate response to exercise
Increase red blood cell production
qs.x: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandins, leading to sodium and water retention, edema and higher blood pressure.

qs.q: Compared with nonselective NSAIDs, celecoxib mainly offers which advantage?
qs.a: Lower risk of stomach ulcers
w: No cardiovascular risk
No effect on the kidneys
Stronger anti-inflammatory effect
qs.x: COX-2 selective drugs spare stomach protection, but cardiovascular and kidney risks remain.

qs.q: Which statement about acetaminophen is correct for a patient with knee osteoarthritis?
qs.a: It relieves pain but has little anti-inflammatory effect
w: It reduces joint swelling more than NSAIDs
It causes significant stomach bleeding
It is a strong muscle relaxant
qs.x: Acetaminophen is analgesic and antipyretic but not anti-inflammatory; liver toxicity is the main risk with excess use.

qs.q: A patient has taken oral prednisone for a year for rheumatoid arthritis. Which complication is most important to consider when planning manual therapy and resistance exercise?
qs.a: Osteoporosis with fracture risk
w: Increased bone density
Hypertrophy of type II fibers
Faster ligament healing
qs.x: Chronic glucocorticoids reduce bone formation and increase fracture risk, especially in vertebrae.

qs.q: A patient on long-term prednisone has trouble rising from a chair but normal grip strength. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Steroid myopathy affecting proximal muscles
w: Peripheral neuropathy of the hands
Upper motor neuron spasticity
Cerebellar ataxia
qs.x: Steroid myopathy causes painless proximal weakness, mainly of the hip and shoulder girdle.

qs.q: After repeated corticosteroid injections near the Achilles tendon, what is the main tissue concern?
qs.a: Weakened tendon with higher rupture risk
w: Calcification that improves strength
Increased collagen synthesis
Permanent nerve block of the calf
qs.x: Corticosteroids inhibit collagen synthesis and fibroblast activity, so loading should progress cautiously.

qs.q: Which wound finding is expected in a patient on chronic corticosteroids?
qs.a: Slower healing with fewer signs of inflammation
w: Faster healing with more redness
Excess granulation tissue
Healing that is unaffected
qs.x: Steroids blunt inflammation and slow collagen formation, so infection signs may be muted.

qs.q: A patient with Parkinson disease takes carbidopa/levodopa at 8 AM. When is gait training usually best scheduled?
qs.a: During peak 'on' time, often about 1 hour after the dose
w: Right before the next dose is due
Immediately after a high-protein breakfast
Late evening when the drug has worn off
qs.x: Motor performance is best when levodopa is at a good level; coordinating with dose times improves session quality.

qs.q: Why is carbidopa combined with levodopa?
qs.a: It blocks peripheral conversion of levodopa so more reaches the brain
w: It directly stimulates dopamine receptors
It slows dopamine breakdown in the brain
It blocks acetylcholine to reduce tremor
qs.x: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral dopa decarboxylase, reducing nausea and increasing brain levodopa.

qs.q: A patient eats a high-protein lunch right before a levodopa dose and is rigid during afternoon therapy. Best explanation?
qs.a: Dietary amino acids compete with levodopa for absorption and transport
w: Protein converts levodopa to dopamine in the gut
Protein causes dopamine receptors to shut down
High protein causes peak-dose dyskinesia
qs.x: Large neutral amino acids share transporters with levodopa; spacing protein away from doses can help, which should be discussed with the provider or dietitian.

qs.q: Writhing, dance-like movements that appear when levodopa levels are highest are called:
qs.a: Peak-dose dyskinesia
w: Wearing-off tremor
Freezing of gait
Akathisia from withdrawal
qs.x: Peak-dose dyskinesia reflects excess dopamine stimulation and becomes more common with years of levodopa use.

qs.q: A patient's tremor and slowness return an hour before each scheduled dose. This pattern is called:
qs.a: Wearing off
w: Peak-dose dyskinesia
On-state freezing
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
qs.x: End-of-dose wearing off is the most common motor fluctuation; the timing pattern should be documented and reported.

qs.q: During an 'off' period, which therapy focus is most appropriate?
qs.a: Safety, cueing strategies and stretching
w: High-level balance perturbation training
Maximal treadmill speed testing
Introducing a complex new motor skill
qs.x: Off periods limit motor learning and raise fall risk; demanding training fits best in the 'on' state.

qs.q: Which serious reaction can follow abrupt loss of levodopa therapy, for example when doses are missed during a hospital stay?
qs.a: High fever, severe rigidity and confusion resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome
w: Sudden drop in muscle tone with flaccidity
Rapid improvement in gait
Isolated mild headache
qs.x: Abrupt withdrawal can cause a parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome, a medical emergency; missed doses should be reported.

qs.q: Entacapone is added to carbidopa/levodopa mainly to:
qs.a: Extend the duration of each levodopa dose
w: Replace levodopa entirely
Treat orthostatic hypotension
Reduce dyskinesia by blocking dopamine
qs.x: COMT inhibitors slow levodopa breakdown, reducing wearing off; they may increase dyskinesia and can tint urine orange-brown.

qs.q: A patient on pramipexole falls asleep suddenly while seated during a session. What is the best explanation?
qs.a: Sudden sleep onset is a known dopamine agonist effect
w: It is a sign of low blood glucose from the drug
It indicates the drug is not working
It is caused by a high-protein meal
qs.x: Dopamine agonists can cause sudden sleep attacks without warning, which also matters for driving.

qs.q: A family member reports that a patient on ropinirole has begun gambling and shopping compulsively. What is the correct response?
qs.a: Report it to the provider as a possible impulse-control side effect
w: Reassure them it is unrelated to medicines
Recommend higher activity levels to distract him
Document it only as a personality change
qs.x: Dopamine agonists are linked to impulse-control disorders such as gambling, shopping and binge eating.

qs.q: Apomorphine is used in Parkinson disease mainly for:
qs.a: Rapid rescue from sudden 'off' episodes
w: Long-term prevention of dementia
Lowering blood pressure
Treating constipation
qs.x: Apomorphine works within minutes; orthostatic hypotension and nausea are common.

qs.q: Which drug is commonly used to reduce levodopa-induced dyskinesia?
qs.a: Amantadine
w: Trihexyphenidyl
Entacapone
Selegiline
qs.x: Amantadine, an NMDA antagonist, reduces dyskinesia; it can cause leg edema, livedo reticularis and confusion.

qs.q: Why is trihexyphenidyl often avoided in older adults with Parkinson disease?
qs.a: Anticholinergic effects cause confusion, constipation and urinary retention
w: It causes severe dyskinesia
It raises blood pressure sharply
It blocks levodopa absorption
qs.x: Anticholinergic drugs are on the Beers Criteria list because of cognitive and autonomic side effects.

qs.q: Rasagiline improves Parkinson symptoms by:
qs.a: Inhibiting MAO-B to slow dopamine breakdown
w: Blocking peripheral dopa decarboxylase
Directly releasing acetylcholine
Blocking NMDA receptors
qs.x: MAO-B inhibitors prolong dopamine activity and can interact with meperidine, tramadol and some antidepressants.

qs.q: A patient on carbidopa/levodopa becomes lightheaded on standing at the start of therapy. What should the therapist measure?
qs.a: Orthostatic blood pressure and heart rate
w: Grip strength
Peak expiratory flow
Two-point discrimination
qs.x: Levodopa and Parkinson disease itself both cause orthostatic hypotension, a major fall risk.

qs.q: A patient on metoprolol begins cardiac rehab. What is the best way to set exercise intensity?
qs.a: Use the rating of perceived exertion or talk test
w: Use the age-predicted maximum heart rate formula
Target a heart rate rise of 50 beats
Use blood glucose response
qs.x: Beta-blockers blunt resting and exercise heart rate, so heart-rate targets underestimate effort; RPE is preferred.

qs.q: During exercise, a patient on atenolol has a heart rate that barely rises despite heavy breathing. Best interpretation?
qs.a: An expected blunted chronotropic response from the beta-blocker
w: The patient is not working hard enough
The pulse oximeter is malfunctioning
The patient has developed heart block from exercise
qs.x: Beta-blockers limit heart rate increase; monitor symptoms, RPE and blood pressure instead.

qs.q: In a patient with diabetes on propranolol, which hypoglycemia sign may be masked?
qs.a: Rapid heart rate and tremor
w: Sweating
Confusion
Hunger
qs.x: Beta-blockers hide adrenergic signs such as tachycardia and tremor; sweating usually remains.

qs.q: A patient started lisinopril this week and feels dizzy after rising from the mat table. What is the best action?
qs.a: Return to sitting, check orthostatic vitals and report the findings
w: Have the patient walk briskly to raise blood pressure
Ignore it because ACE inhibitors do not affect blood pressure
Perform vigorous neck stretching
qs.x: Antihypertensives commonly cause orthostatic hypotension, especially early; slow position changes and documentation help.

qs.q: Why is an extended cool-down important for a patient on amlodipine?
qs.a: Vasodilation increases the risk of post-exercise hypotension
w: It raises the heart rate too much
It causes hypoglycemia after exercise
It causes bronchospasm after exercise
qs.x: Abrupt stop of exercise plus drug-induced vasodilation can pool blood in the legs and drop blood pressure.

qs.q: A patient on furosemide reports leg cramps and palpitations during exercise. Which lab value is most relevant?
qs.a: Serum potassium
w: Serum calcium only
Hemoglobin A1c
Serum albumin
qs.x: Loop diuretics cause potassium loss, which can cause cramps, weakness and arrhythmias.

qs.q: Which concern is most relevant for an older adult on hydrochlorothiazide exercising in a warm room?
qs.a: Dehydration and orthostatic hypotension
w: Fluid overload and pulmonary edema
Low heart rate from beta blockade
Increased bleeding risk
qs.x: Diuretics reduce fluid volume, which adds to heat stress and lightheadedness on standing.

qs.q: A patient injects rapid-acting insulin before breakfast and comes to therapy about an hour later. Which is the main exercise risk?
qs.a: Hypoglycemia near the time of peak insulin action
w: Hyperglycemia from the meal
Ketoacidosis from exercise
Hyperkalemia from insulin
qs.x: Rapid-acting insulin peaks within about 1 to 2 hours, and exercise further lowers glucose.

qs.q: During a session, a patient on insulin becomes shaky, sweaty and confused. What is the best first response?
qs.a: End exercise, check glucose if possible and give a fast-acting carbohydrate per protocol
w: Continue exercise to raise blood sugar
Give a high-fat snack and resume exercise
Have the patient lie down and rest without checking glucose
qs.x: These are classic signs of hypoglycemia; fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck follow facility protocol.

qs.q: Why should a patient who injected insulin into the thigh be monitored closely before a vigorous leg workout?
qs.a: Exercise of that limb can speed insulin absorption
w: Leg exercise destroys insulin at the site
The thigh absorbs insulin more slowly during exercise
Exercise raises blood glucose after injection
qs.x: Increased blood flow to working muscle speeds absorption from nearby sites, raising hypoglycemia risk.

qs.q: A patient on warfarin slips and strikes her head but feels fine. What is the best action?
qs.a: Report the fall promptly for medical evaluation
w: Document it and recheck next week
Apply ice and continue the session
Reassure her because she has no symptoms now
qs.x: Anticoagulated patients can develop delayed intracranial bleeding; head strikes need prompt evaluation.

qs.q: Which lab value best reflects anticoagulation level for a patient on warfarin?
qs.a: INR
w: Platelet count
Hemoglobin A1c
Serum creatinine
qs.x: Warfarin is monitored with the PT/INR; a high INR increases bleeding risk with manual therapy or falls.

qs.q: A patient on apixaban develops a swollen, painful knee without injury. What should the therapist suspect?
qs.a: Spontaneous joint bleeding (hemarthrosis)
w: Normal response to exercise
Gout from the drug
Tendon rupture from the drug
qs.x: Anticoagulants raise risk of hemarthrosis and soft-tissue bleeding; avoid vigorous manual therapy and report it.

qs.q: An older adult takes zolpidem at bedtime. Which fall risk should be addressed in home safety training?
qs.a: Night-time and early-morning falls from sedation and poor balance
w: Falls only during afternoon exercise
Falls caused by low blood glucose
Falls caused by high heart rate
qs.x: Sedative-hypnotics impair balance and alertness, especially when getting up at night to toilet.

qs.q: Which over-the-counter drug in an older adult is a Beers Criteria concern for confusion and falls?
qs.a: Diphenhydramine
w: Acetaminophen
Topical diclofenac
Calcium carbonate
qs.x: First-generation antihistamines are strongly anticholinergic, causing confusion, urinary retention and falls in older adults.

qs.q: Xerostomia caused by medications most often results from blocking which receptors?
qs.a: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors
w: Dopamine D2 receptors
Beta-adrenergic receptors
Serotonin 5-HT3 receptors
qs.x: Salivary secretion is driven by parasympathetic muscarinic stimulation. Anticholinergic drugs block these receptors and reduce saliva flow.

qs.q: An 80-year-old with overactive bladder reports a sticky mouth and difficulty chewing bread. Which of her medicines is the most likely contributor?
qs.a: Oxybutynin
w: Famotidine
Lisinopril
Levetiracetam
qs.x: Oxybutynin is a bladder antispasmodic with strong anticholinergic effects; dry mouth is its most common side effect.

qs.q: Which antidepressant is known for strong anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth and constipation?
qs.a: Amitriptyline
w: Trazodone
Famotidine
Ramelteon
qs.x: Tertiary-amine tricyclics like amitriptyline block muscarinic receptors strongly, causing xerostomia, constipation and confusion.

qs.q: A patient takes an over-the-counter sleep aid nightly and complains of morning dry mouth. Which ingredient is the likely cause?
qs.a: Diphenhydramine
w: Melatonin
Acetaminophen
Calcium carbonate
qs.x: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation antihistamine with anticholinergic activity, causing dry mouth and next-day sedation.

qs.q: How does reduced saliva most directly affect the oral preparatory phase?
qs.a: Poor bolus cohesion with prolonged chewing
w: Premature spillage of thin liquids
Delayed laryngeal vestibule closure
Reduced upper esophageal sphincter opening
qs.x: Saliva moistens food and binds particles into a cohesive bolus. Without it, chewing is prolonged and the bolus falls apart, leaving residue.

qs.q: A patient with xerostomia has dry crumbly solids scattered in the oral cavity after the swallow. Which compensation is most commonly recommended?
qs.a: Alternating bites of solid with sips of liquid
w: Chin tuck with every liquid swallow
Supraglottic swallow for solids only
Head rotation toward the weaker side
qs.x: Liquid washes help moisten and clear dry solids when saliva is reduced. Moist, sauced foods also help.

qs.q: Pilocarpine improves dry mouth by which mechanism?
qs.a: Stimulating muscarinic receptors on salivary glands
w: Coating the oral mucosa with a lubricant
Blocking histamine release in the mouth
Increasing fluid absorption from the gut
qs.x: Pilocarpine is a cholinergic (muscarinic) agonist, a sialogogue that stimulates remaining salivary tissue.

qs.q: Cevimeline is FDA-approved for dry mouth associated with which condition?
qs.a: Sjogren's syndrome
w: Parkinson's disease
Myasthenia gravis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
qs.x: Cevimeline is a muscarinic agonist approved for dry mouth in Sjogren's syndrome.

qs.q: Which side effect is most commonly reported with pilocarpine tablets?
qs.a: Sweating
w: Dry eyes
Constipation
Urinary retention
qs.x: Because pilocarpine stimulates muscarinic receptors throughout the body, sweating is the most common side effect.

qs.q: Why might a saliva substitute help a patient when pilocarpine does not?
qs.a: Substitutes lubricate even without working salivary tissue
w: Substitutes regenerate damaged salivary glands
Substitutes block anticholinergic drug effects
Substitutes stimulate muscarinic receptors more strongly
qs.x: Sialogogues need functioning glands to stimulate. Saliva substitutes simply coat and moisten the mouth, so they work after extensive gland damage.

qs.q: A child with cerebral palsy is prescribed a medicine to reduce drooling. Which drug is commonly used for this purpose?
qs.a: Glycopyrrolate
w: Pilocarpine
Cevimeline
Donepezil
qs.x: Glycopyrrolate is an anticholinergic used to reduce chronic drooling; it can also thicken secretions and cause constipation.

qs.q: A hospice patient has a patch placed behind the ear to dry secretions. Which drug is this most likely?
qs.a: Scopolamine
w: Fentanyl
Rotigotine
Pilocarpine
qs.x: Transdermal scopolamine is an anticholinergic patch sometimes used to reduce secretions; it can cause dry mouth and confusion.

qs.q: Which oral health problem is a long-term consequence of chronic medication-induced xerostomia?
qs.a: Dental caries
w: Gingival overgrowth
Tooth discoloration from staining
Excessive tooth enamel thickening
qs.x: Saliva buffers acid and clears bacteria; chronic dryness raises the risk of caries and oral candidiasis.

qs.q: The term anticholinergic burden refers to which concept?
qs.a: The cumulative effect of several drugs with anticholinergic activity
w: The single strongest anticholinergic drug in a regimen
The length of time an anticholinergic stays in the body
The dose needed to treat anticholinergic toxicity
qs.x: Several mildly anticholinergic medicines can add up to a large total effect, especially in older adults.

qs.q: Which inhaled medicine for COPD commonly causes dry mouth?
qs.a: Tiotropium
w: Albuterol
Budesonide
Fluticasone
qs.x: Tiotropium is an inhaled long-acting muscarinic antagonist; dry mouth is its most common side effect.

qs.q: Unlike most antipsychotics, which one commonly causes excessive salivation rather than dry mouth?
qs.a: Clozapine
w: Chlorpromazine
Olanzapine
Quetiapine
qs.x: Clozapine frequently causes sialorrhea, especially at night, despite its anticholinergic properties.

qs.q: Shortly after receiving haloperidol, a patient has sustained tongue protrusion and difficulty swallowing. What is this most likely?
qs.a: Acute dystonic reaction
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
qs.x: Acute dystonia appears within hours to days of starting a high-potency antipsychotic and can involve the tongue, jaw and larynx. It needs prompt medical attention.

qs.q: Tardive dyskinesia most commonly produces which oral-motor finding?
qs.a: Involuntary lip smacking and tongue writhing
w: Fixed tongue deviation to one side
Fasciculations with tongue atrophy
Flaccid lips with loss of tone
qs.x: TD causes repetitive involuntary orofacial movements that can disrupt bolus control and the oral phase.

qs.q: Compared with acute dystonia, tardive dyskinesia typically appears when?
qs.a: After months to years of exposure
w: Within hours of the first dose
Only after the drug is withdrawn
Within the first week of therapy
qs.x: TD is a late complication of long-term dopamine blockade and may persist even after the drug changes.

qs.q: Which medication is FDA-approved to treat tardive dyskinesia?
qs.a: Valbenazine
w: Benztropine
Haloperidol
Metoclopramide
qs.x: Valbenazine and deutetrabenazine are VMAT2 inhibitors approved for TD. Anticholinergics like benztropine are not effective for TD.

qs.q: Which GI medicine carries a boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia?
qs.a: Metoclopramide
w: Famotidine
Omeprazole
Pantoprazole
qs.x: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine receptors and has a boxed warning for TD, with risk rising with long-term use.

qs.q: Drug-induced parkinsonism from antipsychotics most often affects swallowing by causing which finding?
qs.a: Reduced tongue movement and delayed swallow initiation
w: Premature velopharyngeal closure
Increased pharyngeal contraction strength
Hyperactive gag reflex with spasm
qs.x: Dopamine blockade can produce bradykinesia and rigidity of oral and pharyngeal muscles, much like Parkinson's disease.

qs.q: A college student takes a pill at bedtime with a small sip of water and wakes with sharp pain when swallowing. Which drug is a classic cause?
qs.a: Doxycycline
w: Famotidine
Levetiracetam
Lisinopril
qs.x: Doxycycline is acidic and a classic cause of pill esophagitis, especially when taken lying down with little water.

qs.q: Alendronate labeling directs patients to remain upright for 30 minutes after a dose mainly to lower which risk?
qs.a: Esophageal irritation and ulceration
w: Orthostatic low blood pressure
Aspiration of the tablet
Rebound bone loss
qs.x: Bisphosphonates irritate the esophagus; staying upright with a full glass of water helps the pill clear quickly.

qs.q: Solid potassium chloride tablets are a known cause of which swallowing-related injury?
qs.a: Pill-induced esophageal injury
w: Vocal fold paralysis
Tongue fasciculations
Oral candidiasis
qs.x: Potassium chloride can injure the esophageal mucosa if it lodges in place, causing odynophagia or ulceration.

qs.q: Which patient factor most increases the risk of pill esophagitis?
qs.a: Taking pills lying down with little fluid
w: Taking pills with a full glass of water
Taking pills while seated upright
Taking pills spaced through the day
qs.x: Recumbent position and low fluid volume let pills stall in the esophagus. Upright posture and adequate fluid aid clearance.

qs.q: Odynophagia means which symptom?
qs.a: Pain with swallowing
w: Difficulty initiating a swallow
Food sticking without pain
Coughing during a swallow
qs.x: Odynophagia is painful swallowing, a hallmark of pill esophagitis; dysphagia is difficulty swallowing.

qs.q: A patient with dysphagia has trouble swallowing an extended-release tablet. What is the best SLP action?
qs.a: Ask the pharmacist or prescriber about alternative forms
w: Crush the tablet into applesauce
Cut the tablet into small pieces
Dissolve the tablet in hot water
qs.x: Many extended-release or enteric-coated products cannot be crushed; the pharmacist can identify a safe alternative form.

qs.q: Two weeks after neck injections for cervical dystonia, a patient reports new trouble swallowing. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: Spread of botulinum toxin to swallowing muscles
w: An allergic reaction to the injection
Tardive dyskinesia of the pharynx
Pill esophagitis from oral medicines
qs.x: Dysphagia is a known effect of cervical botulinum toxin injection due to spread to nearby pharyngeal muscles; distant spread carries a boxed warning.

qs.q: After laryngeal botulinum toxin for adductor spasmodic dysphonia, which early effects are commonly expected?
qs.a: Breathy voice and mild thin-liquid aspiration
w: Strained voice with vocal fold spasm
Hypernasal speech and nasal regurgitation
Complete aphonia lasting several years
qs.x: Temporary breathiness and mild choking on thin liquids are common in the first weeks before voice improves.

qs.q: An SLP notices increasing tongue writhing in a long-term resident on an antipsychotic. What is the most appropriate action?
qs.a: Report the movements to the prescriber or nursing
w: Advise the resident to skip doses
Begin tongue strengthening only
Document as normal aging
qs.x: New or worsening involuntary movements should be reported so the team can assess for tardive dyskinesia.

qs.q: Why do opioids increase aspiration risk?
qs.a: They suppress cough and reduce alertness
w: They increase saliva production
They tighten the vocal folds
They speed esophageal transit
qs.x: Opioids depress the cough reflex and level of consciousness, reducing airway protection.

qs.q: Silent aspiration is defined as which finding?
qs.a: Material entering below the vocal folds without cough
w: Coughing during every swallow
Residue in the valleculae after swallow
Material entering the nasopharynx
qs.x: In silent aspiration, material passes below the true vocal folds with no outward sign such as cough or throat clearing.

qs.q: A patient received lorazepam for agitation one hour before a scheduled bedside swallow evaluation and is drowsy. What is the best plan?
qs.a: Reschedule when the patient is more alert
w: Proceed with thin liquids by straw
Test only solid foods to stay safe
Proceed and rate the patient as normal
qs.x: Sedation lowers alertness and airway protection; results may not reflect true function. Testing when alert gives a valid picture.

qs.q: Which benzodiazepine is commonly used for procedural sedation and can cause transient swallowing impairment afterward?
qs.a: Midazolam
w: Clonazepam
Flurazepam
Quazepam
qs.x: Midazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine used for procedures; residual sedation can briefly impair swallowing.

qs.q: When documenting a swallow evaluation, why should recent sedating medicines be noted?
qs.a: They may affect alertness and performance
w: They determine the diet texture by law
They change the scoring scale used
They replace the need for instrumental testing
qs.x: Medication timing helps the team interpret results and plan re-evaluation.

qs.q: Which pairing of drugs carries an FDA boxed warning for profound sedation and respiratory depression?
qs.a: Opioids with benzodiazepines
w: Proton pump inhibitors with antacids
Saliva substitutes with sialogogues
Inhaled steroids with bronchodilators
qs.x: Combining opioids and benzodiazepines adds sedation and respiratory depression, raising aspiration and overdose risk.

qs.q: Antipsychotic use in older adults is associated with which pulmonary complication?
qs.a: Aspiration pneumonia
w: Pulmonary embolism from vocal strain
Asthma from dopamine blockade
Pneumothorax from cough
qs.x: Sedation, EPS and reduced swallow function from antipsychotics raise aspiration pneumonia risk.

qs.q: A patient took zolpidem late at night and is groggy at an early morning swallow evaluation. What is the concern?
qs.a: Next-morning impairment of alertness
w: Increased saliva causing drooling
Esophageal irritation from the tablet
Hoarseness from vocal fold edema
qs.x: Zolpidem can cause next-day impairment, especially in older adults and women; alertness affects swallow safety.

qs.q: Which antispasticity medicine commonly causes drowsiness and weakness that may affect swallowing?
qs.a: Baclofen
w: Pilocarpine
Pyridostigmine
Albuterol
qs.x: Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist muscle relaxant; drowsiness and weakness can reduce swallow efficiency.

qs.q: The ideal time to schedule a swallow evaluation for a patient on scheduled sedating medicines is when?
qs.a: When the patient is typically most alert
w: Right after the evening sedative
Immediately after a pain injection
During the patient's usual nap time
qs.x: Alertness supports airway protection and valid results; coordinate timing with nursing.

qs.q: Which effect of morphine most directly reduces the ability to clear aspirated material?
qs.a: Cough reflex suppression
w: Increased bronchial secretions
Vocal fold hyperadduction
Increased laryngeal sensation
qs.x: Opioids are antitussives; a weak cough cannot clear material from the airway.

qs.q: A resident's chart shows several sedating medicines. Which screening finding most suggests reduced airway protection?
qs.a: Wet vocal quality without a spontaneous cough
w: Clear voice after each swallow
Prompt cough with a strong throat clear
Complete oral clearance of the bolus
qs.x: A wet voice suggests material at the laryngeal vestibule; absent cough suggests reduced sensation or response.

qs.q: Which drug class is the reversal agent naloxone used for?
qs.a: Opioids
w: Benzodiazepines
Antipsychotics
Anticholinergics
qs.x: Naloxone reverses opioid effects; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines in limited settings.

qs.q: Which statement about sedation and swallowing is most accurate?
qs.a: Reduced alertness can impair both oral control and airway protection
w: Sedation affects only the esophageal phase
Sedation improves swallow timing by relaxing muscles
Sedation increases sensitivity of the cough reflex
qs.x: Sedation slows oral control, delays swallow initiation and blunts protective responses.

qs.q: When should an SLP alert the team about a patient's sedation before a meal?
qs.a: When the patient cannot stay awake for oral intake
w: When the patient asks for a snack
When the patient finishes the meal quickly
When the patient talks during the meal
qs.x: A patient too drowsy to stay alert is at high risk of aspiration; the team should be told so meal and medicine timing can be reviewed.

qs.q: An older adult with new confusion takes diphenhydramine, oxybutynin and amitriptyline. What is the most likely contributing factor?
qs.a: Cumulative anticholinergic burden
w: Vitamin overdose
Serotonin deficiency
Excess dopamine activity
qs.x: Anticholinergic drugs can cause confusion, memory problems and delirium in older adults; the Beers Criteria advise avoiding them.

qs.q: Which reference lists medicines that are potentially inappropriate in older adults, including strong anticholinergics?
qs.a: The AGS Beers Criteria
w: The Mann Assessment of Swallowing
The Penetration-Aspiration Scale
The Western Aphasia Battery
qs.x: The American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria flag drugs such as diphenhydramine and amitriptyline for older adults.

qs.q: A patient with asthma uses an inhaled corticosteroid and develops hoarseness. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Inhaled steroid effect on the larynx
w: Albuterol-induced vocal nodules
Acid reflux from the inhaler
Allergy to the inhaler propellant
qs.x: Inhaled corticosteroids can cause dysphonia through laryngeal muscle effects and candidiasis.

qs.q: Which practice is recommended after using an inhaled corticosteroid to reduce oral and laryngeal side effects?
qs.a: Rinsing the mouth and spitting
w: Lying flat for several minutes
Drinking a hot beverage
Using a straw for liquids
qs.x: Rinsing reduces drug deposited in the mouth and throat, lowering thrush and hoarseness risk. A spacer also helps.

qs.q: A patient referred for chronic cough and throat clearing recently started a blood pressure medicine. Which drug is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Lisinopril
w: Famotidine
Albuterol
Pilocarpine
qs.x: ACE inhibitors like lisinopril cause a dry, persistent cough in a notable minority of patients.

qs.q: ACE inhibitor cough is thought to result from accumulation of which substance?
qs.a: Bradykinin
w: Histamine
Dopamine
Acetylcholine
qs.x: ACE also breaks down bradykinin; its buildup in the airway is linked to the dry cough.

qs.q: Pyridostigmine improves strength in myasthenia gravis by what mechanism?
qs.a: Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
w: Blocking dopamine receptors in the brain
Stimulating salivary glands directly
Relaxing skeletal muscle via GABA
qs.x: By slowing acetylcholine breakdown, pyridostigmine increases neuromuscular transmission and muscle strength.

qs.q: A patient with myasthenia gravis has the best speech and swallowing about an hour after a pyridostigmine dose. How should therapy be scheduled?
qs.a: Coordinate meals and sessions with peak medicine effect
w: Schedule sessions just before the next dose
Schedule only in the late evening
Schedule without regard to medicine timing
qs.x: Pyridostigmine onset is about 30 to 60 minutes; aligning activities with peak effect supports best function.

qs.q: Which speech pattern is typical of myasthenia gravis?
qs.a: Hypernasality and weakness that worsen with prolonged speaking
w: Consistent strained-strangled voice
Sudden voice breaks only on vowels
Rapid accelerating speech rate
qs.x: MG causes fatigable flaccid dysarthria; speech deteriorates with use and improves with rest.

qs.q: Which side effect of pyridostigmine might an SLP observe during a swallow session?
qs.a: Increased saliva and secretions
w: Severe dry mouth
Tongue fasciculations from excess dopamine
Hoarseness from candidiasis
qs.x: Cholinergic effects include increased salivation, bronchial secretions, cramping and diarrhea.

qs.q: In Parkinson's disease, when are speech and swallowing usually best?
qs.a: During the 'on' period after a levodopa dose
w: During the 'off' period before a dose
Only on waking in the morning
Only late at night
qs.x: Motor function, including speech and swallowing, often improves when levodopa is working; sessions are often timed to 'on' periods.

qs.q: A patient with Parkinson's develops 'wearing off' before each dose. How might this appear in therapy?
qs.a: Softer voice and slower swallow near the next dose
w: Improved loudness right before the next dose
Excess drooling only during 'on' time
Stuttering that appears only after meals
qs.x: As levodopa wears off, hypophonia, reduced articulation and dysphagia can return; reporting the pattern helps the team.

qs.q: Which hyperkinetic speech change can result from levodopa peak-dose dyskinesia?
qs.a: Irregular articulation from involuntary movements
w: Monotone, quiet voice
Flaccid hypernasal resonance
Slow, labored speech with spasticity
qs.x: Peak-dose dyskinesias are involuntary movements that can disrupt articulation and respiration for speech.

qs.q: Which antiseizure medicine is known for word-finding difficulty and slowed thinking?
qs.a: Topiramate
w: Levetiracetam
Phenytoin
Baclofen
qs.x: Topiramate commonly causes cognitive slowing and word-finding problems that can resemble mild aphasia.

qs.q: Donepezil is used to treat which condition?
qs.a: Alzheimer's disease dementia
w: Parkinson's tremor
Myasthenia gravis
Spasmodic dysphonia
qs.x: Donepezil is a cholinesterase inhibitor that modestly improves cognition in Alzheimer's disease.

qs.q: Why are anticholinergic medicines concerning in a patient taking donepezil?
qs.a: They oppose the drug's cholinergic effect
w: They double the drug's benefit
They prevent its absorption in the stomach
They have no interaction at all
qs.x: Anticholinergics block acetylcholine while cholinesterase inhibitors increase it, working against each other and worsening cognition.

qs.q: Compared with bupivacaine, lidocaine has which profile?
qs.a: Faster onset and shorter duration
w: Slower onset and longer duration
Faster onset and longer duration
Slower onset and shorter duration
qs.x: Lidocaine works within minutes and lasts about 1-2 hours plain. Bupivacaine is slower to set up but lasts several hours.

qs.q: A surgeon wants a local anesthetic that will give the longest postoperative pain relief after a hernia repair. Which drug is most likely requested?
qs.a: Bupivacaine
w: Lidocaine
Chloroprocaine
Tetracaine
qs.x: Bupivacaine is a long-acting amide, commonly infiltrated at closure for prolonged pain relief.

qs.q: Which local anesthetic carries the greatest risk of cardiotoxicity if absorbed into the bloodstream?
qs.a: Bupivacaine
w: Lidocaine
Mepivacaine
Chloroprocaine
qs.x: Bupivacaine binds cardiac sodium channels tightly and can cause hard-to-treat dysrhythmias and arrest.

qs.q: Why is epinephrine added to a local anesthetic?
qs.a: It constricts vessels, prolonging the block and reducing bleeding
w: It speeds the onset by dilating local vessels
It neutralizes the acidity of the anesthetic
It prevents allergic reactions to the anesthetic
qs.x: Vasoconstriction slows absorption, so the drug stays at the site longer, toxicity risk drops and the field is drier.

qs.q: Local anesthetic with epinephrine has traditionally been avoided in which surgical site?
qs.a: Fingers and toes
w: Abdominal wall
Scalp
Lower back
qs.x: End-artery areas such as fingers, toes, nose, ears and penis were traditionally avoided because of concern for ischemia.

qs.q: Which statement about lidocaine with epinephrine compared with plain lidocaine is correct?
qs.a: It lasts longer and reduces bleeding at the site
w: It acts faster and lasts a shorter time
It has no effect on bleeding at the site
It is safe to use for IV regional block
qs.x: Epinephrine prolongs lidocaine's effect and narrows nearby vessels. Epinephrine-containing solutions are not used for Bier block.

qs.q: Which local anesthetic is used for an intravenous regional (Bier) block?
qs.a: Plain lidocaine
w: Bupivacaine
Lidocaine with epinephrine
Bupivacaine liposomal
qs.x: Plain lidocaine is the standard Bier block agent; bupivacaine is avoided because of cardiotoxicity, and epinephrine is not given IV this way.

qs.q: A patient receiving local infiltration reports a metallic taste, ringing in the ears and numbness around the mouth. What do these signs suggest?
qs.a: Early local anesthetic systemic toxicity
w: Normal effect of local anesthetic
Allergic reaction to latex
Vasovagal response to the injection
qs.x: Circumoral numbness, metallic taste and tinnitus are early CNS signs of LAST. Report them to the surgeon and anesthesia right away.

qs.q: Which finding represents severe local anesthetic systemic toxicity?
qs.a: Seizures followed by dysrhythmias
w: Mild itching at the site
Brief lightheadedness
Redness at the injection site
qs.x: LAST can progress from CNS excitation to seizures and then cardiovascular collapse.

qs.q: What is the specific treatment that should be available when local anesthetic systemic toxicity is suspected?
qs.a: Lipid emulsion
w: Naloxone
Flumazenil
Protamine
qs.x: Lipid emulsion therapy is the specific rescue for LAST, alongside airway support and seizure control.

qs.q: Why does the surgeon aspirate before injecting local anesthetic?
qs.a: To avoid injecting into a blood vessel
w: To mix the drug with tissue fluid
To speed the onset of the block
To measure how much drug was used
qs.x: Aspiration helps detect intravascular placement, which is a common cause of systemic toxicity.

qs.q: Two vials on the back table look identical except one reads 'with epinephrine.' What is the best way for the CST to prevent a mix-up?
qs.a: Read the full label aloud and label each syringe including 'with epinephrine'
w: Use a different size syringe for each drug
Rely on the color of the solution to tell them apart
Draw both drugs into one syringe for the surgeon
qs.x: Plain and epinephrine-containing solutions are both clear. The label on every container must state the drug, strength and whether epinephrine is present.

qs.q: Which local anesthetic is an ester with a very rapid onset and short duration?
qs.a: Chloroprocaine
w: Bupivacaine
Ropivacaine
Mepivacaine
qs.x: Chloroprocaine is an ester broken down quickly by plasma cholinesterase, so it acts fast and wears off quickly.

qs.q: Which statement about liposomal bupivacaine (Exparel) is correct?
qs.a: It provides infiltration analgesia lasting up to about 72 hours
w: It is mixed freely with lidocaine on the field
It is given intravenously for sedation
It works within seconds as an eye drop
qs.x: Liposomal bupivacaine releases drug slowly over days. Other local anesthetics can trigger rapid release, so mixing is restricted per labeling.

qs.q: Ropivacaine is often chosen over bupivacaine for nerve blocks because it:
qs.a: Has less cardiotoxicity with a similar long duration
w: Has a much faster onset than lidocaine
Contains epinephrine in every vial
Is an ester that rarely causes allergy
qs.x: Ropivacaine is a long-acting amide with a better cardiac safety profile than bupivacaine.

qs.q: What is the most important safety rule for topical thrombin?
qs.a: It must never be injected into a blood vessel
w: It must be mixed with sterile water only
It is applied only to bone surfaces
It must be given intramuscularly
qs.x: Topical thrombin can cause extensive clotting and death if it enters the circulation. It is for topical use only.

qs.q: How does topical thrombin promote hemostasis?
qs.a: It converts fibrinogen to fibrin
w: It activates platelets mechanically
It constricts arterioles at the site
It plugs bleeding bone surfaces
qs.x: Thrombin acts on the patient's fibrinogen to form a fibrin clot at the bleeding surface.

qs.q: Thrombin-JMI is bovine-derived. What is a known risk of bovine thrombin?
qs.a: Antibody formation that can cause bleeding problems
w: Severe hypoglycemia
Kidney stones
Permanent hair loss
qs.x: Bovine thrombin can trigger antibodies to clotting factors, leading to coagulopathy. Recombinant human thrombin (Recothrom) lowers this risk.

qs.q: An absorbable gelatin sponge (Gelfoam) is often prepared by soaking it in:
qs.a: Topical thrombin or saline
w: Sterile water and alcohol
Povidone-iodine
Heparinized saline
qs.x: Gelfoam can be used dry or moistened with saline or thrombin to enhance its hemostatic effect.

qs.q: Why should excess absorbable gelatin sponge or oxidized cellulose be removed near the spinal cord or bony foramina?
qs.a: Both swell and can compress nerves
w: Both dissolve bone tissue
Both block absorption of antibiotics
Both cause hemolysis of nearby blood
qs.x: These agents expand as they absorb fluid, which can compress nerves in closed spaces.

qs.q: Oxidized regenerated cellulose (Surgicel) should not be soaked with thrombin because:
qs.a: Its acidity inactivates thrombin
w: It dissolves instantly in thrombin
It becomes toxic when wet
It turns the thrombin into heparin
qs.x: The low pH of oxidized cellulose deactivates thrombin, so it is applied dry.

qs.q: How should microfibrillar collagen (Avitene) be handled?
qs.a: With dry gloves and dry instruments
w: Soaked in sterile water first
Mixed with antibiotic irrigation
Warmed in saline before use
qs.x: Microfibrillar collagen sticks to wet gloves and instruments, so it is handled dry.

qs.q: Which hemostatic agent should be kept out of cell-saver (blood salvage) suction?
qs.a: Microfibrillar collagen
w: Normal saline
Lactated Ringer's
Bone wax
qs.x: Collagen fibers can pass through cell-saver filters and be reinfused, so it should not be suctioned into salvage systems.

qs.q: Which irrigation solution is most commonly used for wound and body cavity irrigation?
qs.a: 0.9% sodium chloride
w: Sterile water
Glycine
Hydrogen peroxide
qs.x: Normal saline is isotonic, so it does not damage cells or shift fluid significantly.

qs.q: Why is sterile water avoided when large volumes may be absorbed into the bloodstream?
qs.a: It is hypotonic and can cause hemolysis
w: It is hypertonic and causes dehydration
It is too acidic for tissue
It conducts electricity strongly
qs.x: Water entering the circulation moves into red cells and ruptures them. It is used for rinsing instruments, not for routine wound irrigation.

qs.q: During a monopolar transurethral resection, why is normal saline not used as the irrigant?
qs.a: It conducts electricity and disperses the current
w: It is hypotonic and causes hemolysis
It stains the bladder wall
It causes the scope lens to fog
qs.x: Monopolar resection needs a non-conductive fluid such as glycine or sorbitol. Bipolar systems can use saline.

qs.q: Which is a feature of lactated Ringer's as an irrigation solution?
qs.a: It is isotonic and contains calcium and lactate
w: It is hypotonic like sterile water
It contains heparin to prevent clotting
It is non-conductive for monopolar resection
qs.x: LR is a balanced isotonic solution often used for arthroscopy irrigation.

qs.q: In 2020, the FDA requested removal of bacitracin for injection from the market. Why?
qs.a: Risk of kidney injury and anaphylaxis
w: It was replaced by a generic
It caused low blood sugar
It stained surgical instruments
qs.x: FDA cited nephrotoxicity and anaphylaxis risk; facilities now often choose other irrigation antibiotics.

qs.q: Before antibiotic irrigation is prepared, which check is most important?
qs.a: The patient's allergy history
w: The patient's blood type
The patient's last meal
The patient's height
qs.x: Antibiotics in irrigation can cause allergic reactions, so allergies are confirmed before preparation.

qs.q: Why are irrigation solutions usually warmed before use?
qs.a: To help prevent patient hypothermia
w: To increase the antibiotic strength
To make them more hypotonic
To shorten the surgery time
qs.x: Large volumes of cold irrigation can lower core temperature, so fluids are warmed to near body temperature.

qs.q: Tropicamide is used before cataract surgery because it:
qs.a: Dilates the pupil
w: Constricts the pupil
Lowers intraocular pressure
Numbs the cornea
qs.x: Tropicamide is an anticholinergic mydriatic that also causes short-lived cycloplegia.

qs.q: How does phenylephrine eye drop differ from tropicamide?
qs.a: It dilates the pupil without paralyzing focus
w: It constricts the pupil
It numbs the cornea
It paralyzes focus without dilating
qs.x: Phenylephrine is an alpha agonist that contracts the dilator muscle; it does not cause cycloplegia.

qs.q: Which systemic effect should be watched for with phenylephrine eye drops?
qs.a: Elevated blood pressure
w: Low blood sugar
Slow breathing
Excess urination
qs.x: Systemic absorption of phenylephrine can raise blood pressure, especially in sensitive patients.

qs.q: Under the standard ophthalmic cap color code, mydriatic eye drops have which cap color?
qs.a: Red
w: Green
Tan
Pink
qs.x: Mydriatics and cycloplegics are red; miotics green; anti-infectives tan; steroids pink.

qs.q: What is proparacaine used for in eye surgery?
qs.a: Topical anesthesia of the cornea
w: Dilating the pupil
Constricting the pupil
Staining the lens capsule
qs.x: Proparacaine drops numb the eye surface within seconds for a short time.

qs.q: What is a concern with repeated use of topical anesthetic eye drops like tetracaine?
qs.a: Damage to the corneal epithelium
w: Permanent pupil dilation
Increased tear production
Allergy to latex
qs.x: Repeated topical anesthetic use can delay healing and damage the corneal surface.

qs.q: Intraocular acetylcholine (Miochol-E) is given during cataract surgery to:
qs.a: Constrict the pupil quickly
w: Dilate the pupil
Numb the cornea
Prevent infection
qs.x: Acetylcholine is a miotic that constricts the pupil within seconds after lens placement.

qs.q: How does intraocular carbachol (Miostat) compare with intraocular acetylcholine?
qs.a: Slower onset but longer-lasting miosis
w: Faster onset but shorter miosis
It dilates rather than constricts
It numbs rather than constricts
qs.x: Carbachol works over minutes and its effect can last about a day; acetylcholine acts in seconds and is short-lived.

qs.q: Why is hyaluronidase added to local anesthetic for an eye block?
qs.a: To help the anesthetic spread through tissue
w: To prolong vasoconstriction
To dilate the pupil
To reverse heparin
qs.x: Hyaluronidase breaks down hyaluronic acid in connective tissue, improving anesthetic spread.

qs.q: Which serious interaction is associated with methylene blue?
qs.a: Serotonin syndrome with serotonergic antidepressants
w: Severe hypoglycemia with insulin
Bleeding with acetaminophen
Kidney stones with calcium
qs.x: Methylene blue inhibits MAO-A, so the FDA warns of serotonin syndrome with SSRIs, SNRIs and similar drugs.

qs.q: After methylene blue is given, which monitoring change may occur?
qs.a: A falsely low pulse oximetry reading
w: A falsely high blood glucose
A falsely low heart rate
A falsely high temperature
qs.x: Blue dye in the blood interferes with pulse oximeter light absorption.

qs.q: Isosulfan blue is used for which procedure?
qs.a: Sentinel lymph node mapping
w: Cataract extraction
Ureteral stent placement
Coronary bypass grafting
qs.x: Isosulfan blue travels through lymphatics to stain the first draining node. Anaphylaxis is a known risk.

qs.q: Before indocyanine green (ICG) is used, which allergy should be confirmed?
qs.a: Iodide allergy
w: Egg allergy
Latex allergy
Peanut allergy
qs.x: ICG formulations contain sodium iodide, so iodide allergy is a caution.

qs.q: Heparinized saline on a vascular case is used to:
qs.a: Irrigate vessel lumens to prevent clotting
w: Reverse anticoagulation at closure
Stain vessels for identification
Constrict bleeding vessels
qs.x: Heparinized saline keeps clots from forming in vessels and catheters during vascular work.

qs.q: Which drug reverses heparin at the end of a vascular procedure?
qs.a: Protamine
w: Vitamin K
Tranexamic acid
Thrombin
qs.x: Protamine binds heparin. Watch for hypotension and anaphylaxis, especially with fish allergy or prior protamine-insulin use.

qs.q: According to The Joint Commission, which containers on the sterile field must be labeled?
qs.a: Every syringe, cup and basin containing medication
w: Only containers with controlled drugs
Only syringes handed to the surgeon
Only when more than one drug is present
qs.x: All medications and solutions on and off the sterile field must be labeled, even if only one is present.

qs.q: When should a medication container on the sterile field be labeled?
qs.a: Immediately when the drug is placed in it
w: At the end of the procedure
When the surgeon asks for it
After the count is completed
qs.x: Labeling at once prevents mix-ups between clear solutions.

qs.q: When receiving a medication from the circulator, what should be verified aloud?
qs.a: Drug name, strength and expiration date
w: Lot number and manufacturer only
Price and storage location
Pharmacy and ordering date
qs.x: Both the circulator and scrub confirm name, strength and expiration before the drug is transferred.

qs.q: How should a medication in a vial be transferred to the sterile field?
qs.a: Using a sterile transfer device or sterile syringe
w: By the circulator reaching over the field
By pouring after removing the stopper with fingers
By the scrub touching the outside of the vial
qs.x: Sterile technique is maintained during transfer; the circulator never reaches over the sterile field.

qs.q: The CST finds an unlabeled cup of clear fluid on the back table. What is the correct action?
qs.a: Discard it and obtain a fresh, labeled supply
w: Assume it is saline and use it
Smell it to identify it
Ask the surgeon to guess
qs.x: An unlabeled solution can never be identified with certainty, so it is discarded.

qs.q: When handing a syringe of local anesthetic to the surgeon, the CST should:
qs.a: State the drug name and strength aloud
w: Pass it silently to avoid distraction
State only the volume in the syringe
Announce the patient's name only
qs.x: Stating the drug and strength allows the surgeon to confirm before injecting.

qs.q: Why are original medication vials kept in the room until the case ends?
qs.a: To allow verification if a question arises
w: To return them to pharmacy for credit
To use as spare containers
To meet fire safety rules
qs.x: Original containers allow the team to recheck drug, strength and amount used.

qs.q: During a scrub relief, what should happen with medications on the field?
qs.a: Both scrub persons review each labeled medication together
w: The relief assumes labels are correct
All medications are discarded
Only the surgeon reviews them
qs.x: A hand-off review prevents errors when staff change.

qs.q: Cefazolin for surgical prophylaxis should be infused within what time before incision?
qs.a: 60 minutes
w: 120 minutes
180 minutes
24 hours
qs.x: Most prophylactic antibiotics, including cefazolin, should start within 60 minutes before incision so tissue levels are adequate.

qs.q: Why may vancomycin prophylaxis begin up to 120 minutes before incision?
qs.a: It must infuse slowly to avoid a reaction
w: It needs time to be absorbed orally
It only works after a long delay
It must be given after induction drugs
qs.x: Vancomycin is infused slowly to prevent infusion-related flushing, so it starts earlier.

qs.q: A patient receiving vancomycin develops flushing and itching of the face and upper body. What is the likely cause?
qs.a: Infusion running too fast
w: Allergy to cefazolin
Local anesthetic toxicity
Methylene blue reaction
qs.x: Vancomycin infusion reaction (formerly red man syndrome) is related to infusion rate. Report it to anesthesia.

qs.q: Cefazolin is the most common surgical prophylactic antibiotic mainly because it:
qs.a: Covers common skin organisms like Staphylococcus aureus
w: Covers all anaerobic bacteria
Is never associated with allergy
Has no need for redosing
qs.x: Cefazolin targets typical skin flora that cause surgical site infections.

qs.q: For a patient with a severe beta-lactam allergy, which antibiotic is a common prophylaxis alternative?
qs.a: Clindamycin
w: Cefazolin
Ampicillin
Cefoxitin
qs.x: Clindamycin or vancomycin are common alternatives when beta-lactams must be avoided.

qs.q: During a long procedure, what may happen with cefazolin prophylaxis?
qs.a: It is redosed at set intervals or after major blood loss
w: It is replaced with sterile water irrigation
It is given only after closure
It is mixed into the local anesthetic
qs.x: Cefazolin is redosed for prolonged cases or significant blood loss to keep tissue levels adequate.

qs.q: When is the patient's allergy status confirmed with the whole team before incision?
qs.a: During the surgical time-out
w: After the skin is closed
During the final count
When the patient leaves PACU
qs.x: Allergies are reviewed in the time-out because they affect antibiotics, dyes and irrigation choices.

qs.q: Propofol has a milky white appearance because it is formulated as which of the following?
qs.a: A lipid emulsion containing soybean oil and egg lecithin
w: A crystalline suspension in normal saline
A protein-bound solution in albumin
A colloid dissolved in hydroxyethyl starch
qs.x: Propofol is an oil-in-water emulsion. Its lipid base explains the white color and the strict handling rules.

qs.q: Why does propofol labeling require strict aseptic technique and prompt discard of opened vials and syringes?
qs.a: Its lipid emulsion supports bacterial growth
w: It breaks down into a toxic compound in light
It loses all potency within minutes of opening
It crystallizes when exposed to room air
qs.x: Contaminated propofol has caused outbreaks of sepsis. Labeling limits how long a drawn syringe or spiked vial may be used.

qs.q: Which induction agent is chosen for its hemodynamic stability but can briefly suppress adrenal cortisol production?
qs.a: Etomidate
w: Propofol
Ketamine
Methohexital
qs.x: Etomidate inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase in the adrenal cortex. It causes little change in blood pressure or heart rate.

qs.q: Which feature best distinguishes ketamine from other IV induction agents?
qs.a: It keeps spontaneous breathing and airway reflexes largely intact
w: It reliably lowers heart rate and blood pressure
It never causes dreams or emergence reactions
It markedly dries oral and airway secretions
qs.x: Ketamine is a dissociative NMDA antagonist. It tends to raise heart rate and BP and increases secretions.

qs.q: A hypotensive trauma patient with a history of severe asthma needs induction. Which agent's properties fit best?
qs.a: Ketamine, because it bronchodilates and supports blood pressure
w: Propofol, because it bronchodilates and raises blood pressure
Methohexital, because it relaxes airway smooth muscle best
Midazolam, because it supports blood pressure and the airway
qs.x: Ketamine's sympathomimetic effect supports blood pressure, and it relaxes bronchial smooth muscle.

qs.q: Why is methohexital commonly used for anesthesia during electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)?
qs.a: It does not strongly raise the seizure threshold, so the therapeutic seizure is preserved
w: It is a benzodiazepine that reliably prevents all seizure activity
It provides strong analgesia through NMDA receptor blockade
It can be fully reversed with flumazenil after the treatment
qs.x: Methohexital is a short-acting barbiturate with less anticonvulsant effect than many agents. It can cause myoclonus and hiccups.

qs.q: Which volatile anesthetic is preferred for inhalational (mask) induction, especially in children?
qs.a: Sevoflurane, because it is nonpungent and well tolerated
w: Desflurane, because it has the fastest onset of all
Isoflurane, because it is the least irritating agent
Halothane, because it is the current US standard
qs.x: Sevoflurane does not irritate the airway. Desflurane and isoflurane are pungent and can cause coughing and laryngospasm.

qs.q: Why does desflurane require a special heated, pressurized vaporizer?
qs.a: Its boiling point is close to room temperature
w: It is rapidly broken down by light
It is too viscous to vaporize normally
It corrodes standard vaporizer metals
qs.x: Desflurane's high vapor pressure would give unpredictable output in a standard variable-bypass vaporizer, so it is heated and pressurized.

qs.q: A provider uses desflurane to speed wake-up after a long case. Which property explains its rapid emergence?
qs.a: Low solubility in blood
w: High potency (low MAC)
Extensive liver metabolism
High solubility in fat
qs.x: Less soluble agents equilibrate and wash out quickly. Desflurane has the lowest blood-gas solubility of the modern volatiles.

qs.q: Which inhaled anesthetic is the most potent, meaning it has the lowest minimum alveolar concentration (MAC)?
qs.a: Isoflurane
w: Sevoflurane
Desflurane
Nitrous oxide
qs.x: MAC is the alveolar concentration that prevents movement to incision in half of patients. Potency order is isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane, then nitrous oxide.

qs.q: Why is nitrous oxide usually avoided in patients with a pneumothorax or bowel obstruction?
qs.a: It enters closed air spaces faster than nitrogen leaves, expanding them
w: It is a potent trigger of malignant hyperthermia
It causes severe bronchospasm in damaged lungs
It stimulates bowel motility and raises gut pressure
qs.x: Nitrous oxide is far more soluble in blood than nitrogen. Air-filled cavities such as the middle ear and eye gas bubbles are also affected.

qs.q: Why does the pressure gauge on a nitrous oxide E-cylinder poorly reflect how much remains?
qs.a: It is stored as a liquid, so pressure stays steady until the liquid is nearly gone
w: The gauge reads only the oxygen mixed into the cylinder
The cylinder is filled with helium to keep pressure constant
Its pressure rises steadily as the cylinder is emptied
qs.x: Liquid nitrous oxide keeps the gas above it at constant pressure. Weighing the cylinder is the reliable way to estimate contents.

qs.q: What causes diffusion hypoxia at the end of an anesthetic that used nitrous oxide?
qs.a: Nitrous oxide leaving the blood floods the alveoli and dilutes oxygen
w: Residual opioids depress the brain's response to carbon dioxide
Carbon monoxide from dry absorbent binds hemoglobin
Leftover blockers weaken the diaphragm at extubation
qs.x: Large volumes of nitrous oxide move from blood into the lungs once it is turned off. High-flow oxygen for several minutes prevents it.

qs.q: Which statement about remifentanil is correct?
qs.a: Blood and tissue esterases break it down, so effects fade within minutes after infusion ends
w: The liver clears it slowly, so effects last hours after infusion ends
The kidneys clear it, so effects are prolonged in renal failure
It accumulates in fat, so long infusions cause delayed waking
qs.x: Remifentanil's context-sensitive half-time stays short regardless of infusion length. A plan for postoperative pain is needed.

qs.q: After a remifentanil infusion ends, why is clearing the IV line important?
qs.a: Drug left in the line can later be flushed in, causing apnea or rigidity
w: The drug crystallizes in tubing and blocks the IV catheter
Remifentanil reacts with saline to form a toxic product
Residual drug in tubing loses potency and contaminates fluid
qs.x: Even a small inadvertent bolus of remifentanil can cause sudden apnea and chest wall rigidity in the PACU.

qs.q: A rapid, large IV bolus of fentanyl can cause which effect that makes mask ventilation difficult?
qs.a: Chest wall and glottic rigidity
w: Severe histamine-related bronchospasm
Sudden rise in seizure activity
Profound malignant hyperthermia
qs.x: Opioid-induced muscle rigidity (wooden chest) is treated by the provider, often with a neuromuscular blocker.

qs.q: Brief, visible muscle twitching right after succinylcholine is given is caused by what?
qs.a: Depolarization of the motor end plate before paralysis
w: Histamine release from mast cells in the skin
An early sign of local anesthetic toxicity
Anticholinergic stimulation of skeletal muscle
qs.x: Succinylcholine acts like acetylcholine at the nicotinic receptor, producing fasciculations and then a depolarizing block.

qs.q: A patient remains paralyzed for hours after a single intubating dose of succinylcholine. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Reduced or atypical plasma cholinesterase activity
w: Unrecognized malignant hyperthermia susceptibility
Rapid liver metabolism to an active metabolite
Accidental sugammadex given before the case
qs.x: Succinylcholine is broken down by plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase. Inherited or acquired deficiency prolongs the block; supportive ventilation and sedation follow.

qs.q: Which patient is at greatest risk of life-threatening hyperkalemia from succinylcholine?
qs.a: An adult with extensive burns sustained several days ago
w: A healthy adult having an outpatient appendectomy
An adult with well-controlled essential hypertension
A teenager with mild, intermittent asthma
qs.x: Burns, crush injury, denervation and prolonged immobility upregulate receptors, so potassium release surges after the first day or two.

qs.q: What does the boxed warning for succinylcholine describe?
qs.a: Hyperkalemic cardiac arrest in children with undiagnosed muscle disease
w: Delayed liver failure after repeated use in adults
Severe hypoglycemia in children younger than two
Permanent hearing loss after rapid IV injection
qs.x: Children with undiagnosed myopathies such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy can develop rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalemic arrest.

qs.q: How is succinylcholine normally stored on anesthesia workstations?
qs.a: Refrigerated, with a limited beyond-use period once kept at room temperature
