w: Frozen, then thawed in warm water before use
At room temperature, protected only from light
In a warming cabinet to prevent crystallization
qs.x: Labeling allows a limited time at room temperature. Carts should show the date it left the refrigerator.

qs.q: When succinylcholine is contraindicated, which nondepolarizing blocker is usually chosen for rapid sequence intubation?
qs.a: Rocuronium
w: Pancuronium
Vecuronium
Atracurium
qs.x: Rocuronium has the fastest onset of the nondepolarizers at intubating doses, and sugammadex can reverse it.

qs.q: Which neuromuscular blocker is supplied as a powder that must be reconstituted before use?
qs.a: Vecuronium
w: Rocuronium
Succinylcholine
Cisatracurium
qs.x: Vecuronium is a lyophilized powder; the tech should know it takes extra preparation time in an emergency.

qs.q: Why is cisatracurium often selected for patients with kidney and liver failure?
qs.a: It undergoes Hofmann elimination, which does not depend on organ function
w: It is cleared entirely unchanged by the kidneys
It is fully reversed by sugammadex in seconds
It is metabolized only by plasma cholinesterase
qs.x: Hofmann elimination is a spontaneous breakdown that depends on temperature and pH. Cisatracurium also releases little histamine.

qs.q: A patient given pancuronium develops a fast heart rate. Which property explains this?
qs.a: Vagolytic (anticholinergic) effect at the heart
w: Direct beta-1 agonist activity
Marked histamine release
Stimulation of catecholamine reuptake
qs.x: Pancuronium is a long-acting aminosteroid with vagolytic effects. It is cleared largely by the kidneys.

qs.q: How does sugammadex reverse rocuronium?
qs.a: It encapsulates rocuronium in plasma, drawing it away from the neuromuscular junction
w: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase so more acetylcholine reaches receptors
It blocks muscarinic receptors to prevent bradycardia
It speeds up liver metabolism of rocuronium
qs.x: Sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin. It works even in deep block and needs no paired anticholinergic.

qs.q: Sugammadex would be expected to reverse a block produced by which agent?
qs.a: Vecuronium
w: Cisatracurium
Atracurium
Succinylcholine
qs.x: Sugammadex binds aminosteroid blockers, mainly rocuronium and vecuronium. It has no effect on benzylisoquinolines or succinylcholine.

qs.q: What should patients taking hormonal contraceptives be told after receiving sugammadex?
qs.a: Contraceptive effect may be reduced, so a backup method is advised for 7 days
w: Their contraceptive will become stronger for the next month
Sugammadex has no known effect on hormonal contraception
Their contraceptive effect will be reduced for one day only
qs.x: Sugammadex can bind progestogen, lowering exposure similar to a missed pill. Labeling advises backup contraception for 7 days.

qs.q: Why is glycopyrrolate given along with neostigmine for reversal?
qs.a: To block muscarinic effects such as bradycardia and secretions
w: To speed the onset of neostigmine at the muscle
To encapsulate residual rocuronium in plasma
To provide sedation during emergence
qs.x: Neostigmine raises acetylcholine at both nicotinic and muscarinic sites. Glycopyrrolate's onset roughly matches neostigmine's.

qs.q: The train-of-four shows zero twitches near the end of surgery. Why is neostigmine unlikely to work at this point?
qs.a: It can only enhance recovery that has already begun and has a ceiling effect
w: It is inactivated by the volatile anesthetic still in use
It reverses only depolarizing blockers like succinylcholine
It takes several hours to reach peak effect
qs.x: Once acetylcholinesterase is fully inhibited, more neostigmine adds nothing. Some twitches should be present before it is used.

qs.q: Which train-of-four ratio is generally considered adequate neuromuscular recovery before extubation?
qs.a: 0.9 or greater, measured quantitatively
w: 0.5 or greater, judged by eye
0.7 or greater, judged by touch
0.25 or greater, judged by eye
qs.x: Visual and tactile assessment cannot reliably detect fade above about 0.4, so quantitative monitors are preferred.

qs.q: What does train-of-four monitoring typically show during a phase I succinylcholine block?
qs.a: All four twitches reduced equally, without fade
w: Progressive fade from the first to the fourth twitch
Strong post-tetanic potentiation of twitches
Four normal twitches with absent tetanus
qs.x: Fade is the hallmark of nondepolarizing (and phase II) block. Phase I depolarizing block reduces twitches evenly.

qs.q: Where are nerve stimulator electrodes most commonly placed for train-of-four monitoring?
qs.a: Over the ulnar nerve at the wrist, watching thumb adduction
w: Over the median nerve, watching wrist flexion
Over the femoral nerve, watching knee extension
Over the radial nerve, watching finger extension
qs.x: The adductor pollicis is the standard site. Facial sites recover sooner and may overestimate recovery.

qs.q: Which group of drugs can trigger malignant hyperthermia?
qs.a: Volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine
w: Propofol and nondepolarizing blockers
Opioids and benzodiazepines
Nitrous oxide and local anesthetics
qs.x: Sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane and succinylcholine are triggers. The other listed agents are considered safe.

qs.q: Which inhaled agent is considered safe for a patient who is susceptible to malignant hyperthermia?
qs.a: Nitrous oxide
w: Sevoflurane
Desflurane
Isoflurane
qs.x: All potent volatile agents are triggers. Nitrous oxide, propofol, opioids and nondepolarizers are not.

qs.q: Which is often the earliest sign of malignant hyperthermia under general anesthesia?
qs.a: Unexplained rising end-tidal CO2 despite increased ventilation
w: Core temperature above normal range
Cola-colored urine in the Foley bag
Low serum potassium on the first gas
qs.x: Hypermetabolism produces CO2 quickly. Hyperthermia and myoglobinuria usually come later.

qs.q: Which statement about body temperature in malignant hyperthermia is correct?
qs.a: Temperature often rises after earlier signs such as rising EtCO2 and tachycardia
w: Fever is always the first sign and is required for diagnosis
Temperature typically falls as the crisis begins
Temperature changes are not seen in malignant hyperthermia
qs.x: Waiting for fever delays recognition. Hyperthermia can then climb very quickly.

qs.q: After succinylcholine, a child's jaw becomes rigid and the mouth cannot be opened. Why is this finding important?
qs.a: Masseter muscle rigidity can be an early warning of malignant hyperthermia
w: It confirms the block is complete and intubation is ideal
It indicates local anesthetic toxicity from the IV
It is a normal effect that needs no further attention
qs.x: Masseter spasm should be reported. The team watches closely for other MH signs and checks CK and urine myoglobin.

qs.q: How does dantrolene treat malignant hyperthermia?
qs.a: It reduces calcium release from the muscle's sarcoplasmic reticulum
w: It blocks acetylcholine receptors at the end plate
It lowers the hypothalamic temperature set point
It binds and removes volatile anesthetic from blood
qs.x: Dantrolene acts at the ryanodine receptor to stop the runaway muscle hypermetabolism.

qs.q: Which diluent is used to reconstitute dantrolene?
qs.a: Sterile water for injection without a bacteriostatic agent
w: 0.9% sodium chloride for injection
Dextrose 5% in water
Bacteriostatic water for injection
qs.x: Saline and dextrose can cause precipitation. Labeling specifies sterile water without preservatives.

qs.q: What is a practical advantage of Ryanodex compared with older dantrolene products (Dantrium, Revonto)?
qs.a: It needs far less diluent and fewer vials, so it is ready faster
w: It is given orally, so no IV access is needed
It is a premixed bag that needs no preparation
It also reverses residual neuromuscular blockade
qs.x: Older forms need many vials, each mixed with a large volume of water and shaken. Ryanodex is a concentrated suspension.

qs.q: Which drug class should not be combined with dantrolene during an MH crisis because of hyperkalemia and cardiovascular collapse?
qs.a: Calcium channel blockers such as verapamil
w: Loop diuretics such as furosemide
Short-acting insulin with dextrose
Benzodiazepines such as midazolam
qs.x: Arrhythmias in MH are treated with standard drugs other than calcium channel blockers. Insulin with dextrose is used for hyperkalemia.

qs.q: What is the purpose of activated charcoal filters on the anesthesia circuit in an MH event?
qs.a: They rapidly lower volatile anesthetic in inspired gas
w: They absorb carbon dioxide in place of soda lime
They warm and humidify inspired oxygen
They filter bacteria from the expiratory limb
qs.x: Filters on both limbs of the circuit remove residual vapor quickly, without waiting to swap the machine.

qs.q: Preparing an anesthesia machine for a known MH-susceptible patient includes which step?
qs.a: Removing or securing vaporizers, flushing per the maker, and adding charcoal filters
w: Filling every vaporizer to the top before the case
Keeping the old circuit to save setup time
Switching to a lower oxygen flow during the flush
qs.x: A fresh circuit and CO2 absorbent are also used. Follow the machine manufacturer's MH preparation guidance.

qs.q: Which cooling measures are used during a malignant hyperthermia crisis?
qs.a: Cold IV saline and ice packs to the groin, axillae and neck
w: Warm blankets to prevent shivering
Room-temperature IV fluids only
Fans alone with no other cooling
qs.x: Active cooling continues until temperature approaches normal, to avoid overshooting into hypothermia.

qs.q: Which lab pattern is expected during a malignant hyperthermia crisis?
qs.a: Mixed acidosis, high potassium, rising CK and myoglobin
w: Alkalosis, low potassium, normal CK and myoglobin
Normal blood gases, low glucose, low calcium
Isolated low sodium with a normal CK
qs.x: Muscle breakdown releases potassium, CK and myoglobin. Both respiratory and metabolic acidosis develop.

qs.q: After an MH episode is controlled, why is the patient monitored in the ICU for at least 24 hours?
qs.a: Symptoms can recur (recrudescence) after initial control
w: Dantrolene causes delayed seizures in all patients
The patient cannot breathe without a ventilator
Cooling must continue for the full day
qs.x: Recrudescence occurs in a meaningful share of cases, so monitoring and dantrolene continue under the team's direction.

qs.q: During an MH crisis, which resource provides 24-hour expert consultation by phone?
qs.a: The MHAUS MH Hotline
w: FDA MedWatch reporting line
The hospital blood bank
The local poison center only
qs.x: MHAUS (Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States) runs the hotline and the North American MH Registry.

qs.q: Which tasks typically fall to the anesthesia technologist during an MH crisis?
qs.a: Bringing the MH cart, mixing dantrolene, gathering ice and cold fluids
w: Choosing the dantrolene dose and pushing it
Deciding when to end the surgical procedure
Interpreting the arterial blood gas for the team
qs.x: Techs also help change the circuit, place charcoal filters, set up lines and run labs, then restock the cart.

qs.q: Which local anesthetic is the most cardiotoxic, with cardiac arrest that is notably hard to resuscitate?
qs.a: Bupivacaine
w: Lidocaine
Chloroprocaine
Mepivacaine
qs.x: Bupivacaine binds cardiac sodium channels tightly. Ropivacaine was developed partly to lower that risk.

qs.q: Chloroprocaine has a very short duration because it is metabolized by what?
qs.a: Plasma cholinesterase, since it is an ester
w: The liver, since it is an amide
The kidneys, unchanged in urine
Hofmann elimination in plasma
qs.x: Ester local anesthetics are rapidly hydrolyzed in plasma. Amides have two i's in their names and rely on the liver.

qs.q: A patient receiving a nerve block reports a metallic taste, ringing in the ears and numbness around the mouth. What do these suggest?
qs.a: Early local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)
w: An expected sign that the block is working
A vasovagal reaction to needle placement
An allergic reaction to the skin prep
qs.x: CNS symptoms often come first and can progress to seizures and cardiac collapse. Report them right away.

qs.q: Which specific treatment for LAST should be in the LAST kit wherever nerve blocks are performed?
qs.a: Lipid emulsion 20%
w: Sodium bicarbonate
Dantrolene
Hyaluronidase
qs.x: Lipid emulsion is thought to draw local anesthetic away from heart and brain and supports cardiac function.

qs.q: How does ASRA guidance modify ACLS for cardiac arrest from LAST?
qs.a: Smaller epinephrine doses; avoid vasopressin, beta blockers and local anesthetics
w: Higher epinephrine doses and early amiodarone with lidocaine
Vasopressin first, then calcium channel blockers
Standard ACLS with lidocaine for every rhythm
qs.x: Lipid emulsion is given alongside high-quality CPR. Recovery may take a long time, so resuscitation is prolonged.

qs.q: Why is epinephrine sometimes added to a local anesthetic for a nerve block?
qs.a: To prolong the block and signal intravascular injection by raising heart rate
w: To lower blood pressure during the block
To reverse sedation after the block
To speed liver metabolism of the anesthetic
qs.x: Vasoconstriction slows absorption. A sudden rise in heart rate during injection suggests the needle is in a vessel.

qs.q: Why does liposomal bupivacaine (Exparel) labeling warn about giving lidocaine at the same site around the same time?
qs.a: Lidocaine can cause immediate release of bupivacaine from the liposomes
w: Lidocaine permanently inactivates the liposomal bupivacaine
Lidocaine and bupivacaine form a solid precipitate
Lidocaine shortens the block to only a few minutes
qs.x: Labeling advises waiting at least 20 minutes after lidocaine before liposomal bupivacaine is given locally.

qs.q: A patient becomes cyanotic with low pulse oximetry readings after a dental block with prilocaine. What complication should be suspected?
qs.a: Methemoglobinemia
w: Malignant hyperthermia
Anaphylaxis to latex
Air embolism
qs.x: Prilocaine and benzocaine can oxidize hemoglobin. Methylene blue is the usual treatment.

qs.q: An anesthetized patient has low blood pressure with a heart rate of 110. Which vasopressor fits this picture best?
qs.a: Phenylephrine, a pure alpha-1 agonist that may slow the heart rate
w: Ephedrine, which raises both heart rate and blood pressure
Atropine, which mainly increases heart rate
Epinephrine, which strongly increases heart rate
qs.x: Phenylephrine constricts vessels and can cause reflex bradycardia, which is helpful when the heart rate is high.

qs.q: Which vasopressor is typically chosen for hypotension with a slow heart rate, and shows tachyphylaxis with repeat doses?
qs.a: Ephedrine
w: Phenylephrine
Vasopressin
Esmolol
qs.x: Ephedrine works directly and by releasing norepinephrine, so repeated doses become less effective.

qs.q: How does atropine differ from glycopyrrolate?
qs.a: Atropine crosses into the brain and can cause confusion; glycopyrrolate does not
w: Atropine slows the heart; glycopyrrolate speeds it up
Atropine is a cholinesterase inhibitor; glycopyrrolate is not
Atropine has no effect on secretions; glycopyrrolate does
qs.x: Both are anticholinergics. Atropine is a tertiary amine; glycopyrrolate is quaternary and stays outside the CNS.

qs.q: Epinephrine is stocked in more than one concentration. Which cart practice best prevents mix-ups?
qs.a: Store each concentration in its own labeled spot and verify the label before handing it off
w: Store all concentrations together so they are easy to find
Remove the labels so the vials are not confused
Mix concentrations in one bin sorted by expiration date
qs.x: Concentration errors with epinephrine are a known cause of serious harm. Separation and label checks are key safeguards.

qs.q: On ASTM color-coded anesthesia syringe labels, which color identifies neuromuscular blockers?
qs.a: Fluorescent red
w: Blue
Yellow
Violet
qs.x: Induction agents are yellow, opioids blue, vasopressors violet, local anesthetics gray and anticholinergics green.

qs.q: A technologist moves refrigerated rocuronium into a room-temperature cart drawer. What should be done?
qs.a: Label it with the date removed and the new beyond-use date
w: Nothing, since refrigeration has no effect on its shelf life
Return it to the refrigerator every night after cases
Discard it at once because it cannot be kept at room temperature
qs.x: Refrigerated blockers have a shorter shelf life at room temperature, so dating is required.

qs.q: When restocking the cart, where should newly delivered drugs with later expiration dates be placed?
qs.a: Behind existing stock so the earliest-expiring items are used first
w: In front of existing stock so they are used first
In a separate bin away from the drug's usual slot
Mixed randomly with older stock in the same bin
qs.x: First-expiring, first-out rotation keeps expired drugs off the cart.

qs.q: What is the purpose of a numbered breakaway seal on an emergency or MH cart?
qs.a: To show whether the cart has been opened since its last check
w: To keep controlled substances counted automatically
To prevent anyone from opening it during a code
To track the cart's location in the department
qs.x: The seal number is recorded on the check log. A broken or changed seal means the cart needs a full check and restock.

qs.q: According to Joint Commission standards, which syringes on the anesthesia workstation must be labeled?
qs.a: Any syringe of medication not given right after it is drawn up
w: Only syringes containing controlled substances
Only syringes prepared by a pharmacist
Only syringes holding more than one drug
qs.x: Labels include the drug name, strength and expiration. Unlabeled syringes are a common cause of wrong-drug errors.

qs.q: Why is epinephrine added to dental local anesthetic cartridges?
qs.a: To slow systemic absorption and lengthen duration
w: To speed the onset of the nerve block
To buffer the acidic anesthetic solution
To prevent allergic reactions to the anesthetic
qs.x: Vasoconstriction keeps anesthetic at the site longer, prolonging the block, lowering blood levels and toxicity risk, and improving hemostasis.

qs.q: Which amide local anesthetic is partly metabolized in plasma because it contains an ester side chain?
qs.a: Articaine
w: Lidocaine
Bupivacaine
Mepivacaine
qs.x: Articaine's ester group is hydrolyzed by plasma esterases, giving it a short half-life even though it is classed as an amide.

qs.q: Prilocaine's metabolite o-toluidine can cause which adverse effect?
qs.a: Methemoglobinemia
w: Malignant hyperthermia
Serotonin syndrome
Hemolytic uremic syndrome
qs.x: o-Toluidine oxidizes hemoglobin to methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen.

qs.q: A child develops gray-blue skin after heavy use of a topical anesthetic gel; pulse oximetry stays low despite oxygen. Which agent is most likely?
qs.a: Benzocaine
w: Lidocaine
Tetracaine
Bupivacaine
qs.x: Benzocaine is a well-known cause of methemoglobinemia; FDA warns against its use for teething in children under 2.

qs.q: Which finding is most characteristic of methemoglobinemia?
qs.a: Cyanosis that does not improve with supplemental oxygen
w: Bright red flushing of the face and neck
Pinpoint pupils with slow respirations
Hives and wheezing soon after injection
qs.x: Methemoglobin cannot carry oxygen, so cyanosis persists and blood may look chocolate-brown. Methylene blue is the treatment.

qs.q: A patient taking propranolol receives epinephrine-containing anesthetic. What reaction is the clinician watching for?
qs.a: Hypertension with reflex bradycardia
w: Hypotension with reflex tachycardia
Prolonged bleeding at the injection site
Hypoglycemia with sweating and tremor
qs.x: Nonselective beta blockade leaves epinephrine's alpha effects unopposed, raising BP; the baroreceptor reflex slows the heart.

qs.q: Compared with propranolol, why is metoprolol less likely to interact with dental epinephrine?
qs.a: It is cardioselective, leaving beta-2 vasodilation intact
w: It is a calcium channel blocker, not a beta blocker
It speeds the hepatic breakdown of epinephrine
It blocks alpha receptors as well as beta receptors
qs.x: Metoprolol mainly blocks beta-1 receptors, so beta-2 mediated vasodilation still offsets epinephrine's alpha effect.

qs.q: Why are vasoconstrictors used cautiously in patients taking amitriptyline?
qs.a: It blocks norepinephrine reuptake, exaggerating the pressor response
w: It inhibits liver metabolism of amide anesthetics
It causes methemoglobinemia with articaine
It lowers the seizure threshold only with esters
qs.x: Tricyclics enhance adrenergic effects; levonordefrin is avoided and epinephrine is limited.

qs.q: Which local anesthetic is chosen for long procedures and postoperative pain control because of its long duration?
qs.a: Bupivacaine
w: Mepivacaine
Prilocaine
Lidocaine
qs.x: Bupivacaine is a long-acting amide; patients should be warned about prolonged numbness and lip biting.

qs.q: When a vasoconstrictor should be avoided, which anesthetic works well plain because it causes only mild vasodilation?
qs.a: Mepivacaine
w: Bupivacaine
Tetracaine
Articaine
qs.x: Mepivacaine's minimal vasodilation gives useful duration without epinephrine.

qs.q: Which statement about lidocaine is correct?
qs.a: It is an amide metabolized mainly by the liver
w: It is an ester metabolized by plasma cholinesterase
It is metabolized to PABA in the plasma
It is excreted unchanged without metabolism
qs.x: Lidocaine is the prototype amide; severe liver disease slows its clearance.

qs.q: Which topical anesthetic is an ester and is metabolized by plasma pseudocholinesterase?
qs.a: Tetracaine
w: Lidocaine
Prilocaine
Articaine
qs.x: Tetracaine and benzocaine are esters; esters produce PABA, a source of allergy.

qs.q: What are typically the earliest signs of local anesthetic overdose?
qs.a: Circumoral numbness, tinnitus and slurred speech
w: Bradycardia and profound hypotension
Generalized hives and facial swelling
Unconsciousness without prior symptoms
qs.x: CNS excitation comes first (numbness, metallic taste, ringing ears, talkativeness, twitching) before seizures and depression.

qs.q: Minutes after an injection, a patient reports a pounding heart, tremor and anxiety that fade quickly. The most likely cause is:
qs.a: A transient reaction to the epinephrine
w: An allergic reaction to the amide
Methemoglobinemia from the anesthetic
Local anesthetic toxicity to the heart
qs.x: Brief tachycardia, palpitations and tremor are typical of absorbed epinephrine and resolve as it is metabolized.

qs.q: Which practice best reduces the risk of local anesthetic toxicity?
qs.a: Aspirating before and injecting slowly
w: Warming the cartridge before injection
Using a longer needle for every block
Injecting rapidly to shorten exposure
qs.x: Aspiration helps avoid intravascular injection, and slow injection limits peak blood levels.

qs.q: Which complication has been reported more often with articaine used for inferior alveolar nerve blocks?
qs.a: Prolonged paresthesia of the lip or tongue
w: Gingival overgrowth near the site
Delayed bleeding from the tissue
Permanent tooth discoloration
qs.x: Higher-concentration agents such as articaine have been linked to more paresthesia reports after mandibular blocks.

qs.q: A young adult with epilepsy has firm, enlarged interdental papillae. Which medicine is most likely responsible?
qs.a: Phenytoin
w: Levothyroxine
Metformin
Acetaminophen
qs.x: Phenytoin is the classic cause of drug-induced gingival overgrowth.

qs.q: A kidney transplant recipient has gingival enlargement. Which immunosuppressant is most associated with this?
qs.a: Cyclosporine
w: Prednisone
Fluconazole
Valacyclovir
qs.x: Cyclosporine causes gingival overgrowth, which can be worse when combined with a calcium channel blocker.

qs.q: Which antihypertensive class is linked to gingival overgrowth, with nifedipine the most cited example?
qs.a: Calcium channel blockers
w: ACE inhibitors
Thiazide diuretics
Beta blockers
qs.x: Nifedipine, amlodipine, diltiazem and verapamil can all cause gingival enlargement.

qs.q: Which factor most reduces the severity of drug-induced gingival overgrowth?
qs.a: Meticulous plaque control
w: Switching to a whitening toothpaste
Avoiding all fluoride products
Using an alcohol-based rinse
qs.x: Plaque-induced inflammation worsens overgrowth; frequent recall and good home care help.

qs.q: A patient taking oxybutynin for overactive bladder is most at risk for which oral problem?
qs.a: Xerostomia with increased caries risk
w: Gingival overgrowth
Intrinsic tooth staining
Osteonecrosis of the jaw
qs.x: Anticholinergic drugs reduce saliva, raising the risk of root and cervical caries and candidiasis.

qs.q: Why does diphenhydramine commonly cause dry mouth?
qs.a: It has anticholinergic effects
w: It is a muscarinic agonist
It blocks calcium channels
It inhibits prostaglandins
qs.x: First-generation antihistamines block muscarinic receptors in salivary glands.

qs.q: Pilocarpine relieves dry mouth by which mechanism?
qs.a: Stimulating muscarinic receptors in salivary glands
w: Blocking histamine receptors in the mucosa
Replacing saliva with a lubricating gel
Reducing inflammation in salivary ducts
qs.x: Pilocarpine and cevimeline are cholinergic agonists; sweating and flushing are common effects.

qs.q: Cevimeline is used cautiously in patients with which condition?
qs.a: Uncontrolled asthma
w: Hypothyroidism
Osteoporosis
Type 2 diabetes
qs.x: As a muscarinic agonist it can increase bronchial secretions and constriction; narrow-angle glaucoma is another caution.

qs.q: Which preventive measure is most important for a patient with medication-induced xerostomia?
qs.a: Daily fluoride use and frequent recall
w: Sugar-free gum avoidance
Daily alcohol-based rinses
Fewer professional cleanings
qs.x: Loss of saliva removes buffering and remineralization; fluoride, xylitol and saliva substitutes help.

qs.q: A patient taking alendronate for osteoporosis needs an extraction. Which complication is the concern?
qs.a: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw
w: Drug-induced gingival overgrowth
Methemoglobinemia from anesthetic
Black hairy tongue
qs.x: Bisphosphonates reduce bone turnover; extractions are the most common trigger for MRONJ, though risk is low with oral osteoporosis therapy.

qs.q: Which patient has the highest MRONJ risk?
qs.a: A cancer patient receiving IV zoledronic acid
w: An adult taking oral alendronate briefly
A patient taking calcium and vitamin D
A patient taking inhaled corticosteroids
qs.x: IV antiresorptive therapy for bone metastases or myeloma carries far higher risk than oral osteoporosis therapy.

qs.q: How does denosumab differ from bisphosphonates?
qs.a: It inhibits RANKL and does not bind to bone
w: It binds bone mineral for many years
It is a calcium channel blocker
It causes gingival overgrowth
qs.x: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL; its effect on bone fades over months after the last injection.

qs.q: MRONJ is defined in part by exposed bone in the maxillofacial region lasting longer than:
qs.a: 8 weeks
w: 3 days
2 weeks
1 year
qs.x: The definition also requires current or past antiresorptive or antiangiogenic therapy and no history of jaw radiation.

qs.q: An asthmatic using an inhaled corticosteroid has white plaques that wipe off. Which advice helps prevent recurrence?
qs.a: Rinse the mouth and spit after each inhaler use
w: Swallow water before each inhaler use
Use the inhaler only at bedtime
Brush the tongue with baking soda once weekly
qs.x: Pseudomembranous candidiasis is common with inhaled steroids; rinsing and a spacer reduce oral deposition.

qs.q: Which agent is a topical antifungal used for oral candidiasis?
qs.a: Nystatin
w: Acyclovir
Metronidazole
Doxycycline
qs.x: Nystatin suspension or clotrimazole troches treat oral candidiasis topically; fluconazole is systemic.

qs.q: Intrinsic gray-brown banding of the permanent teeth suggests exposure to which drug during tooth development?
qs.a: Tetracycline
w: Amoxicillin
Penicillin VK
Cephalexin
qs.x: Tetracyclines bind calcium in developing teeth, so they are avoided in pregnancy and young children.

qs.q: Which lab test is used to monitor warfarin?
qs.a: INR
w: aPTT
Platelet count only
Hemoglobin A1c
qs.x: The INR standardizes the prothrombin time; a common therapeutic range is 2-3.

qs.q: Warfarin works by which mechanism?
qs.a: Antagonizing vitamin K-dependent clotting factor production
w: Directly inhibiting factor Xa
Irreversibly blocking platelet COX-1
Directly inhibiting thrombin
qs.x: Warfarin reduces synthesis of factors II, VII, IX and X.

qs.q: For a patient on warfarin scheduled for scaling and root planing, what should the clinician confirm?
qs.a: A recent INR, ideally within 24 hours
w: A fasting blood glucose level
A recent hemoglobin A1c value
A recent thyroid function panel
qs.x: A current INR in the therapeutic range lets most dental care proceed with local hemostasis.

qs.q: Why is INR not used to assess bleeding risk in patients taking apixaban?
qs.a: It inhibits factor Xa and INR does not reliably reflect its effect
w: It is an antiplatelet drug measured by bleeding time
It is monitored with hemoglobin A1c
It has no effect on clotting
qs.x: DOACs need no routine monitoring; the timing of the last dose matters more.

qs.q: Rivaroxaban belongs to which drug class?
qs.a: Direct factor Xa inhibitor
w: Vitamin K antagonist
P2Y12 inhibitor
Low molecular weight heparin
qs.x: Rivaroxaban and apixaban are oral factor Xa inhibitors.

qs.q: Dabigatran works by:
qs.a: Directly inhibiting thrombin
w: Antagonizing vitamin K
Blocking platelet P2Y12
Inhibiting factor Xa
qs.x: Dabigatran is an oral direct thrombin inhibitor cleared largely by the kidneys.

qs.q: Why does a single exposure to aspirin affect platelets for about a week?
qs.a: It irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1
w: It permanently depletes vitamin K
It destroys circulating clotting factors
It reversibly binds to thrombin
qs.x: Platelets cannot make new COX-1, so the effect lasts their lifespan of about 7-10 days.

qs.q: A patient on aspirin and clopidogrel after a recent coronary stent needs periodontal therapy. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Proceed with local hemostasis and consult the cardiologist with any concerns
w: Tell the patient to skip clopidogrel for a week
Postpone all dental care for one year
Prescribe vitamin K before treatment
qs.x: Interrupting dual antiplatelet therapy risks stent thrombosis; bleeding is usually managed locally.

qs.q: Which antibiotic is most likely to raise the INR in a patient taking warfarin?
qs.a: Metronidazole
w: Amoxicillin
Penicillin VK
Cephalexin
qs.x: Metronidazole inhibits warfarin metabolism (CYP2C9); fluconazole has a similar effect.

qs.q: A warfarin patient is prescribed fluconazole for oral candidiasis. What is the concern?
qs.a: Increased INR and bleeding risk
w: Reduced antifungal effect
Gingival overgrowth
Xerostomia and root caries
qs.x: Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9 and can markedly increase warfarin's effect; the prescriber should be informed.

qs.q: Which analgesic is usually preferred for a patient taking warfarin?
qs.a: Acetaminophen
w: Ibuprofen
Naproxen
Aspirin
qs.x: NSAIDs add antiplatelet effects and GI bleeding risk; acetaminophen is generally preferred.

qs.q: Why is ibuprofen a concern for a patient taking apixaban?
qs.a: It adds antiplatelet and GI bleeding risk
w: It speeds apixaban clearance
It causes methemoglobinemia
It raises blood glucose
qs.x: Combining NSAIDs with anticoagulants increases bleeding risk.

qs.q: Unfractionated heparin is monitored with which test?
qs.a: aPTT
w: INR
Hemoglobin A1c
Serum creatinine
qs.x: Heparin enhances antithrombin; the aPTT reflects its effect.

qs.q: Which is a local hemostatic measure after an extraction in an anticoagulated patient?
qs.a: Oxidized cellulose placed in the socket
w: Vigorous rinsing right after surgery
Drinking through a straw
Applying heat to the cheek
qs.x: Pressure, sutures, gelatin sponge, oxidized cellulose and tranexamic acid rinses help control bleeding.

qs.q: What is the most important first step in assessing bleeding risk before treatment?
qs.a: Reviewing the full medication list, including supplements
w: Checking the patient's blood type
Measuring blood pressure only
Asking about dietary fat intake
qs.x: Anticoagulants, antiplatelets, NSAIDs and supplements such as ginkgo or fish oil can all affect bleeding.

qs.q: According to the AHA, which patient should receive antibiotic prophylaxis before scaling?
qs.a: A patient with a prosthetic heart valve
w: A patient with mitral valve prolapse
A patient with a coronary artery stent
A patient with a pacemaker
qs.x: Prophylaxis is reserved for highest-risk conditions: prosthetic valves, prior endocarditis, certain CHD and transplant valvulopathy.

qs.q: Which history alone qualifies a patient for endocarditis prophylaxis?
qs.a: Previous infective endocarditis
w: Coronary artery bypass surgery
Controlled hypertension
Functional heart murmur
qs.x: Prior infective endocarditis places a patient in the highest-risk group.

qs.q: Which antibiotic is first-line for AHA endocarditis prophylaxis in a patient who can take oral medicine?
qs.a: Amoxicillin
w: Clindamycin
Metronidazole
Doxycycline
qs.x: Amoxicillin is first-line, given as a single dose 30-60 minutes before the procedure.

qs.q: A patient with a mild rash to penicillin (no anaphylaxis) needs prophylaxis. Which is an appropriate alternative?
qs.a: Cephalexin
w: Ampicillin
Amoxicillin
Metronidazole
qs.x: Cephalexin is acceptable if there is no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria with penicillins.

qs.q: A patient with penicillin anaphylaxis needs prophylaxis. Which oral option fits current AHA guidance?
qs.a: Azithromycin
w: Cephalexin
Clindamycin
Amoxicillin
qs.x: Azithromycin, clarithromycin or doxycycline are options; cephalosporins are avoided after anaphylaxis.

qs.q: What did the 2021 AHA update change about clindamycin for dental prophylaxis?
qs.a: It is no longer recommended
w: It became the first-line choice
It is now required with amoxicillin
It replaced azithromycin for allergy
qs.x: Clindamycin was removed because of higher C. difficile risk and adverse effects.

qs.q: If prophylaxis was not taken before the appointment, when may it still be given?
qs.a: Up to 2 hours after the procedure
w: Only the day before the visit
Up to 1 week after the visit
Only with the next appointment
qs.x: The dose is ideally 30-60 minutes before but may be given up to 2 hours after.

qs.q: Which dental procedure does NOT require prophylaxis in a high-risk cardiac patient?
qs.a: Dental radiographs
w: Periodontal probing
Scaling and root planing
Tooth extraction
qs.x: Radiographs, anesthetic injections through noninfected tissue and adjusting appliances do not need prophylaxis.

qs.q: Under ADA guidance, what is the usual recommendation for patients with prosthetic joints before dental care?
qs.a: Prophylaxis is generally not recommended
w: Prophylaxis is always required
Prophylaxis only for radiographs
Prophylaxis only after a cleaning
qs.x: The ADA does not generally recommend prophylaxis for joint replacement; decisions may be individualized with the surgeon.

qs.q: A patient prescribed metronidazole for necrotizing periodontal disease should be warned about which interaction?
qs.a: A disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol
w: Tooth staining with dairy products
Photosensitivity with dairy foods
Gingival overgrowth with citrus
qs.x: Flushing, nausea and vomiting can occur with alcohol during and shortly after therapy.

qs.q: Per ADA guidance, antibiotics are NOT indicated for which condition?
qs.a: Irreversible pulpitis without systemic signs
w: Spreading facial cellulitis with fever
Abscess with trismus and fever
Infection with swollen lymph nodes
qs.x: Localized pulpal and periapical conditions are treated with definitive dental care; antibiotics are for systemic involvement.

qs.q: How does subantimicrobial-dose doxycycline help in periodontitis?
qs.a: It inhibits collagenase that breaks down connective tissue
w: It kills all periodontal pathogens directly
It stimulates salivary flow
It forms fluorapatite on root surfaces
qs.x: At subantimicrobial levels doxycycline acts as a host modulator, reducing tissue destruction.

qs.q: What is the most common side effect of chlorhexidine rinse?
qs.a: Extrinsic brown staining of teeth
w: Gingival overgrowth
Intrinsic tooth staining
Xerostomia with root caries
qs.x: Chlorhexidine also alters taste and increases calculus; the stain is removable by polishing.

qs.q: Why is chlorhexidine rinse used separately from toothpaste?
qs.a: Sodium lauryl sulfate in toothpaste inactivates it
w: Toothpaste fluoride makes it toxic
It dissolves the toothpaste abrasive
It turns toothpaste into a gel
qs.x: Chlorhexidine is cationic and binds anionic detergents; spacing use about 30 minutes apart preserves activity.

qs.q: Why is acidulated phosphate fluoride avoided on patients with porcelain or composite restorations?
qs.a: It can etch the restoration surface
w: It stains composite resin yellow
It causes gingival overgrowth
It interferes with local anesthetic
qs.x: The low pH of APF can roughen porcelain and composite; neutral sodium fluoride is used instead.

qs.q: Which is the main way topical fluoride reduces caries?
qs.a: Promoting remineralization and forming fluorapatite
w: Killing all oral bacteria on contact
Increasing salivary flow
Blocking sugar absorption from food
qs.x: Fluoride enhances remineralization, makes enamel more acid-resistant and inhibits bacterial enzymes.

qs.q: A patient taking warfarin has blood drawn to check how well the medicine is working. Which test is ordered?
qs.a: PT/INR
w: aPTT
Anti-Xa
Platelet count
qs.x: Warfarin lowers vitamin K-dependent clotting factors and is followed with PT reported as INR.

qs.q: A patient on a continuous IV heparin infusion is most commonly monitored with which test?
qs.a: aPTT or anti-Xa
w: PT/INR
Bleeding time
Fibrinogen
qs.x: Unfractionated heparin is followed with aPTT or an anti-Xa assay, both drawn in a light blue citrate tube.

qs.q: Which tube is used for PT/INR and aPTT?
qs.a: Light blue sodium citrate
w: Lavender EDTA
Green lithium heparin
Gray sodium fluoride
qs.x: Coagulation tests need 3.2% sodium citrate, which binds calcium so clotting can be measured in the lab.

qs.q: Why must a light blue citrate tube be filled to the fill line?
qs.a: To keep the blood-to-citrate ratio at 9 to 1
w: To prevent the gel barrier from failing
So the tube can be centrifuged sooner
So the lab has enough for repeat tests
qs.x: Underfilling leaves extra citrate relative to blood, which falsely prolongs clotting times; underfilled coag tubes are rejected.

qs.q: An underfilled light blue tube is sent for aPTT. What is the likely effect?
qs.a: Falsely prolonged result
w: Falsely shortened result
No effect on the result
Falsely low platelet count
qs.x: Excess citrate binds the calcium added in the test, so clotting takes longer and the result reads falsely long.

qs.q: You draw a PT using a butterfly, and the light blue tube is the first tube. What should you do?
qs.a: Draw a discard tube first
w: Fill the light blue tube halfway
Draw the light blue tube last
Tap the tubing to remove air
qs.x: Air in the butterfly tubing would underfill the first tube, so a discard tube clears the dead space before the citrate tube.

qs.q: A patient says he takes apixaban. What should you expect after the venipuncture?
qs.a: The site may bleed longer than usual
w: The vein will be harder to find
The sample will clot in the tube
The patient will need a fasting draw
qs.x: Apixaban is an oral factor Xa inhibitor; plan for extra pressure and check the site carefully before bandaging.

qs.q: When anti-Xa monitoring is ordered for a patient on subcutaneous enoxaparin, the draw is usually timed for about when?
qs.a: About 4 hours after the dose
w: Right before the dose
About 30 minutes after the dose
At any time of day
qs.x: Peak anti-Xa activity for low-molecular-weight heparin is about 4 hours after a subcutaneous dose, so timing must be documented.

qs.q: Clopidogrel affects which part of clotting at the puncture site?
qs.a: Platelet plug formation
w: Vitamin K clotting factors
Thrombin directly
Red cell production
qs.x: Clopidogrel is a P2Y12 antiplatelet; the platelet plug forms more slowly, so the site can ooze.

qs.q: An outpatient takes daily aspirin. Which practice best prevents a hematoma?
qs.a: Firm pressure with the arm straight until bleeding stops
w: Bending the arm up over the gauze
A tight bandage right after needle removal
Rubbing the site to speed clotting
qs.x: Straight-arm pressure until the site is sealed prevents a hematoma; bending the elbow traps blood under the skin.

qs.q: A patient received alteplase for a stroke an hour ago. Why should venipunctures be kept to a minimum?
qs.a: Very high risk of bleeding at puncture sites
w: The drug makes veins collapse
Results are invalid for 24 hours
The drug causes blood to clot in tubes
qs.x: Thrombolytics dissolve clots throughout the body, so every puncture is a bleeding risk and needs prolonged pressure.

qs.q: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor. Which coag result may it prolong?
qs.a: aPTT and thrombin time
w: Platelet count
Hemoglobin
Fibrinogen only
qs.x: Dabigatran blocks thrombin, so thrombin time is very sensitive to it and aPTT is often prolonged.

qs.q: A blood sample for aPTT on a heparin patient sits at room temperature for several hours before processing. Why is that a problem?
qs.a: Platelets release a factor that neutralizes heparin
w: The citrate evaporates from the tube
Red cells absorb the heparin
The sample turns into serum
qs.x: Platelet factor 4 released over time neutralizes heparin and falsely shortens the aPTT, so these samples are processed within about 1 hour.

qs.q: After a draw on a patient taking warfarin, the site keeps oozing after extended pressure. What is the best action?
qs.a: Keep pressure on and notify the nurse
w: Apply a bandage and dismiss the patient
Have the patient hold the gauze and leave
Apply a tourniquet above the site
qs.x: Never leave a bleeding site unattended; continue pressure and report it so the nurse or provider can assess.

qs.q: Protamine is given to reverse which anticoagulant?
qs.a: Heparin
w: Warfarin
Aspirin
Apixaban
qs.x: Protamine binds and neutralizes heparin; vitamin K (phytonadione) is used for warfarin reversal.

qs.q: A patient with a very high INR receives phytonadione. Which test will be redrawn to see if it worked?
qs.a: PT/INR
w: aPTT
Anti-Xa
Platelet function test
qs.x: Vitamin K restores warfarin-affected clotting factors, which is tracked with PT/INR.

qs.q: What is a trough level?
qs.a: The lowest drug level, drawn just before the next dose
w: The highest level, drawn right after the dose
A level drawn at any random time
A level drawn after the first dose only
qs.x: Troughs are drawn just before a scheduled dose, usually within about 30 minutes of it.

qs.q: Why must the phlebotomist record the exact collection time on a drug level?
qs.a: The result is interpreted against the last dose time
w: The lab bills by collection time
Drug levels expire after one hour
It sets the order of draw
qs.x: A level means nothing without timing; the same value can be fine as a peak and toxic as a trough.

qs.q: A vancomycin trough is ordered with the next dose due at 1000. When is the trough usually drawn?
qs.a: Shortly before 1000, within about 30 minutes
w: At 1000 as the infusion starts
One hour after the infusion ends
Any time that morning
qs.x: Troughs represent the lowest level, just before the next dose begins.

qs.q: A gentamicin peak is ordered after a 30-minute infusion. When is it typically drawn?
qs.a: About 30 minutes after the infusion ends
w: Right before the infusion starts
Halfway through the infusion
Six hours after the infusion ends
qs.x: Aminoglycoside peaks are drawn after distribution, usually 30 minutes after a 30-minute infusion is complete.

qs.q: Why are tobramycin levels monitored closely?
qs.a: High levels can harm the kidneys and hearing
w: High levels cause severe bleeding
Low levels cause high blood sugar
The drug changes the order of draw
qs.x: Aminoglycosides are nephrotoxic and ototoxic, so peaks and troughs guide safe dosing.

qs.q: When is a routine digoxin level usually drawn?
qs.a: At least 6 to 8 hours after the last dose
w: Within 1 hour after the dose
Exactly at the time of the dose
Only after a meal
qs.x: Digoxin takes hours to distribute into tissue; an early draw reads falsely high.

qs.q: Which tube should NOT be used for a lithium level?
qs.a: Green lithium heparin
w: Red plain serum
Gold or tiger-top serum
Royal blue per lab policy
qs.x: Lithium heparin contains lithium and falsely raises the result.

qs.q: A lithium level is usually drawn about how long after the last dose?
qs.a: About 12 hours
w: About 30 minutes
About 2 hours
About 48 hours
qs.x: Standard lithium levels are 12-hour post-dose levels, so dose and draw times must be recorded.

qs.q: A patient with low albumin has a phenytoin level ordered. Which test may the provider also order?
qs.a: Free phenytoin level
w: Phenytoin peak only
Serum albumin in a gray tube
PT/INR
qs.x: Phenytoin is highly protein bound; with low albumin, the total level can look normal while the active free drug is high.

qs.q: A valproic acid level for routine monitoring is usually drawn when?
qs.a: As a trough before the next dose
w: One hour after a meal
At any random time
Immediately after the dose
qs.x: Routine anticonvulsant levels such as valproate are troughs, drawn before the next dose.

qs.q: Tacrolimus levels for a transplant patient are drawn in which tube?
qs.a: Lavender EDTA whole blood
w: Light blue citrate
Gray sodium fluoride
Green lithium heparin
qs.x: Tacrolimus concentrates in red cells, so it is measured in whole blood from an EDTA tube, usually as a trough.

qs.q: When is a routine cyclosporine level most often drawn?
qs.a: Trough, just before the next dose
w: At bedtime only
Peak right after the dose
Random time with a meal
qs.x: Cyclosporine is most often monitored with a trough whole-blood level.

qs.q: The vancomycin trough is drawn 2 hours late, after the dose has started. What should you do?
qs.a: Notify the nurse and document the actual time
w: Label it with the scheduled time
Discard the sample without telling anyone
Draw from the IV arm to save time
qs.x: A level drawn during the infusion is not a trough; accurate time documentation and communication prevent wrong dosing decisions.

qs.q: Why is theophylline a drug that needs level monitoring?
qs.a: It has a narrow therapeutic range
w: It turns serum cloudy
It only works when drawn fasting
It interferes with coag tubes
qs.x: Small changes in level can cause toxicity such as seizures or arrhythmias, so levels guide therapy.

qs.q: A carbamazepine level is ordered. What information must accompany the sample?
qs.a: Collection time and time of last dose
w: Patient's blood type
Tourniquet brand used
Tube lot number only
qs.x: Collection time and last dose time let the provider decide whether the level is a trough and interpret it correctly.

qs.q: Some labs ask for drug levels in a red top tube without gel. Why?
qs.a: Gel separators can absorb some drugs
w: Gel causes the sample to clot faster
Red tubes keep drugs frozen
Gel adds extra drug to serum
qs.x: Certain drugs can be absorbed into gel separators, lowering results, so follow the lab's tube requirements.

qs.q: Methotrexate levels after high-dose therapy are drawn at exact timed points. Why?
qs.a: Timing guides leucovorin rescue decisions
w: It changes the order of draw
It is always drawn with blood cultures
It only matters for outpatient draws
qs.x: Methotrexate clearance is followed at set times after the infusion; the result decides how long rescue therapy continues.

qs.q: Which drug class does amikacin belong to, making peak and trough levels common?
qs.a: Aminoglycoside antibiotics
w: Anticoagulants
Anticonvulsants
Cardiac glycosides
qs.x: Amikacin, gentamicin and tobramycin are aminoglycosides monitored for kidney and hearing toxicity.

qs.q: A patient has an IV infusing in the left arm. Which site is preferred for a routine draw?
qs.a: The right arm
w: Above the IV in the left arm
The left hand near the IV
Directly through the IV catheter
qs.x: Drawing from the arm opposite the IV avoids dilution and contamination by the infusing fluid.

qs.q: A glucose result is extremely high in a patient with no diabetes; the sample was drawn above a running IV. What fluid most likely contaminated it?
qs.a: Dextrose solution
w: Lactated Ringer's
Potassium-free saline
Sterile water flush
qs.x: Dextrose-containing IV fluid in the sample falsely raises glucose; drawing above an IV is never acceptable.

qs.q: A sample drawn above an IV running potassium chloride will most likely show what?
qs.a: Falsely high potassium
w: Falsely low potassium
Falsely high glucose
Prolonged PT/INR
qs.x: The infused potassium mixes with the sample and raises the result.

qs.q: A sample contaminated with lactated Ringer's may show which change?
qs.a: Unexpected rise in lactate
w: Very high glucose
Prolonged aPTT
Very low sodium only
qs.x: Lactated Ringer's contains lactate, potassium and calcium, and also dilutes other analytes.

qs.q: An aPTT drawn from a line that was just flushed with heparin will most likely be:
qs.a: Falsely prolonged
w: Falsely shortened
Unaffected
Hemolyzed
qs.x: Heparin contamination prolongs aPTT; line draws need a proper discard per protocol.

qs.q: Both arms have IVs. What is the acceptable approach?
qs.a: Draw below an IV site and document it
w: Draw above the IV for better flow
Draw through the IV catheter yourself
Mix samples from both arms
qs.x: Below the IV is acceptable when no other site exists; the nurse decides whether the infusion can be interrupted, and the site is documented.

qs.q: Per CLSI order of draw, which tube comes right after blood cultures?
qs.a: Light blue citrate
w: Lavender EDTA
Gray fluoride/oxalate
Green heparin
qs.x: Order: cultures, light blue, red/gold serum, green heparin, lavender EDTA, then gray.

qs.q: Drawing a lavender EDTA tube before a chemistry tube can cause which result?
qs.a: Falsely high potassium and low calcium
w: Falsely high glucose
Falsely prolonged PT
Falsely low sodium only
qs.x: K2 or K3 EDTA carryover adds potassium and chelates calcium, causing misleading results.

qs.q: Why is the green heparin tube drawn after the light blue citrate tube?
qs.a: Heparin carryover would prolong coag results
w: Heparin clots the citrate tube
Citrate falsely raises potassium
Green tubes need the most blood
qs.x: Even small amounts of heparin carried into a coag tube can falsely prolong clotting times.

qs.q: A patient takes high-dose biotin supplements. Which test is known to be falsely affected on some immunoassays?
qs.a: Troponin
w: Hemoglobin
Platelet count
Blood culture
qs.x: The FDA has warned that biotin can cause falsely low troponin on biotin-streptavidin assays, risking a missed heart attack.

qs.q: How can biotin affect thyroid immunoassays?
qs.a: Falsely low TSH and falsely high T4
w: Falsely high TSH only
No effect on thyroid tests
It clots the serum tube
qs.x: Biotin interference can mimic hyperthyroidism; report supplement use per lab policy.

qs.q: What is the phlebotomist's role when a lab requires biotin screening?
qs.a: Ask about biotin use and record it per policy
w: Advise the patient to stop biotin
Draw the sample in a gray tube
Dilute the sample with saline
qs.x: The phlebotomist gathers and documents the information; the lab and provider decide how to handle interference.

qs.q: A patient on an IV insulin drip has a glucose drawn above the IV. What result might be misleading?
qs.a: Glucose not matching the patient's true level
w: Hemoglobin falsely high
PT falsely prolonged
Potassium falsely high only
qs.x: Infused fluid dilutes and alters the sample; glucose checks must come from the opposite arm or as directed.

qs.q: A vancomycin level is drawn from the same arm the vancomycin is infusing in. What is the likely result?
qs.a: A falsely very high level
w: A falsely low level
A clotted specimen
An accurate trough
qs.x: Drug from the infusion contaminates the sample; always draw drug levels from the arm without the infusion.

qs.q: Saline contamination of a sample typically shows which pattern?
qs.a: High sodium and chloride with diluted other values
w: Very high glucose and potassium
Prolonged PT with low platelets
High calcium and low sodium
qs.x: Normal saline adds sodium and chloride and dilutes everything else, such as protein and calcium.

qs.q: A patient started on metoprolol now has a heart rate in the 40s with a normal P before every QRS. What rhythm is this most likely?
qs.a: Sinus bradycardia
w: Atrial flutter
Junctional tachycardia
Idioventricular rhythm
qs.x: Beta-blockers slow the SA node, producing sinus bradycardia with normal P-QRS relationships.

qs.q: Diltiazem is given to a patient in rapid atrial fibrillation. What change on the monitor shows the intended effect?
qs.a: Slower ventricular rate
w: Return of U waves
Narrower QRS complexes
Taller P waves
qs.x: Diltiazem slows AV node conduction, so fewer atrial impulses reach the ventricles and the ventricular rate falls.

qs.q: Which effect of verapamil explains why it can cause AV block?
qs.a: It slows conduction through the AV node
w: It speeds up the SA node
It shortens the QT interval
It blocks potassium channels in the ventricles
qs.x: Verapamil is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that slows AV nodal conduction, lengthening the PR and possibly causing block.

qs.q: A patient on atenolol shows a PR interval that is long but constant, with every P followed by a QRS. What is this?
qs.a: First-degree AV block
w: Mobitz I second-degree block
Mobitz II second-degree block
Third-degree AV block
qs.x: A prolonged but constant PR with no dropped beats is first-degree AV block, a common beta-blocker effect.

qs.q: A patient on both metoprolol and diltiazem has a new slow rhythm. Why is this combination watched closely?
qs.a: Their AV node slowing effects add together
w: Diltiazem speeds up metoprolol's removal
They cancel each other out
Metoprolol raises potassium dangerously
qs.x: Beta-blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers both slow the SA and AV nodes, so together they raise the risk of bradycardia and heart block.

qs.q: What is atropine's main use in an emergency cardiac setting?
qs.a: First-line drug for symptomatic bradycardia
w: Converting stable SVT
Treating torsades de pointes
Slowing rapid atrial fibrillation
qs.x: Atropine blocks vagal tone, increasing SA node firing and AV conduction in symptomatic bradycardia.

qs.q: After atropine, what change would the monitor tech expect to see?
qs.a: An increase in heart rate
w: A brief period of asystole
Longer PR intervals
Peaked T waves
qs.x: Atropine removes vagal slowing, so the sinus rate and AV conduction usually increase.

qs.q: For which rhythm is atropine least likely to help?
qs.a: Third-degree block with wide ventricular escape
w: Sinus bradycardia from high vagal tone
Mobitz I second-degree block
Symptomatic first-degree block
qs.x: Atropine acts on the SA and AV nodes; blocks below the AV node with wide escape rhythms often do not respond, and pacing may be needed.

qs.q: Adenosine is given for a narrow-complex tachycardia. What should the tech expect on the strip right after it is given?
qs.a: A few seconds of asystole
w: Gradual slowing over an hour
Sudden ventricular fibrillation
Widening of every QRS
qs.x: Adenosine briefly blocks the AV node; a short pause or asystole for a few seconds is expected before the rhythm resumes.

qs.q: Adenosine is mainly used to treat which rhythm?
qs.a: Stable narrow-complex reentrant SVT
w: Ventricular fibrillation
Third-degree heart block
Torsades de pointes
qs.x: Adenosine interrupts reentry circuits that use the AV node, converting many SVTs to sinus rhythm.

qs.q: Why is a continuous rhythm strip recorded while adenosine is given?
qs.a: To capture conversion or reveal an underlying rhythm
w: To measure the patient's potassium
To check for U waves
To calculate the dose
qs.x: Recording during adenosine documents conversion and can unmask flutter waves or atrial fibrillation hidden by a fast rate.

qs.q: A patient with a fast regular rhythm gets adenosine. The rate slows briefly and sawtooth waves appear. What rhythm was hidden?
qs.a: Atrial flutter
w: Sinus tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia
Junctional rhythm
qs.x: Adenosine slows AV conduction briefly, uncovering flutter waves; it does not convert atrial flutter itself.

qs.q: How long does adenosine's effect usually last?
qs.a: Seconds
w: Several hours
About a day
Several weeks
qs.x: Adenosine has a half-life of under ten seconds, so its pause is brief.

qs.q: Isoproterenol is a beta-agonist. What strip change is expected when it is running?
qs.a: A faster heart rate
w: A longer QT interval
More AV block
A slower sinus rate
qs.x: Isoproterenol stimulates beta receptors, increasing heart rate and AV conduction; it is used for some bradycardias and pause-dependent torsades.

qs.q: Esmolol is a very short-acting beta-blocker. Which strip change should be reported while it is infusing?
qs.a: New heart block or marked bradycardia
w: Mild slowing of sinus tachycardia
A slightly lower ventricular rate in A-fib
Fewer PACs
qs.x: Some slowing is the goal, but new AV block or marked bradycardia is an adverse effect to report.

qs.q: Ivabradine lowers heart rate by acting on which part of the conduction system?
qs.a: The SA node
w: The AV node
The bundle branches
The Purkinje fibers
qs.x: Ivabradine blocks the funny current in the SA node, slowing sinus rate without affecting AV conduction much.

qs.q: What does the QT interval measure?
qs.a: Start of the QRS to the end of the T wave
w: Start of the P wave to start of the QRS
End of the QRS to start of the T wave
Peak of one R wave to the next
qs.x: The QT reflects ventricular depolarization and repolarization, from QRS onset to T-wave end.

qs.q: Why is the QTc used instead of the raw QT?
qs.a: It corrects the QT for heart rate
w: It corrects for patient age
It removes the U wave
It measures only the ST segment
qs.x: QT shortens as heart rate rises, so the corrected QT allows comparison across different rates.

qs.q: At a normal heart rate, which quick visual check suggests a long QT?
qs.a: The QT is longer than half the R-R interval
w: The PR is longer than one large box
The QRS is narrower than the P wave
The T wave is upright in lead II
qs.x: If the T wave ends past the midpoint between two R waves at a normal rate, the QT is likely prolonged.

qs.q: Which rhythm is most associated with a prolonged QT?
qs.a: Torsades de pointes
w: Atrial flutter
Wandering atrial pacemaker
Sinus arrhythmia
qs.x: A long QT increases the risk of torsades de pointes, a polymorphic VT.

qs.q: On the strip, torsades de pointes looks like:
qs.a: Polymorphic VT whose QRS height twists around the baseline
w: Regular narrow complexes with sawtooth waves
Wide complexes of identical shape and height
Irregular narrow complexes with no P waves
qs.x: Torsades means 'twisting of the points': the QRS amplitude waxes and wanes around the baseline.

qs.q: Which medicine is the usual first treatment for torsades with a pulse?
qs.a: Magnesium sulfate
w: Adenosine
Diltiazem
Digoxin
qs.x: Magnesium stabilizes the cell membrane and is the common first-line treatment for torsades.

qs.q: A patient on amiodarone has a QT that has lengthened. How is this best described?
qs.a: An expected drug effect that still needs monitoring
w: A sign the drug has stopped working
A finding that rules out torsades
Evidence of high potassium
qs.x: Amiodarone prolongs the QT by design, though torsades is less common than with some other drugs; trends should still be reported.

qs.q: Why are patients usually placed on telemetry when sotalol is started?
qs.a: To monitor the QTc for prolongation
w: To watch for peaked T waves
To check for U waves from high calcium
To confirm a faster heart rate
qs.x: Sotalol is a beta-blocker with class III effects; it can prolong the QT and cause torsades, so starts are monitored.

qs.q: Besides QT prolongation, what other strip change would you expect from sotalol?
qs.a: Bradycardia
w: Sinus tachycardia
Peaked T waves
Short PR interval
qs.x: Sotalol also has beta-blocking activity, so it slows heart rate and can lengthen the PR.

qs.q: Dofetilide is started in a monitored setting for several days mainly because of which risk?
qs.a: QT prolongation and torsades
w: Severe hyperkalemia
Sinus tachycardia
Digoxin-like scooped ST segments
qs.x: Dofetilide labeling requires an inpatient start with continuous ECG monitoring and repeated QTc checks.

qs.q: Which antiemetic commonly given in hospitals can prolong the QT?
qs.a: Ondansetron
w: Diphenhydramine
Famotidine
Simethicone
qs.x: Ondansetron has a dose-related QT effect, especially with other QT drugs or low electrolytes.

qs.q: A patient receiving IV haloperidol for agitation should be watched for which strip change?
qs.a: QT prolongation
w: Peaked T waves
Shortened PR interval
Delta waves
qs.x: Haloperidol, especially given IV, can prolong the QT and has been linked to torsades.

qs.q: Which opioid is best known for prolonging the QT interval?
qs.a: Methadone
w: Morphine
Hydromorphone
Fentanyl
qs.x: Methadone blocks cardiac potassium channels and can prolong the QT; ECG monitoring is often recommended.

qs.q: A patient on amiodarone is started on azithromycin. Why might the provider want ECG follow-up?
qs.a: Both drugs can prolong the QT
w: Azithromycin raises potassium
Both drugs cause peaked T waves
Azithromycin speeds AV conduction
qs.x: Azithromycin is a macrolide that can lengthen the QT; combining it with another QT drug adds risk.

qs.q: Which antidepressant has an FDA warning about QT prolongation?
qs.a: Citalopram
w: Bupropion
Mirtazapine
Sertraline
qs.x: Citalopram carries an FDA warning for dose-dependent QT prolongation.

qs.q: Which antibiotic class, which includes levofloxacin, is linked to QT prolongation?
qs.a: Fluoroquinolones
w: Penicillins
Cephalosporins
Tetracyclines
qs.x: Fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin and moxifloxacin can prolong the QT.

qs.q: A patient on digoxin has sagging, scooped ST segments but no new arrhythmia. What is this most likely?
qs.a: Expected digoxin effect
w: Digoxin toxicity
Acute anterior MI
Severe hyperkalemia
qs.x: The scooped ST ('Salvador Dali mustache') is a common digoxin effect and does not by itself mean toxicity.

qs.q: Which strip finding in a patient on digoxin suggests toxicity rather than normal effect?
qs.a: New frequent PVCs in a bigeminy pattern
w: Scooped ST segments
Slightly shortened QT
Flattened T waves
qs.x: Ventricular ectopy such as bigeminy is one of the most common signs of digoxin toxicity.

qs.q: A patient on digoxin with A-fib suddenly has a slow, regular rhythm. Why is this concerning?
qs.a: It may be a junctional rhythm from digoxin toxicity
w: It means the A-fib has safely resolved
It shows the potassium is high
It is a normal adenosine effect
qs.x: Regularization of A-fib can mean complete heart block with a junctional escape, a digoxin toxicity sign.

qs.q: Which rhythm is classically linked to digoxin toxicity?
qs.a: Atrial tachycardia with block
w: Wolff-Parkinson-White
Sinus arrhythmia
Wandering atrial pacemaker
qs.x: Digoxin increases automaticity while slowing AV conduction, producing atrial tachycardia with AV block.

qs.q: Which electrolyte problem raises the risk of digoxin toxicity?
qs.a: Low potassium
w: High potassium
Low calcium
High sodium
qs.x: Hypokalemia makes heart cells more sensitive to digoxin, increasing the risk of toxic arrhythmias.

qs.q: A patient on digoxin reports nausea and yellow-green halos around lights. What should the tech do with this information?
qs.a: Report it with a current rhythm strip
w: Document it only at shift end
Reassure that it is normal
Ask the patient to skip meals
qs.x: Nausea and vision changes are signs of possible digoxin toxicity and should be reported promptly.

qs.q: What is usually the earliest ECG sign of hyperkalemia?
qs.a: Tall, narrow, peaked T waves
w: U waves
Delta waves
Scooped ST segments
qs.x: Peaked T waves usually appear first, before PR prolongation and QRS widening.

qs.q: As hyperkalemia worsens, which change is most dangerous?
qs.a: Widening QRS heading toward a sine-wave pattern
w: Slightly taller T waves
Mild sinus tachycardia
Upright P waves
qs.x: A widening QRS and sine-wave pattern signal severe hyperkalemia and can quickly progress to VF or asystole.

qs.q: In severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes, which medicine is commonly given to protect the heart?
qs.a: Calcium chloride
w: Potassium chloride
Digoxin
Adenosine
qs.x: IV calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane against high potassium; it does not lower potassium itself.

qs.q: A patient on spironolactone and lisinopril develops peaked T waves. Which electrolyte is most likely high?
qs.a: Potassium
w: Sodium
Calcium
Chloride
qs.x: Spironolactone and ACE inhibitors both raise potassium, which can cause peaked T waves.

qs.q: A patient on furosemide has small extra waves after the T wave. What are these and what do they suggest?
qs.a: U waves, suggesting low potassium
w: Delta waves, suggesting WPW
J waves, suggesting high calcium
Flutter waves, suggesting atrial flutter
qs.x: Loop diuretics waste potassium; prominent U waves are a classic sign of hypokalemia.

qs.q: Which ECG change is linked to hypocalcemia?
qs.a: Prolonged QT from a long ST segment
w: Short QT
Peaked T waves
U waves
qs.x: Low calcium lengthens the ST segment, which prolongs the QT.

qs.q: Which ECG finding is linked to hypercalcemia?
qs.a: Short QT interval
w: Long QT interval
Tall peaked T waves
Wide sine-wave QRS
qs.x: High calcium shortens the ST segment and QT interval.

qs.q: Low magnesium is most closely linked to which dangerous rhythm?
qs.a: Torsades de pointes
w: Atrial flutter
Sinus bradycardia
First-degree AV block
qs.x: Hypomagnesemia prolongs the QT and raises the risk of torsades; it often occurs with low potassium.

qs.q: Which electrolyte finding should be reported to the nurse or provider immediately?
qs.a: Peaked T waves with a widening QRS
w: A single PAC
A slightly flattened T wave
Normal sinus rhythm with artifact
qs.x: Peaked T waves with QRS widening suggest severe hyperkalemia, which can cause cardiac arrest.

qs.q: A patient started lisinopril 6 weeks ago and now has a dry, tickling cough. Lungs are clear and weight is stable. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Bradykinin buildup from ACE inhibition
w: Fluid backing up into the lungs
Beta-2 receptor blockade in the airways
Low potassium from the kidneys
qs.x: ACE also breaks down bradykinin, so ACE inhibitors cause a dry cough in a notable minority of patients. Clear lungs and stable weight argue against HF fluid overload; ARBs rarely cause this cough.

qs.q: A patient who has taken enalapril for 4 years has sudden swelling of the lips and tongue. Which statement is correct?
qs.a: ACE inhibitor angioedema can first appear even after years of use
w: Angioedema only occurs within the first few doses
This swelling is a sign of high potassium
This is fluid overload from worsening heart failure
qs.x: ACE inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, can occur at any time, and threatens the airway. It responds poorly to antihistamines alone.

qs.q: A discharge list shows both lisinopril and sacubitril-valsartan as active. Why is this a concern to report?
qs.a: Taking them together greatly raises angioedema risk
w: They cancel each other's blood pressure effect
Together they cause severe low potassium
Sacubitril-valsartan only works with a diuretic
qs.x: Neprilysin inhibition plus ACE inhibition sharply raises bradykinin and angioedema risk. A washout of at least 36 hours is required when switching from an ACE inhibitor.

qs.q: Which counseling point appears in carvedilol labeling for patients with heart failure?
qs.a: Taking it with food slows absorption and lowers orthostatic dizziness
w: It should be taken only at bedtime on an empty stomach
It must be separated from all meals by several hours
It is a rescue medicine used only when short of breath
qs.x: Carvedilol is a nonselective beta-blocker with alpha-1 blockade. Taking it with food reduces the risk of orthostatic hypotension.

qs.q: A patient ran out of metoprolol succinate several days ago. Which problem is most associated with abruptly missing a beta-blocker?
qs.a: Rebound tachycardia, hypertension, or angina
w: Sudden severe low blood sugar
Bradycardia and heart block
Wheezing and bronchospasm
qs.x: Abrupt beta-blocker withdrawal can cause rebound sympathetic activity, angina and even MI. Running out of medicine should be reported and resolved promptly.

qs.q: A heart failure patient on furosemide is taught to report weight gain. Which threshold is most commonly used?
qs.a: A gain of 2-3 lb in one day or about 5 lb in a week
w: Any gain of a half pound over a month
Only gains greater than 15 lb in a week
Weight gain only if legs are also swollen
qs.x: Rapid weight gain reflects fluid retention and often precedes dyspnea by days. Early reporting allows diuretic adjustment and can prevent admission.

qs.q: Which method gives the most reliable daily weights for a heart failure patient?
qs.a: Same scale each morning, after urinating, before eating
w: Any scale at any time, as long as it is daily
Each evening after dinner, fully dressed
Once a week at the clinic on its scale
qs.x: Consistent timing, scale and clothing removes day-to-day noise so true fluid trends can be seen.

qs.q: A patient on lisinopril and spironolactone recently began using a salt substitute to cut sodium. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Salt substitutes contain potassium chloride and can cause hyperkalemia
w: Salt substitutes block spironolactone absorption
Salt substitutes cause severe low sodium
There is no concern; salt substitutes are recommended
qs.x: Most salt substitutes are potassium chloride. Combined with an ACE inhibitor and a potassium-sparing diuretic, this can cause dangerous hyperkalemia.

qs.q: A patient on furosemide reports leg cramps, weakness and palpitations. Which electrolyte problem is most likely?
qs.a: Hypokalemia
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypercalcemia
Hypernatremia
qs.x: Loop diuretics waste potassium and magnesium. Hypokalemia causes cramps, weakness and arrhythmias and should be reported for lab testing.

qs.q: An older patient on digoxin and furosemide has nausea, poor appetite and sees yellow-green halos around lights. What is the concern?
qs.a: Digoxin toxicity, made more likely by low potassium
w: Expected side effects that will fade with time
Furosemide allergy
Early heart failure exacerbation only
qs.x: Visual changes, GI symptoms and arrhythmias suggest digoxin toxicity. Hypokalemia from diuretics and declining kidney function increase toxicity risk.

qs.q: Which finding meets the usual definition of orthostatic hypotension?
qs.a: Systolic drop of 20 or diastolic drop of 10 within 3 minutes of standing
w: Any heart rate rise of 5 beats on standing
Systolic drop of 5 within 10 minutes of standing
Diastolic rise of 10 after sitting up
qs.x: Orthostatic hypotension is a sustained fall of at least 20 systolic or 10 diastolic mmHg within 3 minutes of standing. It is a major fall risk with antihypertensives and diuretics.

qs.q: A patient on clonidine has missed doses for 2 days and now has headache, agitation and very high blood pressure. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: Rebound hypertension after abrupt clonidine interruption
w: An allergic reaction to clonidine
Clonidine overdose
Expected first-dose effect
qs.x: Clonidine is a central alpha-2 agonist. Abrupt loss of effect causes sympathetic rebound with severe hypertension, which should be reported promptly.

qs.q: A patient on amlodipine has ankle swelling, but stable weight, clear lungs and no dyspnea. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Calcium channel blocker vasodilatory edema
w: Worsening heart failure fluid overload
Deep vein thrombosis in both legs
Low potassium
qs.x: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers dilate arterioles, causing dependent edema that responds poorly to diuretics. Treating it with a diuretic can start a prescribing cascade.

qs.q: A patient on lisinopril and furosemide has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days and is dizzy on standing. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Volume depletion with hypotension and acute kidney injury
w: Fluid overload from heart failure
Hyperglycemia from the diuretic
Angioedema from the ACE inhibitor
qs.x: Diuretics plus ACE inhibitors or ARBs during dehydrating illness raise the risk of hypotension and AKI. Many patients have sick-day plans; poor intake should be reported.

qs.q: Why can a beta-blocker be a concern for a patient with insulin-treated diabetes?
qs.a: It can mask warning signs of hypoglycemia such as tremor and fast heart rate
w: It causes rapid weight gain that raises insulin needs
It makes insulin work much more slowly
It reliably causes diabetic ketoacidosis
qs.x: Beta-blockers blunt adrenergic symptoms of low sugar like tachycardia and tremor. Sweating is usually preserved, so it remains a useful warning sign.

qs.q: A patient injected insulin lispro for lunch, then skipped the meal. When is hypoglycemia risk highest?
qs.a: About 1 to 3 hours after the injection
w: About 8 to 12 hours after the injection
The following morning
Only after 18 hours
qs.x: Rapid-acting insulin starts in about 15 minutes and peaks around 1-2 hours. Skipping the meal leaves that peak unopposed.

qs.q: Which statement best describes insulin glargine?
qs.a: Long-acting basal insulin with no pronounced peak
w: Rapid-acting insulin given right before meals
Intermediate insulin that peaks at 4 to 12 hours
Insulin that may be mixed with any other insulin
qs.x: Glargine lasts about 24 hours with a relatively flat profile and should not be mixed with other insulins in the same syringe.

qs.q: A patient taking NPH insulin at bedtime reports night sweats, nightmares and morning headaches. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: NPH peaking overnight causing nocturnal hypoglycemia
w: Insulin resistance from too little insulin
Normal dreams unrelated to medicine
Sleep apnea from weight gain
qs.x: NPH peaks around 4-12 hours, so a bedtime injection can peak in the early morning hours. Night sweats and nightmares are classic nocturnal hypoglycemia clues.

qs.q: An alert patient with a low glucose takes fast-acting carbohydrate. When should glucose be rechecked under the Rule of 15?
qs.a: About 15 minutes later
w: About 1 hour later
At the next scheduled meal
Only if symptoms return
qs.x: The Rule of 15 pairs about 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate with a recheck in about 15 minutes, repeating if still low, then a snack or meal.

qs.q: Which statement about nasal glucagon is correct?
qs.a: It is absorbed through the nasal lining, so the patient does not need to inhale
w: It only works if the patient takes a deep breath
It must be mixed with sterile water before use
It is ineffective when the patient is unresponsive
qs.x: Nasal glucagon is absorbed passively across the nasal mucosa and works in unresponsive patients, making it easy for family members to use.

qs.q: In which home patient is glucagon least likely to raise blood glucose effectively?
qs.a: A malnourished patient who has been drinking heavily
w: A well-fed patient with type 1 diabetes
A patient who took extra rapid-acting insulin
A patient on a sulfonylurea who ate breakfast
qs.x: Glucagon works by releasing liver glycogen. Starvation and alcohol deplete glycogen stores, so the response may be weak.

qs.q: Which situation most raises the risk of lactic acidosis in a patient taking metformin?
qs.a: Severe dehydration or acute kidney injury
w: Mild constipation
A high-protein diet
Taking it with meals
qs.x: Metformin is cleared by the kidneys. Dehydration, AKI, iodinated contrast and hypoxia raise the risk of rare but serious lactic acidosis.

qs.q: A patient on metformin for many years reports new numbness and tingling in both feet. Which deficiency is associated with long-term metformin use?
qs.a: Vitamin B12 deficiency
w: Vitamin K deficiency
Vitamin C deficiency
Iron deficiency
qs.x: Long-term metformin reduces B12 absorption, which can cause or worsen neuropathy. Periodic B12 checks are recommended.

qs.q: A patient on empagliflozin has vomiting, abdominal pain and rapid breathing. Fingerstick glucose is only mildly elevated. What should be suspected?
qs.a: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis
w: Gastroenteritis only, since glucose is near normal
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
Hypoglycemia unawareness
qs.x: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose. Ketones and a blood gas or metabolic panel are needed; a normal-looking glucometer reading does not rule it out.

qs.q: Why do sick-day plans for diabetes specifically address SGLT2 inhibitors?
qs.a: Vomiting and poor intake raise the risk of ketoacidosis and kidney injury
w: They cause severe hypoglycemia during any illness
They stop working when the patient has a fever
They interact with all antibiotics
qs.x: Fasting and dehydration promote ketosis and volume depletion on SGLT2 inhibitors. Patients should have a written plan from their prescriber for acute illness and before surgery.

qs.q: Which adverse effect is common with SGLT2 inhibitors such as canagliflozin?
qs.a: Genital yeast infections
w: Severe constipation
Hair loss
Weight gain
qs.x: Glucose in the urine promotes genital mycotic infections and UTIs. Rare Fournier gangrene (perineal pain, swelling, fever) needs emergency evaluation.

qs.q: A patient on semaglutide has severe, constant upper abdominal pain radiating to the back with vomiting. What should be suspected?
qs.a: Acute pancreatitis
w: Expected mild GI side effect
Hypoglycemia
Constipation from slowed digestion
qs.x: Nausea is common with GLP-1 agonists, but persistent severe pain radiating to the back suggests pancreatitis, which needs prompt evaluation.

qs.q: Which history is a labeled contraindication for GLP-1 agonists such as dulaglutide?
qs.a: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma
w: History of type 2 diabetes for over 10 years
Past history of gestational diabetes
History of controlled hypertension
qs.x: GLP-1 agonists carry a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors and are contraindicated with a personal or family history of MTC or MEN2.

qs.q: A patient on tirzepatide and glipizide has lost weight and now logs several low readings. What is the best explanation?
qs.a: Improved glucose control plus the sulfonylurea is raising hypoglycemia risk
w: Tirzepatide alone commonly causes severe lows
The glucometer is broken
Weight loss always raises blood glucose
qs.x: GLP-1 and GIP/GLP-1 agonists rarely cause lows alone, but combined with insulin or sulfonylureas they can. The pattern should be reported for medication review.

qs.q: Reviewing a glucose log, which pattern most needs prompt reporting to the provider?
qs.a: Repeated low readings, including overnight
w: One high reading after a holiday meal
Slightly higher readings before dinner
Readings recorded in a different notebook
qs.x: Recurrent hypoglycemia is dangerous, especially in older adults, and usually means a medication or meal-timing mismatch that needs adjustment.
