qs.q: What is the usual INR target range for a patient taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation?
qs.x: Most warfarin indications, including AF and VTE, target an INR of 2-3. Some mechanical valves need higher ranges.

qs.q: A patient on warfarin asks about eating leafy green vegetables. What is the correct teaching point?
qs.a: Keep vitamin K intake consistent from week to week
w: Avoid all green vegetables completely
Eat as many greens as possible to prevent bleeding
Greens do not affect warfarin at all
qs.x: Vitamin K counteracts warfarin. Sudden changes in intake shift the INR; a steady diet allows stable dosing.

qs.q: A patient on warfarin was just prescribed an antibiotic for a UTI. Which antibiotic is most likely to markedly raise the INR?
qs.a: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
w: Nitrofurantoin
Amoxicillin
Cephalexin
qs.x: TMP-SMX inhibits warfarin metabolism (CYP2C9) and can sharply raise the INR. An early INR check after starting interacting antibiotics is common.

qs.q: Which agent reverses the effect of warfarin?
qs.a: Vitamin K (phytonadione)
w: Protamine sulfate
Idarucizumab
Naloxone
qs.x: Vitamin K restores clotting factor production; four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate is used for rapid reversal in serious bleeding.

qs.q: Why is adherence especially critical for direct oral anticoagulants like apixaban?
qs.a: Short half-lives mean protection fades within about a day of missed doses
w: They build up for weeks before working
Missed doses cause sudden severe bleeding
They require daily INR checks
qs.x: DOACs act quickly and wear off quickly. Missed doses leave patients unprotected against stroke or clot, unlike warfarin's slower offset.

qs.q: Which administration point is important for the higher-strength rivaroxaban tablets?
qs.a: They should be taken with food for adequate absorption
w: They must be crushed and mixed with juice
They must be taken on an empty stomach
They should be taken with an antacid
qs.x: The higher-strength rivaroxaban tablets are absorbed much better with food, typically the evening meal for once-daily AF dosing.

qs.q: Which storage point applies to dabigatran capsules?
qs.a: Keep them in the original bottle or blister to protect from moisture
w: Store them in a weekly pill organizer
Keep them refrigerated
Open the capsules to make swallowing easier
qs.x: Dabigatran is moisture-sensitive and capsules should not be opened, which can greatly increase absorption and bleeding risk.

qs.q: An 84-year-old on apixaban tripped and hit her head an hour ago. She is alert with no complaints. What is the best action?
qs.a: Arrange emergency evaluation for possible intracranial bleeding
w: Reassure her since she is alert
Recheck her in one week
Apply ice and have family watch her for a month
qs.x: Anticoagulated patients with head trauma are at risk of delayed intracranial hemorrhage and generally need imaging even when they appear well.

qs.q: A patient on warfarin has been taking OTC ibuprofen for knee pain. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Increased risk of GI and other bleeding
w: Ibuprofen makes warfarin ineffective
Ibuprofen causes clotting
There is no interaction
qs.x: NSAIDs impair platelet function and injure the GI lining, adding to anticoagulant bleeding risk. Acetaminophen is usually preferred, within limits.

qs.q: A COPD patient has been refilling an albuterol inhaler far more often than before. How should this be interpreted?
qs.a: Worsening disease control that should be reported
w: A sign the inhaler is defective
Normal use for stable COPD
Evidence of albuterol allergy
qs.x: Rising rescue inhaler use is an objective marker of worsening control and may precede an exacerbation.

qs.q: Which statement about tiotropium is correct?
qs.a: It is a once-daily maintenance bronchodilator, not a rescue inhaler
w: It is the preferred inhaler for sudden breathlessness
It is an inhaled corticosteroid
It is taken only during exacerbations
qs.x: Tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) used daily to prevent symptoms. A short-acting bronchodilator is used for rescue.

qs.q: When using a metered-dose inhaler, what should the patient do right after the puff is inhaled?
qs.a: Keep the breath in for about 10 seconds if possible
w: Exhale forcefully right away
Take a second puff immediately
Cough to clear the airway
qs.x: Breath-holding lets the medicine settle in the airways. Technique: exhale, seal lips (or use a spacer), press at the start of a slow deep breath, then hold.

qs.q: What is the correct inhalation technique for a dry-powder inhaler such as fluticasone-salmeterol (Diskus)?
qs.a: A quick, forceful, deep breath in
w: A slow, gentle breath in over several seconds
Use with a spacer to slow the powder
Exhale into the device before inhaling
qs.x: Dry-powder inhalers rely on a strong inspiratory effort to break up the powder. Exhaling into them can clump the dose; spacers are not used.

qs.q: A patient using an inhaled corticosteroid has white patches in the mouth. Which teaching point helps prevent this?
qs.a: Rinse the mouth with water and spit after each use
w: Use the inhaler only at night
Swallow the medicine instead of inhaling
Shake the inhaler for one minute
qs.x: Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) is a common local effect of inhaled steroids. Rinsing and spitting, and using a spacer with MDIs, reduces it.

qs.q: A COPD patient with diabetes is on a prednisone burst for an exacerbation. Which change is most expected in the glucose log?
qs.a: Higher readings, especially in the afternoon and evening
w: Frequent morning lows
No change in readings
Lower readings throughout the day
qs.x: Glucocorticoids raise glucose by increasing insulin resistance. Morning prednisone typically peaks its effect later in the day.

qs.q: During home medication reconciliation, which approach gives the most complete picture?
qs.a: Review every bottle in the home, including OTCs and supplements, against all lists
w: Rely on the most recent discharge summary
Ask the patient to list medicines from memory
Use only the primary care office list
qs.x: A brown-bag review often reveals duplicates, discontinued drugs still in use, and OTC or herbal products missing from every official list.

qs.q: An 80-year-old uses diphenhydramine nightly for sleep and has new confusion and urinary retention. Why is this drug on the Beers list?
qs.a: Strong anticholinergic effects cause confusion, retention and falls
w: It raises blood pressure dangerously
It causes severe low blood sugar
It thins the blood
qs.x: The AGS Beers Criteria list first-generation antihistamines as potentially inappropriate in older adults because of anticholinergic burden.

qs.q: Why are benzodiazepines such as lorazepam listed in the Beers Criteria for older adults?
qs.a: Higher risk of falls, fractures and cognitive impairment
w: They cause high potassium
They raise blood glucose
They cause dry cough
qs.x: Older adults are more sensitive to benzodiazepines and clear some of them slowly, raising the risk of sedation, delirium and falls.

qs.q: Why is glyburide considered potentially inappropriate in older adults?
qs.a: It causes prolonged hypoglycemia, especially with reduced kidney function
w: It causes severe weight loss
It raises blood pressure
It commonly causes lactic acidosis
qs.x: Glyburide is long-acting with active metabolites. Beers Criteria advise avoiding it in favor of options with lower hypoglycemia risk.

qs.q: At a home visit, a patient has bottles labeled Zestril and lisinopril from two pharmacies and takes both. What is this?
qs.a: Therapeutic duplication of the same drug
w: A planned combination therapy
A drug-food interaction
A normal brand-generic switch
qs.x: Zestril is brand-name lisinopril. Brand-generic duplication, often across pharmacies, is a common reconciliation finding to report.

qs.q: A patient takes Tylenol for arthritis and an OTC nighttime cold product. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Hidden acetaminophen in the cold product raising liver injury risk
w: The cold product blocks acetaminophen
Acetaminophen causes bleeding with cold products
No concern; they have different uses
qs.x: Many combination cold, sleep and prescription opioid products contain acetaminophen. Unrecognized stacking is a leading cause of liver toxicity.

qs.q: Which medicine should stay in its original container instead of a weekly pill organizer?
qs.a: Sublingual nitroglycerin tablets
w: Amlodipine tablets
Lisinopril tablets
Atorvastatin tablets
qs.x: Sublingual nitroglycerin loses potency with exposure to air, light and moisture and should be kept in its original glass bottle.

qs.q: A patient developed ankle edema on amlodipine and was then prescribed furosemide for it. What is this pattern called?
qs.a: A prescribing cascade
w: Therapeutic substitution
Drug tolerance
Synergy
qs.x: A prescribing cascade occurs when a drug side effect is mistaken for a new condition and treated with another drug, adding risk.

qs.q: Which medication groups cause the most ER visits for adverse drug events in older US adults?
qs.a: Anticoagulants, insulin, and oral diabetes medicines
w: Statins, vitamins, and antacids
Antibiotics, eye drops, and laxatives
Thyroid medicines, inhalers, and antihistamines
qs.x: CDC surveillance shows anticoagulants, diabetes agents and antiplatelets account for a large share of emergency hospitalizations for adverse drug events in older adults.

qs.q: A patient with heart failure on lisinopril and furosemide has been taking daily ibuprofen. What is the main risk?
qs.a: Fluid retention and acute kidney injury
w: Low blood sugar
Bradycardia
Thrush
qs.x: NSAIDs cause sodium retention and reduce kidney perfusion. Combined with an ACE inhibitor or ARB and a diuretic, this is the 'triple whammy' for AKI.

qs.q: Which technique best confirms that a patient understands a new medication schedule?
qs.a: Ask the patient to explain in their own words how they take each medicine
w: Ask whether they have any questions
Give a printed handout
Have a family member sign the list
qs.x: Teach-back reveals misunderstandings that yes-or-no questions miss and is a core adherence strategy.

qs.q: A patient admits skipping doses of an expensive inhaler to make it last. What is the best response?
qs.a: Discuss cost openly and connect them with pharmacy or social work resources
w: Tell them the inhaler is optional
Document nonadherence without discussion
Advise buying a similar product online
qs.x: Cost-related nonadherence is common. Pharmacists, assistance programs and prescribers can often find affordable alternatives.

qs.q: Which home medication combination most strongly warrants a conversation about having naloxone available?
qs.a: An opioid plus a benzodiazepine
w: A statin plus aspirin
Metformin plus a GLP-1 agonist
An ACE inhibitor plus a diuretic
qs.x: Opioids combined with benzodiazepines or other sedatives sharply raise respiratory depression risk; naloxone in the home is recommended.

qs.q: An 82-year-old has new confusion that began about a week after a medication change. What is the best reconciliation approach?
qs.a: Treat any recently started or changed medicine as a possible cause and report
w: Assume dementia progression
Attribute it to normal aging
Wait for the next annual visit
qs.x: Adverse drug events often present atypically in older adults, with confusion, falls or functional decline. Recent changes are prime suspects.

qs.q: Which finding gives the most objective evidence of nonadherence at a home visit?
qs.a: Pill counts and refill dates that don't match the prescribed schedule
w: The patient says they never miss doses
The pill bottles are neatly organized
The patient knows the names of the medicines
qs.x: Self-report overestimates adherence. Comparing remaining pills and pharmacy refill history to the expected use is more objective.
